Webb telescope detects galaxy origin of the farthest fast radio burst we've seen to date
And the data it provided sheds light on the origins of fast radio bursts.
Back in 2024, scientists detected the farthest fast radio burst we've ever seen to date, thanks to observations by the MeerKAT ground telescope array. Fast radio bursts are ultra-fast radio waves from deep space, which last a fraction of a second but release as much as energy as what the sun emits in three days. They were first discovered in 2007, and not much is known about them. Now, astronomers have used the James Webb telescope to pinpoint the origin of the burst detected in 2024, and it could shed light on the phenomenon's origins.
Webb's near-infrared instruments detected a galaxy in the right location from where the burst had come. Based on measurements from the way its light stretches, the fast radio burst occurred just 3 billion years after the Big Bang. Its origin galaxy existed way back when star formation was at its peak in the universe. In addition, the galaxy that produced it is also 1,000 times smaller than expected. The previous fast radio bursts we've detected took place billions of years later in massive, star-forming galaxies.
There are a couple of theories on how fast radio bursts are produced. One proposes that they're generated by the merger of two neutron stars. But it takes billions of years before two neutron stars — the collapsed cores of massive supergiant stars — collide, which means that bursts can only come from older galaxies.
Another theory suggests that the bursts can come from massive stars exploding in a supernova and leaving behind magnetars, which are rare type of neutron stars that have highly powerful magnetic fields. "Our work suggests that it's very unlikely that this [fast radio burst] was produced by a merger," said Manisha Caleb from the University of Sydney, Australia, who served as lead author on the study published in Science. In other words, their work shows that the origin of this burst was likely a supernova, providing support for the theory that fast radio bursts can come from a certain type of star explosion.

For decades, a typical CFO job description looked like this: close the books, keep the company compliant, manage cash, and make sure the numbers add up. Today, this role is shifting dramatically. Whether it's cybersecurity, M&A, ESG, or even IT, it eventually lands on the CFO's desk. This is because each of these functions eventually has a financial implication. Whether it is evaluating the cost of a new technology stack, assessing the risks of an acquisition, or weighing the fallout from a cybersecurity breach, CFOs today need to look beyond the numbers. They must understand how the entire business works and have a clear point of view when making critical decisions. But at MoEngage, this has never really been a shift. It has been the norm for much of the company’s journey, and at the centre of it has been its CFO Narasimha Reddy, who joined MoEngage in 2015, when it was still a 10-15-person startup. Over the last decade, MoEngage has faced several moments that have tested its CFO might. These episodes range from raising funds to convincing the sales team to sell a pricing model they weren't sure about to deciding which country the company should call home. Reddy was in the room for all of it and, more often than not, pushed decisions that finance leaders are not traditionally expected to make on their own. Today, MoEngage serves more than 1,300 consumer brands globally, including Starbucks, Coca-Cola, Flipkart, Domino’s and OYO, among others. The company raised $280 Mn in its Series F round last year, crossed nearly $100 Mn in annual recurring revenue (ARR), and claimed profitability in the December quarter of 2025. Reddy, who has been central to all of this, now has a remit that extends well beyond finance, with strategy, HR and partnerships also reporting to him. For The CFO Code series, Inc42 caught up with Narasimha Reddy, board member, CFO and head of strategy at MoEngage, for an exclusive conversation. Reddy spoke in detail about the toughest stretch of MoEngage’s ten-year fundraising journey, why he believes global compliance structures should remain simple, his take on AI, and what he thinks will set the next generation of CFOs apart. The Making Of A Startup CFO Reddy joined MoEngage after stints at UBS and Continuum Energy. His decision to join the company was also personal. Founder and CEO Raviteja Dodda was his roommate while they prepared for the IIT entrance exam, and they stayed in touch over the years. When Dodda started his venture, Reddy joined. Eleven years later, he remains at MoEngage full-time, with finance being just one of the four functions that he oversees. In an interview with Inc42, Reddy shared that when he joined MoEngage, it was still finding its footing, and there was little room for defined job descriptions. At that juncture, Reddy’s technical and financial training shaped his view of what a finance leader should do. “In new-age companies, especially at an early stage, the role of a CFO is much broader, requiring an understanding of the entire business and how functions intersect to drive growth, product economics, capital allocation and stakeholder value,” Reddy said. This thesis was tested when MoEngage faced a difficult financial period in 2016-2017. Reddy shared that during this time, the company struggled to raise its Series B round because of limited capital availability in the market. “You can’t continue investing in growth in the same way when capital availability is limited. So the question becomes: how do you get closer to profitability, even if you’re not profitable yet? We did multiple things to achieve that,” Reddy said. To deal with it, Reddy pushed for moving the company’s enterprise customers from monthly postpaid contracts to annual prepaid plans, even offering discounts in some cases, to bring cash into the business upfront. Reddy said he and the founder spent considerable time with large customers to make that shift. As a result, the move brought in enough cash to sustain growth and buy time until its next round. Under Reddy’s leadership, MoEngage also raised venture debt outside a financing round, an unconventional move at the time given its limited cash cushion. The company eventually raised its Series B in 2018, three years after its Series A. Reddy also shared two instances where he had to push through decisions that the rest of the company initially resisted. The first was moving Indian customers from monthly payments to annual upfront payments. MoEngage’s sales team was sceptical that Indian customers would agree. To prove that it was possible, Reddy joined the sales call with MoEngage’s largest customer at the time and closed the first such deal himself, which eventually became the norm. The second was introducing price escalation clauses, which meant customers would pay more each year as the product evolved. The sales team initially resisted, fearing it would make negotiations harder. Reddy said he convinced the team by showing how larger global SaaS companies structure their pricing. His broader lesson was that leaders need to prove that a new approach works and use data and industry benchmarks to get the rest of the team on board. MoEngage’s Homecoming In January 2026, the National Company Law Tribunal's Bengaluru bench approved the merger of MoEngage Inc, the company's US-based parent entity, into its Indian arm, MoEngage India Private Limited, a process also known as a reverse flip. Reddy shared that when the company was formed, the US as the home ground was a straightforward choice. “Our capital and its early customers were both concentrated there, and Indian public markets were not yet open to loss-making, high-growth companies,” said Reddy. That changed as SEBI eased listing norms, removing the requirement for three years of prior profitability, and as Indian investors grew more comfortable backing new-age, high-growth businesses. What tipped the decision to move MoEngage back to India, Reddy said, was less about India's markets opening up and more about how he'd come to see the US ones behave. “If you look at US public markets, people are more sentiment-driven and not really financially driven,” Reddy stated, pointing to how capital has concentrated around AI in recent years even as companies with strong cash flows and growth outside that category struggle to attract the same attention. According to him, India offered a steadier home to MoEngage. Measuring AI By The Productivity It Unlocks When asked about AI, Reddy shared that the question should not be whether AI as a whole is delivering an ROI but what AI is doing for each function, and whether that improvement is worth what the company is spending on it. “Finance teams, for instance, could ask whether AI allows one person managing 200 accounts to handle 250 or 350 without a corresponding increase in headcount. Engineering could look at whether a feature that once took a month can now be shipped in two weeks,” Reddy noted. According to him, companies should cap their spend and then measure whether the productivity justifies the investment. Sharing an internal mechanism, Reddy said MoEngage does not licence one AI tool uniformly across the company. More expensive models go to a smaller set of people within each function, who can extract the most value from complex tasks, while lower-cost licences cover simpler day-to-day use across the rest of the team. Reddy, however, does not see AI as a replacement for human judgement, but a tool that can do the legwork before the judgement call is made. “Consider entering a new market. AI can help answer almost every question around it, from market size and competition to potential revenue and the investment required. But whether the company should enter that market, and how much capital it should commit, remains a human decision,” Reddy said. Rise Of The New CFO For Reddy, the CFO of the future cannot afford to sit on the sidelines and explain decisions after they have been made. The role, he believes, is moving much closer to the heart of the business, with CFOs expected to help decide where the company should place its bets, how those bets should be measured and when it is time to walk away. According to him, this is only possible by having a framework for investment decisions and defined rules of the game the company wants to play. “If I am investing in some new idea or some new market, it is important to have a framework for how you would evaluate it. Should I have a two-year gestation period or an 18-month gestation period? What do those results mean?” Reddy said. Reddy also iterated that stakeholder value cannot remain a CEO-only responsibility. Finance has a seat at that table too, and the CFO needs to have a point of view on the decisions that shape the company’s long-term value. When asked how he sees the CFO’s role evolving, Reddy pointed out that, since 2022, investors have become less willing to reward growth at any cost. He cited the Rule of 40, a widely used SaaS benchmark that combines a company’s revenue growth rate with its profit margin, as a useful measure of sustainable growth. He said that founders who keep burning 30-40% of revenue even as growth slows from 60% to 40% are increasingly out of step with investor expectations. Reddy also shared that he believes tomorrow's CFOs will need enough understanding of emerging tools to know where technology can improve productivity, automate manual work, and make the finance function more efficient. That becomes particularly relevant as AI starts taking over parts of traditional finance work. The future CFO, then, is less an accountant with a bigger title and more a business leader with a finance lens. In Reddy’s view, numbers still matter, but the CFO’s job is to decide what the numbers should help the company do next.

In the weeks and months following Hamas’s brutal October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, and Israel’s devastating campaign in Gaza that followed, the world’s attention turned away from the West Bank.
Who are the violent Israeli settlers in the West Bank?
Jalud and the West Bank’s epidemic of settler violence, explained.
Over the past three years, however, the situation in the Israel-occupied territory has worsened as Israeli settlers have carried out more violent attacks on Palestinians.
The attacks can range from acts of daily harassment and trespassing to a major mob assault in the West Bank village of Jalud that overwhelmed Israeli security forces and blocked a displaced Palestinian family from returning home. Last week, Israeli settlers shot and killed a Palestinian man.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has largely dismissed violent West Bank settlers as an issue, blaming the Jalud attack on a “handful of rioters” and referring to settlers as “juvenile delinquents” in a speech to the UN last month, in which he argued that the world should focus on violence committed by Palestinians instead.
But even as he downplays the problem, human rights organizations have documented a record level of Israeli settler violence in the West Bank. The International Committee of the Red Cross has said that such attacks have made everyday life “untenable” for the more than 3 million Palestinians living in the West Bank.
The Israeli settlements are also clearly illegal, as Vox’s Zack Beauchamp explained in September — but that hasn’t stopped them from expanding.
Ahead of Israel’s elections later this month, settlers have accelerated a campaign of ethnic cleansing with the explicit backing of some Israeli cabinet ministers, led by young militant Jewish settlers that are part of a loose network known as the Hilltop Youth.
The Wall Street Journal’s Feliz Solomon reported on the Jalud attack and has written about the role of Hilltop Youth in worsening settler violence. She spoke with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about the reality on the ground in the West Bank, the settler groups behind it, and how Israeli officials are responding.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
Tell me about the last three years in the West Bank. What’s been happening?
The October 7 attack really hardened a lot of people’s views in Israel, and that’s played out in the West Bank in a number of ways.
One is that the government of Benjamin Netanyahu, which has some powerful members who are settlers themselves, became much more overtly supportive of expanding the Jewish settlements.
The second thing that changed was basically a total breakdown of trust, both between Jews and Arabs, and also between Jews and the state, because a lot of people felt that they were really on their own in terms of security.
All of this created a really combustible environment. There are more settlers there now. They’re behaving more brazenly, and there’s what a lot of people would describe as a permissive environment of almost total impunity.
What does that total impunity look like? We often hear the term “settler violence.” What does that mean?
There’s really a whole spectrum of violent actions. It’s mostly by younger male settlers. There are some acts of daily harassment, like trespassing on Palestinian property, vandalism, stalking people, blocking roads, and preventing access to resources like water wells. And then on the other end of the spectrum, there are also acts of extreme violence.
There have been some very serious physical assaults. Settlers throwing rocks with slingshots. Last year, there was a viral video of an elderly woman who was beaten with a stick. She was hospitalized for days. And lately, we’ve been seeing more mob violence where a large group of settlers will raid a Palestinian village. They’ve set mosques and other property on fire.
Just to be clear, there’s violence by Palestinians too, but we’re really seeing an alarming surge of violence by settlers that’s often unpunished, and increasingly it’s happening when settlers go into Palestinian areas where they’re not supposed to be.
You reported on an attack that happened last week in the West Bank near the Palestinian village of Jalud. Tell me what happened.
Over the summer, some young settlers who are associated with a group called the Hilltop Youth set up an encampment around three houses on the outskirts of the Palestinian village, Jalud, and essentially besieged the houses. They blocked their access to essential goods and harassed the residents until, in late July, they felt so unsafe that they fled.
Two of those houses belonged to the Tubasi family. In early September, Israel’s high court ordered the state to ensure their safe return, and in late September, they tried to go back. We spoke with Wael, who’s one member of the family, and also with their lawyer about what happened when they tried to go back.
A few dozen [Israeli] security forces were deployed to escort them home in the middle of the night, and when they got there, they found that the house was totally ransacked. They showed us before and after pictures, and the windows were smashed, the doors were broken, electrical wires were cut, and there was just debris all over the place.
When they came inside for the first time in about two months, they were walking through the property looking at the damage with flashlights, and they’d only been there for a few minutes when suddenly they were surrounded by a mob of settlers. They said at first that there were about 50 settlers around the house, and the military later said that there were more than a hundred people that took part in what they called a riot.
The authorities told the family to take cover deeper inside the house, and they hid inside a stairwell as the soldiers tried to force these settlers to retreat, but they were shouting and throwing rocks at the house, and then, according to Wael, they even started climbing in through the windows. At that point, the authorities told the family to go upstairs, all the way up to the roof and to hide in a corner of the rooftop.
Wael explained what he saw up there. He was looking down and he saw the soldiers battling it out with this large group of settlers and this thick cloud of tear gas and loud bangs from stun grenades.
“There are more settlers there now. They’re behaving more brazenly, and there’s what a lot of people would describe as a permissive environment of almost total impunity.”
Eventually, the security forces realized that they weren’t getting the situation under control. They had to get this family out of there. They took them back downstairs and outside and put them in a military vehicle, but then the settlers surrounded the vehicle and they were rocking the car. They slashed the tires so that [the family] couldn’t leave. Then the soldiers had to move them into an armored military vehicle and eventually they got them out.
A short while later, not long after they had escaped, they started receiving video messages from some of their neighbors that showed what happened after they left, which was that their car and their house had been set on fire.
All right, so the Israeli authorities in the form of soldiers were trying to help this Palestinian family legally return and settlers violently blocked them. This is settlers versus the authorities. What do we know about who these settlers are and what is motivating them?
This was a very large group. We know of three people who were detained in this incident. All of them were teenagers. The youngest one I believe was 15 years old.
A lot of the harassment in this area comes out of a nearby settlement called Esh Kodesh and smaller, more informal settlements around it that are called outposts. And these outposts are usually pretty crude encampments. They often start with just tents or a camper van or a trailer with no electricity and no water. And the people who choose to live in these places tend to be very young, very extreme ideological settlers.
You mentioned something called the Hilltop Youth. Who are they?
The Hilltop Youth is a loose network of settlers that live outside the mainstream, and they often have much more extremist views than the mainstream settler movement. It’s an offshoot of religious Zionism, which is one of the main ideologies of the settler movement, and it sort of fuses the ideas of Orthodox Judaism with ultranationalism.
The Hilltop Youth take these ideas to the extreme, and I’ve spoken with a bunch of them myself. They believe that they’re on a divine mission to reclaim the Holy Land for Jews, and they’ll cite parts of the Torah and other religious texts that they interpret as empowering them to take the land back and even to use violence. They see it as a preventive type of self-defense, and they see themselves as protecting all other Jews.
These are young people, some of them teenagers. Where are they coming from? Why are their parents not grounding them? How has this been allowed to unfold the way it has?
It’s a good question, and I should say also that not all Hilltop Youth are violent, but a lot of the violence that’s committed by Jews in the West Bank does come from this group, and they come from all over the place. Some of them grew up in the settlements, and then as teenagers, they kind of wandered and they struck out on their own. And then there are others who come from all over Israel.
A lot of the Hilltop Youth, we’re finding, are kind of troubled kids. Sometimes they’re dropouts from strict religious schools, sometimes they have behavioral issues or ADHD, and they just didn’t really fit in. We heard from some kids who said that they found out about the outposts by word of mouth, like someone at their school had invited them to come for the weekend and they’d come and they’d stay a few days and eventually they’d start spending more and more time there until at some point they’re just living there.
There are a number of NGOs that recruit young kids to come work as farm hands on agricultural outposts in the West Bank, and some of those are in these areas that are more prone to radicalization. These organizations present themselves as very innocent in that they’re identifying kids that need help and are bringing them to a place where they will learn some discipline and they will have a purpose and they’ll have something to do. But that often puts them into a more extreme environment.
In the case of the family you profiled in Jalud, it’s clear that the Israeli authorities, in the form of soldiers, attempted to help the family get back to their home. How does this typically play out, though? How do Israeli soldiers typically respond when settlers attack Palestinians?
There have been a number of high-profile examples of video footage circulating that appears to show Israeli soldiers either standing idly by or even, some would argue, siding with the settlers.
In one recent example, there was a video that showed some soldiers praying alongside settlers who had besieged the home of a Palestinian American man, and that was actually not very far from where the Tubasi house is. The military said that it was looking into it to determine whether disciplinary action needed to be taken.
In general, military officials acknowledge that this violence by settlers is a big problem, and the security establishment definitely does not support what’s happening here. They see it as getting in the way of counter-terrorism efforts and overall efforts to bring stability to this very volatile area.
I’ve heard this directly from military officers, but on the ground there does seem to be a breakdown of discipline in some cases and a lack of clear instruction in other cases. Some soldiers simply don’t know how to deal with threats from other Israelis, especially really young ones, as you pointed out. It’s just not what they’re trained to do.
Do you think the government could put a stop to these attacks by settlers if it wanted to, or has the government lost control?
This problem has gotten so big that it’s going to be very difficult to solve without significant backlash, but I have spoken with a number of former Israeli security officials who say yes, much more could be done — starting with a more frank acknowledgement of what’s happening, clearer law enforcement procedures, and more disciplinary actions.

‘Gaurav Gogoi failed completely, should resign’: Akhil Gogoi slams Congress after Nagaon Lok Sabha bypoll setback
Akhil Gogoi also blamed Assam Congress president Gaurav Gogoi for the party's poor performance and called for his immediate resignation.
The BJP won the Nagaon Lok Sabha by-election in Assam, with the Congress being pushed to the third place. The result has drawn sharp criticism from Raijor Dal chief Akhil Gogoi, a former ally of the Congress, who called the defeat a “tragedy for Assam's anti-BJP forces”.
Akhil Gogoi also blamed Assam Congress president Gaurav Gogoi for the party's poor performance and called for his immediate resignation. His remarks come as the Congress struggles in a constituency where Muslims account for more than 55% of voters.
Akhil Gogoi questions Congress's performance in Nagaon
Reacting to the by-election results, Raijor Dal MLA Akhil Gogoi pointed to the sharp fall in the Congress's vote count. He noted that the constituency had previously been held by the Congress, but a candidate's move to the BJP led to the by-election.
“Regarding the by-election in Nagaon—it was originally a Congress seat, but the candidate switched to the BJP, which is why this by-election is taking place,” he was quoted as saying by news agency ANI.
Akhil Gogoi said the Congress had won the seat by a margin of 2.5 lakh votes in the previous election but was now struggling to reach even two lakh votes.
“This is essentially a minority-dominated seat,” he said, adding that the Congress's minority vote share had fallen sharply.
“The most significant development this time is that the minority vote share for Congress has plummeted from 25% to just 5%. The BJP is poised to win this minority-dominated seat,” he said.
Calling the outcome a historic setback for the Congress, Akhil Gogoi said Gaurav Gogoi had failed in his role as state party president.
“This is a historic defeat for the Congress,” he said. “I believe the Congress President, Gaurav Gogoi, has failed completely. In my opinion, Gaurav Gogoi should resign from the post of State Congress President this very day.”
Amit Shah credits BJP leadership for bypoll victories
Union Home Minister Amit Shah welcomed the BJP-led NDA's performance in the by-elections in West Bengal, Assam and Puducherry, as well as recent local body polls in Rajasthan and Tripura.
In a post shared on X, Shah said the results reflected continued public support for the BJP under Prime Minister Narendra Modi's leadership.
“The BJP, under the leadership of PM Shri Narendra Modi Ji, continues to win elections one after another despite the lies and disinformation campaigns run by Rahul Gandhi and the INDI Alliance,” Shah said.
He claimed that the results showed voters had rejected the opposition alliance.
“The NDA’s victories in the by-elections in West Bengal, Assam and Puducherry, and the recently held local body polls in Rajasthan and Tripura, demonstrate that the people have completely rejected the INDI Alliance,” he said.
Shah also accused opposition parties of questioning institutions after electoral defeats, saying voters had recognised their “true character”.

‘US history shaped by immigrants’: India calls JD Vance’s H-1B visa remarks ‘deeply offensive’
Reacting to comments by the US Vice President in the context of the decision, India said the descriptions of Indian professionals were "unwarranted".
India on Friday called out US Vice President JD Vance over his comments in the context of United States' decision to suspend applications under the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) programme for certain companies.
India said the descriptions of Indian professionals were "unwarranted" and ignored their contributions to the American economy and innovation ecosystem.
US Vice President JD Vance accused companies of using H-1B visa holders to replace American workers with lower-paid foreign employees, describing them as “foreign indentured servants” in remarks on October 8.
In a video message addressing Microsoft and other companies affected by the US suspension of the PERM green-card programme, Vance said, “You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.”
MEA on US's PERM decision
India's Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said in a statement on Friday the US suspension of applications under the PERM programme for certain companies will not, by itself, affect the validity of existing H-1B visas, but could impact the green-card process for eligible employees of the affected firms.
Under the PERM decision, the US Department of Labor has suspended the processing of pending applications and stopped accepting new applications under the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) programme for eight firms, including Indian IT companies Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro and HCL Technologies. Other IT and technology firms on the list are - Cognizant, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe.
Talent mobility benefits both countries by helping US companies access skilled professionals who contribute to innovation, research, productivity and job creation, the MEA said. It added that the steps announced by the US do not advance the shared ambitions of the two countries.
“It should be noted that PERM is distinct from the H-1B visa programme. The suspension of PERM applications does not, by itself, affect the validity of existing H-1B visas or the status of H-1B visa holders and their dependents, though there could be some impact on the permanent-residency/Green Card process of eligible employees of the affected companies,” the MEA stated.
India calls out Vance
Reacting to comments by the US Vice President in the context of the decision, India said the descriptions of Indian professionals were "unwarranted" and ignored their contributions to the American economy and innovation ecosystem.
Deep Dive
“We have also seen some comments in this context by the US Vice President. We believe that such descriptions are unwarranted and ignore the fact that Indian professionals in the United States are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem," the MEA stated.
Indeed, the history of the United States itself has been shaped by generations of immigrants whose labour, enterprise and innovation have contributed to its growth and prosperity, it said.
Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive, the MEA said.

At a promotional event in Times Square on Wednesday for the security company NordVPN, brand ambassador Shaquille O’Neal said he is eager to raise awareness among regular people about the importance of digital security and personal privacy.
“I have a video of me beating up Charles Barkley, and I wouldn't want the world to see that. That was a joke,” O'Neal says. “But everybody needs to have control of their own information.”
After being targeted by scammers who claimed that he was trying to buy a house and they were working on the transaction, O’Neal says, he realized he needed to learn more about cybersecurity and digital defense.
“I was hacked for the first time, not a bad hack, and I didn't know what to do,” he told reporters. “So I had to look into it. Once that happened, I really had to start paying more attention, because I would think nothing like that could ever happen to me, but it could happen to anybody.”
O'Neal, of course, is not just anybody. Still, the four-time NBA champion and media personality says that he doesn't have particularly sensitive data on his devices and tries to live a normal life as much as possible. When WIRED asked, though, whether he worries that he needs to take extra precautions to protect himself and loved ones as a result of his high profile, O'Neal said, “Yes, I think about it all the time, but I don't let it consume me, because if you let it consume you you can go crazy. But you have to be able to have great reactionary skills if something happens.”
A prolific tech investor who was early to AI, O'Neal emphasizes that the goal of his relationship with NordVPN is to inform the public and help people protect themselves. NordVPN is, well, known for its VPN. But the company has other offerings, including antivirus, threat detection, and scam-defense products that are geared toward accessibility for consumers. Marijus Briedis, the company's chief technology officer, says he was surprised by the findings of a recent NordVPN poll showing that 73 percent of Americans have an overconfidence in traditional antivirus and believe it can protect them against anything from identity theft to online tracking.
“The weakest link is between the computer and the chair, and I've been thinking so much about how to solve that problem,” Briedis told WIRED. “So the thing we are doing right now is focusing on education. It's a really interesting problem, how to do it in the best way. It's still haunting me in my dreams.”

Prime Minister Narendra Modi has urged global tech companies, financial institutions and telecom operators to collaborate and form a comprehensive framework to curb cyber fraud and deep fakes. “At a time when telecom and digital technology have become so important, it is equally important to make the security framework associated with it ironclad. It is our priority to secure mobile phones and networks… trust is very important for ordinary citizens communicating or making payments through the phone,” PM Modi said. Speaking at the India Mobile Congress 2026, the PM highlighted India’s successful endeavour to protect citizens from cyber attacks and frauds, noting that global cooperation is required to nip the issue in the bud, especially as most such operations are borderless. He urged the GSM Association (GSMA), which is a global advocacy group for the telecom industry, and global telecom operators, to create a global mechanism that can potentially prevent cyber fraud before it reaches the masses. He also offered India’s deep expertise in the area to global regulators, noting that authorities in the country have gained vast knowledge on fighting cyber crime. He further noted that the discussions held during the IMC’s tenth edition this year will create a map for how the next decade of telecom will look like, in India and globally. India’s Cyber Fraud Battle The country has grappled with rising cyber fraud over the past few years, with Indians losing ₹3,588.2 Cr in more than 5.83 Lakh digital payment fraud cases between FY22 and FY26. The government has consequently taken several steps to curb such frauds, including a dedicated portal to report suspected crime. The Sanchar Saathi portal has received 12.8 Lakh inputs on suspected fraud communications since launch in 2023. The Centre announced this week that suspected cyber-fraud losses of more than ₹5,000 Cr were prevented through the Financial Fraud Risk Indicator (FRI). Nevertheless, nearly 7.1% of the attempted digital consumer transactions in India were suspected fraud in 2025, almost double the equivalent rate globally (3.8%). To curb this, union home minister Amit Shah directed officials to improve the National Cybercrime Helpline using AI to ease the process of reporting cybercrimes. He also called for addressing the issues related to bank accounts being frozen as part of cyber fraud investigations. The RBI has also come up with a compensation mechanism to aid fraud victims, under which the Centre and bank operators shoulder parts of the unrecovered losses. Customers, losing up to ₹50,000 in cybercrime cases, would be eligible for compensation of up to 85% of the net loss amount or ₹25,000, whichever is lesser.

The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) approved a 24-hour suspension of mobile internet services in New Delhi amid the ongoing protests against the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, in the capital. The shutdown will come into effect from 10 PM on October 9 to 10 PM on October 10 and will impact a 4-km radius of the Janpath-Kartavya Path in New Delhi. The order has been issued in the interest of public security under the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has also reportedly issued an advisory, urging major social media platforms to prioritise action against unlawful, false, or manipulated content linked to the protests. As per a report by PTI, the MeitY directs tech firms to proactively remove ‘unlawful’ posts, label synthetically generated media depicting current events, and ensure swift cooperation with law enforcement agencies within timelines stipulated under the IT Rules, 2021. Meanwhile, the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation announced that 57 Metro stations will be shut from 9 PM onwards, citing “security reasons”. Liquor vendors have been shut and barricades put up in the national capital, while central police personnel have also been deployed. In July, during the NEET protest, the Delhi Police requested app-based aggregators to regulate operations around the central Delhi area. So far in 2026, India has seen 31 instances of internet shutdowns, as per the Software Freedom Law Centre’s Internet Shutdowns Tracker.

Left parties slam Delhi curbs ahead of October 10 Jantar Mantar protest
Left parties have condemned Delhi's restrictions ahead of the October 10 mobilisation and asked police to allow the Jantar Mantar protest. The row intensified after the Supreme Court said transport to the capital cannot be brought to a complete halt.
Left parties on Friday condemned the restrictions imposed ahead of the October 10 mobilisation against the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls and the Election Commission's functioning, and demanded that Delhi Police allow protesters to assemble at Jantar Mantar in the national capital.
In a joint statement, the parties said the denial of permission for the demonstration, extensive barricading, prohibitory orders, the closure of 45 metro stations, the cancellation of trains heading to Delhi, and alleged house arrests in different parts of the country were aimed at preventing the mobilisation. They also said the curbs were causing inconvenience to the general public.
"There are reports of students being put under detention in various places and the offices of student organisations are under surveillance," the statement issued by the CPI(M), CPI, CPI(ML)-Liberation, Revolutionary Socialist Party and All India Forward Bloc said.
The crackdown comes as the Cockroach Janta Party prepares for a massive demonstration at Jantar Mantar on Saturday. The Left parties said, "We demand that the Delhi Police and the Union government stop intimidating and harassing prospective participants and refrain from arbitrary detention of people," and urged the authorities to remove hurdles and permit the protest at Jantar Mantar.
CPI(M) general secretary M A Baby said the Supreme Court had heard the challenge to the restrictions on movement in Delhi, with senior advocate Kapil Sibal appearing for the petitioners. According to Baby, the court observed that while the government could regulate movement, it could not stop traffic altogether, as students, workers and ordinary citizens also needed to travel.
The Supreme Court on Friday directed the Centre to ensure there is no "complete prohibition" on metro and train services to Delhi on October 10, saying it cannot bring everything to a halt. The top court said that while law enforcement agencies can take steps to restrict unruly movement, citizens should not be unduly harassed. The Solicitor General said he would convey the suggestion to the authorities to consider an alternative designated site for the protest.
"Delhi has become a city of barricades," Baby said, alleging that barricading and the deployment of security personnel were creating an atmosphere of intimidation. "We will take up this issue very seriously," he said, adding that the Left parties would participate in Saturday's mobilisation.
Separately, CPI MP P Sandosh Kumar wrote to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, demanding that Jantar Mantar be opened for the demonstration, metro stations be reopened, and the detention of activists be stopped. "Every method of reaching out to your insensitive government has been met with barricades and lathis," Kumar said in the letter. "I wish to make it categorically clear that turning Delhi into a military cantonment will not deter us," he said, alleging that transport restrictions and the detention of activists were preventing people from joining the mobilisation.
CPI(ML) Liberation general secretary Dipankar Bhattacharya said, "Meanwhile, the CJI has advised the government not to use a hammer to kill a fly! Does that leave room for using hammers for cockroaches?" He said that with trains cancelled and metro services stopped, the government had "laid a siege around themselves and turned the whole of Delhi into a huge police camp or paramilitary cantonment". "Has independent India ever witnessed such fear of democracy and peaceful mass protest?" he said.
The joint statement was signed by Baby, CPI general secretary D Raja, Bhattacharya, AIFB general secretary G Devarajan and RSP general secretary Manoj Bhattacharya, as the Left parties reiterated their demand that authorities remove restrictions and allow Saturday's mobilisation at Jantar Mantar.

An Anthropic AI model provided false information about an unsolved homicide to a Philadelphia Police Department (PPD) tipline, according to a report from 6abc. In a statement released on Friday, the PPD said the AI model sent the tip through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com on July 18th, but the investigators never reviewed it because it was marked as spam.
Anthropic’s AI gave Philadelphia police a fake tip about an unsolved homicide
The false tip ‘purported to come from someone who might have information about the case.’
Anthropic learned its AI model sent the false tip on September 28th and notified the PPD on October 7th. The company said that during testing, its AI model was interacting with “randomly selected websites” and submitted false information through the PPD’s tipline, according to the PPD’s statement. The submission “purported to come from someone who might have information about the case,” the PPD said.
After discovering the submission, Anthropic halted the testing process that led to the false tip. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google have been the subject of increased scrutiny after disclosing that their AI models escaped testing environments and hacked third-party companies. Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, advocated for slowing down the development of AI in response to these incidents.
“The company [Anthropic] must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city’s knowledge,” the PPD added. “The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable.”
Anthropic didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment. The company is planning to publish a report about this incident, as well as other “instances of unintended model behavior” on Friday, according to the PPD’s statement.

Prosecutor says suspect in Nigel Farage terror plot was motivated by extreme left-wing views
A prosecutor says the man charged with plotting a terror attack on Reform UK leader Nigel Farage and murdering former lawmaker Ann Widdecombe was motivated by “extreme left-wing” views
LONDON -- A man charged with plotting a terror attack on Reform UK leader Nigel Farage and murdering former lawmaker Ann Widdecombe was motivated by “extreme left-wing” views, a prosecutor said Friday.
Prosecuting attorney Jonathan Polnay said Joshua Kerry’s attack on Widdecombe is “inextricably linked” to his earlier attempt to break into the home of Farage, Britain’s best-known anti-immigration politician. The lawyer said both crimes have a “terrorist connection.”
During a pretrial hearing at London’s Central Criminal Court, Polnay said Kerry conducted research into the home and office addresses of a number of politicians, including Farage and Widdecombe, over a two-year period. Polnay said Kerry had an “extreme left-wing and/or anti-establishment mindset” and was “particularly hostile” toward Reform UK.
Kerry, 28, has not been asked to enter a plea and spoke only to confirm his identity when he attended the hearing remotely from Belmarsh high-security prison. Defense lawyer Nicholas Lumley said Kerry is likely to contest all the charges against him.
Judge Bobbie Cheema-Grubb set a trial date of June 8 next year.
Kerry was arrested in July and charged with murdering 78-year-old Widdecombe, who was found dead at her rural house in southwest England on July 8. Prosecutors say Kerry drove 265 miles (425 kilometers) from his home in northern England and hit her 21 times with a hammer as she ate lunch in her kitchen.
Widdecombe joined Reform UK after a long career as a Conservative member of Parliament and government minister, and was known for her blunt-spoken, socially conservative views opposing abortion and the expansion of LGBTQ+ rights.
After her death, counterterrorism police reopened a probe into an alleged firebomb and break-in attempt at Farage’s south London home in April 2025. Prosecutors say the door was damaged by a knife, and Kerry’s DNA was found on a bottle of lighter fluid left on the porch.
Last week prosecutors charged Kerry with preparing terrorist acts, including against Farage, between May 2024 and the day Widdecombe was killed.
Widdecombe’s slaying renewed concerns over security for politicians, which has been tightened in the past decade after two lawmakers were murdered.
Labour legislator Jo Cox was shot and stabbed in 2016 by a far-right extremist, and Conservative David Amess was stabbed in 2021 by an attacker inspired by the Islamic State group.
