I thought I'd get sick of the food by the end of my seven-day voyage in April 2022. I'd never been on a cruise before, but I imagined my dining options would be limited at sea.
And they might have been if I weren't on board Royal Caribbean's Wonder of the Seas, one of the largest cruise ships in the world. The megaship has 20 eateries, from coffee shops and buffets to fast-food joints and upscale restaurants.
I was overwhelmed with options every time I got hungry on my Caribbean cruise. I ate at as many different restaurants as I could — more than half of them.
There were 10 standout dishes that I still think about when my stomach grumbles.
Some of the best meals were included in the cruise rate. Others came from specialty restaurants.
Wonder of the Seas has some restaurants that are complimentary as part of the cruise rate, while specialty dining incurs an additional cost.
For the latter, guests often pay a cover charge for a three-course meal. I made reservations at five specialty restaurants. I recommend booking your reservation as soon as possible, because the cost tends to rise the longer you wait.
Two of my favorite dishes came from the main dining room.
The main dining room is complimentary for guests and serves breakfast and a three-course dinner each day.
One was a dinner entrée — garlic tiger shrimp with jasmine rice, seasonal veggies, and herb butter.
The shrimp was juicy and had great flavor. The rice was sticky, which I like, and the asparagus and tomatoes were well-seasoned.
The other was a French toast breakfast. The bread was thick, crispy on the outside, and fluffy on the inside.
A delicious berry compote on top paired nicely with maple syrup. Two crispy strips of bacon added a savory crunch to each bite. This was my favorite breakfast of the whole trip.
I also particularly enjoyed El Loco Fresh, an outdoor DIY taco bar.
It's included for guests and serves a selection of meats, cheeses, and toppings, like pico de gallo, guacamole, and sour cream.
I grabbed a bowl of chips and made myself some nachos.
The queso had great texture and flavor. The bar had every topping I could want, satisfying my Tex-Mex craving on the ship.
When I wanted an upscale meal, I splurged on dinner at Chops Grille, a steakhouse.
I paid $55 for a three-course dinner here.
The highlight was the appetizer — a crispy goat cheese salad with green apples, candied walnuts, cranberries, and balsamic dressing.
It was an eclectic mix of textures and flavors, yet it blended perfectly in my mouth.
I treated myself to another fancy dinner at 150 Central Park.
On a plant-filled outdoor deck, 150 Central Park served a variety of meat, seafood, and other "locally sourced ingredients," according to Royal Caribbean. I had a three-course dinner for $50.
My favorite dish was the fried cheesecake for dessert.
The dessert was soft, fluffy, and light, with a cream cheese filling. Caramelized popcorn, whipped cream, and a Nutella drizzle complemented it perfectly, making it even more satisfying than the main course.
To get my seafood fix, I went to the New England-style Hooked Seafood restaurant.
The menu draws inspiration from Maine to Maryland. I paid $53 for a three-course dinner.
The lobster roll was fantastic.
The toasted roll was generously loaded with thick chunks of lobster and a layer of crisp lettuce. I squeezed the grilled lemon across the top and bit into the refreshing mess of a sandwich. It reminded me of lobster rolls I've had back home on the East Coast.
For dessert, I went with the chef's suggestion: a lemon tart.
I took one bite, and it was easy to see why it came highly recommended. The lemon custard was tangy with a bit of sweetness, and it filled up a flaky, buttery crust. It was the best lemon tart I've ever had.
The Mason Jar serves southern comfort food. It ended up being my favorite restaurant on the ship.
I booked a three-course dinner at the Mason Jar for $40, and everything I ordered made my top 10 list.
I'm glad I booked it for a three-course dinner, which started with crab beignets.
I ordered the crab beignets appetizer at the Mason Jar. Although I'd never had one before, I love crab, and I love beignets. So I gave it a try.
They were the perfect texture — soft and fluffy with a crisp outer layer. The crab flavor was subtle, with cinnamon on top for an interesting twist. The accompanying crap dip was refreshing, too.
For my main, I ordered fried chicken with mashed potatoes and mac and cheese.
The chicken was tender and well-seasoned, with a crispy outer layer. The sides had good flavor as well.
My dessert at The Mason Jar was served in one.
Called "Gone Bananas," the dessert consisted of layers of vanilla pudding and graham cracker crumbs inside a jar. It was topped with brûléed bananas, whipped cream, and toffee. The dessert was fluffy, light, and rich in banana flavor.
It was a fitting ending to my favorite meal of the trip.
If I were to cruise with Wonder of the Seas again, I'd spend less money on specialty restaurants and more evenings in the main dining room.
While the specialty restaurants served delicious dishes, I thought the food quality was just as high in the main dining room, where I ate only twice.
But I'd absolutely pay to go back to The Mason Jar for all three standout courses.

What to expect at Apple's 'Welcome home' event next week
The company is reportedly rebooting its smart home ambitions with a smart display and a whole bunch of other accessories.
Apple is hosting its second fall event on October 13, and the "Welcome home" tagline on its invitation heavily suggests it will be focused on smart home products. Depending on your perspective, you could trace the company's entry into the space with the introduction of the Apple TV, HomeKit or the first HomePod, but this new push is reportedly built around the improved functionality of Siri AI and several new pieces of hardware that will run it.
The star of that new hardware lineup will reportedly be the company's first smart display, but it's also expected to introduce updates to the Apple TV and HomePod mini alongside it, too, and possibly a whole lot more. Here's the full rundown of new products Apple could announce at its smart home event.
An Apple smart display or 'HomePad'
All recent reporting indicates Apple is ready to launch its first smart display, a device that marries the audio and AI assistant capabilities of a HomePod with a display that can showcase photos, run apps and act as a dedicated FaceTime device.
Bloomberg reports Apple's so-called "HomePad" will feature a 6-inch square display that will be available attached to a round, HomePod mini-style speaker or a smaller audio set-up that can be mounted alongside the display on a wall. The primary method for interacting with the HomePad is Siri AI, but the device's new tvOS-based "homeOS" will also support touchscreen interactions and include some of the customizable interface elements of the Apple Watch and the iPhone's StandBy mode. The smart display will also be able to run iPadOS-style apps, according to Bloomberg, which opens up the possibility for video streaming and other functionality if developers decide to support it.
Besides acting as a showcase for Siri AI's ability to interact with Apple's HomeKit platform, Apple reportedly also plans for the device to be able to detect who's looking at it and adjust its interface and apps accordingly, though it apparently won't rely on Apple's Face ID technology from the iPhone to make that happen. The feature could let the HomePad switch which calendar or notifications it displays depending on who's looking at the screen — personalization features few other Apple devices offer.
Updates to the HomePod mini and Apple TV
Apple limits access to Siri AI based on a device's A-series or M-series chip, so it makes sense the aging chips in the current HomePod mini (an S5 chip from the Apple Watch Series 5) and the Apple TV 4K (an A15 Bionic chip from the iPhone 13) would need to be swapped out for something new. Bloomberg reports that both the Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini will be updated with faster chips that can run Siri AI, along with modest design updates.
The new Apple TV 4K will reportedly be powered by at least an A19 chip from the iPhone 17 lineup and feature a slightly redesigned remote along. The HomePod mini will come in new colors including green, pink, blue, black and white, according to MacRumors, and will likely feature a chip from a recent Apple Watch so it can handle Siri AI prompts. Apple is also reportedly working on supporting surround sound setups with HomePods, an expansion of the stereo HomePod setups it currently offers through the Apple TV.
Third-party doorbells, locks and cameras
Previous reports suggested Apple was working on its own privacy-focused cameras as part of its smart home lineup, but now Bloomberg reports they might not be sold under Apple's name. The company is reportedly collaborating with LG Electronics to create a series of smart locks, doorbells, thermostats and temperature sensors. The devices will work with Apple's smart home ecosystem but will apparently be manufactured, sold and supported by LG. A later leak suggested similar third-party devices will also come from Schneider Electric, which is apparently making a thermostat for the launch.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

The zardozi embroidery on a Dior dress, the T-strap leather sandals at a Prada show, the mirror-work technique used on a Fendi bag – for decades, the skill of Indian artisans has been an invisible force behind some of the world’s most coveted fashion.
Now, that work is beginning to claim its own place in the spotlight, and the Mumbai-based textile and embroidery atelier Chanakya International is at the forefront.
Chanakya marked its 40th anniversary this month, celebrating with three exhibitions that trace its journey from an embroidery powerhouse to a present-day craft and cultural institution. The person steering it is 49-year-old Karishma Swali, whose father set up the group’s operations in the 1980s.
“What we have as a country is unique,” she tells me of India’s rich textile and craft heritage. “It’s unparalleled in many ways, and it’s the only place where we continue to practise it.” During the Renaissance, she says, France and Italy had established and varied traditions. “But what we have in India today is [what] other parts of the world have lost.”
Chanakya has a network of 1,400 artisans, and says that some are 13th-generation craftspeople, skilled in hundreds of embroidery traditions and supplying almost every luxury label you can imagine. Among the techniques they have revived is the Mughal-era silver filigree lace, or chaand jaal, reintroduced in a lighter form that has since become a regular feature in couture collections.
In 2023, Dior held a show at Mumbai’s Gateway of India, showcasing its partnership with Chanakya, in a high-profile acknowledgment of Indian craftsmanship. The runway saw sari-inspired skirts, vibrant madras-checks sets and Nehru-collar jackets.
These collaborations are supported by expert craft knowledge passed down and refined over generations, and they need institutional support to survive. The Kalhath Institute, a craft-preservation centre in Lucknow, runs residencies that pair artists from across the world with local artisans.
Kalhath’s co-founder Mohammed Amine Dadda tells me that Indian craftsmanship’s defining quality is “intelligence of the hand” – a sensitive, slow and cumulative process underpinned by patience and dexterity. “Without this technical mastery, and the considerable time required to create the most demanding pieces, haute couture and contemporary luxury simply could not bring their most ambitious creative visions to life.”
This mastery is not limited to textiles. When it comes to jewellery, global luxury brands have long sought Jaipur-based the Gem Palace, established in 1852 by the Kasliwal family, who still run it today. Samarth Kasliwal, 33, says part of the appeal lies in the visual language of Indian artistry itself. “There is something about Indian artistry that is inspired by nature,” he tells me, pointing to the recurring use of floral patterns and animals across Indian art and design. These motifs are universal, and travel across the lines of culture and language.
One recent collaboration Kasliwal is particularly proud of is a collection for Dior featuring green onyx and rock crystals, with engravings of birds, animals and flowers. The combination, he says, is reminiscent of traditional Indian jewellery, while drawing on techniques that remain central to the atelier’s work today.
With increased visibility, the question of credit and appropriation has become harder to ignore. Last week, a Ralph Lauren gown from the designer’s spring 2027 collection attracted criticism after many Indians pointed out that the embroidery the brand described as “embellishments” looked a lot like Indian zardozi, but without any accompanying credit. (Ralph Lauren did not respond to my request for comment.)
Then, Fendi came under fire when people noticed that a baguette bag from its autumn/winter collection featured mirrorwork often seen in Gujarati crafts. In April, Fendi credited Chanakya artisans in a social media video showcasing the same embroidery. But the product description on its site failed to mention any Indian inspiration, and its final label read “Made in Italy”.
After I asked Fendi about the discrepancy, the brand cited its “creative partnership” with Chanakya of more than three decades, saying it “remains committed to supporting and recognizing India’s rich craft heritage”. The website descriptor now reads: “Made in Italy and India with Chanakya”.
A recent Financial Times report noted that under EU rules, garments embroidered in India can still end up with a European label – so long as the final construction and finishing take place in Europe.
Last year, Prada was accused of appropriating Indian culture with Kolhapuri-inspired sandals, a controversy that showed us these debates around recognition can sometimes produce a more structural response. “We acknowledge the sandals … are inspired by traditional Indian handcrafted footwear, with a centuries-old heritage,” Lorenzo Bertelli, the corporate social responsibility chief at the Italian fashion house, had written in a letter to the Maharashtra chamber of commerce at the time.
Prada subsequently partnered with state-backed organisations in Maharashtra and Karnataka to produce a limited-edition collection, Made in India, and committed to a three-year training programme for artisans specialising in the craft.
Might these collaborations, controversies and corrections represent a shift in India’s place in the fashion industry? Anthropologist Phyllida Jay, author of Inspired by India: How India Transformed Global Design, appears to think so, placing the debate in a longer arc. “The stories of the ateliers producing highly skilled Indian craft in the elevated realm of European luxury and high fashion is part of a broader paradigm shift,” she writes, “where over 70 years after the end of colonial rule, India is being looked at in a different way on the world stage.” It is, in a way, a reversal, moving from a colonial history of extraction toward one in which Indians themselves get a voice in how their craft is represented.
Swali is ensuring this visibility also lives on through the Chanakya School of Craft, which she set up in 2016. Its 18-month programme provides free embroidery training and a travel honorarium to dozens of women, some of whom have gone on to work at the main atelier. Others have set up their own independent studios.
I had a chance to visit the space – inside a high-rise in Lower Parel, where those as young as 18 learn intricate needlework alongside grandmothers in their 60s. “Craft in India has never been institutionalised,” Swali says of the ethos behind the initiative. “It’s intergenerational,” she says, adding that women have often been excluded.
India’s culture of craft has always been precious. Growing up, I loved having the choice to affordably create any type of clothing. At one point, I had a small army of tailors, each with a different specialisation, whom I’d go to for different needs. I’d buy ajrakh and mashru silks from Dastkar or Nalli, and hand it to the right Masterji to stitch, embroider and tweak to my size. So, to me, Indian craftsmanship is not just a part of luxury, but a luxury itself.

Fashion designer Payal Khandwala, whose spring-summer ’26 collection featured handwoven silks, cottons and brocades, recommends the perfect saree weave: “The delicate poetry of a Jamdani saree is definitely my favourite. A 2,000-year-old craft, typically woven in fine muslin and of Bengali origin, it’s somewhat an unsung hero. The weaving process itself is exceptionally intricate. Using a supplementary weft technique, thousands of markings are meticulously mapped on to the warp to recreate the pattern, interlaced by hand with a wooden shuttle and metallic needle to guide the motifs in silver and gold yarn, on fine mulberry silk and organza.”

The true measure of my love for my friends is in the number of memes I send them. One of the accounts I rely on is Bahaish Kapoor’s. What makes an image meme-worthy? “I always look for people who are in a deep philosophical, romantic, dramatic action moment which I can repurpose to bring in a whole new meaning,” he tells me. “I try to mix and match and see what’s working.” His 340,000-plus followers include Sharon Stone and Hrithik Roshan.

Adidas sues Australian label White Fox over four stripes design
- Published
Adidas is suing Australian label White Fox for selling and advertising clothes with a four-striped design, arguing it is "deceptively similar" to the German brand's distinct logo.
The sportswear giant said it had repeatedly asked White Fox to stop selling and promoting the clothes since March, but the Sydney-based company refused.
The fast-fashion online retailer is popular with teenagers and young adults in Australia, the UK and the US, and has relied on billboards, bus advertising and influencers - often university-aged - to grow its profile.
The Australian law firms representing Adidas and White Fox both declined to comment on the case, the first hearing due to begin on Friday.
In Federal Court documents, Adidas states that its three-striped design has a "substantial and valuable reputation" in Australia, where it has been trademarked since 1957.
The company says since at least March, White Fox has been selling and advertising clothes with four parallel stripes of equal width, which it claims is an infringement of Adidas's trademark.
White Fox's designs are "substantially identical with or otherwise deceptively similar" to Adidas, the company claims.
It also argues that White Fox's advertisements for its four-striped clothes and White Fox-branded socks feature people wearing "genuine" Adidas items.
This might lead Australians to think Adidas is associated with White Fox and has approved of the design, the documents claim.
The company says White Fox is "taking advantage" of Adidas's reputation, "drawing an association in the minds of consumers" of the two brands, or at least "sailing close to the wind".
Adidas, which reported €24.8 billion (£21bn; $28bn) in revenue in 2025, is also seeking damages, saying White Fox must pay them the profit from the products plus interest and costs.
Evidence provided by Adidas included side-by-side comparisons of its products with White Fox clothes which include sweatpants and lounge shorts, as well as images of billboards on buses and at bus stops.
In one example, Adidas claimed that an online listing from June 2025 showed a pair of White Fox-branded socks being modelled by someone wearing pink Adidas shoes.
A few days after the court proceedings were lodged last month, the Adidas logo on the shoes were digitally altered to remove one of the stripes, the documents alleged, and a week later, all three stripes were scrubbed from the image.
In 2013, Adidas successfully sued Pacific Brands in Australia for selling shoes with four stripes.
White Fox was launched in 2013 by Georgia and Daniel Contos and is privately-owned by the Greek-Australian couple and Daniel's mother Melina Maceri. It has a growing presence in the US and expanded into the UK market in 2024.
In the 12 months to June 2025, the company generated AU$542m (£286m; $377m) in revenue, a four-fold jump from its 2022 figure of $121m, according to the Australian Financial Review.

The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.
The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.
“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.
That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.
“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.
Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.
“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.
“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”
In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.
“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.
“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.
The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded in disbelief.
“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.
“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”
Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.
South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel Prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”
Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the Prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.
“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.
Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.
“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.
In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.
“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.
Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Donald Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.
On Monday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”

Why Elon Musk is taking on India's richest man over Starlink
- Published
Elon Musk has questioned whether billionaire Mukesh Ambani is the "real boss of India" as his satellite internet company Starlink struggles to secure final approval to launch in the country.
The remark came a day after Musk accused unnamed powerful business interests of trying to block Starlink's entry into India. He then singled out Ambani, whose Reliance conglomerate owns Jio, India's biggest mobile network operator.
India has rejected Musk's allegations, saying its satellite communications rules are fair and non-discriminatory.
Ambani and Reliance Group have not responded to Musk's remarks. The BBC has reached out to them for comment
The row comes as competition grows in India's satellite internet market, with Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel also preparing to launch services.
The rivalry is complicated by the fact that Starlink has also partnered with Ambani's Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel.
In March 2025, both companies signed agreements with SpaceX to distribute Starlink equipment and services in India, subject to government approval. The companies also said they could explore sharing network infrastructure. The BBC has also reached out to Bharti Airtel for comment.
Musk first made the allegations on Wednesday, accusing "certain oligarchs" of maintaining a "monopolistic chokehold" on Indian consumers.
"You can guess who they are," he wrote on X, external, adding that blocking Starlink was "a crime against the people of India".
On Thursday, India's Ministry of Communications responded, saying that three operators - Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio Satellite Communications - were at broadly the same stage of the approval process, with all three awaiting security clearances and spectrum allocation before they can launch commercial services.
"The suggestion that the framework or its application is unfair or discriminatory is baseless and misconceived," the ministry said, without naming Musk directly.
Musk continued to question the delay, saying Starlink was already licensed in more than 165 countries.
"Starlink is licensed in over 165 countries and has spent five years complying with every single law and requirement of the government of India, so why still no license? Is Ambani the real boss of India?" he wrote on X on Thursday.
Starlink, owned by Musk's SpaceX, uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas where mobile networks and broadband cables are difficult or expensive to install.
The company has been trying to enter India since 2021 and has secured key licences. But it still needs final security clearances and spectrum allocation before it can begin commercial services.
Wednesday's row unfolded as senior executives from Starlink, Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel gathered at the India Mobile Congress in Delhi, where all three companies discussed their plans for satellite internet services.
Speaking at the event, Akash Ambani, chairman of Reliance Jio Infocomm and Mukesh Ambani's son, said the company was developing its own satellite communications technology and working towards regulatory approvals.
Asked by a reporter about Musk's allegations, Akash declined to comment and only said, "We want to be heads down and deliver value to our Indian consumers."
Bharti Airtel chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal said his company's satellite venture was also awaiting government approvals.
SpaceX executive Lauren Dreyer, who oversees Starlink's business operations, said the company had spent years working with Indian regulators and had built security controls into its network to meet the country's requirements.
Security has been a key concern surrounding Starlink's entry into India. In 2024, Indian authorities said they had recovered Starlink equipment during a drug-smuggling investigation in the remote Andaman and Nicobar Islands and an army operation in the northeastern state of Manipur.
Musk said at that time that Starlink's service had never been active in India, arguing that the equipment recovered by authorities could not have been using its satellite network.
Questions also remain over how affordable the service would be for Indian consumers, particularly those in rural areas.
India is one of the world's largest internet markets but access remains uneven, particularly in remote areas where mobile networks and broadband cables are difficult or expensive to build.
Musk has argued that Starlink could help bridge this gap. "Starlink in India would enable high-speed, affordable internet connectivity for those who can't afford current prices or who don't have a connection at all!" he wrote on X on Wednesday.
The company has yet to announce prices for India, but some experts say its plans elsewhere suggest the service could be beyond the reach of many Indian households.
In the US, Starlink's residential plans start at $55 a month, although prices and equipment costs vary by plan and location.

New Delhi, Oct 9: An unprecedented security clampdown has been enforced in the Capital ahead of Saturday, after Delhi Police denied permission to the Cockroach Janta Party to hold a protest at Jantar Mantar, with the deployment of 25,000 police and paramilitary personnel, closure of 57 metro stations, suspension of internet services and intensive checks at city's border points, railway stations, bus terminals, hotels and other sensitive locations.
According to police, the elaborate security arrangements are aimed at preventing protesters from staging an unauthorised sit-in at Jantar Mantar and to maintain law and order across the city amid the possibility of large-scale mobilisation of people.
Internet services will be suspended within a 4-kilometre radius of Jantar Mantar from 10 pm on October 9 to 10 pm on October 10, sources said. The Union home ministry has approved the decision, they said. The suspension will apply to all mobile internet services. Internet services in the rest of Delhi will remain unaffected, they said.
The New Delhi district has been divided into 20 zones to strengthen security arrangements and maintain law and order. Each of the 20 zones will be monitored by a Joint Commissioner of Police, a Deputy Commissioner of Police and an Additional Deputy Commissioner of Police to ensure close supervision of the security arrangements, the sources said.
Special Commissioners of Police heading various units will also closely monitor the zones and coordinate with senior officers whenever required to respond to any law-and-order situation, they added.
Addressing a press conference, Joint Commissioner Nupur Prasad said on Friday that police have denied permission for the proposed October 10 demonstration, citing the short notice given for the event and alleged violations of rules and directions during an earlier protest.
She said the application seeking permission for the demonstration was submitted on October 7, just three days before the proposed gathering, adding that according to rules, such applications have to be submitted at least 10 days in advance
Police said the application did not meet the stipulated notice period and that the conduct of the July demonstration had raised concerns over compliance with directions issued by authorities.
The restrictions have been proposed in view of the Cockroach Janata Party's protest at Jantar Mantar on October 10 against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Kumar is facing allegations of voter-list tampering under the guise of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and of bypassing his two colleagues to alter Form 6, a key document to register as a voter.
As part of the security arrangements, Delhi Police conducted mock drills at several locations.
More than 120 companies of Central Armed Police Forces are expected to be involved in the security arrangements.
Liquor shops across Delhi have been ordered to remain closed on October 9 and 10 as a preventive measure. Entry and exit gates at 57 Delhi Metro stations, including Rajiv Chowk, New Delhi, Central Secretariat, Patel Chowk and Kashmere Gate, will remain closed from 9 pm on Friday till further notice.
According to the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC), restrictions will also continue on October 10, with the interchange facility remaining available at all affected stations except for the New Delhi metro station.
Other prominent stations where entry and exit gates will remain closed include Janpath, Mandi House, Barakhamba Road, Supreme Court, Indraprastha, ITO, Delhi Gate, Khan Market, Jama Masjid, Chandni Chowk, Hauz Khas and INA.
The list also includes Shaheen Bagh, Jamia Millia Islamia, Okhla Vihar, Kalindi Kunj, Lajpat Nagar, Ashram, Sarai Kale Khan-Nizamuddin, Welcome, Shahdara, Rithala, Rohini, Azadpur, Kashmere Gate and Shivaji Stadium, among others.
Railway services are also expected to be disrupted, with several trains scheduled to arrive at or depart from New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin railway stations between 4 am and 2 pm on Saturday reported cancelled.
The restrictions are intended to prevent large groups from converging on sensitive locations and moving towards areas where demonstrations are not permitted.
The proposed measures could affect office-goers, students, shoppers and other commuters who rely on the metro for daily travel. Passengers have been advised to check official announcements.
Meanwhile, police have stepped up monitoring of social media platforms, with more than 200 content creators reportedly under scrutiny in connection with mobilisation for the protest.
Borders of the national capital will also face heightened surveillance and additional security cameras have been installed.
There is a possibility of restrictions on vehicles entering New Delhi after 6 am on Saturday, depending on the security assessment and the situation on the ground, police sources said.
Hotels, lodges, guest houses and dharamshalas are being checked as part of the preventive security exercise. Police are also issuing appeals from various mosques and temples, urging people to maintain peace.
Bus terminals across the Capital will witness heightened vigilance, with security personnel monitoring passengers and vehicles arriving from neighbouring states.
The airport and its approach roads are expected to remain under heightened security, with additional checks and surveillance to ensure that passenger movement remains orderly. Travellers heading to the airport have been advised to account for possible congestion and security checks while planning their journeys.
Police will keep a close watch on people associated with the protest and assess attempts to mobilise supporters through social media platforms.
More than 200 content creators have reportedly come under scrutiny as part of the monitoring exercise. Police teams are examining online posts and messages relating to mobilisation, gathering points and the proposed demonstration.
Police said security personnel will monitor developments throughout Saturday and respond to any incidents, including crowd build-up, traffic obstructions and attempts to breach barricades.

Betsy Pleasants was studying one historic disruption to abortion access when a more seismic one emerged.
In spring 2022, as a graduate student at UC Berkeley School of Public Health, Pleasants was researching the effects of the Covid-19 pandemic on abortion services when a leaked draft opinion indicated that the U.S. Supreme Court would overturn Roe v. Wade. The court finalized its decision that June, ending the nearly 50-year-old constitutional right to abortion and ushering in an era of rapid change and increased state restrictions.
Working with her thesis committee, Pleasants, who is interested in expanding access to abortion and other reproductive health care, adapted her dissertation to study conversations on the social network Reddit. Her new focus was tracking emerging barriers to abortion access in real time and examining the role of online resources in connecting people with evidence-based health information and services.
“When it became clear that Roe v. Wade was going to be overturned, we all agreed that we had to shift the project,” said Pleasants, now a postdoctoral research associate at the Center for Women’s Health Research at the University of North Carolina. The Supreme Court decision “is something that required a response, and this project was positioned to offer timely insights into what this policy change means in people’s lives.”
Pleasants and her colleagues plumbed thousands of posts from the Reddit forum r/abortion using natural language processing (NLP) — a type of computational analysis used to identify patterns in human language — alongside a qualitative close reading of a subset of posts. Through this dual approach, grounded in safeguards for user privacy, Pleasants is defining a framework for using artificial intelligence tools without losing sight of the context, complexity, and people behind the data.
“We are in a complex policy moment for reproductive health,” said Pleasants, who was recently named a STAT Wunderkind. This type of research “is an act of documenting in an effort to work towards evidence-based policy change over time, and to advocate for the change that’s needed to promote access to reproductive health care.”
Findings by Pleasants and her colleagues reaffirmed well-established barriers to access, including high costs and limited appointment availability, while also revealing lesser-known challenges, such as delays in receiving abortion medications by mail, low credibility of online ordering platforms, and concerns about the legal risks of seeking abortion or related medical care.
“Embracing this opportunity and new methods was visionary,” said Ushma Upadhyay, professor in the Department of Obstetrics, Gynecology, & Reproductive Sciences at the University of California San Francisco, who mentored Pleasants during her doctoral research. “At the time, I didn’t know of any other studies using NLP to study online discourse on abortion. Most researchers will just take a random sample of a manageable number that they can analyze, and so this approach was really great because Betsy was able to get a more complete picture.”
For scientists like Pleasants, the value of NLP goes beyond making large-scale research more efficient. It offers a broader view of how people communicate and behave at a scale that would otherwise be difficult to capture.
“Computational research is like a stepping stool over a tall fence that lets you look at the other side and see everything that’s around you,” said Danny Valdez, associate professor of public health at the Indiana School of Public Health-Bloomington, who has employed NLP to study vaccine misinformation, addiction and recovery, and cancer care. “NLP, machine learning, and, increasingly, AI methods give you a 1,000-foot overview of how people communicate when they need help. You can learn a lot about the pulse of the nation, which helps us understand and inform where future policy could be headed.”
A new model for studying online discourse
Growing up in North Carolina, Pleasants got her first window into how people access health information, sparking an interest that would eventually shape her career. Even in Durham, a liberal core city of North Carolina’s Research Triangle, she recalled receiving abstinence-only sex education from a gym teacher. The contrast between the information she received at school and at home made her aware of how unevenly health knowledge and resources could be distributed.
“I saw peers and other people in the community navigating not having good sex education, not having access to desired health services, and stigma,” said Pleasants. “All of these things really shaped the capacity they had to make decisions for themselves about their reproductive health.”
Those early observations would become a throughline in Pleasants’ career, from earning her undergraduate degree at the University of North Carolina to completing her master’s and doctorate at UC Berkeley, and ultimately returning to UNC for her postdoctoral research.
Pleasants entered college with an eye on becoming a physician, but was instead drawn to medical anthropology and broader discussions of how history, politics, and culture have shaped, and continue to shape, the U.S. health care system.
“A big question that came up for me was: ‘Do I want to work within that system or do I want to critically engage with it?’” said Pleasants. “So, I ended up on this trajectory of research with an interest in asking questions of how we offer health services, particularly for women, and seeking to understand how we can make that better for all people as much as possible.”
Analyzing r/abortion while at Berkeley allowed Pleasants to capture perspectives often overlooked by conventional research methods. The platform’s relative anonymity gave people space to speak candidly about personal experiences they might hesitate to share elsewhere. And because most community members had not interacted with the health care system, their experiences would often be missed by practice-based analysis.
“Following the reversal of Roe v. Wade, a lot of people were turning to Reddit for support,” said Upadhyay.
Pleasants and her collaborators used NLP to analyze more than 7,000 posts from the months before, during, and after the leak of the Supreme Court’s draft decision, identifying 55 distinct topics. Human oversight was integral throughout, both to validate the computational approach and to guide deeper qualitative analysis. The team closely examined posts within the identified topics to understand not only what people were discussing, but how they were navigating their experiences.
The research revealed a wide range of barriers to abortion care, from state bans, high costs, and long travel distances to stigma and lack of social support. It also surfaced emerging challenges, including delays receiving abortion medications by mail, uncertainty about the legitimacy of online services, and concerns about potential legal risks. The qualitative analysis provided further insight into the impacts of these barriers, including anxiety and isolation and, in some cases, the need to self-manage abortions.
The emphasis on human supervision also extended to protecting the privacy of Reddit users. As NLP and AI tools become more widely integrated into public health research, their use has fueled broader discussion, both within the research community and among the public, about the ethical use of online data. Pleasants said the stakes are particularly high in reproductive health research.
“We are studying issues that are, at minimum, sensitive and stigmatized, and in some cases even pose risks for prosecution,” she said. “This becomes even more complex when you’re working with publicly available data where people may not be aware that their posts could be used for research.”
To protect Reddit users, the team employed a “heavy disguise” process, replacing potentially identifiable posts with composite quotations that combined and rephrased similar experiences. The researchers then tested these composites using online searches and plagiarism-detection tools to help ensure they could not be traced back to their original sources.
Together, these practices have established a model for studying sensitive online discourse at scale.
“As this technology keeps getting faster and faster and faster, you do have very talented and forward-thinking researchers like Betsy, who are slowing things down and looking at how to make this as rigorous and concrete as possible through a very firm qualitative lens,” said Valdez, who was not involved in Pleasants’ research, though both have received funding from the Society of Family Planning. “We need work like Betsy’s that’s already acknowledged the difficulties of social media mining … and to show very high regard for the content that people are leaving on social media.”
Today, Pleasants said her research, which has now expanded to include contraception and misinformation online, has taken on greater urgency as shifting policies increasingly constrain access to reproductive health care. She noted that researchers, advocates, and clinicians in the field have long worked amid scrutiny and uncertainty.
“The importance of the research doesn’t lessen just because policies make the work harder. Rather, the opposite seems true right now,” she said.

A Newfoundlander got a random call from a bunch of Hollywood stars — and just went with it
Paul Matthews jokes he might need a publicist after appearing in Netflix promo
Paul Matthews was at home washing blueberries in Brigus, N.L., last month, when he got a call from a woman he didn’t know. He told her she’d called a wrong number, but then they started chatting — and Matthews stayed on the line.
“Why not?” Matthews told The Current on Friday. “I'm just picking through blueberries and life is good and I'm just relaxed.”
The woman said her “chubby fingers” must have dialled the wrong number — but that was a fib. On the other end of the line, it was really Jax Irwin, a broadcaster who makes viral videos cold calling phone numbers on the East Coast, just to chat.
On that particular day, she was calling random numbers to film a promotional video with the cast of a new Netflix show, Below, filmed and set in Newfoundland and starring Josh Hartnett, Charlie Heaton and Mackenzie Davis.
“We wanted to stay true to calling completely random numbers,” Irwin told The Current.
“Mackenzie and Charlie and Josh, they've spent, obviously, a lot of time in Newfoundland. So they were equally pleased, excited, and also familiar with how lovely folks from Newfoundland can be.”
I couldn't have asked for a better person to pick up the phoneJax Irwin
Matthews delivered. They chatted about Brigus, its beautiful rock walls and winding paths. He told her he used to be the town’s deputy mayor but was getting older now. When Irwin called him a mover and a shaker, he said these days he’s “moving slower and shaking more.”
But Matthews had his own surprise in store. He’d heard an interview with Irwin on The Current, just the week before.
“I was listening to CBC Radio and they had this lady on and she does this as a sort of a hobby, she cold calls people,” he told her that day, prompting a stunned Irwin to respond: “Can I tell you a secret? That's that lonely woman who calls people, calling you right now.”
“I wouldn’t be surprised," Matthews replied.
Irwin told The Current she “couldn't have asked for a better person to pick up the phone.”
Netflix released the video of their call on social media this week, where it’s already racked up almost 900,000 views across TikTok, Facebook and Instagram.
Matthews said he’s had a lot of calls and texts from family and friends who’ve seen the video. He joked he might need to hire a publicist.
“I think I am on second nine of the 10 seconds of fame,” he laughed.
Newfoundland has its 'own type of magic'
Below, which premiered this week on Netflix, stars Hartnett as a fisherman in a small Newfoundland town that is terrorized by an unknown sea creature.
Harnett spoke to CBC Radio’s Q this week and said the people of St. John’s really helped him prepare for the role, from a fisherman who showed him how to tie nets, to locals who taught him how to properly use “skeet” in a sentence.
“You get this sort of feeling of being in a place that has its own type of magic,” he told Q. “What that is, I can't really put a finger on, but it feels unlike anything else.”
Matthews, second from right, ended up attending a screening of Below with his wife Tina Matthews, right, and daughter Zara Tai Matthews. They met the star of the show, actor Josh Hartnett. (Netflix)
Hartnett also listened to hours of CBC’s Newfoundland show, The Broadcast, to nail the accent — with Matthews saying the overall cast did “reasonably well” on that score.
The streaming giant also invited Matthews and his family to attend a screening of the show in St. John’s, where he said they got to chat with Hartnett and were very well looked after. In another coincidence, his daughter, Zara Tai Matthews, appears in the show’s sixth episode.
Irwin started making the calls in part because she felt lonely and homesick after moving to Toronto from Dartmouth, N.S. She’s not too worried about people knowing it’s her calling, if the extra publicity blows her cover.
“I also don't want to be too much of a sneaky snake, right? So if people know what I'm doing, I'm just always happy to connect with anybody who will pick up the phone,” she said.
Matthews thinks Irwin is doing good by making these connections, and he can see why she calls smaller communities on the East Coast to have these chats.
“People in those big cities are just so rushed, and I well appreciate that,” he said.
“What may be one of the very attractive features of our lifestyle is that we take time to live and enjoy the vagaries of life, wherever they come.”

The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season has been mercifully dull, but that’s set to change this week. Tropical Storm Isaias is forecast to become the season’s first hurricane before making landfall somewhere between Mississippi and Florida by the weekend.
El Niño has turned the Atlantic basin into a graveyard by changing winds high in the atmosphere so that they rip apart storms. That’s helped depress tropical cyclone activity to near-record-low levels and resulted in zero hurricanes. That could change imminently, though.
Isaias is churning in the Gulf of Mexico with winds of 65 mph, according to the latest update from the US National Hurricane Center. That’s just a shade below hurricane strength. The storm is forecast to pass over a patch of abnormally warm water, providing fuel for it to blossom into a hurricane. It could peak as a Category 2 storm with winds of 110 mph as it lumbers to the northeast. The storm is expected to weaken due to those aforementioned gnarly winds shortly before it makes landfall somewhere along the Gulf Coast.
The NHC has issued hurricane watches for all the coastline in Mississippi and Alabama as well as parts of the Florida Panhandle. (Tropical storm watches extend into Louisiana as well.)
Folks in that region can expect rainfall totals of up to 7 inches, though some spots in the Panhandle could see as much as 10 inches and storm surge as high as 7 feet. Tornadoes aren’t out of the question either. In other words, it’s a storm to take seriously.
Isaias could make also (or at least tie) history as the latest first Atlantic hurricane to form on record. The current record was set in 1905, when the season’s first hurricane formed on October 8. There’s still one more update scheduled for Isaias on Wednesday, so it’s possible it could just miss out on tying that mark.
Record or not, Isaias is indicative of the hurricane season that wasn’t. This year’s Atlantic hurricane season was forecast to be below average. But it’s been even quieter than expected owing to an El Niño that’s been dubbed “super,” “Godzilla,” and “supersized.” The superlatives—which meteorologists will be quick to tell you are not official designations—are indicative of the strength of this year’s event. El Niño is measured by ocean temperatures in a part of the tropical Pacific, and this year’s iteration has seen record highs throughout the summer and first part of fall.
The intensity has had a heavy hand in rearranging the atmosphere around the world, including over the Atlantic. Saharan dust has also played a role in quieting things by making the air in one of the major areas where hurricanes develop too damn dry.
For a sense of how that has impacted the Atlantic hurricane season, we can look at some averages. From 1991 to 2020, the basin saw an average of 14 named storms, seven hurricanes, and three major hurricanes—that is, storms of Category 3 or greater—annually, according to NHC data. This year has seen eight tropical storms and one soon-to-be hurricane.
Another metric to measure the season is accumulated cyclone energy (ACE for short), which takes into account not just the number and intensity of storms but how long they stick around. The ACE to date for 2026 is 10.8 units. The average for this time of year? Nearly 102, according to data maintained by Colorado State University. Most of that energy typically accumulates from mid-August through late September.
None of this is to say there might not be another surprise storm in the coming weeks. But with El Niño continuing to intensify and the peak of the season well past, the odds of this season seeing a sudden spurt of activity are minimal at best.

NEW DELHI: Delhi police has justified its restrictions on a proposed protest by the Cockroach Janta Party at Jantar Mantar, citing past violence, alleged assaults on women constables and the need to maintain public safety. The police said the organisers were proceeding without permission and stressed that the temporary curbs were necessary to prevent overcrowding and keep the capital functioning.In a statement posted on X, the force said, "The right to protest must be protected, but so must the right of a city to function safely. Responsible policing is about balancing both."
The police cited violence during a protest in July to explain its concerns.According to the statement, permission had been granted for a one-day demonstration, but it continued for a month. More than 200 police personnel were injured, while over 2,000 people with criminal antecedents joined the protest, contributing to the violence.The police said the situation eventually spiralled out of control, leading to clashes in which students were also injured. It added that women constables had been molested and assaulted by protesters at Jantar Mantar in the past week.
Crowd management and public safety
The police also pointed to the limited capacity of Jantar Mantar, saying the site could accommodate only 1,000 people at a time. It said restrictions were needed to prevent overcrowding and protect protesters, residents, shopkeepers and others in the area.The force said Delhi Police had to balance the right to protest with the safety of residents and the capital's economic interests. It added that the city could not be brought to a halt every time a demonstration took place.According to the statement, seeking permission allows authorities to estimate crowd numbers and plan traffic diversions, emergency access and safe movement around the protest site. The police said this would help demonstrators raise their concerns while allowing residents, workers and businesses to continue with their daily activities.
Police cite legal position on unauthorised protests
The police said the Cockroach Janta Party was proceeding with its planned gathering without permission. Citing the Supreme Court's position, the statement said a protest held without permission was unlawful and participants could face prosecution.It added that organisers were responsible for explaining the legal position to those they invited to attend."The restrictions being put in place today are temporary. They are intended to regulate the flow of people, prevent overcrowding and keep protesters, residents, shopkeepers and others in the area safe," the statement read.The police said the precautions were intended to ensure that people could raise their concerns peacefully without compromising public safety or disrupting the functioning of the city.

The Supreme Court on October 5 said it had not approved any modification to the contents of Form 6, directly contradicting the Election Commission’s (EC) recent claim that it alterations made in the form were upheld by the court. Form 6 is the document used by citizens to apply for inclusion of their names in the electoral roll.
The apex court was hearing a bunch of petitions challenging the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process and seeking the suspension of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar who has come under intense scrutiny following an Indian Express report published on September 25. It showed that Kumar had overruled written objections from election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi at least on 14 occasions in 10 months. One of the points of contention was modifications to Form 6.
On September 26, the ECI issued a press note saying that the “declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR” had been upheld by the Supreme Court.
On Monday, while arguing in front of a Bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, senior advocates Menaka Guruswamy and Vikas Singh questioned the decision-making process followed by the three-member Election Commission. Guruswamy raised concerns over the use of a modified Form 6 during the SIR process.
“Let us see how the SIR was conducted in Delhi. Form 6 has two new conditions added. The modified Form 6 was circulated. The Schedule to the RPA contains Form 6. It cannot be modified in this manner,” she submitted.
In response, chief justice Surya Kant made the court’s position clear: “We have not approved Form 6. A modified Form 6 has not been approved by us. Let us be very clear.”

— Bar and Bench (@barandbench) October 5, 2026
Guruswami also noted that the supposed ‘illegality’ of the SIR process had prevented the conduct of free and fair elections in India. “We have grown up with free and fair elections in this country. They do not exist today,” she said.
The court issued notices to the central election commission, the chief election commissioner and the two other commissioners, seeking their responses. The Bench further mentioned that if any decision taken by the Election Commission was found not to be in accordance with the law, it would be annulled.
The Controversy Regarding Form 6
Form 6 is a statutory form prescribed under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, framed under Section 28 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950. This means the ECI cannot simply change the form or add new requirements whenever it wants. Any change to the statutory format has to be made through the parliament, rather than through an internal decision of the poll panel.
In states where the SIR is currently ongoing, such as Delhi and Karnataka, the online Form 6 available on the Election Commission’s website contains an additional declaration section between Sections J and K. In this section, an applicant has to state whether their name appears in the electoral roll from the previous SIR, whether their parents’ or grandparents’ names appear in that roll, or whether neither their name nor their parents’ names appear in the previous SIR electoral roll.
Although this declaration is not marked as mandatory, applicants cannot submit the online Form 6 without filling it in.
However, in states where the SIR has already been completed or has not yet started, such as West Bengal, the Form 6 link on the ECI website does not show this additional declaration.
Interestingly, if the Form 6 PDF is downloaded from the same ECI website for offline submission, there is no section asking for any SIR-related information. This means that the additional declaration appears to be present only in the online version of Form 6 being used in states where the SIR is underway.
SC’s May 2026 Bihar SIR Judgement
In a May 27, 2026 judgment on the Bihar SIR, the Supreme Court had said that the EC had some power to decide what documents it could ask voters to provide during an SIR.
On October 5, the ECI cited this to seemingly claim that the declarations added to Form 6 had been upheld by the Supreme Court. However, the SIR declarations in question added to Form 6 are different from what the Supreme Court had examined in the Bihar case. During the Bihar SIR, the ECI used a separate document called Annexure D.
The new declaration started appearing on the ECI’s online voter-registration system from July 2026.
Reacting to the controversy, Calcutta high court advocate Samim Ahammed said, “Despite being the holder of a constitutional post, the chief election commissioner’s conduct over the past few years has been arbitrary, with the Commission acting in violation of the Constitution and the laws of the land. The Commission does not have the power to legislate or make changes to a statute. The rules have to be laid before Parliament before they can be enforced. But the way in which the Commission has tried to bypass this process is extremely unfortunate for the health of our democracy.”
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi commented on X that the SC observation “established beyond doubt that Gyanesh Kumar changed Form 6 illegally and unilaterally.”
