One of the regulations that make vehicles in the US different from those in Europe or Japan is our headlight rules. They’re laid out in the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS), and changing them is—or used to be—a lengthy, laborious process, which is a major reason automotive lighting technology has lagged in the US. But the current administration says it’s time for “bolstering driver safety, slashing red tape, and embracing new technologies,” so it’s going to start a negotiated rulemaking process to rewrite the regulations to suit 2026.
“Today’s standards do not allow automakers to deploy the latest safety-improving lighting technologies, so we are bringing key experts and stakeholders together to modernize our standards and address potential causes of glare,” the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Jonathan Morrison said. “This collaborative approach will allow us to update outdated regulations, foster innovation, and keep everyone on our roads safer.”
While it is fair to be skeptical of the government’s efforts to streamline bureaucracy, it is also fair to say US headlight regulations really could use an update.
When Ars started covering cars, automakers like Audi, BMW, Mercedes, Toyota, and Volvo were trying to import adaptive headlight technology. At the time, the FMVSS only allowed for “dumb” high- and low-beams, nothing else. Meanwhile, lighting technology evolved, adopting first lasers and then LEDs with addressable pixels that can block out those that would otherwise illuminate oncoming cars.

Meta bans TikTok ads from its platforms in tit-for-tat row
It called the move 'a normal business practice.'
Meta confirmed that it has banned ads from rival platform TikTok, saying that "declining promotional services to a competitor is a normal business practice," Bloomberg reported. The news follows TikTok's own ban of Instagram and Facebook profile links and Meta ads pressuring TikTok and other social media sites to follow its lead with safety features for minors.
On Thursday, Meta placed a complete ban on ads and marketing from TikTok's US minority owner, China's ByteDance. The ban is in effect in the US, Canada, Egypt, Indonesia, Japan, Thailand and Vietnam, the company said. It also applies to third-party advertisers running TikTok-linked campaigns in those countries. "We don't have to run ads from a competitor whose goal is to pull people off our apps," Meta spokesperson Chris Sgro told Bloomberg.
In August, Meta agreed to an $18 billion settlement with US states that also forced it to implement child safety features on Facebook and Instagram. Legal experts said that could pressure the company's competitors, particularly TikTok and YouTube, to reshape their apps as well. This summer, the European regulators wrote that TikTok hasn't done enough to ensure minors' safety and that it could impose a fine of up to six percent of the platform's annual revenue.
That puts TikTok and YouTube on the back foot, with both government regulators and Meta itself pressuring them to follow Meta's child safety lead. Meta recently placed ads in major newspapers demanding similar moves from its rivals, while calling out TikTok for failing to show at several US government meetings around screen time and child safety. TikTok, now owned by a consortium of US and UAE investors (including Larry Ellison's Oracle), has so far said very little on the issue.

Omnichannel menswear brand KISAH has raised ₹35.9 Cr (about $3.7 Mn) in a Series A funding round led by Fireside Ventures at a post-money valuation of around ₹211 Cr (about $22 Mn). The startup plans to use the capital primarily to expand its retail network, while also investing in supply chain, warehousing, technology and backend infrastructure. “We are learning retail right now. We've had very good positive early signs for us. The idea is that we are using this money to create our playbooks, and then the retail expansion is something which should be funded by franchisees,” cofounder Yash Sarawagi told Inc42. Prior to this, the D2C startup had raised around ₹10 Cr from angel investors, including Sagar Daryani, founder of Wow! Momo, and Apoor Salarpuria of the Salarpuria Group. Founded in 2018 by Sarawagi, KISAH is a Kolkata-based menswear and kidswear brand. Sarawagi’s sister Yashvi Lathsarya later joined the business as its cofounder, followed by Saurav Kothari as its third cofounder. KISAH began as a marketplace-led brand before expanding its own D2C platform as well as presence in physical stores. The brand sells through marketplaces including Myntra, Amazon, AJIO and Nyka. It sells contemporary ethnic and occasion wear, targeting wedding guests and consumers beyond the traditional groom market. Its range includes kurtas and sherwanis alongside more contemporary pieces such as bomber jackets, flared trousers and sneakers. KISAH sits at the premium end of online ethnicwear but remains more affordable than traditional offline brands. Its products sell for an average of about ₹4,000 on Myntra, compared with roughly ₹1,000 for the platform’s wider ethnicwear category, according to Sarawagi. KISAH’s Offline Push KISAH began its offline expansion with a store in Kolkata’s Gariahat in 2025. The store generated around ₹45-50 Lakh in its first partial year of operations before reaching annual sales of about ₹70 Lakh, as per the cofounders. The performance encouraged KISAH to accelerate its retail expansion. It opened its first flagship store in Bengaluru’s Indiranagar in September 2025, followed by a store at Hyderabad’s Sarath City in November last year. As of now, KISAH operates a total of 12 stores across Bengaluru, Kolkata, Hyderabad, Mumbai and Visakhapatnam, among other markets. It plans to expand further in Bengaluru and test markets such as Jaipur and Visakhapatnam. The brand plans to reach around 100 stores and ₹500 Cr in revenue before expanding into broader categories. Over the next 12-18 months, it also plans to integrate its online and offline operations as it builds an omnichannel shopping experience. On the financial front, the startup claims to have clocked a revenue of ₹65 Cr in FY26 while maintaining profitability, with an EBITDA margin of around 5-6%. It expects its revenue to cross ₹100 Cr in FY27, implying growth of about 70%, with retail expected to be the main growth driver. The offline business is projected to grow four-fivefold during the year and contribute 25-30% to its overall business in FY27. As of now, D2C contributes around 20% of KISAH’s business, while marketplaces account for most of its online sales. International markets contribute around 8-10% of revenue, with the US its primary overseas market.

Global sportswear brand Adidas claims Australian label White Fox is trying to trade off its reputation by infringing its distinctive three-stripe trademark.
Adidas is suing the online fast-fashion retailer in the Federal Court for selling clothes with a four-stripe design, which it argues is deceptively similar to its classic design.
White Fox rejected repeated requests to stop selling and promoting clothing bearing the four parallel stripes, its rival claims.
During the first mention of the dispute on Friday, Adidas’s barrister Patrick Flynn SC argued the Sydney-based company had been using the stripes as a trademark for months.
He pointed to a picture of a White Fox-endorsed influencer wearing the company’s four-stripe shorts with genuine Adidas shoes as a promotion that would confuse consumers.
“There’s an intention to trade off our reputation,” Flynn said.
Adidas has held the trademark for a three-stripe design in Australia for more than 50 years and successfully sued another retailer for infringement over shoes bearing four stripes in 2013.
It meant the action filed against White Fox in September was “not uncharted territory”, Flynn noted.
“This is a pretty simple matter,” he said.
White Fox’s barrister Ed Heerey KC said the Australian company would argue the four stripes emblazoned on the label’s clothing were simply decorative rather than a trademark.
He highlighted similar items bearing the four stripes from other brands such as fast-fashion labels Princess Polly, Glassons, and Shein.
“Obviously Adidas has a reputation,” Heerey said.
“Their own slogan is that it’s the brand with three stripes. Emphasis on the three.”
The boutique will interrogate whether the use of four stripes was deceptively similar to Adidas’s trademark and whether any consumers would actually be misled.
He noted the 2013 judgment in favour of Adidas found it was common for branding to be placed on the side of shoes, but there was no such common practice for clothing.
Adidas is seeking orders that will prevent White Fox making clothing with four stripes and force it to hand over profits it made on the products.
Justice Ian Jackman – brother of one of Australia’s most famous exports Hugh Jackman – set the dispute down for a hearing in early 2027.
It marks the first high-profile litigation of this kind against White Fox Boutique, which has become a major player in the retail industry since it was launched in Sydney in 2013.
Co-founders Georgia and Daniel Contos, who own the company with Daniel’s mother Melina Maceri, focused on social media and influencer marketing to build their brand.
The online retailer later expanded to the US and UK and generated $542m in revenue in the year to June 2025.
Meanwhile Adidas, which generated a record $39.9bn in 2025, has vigilantly defended its three-stripe trademark across the globe with varying success.
The sportswear giant recently lost its trademark infringement cases against luxury brand Thom Browne in the US, UK, and Germany.
The upcoming battle in the federal court could prove to be a battleground for Adidas in a world of fast fashion and prolific imitation.

CPU makers have noticed that the seemingly unending RAM price hikes are making it tough for a lot of us to upgrade our PCs. Their solution? A return to last-gen DDR4 RAM. Intel and AMD are making new CPUs that’ll support the older, more affordable type of memory.
Decade-old RAM is making a comeback
The RAM shortage is bringing back DDR4, with new Intel and AMD CPUs for older RAM, sockets, and chipsets.
On Friday, Gigabyte announced that two of its motherboard lines will support “upcoming” processors built on Intel’s LGA 1700 socket. That socket debuted in 2021 with the 12th gen Alder Lake CPUs and supported both DDR4 RAM and the then-new DDR5 RAM. Intel dropped it for a DDR5-only approach in 2024. But according to Gigabyte, the dual format support is now being revived, with new LGA 1700 chips “expected to launch in early 2027.”
Intel did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
This backtrack stems from LGA 1700’s cross-compatibility with both kinds of RAM — an advantage over its successor that’s recently become much more important. Intel’s strategy may be to offer users the choice of a new CPU that doesn’t require them to switch to new, and very expensive, DDR5 memory, too. AMD is doing something similar: in August, Gigabyte also announced a new series of motherboards for AMD’s last-gen, DDR4-compatible AM4 platform to go along with the 10th-anniversary relaunch of the Ryzen 7 5800X3D CPU.
DDR4 started hitting the market in 2014 and has since been succeeded by the much faster DDR5. Under normal circumstances, buying new hardware to use technology that’s over a decade old would probably be a bad investment. But the RAM shortage is changing the math, with DDR4 RAM seemingly feeling the sting of price hikes much less than DDR5.
I recently saw the price disparity first-hand while shopping around for new RAM after a DDR4 kit abruptly died on me. Right now, a DDR5 32GB Corsair Vengeance RAM kit costs $620, while the corresponding DDR4 kit costs $260. Even though it’s more than 32GB of DDR4 RAM typically cost back in mid-2025, that’s more than double the price for DDR5! Of course, DDR5 has significant advantages, like higher speeds and better power efficiency. But those perks might not be worth the current price of admission.
It could be years before prices drop again, a reality that’s starting to really sink in with the official return of older sockets and chipsets. But at least it’s a good time to hang onto your DDR4 RAM.

World Mental Health Day, October 10, 2026; this year’s theme—“Lived experiences heard: real voices, real change”—deserves more than an awareness programme, a poster or a social media message. It asks an uncomfortable question: we talk a lot about mental health in Kashmir, but have we really taken the time to listen to those who live it?
Mental health has become increasingly visible in public discourse. Schools, colleges and healthcare institutions organise awareness programmes, and professionals speak about depression, anxiety, suicide prevention and substance use. That is welcome. But awareness and understanding are not the same. We may know what depression is and still judge the person who suffers from it. We may discuss anxiety and tell an anxious student to “just be confident”. We may call addiction a disease and still look at a person recovering from substance use with suspicion. Somewhere between awareness and acceptance lies the human being whose voice often remains unheard.
As psychiatrists, we meet patients every day. Each arrives with a diagnosis, perhaps a prescription and perhaps a family member beside them. But behind every diagnosis is a story. Patients need medicines, but they also need to be heard, understood and involved in decisions about their care. A young person with examination anxiety is not merely an “anxiety case”; a person with depression is not merely a “depressive patient”; a person struggling with addiction is not merely an “addict”. There are dreams, fears, relationships, disappointments, expectations and circumstances. Sometimes, listening to that story is itself therapeutic.
A young student once came to us after three difficult attempts at the NEET examination. She had worked hard, had the academic ability and wanted to become a doctor, but performance anxiety became overwhelming. She missed the qualifying mark by only a few marks. Three attempts can make a young person question intelligence, worth and future. Eventually, she found the courage to seek psychiatric help—a difficult step in a setting where stigma remains strong. She received a simple, focused intervention, including medication for a limited period around the examination, with support and reassurance. Sometimes a small intervention at the right time can prevent a young person from losing faith in herself.
Recently, she returned to the same hospital—not as a patient, but as a young aspiring doctor who had qualified NEET and secured admission in the very hospital where she had once sought help. The hospital that had witnessed her anxiety was now witnessing her achievement. Her story reminds us what can happen when judgement is replaced with understanding. Instead of “Study harder”, “Everyone gets nervous” or “Just be positive”, she was heard—and that listening became part of her journey towards change.
We encountered another story: a school-going boy battling depression whose illness was being dismissed as “drama”. His family interpreted his difficulties as an attempt to escape studies, while he was actually struggling under the weight of illness. He did not need another lecture; he needed somebody to say, “We believe that you are struggling.” A child’s suffering does not become less real because adults cannot immediately understand it.
Another young woman presented after a suicidal act. When asked why she had reached that point, her answer was painfully simple: “Doctor, nobody listened to me.” Her anger and behaviour had been noticed, but had anyone stopped to ask where that anger was coming from? We are often quick to call someone “difficult”, “attention-seeking”, “dramatic” or “angry”. Yet behaviour may be the visible surface of an invisible struggle. If we only judge behaviour, we may miss the pain beneath it.
Another young woman with severe depression and recurrent suicidal thoughts had made multiple attempts at self-harm. Despite treatment, improvement was minimal. We sat with her for a one-to-one conversation—not simply about symptoms, but about her life. She spoke of parental disputes, marital difficulties, allegations of extramarital relationships within the family and emotional turmoil that had never found a safe space for expression. Perhaps these circumstances could not be changed overnight, but something changed when she was finally able to speak. This is why listening matters. A patient is not merely a diagnosis that needs to improve; the person’s circumstances need to be understood. When patients participate in treatment decisions, we understand not only what treatment we want to give, but what treatment they are able and willing to live with.
Think of a person with OCD. Repeated checking, washing or reassurance-seeking may appear strange or amusing from outside, but inside is a relentless battle with intrusive thoughts and anxiety. A person with depression may experience what Winston Churchill described as his “black dog”. A person with psychosis may hear voices or hold beliefs others cannot understand. A person with bipolar disorder may move between extremes of mood, energy and functioning. From outside, we see behaviour; from inside, they are fighting a battle. All of them have stories to tell.
Mental-health care is not always confined to a prescription pad. Sometimes a song, ghazal or poem can help connect with feelings that are difficult to express in ordinary conversation. Recently, we suggested a song to a patient struggling with suicidal thoughts. The song, from Aakhir Kyun, carries a message of hope:
Aik andhera, laakh sitare
Aik nirasha, laakh saharay
Sab se badi sogaat hai jeevan
Nadaan hai jo jeevan se haaray
The song continues:
Beete hue kal ki khaatir
Tu aane wala kal mat khona
Jaane kaun kahan se aakar
Raahen teri phir se sawaaray
Sometimes words reach places where clinical language cannot. A patient may not remember everything about neurotransmitters or diagnostic criteria, but may remember a sentence, a poem, a song—or simply the feeling that someone sat beside them and understood. Perhaps that too is part of healing.
There is a paradox in Kashmir today. We speak about mental health more than before, yet stigma has not disappeared. We organise programmes, but how often do we invite people with lived experience to tell us what they actually went through? How often do we ask students what academic pressure feels like, people recovering from substance use what makes returning to society difficult, or families what prevents them from seeking help? And most importantly, how often do we change something after listening?
Awareness tells us that depression is an illness; listening tells us what depression feels like. Awareness tells us examination anxiety exists; listening tells us what happens inside the mind of a student who cannot perform despite years of preparation. Awareness tells us addiction is a disorder; listening tells us about loneliness, stigma, family conflict and social exclusion during recovery. We need both awareness and listening—but listening is where empathy begins.
“Lived experiences heard” should not mean merely giving patients an opportunity to speak. Their experiences should influence what we do next. If students describe overwhelming academic pressure, institutions need better psychological support. If stigma prevents treatment, services need to become more approachable. If people recovering from substance use say society refuses them a second chance, rehabilitation must include social reintegration. If families do not know where to seek help, services must become more visible and accessible. Listening without action can become another form of tokenism. The second half of the theme therefore matters just as much: Real voices. Real change.
Mental healthcare has increasingly moved beyond asking only, “What is wrong with you?” We must also ask, “What happened to you?” The first question looks for a disorder; the second seeks a story. And mental health is often inseparable from that story—examination pressure, grief, unemployment, family conflict, trauma, substance use, loneliness, or simply the feeling that something is wrong without having words to explain it.
The young woman who returned after qualifying NEET reminds us that psychiatric care can help someone reclaim a dream. The depressed schoolboy needs someone to believe his suffering is real. The young woman who said, “Nobody listened to me,” reminds us that anger may have a story behind it. The girl who had so much to say reminds us that a conversation can uncover what months of treatment could not. The person with OCD is fighting thoughts we cannot see; the person with depression is fighting a darkness we may not understand; the person with psychosis may be living in a frightening reality; and the person with bipolar disorder may be fighting battles that change with mood. They all have voices. They all have stories.
So, this October 10, perhaps we should do something simple. Let us hear them—not merely to complete an awareness campaign or fulfil a theme, but to understand, involve and change. The success of mental-health awareness should not be measured only by seminars conducted or posters displayed, but by how many people felt safe enough to speak, how many felt genuinely heard, and how many lives became a little different because somebody listened.
Let patients tell us what the problem feels like. Let their experiences inform our solutions. Let their voices influence our policies. Because the person living with an illness often knows something about it that textbooks cannot teach.
Listen to them. Believe them. Include them. Act on what they tell us. Let their voices be heard. Let their experiences shape our care. Let real voices bring real change.
Dr Mansoor Ahmed, Professor, Department of Psychiatry, GMC Anantnag
Dr Mohammad Younis, Resident Doctor, GMC Anantnag

FBI agents could soon get a new training course - from athletes in one of the president’s favorite sports.
Director Kash Patel has launched a bid to bring in Dana White’s UFC trainers to teach special agents mixed martial arts techniques, according to a report.
Patel, who attended President Donald Trump’s UFC birthday bash at the White House, is now seeking a one-year “sole source” contract with the UFC to provide a training program for agents in “defense tactical techniques,” according to an agency document released in September.
“The purpose of the training is to enhance physical combat abilities, mental toughness, and tactical awareness, which are crucial for special agents in high-risk situations,” the document, which was first reported by MS NOW, read. It’s unclear how much the contract is worth, as the estimated figure was redacted.
White is the president of the UFC and a longtime friend of Trump. The president has attended numerous UFC matches throughout the years, and even brought the Octagon to the White House South Lawn in June to celebrate America’s 250th birthday — and his 80th birthday. Patel is also a fan of the sport and has been seen at events.
The FBI said the UFC was “uniquely qualified” to conduct the training in its document, noting the trainers’ skills in “striking techniques, grappling/takedowns, weapon defense, ground control, as well as conditioning to the standard that the FBI expects and requires.”
The proposed deal would bypass the bidding process required for federal contracts, something the Trump administration has done in the past.
During the botched renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, the National Park Service awarded Greenwater Services, an Ohio-based firm with ties to a Trump donor, a $1.7 million no-bid contract to install a water-purification system, The New York Times reported in June. Days after the project was complete, the basin turned green from algae blooms.
The FBI said in the newly revealed document that the proposed contract’s one-year term “will allow for more market research to be conducted and allow for vendors to become more equipped to handle this requirement.
“The long-term contract that will be created in the future will be done so on a competitive basis.”
The Independent has reached out to the FBI for comment on the proposed deal.
This would not be the first time the FBI worked with the UFC.
The UFC announced in early March that its current and former athletes would visit Quantico that week to host a two-day training seminar for FBI Special Agent Academy students and senior FBI staff from around the world.
“This is a tremendous opportunity for our FBI agents to learn and train with some of the greatest athletes on earth - helping the world’s premier law enforcement agency be even better prepared to protect the American people,” Patel said in a statement at the time.
“Dana White has changed the game in the mixed martial arts industry and we’re extremely honored to be partnered with him, the professionals, and the UFC. We are grateful for their shared love of our nation, so that we can better defend her.”

Let’s Encrypt is continuing a push toward tighter security by reducing free SSL/TLS certificate lifetimes from 90 days to 64 days, starting February 10, 2027. For administrators already implementing modern ACME clients that support ARI (ACME Renewal Information), the change should be seamless. For those still relying on hardcoded renewal schedules or manual processes, February will be the deadline to update before certificates start expiring unexpectedly.
Starting on October 14, Let’s Encrypt will begin testing the 64-day certificates, and interested users can opt in to test their setups before production goes live.
Prior to Let’s Encrypt’s launch in early 2016, certificates were often issued for as long as one to three years. The service started with 90-day certificates to force renewal automation that didn’t previously exist. Shorter certificate validity periods limited vulnerabilities from private key thefts and encouraged accelerated HTTPS adoption across the web.
This move shook industry norms at the time, but by limiting the certificate lifetime, the certs are less likely to cause damage if compromised or assigned in error. The move down to 64 days continues this logic, and the lifespans will only continue to get shorter as time goes on, with 45-day defaults planned to follow in 2028.
Just as the initial rollout of Let’s Encrypt aimed to push users toward HTTPS, the shortened certificate windows are aimed at moving users to full ACME automation. The ACME protocol, and, more specifically, ARI (ACME Renewal Information), allows the certificate authority to tell the client when it’s time to renew. Although ARI does this, many deployments are still stuck on scripted update intervals that trigger at fixed offsets like “60 days before expiration.”
I'm positive that Let's Encrypt was fully on board with this change (after all, they pioneered the exact kind of automation which will make this easy to achieve), but they are reducing down to 47 days, because that is the maximum validity that Browsers will soon allow for a CA issued certificate.

A beautiful Himalayan bird is changing its voice due to human activity, research shows
- Published
A sharp increase in human activity is having an impact on the way a Himalayan bird lives and communicates, two studies by Indian researchers have found.
The monal, a pheasant native to Himalayan mountain forests, is deeply woven into the region's cultural, folklore and identity. The eye-catching monal - the male has distinctive green, blue and copper feathers - is the state bird of India's Uttarakhand state and the national bird of Nepal, reflecting its cultural significance across the Himalayas.
But studies show that infrastructure development and tourism are squeezing its habitat, while increasing noise is altering how it communicates with potential mates and rivals.
Researchers from Uttarakhand conducted two separate studies over five years which flagged key threats to the bird.
One study found that the birds are forced to move higher in the mountains as their natural habitat in the alpine meadows above the tree line get crowded. The other says the monal is changing its pitch to cut through human noise in a busy valley.
"These two studies give a useful warning for other more vulnerable species - if the monal is forced to change both its voice and its address, how are the more sensitive species responding?" says Vishal Singh, an environmental practitioner working on ecology and climate issues in the Himalayas.
Dr Rajeev Lochan, lead researcher of both studies, told the BBC that they chose to study the monal as the bird has a narrow habitat range - it moves seasonally between the lower montane zone - an ecological belt found on the lower slopes of the mountains - and high-elevation alpine zones. This, he says, makes it a key indicator of ecosystem health in the north-western Himalayas.
"If the species is facing issues on this particular landscape, there might be a chance that the ecological disturbances are affecting other birds too," said Lochan.
The monal, researchers say, can be seen as a stand-in for the health of a fragile Himalayan ecosystem pushed to a tipping point due to unregulated tourism and heavy urbanisation.
While the region has always drawn tourists, trekkers and researchers given its scenic landscape and biodiversity, rapid infrastructure expansion in the past decade has made more places accessible, increasing footfall and disrupting the wildlife. This, coupled with mounting human pressures, suggests that climate change is emerging as another major threat to the region's already vulnerable biodiversity.
"There are a lot of factors at play but at a broader level, the problem is that the economic development of the region is not aligned to its ecological integrity," Singh said.
According to the first study, climate change is projected to continue shrinking and destabilising the Himalayan monal's habitat across the Indian Himalayas through 2100 under multiple climate scenarios.
Currently, the birds are found in alpine meadows, located high in the mountains above the forests, which form some of the Himalayas' most important seasonal grazing and biodiversity-rich habitats.
The researchers modelled how climate change could shift the monal's suitable habitat across the Indian Himalayan region in the states of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh. It was based on the kind of global climate models and emissions scenarios used for assessments by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the UN's climate science unit.
"These birds are now slowly moving upwards in the Himalayas as the snow is melting and vegetation is growing, making the area accessible to them. They are anyway being pushed upwards as their natural habitats in alpine meadows are being encroached upon by humans," Lochan said.
The model assumes that the bird needs the current climate set-up that exists in alpine meadows in the future too, a reasonable but not certain assumption.
The birds' seasonal migration may become increasingly difficult as changes in climate may force them to move to higher elevations on hills, to smaller and fragmented areas. Their population would be scattered in disconnected pockets, which reduces chances of breeding between groups and increases their risks of long-term decline or local extinction, which is already a threat, the study says.
The second study, also conducted by Lochan, Dinesh Kumar Sharma and Anand Kumar, who work at the Hemvati Nandan Bahuguna Garhwal University, focuses on the bird's behavioural changes. They conducted the study in two valleys in Kedarnath Musk Deer Sanctuary in Uttarakhand - at Chopta, a tourist spot with busy traffic and visitors, and the largely quiet Madmaheshwar.
They recorded more than 700 monal calls across both sites using microphones and passive recording devices and then measured pitch, call length and background noise levels for a year from April 2023.
Birds in noisy environments consistently produced calls with significantly higher peak frequencies compared with those in quieter habitats, the study said.
The researchers found subtle changes in the monal's pitch that could be picked up by recording devices but might go unnoticed by the human ear.
"This does not mean that the species has undergone a permanent or evolutionary change in its vocal frequency; rather, our findings suggest behavioural flexibility in response to different acoustic environments," Lochan said.
Compared with the birds in Madmaheshwar valley, the monal in Chopta also produced shorter call durations likely to cut through low-frequency human noise from traffic and tourist footfall.
Bird calls are one of the most sophisticated forms of sound-based communication in the natural world, and significant changes can interfere with, among other things, their mating success.
"When a species must raise its pitch to be heard over tourist traffic, or climb higher as meadows turn crowded, it reveals how human pressure is rewriting the rules of life in the Himalaya," says Anjal Prakash, a public policy professor at FLAME University and contributor to IPCC reports.
Lochan says he and his team consider this a preliminary study and hope to expand the scope and depth of it.
The research comes with the caveat that it is not conclusive on ecological consequences, and more research is needed. But together, the two studies signal broader ecological stress across the Himalayas.
"In listening to the monal, we hear the Himalayas asking for space, silence and care," says Prakash.

The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) may introduce its proposed insurance commission caps as early as January 2027, amid opposition from brokers over potential revenue losses and job cuts. The regulator is considering January 1 and April 1, 2027 as possible implementation dates for its distribution reforms, Girija Subramanian, whole-time member (distribution) at IRDAI, told Bloomberg in an interview. The proposals seek to curb distribution costs through product-wise commission caps and tighter limits on insurers’ overall expenses. IRDAI has argued that commissions have risen faster than premiums since rules were relaxed in 2023, without a corresponding increase in insurance coverage. Subramanian said commission caps should take effect sooner, arguing that phased reductions could encourage distributors to rush sales and increase the risk of mis-selling. Separately, IRDAI’s consultation paper proposes a five-year transition to lower expense limits for insurers, with the first interim milestone in FY29. “There is an earlier-the-better case, but getting the reforms right is more important than getting them early,” she told Bloomberg. The proposals have implications for listed insurance distributors such as Policybazaar parent PB Fintech and Turtlemint, whose businesses depend on commissions from insurance sales. Shares of PB Fintech and Turtlemint have slumped over 47% each since IRDAI proposed the commission caps on September 23. However, the framework is still under consultation. Stakeholders have until October 25 to submit comments, after which IRDAI will review the feedback and publish draft regulations for another round of consultation before issuing the final rules. Brokers Flag Revenue, Employment Risks The Insurance Brokers Association of India (IBAI) has warned that the proposed norms could cut broking sector revenues by 60–70% and result in the loss of up to 10 Lakh jobs across insurance distribution. At a press briefing, the association’s representatives said the distribution sector employs more than 83 Lakh people. While supporting IRDAI’s objective of making insurance more affordable and accessible, they argued that the proposed changes threaten small businesses and MSMEs. The resulting job losses could affect insurance awareness, policy renewals, assistance to policyholders, and insurance penetration among underserved communities, they added. The association has sought an extension of the feedback deadline to December-end from October 25 and submitted letters to the Prime Minister’s Office and the finance ministry. The IBAI also disputed IRDAI’s interpretation of data showing that general insurance premiums sourced through brokers grew 37%, while commission payouts rose 173%. It argued that the increase in commissions since FY23 largely reflected the reclassification of previously off-book marketing expenses following regularisation, rather than inflationary pressures on insurance consumers. The association claimed that general insurers’ operating expenses averaged around 26.5% of gross premiums, below the mandated 30% limit. It also said policyholders received ₹84.4 in non-life insurance claim payouts for every ₹100 of premiums paid over five years, compared with a global average of 72–75%. The representatives said the association was ready to work with IRDAI to address specific market anomalies, including mis-selling and disproportionate remuneration. IRDAI Backs Wider Distribution IRDAI, meanwhile, has pointed to rising expenses at private insurers. Expenses at private life insurers increased to about 22% of total premiums from 16% in FY21, while those at private general insurers rose to roughly 32% from 25% in FY19. Additional rewards have also pushed distributor remuneration 30–60% above base commissions in some cases. Subramanian rejected concerns over large-scale job losses, arguing that the reforms would create employment by widening the distribution network and lowering entry barriers. To encourage expansion beyond major cities, IRDAI has proposed allowing distributors to earn an additional 10% of the applicable commission limit on business generated in towns with populations below 10 Lakh. This would rise to 20% for areas with fewer than 50,000 residents. Other proposals include allowing distributors to undertake financial and non-financial activities beyond insurance.

US says China's maritime actions off Taiwan 'deeply destabilising'
"By asserting authorities around maritime areas that Taiwan has peacefully administered for over 70 years, China only exacerbates tensions and undermines the peaceful resolution of issues that it claims to seek," a US State Department spokesperson said.
TAIPEI: China's maritime actions off Taiwan's east coast are "deeply destabilising" and only worsen tension, the US State Department said, after Reuters reported the first known sighting of a Chinese militia boat in those waters in August.
China, which views Taiwan as its own territory, has stepped up activity off the island's east coast since June with regular coast guard patrols.
Officials in Taiwan, which rejects Beijing's sovereignty claims, say they believe China is practicing for a possible maritime blockade using overlapping military, paramilitary and civilian assets.
Taipei regards the area off its east coast as critical to wartime supply routes from allies in the event of a blockade or conflict.
The United States remains concerned by China's activity east of Taiwan, a State Department spokesperson said, responding to a question on the sighting of the militia boat.
"China's actions are deeply destabilising," the spokesperson added.
"By asserting authorities around maritime areas that Taiwan has peacefully administered for over 70 years, China only exacerbates tensions and undermines the peaceful resolution of issues that it claims to seek."
The US urges Beijing to cease its pressure against Taiwan and instead engage in "meaningful dialogue with Taiwan's democratically elected authorities", the spokesperson added.
China's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. China recognises no claims of sovereignty by Taiwan, including over waters surrounding it.
The US is Taiwan's most important international backer, though President Donald Trump has yet to approve a new US$14 billion arms sale package for the island.
Taiwan's Coast Guard said in a statement about the militia boat and its accompanying vessels that their activities were all located outside of "restricted waters".
In a practice dating to the 1950s, China's maritime militia, more commonly seen around South China Sea flashpoints, consists of fishing vessels whose crews receive training and support to operate in disputed waters, often alongside coast guard ships.
In June, Britain, France, Germany and the US, all expressed concern over Chinese activities off Taiwan's east coast as a threat to regional stability and freedom of navigation.

Newcastle University is facing a backlash from conservationists over the appointment of the heir to an Indian oil and gas fortune who runs a controversial mega-zoo as a professor of sustainability.
The university announced that Anant Ambani had been given a professorship of practice for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship” and “significant contributions to advancing a more sustainable future”.
Ambani is the son of India’s richest person, Mukesh Ambani, who made his fortune primarily in oil and gas, owns the world’s largest oil refinery and has close ties with the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Mukesh Ambani has enthusiastically praised BJP policies, and firms linked to his Reliance conglomerate have recently made significant donations to the party. The prime minister, Narendra Modi, attended Anant Ambani’s lavish 2024 wedding in Mumbai.
Anant Amabani, 31, who is leads on renewable energy on the Reliance Group’s executive board and is worth an estimated £90bn, has set up Vantara, a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo near the family’s oil refining facilities in Gujarat, which reportedly has more than 150,000 animals including 200 lions, 250 leopards and 900 crocodiles, and where he hosted his opulent pre-wedding celebrations attended by celebrity guests and politicians.
Conservation groups have previously raised questions about how some of the animals were sourced, given many were endangered species. Vantara has never been found guilty of any wrongdoing.
The university’s announcement was met with incredulity and derision from academic staff and Indian and international conservationists and environmentalists.
Ramachandra Guha, a leading Indian public intellectual and the author of the book Speaking With Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism, said: “I must say that it is a rather mystifying choice. As a scholar of Indian and global environmentalism, I can name at least 50 – perhaps 100 – individuals who are far better qualified to be thus honoured. They include soil scientists, energy scientists, water conservation experts, community forest workers, ecologists, pollution abatement experts etc who have made real and tangible contributions to a more sustainable future for India and Indians.
“I wonder on whose advice Newcastle University has acted, and whether it did due diligence on what has and has not been done in these fields. Its appointment of Mr Ambani is puzzling in the extreme, and is likely to adversely affect the university’s institutional credibility and intellectual standing.”
Bhuvan Mangalore, an Indian investigator into illegal wildlife trade who is completing a dissertation on Vantara at Anglia Ruskin University, asked: “Is this a joke?”
Prof Matt Perry, the chair of the University and College Union branch at Newcastle University, said staff members had objected to the appointment citing environmental concerns.
Prof Lyla Mehta, the head of the climate, environment and sustainability department at the University of Sussex’s Institute of Development Studies, shared concerns that “as public funding for universities falls, there is a real danger that billionaire and corporate money begins to shape academia”.
She said: “Universities are supposed to be places that question power and hold corporations to account, not give them academic legitimacy.”
In April, Anant Ambani launched Vantara University, billed as the world’s first global university dedicated to wildlife conservation and veterinary science.
Lorne Stockman, a research co-director at Oil Change International, said: “At a time when the climate crisis demands an urgent phaseout of oil and gas, we must demand our publicly funded institutions do better.”
In 2025, an investigation by the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung found that many animals delivered to Vantara arrived through countries with opaque wildlife trading networks such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the United Arab Emirates, raising concerns that endangered species may have been illegally trafficked.
In August last year, an investigation by India’s supreme court, which lasted less than three weeks, cleared the zoo’s operators of any wrongdoing. A subsequent fact-finding mission into the zoo by Cites, the UN body that regulates the trade of endangered species, found that some of the permits used to bring animals to Vantara were probably forged.
Its report said: “There is a need for caution to ensure that imports of large numbers of animals by these facilities are not inadvertently creating a demand for illegally sourced animals.”
Cites recommended restrictions on India’s imports of endangered wild animals. However, it subsequently reversed its decision after objections from India, the US and Japan at a Cites meeting after they argued there was not enough proof of illegal imports.
In August, the zoo launched a “reset” in its operations by appointing a former Cites head to oversee its operations and said it would voluntarily pause all wildlife imports until June next year.
Vantara has declined to comment. The Ambani family and Vantara have previously denied the allegations of wildlife trafficking. They have said: “Our mission and focus continues to be the rescue, rehabilitation and care of animals.”
A Newcastle University spokesperson said: “The award of a professorship of practice recognises Mr Ambani’s contributions to conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship through his work with Vantara, a wildlife rescue and conservation initiative, and as the executive lead for the Reliance Group’s transition toward a green energy future.”

America’s good hurricane luck is about to run out
Hurricane Isaias is almost here. Are we ready?
The first hurricane of the fall season is expected to strike the Gulf Coast overnight, marking the latest onset of hurricane season in living memory. As of early Friday afternoon, Hurricane Isaias had grown to a Category 3 storm, with sustained winds of 120 miles per hour. It will strike along the shores of the Florida Panhandle, Alabama, and Mississippi, posing a threat to life and property for millions of Americans. Weather forecasters anticipate between 8 and 12 inches of rain in the areas near where the storm makes landfall.
Isaias’s imminent arrival signals the end of a period of unusual good luck when it comes to hurricanes striking the United States. Last year, no hurricanes reached the US mainland at all. And this year, Isaias is breaking a more than 100-year-old record: October 9 is the latest date since 1905 for the first Atlantic hurricane of the season to take shape. August and September have historically been the busiest periods of hurricane season.
Not lately, though. It’s a strange recent phenomenon, and it’s been even more fortuitous than it would ordinarily be. That’s because the Trump administration has slashed weather forecasting and emergency relief funding over the past two years, leaving us less prepared for a disaster.
And now our luck seems to be running out — with even more rough weather on the way.
Hurricane season may be quieter than usual — but El Niño is on the way
Here’s the secret ingredient that’s pushed off hurricanes even as warming planetary temperatures raise concerns about more extreme weather events: El Niño. This notorious shift in global wind patterns, which occurs every two to seven years, moves warm water around the oceans, disrupting traditional weather patterns and leading to intense rain and sometimes disastrous flooding, as well as droughts. If there is an upside, however, it’s that this temporary change in ocean conditions prevents hurricanes from forming as frequently as they otherwise would.
The downside is, well, El Niño is still on its way. Forecasters expect this year’s version to be historically bad — using words like “super” or “Godzilla” to describe it. The worst of the bad weather is projected to arrive in December: The southern half of the continental US is expected to see unusually rainy and stormy weather, while areas of the Great Lakes and Pacific Northwest could see extreme dry spells.
It will also serve as a crucial test of our reduced capacity for predicting and responding to disasters. Trump’s “big beautiful bill” cut funding for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s weather forecasting and public alert programs by $200 million, and 17 percent of FEMA’s workforce left the agency in 2025 amid the administration’s DOGE purge.
For now, if you’re in the danger zone for Isaias, please pay attention to local and national weather alerts this weekend. If you’re not, count yourself lucky — but there are storm clouds on the horizon.

Passengers stranded in Jammu, Katra as 4 trains cancelled ahead of CJP protests
More than 250 trains were cancelled ahead of the CJP's October 10 protest in Delhi, leaving passengers stranded at Jammu and Katra railway stations with little prior notice
Passengers travelling from Jammu and Katra to different parts of the country faced major disruption on Friday after four trains were cancelled at short notice. The cancellations were linked to anticipated congestion around New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin railway stations ahead of the Cockroach Janta Party's October 10 protest seeking the removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
The Railway Board cancelled more than 250 trains connected to New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin stations, affecting services across the country. In Jammu and Katra, passengers were left stranded at stations with luggage, with many saying they had learnt about the cancellations only after arriving for their journeys.
According to officials, the cancellations covered passenger trains scheduled to leave their originating stations after 2 pm on October 9, as well as those due to arrive at New Delhi or Hazrat Nizamuddin between 4 am and 2 pm on October 10. Trains scheduled to depart from these two stations for other destinations, along with local trains, were also cancelled.
The Jammu railway division said it had made special arrangements to help passengers. A spokesperson said help desks had been set up at major stations, including Jammu Tawi, Katra, Kathua and Pathankot Cantt, and extra staff had been deployed to manage crowds, assist passengers and run special refund counters.
The spokesperson said passenger information was being shared through bulk SMS, public announcements, display boards and social media. He added that the Railway Protection Force and Government Railway Police had also been deployed and a dedicated helpline had been activated.
At Jammu Tawi and Katra railway stations, scores of passengers were seen waiting for updates and trying to find alternative transport. Several said they had booked tickets two to three months in advance but received no prior notice before reaching the station.
"We booked our tickets two months ago, and our train was scheduled for today. However, we learnt just half an hour to an hour before departure that it had been cancelled. We have to reach Delhi, but no alternative arrangements are available. We are travelling with our family and are extremely troubled and worried," said Narinder Singh, a passenger from West Bengal.
He questioned why passengers had not been informed in advance and said they had approached the administration for help. "Many people are facing the same problem. Somehow, everyone has to reach Delhi. We are stranded at Katra railway station and are waiting to see what arrangements can be made," he said.
At Katra railway station, Raj, a visitor from Dehradun, said he and his companions had booked their tickets two months earlier and were to travel to Delhi before going on to Dehradun. He said the cancellation had disrupted their itinerary, forcing them to look for alternative transport and extend their stay in Katra.
Raghav Kumar, a passenger from Sitamarhi in Bihar, said he had completed his pilgrimage to the Shri Mata Vaishno Devi shrine and came to know about the cancellation of his return train only after reaching the railway station. He said he had booked his ticket online nearly three months ago.
"I am facing a lot of difficulties. I do not know where I will have to stay tonight or what problems I may face. I need help to reach home," he said, appealing to the government and railway authorities to arrange alternative transport or provide financial assistance for the journey.
In Jammu, another passenger, Narinder Singh, said the disruption had created chaos for people trying to reach their destinations. "Look at how much chaos has been created here. People are facing difficulties, and everyone is stranded. Those who need to reach their respective destinations are stuck here," he said.
Sunita, a passenger from Mumbai, also expressed displeasure over the cancellations and said the disruption had caused considerable hardship to passengers travelling with their families.
Officials advised passengers to plan their journeys accordingly and seek assistance through railway helpline 139 or the National Train Enquiry System app. The cancellations left many passengers in Jammu and Katra stranded, even as railway authorities said support measures had been put in place to help them.

Women account for 43% of the workforce in India’s Ayush services sector, with their representation crossing 50% in several organised segments, including hospitals, day-care centres, educational institutions and wellness establishments, according to a new assessment of the sector released by the Central government on Thursday (October 8, 2026).
The Ayush Services Sector Report, prepared by the Research and Information System for Developing Countries (RIS) and released on Ayurveda Day 2026, estimates that the sector supports 1.76 million livelihoods across healthcare, wellness, education and allied services.
Women’s representation is highest in spas and wellness resorts, where it exceeds 60%, followed by educational institutions at 58%, day-care centres at 57% and hospitals at 53%, says the report.
The findings come as the Ayush services economy expands beyond traditional clinical practice into wellness, education, preventive health and medical value travel.
16.91% growth
The sector, comprising Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy, was estimated at $36.92 billion in 2024-25. It has registered a compound annual growth rate of 16.91% since 2022-23.
Standalone clinics remain the largest segment, generating an estimated $16.21 billion, or 43.9% of the sector’s revenue. Day-care centres contribute another $10.13 billion. Together, the two segments account for more than 70% of the sector’s revenue.
“More than one million livelihoods are concentrated in local and standalone clinics, underlining the sector’s employment footprint across urban and rural areas,’’ says the report.
The wellness segment has recorded a 21.29% compound annual growth rate, while yoga centres registered about 75% growth in revenue over two years, according to the assessment.
Ayurveda remains the largest individual Ayush system, accounting for $17.73 billion, or about 48% of the total services revenue.
The sector is also gaining a foothold in medical value travel. Ayush-related medical value travel generated an estimated $1.77 billion in 2024-25. Although international patients account for only around 5% of patient volumes, they contribute an estimated 15-25% of hospital-segment revenue, with therapeutic programmes typically involving stays of five to 11 days.
The assessment projects that the Ayush services economy could expand to between $216 billion and $318 billion by 2047.
Job opportunities
Union Minister of State for Ayush Prataprao Jadhav said the sector’s expansion was creating employment opportunities across healthcare, wellness, education and allied services, while also opening avenues for entrepreneurship and women’s participation.
The report projects further employment opportunities in healthcare delivery, wellness, education, medical travel, research, digital health and allied services as the sector expands.

Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky criticises 'gift to Putin'
- Published
US President Donald Trump says he has reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin allowing Moscow to "immediately release" diesel to the US and globally.
Trump said the proposed release of hundreds of thousands of tonnes of Russian diesel, in tranches, would see prices "COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!".
It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April 2027 as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.
Ukraine's president criticised the decision, saying any easing of sanctions on Russia played into Moscow's hands and would prolong the war between the two countries.
Trump said Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another million after that.
He added that a further three million tonnes of Russian diesel would be delivered "within a short period" after, dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have seen attacks by Ukraine.
Putin later said Russia was willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products, but his statement did not specify amounts.
The BBC has asked the White House for clarity on what Russia will get from the US in return for the commitment.
Friday's announcement is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US, as he has spent months grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which began in February, and its impact on global energy prices.
That conflict has sent the cost of petrol and, in particular diesel, skyrocketing in America in recent months, which has soured his standing with the public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation.
The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.
Shortly after Trump's announcement, the US Treasury formally issued a temporary licence allowing Russian diesel into the market.
Putin said in a statement that he had spoken to Trump about the global energy situation on Friday, adding: "The Russian side confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large."
An envoy for Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, welcomed the deal on social media, saying: "Russia-US co-operation on diesel and energy will benefit the world."
But Zelensky hit out at it, saying "gifts to Putin will not work for peace" and that Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror".
"Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on social media.
Russia has this year experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, and introduced a ban on diesel exports.
According to the International Energy Agency, its diesel production is estimated to have fallen by nearly 30%.
Trump has expressed his displeasure over those attacks, blaming them for rising fuel prices.
But Zelensky defended the strikes on Friday, saying there were in response to "Russia's years-long campaign of terror against Ukraine's energy sector".
"Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure," he said.
- Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work? 
  - Published3 hours ago
Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information and the details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return is unclear.
But the announced deal represents a remarkable about-face, as the US Congress recently enacted legislation - signed by the president - to authorise new American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.
The agreement with Russia also opens Trump up to criticism from European allies and pro-Ukraine politicians in the US, that the American president is now helping to fund Moscow's war machine.
What impact the deal with Russia will have on fuel prices also remains unclear. The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent, remains above $103 a barrel. Before the war with Iran, Brent crude was trading at about $73 a barrel.
With the looming US midterm congressional elections - which will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress - Trump has been searching for ways to ease his Republican party's political pain.
Earlier this week, he said he was "thinking about" suspending the federal tax on gasoline and also announced that he would allow so-called red dye diesel to be used on US highways without facing federal tax.
Trump has also successfully pressured G7 nations into releasing 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from stockpiles to help ease supply concerns, and previously supported calls for a ban on diesel exports from the US.

The Confederation of African Football (CAF) is reconsidering its decision to stage the Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) every four years, with president Patrice Motsepe indicating that a return to the biennial format remains a possibility.
Motsepe, who announced last December that AFCON would switch to a four-year cycle from 2028, said discussions at CAF’s three-day strategy conference in Cape Verde had prompted a fresh review of the competition’s future.
The original decision attracted criticism from those who believed the revised schedule prioritised European football interests and FIFA’s international calendar over African football.
However, Motsepe dismissed suggestions that CAF was acting under pressure from FIFA or UEFA, calling the allegations “nonsense, absolute rubbish”.
The South African businessman insisted that protecting and promoting African football remained his foremost responsibility.

He confirmed that CAF had been examining several possibilities, including restoring AFCON’s traditional two-year cycle, although no final decision has been announced.
Motsepe, who is also a FIFA vice-president, spoke a day after CAF reiterated its unanimous support for FIFA president Gianni Infantino, who highlighted the governing body’s investments in African football during his decade in office.
The CAF president also addressed concerns surrounding the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations, reaffirming that Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda would host the tournament as scheduled.
His assurance followed reports questioning the progress of infrastructure projects and suggesting that some CAF officials wanted the competition moved elsewhere.
Motsepe acknowledged that challenges could arise during preparations but maintained his confidence in the three East African host nations.
“You have to believe in Africa,” he said, emphasising the importance of supporting the continent’s ability to organise major sporting events.

Working with Iraola, car clauses and hope - the Liverpool academy approach
- Published
One of the first things you notice in Alex Inglethorpe's office at Liverpool's AXA Training Centre is a framed image gifted by Trent Alexander-Arnold.
It is a picture from 2019 of the academy director and player watching a game together. Alexander-Arnold left for a new challenge at Real Madrid last year, after 20 years on Merseyside, but his story is one of inspiration for everyone that enters Liverpool's academy.
He joined as a six-year-old in 2004 and went on to win the Premier League, Champions League, FA Cup, League Cup, Community Shield, Uefa Super Cup and the Fifa Club World Cup with Liverpool.
"The ideal for any academy, and certainly for us, is wanting young players - and hopefully they're local players - to improve the first team and in doing so, they come and win trophies," says Inglethorpe.
"At Liverpool the bar is high, so to have a player capable of winning everything that you could possibly win is a dream."
Inglethorpe and his team oversee the development of younger players and ensure there is alignment between the academy and the first team.
One of the phrases used is 'the first team pitch is only 300 metres away from the academy building in Kirkby, but the journey might take 10 years to get there'.
Under new boss Andoni Iraola, players like Rio Ngumoha, Trey Nyoni, Lewis Koumas and James McConnell, who have spent time at the academy, have all featured this season.
"We were fortunate because of how the calendar worked, with players still at the World Cup and a delayed return. Andoni and his staff spent a lot of his first week here watching the academy," says Inglethorpe.
"So we felt ahead, in terms of building a relationship from the outset."
Adapting to a 'distorted' market
At the Kirkby academy, phones are handed in on a morning and there is a clause in contracts with a maximum engine size limit for cars that are driven into academy premises.
"It comes back to passing your audition. First impressions matter," says Inglethorpe.
"Often before you've kicked a ball, the car you drive or the watch you wear can have an impact on how you're thought of - and that could be first team staff or players looking at you.
"We've believed in the idea of 'earning the right' for some time."
Last week, Manchester United signed 16-year-old winger Isaac Konde from Liverpool on a one-year scholarship followed by a five-year professional deal. Both clubs are now in talks over a compensation package.
In February, a tribunal ruled Liverpool must pay at least £2.8m to Chelsea for Ngumoha. The 18-year-old left Chelsea in September 2024 to join the Reds and signed his first professional contract a year later.
Both are recent examples of the current climate around talent.
At Liverpool, the belief is they have been sensible and responsible with a view to deferred gratification in most cases, but the wage structure is currently under review.
"It's always a compliment when other clubs want your players as it means you're doing something right," says Inglethorpe.
"But I think the market of players at 16 is distorted because of Brexit and because you can't recruit like you would do before. There's always been movement of players but it feels a little more extreme now.
"When there's a clamour for talent - fees, wages and everything else will shift accordingly, so it's dealing with what we have and adapting to a new situation."
Do Liverpool need a Scouser in the first team?
When Curtis Jones moved to Inter Milan in the summer, it left Liverpool without a first team player born in the city.
"I acknowledge the fact that ideally Liverpool would love to have a team full of Scousers," says Inglethorpe.
"But it is testament to the supporters that if you adopt the characteristics of a Scouser - and you only have to see the likes of Bill Shankly, Kenny Dalglish and others over the years - you can be treated as one of their own.
"So if you are fearless, passionate, play tough and demonstrate those qualities, then it doesn't matter if you've come from an L1 postcode and got a purple bin or not. That's the beauty of the club and the crowd."
One name to keep an eye on is 15-year-old Luca Eden. The midfielder was born in the Wirral and has already represented England at youth level.
Last month, he became the youngest player to feature in the Uefa Youth League for Liverpool, beating a record previously held by Joshua Abe, Ngumoha and Alexander-Arnold.
"We've got plenty of Scousers in the academy and plenty who I think will play for the club. But if not and a lad comes from Warrington or wherever, that's not a problem," Inglethorpe insists.
Getting proven wrong by Jarell Quansah
One of the most challenging aspects of Inglethorpe's role is letting players go. Liverpool released eight players from their academy set-up at the end of last season.
Inglethorpe explains how the likes of Harry Kane, who was coming through the academy at Spurs when he was a youth coach there, and Alexander-Arnold weren't necessarily the best in their respective youth cohorts.
"At that stage, there's too many unknowns. You can't predict how players will react to adversity and natural bumps in the road," says Inglethorpe.
"I've been proven wrong so many times in the past. A good example would be Jarell [Quansah] - someone who was always liked and never in danger of leaving but probably never seen in the top three in the group."
Quansah left Liverpool for Bayer Leverkusen in 2025 and has since won eight caps for England.
"There are no certainties - the point of the academy is to allow them to fulfil their potential," says Inglethorpe.
"Sometimes players need to leave to gain an opportunity. There are lots of lovely examples of boys leaving and having good careers, and I'm not convinced they would have had the same career if they stayed at Liverpool.
"The linear and most productive way is to break in, but there's different pathways that can lead back to playing for Liverpool - and that is the dream."
'There are exciting times ahead'
Just before the academy players go on the pitch, there is a sign that says: "Don't look sideways" - referring to where the first team train.
Next month will mark 14 years at Liverpool for Inglethorpe. So what's his definition of success?
"Anyone would want to take something on and leave it in a better place, and I think we've done that," he says. "Ultimately we have had players in the first team winning major trophies and we're fortunate to be part of that era."
There is one standout moment.
The 'Kids Cup', when Liverpool beat Chelsea in the 2024 Carabao Cup final. Faced with an injury crisis, Jurgen Klopp relied heavily on academy players and his side finished the match with a team whose average age was under 22. Klopp called it his "most special trophy".
"It's definitely a moment in time. The longer the game went on, Jurgen was taking off the seniors and putting another one of the boys on. It was an incredible show of belief," says Inglethorpe.
On another wall in Inglethorpe's office is a magnetic board with headshots of every player in the academy on the left and the first team squad on the right. Ultimately, the motive is for everyone to make the journey across the board.
With a £20m revamp to the academy facility planned to be completed by 2028, the determination to carry on producing first team players is stronger than ever.
"There are exciting times ahead with the potential for the other end, and I'm really excited for the future," says Inglethorpe.
"In Julian Ward [the new sporting director], we have someone who is hugely invested in the academy and has been on this journey for a long time."

US public executions were once a community spectacle. The country thought they stopped
Parents and teachers would often bring children to executions

For about nine decades, executions in the U.S. have been private affairs, often shrouded in secrecy. The stunning Pentagon announcement Thursday that the first military execution in more than 65 years will be livestreamed could change that.
Allowing the world to watch Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan face the firing squad in December would make it the first public execution since two hangings in the 1930s in Kentucky and Missouri drew crowds.
In 1936, a man who reportedly confessed to the rape and murder of a woman was hanged in front of thousands in Owensboro, Kentucky, while the following year, hundreds watched a man in Missouri be hanged.
A livestreamed execution is reminiscent of a bygone period in America's history in which public executions were seen as deterrents to crime as well as popular ceremonies, said Michael L. Radelet, professor emeritus at the University of Colorado Boulder, who has done extensive research on executions.
Parents and teachers would often bring children along to teach them a lesson. The events would sometimes feature a choir, a preacher giving an “execution sermon” and the condemned, who was typically a man being hanged, giving a long speech to the crowd.
In an execution in Leadville, Colorado, in the late 1800s, Radelet said Cyrus Minich, who was being put to death, told the crowd, “Therefore I apologize and I’m ready to go. Goodbye, goodbye.”
The crowd reportedly responded: “Goodbye Cy, goodbye Cy.”
“This is in the days before TV, so not much going on often in big cities, certainly in rural areas, too, so they were there just for the spectacle,” Radelet said, adding that sometimes it would draw a crowd because the person was so hated.
Thousands watched country's last public execution
The 1936 hanging in Kentucky of Rainey Bethea is often considered the last public execution in the country, said Radelet.
Bethea was a Black man who reportedly confessed to the rape and killing of a 70-year-old white woman, but was never charged with murder, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Thousands of people attended the event, which was held in a parking lot so the courthouse lawn wouldn’t be damaged by the crowd, according to the center.
But there was also one the following year in which Roscoe “Red” Jackson in Missouri was hanged. The Los Angeles Times reported that some people were given passes to watch, while others climbed trees or cut peepholes to catch a glimpse of the morning execution.
States started to change the policy as an increasing number of people witnessed botched hangings and as broader concerns grew over the events, Radelet said.
“Instead of promoting the sanctity of life and how solemn the circumstance was, with people applauding and having a carnival-like atmosphere, that really turned people off," he said.
Oklahoma City bomber's execution was on CCTV
Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said they have no record of any execution being livestreamed.
The closest came in 2001, when Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh was executed at a federal prison in Terre Haute, Indiana. Then-U.S. Attorney General John Ashcroft announced that victims could attend in person or view it through a closed-circuit television
But will the Army's announcement about livestreaming the execution of Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding many others in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, change the situation?
Maher said she sees Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's comments as “simply aspirational.”
“There is currently no regulation or precedent for an execution to be livestreamed on the internet or otherwise made widely available to the public,” she said in a statement.
Hasan could choose to resist execution and file a habeas petition — a legal request to review the legality of a detention — in civilian court, which could significantly delay the execution, experts said.
Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at UC Berkeley Law, said the announcement raises many legal and public policy questions, including concerns for the dignity of the defendant, who will be eligible to view the execution and what the Trump administration has in mind in opting for an unusual spectacle.
“This is a president who’s about spectacle and that’s, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver,” Semel said, adding that she was skeptical that the administration had given a second thought to the legal and social questions being presented by the decision.
Deborah Denno, a death penalty expert and law professor at Fordham University, said livestreaming an execution could make the process “much more transparent” and inform the public about all that capital punishment entails. Those are benefits that she said would be useful at a time when a botched execution in Tennessee has raised fresh questions about the manner by which criminal defendants are put to death for their crimes.
“I think it could possibly be a good idea because it would be transparent and the public would be fully aware that it’s happening,” she said.
