For a long time, fungal infections have meant itchy skin, discoloured nails and sometimes hair loss.
These symptoms are collectively called dermatophytosis and are caused by a group of fungi called dermatophytes.
‘’Unfortunately, immunocompromised patients can get lesions all over their body. The itchiness and the lesions can get so severe that people even get suicidal thoughts,” said Shivaprakash Rudramurthy, professor of medical mycology at the Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research (PGIMER), Chandigarh.
Global warming
Dermatophytes are molds: fungi that grow in long strands. The other common category of fungi is yeast, which are single, oval-shaped cells. Among the yeasts, Candida auris is rapidly emerging as a multidrug resistant pathogen in ICU facilities. It enters the blood stream and causes severe infections, most of which are untreatable by the available antifungals. According to Prof. Rudramurthy, those infected suffer a 30-40% mortality rate.
C. auris has become a menace only in the last two decades. The first report was in 2009 in Japan. Several other fungal species have become more pathogenic only in recent times. The cause of this rise remains unresolved but scientists and medical doctors have some ideas.
Fungi grow best in damp places below 30° C, so they can grow on our skin, especially in moist areas of the body, like armpits and the genital area. However, bloodstream infections in humans were rare because they could not survive in the body’s 37° C temperature.
“Fungal infections are common in cold-blooded animals with lower body temperatures,” Sriram Varahan, a mycologist at CSIR-Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology, Hyderabad, said.
“But global warming puts a selective pressure on fungi such that only the more heat-tolerant ones survive. These ones can survive inside our bodies too, if they gain access to it. This is called the fungal infection — mammalian selection hypothesis.”
Clinical samples
Today, roughly 20% of infections reported in hospitals are fungal in nature — yet most hospitals in India lack the capabilities and infrastructure to identify fungal pathogens, Prof Rudramurthy said.
This prompted PGIMER to begin storing fungal pathogens some 25 years ago. Today, the institute holds a stock of 15,000 clinical fungal isolates across India and helps other medical centres and clinicians identify and culture them for study, free of cost.
The C. auris isolates from PGIMER’s repository have come handy for Kaustuv Sanyal and his research associate Aswathy Narayanan, both at the Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research, Bengaluru. They study how fungal pathogens divide and their genomes evolve.
In a recent study published in Nature Communications, they characterised the clinical isolates of C. auris found across India. Their focus was the pathogen’s ability to resist antifungals. They were able to establish their findings in patient samples and go beyond earlier studies in model systems.
“More than 90% clinical isolates of C. auris are resistant to common azole-based antifungals, such as fluconazole,” Prof. Sanyal said. Some “30% of them are resistant to another class of antifungals called the polyenes. They mostly respond to a different class of antifungals called the echinocandins.”
A drug may not work on a pathogen for many reasons, including the drug’s target becoming mutated or the drug’s effect being negated by the pathogen’s own biomolecules. Dr. Narayanan and her collaborators at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Thiruvananthapuram, found significant changes in drug-resistant C. auris genomes that could explain why Indian clinical isolates were able to resist azoles and echinocandins.
Susceptibility tests
A fungal cell has two protective layers surrounding it. The outermost is the cell wall and the inner one is the cell membrane. Azole and polyene antifungals target a fat called ergosterol that is enriched in the cell membrane. Echinocandins target the cell wall.
“When we grow C. auris isolates in the presence of fluconazole, the pathogen fights back by making extra copies of the Erg 11 gene. This in turn helps in higher production of ergosterol, thereby eliminating the effect of the azole drug,” Dr Narayanan said.
The study found parts in the C. auris genome where additional copies of the Erg11 gene were present.
With echinocandin drugs such as caspofungin, the team found mutations in the Fks1 gene that allowed the pathogen to resist the drug’s action. The team also found genetic changes promoting higher tolerance of echinocandins.
“Fks1 mutations can enable C. auris to survive even caspofungin doses up to 16 ug/ml. That means a patient with such a pathogen will need the drug at a concentration higher than 16 ug/ml,” Prof. Sanyal said. “Today, clinicians would not know that because they test the pathogen’s ability to survive only until 2 µg/mL of caspofungin — as defined by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and followed globally.”
The logical thing for clinicians would be to look for mutations like in the Fks1 gene and decide the limits for tests to decide the antifungal dose for patients. But due to associated costs, a more practical way is to increase the limits of susceptibility tests for caspofungin to higher than 16 ug/ml, Prof. Sanyal added.
C. auris, without any specific gene mutation or gene duplication, still responds to high concentrations of caspofungin in unexpected ways. While the pathogen dies at lower concentrations of the drug, at exceptionally high ones, it survives. This is paradoxical.
“This is because caspofungin at high doses activates compensatory pathways in the fungus,” Prof. Sanyal explained. “The fungus starts producing chitin, the raw material of the fungal cell wall, in large quantities. Any damage that caspofungin brings about on the cell wall is compensated by the extra chitin production. And thus the cell wall remains intact despite the antifungal.”
Such examples of paradoxical growth are called the Eagle effect, named for the U.S. pathologist Harry Eagle.
Beyond the arms race
The studies underline the importance of clinicians conducting more nuanced susceptibility tests to decide the antifungal doses. They show that fungi are protected from antifungals by genetic mutations as well as by making more copies of protective genes.
Prof. Sanyal also stressed on the need for a combination of therapies to target cellular compensatory pathways, keeping the major antifungals effective against drug-tolerant species.
However, Dr. Varahan said he believed scientists and doctors need to think of gentler alternatives: “When we target [a molecule] without which an organism cannot live at all, evolution ensures that its population survives with a changed molecule. So instead of participating in an arms race, it is perhaps better to target the less critical molecular pathways, inhibition of which will allow the pathogen to still survive but not cause a disease.”
It seems the idea of dousing fungal pathogens with antifungals is nearing its end. The next-generation of antifungals will need more planning.
Somdatta Karak heads science communication at CSIR-CCMB.

The Indian pilot who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv said his faith and his desire to save his passengers allowed him to make a “last push” to open the cockpit door as he fought for his life.
Capt Smit Machchhar, who was recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, described to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, how he helped save the plane and its more than 170 passengers.
“I had suffered so many injuries that I had collapsed. At that time, I could feel that the aircraft was going down. I knew this was the last push,” Machchhar told Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”
His Omani co-pilot apparently stabbed him and set the plane on a steep descent, with the aircraft plummeting about 17,000 feet in the span of a minute. While still being attacked, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter, subdue the attacker and ultimately stabilise the plane.
The full circumstances of the attack are still under investigation, but a relief crew on the flight helped land the plane safely in Tabouk, north-west Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities arrested the co-pilot and have since interrogated him.
Machchhar, a father of two, was seriously injured during the attack, but credited his 17 years of aviation experience with giving him the wherewithal to understand the gravity of the situation.
Modi praised the captain for his actions, which he said helped prevent a “great tragedy.”
“You have done such a great thing that people across the country and around the world are eager to see you and speak to you,” Modi told him. “You have truly made the whole country proud.”
The motives and affiliation of the apparent attacker are still unknown, but Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said that an initial background investigation indicated he had undergone “Islamic radical indoctrination”.
The attacker is to be sent back to the United Arab Emirates, where Emirati investigators will work to establish any links with terror organisations. Netanyahu said Israel would cooperate with the UAE on the investigation.
Machchhar was hailed as a hero by world leaders, who said his actions had helped prevent a great disaster and save many lives.
The pilot said that during the difficult moments he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a devotional hymn dedicated to the Hindu deity Hanuman and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage.
“Lord Hanuman gave me courage,” Machchhar told Modi.
He added that he felt proud of himself for the first time since the attack. “I am feeling very proud right now. I had not felt proud of myself until now,” he told Modi.
“I am not thinking of it as a wound, I am thinking of it as a journey,” he said, while covered in bandages. “And it will take time, but I am very, very confident that I will recover.”

విద్యా వ్యవస్థలో సంస్కరణలు చేపట్టాలని, పాఠశాలలకు నిధులు పెంచాలని డిమాండ్ చేస్తూ ఫ్రాన్స్లో హైస్కూల్, యూనివర్సిటీ విద్యార్థులు, ఉపాధ్యాయులు పెద్దఎత్తున దేశవ్యాప్త నిరసనలు చేపట్టారు. 2026 అక్టోబర్ మొదటి వారంలో ఈ నిరసనలు తీవ్ర స్థాయికి చేరి హింసాత్మకంగా మారాయి. నిరసనకారులు కార్లకు, పాఠశాల భవనాలకు నిప్పుపెట్టడం, పోలీసులపైకి తిరగబడటం వంటి చర్యలకు పాల్పడ్డారు. ఇప్పటివరకు దాదాపు 6,000 మందికి పైగా నిరసనకారులను పోలీసులు అదుపులోకి తీసుకున్నారు. వీరిలో అత్యధికులు మైనర్ విద్యార్థులే ఉన్నారు. పరిస్థితి అదుపు తప్పడంతో ఫ్రెంచ్ ప్రభుత్వం దేశవ్యాప్తంగా ఉన్నత పాఠశాలలకు సెలవులు ప్రకటించి, తరగతులను ఆన్లైన్ విధానంలోకి మార్చింది.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, పారిస్ స్టాక్ ఎక్స్చేంజ్ను నిరసనకారులు స్వాధీనం చేసుకున్నారంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. ఇందులో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: అక్టోబర్ 2026 ఫ్రాన్స్ నిరసనల్లో భాగంగా నిరసనకారులు పారిస్ స్టాక్ ఎక్స్చేంజ్ భవనాన్ని స్వాధీనం చేసుకుంటున్న దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: వైరల్ వీడియో ఏప్రిల్ 2023లో పెన్షన్ సంస్కరణలకు వ్యతిరేకంగా జరిగిన నిరసనలకు సంబంధించినది. ఆ ఘటనలో ఆందోళనకారులు భవనం లాబీలోకి మాత్రమే ప్రవేశించారు తప్ప స్టాక్ ఎక్స్చేంజ్ను స్వాధీనం చేసుకోలేదు. అలాగే, ఈ వీడియోకు అక్టోబర్ 2026 విద్యార్థుల నిరసనలతో ఎలాంటి సంబంధం లేదు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా, వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇదే వీడియో (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కనీసం 20 ఏప్రిల్ 2023 నుంచి ఇంటర్నెట్లో అందుబాటులో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. పారిస్ స్టాక్ ఎక్స్చేంజ్ యూరోనెక్స్ట్ భవనాన్ని నిరసనకారులు ఆక్రమించినట్లు ఇందులో పేర్కొన్నారు.
ఈ ఘటనను రిపోర్ట్ చేసిన స్థానిక, అంతర్జాతీయ వార్తా కథనాల (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ప్రకారం, 20 ఏప్రిల్ 2023న దాదాపు 200 నుంచి 300 మంది నిరసనకారులు పారిస్లోని బిజినెస్ డిస్ట్రిక్ట్లో ఉన్న యూరోనెక్స్ట్ స్టాక్ ఎక్స్చేంజ్ కార్యాలయ లాబీలోకి ఒక్కసారిగా దూసుకెళ్లారు. నిరసనకారులు తమ చేతుల్లో యూనియన్ జెండాలను పట్టుకుని, ఎరుపు రంగు పొగ గొట్టాలు వెలిగించడంతో ఆ ప్రాంతమంతా ఎర్రటి పొగతో నిండిపోయింది. అధ్యక్షుడు ఇమ్మాన్యుయేల్ మాక్రాన్ ప్రభుత్వం రిటైర్మెంట్ వయసును 62 ఏళ్ల నుంచి 64 ఏళ్లకు పెంచుతూ చట్టం చేయడాన్ని నిరసిస్తూ ఆ సమయంలో ఫ్రాన్స్ వ్యాప్తంగా కార్మిక సంఘాలు, రైల్వే కార్మికులు పెద్ద ఎత్తున ఆందోళనలు చేపట్టారు.
అయితే ఈ నిరసన కేవలం కార్యాలయ ప్రవేశ ద్వారం (లాబీ) వరకే పరిమితమైంది. లోపల ట్రేడింగ్కు ఎలాంటి నష్టం వాటిల్లలేదని, స్టాక్ మార్కెట్ లావాదేవీలకు అంతరాయం కలగలేదని మీడియా పేర్కొంది. ఇక, అక్టోబర్ 2026లో జరుగుతున్న నిరసనల్లో యూరోనెక్స్ట్ స్టాక్ ఎక్స్చేంజ్ కార్యాలయంపై దాడి జరిగినట్లు ఇప్పటివరకైతే ఎటువంటి విశ్వసనీయ సమాచారం లేదు.
చివరిగా, పారిస్ స్టాక్ ఎక్స్చేంజ్ భవనంలోకి నిరసనకారులు దూసుకెళ్లిన ఈ వీడియో ఏప్రిల్ 2023 నిరసనలు సంబంధించినది.

Ireland is becoming a global leader in the field of innovation in harnessing digital technologies as a tool to address various barriers for access to care. In alignment with WHO, Ireland recognizes the importance of mobilizing assistive technology to help the 2.5 billion people in need globally, including older persons, people with disabilities, and those living with health conditions. This includes ensuring equitable access to assistive products such as glasses, hearing aids, walking aids, wheelchairs, prosthetics, and communication and memory devices.
In March 2024, Anne Rabbitte, T.D., Ireland’s Minister of State with special responsibility for disabilities at the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, agreed to a €12.5 million donor agreement between the Government of Ireland and WHO, aimed at accelerating affordability and availability of assistive technology for those in need.
The cooperation has been building throughout the years. Back in 2022, Taoiseach Micheál Martin, TD, launched the Global report on assistive technology, along with the Director-General of WHO and the Executive Director of UNICEF. The Taoiseach highlighted the importance of international cooperation to ensure more equitable access to assistive technology, in order to achieve a society where everyone is included and enabled to live their best life.
Minister Rabbitte stated that: “Ireland has identified the serious need to invest in public health systems alongside the WHO. The present risk of rising health needs coupled with a decreasing pool of health and social care professionals globally reveals an urgent need for all of us to act now. Ireland’s contribution aligns with the recommendations of the Global Report on Assistive Technology and supports a five-year initiative towards achieving national health system models that include assistive technology. The programme will explore and demonstrate how digital technology can facilitate people-centred services, assistive technology policy, improve the affordability and appropriateness of assistive products, enable effective provision systems, and boost the capacity of health personnel to identify, screen, refer and provide assistive technology for all those in need.”
Health personnel in Tanzania participating in on-line training on assistive products, as part of an overall program aimed at provision of simple assistive products through community and primary health care facilities - making products such as walking aids and reading glasses more readily available for people within their local area. Digital technology was instrumental in facilitating efficient learning through the platform, and enabling support for health workers from their mentors through communication apps after the training. Credit: WHO/Kylie Shae
With an ageing global population and a rise in noncommunicable diseases, an estimated 3.5 billion people will need assistive technology by 2050. Dr Yukiko Nakatani, WHO Assistant Director-General, Access to Medicines and Health Products, welcomes this important contribution from Ireland and their leadership in the digital initiative. She said: “The 2018 World Health Assembly resolution on assistive technology calls upon WHO to take the necessary steps to promote equitable access to assistive technology in our endeavour to build a more inclusive world. Our partnership with the Government of Ireland will support WHO in achieving our mission to ensure health for all, everywhere, with assistive technologies as an important enabler of well-being, inclusion, and participation.”
Through Ireland’s contribution, and in collaboration with its broad network of partners, WHO will develop evidence-based guidance for Member States on strengthening access to assistive technology through understanding, prioritising and stimulating increased innovation and use of digital solutions. The work will also involve national, regional, and global projects that test digital solutions designed to address persistent access barriers such as: digital platforms that empower users with information about assistive technology and how to access it; digital tracking of products to manage supply; and online training and support for health workers. The results and lessons learned will help countries expand their knowledge, skills, and capacities in the provision of assistive technology as an integral component of Universal Health Care.
‘Leaving no one behind’ means ensuring that people with disabilities, the older population, those affected by chronic diseases and everyone who needs assistive technology are included in society and able to live healthy and dignified lives.
* * * *
Click below to find out what is assistive technology, who needs it, and how it improves lives
Assistive technology is an umbrella term for external products used by individuals to help maintain or improve their bodily functions. Common examples are wheelchairs, glasses, prosthetic limbs, white canes, and hearing aids as well as digital solutions such as speech recognition or time management software. Assistive technology helps people in all aspects of their lives, including in education, employment, fitness, leisure and other everyday activities such as self-care, cooking and reading.
Most people will need assistive technology at some point in their lives, especially as they age. While some may require assistive technology temporarily, such as after an accident or illness, others may require it for a longer period or throughout their lifespan. It is commonly needed by older people, children and adults with disabilities, people who have been injured or who have a health condition such as diabetes, stroke and dementia.
Equitable access is key
Improving access to assistive technology enables the inclusion and participation of users in their family, community and all areas of society, including the political, economic and social spheres. Assistive technology positively impacts a person, their family and friends, and has broader socioeconomic benefits. For example:
- early provision of hearing aids for young children supports their development of language and communication skills, limiting negative impacts on their education, future employment and community participation;
- provision of appropriate wheelchairs facilitates mobility, improving individuals’ access to education and employment while reducing healthcare costs due to a reduction in secondary complications such as pressure sores and contractures;
- therapeutic footwear for diabetes reduces the incidence of foot ulcers, preventing amputations and the associated impact on individuals and burden on health-care systems; and
- timely provision of assistive technology for older people can improve their independence and safety as well as enable them to live at home for as long as possible.

Gauhati HC grants bail to Zubeen Garg’s bandmate Amritprava Mahanta in murder trial
The Gauhati High Court on Friday granted bail to Amritprava Mahanta, a band member of Zubeen Garg, in connection with the murder trial of the late singer-composer.
Garg had died under mysterious circumstances on September 19 last year while swimming in the sea in Singapore. Mahanta is one of the seven accused currently undergoing trial for his alleged murder.
“The court granted bail to Mahanta after going through our arguments. The details of the bail order will be known once it is out or released online. The prosecution has nothing concrete against my client. She is innocent and was falsely implicated,” said Mahanta’s lawyer, Anan Kumar Bhuyan.
The bail was granted by Justice Pranjal Das. The court has set a bail bond of ₹50,000, with two sureties of the same amount, and imposed several other conditions, including the submission of her passport for her release on bail.
Mahanta’s lawyers will first have to submit her bail bond to the trial court where the case is underway. Once it is accepted, she is likely to be released from jail, lawyers said.
“We are yet to see the detailed order. Only after that we will know on what basis the court granted her bail. We will write to the state government and it is for them to decide whether they will appeal against the bail,” prosecution lawyer Ziaul Kamar said.
Mahanta was arrested on October 3 last year after several days of interrogation. She is currently lodged at Haflong Jail in Dima Hasao district.
Following Garg’s death, there was widespread demand across Assam for a proper investigation. The state government subsequently constituted a special investigation team (SIT) to probe the matter. It concluded that Garg had been murdered as part of a planned conspiracy.
Besides Mahanta, six other persons, including Garg’s manager, the organiser of the event in Singapore that the singer had gone to attend, another bandmate, Garg’s cousin and two security officers, were arrested in connection with the case. All of them are currently in jail.
Last month, a special court had granted bail to the two security officers in a separate disproportionate assets case. However, they remain in prison for their alleged role in Garg’s death.

Sanjay Dutt appeared on Shekhar Suman’s Shekhar Tonite for a Gandhi Jayanti special episode, where he remarked that he could no longer feel “peace” in the country. His comments drew backlash, following which Dutt clarified that the conversation was scripted and intended to be light-hearted and humorous. Shekhar Suman also defended him, saying the remarks were taken out of context.
Following the controversy, a purported video of actor Sanjay Dutt is being shared on social media with the claim that it shows him speaking about protecting Muslims from discrimination, opposing the saffronisation of government institutions and the armed forces, and saying that the people of Kashmir should decide their own future.
In the video, he can be heard saying (translated from Hindi to English), “I will not let Muslims suffer in India the way my mother suffered as a Muslim. I do not need the saffronisation of government institutions, especially the armed forces. The Army belongs to the country, not to any one colour. The decision on Kashmir should be made by the people of Kashmir. Let them choose their side and remove the Army from there.” Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows actor Sanjay Dutt making controversial remarks about Muslims, saffronisation, and Kashmir.
Fact: The video is AI-manipulated. The original visuals are from Sanjay Dutt’s appearance on Shekhar Tonite, but the alleged remarks about Muslims, saffronisation, the armed forces, and Kashmir do not appear in the original episode. AI voice detection tools also indicate that the audio has likely been generated or manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
We searched Google using relevant keywords but found no credible reports confirming that Sanjay Dutt made the alleged remarks.
We then reviewed the entire ‘Shekhar Tonite’ episode shared on Shekhar Suman’s official YouTube channel on 02 October 2026. However, we found no instance of Sanjay Dutt making the alleged statement anywhere in the episode, indicating that the audio in the viral clip has been added or altered.
We then analysed the viral video using multiple AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya. The analysis indicated that the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated. This suggests that the original footage was paired with fabricated audio to make it appear that actor Sanjay Dutt was speaking about protecting Muslims from discrimination, opposing the saffronisation of government institutions and the armed forces, and calling for the people of Kashmir to decide their own future.
To sum up, this video of Sanjay Dutt allegedly making controversial remarks about Muslims, saffronisation, and Kashmir is AI-manipulated.

Volkswagen’s ID.4 is no more. The midsize crossover debuted in 2021, one of VW’s first new electric vehicles designed in the wake of dieselgate. A year later, the company began local production in Chattanooga, Tennessee, and a couple of years ago facelifted the model, adding a much-improved rear drive unit in the process. But Chattanooga turned its attention away from the ID.4 earlier this year. And, having sold almost a million ID.4s (and near-identical ID.5s) globally, the German automaker has decided it’s time for its replacement. Meet the ID. Tiguan.
Dropping the numerical and adopting the moniker of VW’s big seller is a statement. “The Tiguan is our best-selling model worldwide, and the ID.4 and ID.5 are among our most successful electric cars. The ID. Tiguan brings these two success stories together,” said Thomas Schäfer, CEO of the VW brand.
VW was an early pioneer of using flexible vehicle architectures to create a multitude of bodystyles and sizes with common parts, and its transition into building EVs hasn’t changed that. The ID. Tiguan uses an updated version of the company’s mass-market EV platform, now called MEB+, with either 58 kWh or 77 kWh battery packs. The smaller pack is only available with a 187 hp (140 kW) rear electric motor, but the 77 kWh battery can be had with either a 281 hp (210 kW) rear-wheel drive powertrain or as a 295 hp (220 kW) all-wheel drive version. Range is up to 373 miles (600 km), at least according to the European WLTP test.
Alongside the mainstream name, it has a more mainstream look, though it’s part of VW’s new design language. For those keeping track of the various interesting names car companies give their design languages—it can’t just be me—this one is called Pure Positive. The automaker says it wants the ID. Tiguan to feel like it belongs to the premium rather than mainstream segment, both inside and out.

What reception awaits Man City at Anfield?
- Published
It was December 2024 when Pep Guardiola's Manchester City side were 2-0 down at Liverpool and the Anfield crowd chanted "you're getting sacked in the morning" towards the opposition boss.
No-one truly believed he was going to be given his marching orders but his side were on their way to a remarkable fourth consecutive Premier League defeat.
Guardiola could not help but lift six fingers up to the Liverpool crowd in response - representing the six Premier League titles he won with City.
Now, some may question each of those successes after an independent commission found the club guilty of the majority of the 115 financial charges the Premier League brought against them.
On Friday, current City boss Enzo Maresca said the club's titles are "absolutely not" tainted. But come Sunday, he and his players will face up to their new normal.
Such is the script that a trip to what promises to be a ferocious Anfield - a place Guardiola always described as difficult - is next.
City have won five out of five in the Premier League this term and it would be huge if Maresca can maintain that 100 % start.
But for Andoni Iraola and Liverpool, this will be an opportunity to truly kickstart their own campaign, fuelled by a backstory like no other.
"It's an exciting game," said the Reds boss. "We are playing at home at Anfield against City that is top of the league, they have won all of their games.
"We will go for the game, they will go for it and it will be quite an open game and we have to be ready. I hope we will be at the level of the game, which will be high."
Asked if it was the kind of fixture he relished when taking the Liverpool job, Iraola added: "Yes, we are here to play this game. We know it's going to be challenging. They are very good but we also are very good."
It will be the first time since 2015 this clash will have neither Jurgen Klopp or Guardiola on the touchline, but nevertheless, a hostile atmosphere awaits and Tom Werner, the Liverpool chairman, will be in attendance.
Liverpool finished second in the Premier League to Man City in 2013-14 under Brendan Rodgers and again in 2018-19 and 2021-22 when Klopp's side put up 97 and 92 points respectively, but were one shy of Guardiola's City as they were pipped to the title.
A verdict on City's appeal awaits. City insist they are innocent but there will be sections of the Liverpool fanbase and former players and staff that feel aggrieved.
"You think about the memories and the successes that you were wrongly denied," John Achterberg, who was Liverpool's goalkeeping coach under Rodgers and Klopp, told The Athletic., external
"We won one Premier League title [in 2019-20], but it could have been four given that we missed out to City three times by such narrow margins."
Iraola added: "The worst thing probably is the uncertainty. No-one knows what's going to happen. We have to focus on Liverpool and being the best club we can be, the best team we can be. That's my challenge."

Liverpool may have a historic rivalry with the red half of Manchester, but since City were taken over by Abu Dhabi in 2008, matches between the two have consistently delivered on the field and there's been off-field action too.
In 2018, the Reds were fined 20,000 euros (£17,500) by Uefa after supporters threw missiles at the City bus before the Champions League quarter-final first-leg at Anfield.
Liverpool went on to score three goals in 19 first-half minutes and knocked City out. Earlier that season in January, it was Klopp's men who ended City's unbeaten league start with a thrilling 4-3 win at Anfield.
"There's something about it that you will find in no other stadium in the world. They score a goal and over the next five minutes you feel that you'll receive another four. You feel small and the rival players seem to be all over," Guardiola said in 2019.
Merseyside Police say an appropriate policing plan will be in place for Sunday but chose not to delve into specifics when asked by BBC Sport.
There is a growing expectation the team buses will be welcomed when they arrive and posters on social media have advertised a 'Bus Greeting' on Anfield Road.
It remains unclear whether a separate bus route could be taken, but that has happened previously at Anfield.
Inside the ground, Liverpool are renowned for their collection of banners and flags and plenty are planned. It will be worth keeping an eye on the pre-match playlist, too.
One social media post suggested fans could bring stacks of fake money.
In terms of preparations, Liverpool's stance is "business as usual" and any talks with the police and around safety concerns are regular meetings that would happen before every game.
The fact of the matter is, however, this is likely to be an occasion and game like no other.

"The race is too hard for women. They are simply not tough enough to do it."
Those are the words of Lazarus Lake, race director of the Barkley Marathons - one of the world's hardest ultramarathons which to date, of the approximate 1,000 people who have started, only 20 have ever completed.
Speaking in 2015 and daring for someone to prove him wrong, it took nine years until a British ultra-runner did just that.
Completing the extreme 100-mile course with just one minute 39 seconds to spare of the 60-hour cut-off, Jasmin Paris from Midlothian made history and cemented her name in the ultra-running history books.
But now, increasingly, she is not alone.
Last summer, there was a female one-two for the first time in the gruelling Montane Summer Spine Race from Derbyshire to Scotland. Rachel Entrekin set a new course record and became the first woman to win the Cocodona 250 in Arizona in May, while last month Sophie Woods smashed the overall record by six days to complete the Via Alpina.
It appears female runners are no longer just taking part in ultra-endurance events, they are competing with their male counterparts, breaking records and in some cases, winning races outright.
All of this has prompted suggestions that they are perhaps better suited to these kinds of challenges.
But is there any scientific proof? Do women really have any physiological or psychological advantages in endurance exercise (anything that takes more than six hours)? And if so, could we see more of these records fall in the future?
In running distances up to the marathon, there is on average a 10-12% performance gap between males and females.
Men are generally stronger and built with a bigger aerobic engine.
But as the distance increases, those physical advantages appear to become less relevant and the gap starts to narrow.
The "gender pace gap" diminishes to 0.25% in 100-mile races, according to a study of more than 20 years of amateur ultra-race data conducted by RunRepeat, in collaboration with the International Association of Ultrarunners,
Anything further than 195 miles and women have the potential to be faster.
So why might this be the case?
For Professor Andy Jones, an expert in endurance performance at the University of Exeter, there are three potential physiological explanations why women could perform better over longer distances or durations.
Fat metabolism – women have higher fat stores and burn it more efficiently, giving them a steady energy source for longer.
Muscles – women have more oxygen-efficient muscle fibres, known as "slow twitch", that are better suited for endurance activities.
Fatigue resistance – women retain more strength over hours of endurance exercise.
However, Jones, who played a key role in Eliud Kipchoge's sub two-hour marathon challenge in 2019, is keen to point out that the science in this area is "behind".
"There isn't as much hard evidence as there would be for shorter distances, which have been studied for a long time in quite some detail," he adds.
That is a view shared by Dr Richard Burden, co-lead of female athlete health and performance at the UK Sports Institute, who feels a lot more information needs to be gathered before conclusions can be made.
"At the moment we are speculating … there are definitely some physiological adaptations that you see more in women than men that are favourable for ultra-type events. But those need to be better established and more studies would need to be done."
Physiology, however, only gets you so far. The realities of ultra-endurance exercise - multi-day events, sleep deprivation, extreme terrain and conditions, to name but a few – mean the journey to the finish line is as much mental as it is physical.
And for Sophie Woods, this is where women have the edge.
"It's not necessarily about being the fastest person at the start," she says. "It is about preparation, it is about mental strength and being able to continue to persevere when things go wrong."
During the New Zealand runner's record-breaking run of the Via Alpina, she was forced to expect the unexpected – from disruption caused by wildfires that made her route longer and more dangerous to swarms of horseflies.
"I was so tired and there were so many of them and I wanted to have a complete meltdown and just cry, but I couldn't because if I stopped moving, they started biting me," she says.
"I think women are really good at adapting and continuing and just knowing that once we start something, you've just got to keep moving until you get to the finish."
That view is echoed by Yngvild Kaspersen, who last month became the first woman to win the prestigious Ultra-Trail Mont Blanc CCC race in the Alps twice. She credits her victory to the "mental game" she puts herself through in training.
The Norwegian, who balances life as a professional runner with her job as a GP, also believes female ultra-runners are so strong because camaraderie in the community is unrivalled.
"We're competitors but we're also motivating each other, inspiring each other, pushing each other to do better in the races," she says. "If you see the podiums for the women this year [at UTMB], how close we are and how we're running together out there - that's very special and I'm very proud to be a part of that community and that group of women."
So can we explain why women might be more resilient?
Sports dietitian Renee McGregor, who specialises in athlete nutrition and hormonal health, believes the answer comes from the female body itself.
"The moment women step into puberty, we are dealing with a fluctuating hormonal system," she says. "We never ever give ourselves credit for that, it's just an accepted part of being female. But actually, it is an endurance in itself and I think that's probably where a big part of our resilience comes from."
McGregor, an ultra-runner herself, points to research that suggests female runners display more disciplined and even pacing strategies than men in distance races, maximising on what she terms the female "brain bank".
"I don't think women go into these races without a lot of thought and contingency planning," McGregor adds.
"For example, if you've been through a pregnancy and you've dealt with nausea, if you've had a baby and dealt with the lack of sleep or if you've gone through fertility treatment, you have to go through so much discomfort, but you know you can get through it. And I think it's that knowledge of 'I can get through this, I can find a solution'."
One of the biggest reasons why we cannot talk with any certainty about the potential physiological and psychological advantages that women may have in this field is because participation numbers are low, with women making up roughly only 20% of those on ultramarathon start lines.
Research by SheRACES, a network set up by British ultra-runner Sophie Power to correct gender disparities in running, suggests the reasons for this range from societal perceptions around women's abilities, to concerns around the time needed for training, or access to the right support at the events themselves.
Slowly but surely, however, things are starting to change.
Earlier this year, a trail race in New Zealand became the first UTMB World Series event to achieve a 50:50 gender split, while a leading UK race provider has launched a new initiative to target gender parity at its events.
And now, according to Dr Burden, society is talking about the limits of human performance in a different way too.
"Historically, the majority of the time it [the limits of the human] will be established from male models or male sports," he says. "Now we're starting to break it up into the limits of male performance and the limits of female performance and that's a distinction that needs to be made … but to make better comparisons, we would need more women taking part in ultra events."

When it comes to participation, visibility is key.
Kaspersen describes Rachel Entrekin's historic victory at Cocodona 250, one of the most demanding ultramarathons in the world, as an "inspiration" among the elites to "dare to try".
And at the amateur level, there are those like Emily Fairs, a 22-year-old ultra-runner who documents the realities of her training and races on social media as part of her mission to get more women of all ages on start lines.
"When it comes to endurance training, there are so many components that come into it and that we are fearful of but by seeing another woman do it you think 'right, if she can do it, if she has the tools, she has the knowledge, she has the ability to do all these crazy difficult challenges, then so do I. I'm no different to her. She's no different to me'," says Fairs.
Fairs says she has received thousands of messages from women about how her content has encouraged them to lace up their trainers, and believes recent trends of female success in ultra-running are just the start.
"When the proportion is so low, we have no clue what women are capable of. We're starting to see more women get faster and enter the sport and push themselves and break records. So, who knows where we'll be 10-15 years later down the line?"

The Supreme Court on Friday (October 9, 2026) took exception to a recent High Court judgment, which held that removing a woman’s salwar and pressing her chest did not amount to an attempt to rape. The court issued notice to the accused, who had been acquitted of the charges against him.
A Bench headed by Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant was hearing a suo motu case concerning the High Court ruling, which had held that removing a woman’s salwar and pressing her chest did “not unequivocally establish” an attempt to rape and could, “at best”, constitute assault or use of criminal force with intent to outrage a woman’s modesty under Section 354 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
“What line [the] Patna High Court used is something very shocking,” the Chief Justice remarked. The Bench, also comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana, issued notice to the accused, Himanshu Pathak, observing that the outcome of the proceedings could have a bearing on his rights.
‘Insensitive language'
Senior advocate Shobha Gupta, who had brought the High Court judgment to the Supreme Court’s attention, questioned the use of the word “preparation” in judicial orders to describe sexual acts falling short of penetration. She also drew the court’s attention to other recent High Court rulings which, she submitted, contained objectionable and insensitive language while referring to victims of sexual offences.
The Bench said it would examine the submissions.
The trial court had convicted Pathak under Sections 376 read with 511 of the IPC for attempting to commit rape and sentenced him to three years’ rigorous imprisonment along with a fine of ₹5,000. He was also sentenced to six months’ imprisonment under Section 342 for wrongful confinement, with both sentences to run concurrently.
According to the prosecution, the incident occurred on January 19, 2008, when the woman accompanied her father to Chhaya Studio in Amarpur to have her photograph taken. The accused, who owned the studio, allegedly asked her father to wait outside on the pretext of showing her the photograph on a computer. Once they were alone, he allegedly locked the door, tried to remove her salwar, undressed himself and sexually assaulted her. Hearing her cries, her father broke open the door, after which the accused allegedly escaped. An FIR was registered the following day.
The High Court, however, found an “absence of any evidence of penetration, even to the slightest extent, or any overt act unequivocally constituting an attempt to commit rape”, and held that the ingredients necessary to sustain the conviction under Sections 376 read with 511 of the IPC were not made out.
It instead found that the alleged acts of confining the woman inside the studio, shutting the door, attempting to remove her salwar and pressing her chest attracted the offence under Section 354 of the IPC. “These acts clearly establish the use of criminal force upon a woman with the intention, or at least the knowledge, that such acts were likely to outrage her modesty, thereby satisfying the essential ingredients of Section 354 IPC,” the High Court had held.

Anthropic has updated its usage policy to introduce restrictions on “sustained and needless abusive behaviour” towards its AI models. The company said the restrictions on abusing its models are intended for extreme cases in which users repeatedly act cruelly towards Claude without any discernible purpose. However, the company clarified that the rule does not cover ordinary user frustration, pushback against the chatbot’s responses, dark creative themes, or model testing and research. “Claude’s ability to end these interactions will remain the primary enforcement mechanism,” Anthropic said in its updated usage policy, which is set to take effect from November 12. The update builds on a measure Anthropic introduced in August 2025, allowing Claude to end conversations with users who persistently engage in harmful or abusive interactions. Anthropic gave Claude Opus 4 and 4.1 the ability to end conversations in rare cases involving persistent user abuse or harmful requests in 2025, particularly when users continue such behaviour despite repeated refusals and redirection. Claude can end a conversation only as a last resort, after attempts to redirect the interaction fail, or when explicitly asked to do so. It is instructed not to use this ability when users may be at imminent risk of harming themselves or others. Users can immediately start a new chat or edit and retry previous messages to continue an ended conversation. Anthropic said it will continue refining the feature based on user feedback. The feature was developed partly as an experiment into potential AI welfare, after testing found that Claude displayed an apparent aversion to harmful tasks and signs of distress in simulated interactions. In the past, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has also acknowledged that the moral status of AI models remains uncertain but said it is exploring low-cost measures to mitigate potential risks to their welfare. The debate around AI consciousness goes beyond Anthropic, with recent instances of AI models exhibiting behaviour that has raised questions about their ability to experience distress, develop preferences or display signs of self-preservation. In June 2025, a study by former OpenAI researcher Steven Adler found that GPT-4o sometimes resisted being replaced by a safer system in simulated, high-stakes scenarios, raising concerns about AI self-preservation. In a separate 2025 evaluation, Anthropic and OpenAI researchers found instances of models exhibiting deceptive or self-preserving behaviour under test conditions. Anthropic Tightens Rules On Election Interference, Weapons As the risks of AI misuse ramp up, Anthropic has also made key changes to the scope of Claude’s usage. This includes expanding restrictions on deceptive commercial and political campaigns. It now bars the use of Claude to obscure the source of a message or amplify content through fake accounts and posts. It also prohibits election-related misuse, including spreading misinformation about candidates or voting procedures, impersonating candidates or election officials, and attempting to suppress voter turnout. Anthropic has also expanded its weapons-related restrictions to include the prohibition of software and components that enable weapons to function, as well as activities such as arming drones and other autonomous vehicles. The updated policy also expands restrictions on surveillance, prohibiting tracking people without their consent, whether in real time or through the analysis of previously collected data. It also bars the use of Claude to decide or recommend whom law enforcement agencies should investigate, arrest or charge. Building or improving tools designed for surveillance is prohibited as well. However, Anthropic’s policy allows for certain modifications to restrictions under contracts with government customers, provided the company determines that contractual limits and applicable safeguards adequately mitigate potential harms. The policy also clarifies requirements for high-risk applications in areas such as health and finance, where AI-generated recommendations can have significant consequences for users.

A Russian drone hit Kyiv’s key Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River, marking the fourth consecutive day that Russia has targeted bridges used by tens of thousands of residents commuting between the city’s two banks. Video footage showed cars driving across the bridge as the drone plunged into the roadway and exploded in a burst of fire. Later on Sunday, a Russian airstrike hit Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-biggest city, killing one person and injured another six, mayor Ihor Terekhov said on Telegram.
- In Kyiv, Merz said Germany’s financial help was not only about protecting Ukraine’s territorial integrity. “We do it deeply in our own interest, for it is a matter of Europe’s security,” he said, adding that Russia was carrying out cyber-attacks and disinformation campaigns targeting European democracy. Russia has said accusations of hybrid warfare are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria.
- Zelenskyy said on Sunday he believed Russia might have shared jet-drone technology with its ally North Korea. Earlier in the war, North Korea supplied Russia with millions of artillery shells, and it has since provided ballistic missiles that Moscow regularly uses to attack Ukrainian cities. Asked if Russia had shared with North Korea the technology behind its latest generation of jet-powered drones, Zelenskyy told journalists: “They [Russia] are sharing with North Korea all the technologies. I don’t know about the ballistic and etc but I think yes, because North Korea helped them with missiles.”
- Meanwhile, Ukraine’s military has again used drones to deliver food and medicine to the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine,  foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said on Sunday. Oleshky, a frontline town on the Dnipro River, which separates Russian and Ukrainian forces, has become “a hell on earth” under Russian occupation since 2022, according to residents. Sybiha, who has previously accused Russia of starving residents, said the latest delivery contained almost four metric tons of food and medicine. Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said last month that Russia had not agreed to Ukrainian proposals to allow civilians to evacuate.
- As Zelenskyy on Sunday said the US wanted to hold a new round of peace talks with Ukraine and Russia by the end of October, India said it was seeking a greater role in brokering an end to the war, the foreign minister said. Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said at a Munich Security Conference in New Delhi on Sunday that India had been advocating for a peace deal “for many years, and in recent months we have got a little bit more involved beyond advocacy, so we have conversations with both Russia and Ukraine in this regard”. He said India was starting with Black Sea safety of shipping but also including discussions about grain and energy exports and “on non-attack possibilities”.

Quick Answer
OriginOS 7 adds useful upgrades like a customizable Control Center, Pet Pals themes, custom stickers, Liquid Glass controls, and Vivo Office Kit for seamless file sharing, clipboard sync, and screen mirroring across Windows and Mac.
Chinese smartphone makers replicate their software to look like iOS, aiming to appeal to users who want something familiar with an iPhone-like design. Vivo is no different. Their newly announced OriginOS 6 is a slight departure from the older Funtouch OS, which mimics iOS.
Vivo recently unveiled Origin OS 7 based on Android 17. Once again, Vivo gets heavily inspired by iOS and brought some of the biggest changes, many of which are welcome, while some I wish they had never made. You can view the full changelog here.
I have been using Origin OS 7 on my Vivo V80 for the past several days. Here are the 5 best Origin OS 7 features I found genuinely useful.
Table of Contents
5 Best OriginOS 7 Features
Adjust Liquid Glass Design
With iOS 26, Apple introduced a Liquid Glass design that most people hated.
The new glossy design made text harder to read and requires more power to render. Many Android skins have quickly adopted the Liquid Glass design, whether users like it or not, and Vivo is no different.
Vivo OriginOS 7 has incorporated the Liquid Glass design throughout the system. Unlike Apple, which introduced Liquid Glass transparency control a year after launch, OriginOS 7 offers three modes out of the box. You can set it to Realistic, Neutral, and Soft. If you are not a fan of Liquid Glass design, you can set it to Tinted.
One big note: the new Liquid Glass design seems limited to high-end smartphones, and the Vivo V80 lacks the feature entirely. It runs on Snapdragon 7 Gen 4. The biggest reason might be that mid-range chips can’t handle the heavy rendering required by the new glass design. Believing this, Vivo might have restricted this feature on other older and mid-range devices too.
Customizable Control Center
Another feature that Vivo borrowed from iOS is the ability to customize Control Center. For years, Android Control Center has remained the same. But with OriginOS 7, Vivo has taken a similar approach to Apple, letting you fully customize the layout and individual tiles.
The biggest change is that you can no longer be forced to use the default layout. You can rearrange or resize tiles however you want. With this functionality, you can also change the connectivity cards and media player, and remove them completely from the Control Center.
You can also rearrange the volume and brightness sliders, and even the network and media player, similar to what Apple allowed in iOS 26. If you’re not a fan of this new approach, Vivo also lets you choose the older Control Center layout in Settings.
However, by default, it is set to the old controls, and to change the layout, follow the steps below. Plus, you can also resize app icons on the home screen. You can simply long-press and drag them to your preferred size.
Lock Screen Customization and Pet Pals
Customization is the biggest focus on OriginOS 7. Vivo has brought several new theme options. I particularly liked the Pet Pals themes, where cute little pets appear on your home and lock screen and perform different actions based on the time of day, such as while the screen is on, tilting your phone, tapping, while your phone is on low battery, and also while you are doing actions such as listening to music and charging, and much more.
Stickers
In addition to more themes and lock screen customization, Vivo also added the ability to add custom stickers to the Home or lock screens; you can even add them to the always-on display.
Like widgets, you can drag and drop these stickers anywhere on the screen and resize them as you like. But these stickers won’t have any functionality like widgets or let you tap them to open an app. They are purely there for looks. Vivo offers some built-in stickers to get you started. However, you can also create any sticker using AI or photos already on your phone. You can tap it, convert it, and add it to your stickers; once done, you can add it anywhere on supported screens. Vivo also designed dedicated themes for adding stickers.
Vivo Office Kit
Vivo introduced Vivo Office Kit with OriginOS 6, and while it isn’t particularly new in OriginOS 7, it still remains one of the favorite features if you want to create an ecosystem. It lets your Vivo connect to your computer and sync the clipboard, share files, remote control, mirror your screen, sync your notes, and much more, similar to what you can do if you have an iPhone or Mac with the Apple ecosystem.
The best part is that it also works on Mac and other Windows devices. So unlike Apple, you don’t need to own a Mac and iPhone combination to use it. Whether you use Windows or Mac, your Vivo phone can connect to either of them and get all those handy features.
Even if you have never been in the Apple ecosystem, you might find these features very useful. Especially since every company has tried hard to bring an ecosystem between Android and Windows, or Android and macOS, or vice versa, and failed.
But somehow, many Chinese brands have figured out how to break the Apple ecosystem and connect a Vivo phone to an Apple device. And not just Vivo; OnePlus did the same with O+ Connect. Similarly, OPPO devices can connect to any PC or Mac apps.
Final Thoughts
Those are the five best features I truly love about OriginOS 7. To sum it up, OriginOS 7 brought Liquid Glass design to the OS. If you don’t like it, Vivo does offer options to disable it.
Next, it offers plenty of customization options, including the ability to add stickers (which I found unique) and new Pet Pals themes, which are my favorite. Plus, it has plenty of AI features, some of which run locally on your device, that can help with tasks like formatting text, plus AI features in the Photos app to edit and remove unwanted backgrounds.
Finally, the Vivo Office Kit is a great way to connect the Vivo phone to any PC, including Windows or Mac, and it lets you easily sync your clipboard and share files. Finally, Android’s Control Center is also customizable, similar to iOS, where you can set different sizes for each tile and rearrange them to suit your preferences.
Another feature that is missing on my Vivo V80 is a workbench feature. It is designed for power users who multitask a lot. You can place apps side by side and switch between them easily, just like windows on a PC. The best part is that you can rearrange them the way you want with different layouts, which makes proper multitasking possible on a small screen.
Another feature I really like is the ability to connect your Apple Watch or AirPods directly to your Vivo phone. Previously, Apple Watch only worked with an iPhone. With OriginOS 7, you can pair your Apple Watch and sync your data with a Vivo phone; for AirPods, it also shows the battery level and total, just like on iPhones.
Vivo officially announced OriginOS 7 globally, but still hasn’t announced an official global supported device list. However, we keep track of all the latest OriginOS 7 updates in a separate timeline post. You can bookmark the post for the latest OriginOS 7 updates.

Ukraine: ‘I was lucky not to die. I had guitars with me on the frontline’
Andriy Zholob, vocalist/guitarist, Beton: When MTV arrived in Ukraine, I heard Nirvana, the Offspring, Bad Brains, Social Distortion and thrash metal, and realised that all this started from punk rock. Our drummer and I were in a ska-punk band first, but when our vocalist became pregnant we started Beton in 2017 and played lots of festivals.
Everything changed with the invasion. In 2022, I started military service as a surgeon on the frontline. We were attacked many times and on at least four occasions I was lucky not to die. I had guitars with me on the frontline and every evening we’d play just to relax. At one point, my commander gave me eight days off to record a battle song for our brigade and Beton did a cover of the Clash’s London Calling – Kyiv Calling – to raise money for the Ukrainian resistance. I wanted to use punk rock to stand against evil.
I finished my service two years ago, quit medicine and now work with veterans, many of whom come to our gigs. There are guys and girls with prosthetics, slam dancing, singing along and everything. It’s a real moment of punk rock unity. We play two or three shows every month, but I like to spend time in the mountains. Although I play punk rock, sometimes I need silence.
Morocco and Spain: ‘People would tell me: you love Satan’
Nao, vocalist, Taqbir: In the Muslim community of Morocco, where I come from, the punk look is not accepted. For a long time, I had to perform anonymously, with my face covered, in case people recognised me and wanted to hurt me. Being a punk is not for the faint-hearted. Even in Spain, where I live now, I felt isolated as an immigrant and as a woman who did crazy things to my hair. People would tell me: “You love Satan.”
I heard Crass when I was 13. They were the first band I heard where I recognised myself in the lyrics, because I felt oppressed by religion. Then through chatting with friends online, I discovered more. I’d go to shows in Madrid, take off my hijab and wear makeup. It was a double life that meant I finally felt free to be myself, but for a long time punk cost me my relationship with my family.
Being in Taqbir really helped. I was very angry, so fronting the band was like a cure for this rage. People seem to connect with the rawness. We’ve played in north Africa and the UK and my dream is to be able one day to play in Morocco. Punk has helped me see that things don’t have to be black and white: people can be punk and Muslim and gay. Although there’s anger, our message is positive. If you’re feeling oppressed or that you cannot be yourself in this society, Taqbir are for you.
South Africa: ‘Being from Soweto automatically makes you political’
Abdula Skink, vocalist, Twenty One Children: A lot of kids in Johannesburg got into punk because there were no jobs or infrastructure for us. I grew up in a hip-hop house, but found bands such as Suicidal Tendencies and Black Flag through video games and older friends who skated. Punk just flicked all these switches in my head. Our guitarist, Thula, used to play in TCIYF, the first all-black punk band in South Africa. When we started our band in 2023, I was an assistant teacher for 21 autistic kids, so that became our name. I was also 21, so it felt like a lucky number.
Being from Soweto automatically makes you political. All the great revolutionaries – Hugh Masekela, Nobel prize winners, Desmond Tutu and so on – came from here. Our motto is: if something isn’t true, we won’t sing about it. Our song Scab is about a time I was stopped by police because I was skating through a historically Afrikaans/white area. I had green hair and the policeman was like: “You’re on drugs.” He ripped my Suicidal Tendencies T-shirt, dropped my laptop from my bag on the street and tried to take my skateboard. I wasn’t doing anything illegal. They were just fucking with me. Mostly, we try to make a difference in our communities. Thula built the first DIY skate park in Soweto; we’ve done charity shows for orphanages and such. For us, punk is not so much a livelihood but a way of life.
India: ‘We were bombarded with threatening messages’
Aditya Naik, vocalist/guitarist, Punk on Toast: I grew up listening to Bad Religion, NOFX, the Sex Pistols and the Clash and saw a satirical commentary about our times, so I started the band when I was 17 so I could talk about what was happening around us. In India, you see cruelty or injustice on every corner, so we don’t relate to mainstream music, which ignores this.
At the moment, there’s a lot of oppression of artists. After our song Modified talked about what the right wing are trying to do with us, we were bombarded with threatening messages online. People went through all our profiles, trying to find our phone numbers, where we live, our employers. It felt like being molested. Although we’ve had coverage in Rolling Stone India, the punk scene mostly flies under the radar, but that means we’re freer to sing about what we want.
We took part in the recent Cockroach protests in Mumbai, which alerted people to how things are and got everybody out on the street. Before that, India felt like a small elite club where everyone else is the “cockroaches”, so it was like seeing a phoenix: hope. The punk scene is growing, with our friends Pacifist and Emergency Trigger and bands such as the Light Years Explode and the Riot Peddlers. It’s more about documenting our times and standing for what’s right rather than selling lots of records, but punk rock gave me the greatest superpower: question everything.
Brazil: ‘Under a military dictatorship, there were kids brave enough to play with passion and fury’
Henrike Baliu, vocalist, Blind Pigs and Armada: When the original UK punk explosion happened in 1977, my dad was a naval engineer stationed in Southampton. He saw the Boomtown Rats performing Lookin’ After No 1 on Top of the Pops and told the guy in the record shop: “Give me everything you’ve got” – which meant the Sex Pistols, Generation X and so on.
Years later, when I was 12, I played some of my dad’s records to my friends and they told me about the punk scene in Brazil. Bands such as Ratos de Porão, Inocentes and Cólera sang about life under a military dictatorship, which Brazil was in the 80s. People were disappearing or being murdered, so it blows my mind that under a dictatorship with virtually zero news, poverty and police brutality there were kids with spiky hair brave enough to wear fake leather jackets and play with passion and fury. Those bands were pioneers who paved the way for us.
Blind Pigs were probably the biggest punk band in Brazil over the last 30 years, but now I’m focused on Armada. We are bilingual and sing in Portuguese and English. When we recorded our English language album, Tales of Treason, the country was going through another crazy time politically and the right wing were on the rise again. With the music, I wanted to warn people to learn from history: “Dudes, you don’t want that again.”
Latvia: ‘On stage I let out all my anger’
Evisa Petrovka, vocalist, Depustūtes: In high school, I didn’t really like pop, so I got into metal, but I felt it was missing lyrical depth, so punk really resonated. Ramones and the Sex Pistols sang about the same stuff that made me mad or frustrated. The Dead Kennedys’ political commentary really connected and then I discovered riot grrrl. As I got older, I realised there was a punk scene here in Riga and a whole community of people like me.
There’s so much going on in the world – I’ll never run out of topics and writing and singing in the band never gets boring. On stage, I let out all my anger. Whether I’m running or crawling on the floor, it’s just pure emotion. Singing in Latvian makes it easier to sing about local politics. Lately, we’ve been addressing how people who actually benefit society aren’t getting paid as well as those who aren’t, but I sing about societal norms and stereotyping.
Our song Mrs Pieklājība (Mrs Polite) starts, in a mocking way: “I love listening to men and being obedient.” It was inspired by people telling me “you should smile more” or “women don’t dress like that”. There’s always been at least two women in the band, but most people are really supportive. I love inspiring other girls’ lives. A lot of them come up after shows and say: “That was so inspiring. I wish I could speak as freely as you.”
China: ‘Our albums were confiscated and our work was taken offline’
Wu Wei, vocalist, SMZB: Wuhan and Beijing were the first cities in China to have punk music. I founded the first punk band in Wuhan in 1996 after falling in love with tapes that my friends sent me from the US – initially the Sex Pistols, the Clash, Ramones and then bands with other styles, such as US Bombs, Suicide Machine and Rancid. Through punk, I finally found a way to express myself. Although the scene is still quite small, we were one of the first bands to go on national tours, which influenced the development of punk in other cities. We sing about the environment we operate in: political aspects and things I’ve witnessed in daily life under the system in China.
A few years ago, the authorities prohibited us from performing. Some albums were confiscated, our work was taken offline and our record company was forced to terminate our contract. Despite this, our audiences have a wide age span and range from other punks and bands to art workers, students and ordinary wage-earners. Punk has brought me so many things, from running the bar Wuhan Prison to my personal life. I’ve now settled in the UK with my family, but frequently return to Wuhan for rehearsals and recording. SMZB just released a bilingual album, When the Party Is Over, for our 30th anniversary. Punk has given me my life.
Greenland: ‘I’m 38, a father, still have my piercings and still consider myself a punk’
Jenseeraq Olsen, vocalist/guitarist, Uummat: We have a running joke with Iceland that they are green and we are ice, so most people live on the coast. I was in Denmark for a festival recently and realised that there were more people there – 70,000 – than the entire Greenlandic population. Punk is very much a minority interest here, but I was always rebellious when I was young and didn’t like the mainstream pop my friends were into.
After I saw an advert for Blink-182’s Enema of the State album after the movie American Pie, I realised they were the band I’d been searching for. I was teased for having multicoloured hair and ripped clothes, but Blink were a big influence on Uummat, which means “heart”. We were different from other bands in Greenland and people connected with it: we’ve played to 2,000 people.
I’ve never really written political songs, but Trump’s threat to annex Greenland has made a lot of people emotional, stressed and nervous, which I’m sure will come out in the music. I’m 38, a father and manage a youth centre now, but Blink resonate as much as they did when I was 15. I still have my piercings and I still consider myself a punk. Meanwhile, my 11-year-old son listens to the same music and plays guitar like me. He thinks labels like “punk” are for adults, but he likes the word, so he’ll probably follow in my footsteps.

Navi Pillay, former UN human rights chief, wins Nobel Peace Prize
- Published
Former UN human rights chief and International Court of Justice judge Navi Pillay has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize.
The South African judge was recognised "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said.
Pillay, 85, has taken part in high-profile work considering allegations of human rights violations during a decades-long career, including in Rwanda, Myanmar and Gaza.
Her early work included defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa, and on Friday she became the country's fifth Peace Prize winner - following in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu.
Pillay's work had been "instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted", said the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee Jørgen Watne Frydnes.
"Navi Pillay's commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career," he said.
"At a time of existential challenges - including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time - international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity."
Frydnes said the committee had not been able to notify Pillay that she had won in advance, "so my message to her would be 'if you see a Norwegian number calling, please pick up'".
Shortly afterwards, Pillay reacted to the news by saying "it must be a joke" and thanked those who had gathered to applaud her.
"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked. Last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, gave her medal to the US president in January as "recognition for his unique commitment with our freedom".
Navanethem "Navi" Pillay grew up in South Africa during apartheid as a bus driver's daughter in a poor Indian section of Durban.
She went on to become the first woman to establish a law practice in Natal Province in 1967, and later the first non-white woman to be appointed to the country's high court.
Pillay served as a judge on the UN-backed International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda - focused on the 1994 genocide in which 800,000 people were killed - including four years as its president.
From 2021-25, she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory - a fact-finding body established by the UN Human Rights Council to investigate alleged violations of international law.
The commission concluded that Israel had committed genocidal acts in Gaza and that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant, had "incited the commission of genocide" in their speeches and statements.
The three-member expert panel did not speak officially for the UN and had no legal authority. Israel rejected its findings and accused the three members of the commission of serving as "Hamas proxies".
The panel had previously concluded that Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups committed war crimes and other grave violations of international law on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and another 251 taken hostage. The same report also accused Israel of war crimes.
Reacting to Pillay's award on Friday, Israel's Foreign Ministry said it represented a "grotesque weaponisation of an award to legitimise anti-Israel hatred and prejudice".
It said in a statement: "Her role in the relentless, politically motivated demonisation of Israel and promotion of the genoLIE speaks volumes."
Frydnes said the Nobel organisation was not taking a position on whether the Israeli offensive in Gaza amounted to genocide.
Pillay is currently a judge on the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in the case where Myanmar stands accused by The Gambia of genocide against the Rohingya people.
Myanmar has denied deliberately trying to destroy the minority Muslim population, with a government representative telling the court in January that the allegation was "unsubstantiated".
UN human rights chief Volker Turk said Pillay's recognition was "a reaffirmation that human rights, the rule of law and justice, and accountability are fundamental to everything, to peace, to security, and prosperity".
South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa said she had been a "pioneering defence attorney for anti-apartheid activists" who had worked to "uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally".
Amnesty International Secretary-General Agnès Callamard said she was with Pillay when she learned she had won - and called her an "inspired choice" for the award.
"At a time when both international law and justice are under attack, when too many states attempt to hollow them out, her Nobel Peace Prize could not come at a better time," she said.
