While thousands of Indian students head overseas annually for medical degrees, comprising a heavily monitored segment under the National Medical Commission (NMC) and the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS), parliamentary disclosures indicate that centralised tracking of specific discipline-wise student outflows remains complex.
But for many, the journey culminates in a grueling, high-stakes afternoon inside an Indian examination hall. When the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) released the results for the Foreign Medical Graduate Examination (FMGE) June 2026, the pass rate had plummeted sharply to just 12.4%, triggering nationwide discussions, student protests, and scrutiny over what is locking foreign medical graduates out of medical practice.
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)
The panic after the paper
Dr. Chaynika Soni, a medical intern in a Government Hospital in Rajasthan who cleared the exam in her second attempt after graduating from Belarus in 2024, recalls, “Every single year after the exam, you’ll see the same thing. Students come out saying, ‘The paper was impossible.’ ‘It was too hard.’ ‘Nobody could solve it.’ Coaching centers will upload videos saying, ‘The paper was unexpected.’ Telegram groups will be filled with panic.”
This panic was visible during the June session, where candidates faced sudden structural shifts. Describing his experience with the exam pattern, Dr. Kshitij Anand said, “The questions were relatively long and time-consuming. I felt the questions were completely unrelated to what I studied. There were some questions I could get direct answers for, but it wasn’t much. They give you questions and options in a way that you take time to figure out answers but not enough time to think.”
He adds that the introduction of unfamiliar video modules caught aspirants off guard: “The Board gave us video questions which I agreed were manageable, but it was a new pattern. The FMGE conducted last January was way more image-based, and the options were comparatively easier to tap than this one. Also, the diagrams I have never seen before.”
Acknowledging these pressures, Professor Dr. Karan Juneja, National Convenor of IMA Junior Doctors’ Network, points out that “More video-based questions (this time), clinical-based questions will be tough for FMG’s [as they are] not exposed to Indian setting and less time make the exam tough.”
Inside the recall analysis
As the National Board of Examinations does not release official FMGE question papers, student-reconstructed “recall” papers serve as the baseline for preparation. A look at the high-weightage sections — Community Medicine (PSM), Internal Medicine, and Obstetrics and Gynaecology — reveals distinct hurdles.
Community Medicine heavily tests India-specific public health administration, including domestic health committees like the Bhore or Kartar Singh committees, local staffing norms at Primary Health Centres, and administrative schemes that foreign universities naturally omit. For a student trained overseas, this often translates to unfamiliar civic administration rather than core medicine.
Conversely, Internal Medicine acts as a control case focused on universal clinical reasoning, ranging from ABG analysis to emergency cardiac protocols. Meanwhile, Obstetrics and Gynaecology balances international diagnostic criteria with clinical application, though candidate performance frequently hinges on interpreting embedded clinical images, manoeuvres, or diagnostic scans.
Weighing these system dynamics, Dr. Samar Kumar, National FMG In-charge for the Federation of All India Medical Association (FAIMA), explains, “In departments such as Medicine, Surgery, and Obstetrics & Gynaecology, Indian hospitals generally see a very large number of patients. This gives doctors and students exposure to a wide variety of clinical presentations and allows them to learn how to manage patients even when resources are limited. I would particularly highlight Community Medicine... If an FMG studies Medicine, Surgery, Obstetrics & Gynaecology, and Community Medicine properly, focuses on clinical concepts, and practices clinical and image-based questions, they should find these areas much more manageable in the FMGE.”
Conceptual depth and the gap in coaching materials
Beyond traditional curriculum differences, candidates found that the depth of questioning defied standard coaching modules. Dr. Ruhi Kumari, who appeared in the June session, explains, “We weren’t trained that way. For example, there was a question on cholera; the answer was an increase in cAMP. I knew it was an increase in cAMP (cyclic Adenosine Monophosphate), but the options were given in biochemistry language. Like, you have to know what cAMP is in biochemistry; only then can you answer that. No coaching institute is teaching anyone like this. Only USMLE tutors do. Because USMLE has always asked in-depth questions. Many clinical questions expect you to have clinical experience. But that’s just unfair, because I will only get that experience after I visit the clinic.”
Dr. Kumari further notes the obsolescence of traditional prep material: “Marrow [an online platform) questions were considered the standard before this exam, but I can tell you they are not anymore. There were a lot of questions that weren’t even asked in many previous years' papers, that flustered everyone... Honestly, I am not sure which resource would give me the most apt training, because no institute is teaching you like that at present. Doing INICET papers is not going to help you, or even NEET-PG papers.”
Logistics, exam conditions, and the transparency debate
The academic difficulty was further compounded by severe logistical hurdles on test day. Dr. Samar Kumar outlines the physical toll: “The first issue was related to examination centres. Multiple centres had inadequate facilities. Some did not have coolers or fans, and in some cases, even drinking water was not adequately available. As you know, the FMG examination is five hours, and overall it takes eight hours. Maintaining concentration in such tough conditions, especially during extreme summer, is something beyond the capacity of many students and FMG doctors particularly when they are not provided with adequate facilities.”
He added regarding the sudden format changes, “The second and most important issue was the sudden introduction of video-based questions in the FMG June 2026 examination. FMGs opposed this later as well and conducted protests regarding this issue in Delhi, Gautam Nagar. The demand of the students was to provide compensation for the sudden introduction of video-based questions, but NBEMS denied the demand.”
Adding to student frustration is a perceived lack of institutional accountability. Dr. Kumar said, “Moreover, the FMG examination does not have any kind of transparency. The questions and answers have never been shown to FMGs. Thus, no one knows how they failed by just one mark, five marks, or ten marks... Then why does NBEMS say that they cannot show the questions and answers together? Why can’t the examination questions and their corresponding answers be disclosed?”
FMGE versus NEET-PG and the time crunch
Comparing the screening test to domestic evaluations, Professor Dr. Karan Juneja, National Convenor of IMA Junior Doctors’ Network, notes that “NEET PG exam standard is being given in FMGE exam as the board-making exam is the same NBE.”
While Indian MBBS graduates prepping for NEET-PG sit within a mature ecosystem of shared question banks and peer networks, foreign-trained graduates often experience thinner access to these informal pipelines.
Dr. Samar Kumar contrasts the two exams, “Recently, FMGE has also included video-based and lengthy clinically oriented questions, which adds another dimension to the examination... FMGE continues to have 300 questions, whereas NEET-PG has moved from the earlier 200-question format to 180 questions. Therefore, FMGE tests not only clinical knowledge and application but also a candidate’s ability to maintain concentration and consistency throughout a long examination. NEET-PG, on the other hand, has its own competitive dynamics, including negative marking and a highly competitive selection process. But if you remove these factors from NEET-PG, then it becomes easier than FMGE.”
This time crunch is intensified by structural scheduling. Dr. Anjali Ayappan from Kochi points out, “Two months is simply not enough preparation time for FMG students, especially considering the amount of syllabus and the situation most FMGs are already in. And bringing the next exam forward to October is especially bad for the June pass-outs. They barely get any time to prepare after the result, and then suddenly they’re expected to appear again in October.”
The long road to registration
Clearing the exam is only the first milestone; graduates face a complex administrative labyrinth before they can practice. Dr. Parvathy Sabu, who cleared the exam and works in a Government Hospital in Thiruvananthapuram, said, “Internship posts for FMGs are fewer across almost every State, and protests to increase seats are seen often... By the time you get PR [permanent registration], best-case scenario, approximately 8 years have gone by (including course duration) and a lot of money. Abroad MBBS is a very long-term investment that many don’t realise initially. I think the integration into Indian healthcare and internship issues are the biggest challenges faced by FMGs.”
Reflecting on these cumulative pressures, Dr. Madhavi Gurung, an FMG aspirant who studied in the U.K., concludes, “Many of my friends skipped FMGE and are now doing residency in the U.S., some are working non-training jobs in the U.K., and some are on track to settle in Australia. The struggle doesn’t end after NEET-UG. And with rising competition and reservation quotas, the system is tough. Every year wasted in endless NEET attempts can drain your mental health and confidence. I’m now planning to take AMC Part 1 by the end of this year and hopefully move abroad permanently.”

Hamam al-Hammami, the Omani co-pilot on the flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv who attacked the flight captain in a bid to crash the aircraft at Ben Gurion Airport, was reportedly inspired by the 9/11 attacks, a preliminary investigation has revealed. According to a statement from the United Arab Emirates’ (UAE) Attorney General, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, carried by state media, the suspect wanted to carry out an attack similar to 9/11, which led him to pursue an aviation career. 1. According to a statement from the UAE Attorney General, "The idea of carrying out a similar operation using an aircraft became firmly established in his mind, which, according to his confessions, was connected to his decision to pursue a career in aviation." The statement further said that Al-Hammami wanted to carry out "a premeditated plot with a terrorist objective, aimed at taking control of the aircraft and using it to carry out a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion Airport,” with the intent of causing "the greatest possible number of casualties." 2. The preliminary investigation also revealed that the 30 September flight wasn't Al-Hammami's first to Israel. The suspect had already taken part in two flights to Ben Gurion Airport to become familiar with the route and airport in preparation for the attack. While he told the investigating agencies that it was a lone-wolf attack, an investigation is underway to determine the possible involvement of others. 3. According to the statement, he began gravitating towards extremism and terrorism in 2017 while studying in Australia. His views were shaped by extremist publications and online material that praised terrorist groups and suicide attacks. The statement said Al-Hammami "prepared himself psychologically and physically to carry out his plot by increasing his exposure to material inciting terrorism and training in boxing under a private coach.” 4. The pilot who intervened and prevented the plane from crashing was assigned to the return flight and was near the cockpit when Al-Hammami carried out the attack. State media said, "He noticed the cockpit door opening and closing repeatedly in an unusual manner, which aroused his suspicions," and added that he tried to enter the cockpit using the access code and saw the attack after gaining entry. 5. The UAE said it had reviewed flydubai’s hiring process for Al-Hammami. According to the state-run news agency, investigators confirmed that the suspect fulfilled the employment criteria: he held a pilot’s licence, submitted a good-conduct certificate and passed the required checks. “However, none of the procedures revealed any indications of his extremist views or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot,” it said. On 30 September, Al-Hammami attacked flight captain Smit Machchhar with a crash axe in an attempt to crash the aircraft, which was carrying over 170 people, mostly Israelis. The attempt failed after Machchhar unlocked the cockpit door despite being seriously injured. Crew members and passengers subdued the suspect, while two off-duty pilots made an emergency landing at a civilian and military base in Saudi Arabia's Tabuk. The update from the UAE provides the most detailed account so far of the attack, along with the co-pilot's history and the events that contributed to what the agency described as his extremist views. On Tuesday (October 6, 2026), Kenya confirmed its first Ebola case after a Kenyan national who had returned from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) died in Nairobi. According to media reports that quoted Kenya’s Health Minister Aden Duale, he had lived in the DRC for years and had travelled back home by road before taking a flight to Nairobi.
After the DRC declared an Ebola outbreak in May, Uganda also reported cases and deaths from Ebola. However, after Uganda was declared free of the disease by the World Health Organisation (WHO), the cases have occurred only in the DRC. This is the first case in which an Ebola death has occurred in another country, raising significant concern regarding transmissibility for public health authorities.
What are the details of the case
According to Mr. Duale, the Kenyan national had been living in the DRC for several years and had fallen ill about a month ago. He had been treated in several hospitals in the DRC and died days after arriving in the capital, Nairobi.
He had travelled by road from DRC to Uganda and then boarded a flight to Nairobi, undergoing public screening with other passengers at the airport, but missed being picked up. He went home and was taken to hospital by a relative when he became sicker. He tested positive for the dangerous Bundibugyo strain, which has neither specialised treatment nor a vaccine until now. (Human trials for a vaccine were started in July, and three other candidates are in the pipeline.)
Eight of the patient’s family members and 21 healthcare workers have been quarantined. Screening at all airports. Another 23 passengers and four crew members who travelled on the flight he took from Uganda are also being traced. The traced individuals will remain in isolation for 21 days and will be allowed to leave if they do not show any symptoms.
Why is this fresh cause for concern?
The virus is highly infectious and spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids. This is the 17th outbreak in the DRC and is said to be its deadliest, having claimed over 4,000 lives since May this year. Over 8,300 cases have been confirmed across the country.
Meanwhile, the WHO has warned that the epidemic will surpass the regional 2014-2016 outbreak, which killed over 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
Despite an outbreak in the region, the global health body has not been in favour of imposing travel and trade restrictions on the affected regions. However, not all international travellers are required to fill out a self-declaration form specifying whether they have been in any of the Ebola-affected countries or if they have suffered any symptoms lately.
In Kenya, health authorities explained that the patient who died had managed to pass through the screening without raising any red flags because the medicines he was on probably masked the symptoms as he walked past.
The course ahead
Now that the virus has entered Kenya, the key task for health authorities in the country is firstly to stop the chain of transmission, beginning with the primary contacts already isolated. As per the outbreak protocol, this includes rapid contact tracing, immediate isolation of anyone who develops symptoms, and testing. Strict infection-control measures must be put in place in Kenya, and targeted information on prevention and control disseminated among communities.
Screening and surveillance have been intensified at airports in Kenya. However, at a time when it is impossible to stop global movement, it’s crucial to make sure that all nations maintain vigilance at their entry ports and pick up patients with detectable symptoms. Port authorities should also stress on the seriousness of honestly declaring travel history and symptoms.

- A claim that the U.S. Postal Service plans to begin a pilot program that would attach cameras similar to the dashboard cameras used by police to its delivery vehicles circulated online in late September and early October.
- The claim stemmed from a social media post by the Canton, Ohio, branch of the National Association of Letter Carriers, the union that represents postal workers. The post included an alleged letter from USPS labor relations that outlined the proposed pilot program.
- The claim appears to be true, but Snopes bases its ratings on primary evidence and has not yet independently verified the validity of the letter or its content. As such, we have left this claim unrated.
- Snopes reached out to the USPS, the National Association of Letter Carriers and Next Base, the dashcam company alleged to be partnering with the Postal Service on the pilot program. We will update this article if we hear back.
A claim that the United States Postal Service plan to begin a pilot program that would attach cameras similar to dashboard cameras used by police departments to its delivery vehicles circulated online in late September and early October. 
People across social media platforms and Reddit shared an alleged letter from USPS labor relations to the president of the National Association of Letter Carriers, the union that represents USPS postal workers, that claimed "Next Base, a dash cam manufacturing company, will work with the Postal Service to use the subject cameras to collect infrastructure data within the Washington, DC delivery area."
The posts claimed the cameras would "scan and analyze roads, signage, maps, roadways and sidewalks." The online rumor gained steam as the use of surveillance cameras such as Flock cameras garnered attention and increasing backlash nationwide.
Snopes bases its truth ratings on primary evidence. As such, we've opted to leave this claim unrated until we receive direct confirmation about the implementation of the pilot program from the USPS, the National Association of Letter Carriers and/or Next Base. We've reached out to all parties and will update this article if we hear back.
However, the claim appears to be true, according to a social media post by the NALC's Branch 238, the local union for Canton, Ohio.
On Sept. 25, the union posted a screenshot of the letter and stated, incorrectly, "Please note the cameras are on the OUTSIDE of the vehicles." (The letter in question clearly stated, "These cameras will be forward-facing and installed inside the delivery vehicle.")
The union's post concluded, "Right now, this is just a pilot program. Please do not panic. Please do not call President Smith, he has enough to do! The comments are turned off, too many drama queens again!"
Comments under the post claimed the pilot program was only for the Washington, D.C., area.
Snopes could not locate a Facebook account for Washington, D.C.'s Branch 142 to see if it had also posted about the letter. The primary Facebook account for the NACL had no posts referring to the letter, Next Base or the reported pilot program.
The letter, addressed to NACL president Brian Renfroe on USPS labor relations letterhead, read:
As a matter of general interest, the Postal Service will partner with a company called Next Base to test the use of cameras in our various delivery vehicles.
Next Base, a dash cam manufacturing company, will work with the Postal Service to use the subject cameras to collect infrastructure data within the Washington, DC delivery area.
Next Base cameras will scan and analyze roads, signage, maps, roadways and sidewalks.
The purpose of this pilot is to leverage the Postal Service's unique ability to collect this valuable data due to the scale and frequency with which our fleet of postal vehicles travel the streets of every community across the country.
The cameras will be installed by Next Base on the dashboards of select delivery vehicles. These cameras will be forward-facing and installed inside the delivery vehicle. The cameras will begin recording as soon as the vehicle is in drive and outside the postal facility geofence. The cameras will not hinder the vehicle operator's field of vision, nor does it record audio.
City carrier employees' participation ins this pilot will be limited to operating the modified vehicles during the performance of their regular assigned street delivery duties. All postal insignia and postal employee images will be redacted.
The pilot test is scheduled to begin on September 21 and is expected to run for several months. The Postal Service intends to utilize one hundred delivery vehicles located at the Lammond Riggs Post Office, and the Section 19 Carrier Annex.
The Lammond Riggs Post Office is located at 6200 N. Capitol St. NW in Washington, D.C. The letter and the union's statement were then reported on by credible tech news outlet 404 Media, which also stated it got confirmation from the USPS.
The Postal Service reportedly told 404 Media it was "conducting a limited pilot to assess whether vehicle-mounted cameras can help identify roadway conditions and support community safety. The pilot includes privacy safeguards and requires no additional action from employees. Findings will inform any future decisions."
The story was picked up by other tech news outlets such as Gizmodo, Cybernews and Gadget Review, citing 404 Media's report.
According to its website, Next Base is a U.K.-based company that bills itself as the "largest smart Dash Cam brand in the world" and claims it holds "over 80% of the UK market by volume."

The Indonesian government has been accused of “gross negligence” in a class action lawsuit over its handling of wildfires that have cloaked large parts of South-east Asia in a toxic haze, shuttered schools and caused a spike in respiratory illnesses.
The lawsuit, filed by indigenous and civil society groups in the Indonesian part of Borneo, named President Prabowo Subianto and the governor of West Kalimantan among 10 defendants. The case seeks comprehensive recovery and rehabilitation measures that would include covering the healthcare costs of residents.
None of those named in the lawsuit attended the opening day of court in West Kalimantan’s provincial capital Pontianak on Wednesday, leading judges to adjourn the hearing until 21 October.
“We feel sad and regretful about their absence … But on the other hand, we also understand that perhaps this haze condition caused them to be unable to land in Pontianak,” the plaintiffs’ lawyer, Glorio Sanen, told reporters.
Sanen said the case was “a step to address the problem” of wildfires that flare up annually in Indonesia, where they are often lit as a cheap way to clear land for oil palm planting.
Indonesia, the world’s largest producer of palm oil, has been accused of not doing enough to stop the so-called “slash and burn” land clearances, although the government has vowed a crackdown and deployed the military to fight the fires.
The blazes hit a crisis point this year due to an unusually intense El Niño weather phenomenon, which has created drier-than-usual conditions, sending a putrid smog to Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore, and even the Philippines.
The transboundary haze has angered Indonesia’s neighbours. Schools in the Malaysian state of Johor, just north of Singapore, were to be closed on Thursday and Friday due to deteriorating air quality, local authorities said.
The four plaintiffs in the West Kalimantan lawsuit, which was filed last month, include a chapter of Indigenous NGO AMAN and the local branch of Catholic Youth.
Yakobus Kumis, a plaintiff representing a Dayak ethnic group, indigenous to the island of Borneo, expressed disappointment that government representatives did not attend this week’s hearing, saying it was a “way of the central government teaching the people that violating the law is OK.”
He said the government ignored warning signs ahead of the fires breaking out, and called for the smoke crisis to be classified as a national disaster.
A similar lawsuit filed last year at a court in South Sumatra was dismissed.
The presidential office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report

India’s leprosy programme is falling short of several projections set for 2025-26. The country reported 91,783 new leprosy cases in 2025-26, 41.2% higher than the projected 65,000. New cases among children were 91.6% above the projection while the rate of Grade 2 Disability (G2D) among new cases was 1.34 per million, against a projected one per million.
India’s national prevalence rate was 0.56 cases per 10,000 population at the end of March 2026, below the elimination target of a prevalence rate below one case per 10,000.
But the burden remains concentrated geographically. Chhattisgarh had the highest prevalence among States/UTs at 1.66 cases per 10,000 population, followed by Jharkhand (1.51), Chandigarh (1.49), Odisha (1.25) and Maharashtra (1.14).
At the district level, 14.8% of districts had a prevalence rate above one case per 10,000 in 2025-26, down from 18.6% in 2013-14 but 114 districts still remained above the programme’s elimination target. Moreover, only 148 districts have provisionally achieved interruption of transmission, against a projected 300.
G2D was also concentrated in a few States/UTs. Chandigarh, Delhi, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Odisha together accounted for 42.5% of the 1,945 G2D cases reported in 2025-26. Chandigarh recorded the highest rate at 13.54 per million, followed by Delhi (11.53) and Chhattisgarh (7.87).
Single-Dose Rifampicin Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (SDR PEP), a preventive dose given to people who have been in contact with a leprosy patient, was administered to 91.2% of the 16.94 lakh eligible contacts in 2025-26, up from 71.4% of the 6.48 lakh in 2019-20.
Source: National Leprosy Eradication Programme (2025-26) and National Strategic Plan and Roadmap for Leprosy 2023-2027

It’s rare to see a dramatic feature filmmaker move into the realm of documentary with the craftmanship and authority and insightful power summoned by Ava DuVernay. “13th,” the documentary she made back in 2016, was a revelation — it told the lacerating story of how the 13th Amendment to the Constitution, which abolished slavery, was a revolutionary act of law that, at the same time, opened the door to the way that numerous dimensions of slavery would be perpetuated in America under different names and tactics. The film was despairing and inspiring in equal measure; it cleansed you with the truth.
Tonight, the New York Film Festival presented the premiere of “14th,” a documentary follow-up in which DuVernay sets her sights on the 14th Amendment, a Constitutional addendum, ratified in 1868, that was so monumental — it guarantees equal protection under the law, but also encompasses five intricate sections that deal with issues from insurrection to due process — that one observer calls it “a Constitution in and of itself,” and another hails it as “the everything bagel of democracy.”
Popular on Variety
“14th,” I’m pleased to report, exerts the same kind of historical/topical force that “13th” did. DuVernay, while she works in an extremely accessible and mainstream way, has a singular gift for making the nuances of history come alive. “14th” is steeped in history, but it’s not a dry lecture. Instead, DuVernay cuts through the dusty complacency with which we tend to regard the Constitution (just hearing that word can make you feel like you’re back in school) and shows you that the Constitution is a living, breathing document, one that we fail to heed at our peril. Which is more or less what’s happening today.
A potent movie about history almost has to surprise you. It needs to show you that what you think you know isn’t the half of it. “14th” kicks off with the cutting insight that the three amendments to the Constitution that were passed in the aftermath of the Civil War — the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments — represented nothing less than a restart of American life and society. Yet we don’t necessarily talk about them that way. Everyone knows who “the framers” of the Constitution were (Hamilton, Jefferson, Franklin), but “14th” argues that the period just after the cataclysm of the Civil War had its own framers, who were nearly as significant. Thaddeus Stevens, a member of the House of Representatives who was part of the Radical Republican faction of the 1860s, is a figure who, according to one of the film’s observers, “created the world we live in today.”
With the abolition of slavery, four million people who were formerly enslaved were suddenly added to the fabric of American society. How would that work? DuVernay tell the story of Reconstruction through fresh eyes, and part of the power of her chronicle is that she doesn’t stint on the joy and liberation that were part of it. Black Americans, who were now citizens, formed communities and industries, they became newspaper editors and law enforcers, as well as politicians (there were 1,000 newly elected Black representatives). But it’s more than that. The point is made that Black people, for the first time in American life, could create a fully realized dream of who they wanted to be as individuals. But this would not work unless their citizenship was enshrined. That’s the first thing the 14th Amendment did. It guaranteed equal protection under the law, and it established birthright citizenship for all people born in the United States — a radical idea, one designed to apply to both the children of former enslaved people and the children of immigrants, because what that represented was a stepping up of the rejection of the European aristocratic system (i.e., citizenship by legacy) that had first been overthrown by the American Revolution. Birthright citizenship continued what the original Constitution started.
In recent years, it’s become a stylistic tic in documentaries to keep the talking heads offscreen, letting their words simply flow on the soundtrack without interrupting the images. DuVernay is having none of that. She has assembled an extraordinary roster of scholars, politicians, and commentators, led by the Civil Rights attorney Sherrilyn Ifill, who becomes the film’s oratorical star. We see the speakers and absorb the play of their personalities, as they describe, with a big-picture yet highly personalized passion, how the law of the land actually played out in the creation of the second America that rose from the ashes of the Civil War. DuVernay makes history organic by capturing how the very texture of people’s lives was changed by the law. And she’ll go wherever she needs to illustrate that, even to comedy clips from George Carlin and the great Paul Mooney, who does a bit about the happiness of white people when they were slave owners that must be seen to be believed. (His bit isn’t really about the slave era; it’s about today.)
As the film captures, the rise of the new Black citizenry during Reconstruction was rapid. For one thing, Black Americans did not waste time or spirit on vengeance. But the fall was every bit as rapid, as a culture of systematized violence and murder rose up in the South to try to stuff the genie of emancipation back in the bottle. The Ku Klux Klan was one half of it. The other half is captured in DuVernay’s fascinating portrait of the Lost Cause — the culture of defiance and regret and literal whitewashing that came to represent the Southern consciousness of what life had been before the Civil War. Slavery itself, the obscene horror and inhumanity of it, was washed out of the collective memory, and the Civil War was recast as “the war of Northern aggression.”
What remained were totems and symbols that were somehow infused with nobility. The film traces the history of the Confederate flag as signifier, showing us how rock stars from Tom Petty to ZZ Top used it as a badass backdrop, and spotlighting how the flag was imprinted on the roof of the General Lee, the orange 1969 Dodge Charger driven by the heroes of “The Dukes of Hazzard.” This was one of the most popular TV shows of its time (it debuted in 1979, just as Jimmy Carter’s presidency was winding down), and it was basically using the semiotics of the Civil War — of those who went to war to maintain slavery — as a signifier of cool.
This consciousness extended to the erecting of Confederate monuments in public squares, a movement so widespread — there were 2,629 such monuments built across the South — that it became larger than the sum of its parts. The message to Black citizens, according to one the film’s observers, was, “You matter so little that we’ll celebrate the people who wanted to enslave you.” The film looks at what the movement to remove those monuments, notably the statue of Robert E. Lee that stood in the capital of Virginia (the former capital of the Confederacy), was really about and what it entailed. It’s all part of how the Lost Cause myth became what the film calls “the greatest lie in American history.”
But what does that have to do with the 14th Amendment? DuVernay is getting to that. The true subject of the movie is the power of law, and the erosion of law. The dehumanization of Black people represented by the persistence of Confederate iconography in mainstream culture became an underground signifier of the precariousness of the freedoms enshrined by the 14th Amendment. The rise of the Klan, who took their cross-burning imagery from “The Birth of a Nation” (1915), wasn’t simply a matter of domestic terrorism. It was an attempt “to overthrow biracial democracy.” Between the Civil War and World War II, there were 4,400 lynchings. So entrenched was the backlash against Reconstruction, which was institutionalized with Jim Crow (a system of “law” that was really a culture of fascist violence), that it wasn’t until Brown vs. Board of Education, in 1954, that the might of the 14th Amendment began to reassert itself.
Documentaries tend to lessen in impact when they catch up to recent events, but as “14th” moves into the current era something remarkable happens: The film’s themes of racial oppression begin to mutate into themes of generalized oppression. The section of the 14th Amendment that deals with “insurrection” could not be more explicit. It states that anyone who has been responsible for fomenting an insurrection against the United States government cannot run for public office. This means that Donald Trump, after the unambiguous insurrection of Jan. 6, should not have been allowed to run for president in 2024. In that sense, he trampled on the Constitution simply by being re-elected, and the trashing of the 14th Amendment continued unabated. Birthright citizenship? Ignored. Due process? Out the window with ICE.
The degree to which the United States has been in the ugly thick of a Constitutional crisis since the beginning of 2025 has been persistently understated by the media. But Ava DuVernay states it with meticulous boldness. I don’t agree with her attempt to posit DEI as a Constitutional issue on the level of the Voting Rights Act. (The film itself acknowledges that the DEI movement, whatever one’s opinion of it, represented nothing so much as a “cultural shift.”) But where she shows us the big picture is in capturing how the freedoms of the 14th Amendment have been under siege, and how this may be nothing less than the ritual growing pains — the built-in trauma — of American democracy. Advance, backlash, conflict spilling over into violence…and then re-advance. That’s the rhythm, the moral and spiritual roller-coaster of perfecting our imperfect union. “14th” makes you see that we’re in the heat of the backlash now. But it also lets you feel that a re-advance is waiting in the wings.

South Korea recalls Ukraine envoy over prisoner-of-war row
- Published
South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, the latest escalation in a diplomatic spat between both countries.
It started last month when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul.
Seoul says Ukraine broke an agreement to keep the transfer a secret but Zelensky's office maintains that there was no non-disclosure agreement in place.
The two North Korean soldiers, who were among thousands from the country supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea.
South Korean Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo had in September lodged a formal complaint with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Vieshkin over the matter.
And earlier this week, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said he received an apology from his Ukrainian counterpart, but added that it fell short of Seoul's expectations, according to local reports.
But on Wednesday, Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told reporters at a media briefing that its Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had not apologised, according to Ukrainian news site Liga.
In a statement on Thursday, South Korea's Foreign Ministry said it would "continue consultations with the Ukrainian side", adding that it expected that "various outstanding issues...[would] be resolved smoothly".
- Ukraine says it captured two injured North Korean soldiers in Russia 
  - Published11 January 2025
Zelensky had revealed the transfer at a speech at the UN General Assembly in September, adding that the two North Koreans had not been "easy to capture alive".
It prompted a swift condemnation from South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who called it "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security.
President Lee also faced heavy criticism at home in light of the revelation, with local opposition accusing him of wanting to cover up the transfer to appease Pyongyang.
But his office said that it had been kept confidential partly to protect the North Koreans' families and added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war.
Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer.
The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement.
Seoul later demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations.
Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war.
After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks.
This July, Seoul had announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment.
Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take.
South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US.
Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang.

The Pro Wrestling League (PWL) marked its much-anticipated return to India’s sporting calendar with the official announcement of Season 6 in New Delhi on Friday. Scheduled to take place from January 9-26, 2027 under the aegis of the Wrestling Federation of India (WFI), the flagship league will stage its high-octane bouts at the iconic KD Jadhav Wrestling Arena at the Indira Gandhi Stadium, New Delhi.
The launch event was headlined by the grand felicitation of India’s wrestling contingent following their fruitful campaign at the Asian Games 2026. Star grapplers Sujeet Kalkal, who clinched a historic gold in the Men’s Freestyle 65kg category, and Aman Sehrawat, fresh from adding an Asian Games gold to his Paris 2024 Olympic bronze, were honoured alongside fellow medallists Antim Panghal, Nitesh Siwach, Deepak Punia and Sunil Kumar. The six-member medal-winning contingent was felicitated, celebrating one of India’s strongest wrestling campaigns at the Asian Games in decades.
Hosting Season 6 in Delhi is a key part of the League’s plan to be staged in a different franchise city every season, taking PWL to varied fan bases across the country. Coming to the capital, home to a deep-rooted wrestling culture and one of India’s most passionate sporting audiences, gives the League a landmark stage for its return and brings the action to fans at the heart of the nation.
Season 6 will feature 86 world-class men and women grapplers, including 34 Olympians and Commonwealth, Asian Games, and World Championship medallists. The roster features global luminaries such as Japanese Olympic champion Yui Susaki, alongside India’s finest marquee names.

The competition will be staged across nine Olympic weight divisions:
● Men: 57kg, 65kg, 74kg, 86kg, and 125kg
● Women: 53kg, 57kg, 62kg, and 76kg
Dayaan Farooqui, Chairman, Pro Wrestling League, said, “Wrestling is deeply embedded in India’s sporting culture and our wrestlers have consistently carried the nation’s pride onto the global stage. Season 6 of the Pro Wrestling League is a celebration of that rich legacy, while also taking the sport towards new global benchmarks. Our vision has always been to take the League to a different franchise city each season, bringing world-class wrestling closer to fans across the country. We are delighted to welcome some of the world’s finest wrestlers to Delhi and look forward to delivering an unforgettable experience for fans while further strengthening the sport’s presence in India.”
Aman Sehrawat, Olympic Medallist and Asian Games 2026 Gold Medallist, said, “Winning medals at the Olympics and the Asian Games has been the reward for years of sacrifice, discipline and hard work. To be felicitated for these achievements and to receive this honour in Delhi, in front of the wrestling community and fans, feels truly special. Moments like these remind you of the journey you have undertaken and the people who have supported you along the way. As a wrestler, it is also exciting to see the Pro Wrestling League return to the capital, and I look forward to seeing the sport reach new audiences and inspire the next generation of wrestlers.”
Sujeet Kalkal, Asian Games 2026 Gold Medallist, said, “The Pro Wrestling League has played an important role in my journey as a wrestler and has given me opportunities that have helped me grow both on and off the mat. Competing alongside and against some of the best wrestlers in the world gave me the confidence, exposure and belief to take on bigger challenges. To now be felicitated as an Asian Games gold medallist is a very special feeling, and it makes me realise how far the journey has come. PWL has been an important part of that journey, and I am excited to see it return to Delhi and continue giving young Indian wrestlers the platform to dream bigger.”

A powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake struck Panama on Friday, damaging buildings and roads across the Central American nation and prompting President Jose Raul Mulino to declare a major disaster. There were no immediate reports of casualties. The shallow earthquake was felt across Panama, which has a population of around 4.5 million, according to the National Civil Protection System. The tremor lasted approximately a minute, triggering panic in several areas and forcing people to evacuate buildings, AFP reported. Here is what we know about the earthquake, the damage it caused and its impact on transport and shipping infrastructure. The US Geological Survey (USGS) said the earthquake struck at 1756 GMT, with its epicentre located 10 kilometres (6 miles) from the small town of Pitaloza Arriba in central Herrera province. The USGS initially estimated the earthquake's magnitude at 8.0 before revising it to 7.7. The tremor was felt across the country, including Panama City, which is around 200 kilometres from the epicentre. Residents reported intense shaking, prompting evacuations from high-rise buildings. "I was scared because the shaking was very strong and prolonged. Heavy objects like dressers, the bed, and all the kitchen items were shaking," Salomon Andion, 46, told AFP after evacuating his 15-story building for the second time following aftershocks. Videos circulated on social media showed water spilling from the rooftop pool of a building more than 20 stories tall. Another video showed a bridge over the Panama Canal shaking violently while remaining upright as vehicles travelled across it. Panama's President Jose Raul Mulino described the situation as a major disaster, citing extensive damage to infrastructure. "We are facing a major disaster," Mulino said, adding that some roads had "completely collapsed." Health Minister Fernando Boyd said the worst-affected areas were the provinces of Herrera and Cocle, along with Los Santos in the southeast. The town of Tonosi in Los Santos was completely cut off, complicating efforts to reach residents and assess the damage. "We are trying to figure out how to get there by air, because it's impossible by land," Boyd said. In Penonome, a town in central Cocle province, residents described frightening scenes during the earthquake. "It was horrible, like nothing we ever experienced. My daughter was trapped in school," Juana Alveo, a 38-year-old cashier at a store in Penonome, told AFP. Former president Ricardo Martinelli also posted photographs on Instagram showing his house in the town of Sona in Veraguas province after it collapsed. Images shared by local media showed extensive damage to a church and a hotel in Penonome. President Mulino travelled to Penonome to coordinate the disaster response. Authorities issued a tsunami warning for the eastern Pacific following the earthquake, but the warning was subsequently lifted. The local geosciences institute recorded more than 80 aftershocks, including one with a magnitude above 6.0. The repeated tremors prompted further evacuations, including in Panama City, where residents left high-rise buildings as a precaution. Mulino urged the public to remain calm and avoid spreading unnecessary panic. "What happened should not be used to generate alarms and disorder," he wrote on X, adding that he had requested a report on the damage. The education ministry announced the suspension of classes in schools nationwide. Panama City's international airport, a major aviation hub for the region, was temporarily closed following the earthquake. The Civil Aeronautics Authority said several flights were diverted to other airports as a precaution. Despite the damage to roads and buildings, the Panama Canal Authority said shipping through the canal remained unaffected. The authority confirmed that the waterway, which connects the Pacific and Atlantic oceans, was operating "as normal." The canal is a major international shipping route, making the status of its operations an important consideration in assessing the earthquake's wider transport and economic implications. The leaders of Colombia, Ecuador and Guatemala sent messages of solidarity and offered to provide assistance to Panama. Authorities continued coordinating the disaster response as they assessed damage and explored ways to reach isolated areas. Earthquakes are rare in Panama and typically occur in the western province of Chiriqui, which borders Costa Rica. The latest tremor is at least the fourth earthquake measuring above magnitude 7.0 in Latin America this year, following devastating back-to-back earthquakes in Venezuela's Guaira in June and a powerful earthquake in western Colombia in August. The scale of the damage in Panama, the number of aftershocks and access to affected communities remained key concerns as authorities worked to assess the consequences of the earthquake. A large randomised controlled trial among heart failure patients in India led by the Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute for Medical Sciences and Technology (SCTIMST) in Kerala, has found that hospitalisation episodes and all-cause mortality among heart failure patients can be significantly reduced if patients are systematically followed-up by a nurse, with the help of a mobile health application.
The two-year Telemonitoring and Integrated Multidisciplinary care for Heart Failure (TIME-HF) trial found that heart failure patients with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) who received nurse-led collaborative care had a 22% lower risk of death than those receiving usual care. They were also more likely to remain alive without hospitalisation during the two-year follow-up.
The trial results were published in the American Heart Association’s Journal, Circulation, on August 30, 2026.
What makes the trial relevant is that it addresses critical gaps in heart failure care: in Keralam, heart failure registries have reported high mortality post-discharge — 82.7% mortality over 10 years, alongside the fact fact that only 25.4% of the patients with heart failure receive guideline-based therapies. It also holds lessons for the rest of the country: with nearly 27% of all deaths in India being due to heart disease, and 62% of all deaths due to cardiovascular disease occurring between the ages of 40 and 69 years, there is an urgent need for quality, post-discharge care.
What the trial did
The TIME-HF trial involved 1,507 adults at 22 government and private hospitals in Keralam and neighbouring States, with 755 patients assigned to the intervention and 752 to usual care. The mean age was 61.9 years; 77.6% were men, 57.3% lived in rural areas and 70% had relatively low educational attainment. Ischaemic heart disease was the predominant cause of heart failure, accounting for 77.4% of cases.
Results indicated that nurse-led intervention substantially improved prescription of the four major components of guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure — renin-angiotensin system inhibition/ARNI, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors.
“Our heart failure patients receive sub-optimal care, as most of them do not adhere to therapies or follow up with the doctor on time. There is also the issue of physician inertia. HF Registry evidence indicates that the median survival after diagnosis of heart failure is just 3.7 years. This collaborative care model is proof that survival and quality of life of these patients can be improved if we systematically address the gaps in care so that proven therapies for heart failure become part of routine care,” said lead researcher and additional professor at SCTIMST P. Jeemon.
Centring nursing care
The model put a trained nurse at the centre of the care pathway, who would closely monitor heart failure patients after discharge, educate the patient and family about heart-failure self-care, lifestyle modification and encourage medication adherence.
Nurses reviewed the patients’ medication regimen at discharge to ensure that there was no deviation from the guideline-mediated therapies. This was again reviewed at every follow-up visit with the help of a mobile-health app. The m-health app helped the nurses monitor all physical parameters of the patient real time and to identify warning signs of worsening disease, communicate and connect with patients and physicians so that timely hospitalisation was possible.
All participants underwent scheduled follow-up visits every three months for two years. Adherence to all four guideline-directed medical therapies was only 22.1% in the usual-care group, while it was 37.3% in the intervention group at two years.
“The health system engaging with the patient regularly was the key here. The m-health app gave the patient updates in real time to the nurse. Oxygen saturation levels, weight gain, weight loss, drop in blood pressure or respiratory rate comes as alerts, and then were escalated to the physician,” Dr. Jeemon points out.
The TIME-HF trial thus helped address one of the health system’s persistent weaknesses: that of proper follow-up care of patients with chronic diseases. The model is suited for strengthening chronic disease management and reducing the burden of hospitalisation and mortality in resource-limited settings across the country, experts said.

Nobel Peace Prize winner Navanethem “Navi” Pillay has a connection to India, but it is not the kind one might expect. The South African human rights lawyer’s Indian roots go back generations, to a time when thousands of people were taken from the subcontinent to work on sugar plantations under British colonial rule. Her grandparents were among those who made the journey, linking her family history to a labour system that shaped the lives of Indians overseas. Known as girmit, a term derived from the English word “agreement”, the Indian indentured labour system was a form of contracted overseas employment that expanded during British colonial rule. After slavery was abolished across most of the British Empire in 1833, plantation owners sought alternative sources of labour. In Natal, present-day South Africa, the growing sugar industry turned to India to meet its demand for workers. The expanding sugar industry in Natal needed workers to cultivate and harvest sugarcane. Colonial authorities turned to India, where poverty and economic hardship made overseas recruitment possible. The first ship carrying Indian indentured workers to Natal arrived in November 1860. Over the following five decades, more than 150,000 Indians travelled to the colony under the system. Historical research published in Pacific Historical Review puts the total at 152,641 between 1860 and 1911. Workers generally entered contracts lasting three to five years, although the terms changed over time. They were assigned to employers and expected to carry out demanding agricultural work, often for low wages. The contractual arrangement did not guarantee humane treatment. Historical accounts document harsh working conditions, inadequate accommodation and abuses by plantation employers. Workers could also face legal penalties for breaches of their contracts, including offences relating to absence from work. Their ability to leave was restricted, and the authorities used laws and disciplinary measures to enforce labour obligations. The system therefore created a workforce that was formally contracted but often vulnerable to exploitation. At the end of their contracts, workers had different options, depending on the rules in force at the time. These included signing another contract, remaining in South Africa or returning to India under the applicable repatriation arrangements. For many, returning home was not straightforward. Poverty, the cost and practical difficulties of travel, and changing contractual provisions influenced their decisions. Many stayed and established families, helping shape South Africa’s Indian-origin population. The Indian government eventually prohibited further indentured migration to Natal in 1911, amid mounting evidence of ill-treatment. Pillay’s family history reflects the lasting consequences of indentured migration and the struggles faced by generations of Indians who settled in South Africa under colonial rule. Her own career took a markedly different path, leading her to become a prominent international jurist and a leading voice on human rights. In 2026, Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in recognition of her contribution to international justice and human rights, bringing global attention to a life shaped by the pursuit of equality and dignity. How good is this year's flu shot? Here's what to know about flu season
It may seem like everyone is getting sick right now, but does an early flu season mean a rougher one?
Walking down the street this week, it may seem like everyone is sneezing and hacking up a lung. But as health officials announce the start of an earlier than usual flu season, how worried should Canadians be? And as we head into Thanksgiving weekend, should we be scrambling to update flu and COVID-19 shots?
Some experts say that while this year's flu season may have arrived on our doorstep sooner than usual, it's not necessarily a cause for alarm — but other experts are stressing the importance of prevention in heavy-hit regions such as Toronto and Calgary, where authorities reported one person had already died from the virus.
The strain making up roughly 98 per cent of cases in Canada so far tends to be a milder one, according to Brian Ward, professor emeritus at the Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre in Montreal.
"So far at least, this looks like an H1N1 dominated year, and the years where H1N1 dominates, you can have very large outbreaks, but the number or the proportion of people … who get very sick, is relatively small compared to years that are dominated by H3N2," he told CBC News.
"I'm not convinced yet that we're actually seeing the beginning of a real outbreak. What we're seeing is sort of isolated, small outbreaks."
But where the flu is striking, doctors say it's striking hard. There are currently more than 400 confirmed flu cases in Alberta, where vaccines aren't yet widely available.
- Doctors say flu season is ahead of schedule this year as cases pop up across Ontario
- 1 dead, more than 400 confirmed flu cases ahead of vaccine availability in Alberta
Some regions have started rolling out flu and COVID-19 shots to high-risk populations, with most regions set to offer shots to the general public by mid-October.
Here's what we know.
Is everyone getting sick right now?
According to the latest national numbers, which include data on influenza trends up to Sept. 26, there have been 2,102 detections of influenza across the country since the end of August.
It's an early start to the season. Between Sept. 20 and Sept. 26, 3.7 per cent of influenza tests came back positive, much higher than the average 0.5 per cent rate seen this time of year in 2023-2025.
- Nova Scotia opens COVID-19, flu vaccine bookings ahead of respiratory illness season
- Flu and COVID-19 vaccinations underway in B.C. as respiratory illness season arrives early
- Vaccine-preventable illnesses on the horizon again as Canadian kids head back to school
But much of this national increase is driven by an uptick of cases in B.C. and Yukon, and in large cities such as Toronto and Calgary. The person who died in Alberta lived in the Calgary area and was in the 70-79 years age range, authorities say.
"The rest of the country is really very quiet," Ward said.
He noted that in B.C., outbreaks in long-term care homes are driving the increase in cases, warning that families getting together this holiday weekend could result in further spread.
"That may be the seed that moves the virus … into the schools and universities and marketplaces and so on. But overall, we're still below the 5 per cent [epidemic] threshold."
Official figures don't catch every case of flu, as not everyone seeks out a test when they fall ill.
In hard-hit Toronto, family doctor Joseph Param told CBC News the increase of flu patients he's seeing at his practice is mainly among young adults who are more likely to travel on public transit and may still go to work when feeling under the weather, perhaps because they're used to flu season starting later.
"Over the last couple of weeks, patients who are very healthy who see me rarely have been coming in with severe symptoms," he said.
"So it is important that the general population is aware that we are seeing … early cases now and so that we start taking precautions earlier than expected."
Doctors advise Canadians to stay home if they feel ill and to get vaccinated as soon as shots become available in their area, particularly with the long weekend coming up.
How effective is the flu shot this year?
The protection of flu shots varies from year to year depending on the most dominant strain of influenza in your area.
This year, it's a "good" match, Ward said. Although H3N2 viruses dominated for much of 2025, that subtype hasn't cropped up much in 2026, and this year's vaccine is well-positioned to protect against H1N1.
He said "influenza viruses march to their own drummers" and can mutate even within one flu season.
It's not just flu season in Canada — historically, we see more respiratory illnesses in general cropping up during the fall and going into winter, including colds and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), the latter of which is most dangerous in young children.
Around 98 per cent of lab-confirmed cases of influenza in Canada since the end of August have been of the H1N1 strain, according to government data. (New Africa/Shutterstock)
Rates of COVID-19 are currently trending lower right now than last year, with 3.8 per cent of tests coming back positive in the last week of September compared with 10.3 per cent at the same time in 2025.
The National Advisory Committee on Immunizations (NACI) said in September that it continues to "strongly recommend" the latest COVID-19 booster shots for those at a higher risk of developing severe COVID-19, including health-care workers, adults over the age of 65, those with immunocompromised systems and people in long-term care homes.
When can I get my flu and COVID-19 shots?
Several provinces such as Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia are already advising residents that appointments for flu vaccines and COVID-19 booster shots are available now for residents over the age of six months.
New Brunswick, Saskatchewan and Manitoba are currently allowing residents to book their flu and COVID-19 vaccines, with immunization efforts officially kicking off on Oct. 13.
Those living in Newfoundland and Labrador can receive flu and COVID-19 shots starting Oct. 19.
In Ontario, flu and COVID-19 immunizations have been available since last week for high-risk groups, but don't open to the general public until Oct. 26.
In Quebec, you can start making appointments as of Oct. 13, but the flu and COVID-19 vaccination campaign itself doesn't begin until Oct. 20. It is only free to eligible residents deemed high-risk, meaning non-eligible residents must pay for the shots.

Before heading out to the pharmacy, it's important to check the requirements in your area to be sure that you're eligible. Most regions offer RSV vaccines to eligible patients as well.

‘Build here, scale here’: IIT alumni body urges institution's diaspora to ‘come home’ to India amid US green card crackdown
Pan IIT Alumni India argued that India now offers opportunities in research, deep tech and innovation that previously drove many skilled professionals to leave.
Pan IIT Alumni India, the umbrella body representing alumni of all 23 Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs), on Friday urged the global IIT diaspora to “come home” and “build here, scale here, contribute here”, amid the United States' decision to freeze Green Card filings by eight companies, including Indian IT majors Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) and Infosys.
The alumni body described its appeal as “not a rejection of the world” but “an invitation to come home to a nation that has arrived”, arguing that India now offers opportunities in research, deep tech, and innovation that had previously driven many skilled professionals to leave the country.
Pan IIT Alumni India is a registered society representing more than 500,000 IIT alumni worldwide. The organisation, operating from IIT Delhi, promotes India as a source of innovative technology solutions and serves as a platform for policy engagement, mentorship, and collaboration across the global IIT diaspora.
What the IIT alumni body said
Deep Dive
In a statement, the alumni body expressed concern over the US administration’s action against the permanent labour certification programme, known as Program Electronic Review Management (PERM), and the treatment of skilled Indian professionals on H-1B visas.
While acknowledging the sovereign right of countries to frame their immigration policies, it called for their implementation to be “fairly, transparently, and without stigmatising a community of professionals whose contributions to the American economy and society are well documented”.
“For over five decades, Indian engineers and technologists — a large number of them IIT alumni — have been among the most productive contributors to American innovation, research, and industry,” the statement said, adding that they had built products, filed patents, founded companies and created jobs in the US.
The alumni body also criticised the collective characterisation of Indian professionals as “indentured servants”, calling it “neither accurate nor fair”.
The statement comes amid a widening US crackdown on skilled-worker immigration. On Thursday, the US Labour Department suspended PERM filings involving eight companies — Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCL Technologies, Microsoft, Adobe and Capgemini — and opened investigations into nine universities, citing concerns over fraud and American job losses.
PERM certification is required for most employment-based Green Card applications. Under the process, employers must demonstrate that hiring a foreign worker will not adversely affect the wages, working conditions or job opportunities of American workers. The freeze does not appear to directly affect existing H-1B visa holders, but could disrupt a key route through which employers sponsor temporary foreign workers for permanent residency.
Against this backdrop, Pan IIT Alumni India said the developments should also prompt a reassessment within the Indian diaspora of career opportunities at home. It argued that the factors that once compelled many of India’s brightest engineers to seek opportunities abroad — including the lack of world-class research opportunities, deep-tech infrastructure and patient capital — had changed.
“India today offers the challenges and opportunities that were once only available abroad,” it said, renewing its appeal to IIT alumni overseas: “From Silicon Valley to the Indus Valley — build here, scale here, contribute here.”
Prabhat Kumar, an Indian Revenue Service (IRS) officer and chairman of Pan IIT Alumni India, said the latest developments highlighted the risks of building a career dependent on immigration status.
“For decades, we celebrated when our brightest minds left for American shores. It is time we asked what we lost in the process. A visa was never a stable foundation for a career, and this week's events prove it,” he said.
“The most exciting problems — and the greatest impact — now await our engineers at home. Build here. Scale here. Die here,” he added.

A payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the struggling London Stock Exchange.
Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that has faced a string of recent departures.
The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.
Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.
Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.
“From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao.
“We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.”
Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.”
Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month.
Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 but delayed it to the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict.
Airtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding.
Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa.
The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result of overseas takeovers of UK companies.
Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wise floated in 2021 with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from London to New York.
