The Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) held a protest at Shivaji Park Maidan in Mumbai on 02 October 2026, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. The protesters raised concerns over the alleged exclusion of voters during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and demanded greater transparency in the election process. Although Mumbai Police had denied permission for the meeting, hundreds of people took part in the protest and raised slogans. Police later registered an FIR against the organisers and 400–500 unidentified participants for violating the restrictions.
Against this backdrop, a video circulating on social media (here, here) claims to show footage of the CJP protest at Shivaji Park in Mumbai. Let us verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals of CJP’s protest demanding the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar at Shivaji Park ground in Mumbai on 02 October 2026.
Fact: The viral video is unrelated to the CJP protest in Mumbai. It is an old video showing a public meeting organised by AIMIM leader Asaduddin Owaisi at the Central Library Ground in Bhopal on 15 September, opposing the Uniform Civil Code Bill passed by the Madhya Pradesh Assembly. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to the same footage (here and here) from 18 September 2026, nearly two weeks before the CJP protest in Mumbai.
We found that the video was uploaded on Facebook and Instagram by a Bhopal-based content creator, Amin Siddiqui, on 18 September 2026. We also found several other videos showing the same scenes on his Instagram page (here, here, and here). These videos indicate that the footage is from a public meeting addressed by AIMIM president Asaduddin Owaisi in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh.
News reports (here and here) also confirm that Owaisi addressed a public meeting at the Central Library Grounds in Bhopal on 15 September 2026, opposing the Uniform Civil Code Bill passed by the Madhya Pradesh Assembly.
When we compared the visuals from the viral video with the location on Google Street View, we found that the surroundings match the Central Library Grounds in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh, confirming that the video is related to the Bhopal meeting.
To sum up, an old Bhopal public meeting video is being falsely shared as a CJP protest video in Mumbai.

Greek takeaways: What did we learn from Lionesses' win?
- Published
England came away from Greece with a valuable first-leg lead in their Women's World Cup qualifying play-off - but what did we learn?
Sarina Wiegman's side are looking to secure their place in Brazil next year but have to navigate the play-offs after finishing runners-up in their qualification group.
The back-to-back European champions won 3-1 in Crete on Friday night and will need to finish the job against Greece on Tuesday in Leicester (19:30 BST).
The winner of the tie faces Ukraine or Slovakia in round two to decide who will head to Brazil.
Le Tissier takes her opportunity
Lucy Bronze withdrew from the squad with a minor injury earlier this week, handing a rare opportunity to Manchester United captain Maya le Tissier.
The defender is a key player for her club but struggles to break into the England team with Bronze understandably a tough figure to displace.
Wiegman sees Le Tissier as a right-back as opposed to a centre-back - which is her position at United - and that meant she was handed a start against Greece.
Making her 15th cap, Le Tissier was a standout performer and was rewarded with her first international goal in the 63rd minute, providing optimism for a future without 34-year-old Bronze.
"As soon as we were in possession, she was higher on the pitch and she already came close to a couple of moments with crosses," said Wiegman.
"I'm very happy for her and for the whole team because that was an important goal."
Sloppiness creeps in again
It was just England's third win in their past eight competitive away games.
A 3-1 victory is a pleasing result, but given the gulf in class, Wiegman admitted frustrations at not keeping a clean sheet.
There were familiar lapses in concentration defensively that gave Greece opportunities to pounce. Ioanna Papatheodorou struck the crossbar in the first half, before teeing up Kallisti Brouksair for their goal later on.
Those chances came from England errors and the lack of clean sheet means the door remains open for Greece in the second leg.
"That's up to us. We have to show up on Tuesday, play a good game and then we should be better than Greece," said Wiegman.
"Of course we want to take some more distance [in the scoreline], that's absolutely true, but at the same time we won and that's the most important thing.
"Sometimes we played really well and sometimes we were a bit sloppy. We were a bit frustrated as we wanted to do that better.
"We want to show more than winning, we want to play really well too."
A glimpse of the future
With victory secure, Wiegman was able to hand a debut to 18-year-old Erica Meg Parkinson, as well as Liverpool captain Grace Fisk.
Fisk, 28, had waited more than six years for her debut, having received her first England call-up in 2020 but Parkinson has broken through at pace this season.
The teenager was unexpectedly named in Wiegman's squad in March, having only made the jump up to England's Under-23s a few months earlier.
She secured a move to the United States this summer, joining North Carolina Courage from Portuguese side Valadares Gaia, and came on in the 85th minute.
This week defender Esme Morgan said: "She's a really intelligent player. She has incredibly good movement and timing, picking up pockets for players to find her.
"She's really comfortable receiving [the ball] in tight spaces, she's strong holding off players, very aggressive in her tackling and wins back a lot of balls.
"I've been really impressed with Erica since she came into camp and also from playing against her in the National Women's Soccer League."
- Why England teenager Parkinson has a mindset coach 
  - Published21 July
Who is England's number 10?
Parkinson's debut added to the debate of who Wiegman's preferred number 10 is.
She is one of many options available, including Chelsea forward Lauren James, who was given a creative, free role against Greece.
James showed flashes of quality and nonchalantly lobbed goalkeeper Fafailia Petaloti from 30 yards in the first half, but her effort was ruled out for offside.
Other options include Manchester City's Grace Clinton and Manchester United's Ella Toone, who were both recalled to the squad to cover injuries with Aston Villa's Lucia Kendall among those to drop out.
Laura Blindkilde Brown started in that position with James in Crete, while Beth Mead and Jess Park have also played there before.
The position was a difficult one for Wiegman to nail down at Euro 2025 and more than a year later, the question of who is England's best number 10 remains.
"I see there is a lot of competition in that position, where we have a lot of options with different players, who have different qualities," said Wiegman.
"You can call it a question mark but I call it many options. Today we had two 10s and sometimes three. [James] was one of them."
Job done in strange circumstances
Local media had questioned why the game wasn't being played in Greece's capital city Athens.
And there was an eerie atmosphere with fewer than 4,000 fans in the 26,000-capacity stadium in Heraklion, Crete.
The Lionesses are also not used to being in play-offs, a route they are having to take after finishing runners-up to world champions Spain in their qualifying group.
But Georgia Stanway, this year's top scorer for England, once again turned up when they needed her to and she opened the scoring after a neat, incisive passing move, in a frustrating first half.
That was the spark England needed as they lacked ruthlessness and failed to capitalise on their dominance - an aspect of their game that needs improving.
"I think we made it a bit harder. Greece were well prepared and disciplined. We struggled when they tried to press us," added Wiegman.
"We could have scored more than the three goals. There are lots of things to take. I have seen some fluid moments but I want more.
"The final ball, final cross and the positions can be better. Of course, we are working on that. We have an opportunity to improve that on Tuesday."

Quick Answer
The ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 is a practical, performance-driven business laptop featuring a powerful Intel Core Ultra 7 processor, an exceptional keyboard, excellent port selection, and easy RAM/storage upgradability. However, its main drawbacks are mediocre battery life, a dim display limited to 45% NTSC, and an underwhelming webcam.
ASUS offers the ExpertBook series in many configurations. If you want the best business laptop Asus offers, consider the ASUS ExpertBook Ultra. If you are a business owner who wants a premium design without compromising essential business features, the ASUS ExpertBook B Series is worth considering. Finally, the ASUS ExpertBook P Series is for those looking for an affordable business laptop without paying a premium.
In that regard, the ASUS ExpertBook P3 is a sweet spot for people looking for an affordable business laptop. It doesn’t try to compete with the flashy, ultra-thin consumer aesthetics of the Apple MacBook Air or Dell XPS line; instead, it positions itself as an aggressive challenger to the Lenovo ThinkPad and HP EliteBook ecosystems, as well as other business laptop ranges.
I have been using the ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 version (2026) for the past several days. Overall, it has been a solid business laptop. The model I am testing comes with a powerful Intel Core Ultra 7 255H and delivers excellent performance, a reliable port selection, the best keyboard in its class, and plenty of business-focused features.
ASUS has also expanded the ASUS ExpertBook P3 G2 series, now offering more choices than before with both Intel and AMD configurations across different sizes, while also addressing some of the shortcomings we noticed with the earlier ExpertBook P series.
In this full, detailed review, I will share my experience with the ASUS P3 G1, compare it to the original P3 launched in 2025, and see how it stacks up against the recently announced ASUS P3 G2 series. By the end, you should have a better idea of whether the Asus P3 G1 still makes sense or is worth going for the latest generations instead.
Table of Contents
ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 Review
Design and Build: Practical Over Premium
Asus ExpertBook laptops are easy to spot from miles away. Most models across the lineup look the same and follow a very similar design language, with an understated gray finish and a clean, minimal look.
Asus ExpertBook P3 G1 also follows the same design. It may not impress you with flashy looks or an ultra-slim profile, which is something the ExpertBook P3 isn’t trying to do anyway. This is a practical, business-first laptop.
ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 comes in two chassis variants. The 1A variant has a plastic chassis, and the 2A variant has a metal chassis for those who want an even sturdier, more premium build.
My unit comes with a plastic body, but it doesn’t feel cheap by any means. In fact, it is a step up from some of the older ExpertBook laptops I have reviewed in the past.
Although the chassis is plastic, the matte, grainy finish hides it and gives it a much more premium feel. I love minimal laptop designs, and the ASUS ExpertBook takes that approach even further with nothing but the ASUS logo on the lid. The matte, grainy finish is also fingerprint-resistant; as a result, smudges don’t show up, and it stays clean.
The same treatment continues when you open the lid. The hinge is now slightly stronger. The display is stiffer than ideal to position, but it still wobbles a bit when you type and change its angle.
The lid opens up to 180 degrees, allowing the display to lie completely flat on the surface. It can come in handy if you want to share your screen with someone across the table. One limitation, though: since this variant doesn’t have a touchscreen, you cannot really use the display while it is lying flat.
Build quality is stronger than last generation, but it still has noticeable flex, especially in the center of the keyboard and between the touchpad and the keyboard. Thankfully, I didn’t notice it while typing. The deck doesn’t bend much under normal use unless you press harder.
The rounded corners also make the laptop more comfortable to hold during longer carrying periods.
One thing Asus continues to get right is port selection. In a world where fewer ports have become the norm for a premium experience, Asus ExpertBook P3 supports all major ports, including one Thunderbolt 4 USB-C, one USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-C, two USB 3.2 Gen 1 Type-A ports, a full-size RJ45 Gigabit Ethernet port, HDMI 2.1 TMDS, a 3.5mm audio jack, and a Kensington Nano lock. You get pretty much every port you expect from a business laptop. That also means you can connect most everyday accessories directly to the laptop without carrying a separate dongle.
The chassis is also MIL-STD 810H tested across 24 procedures. The laptop should handle everyday wear and tear. Note that the laptop is not water-resistant.
The keyboard supports backlighting. This makes it easy to see and type in low-light conditions. The backlight also doesn’t leak when you’re looking straight at the laptop. It also has durable keys, and ASUS claims the keyboard is tested for up to 10 million keystrokes to withstand wear and tear over time.
ASUS ExpertBook P3 is available in both 14-inch and 16-inch sizes. My review unit is the 14-inch variant with a WUXGA 16:10 display. The side bezels are fairly noticeable, and there is a rather large chin at the bottom that also houses the Asus ExpertBook logo. Above the display is a physical privacy shutter, which I truly appreciate for business-centric users who want better privacy.
Display: Good for Work, Not for Creative Use
The 14-inch display is a sweet spot if you want something compact without giving up too much screen space.
ASUS ExpertBook doesn’t get the kind of high-end OLED displays Asus offers on some of its high-end laptops or even more affordable VivoBook models. It is a 14-inch IPS-level display with WUXGA 1920 × 1200 resolution, a 16:10 aspect ratio, a 60Hz refresh rate, up to 300 nits of brightness, and 45% NTSC color coverage.
The display quality is decent and gets the job done, especially if you’re buying the ExpertBook primarily for office work. It is perfectly fine for browsing and using office apps like spreadsheets and documents, but if you work on photos or video editing, you will probably want something with better color coverage.
The display also has an anti-glare coating, which does a good job of cutting down reflections and makes it easier to use in bright environments. However, the trade-off is that a matte finish coating removes some of the visual punch you get from glossy panels. Colors aren’t as vibrant, although the text remains sharp.
Watching videos and content on this WUXGA IPS-level panel isn’t a pleasant experience, but as I said, for everyday tasks such as browsing, spreadsheets, and other office applications, it feels comfortable to use, and the text looks sharp enough to read clearly.
Performance: More Power Than Most Office Users Need
Performance is easily one of the ExpertBook P3’s strongest aspects. Asus offers it with either a Core Ultra 5 225H or Core Ultra 7 255H. My unit came with an Intel Core Ultra 7 255H, paired with 16GB DDR5 RAM and a 512GB M.2 NVMe PCIe 4.0 SSD.
At the heart of the configuration is the Intel Core Ultra 7 255H, a high-performance processor with 16 cores, 16 threads, a maximum clock speed of 5.1GHz, and integrated Intel Graphics. In everyday use, this combination handles almost any task without breaking a sweat. Whether you’re using multiple graphics-heavy applications, running dozens of browser tabs, or switching between office apps all day.
Another advantage is upgradability. Asus ExpertBook P3 comes with two DDR5 SO-DIMM slots, and the existing RAM isn’t soldered to the motherboard, so you can upgrade later if you want to, and it won’t cost you a bomb upfront, which is the case with most modern laptops.
It also has two storage slots: one M.2 2280 PCIe 4.0 slot and one M.2 2230 PCIe 4.0 slot, giving you more room to expand the storage later.
One thing I did notice is that the laptop gets quite warm at the bottom even during something as basic as browsing the web. You can definitely feel the heat when using it in your lap. It is not entirely surprising, though, considering the Core Ultra 7 255H is an H-series processor designed for higher performance.
Keyboard and Trackpad: The Keyboard Is the Star
The keyboard is easily one of my favorite things about the Asus ExpertBook P3. It offers one of the best typing experiences I have had on a laptop after Mac. A lot of that comes down to the 1.5mm key travel, which delivers a great typing experience. The keys are also large and well spaced, giving your fingers plenty of room to move around. It didn’t take me long to get comfortable with this keyboard.
The trackpad is also large enough for daily use. The large surface area makes it easy to move the cursor and also use gestures.
I have no issues with the keyboard and trackpad, though some users may find the fingerprint sensor placement inconvenient because it is integrated into the power button. To prevent accidental presses, ASUS made the power button slightly firmer.
Battery Life: The Biggest Compromise
This kind of performance is always welcome, especially if you regularly handle high-demand tasks. The trade-off, though, is battery life. My configuration comes with a 50Wh, 3-cell battery, and the ExpertBook P3 takes a noticeable hit here.
Even for basic use, I was getting only about 8-9 hours. On medium to heavy gaming, the battery life dropped to 4 to 5 hours, which isn’t the performance you want if you plan to use it on battery power all day.
ASUS bundles a 65W USB-C charger in the box, and it can take your laptop from 0 to 100 in less than 2 hours. That’s fairly quick, but I really wish Windows laptop makers offered more travel-friendly options instead of big, bulky charging bricks and three-pin plugs.
Sound: Decent, but Nothing Special
The speakers are decently loud, but they don’t get particularly loud. ASUS uses two built-in speakers with Dirac audio support. Thankfully, Asus includes a built-in 3.5mm headphone jack, so you can plug in wired headphones or earphones directly without relying on the built-in speakers.
Windows 11 Home: Still Too Cluttered
I have never been a fan of Windows’ cluttered experience. If you’ve used Windows for years, you probably won’t mind much, but if you are coming from a Mac or Linux, you’ll have to deal with Windows’ cluttered experience first.
It took me more than three hours to set up the device, including the unwanted Windows updates I had to install during setup. Plus, the Windows update prompts never stop. Even Microsoft has promised to improve the Windows laptop experience by eliminating these unwanted distractions.
Since this is an ExpertBook, ASUS includes business-centric features, including AI ExpertMeet for meetings. However, this configuration lacks some useful Copilot+ AI features for those who care about privacy and want to run AI features locally on the device. The Core Ultra 7 255H delivers up to 13 TOPS of NPU performance, well short of the 40+ TOPS required for a Copilot+ PC. You may need to rely on cloud processing for more demanding AI features.
Camera: Still Needs Work
ASUS has been pretty good at improving the little things in everyday use, but the camera is still one area that needs work. My configuration comes with a 1080p FHD IR camera with Windows Hello support and a physical privacy shutter. Even on the maxed-out ExpertBook Ultra, the camera quality is rather underwhelming, especially on business laptops like this, where it matters a lot.
Even in good lighting, the camera adds plenty of noise, and in low light, it gets worse. However, you can always connect an external camera if camera quality matters to you. But this is something Asus needs to improve.
ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 Review Verdict: Powerful and Practical, but Battery Holds It Back
Overall, if performance is high on your priority list, then the ASUS ExpertBook P3 might be a better choice. Everyday tasks feel quick and responsive, plus it also has plenty of power for more demanding tasks. The excellent keyboard, with 1.5mm key travel, makes typing sessions comfortable, and the full selection of ports lets you connect any peripherals without constantly reaching for or using a dongle. The biggest advantage of the Asus ExpertBook P3 is plenty of room to upgrade later. It offers dual SO-DIMM slots for memory and dual M.2 slots for additional PCIe storage.
Among the pros are also some compromises. Battery life takes a noticeable hit when you push the processor harder, and while the laptop can handle some AI workloads locally, it cannot run the full set of Copilot+ PC features.

- Great keyboard with 1.5mm key travel
- Plenty of ports
- RAM and SSD are upgradeable

BJP’s Dinesh Arya elected unopposed to Rajya Sabha from Uttarakhand
Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP) candidate Dinesh Arya was elected unopposed to the Rajya Sabha from Uttarakhand, officials said on Friday
Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP) candidate Dinesh Arya was elected unopposed to the Rajya Sabha from Uttarakhand, officials said on Friday.
The term of incumbent Rajya Sabha MP Naresh Bansal is scheduled to end on November 25.
Secretary of the Uttarakhand Vidhan Sabha Hem Pant said no other candidate had filed nomination papers for the seat. “We did not receive any nomination apart from that of the BJP’s Dinesh Arya. He was handed over the certificate of election at 3 pm today,” Pant said.
Deep Dive
Arya currently serves as vice-chairperson of the State Drinking Water Monitoring Committee and has previously served as the BJP’s Nainital district president.
A Dalit leader from Kumaon, his election to the Rajya Sabha is being seen as the BJP’s outreach to the Dalit community ahead of the assembly elections, scheduled for February next year.
Arya filed his nomination papers on October 6.
BJP’s Uttarakhand core committee had considered around two dozen names for the Rajya Sabha nomination at a meeting on September 25. A smaller panel was subsequently finalised by CM Pushkar Dhami, state chief Mahendra Bhatt and state BJP general secretary (organisation) Phanindra Nath Sharma and sent to the party’s central leadership for a final decision.
Congress had decided against contesting the election, citing a lack of numbers in the state assembly. “We have 20 MLAs and are short of the required numbers. We cannot ensure the victory of our candidate, which is why we did not contest,” said state Congress vice-president Suryakant Dhasmana.

Contribution To Nation's Progress

The Chief Minister also extended his best wishes to all of them for a bright tenure.

Kupwara, Oct 9: Proper grading and packing of apples can help growers secure better prices in the market, President Fruit Mandi Handwara Mohammad Amin Wani said on Friday, urging growers to maintain quality standards before bringing their produce to the mandi.
Wani said growers had repeatedly been advised to grade apples according to their size and quality and avoid mixing different grades in the same boxes.
“Properly graded and packed apples not only attract better rates but also help build confidence among buyers and traders,” he said.
He said good-quality apples remained the preferred choice of traders visiting Handwara Fruit Mandi from outside the region, adding that proper grading and packing could help growers improve their returns in a competitive market.
Wani said good-quality apples were currently fetching around Rs 1,000 to Rs 1,200 per box. He expressed hope that prices would improve further ahead of Diwali, with a possible rise in market demand.
Expressing concern over losses caused by leaf miner disease this season, Wani said the disease had affected apple production and quality in several areas, adding to growers’ financial difficulties amid rising input and transportation costs.
He urged the government and concerned horticulture authorities to intensify disease-control measures and provide timely technical assistance to affected growers.
“If effective measures are not taken against the disease, it could continue to affect growers as well as traders in the coming seasons,” he said.
On apple arrivals, Wani said the volume of produce reaching the mandi had declined compared with the previous year. He attributed the decline to reduced production in several areas and disease-related damage.

EXCLUSIVE: A number of recent injuries on the set of Season 10 of ABC‘s 9-1-1 has put the production’s safety protocols under scrutiny again.
Deadline understands that four performers, including star Oliver Stark, have sustained stunt-related injuries to varying degrees in recent months. While the incidents do not seem to be connected, the unfortunate timing does highlight the challenges with making a stunt-heavy show like 9-1-1 on a broadcast network schedule.
A spokesperson for 20th Television, which produces the series, declined to comment for this story.
In late August, Stark broke his ankle while performing a stunt and required surgery. Sources close to production say that production continued in the wake of the incident and Stark has since returned to work. While reports of the injury surfaced online, the details of the incident have not yet been shared.
Watch on Deadline
Sources tell Deadline that the stunt involved a firefighter swinging from a car over a set piece to the ladder truck. We understand that, during rehearsals, a stunt double sprained an ankle performing the same stunt and declined medical treatment, so no injury report was submitted to production.
On the 9-1-1 set, production sources say it is typical for stunts to be practiced first with heavyweight bags so the stunt coordinators and other crew members can better understand the necessary weight distribution, etc. Then, the set piece is rehearsed with stunt doubles to work out any issues before the actors come in for their own rehearsal.
In Stark’s case, we’re told the mechanics of the stunt were adjusted after the stunt double was injured. Sources indicate that, still, Stark rolled his ankle over another performer in the scene.
Two other injuries followed in subsequent weeks. In one incident, a stunt person injured their arm on a piece of the set that had jagged metal on it, requiring a hospital visit and stitches. Within the last two weeks, another stunt performer was sent to the hospital after a stunt gone wrong. Sources close to production say the hospital trip was “precautionary” after an “awkward landing” on a platform designed to simulate a ground collapse resulted in a broken rib and minor compressed lung. It’s unclear whether this performer has returned to work.
All SAG-AFTRA signatories, including 20th Television owner Disney, are required to follow certain on-set safety protocols. Stunt performers and coordinators are required to complete a general safety and injury prevention program in order to remain eligible for employment on union productions.
The standards and practices for set safety are developed by Contract Services’ industry wide safety committee. The general guidelines for stunts task production management with ensuring they “allow enough time for rehearsals, training, equipment preparations, and inspections,” per the company’s latest stunt safety bulletin. Contract Services also has more detailed guidelines for specific stunt work.
Typically, the stunt coordinator leads all stunt-related preparations including script review, planning, site selection, preparation, testing, rehearsal, modification, and recommendation of the qualified personnel and equipment to be utilized to perform the stunt. The first assistant director is responsible for holding an on-set safety meeting prior to any stunt work so all involved personnel can see a walk-through of the maneuver and discuss protocol in detail. Another safety meeting is required if there are any “substantive changes” to the stunt.
A concentration of injuries on a single season of television doesn’t necessarily indicate negligence, especially on a high-octane show like 9-1-1. However, it is ambitious for a series like 9-1-1 to pull off massive stunt sequences on a regular basis given the restraints of working within the relatively tight production schedule required of broadcast shows, making it more likely for problems to occur.
Two years ago, a crew member died from a cardiac event while driving home from set after the workday ballooned to 14 hours due to complications with a controlled burn that was being used for a stunt. Still, a production source told Deadline at the time that 9-1-1 was “one of the safest that I’ve ever worked on.”

A Sydney currency trader who was sacked for working from Singapore without approval has won an unfair dismissal case, but failed to be awarded compensation.
The Fair Work Commission ruled on Wednesday that Charles Graham had been unfairly dismissed by HIFX Australia, trading as Xe, in December last year.
Graham was sacked after his manager asked an IT worker to use his “FBI skills” and track the IP address on Graham’s laptop.
They discovered he was working from Singapore. It was also later discovered he had previously worked from Bali after telling his manager he was working from home because he had a plumber “coming around to sort out some recurring bathroom issues”.
Graham was sacked as Xe found he knew he had to get prior approval to work overseas and was to attend the office three times a week.
He said he had been holidaying in Singapore before his partner became ill with a bacterial infection, preventing him from returning to Australia.
He provided documentation, which he said showed his partner required medical treatment.
Graham had previously asked Xe if he could relocate to Singapore, but his request was denied.
Fair Work Commission commissioner Alana Matheson said that after the company sent an email to Graham advising him of its discovery on 17 November last year, the “tone … had clearly pivoted” by the following day, when he was told “there was a case to answer regarding alleged breaches of company policy”.
Over the following 10 days, a series of further email exchanges and a discussion between Xe managers took place.
Graham said in his written response to Xe that he travelled to Singapore for a holiday and that there was no relation to his previous request to relocate there, that the decision to reschedule the return flight to Australia was made over a weekend, and that as there was no expectation or precedent that he contacted his manager outside business hours, he could not inform them of this.
He said that when he did log on from Singapore rather than in Australia “he was bombarded with triaging hundreds of unread emails from his time off, fielding inbound calls and dealing with an eligible complaint from a high-value client”, and this took priority over telling his manager he was stuck overseas.
Among his other responses was that he only intended to spend a short amount of time overseas, he had not been told about specific policies regarding hybrid work, and that he had intended to let his manager know he was overseas as soon as practicable.
The company was not swayed and on 2 December last year sent him a termination letter that stated it had carefully reviewed his written submissions and found that he had not provided flight screenshots with his name, medical evidence that showed his partner was unable to travel, an adequate explanation for not telling his manager he was in Singapore, and had previously complied with “absence and approval processes”, demonstrating that he was familiar with them and had instead made “a conscious choice not to follow” them.
“Your conduct represents a serious breach of company policy, a failure to follow lawful and reasonable instructions, and an irreparable breakdown of trust and confidence,” it said in the letter.
Graham told the commission he worked remotely twice before November 2025: the previous year from Townsville, and in April and May 2025 from Bali. He had been employed by Xe for 20 months.
But his manager said she had not been aware he had ever worked remotely from overseas.
A Microsoft Teams message from Graham to his manager was included in evidence before the commission that detailed his claim he was working from home as he had a plumbing issue during one of the days he also told the commission he worked from Bali.
Matheson found that she was satisfied that the dismissal of Graham was unreasonable because while there was a valid reason for his dismissal, the process followed was procedurally unfair.
This was because Xe failed to fully raise the matters it was relying on in making the decision to dismiss Graham, Matheson said.
She found that reinstatement was inappropriate but also decided against awarding compensation.
This was, she said, in part because his misconduct contributed to the decision to dismiss him, and he was paid four weeks in lieu of notice.

In 2030, U.S. mortality and morbidity rates will suddenly jump. This will happen not because there is a new pandemic or a sudden rise in cases of existing diseases or injuries, or a sudden decline in access to health care. These jumps in rates will occur throughout the U.S., more in some states than others. Within states, these rate changes will be especially noticeable among four groups: college-age people, retirement-age people, people of color, and immigrants.
Even more remarkable, these shocking changes in U.S. health statistics could be averted without any new treatments or changes in access to or quality of health care.
What is the secret to prevention? Ensuring that there is an accurate 2030 U.S. decennial census.
The time is short to carry out this prevention campaign. The threat is imminent and profound.
On Sept. 10, the U.S. Federal Register published an extraordinary notice blandly titled “Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions.” It announced plans for three major unprecedented and untested changes to the U.S. decennial census, which together will reduce, selectively, the number of people counted — and where. Since rates are computed by dividing the number of cases by the population at risk in a specified time period, then by definition, if the number of cases stays the same but the size of the denominator shrinks, the rates will be higher.
The initial window for comments was a scant 33 days, with comments due by Oct. 13. Public pushback has resulted in the comment period being extended to Nov. 2.
What are the three critical changes being proposed?
1) Instead of counting the “whole number of persons in each state,” as commanded by the 14th Amendment of the Constitution, the count will be restricted solely to “citizens or lawful permanent residents of the US.” This excludes all foreign citizen residents who do not meet these criteria, including international students, work visa holders, and recognized refugee and aslyees, and also erases undocumented immigrants.
2) Instead of counting people in relation to their usual residence on Census Day (April 1 of the census year), the changed “rules of residence” will require counting people in relation to where they resided the most between Jan. 3 to April 1, as tied also to the address used in tax records. This will likely mean that college students will be counted as living at their parents’ address, instead of at college, and “snowbirds” and seasonal workers will be counted in the warmer states where they winter, not their primary non-winter residence.
3) Prohibit questions about race and ethnicity (race has been asked about since the first U.S. census in 1790) and prohibit any questions about sexual orientation (first appearing in the 2020 census in a question about household relationships).
Have any of these changes been carefully tested, following usual protocols for reviewing any changes to the census? No. Are they consistent with the Constitution and its amendments? No.
The only reason to make these changes is partisan politics. The Constitution allocates political power — specifically representation in the House of Representatives — and draws political districts in relation to decennial census counts of population size. Change the rules on who is counted where and when, and states’ population counts, political power, and political districts will change. The bet is that the proposed changes will provide partisan advantage to those proposing the change in rules.
Altering the count will affect more than just denominators and the distribution of political power. The predictable data distortions will rupture any understanding of the realities of — and trends in — U.S. morbidity and mortality rates. They will also undermine the data used in federal funding formulas for program eligibility and resource allocation, even as removing people from the census count by political sleight of hand does not disappear their needs.
Furthermore, the distortions will impair the conduct and use of population survey data involving economics, health, education, transportation, etc., by distorting the population-based sampling frames and weights on which all such surveys rely.
The far-ranging potential harms are starkly revealed by the U.S. Census Bureau’s list of 50 common uses of census data for allocation of resources and planning, spanning every sector of the U.S. Those especially germane to health and health services include: “Planning for hospitals, nursing homes, clinics, and the location of other health services”; “Estimating the number of people displaced by natural disasters”; “Creating maps to speed emergency services to households in need of assistance”; “Facilitating scientific research”; and “Assessing the potential for spread of communicable diseases.”
There is no substitute for the granular U.S. decennial census data painstakingly collected by the U.S. Census Bureau, in accord with their longstanding and now threatened mission to “count everyone once, only once, and in the right place.”
Over the past 40 years, virtually all health outcomes tracked in the benchmark U.S. annual federal documents Health, United States and in the Healthy People objectives have used census population data to report rates for both the total U.S. population and by race/ethnicity, as well as occasionally by socioeconomic position. For those who think economic data are sufficient to identify who is at highest risk of poor health outcomes in the U.S. absent racial/ethnic data, think again.
A case in point is maternal mortality. The U.S. stands as an outlier with rates higher than those in all other high-income countries. Reflecting intertwined histories of racialized and economic injustice, not only are there stark disparities by race/ethnicity and by educational level, but there are also racialized inequities within each educational level, and educational inequities within each racialized group. Moreover, these inequities interact: Maternal mortality rates are higher among Black women with a completed college education compared to white women with less than a high school diploma. Maternal mortality is a critical and preventable outcome — but prevention requires accurate data.
Prohibit collecting data on race/ethnicity in the census, and the net result will be to render invisible longstanding and well-known American racialized health inequities, overall and by socioeconomic position, as well as their changes over time. For example, between 1966 and 1980, U.S. socioeconomic and racialized inequities in rates of death before age 65 shrank, only to rise thereafter. These patterns likely reflect the beneficial impacts of the 1960s Great Society programs, followed by the post-1980 conservative and neoliberal backlash.
Erasing data does not erase need or harm, but instead is a time-disgraced method of avoiding accountability via the shameful ruse of “no data, no problem.”
For these and many more reasons, the proposed changes to the 2030 U.S. decennial census must be blocked before they can ever be implemented. Everyone who cares about the health and wellbeing of the U.S. population and the integrity of data can submit comments by Nov. 2.
Nancy Krieger is professor of social epidemiology and American Cancer Society clinical research professor at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. She represents her own views and does not speak on behalf of her institution.

ప్రధాన ఎన్నికల కమిషనర్ జ్ఞానేష్ కుమార్ రాజీనామా చేయాలని డిమాండ్ చేస్తూ కాక్రోచ్ జనతా పార్టీ (CJP) ముంబైలోని శివాజీ పార్క్ మైదానంలో 02 అక్టోబర్ 2026న నిరసన ప్రదర్శన నిర్వహించింది. ఓటర్ల జాబితా ప్రత్యేక సమగ్ర సవరణ (SIR)లో ఓటర్ల తొలగింపు ఆరోపణలు, ఎన్నికల ప్రక్రియలో పారదర్శకతపై నిరసనకారులు ఆందోళన వ్యక్తం చేశారు. ఈ సమావేశానికి ముంబై పోలీసులు అనుమతి నిరాకరించినప్పటికీ, వందలాది మంది నిరసనలో పాల్గొని నినాదాలు చేశారు. సమావేశంపై ఉన్న ఆంక్షలను ఉల్లంఘించారనే కారణంతో నిర్వాహకులతో పాటు, ఇందులో పాల్గొన్న 400-500 మంది గుర్తుతెలియని వ్యక్తులపై పోలీసులు FIR నమోదు చేశారు.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, ముంబైలో జరిగిన ఈ నిరసన సందర్భంగా సీజేపీ వ్యవస్థాపకుడు అభిజీత్ దీప్కేపై దాడి జరిగిందని పేర్కొంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. దీంట్లో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: 02 అక్టోబర్ 2026న ముంబైలోని శివాజీ పార్క్లో జరిగిన నిరసన ప్రదర్శనలో CJP వ్యవస్థాపకుడు అభిజీత్ దీప్కేపై దాడి జరిగినప్పటి దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియో 15 జూన్ 2026 నాటిది. రాజస్థాన్లోని జైపూర్లో పేపర్ లీక్లు, నిరుద్యోగానికి వ్యతిరేకంగా జరిగిన నిరసన సందర్భంగా అభిజీత్ దీప్కేపై గుర్తుతెలియని వ్యక్తులు దాడి చేయడాన్ని ఈ వీడియో చూపుతుంది. ముంబై నిరసనలో అభిజీత్ దీప్కేపై దాడి జరిగినట్లు ఎటువంటి నివేదికలు లేవు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇదే వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కనీసం 15 జూన్ 2026 నుండి ఆన్లైన్లో అందుబాటులో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఈ వీడియోలో ఉన్నవి రాజస్థాన్లోని జైపూర్లో అభిజీత్ దీప్కేపై జరిగిన దాడి దృశ్యాలుగా పేర్కొన్నారు.
మీడియా కథనాల ప్రకారం (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ), 15 జూన్ 2026న రాజస్థాన్ జైపూర్లోని షహీద్ స్మారక్ వద్ద జరిగిన నిరసన ప్రదర్శనలో దీప్కేపై కొందరు వ్యక్తులు దాడి చేసి, ముఖంపై పలుమార్లు కొట్టారు. పేపర్ లీకేజీలు, నిరుద్యోగ సమస్యలపై నిరసన తెలుపుతూ, కేంద్ర విద్యాశాఖ మంత్రి ధర్మేంద్ర ప్రధాన్ రాజీనామా చేయాలని డిమాండ్ చేస్తూ ఆయన ఈ కార్యక్రమాన్ని నిర్వహించారు. మద్దతుదారులు దీప్కేను తమ భుజాలపై ఎక్కించుకుని వేదిక వైపు తీసుకువెళ్తుండగా, గుంపులోంచి కొందరు అతడిని కిందకు లాగి ముఖంపై కొట్టారు. దీంతో సీజేపీ మద్దతుదారులు వెంటనే ఎదురుదాడికి దిగగా, పోలీసులు రంగంలోకి దిగి అనుమానితులను అదుపులోకి తీసుకున్నారు.
అనంతరం దీప్కే ఈ దాడిని ఖండిస్తూ, ఈ ఘటన తన ప్రత్యర్థుల భయానికి నిదర్శనమని పేర్కొన్నారు. అంతేకాకుండా, ముంబై శివాజీ పార్క్ నిరసనలో దీప్కేపై దాడి జరిగినట్లు ఎలాంటి వార్తా కథనాలూ లేవు.

Laotian man deported by US to South Sudan leaves for Laos after year in detention
A Laotian man deported by the U.S. to South Sudan has returned to his home country after more than a year in detention
JUBA, South Sudan -- A Laotian man deported by the United States to South Sudan left for Laos on Thursday after spending more than a year in detention in Africa, an ordeal his attorney said could have been avoided.
Thongxay Nilakout, 49, had been willing to return to Laos before the U.S. deported him to South Sudan, attorney Tin Nguyen said. A Lao consular officer had told his family that a travel document had already been issued.
Nilakout left South Sudan on Thursday afternoon for Vientiane, the capital of Laos, Nguyen said. He had been detained in Juba, South Sudan’s capital, since July 2025.
South Sudan’s Foreign Ministry said Thursday that it had coordinated his repatriation with the government of Laos, which provided assurances against torture or other ill-treatment upon his return.
“Thongxay’s deportation to Laos is not just a relief for his family, it is proof of what we argued from day one. He should have been sent to Laos,” Nguyen said in a statement.
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said it was preparing a response to questions about Nilakout’s case and requested more time to comment.
Nilakout and seven other men were sent to Africa in May 2025, rerouted first to a U.S. military base in Djibouti after a federal judge blocked their deportation to South Sudan midflight. They arrived in Juba aboard a military aircraft after a Supreme Court ruling allowed their removal.
The eight were held in a gated house under armed guard. All had criminal convictions in the U.S. but had served their prison sentences before being taken into immigration custody.
Hundreds have been deported from the U.S. to African countries that aren’t their home nations, according to advocacy groups Human Rights First and Refugees International, which have been monitoring the deportations.
Around a dozen African countries have accepted third-country deportees from the U.S., some in exchange for millions of dollars in payments, though details of the South Sudan deal remain murky.
The choice of South Sudan was particularly controversial given its poor human rights record and political instability. Armed conflict displaced more than half a million people there in 2025, according to the United Nations.
Nilakout resettled in the U.S. as a child in 1980 after his family fled Laos, spending time first in a refugee camp in Thailand, his attorney said.
In 1995, he was sentenced to life in prison without parole for his role in the murder of a German tourist during an armed robbery in southern California. He was 17 at the time of the crime.
His attorney said he became eligible for parole after a 2012 U.S. Supreme Court ruling found mandatory life sentences without parole for juvenile offenders unconstitutional. He was released in 2023 and was working as a restaurant cook when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement took him into custody in March 2025.
Four of the original eight deportees remain in South Sudan, including two Burmese nationals and two Cuban nationals. A Congolese national deported separately has since joined them, bringing the total to five, Nguyen said.
South Sudan’s Foreign Ministry confirmed that five third-country deportees remain in South Sudan and said it was working with the governments concerned and international partners to facilitate their safe and humane repatriation.

National Award-winning actor Parvathy Thiruvothu has taken on a new role in her career with Pradhama Drishtya Kuttakkar, which premiered on Netflix today, October 9. After receiving critical acclaim for its investigative narrative and making an impact in theatres, the film is now available on the streaming platform, allowing a wider audience to watch Parvathy in a different on-screen avatar.
Parvathy Thiruvothu on playing a cop for the 1st time in Pradhama Drishtya Kuttakkar: “A lot of my preparation was about making sure Aleena felt like a real person”
The film marks the first time in Parvathy’s two-decade-long career that she has portrayed a police officer in Malayalam cinema. She plays Aleena Abraham, a woman police constable who navigates an investigation while balancing the demands of her profession with compassion and an understanding of human emotions.
For Parvathy, playing Aleena involved exploring the person behind the uniform rather than relying on familiar portrayals of police officers. Her approach focused on understanding the character’s sense of duty, authority, instincts and vulnerabilities. Through Aleena, the actor aimed to present a police officer who feels grounded and relatable, with her professional responsibilities existing alongside her personal qualities.
Speaking about her experience of playing the character, Parvathy said, “Playing Aleena Abraham was a very new experience for me because I had never played a police officer before in Malayalam. I wanted to understand the person behind the uniform — her sense of responsibility, her compassion, and the authority that comes with the job. A lot of my preparation was about finding that balance and making sure Aleena felt like a real person rather than just a cop on screen. It has been really encouraging to see how the film and the character have been received in theatres, and I’m excited that with the OTT release, a much wider audience will now get the chance to experience Aleena and the story.”
The actor’s performance in Pradhama Drishtya Kuttakkar adds another dimension to her filmography, as she steps into a professional role she had not explored previously in Malayalam cinema. Her portrayal centres on the challenges of investigating a case while navigating the human emotions that accompany the job.
With the film now streaming on Netflix, viewers who missed its theatrical run can watch Parvathy take on the role of Aleena Abraham. The OTT premiere also brings the investigative drama to a wider audience, offering viewers an opportunity to experience the story and the actor’s first Malayalam police officer role.

A landmark survey of the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population has revealed the once endangered species is thriving.
A population of Aldabra giant tortoise lives on an island in Seychelles called Aldabra Atoll.
The most recent survey, led by Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter, revealed there were approximately 180,000 tortoises living on the island.
This is the highest figure ever recorded for the species and far exceeds the human population of Seychelles.
The new figure was obtained by a team who analysed five years of tortoise counts between 2018 and 2022.
It is the first update since a widely cited figure of 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s.
Aldabra Atoll is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises are found in the wild, with a much smaller population living in the Galápagos.
Dr Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, CEO of SIF, said: “More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve.
“This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.”
The study, published in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution, found that the population was relatively stable for this period, with a best estimate of almost 183,000 adult and sub-adult tortoises.
In the 19th century, exploitation of the animals meant there were fewer than 1,000 Aldabra tortoises left on the island.
But a recovery programme meant the island became a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a Unesco site in 1982.
Researchers are now saying it is one of the greatest conservation success stories of the Indian Ocean, with the new study confirming it.
“Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring programme is one of the longest running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said Dr Nancy Bunbury, one of the study’s co-authors.
“By modelling what we didn’t see, as well as what we did, we’ve produced the most reliable baseline yet for this iconic Seychelles species, establishing a benchmark we can use to track the population for decades to come.”
Despite the good news, the study’s authors warn that vigilance is essential. Aldabra’s climate is changing, with longer and more frequent droughts predicted to reduce the shade and food available to tortoises, while rising sea levels threaten low-lying parts of the atoll.
The study authors say invasive mammals remain a key threat including feral cats and black rats that prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings.
The planned eradication of these remaining invasive mammals, the authors say, could lift the last barriers to further growth of the population and help it withstand future climate pressures.
“These results are great news for the tortoises and testament to the fantastic work done in the field,” said Dr Dave Hudson, postdoctoral research associate at the University of Exeter’s Cornwall campus.
“But it’s important to remember that the numbers provide a baseline – not an endpoint.
“Hopefully we have provided the conservation managers the evidence they need to track future change and act early as the tortoises face increasing pressures from climate change, drought and invasive species.”

Roberto De Zerbi has urged bottom-of-the-table Tottenham Hotspur to “react” to the pressure of their crunch clash with fellow strugglers Manchester United.
De Zerbi’s side head to Old Trafford on Saturday in dire need of a first Premier League victory this season.
The north London club has lost three of its first five top-flight matches and crashed out of the League Cup against Liverpool.
De Zerbi has been waiting for the chance to erase the bitter taste of a 3-2 home defeat against Aston Villa in Tottenham’s last match before the international break.
And, with scrutiny mounting on the Italian, the Spurs manager demanded his players rise to the challenge against United.
“I’ve been waiting for this game from three weeks. After the defeat at home against Aston Villa, personally I wanted to play the day after,” he told reporters on Friday.
“It was difficult, it was very tough, especially the first week. But it is football. It is part of the situation in this moment. We have to react, to work in this moment.”
Tottenham failed to score in its first four league games before finally finding the net twice against Villa.
De Zerbi conceded his team has to improve in attack if it is to climb out of the bottom three.
“We created chances to score many other goals in these seven games but we didn’t. We are working to improve in the last third, the assists and the finishing,” he said.
“We are fourth in the table for the team who brings the ball into the opponents’ area the most times.
“It is nothing but it shows we can arrive in the area. We are not good enough to score goals so far when we have clear chances.”
With United manager Michael Carrick also under pressure following its poor start, Tottenham’s trip to Manchester has been dubbed ‘El Sackicko’.
De Zerbi saved Tottenham from relegation after arriving late last season, but that final-day survival feat is unlikely to save him from the axe if results don’t improve soon.
“We are Tottenham. United and Tottenham are still big clubs in the Premier League,” he said.
“We have to deserve to work in this club, playing better and making different results.”

With the Vivo V70 series, Vivo took a premium turn. You can check out our detailed Vivo V70 review. Previously, Vivo V series phones had flashy designs, tall displays, and curved screens, designed to attract people who like flashy looks. But the Vivo V70 changed that rather significantly. Vivo has gone for a more compact form factor and a sturdier build that appeals to anyone looking for flagship-level build quality in a Vivo V series phone.
Now the Vivo V80 continues the tradition. It keeps the same compact form factor and solid build, which feels more like a proper flagship than a typical Vivo design. Now has a bigger 7200 mAh battery, ships with OriginOS 7 out of the box, and is the first non-flagship phone with an excellent 144 AMOLED display and a Zeiss camera setup.
However, it also gets a huge price hike. The base variant now comes with 8GB + 128GB priced at Rs 62,999, 8GB + 256GB at Rs 69,999, and finally 8GB + 512GB at Rs 79,999. Vivo V80 sits next to flagship phones where the competition becomes much harder to ignore.
The Vivo V70 found a speed sweet spot for buyers who cared more about cameras than outright performance. So, with the Vivo V80, has Vivo found that sweet spot again, or has it pushed the Vivo V series a little too far this time? Let’s find out.
Table of Contents
Vivo V80 Review: Great Cameras, Premium Looks and a Price To Match
Compact Build, Flagship-Like Feel
The Vivo V80 looks strikingly similar to the V70 from the front. It keeps the same compact body design with rounded corners on all four sides. In fact, they have almost the same dimensions except the Vivo V80 is now slightly thicker: 157.52 × 74.33 × 7.69 mm (Vivo V70: 157.52 × 74.33 × 7.59 mm), and also slightly heavier at 203g compared to 194g on the Vivo V70 because of the larger battery.
The button placement is also very similar to the V70, with the power and volume buttons on the right being easy to access with one hand. They are clicky and tactile. On the left, it is clean, while on the bottom you will find the SIM ejector, speaker, and Type-C charging port.
You will notice the real difference when you turn the phone around. The camera module now stretches almost across the width of the phone, following the design trend we have been seeing in the phones lately.
Vivo also changed the camera placement to use that extra space better than on the V70, tucking it in with ZEISS branding neatly as well. It comes with a glass back, and the camera module blends neatly into the glass. It also doubles as a natural resting position for your finger while holding the phone. Design-wise, I would rate it 10/10 for its compact form factor and solid in-hand feel.
The device is also IP68 + IP69 rated, so it can protect against dust and water, and it comes in three color options this time. The Stellar Black for those who prefer black phones, Horizon Blue, the one I got, which honestly looks more like olive than blue, and the new Sunrise Anthem color that has a subtle orange, not a contrast look that we found on the iPhone 17 Pro. Here is how all colors look in person.
Sharp 144Hz AMOLED, but Performance Holds It Back
On the front, you get a 6.59-inch 1.5K Amoled edge-to-edge display with minimal bezels on all four sides. Vivo has gone with a flat AMOLED panel once again. The resolution remains the same. But Vivo has bumped the refresh rate to 144Hz from 120Hz.
The processor technically supports it, but pushing both resolution and refresh rate to the highest settings makes the phone noticeably choppier to use. By default, the screen resolution is set to HD, but you can set it to Ultra HD for a sharper display.
OriginOS also lets you choose different screen colors. By default, it is set to natural, but if you want a punchy, vibrant-looking display, you can switch to bright to make on-screen colors pop.
The display is very bright. You get almost all of the advantages of a good AMOLED panel. With its resolution and 459 pixels per inch, the display looks sharp, and the AMOLED panel ensures deep blacks and rich colors. It also has 5000 nits of local peak brightness for HDR content. The display can get very bright, so you can use it comfortably in direct sunlight without visibility issues.
My biggest issue is the same as what I have with the Vivo V70. The phone supports high resolution and the highest refresh rate, but the processor, because of its limitations, struggles to keep the experience smooth. The phone is also Widevine L1 certified, so you can watch Netflix, Amazon, or HD content on other streaming platforms.
Strong ZEISS Cameras, but the Ultrawide Needs an Upgrade
Cameras have long been Vivo phones’ biggest strength. Vivo V80 continues that tradition. Vivo has largely stuck with the same hardware on the V80 as on the V70. That is both a good and a bad thing.
The good thing is these cameras are capable and well-tuned for photography; the bad is Vivo still uses a lower-resolution ultra-wide-angle camera, which definitely needs an upgrade if it wants to compete with flagship phones at this price, especially when it still relies on the camera as its biggest strength.
For starters, it comes with a 50-megapixel ZEISS OIS Main Camera with OIS. It also has a 50-megapixel ZEISS Night Telephoto Camera and a 50MP 3x periscope telephoto zoom. The ultra-wide is the same 8MP ZEISS sensor, with an f/2.2 aperture and a 115-degree field of view.
Vivo V80 vs Vivo X200T: Which Has the Better Camera?
In the past, I compared Vivo V70 cameras with the Vivo X200T, but I also called it an unfair comparison because of the Rs 14,000 price difference between them. But fast-forward to now, after the price increase, the Vivo V70 now sells for the same price as the Vivo X200T, and the latest Vivo V80 is Rs 3,000 more expensive than the Vivo X200T.
I still have the Vivo X200T with me. Now it’s safe to compare both smartphones and decide which one to pick up if you care only about the camera.
Main camera in daylight
First, in daylight, Vivo X200T photos look closer to real life, while Vivo V80 photos look brighter and punchier. The Vivo X200T also handles shadows better than the Vivo V80.
As you can see in the first image, the Vivo V80 loses detail in the bushes, whereas the X200T handles shadows better. The Vivo V80 also has more detail.
Both photos look detailed normally; however, when you zoom in on the Vivo V80, the edges look rough, and the textures look crunchy because of the oversharpening. Both cameras do exceptionally well, but the Vivo V80 might appeal to most users because its contrasty photos work better on social media.
2x Zoom: Vivo X200T Pulls Ahead
Next, both smartphones have a telephoto lens. Side by side, Vivo V80 clearly falls behind in detail. As the images above show, when you zoom in, the Vivo X200T retains more detail than the Vivo V80. As you can see in the image above, the ground behind the cow on the Vivo V80 lacks detail, but on the X200T you can clearly see the grainy structure and other details.
3x Telephoto: Vivo V80 Comes Close
The Vivo V80 comes close to the Vivo X200T in the 3x telephoto shots. When you zoom out, both shots look really good to the eye; the Vivo V80 looks more contrasty and the colors pop, while the Vivo X200T keeps the colors closer to natural.
But again, the Vivo X200T has finer texture. For example, in the second image, when you zoom in, the bird feathers and stone details look better on the Vivo X200T than on the Vivo V80. But the Vivo V80 is also preferable here and retains plenty of detail, though it looks softer when compared side by side with the Vivo X200T. But still, most users prefer Vivo V80 photos simply because of their more vivid and punchy look.
Ultrawide: Vivo V80 Falls Behind
When it comes to the ultra-wide camera, even the specs show that the Vivo V80 falls far behind the Vivo X200T. Vivo still uses the lower 8-megapixel sensor, and it clearly struggles to capture the details. As you can see from the images below, the Vivo X200T shows clear leaves in the bark, whereas the Vivo V80 looks soft. Once again, Vivo oversharpens the image, making it look more contrasty than it does in real life. You can clearly see the difference in the image sample below.
Indoor Shots: The Gap Gets Smaller
Next, in the indoor and close-up shots, once again, Vivo X200T produces natural colors and also natural background blur with crisp and real details, whereas Vivo V80 also does a really good job, and when you look at both samples, the difference is quite small indoors.
Selfies: Both Are Good, X200T Is Slightly Better
Both the Vivo X200T and Vivo V80 produce sharp, detailed-looking selfies. The selfies on the Vivo V80 look cooler than the warmer tones on the Vivo X200T, as you can see in the images below. Both smartphones capture plenty of detail, with the Vivo X200T being slightly better, but not by much.
Shooting Into the Sun: Vivo V80 Struggles More
When shooting directly into the sun, both phones show lens flare. The Vivo V80 struggles more here with the white balance shifting, whereas the Vivo X200T keeps the colors natural and contrasty but still shows a visible ring of light across the frame.
Overall, in comparison, if camera quality is the top priority, and if you want natural-looking colors, a better all-rounder, and also a much better ultra-wide camera, the Vivo X200T takes the lead, while the Vivo V80 is still very capable and comes quite close in many situations. People may also prefer the more punchy look of the Vivo V80 that is ready to post on social media.
The same goes for low-light photos as well. The Vivo V80 is slightly behind the Vivo X200T in terms of retaining details, and some pictures look grainy in comparison.
You can also shoot portraits using the telephoto lens. The portraits look sharp, with strong blur and strong subject separation. You can also use the portrait mode with the telephoto lens to capture close-up portrait shots. Portrait mode also supports several Zeiss portrait styles, which are one of the highlight features of the Vivo V series phones.
And since the Vivo V80 is a camera-focused phone with a ZEISS partnership, you also get camera-focused features that are nice to play around with. It comes with various filters; Zeiss Natural mode is my favorite for getting more natural-looking photos. But still, the Vivo V80 tends to produce slightly punchier colors than expected.
In terms of video quality, the videos shot on the Vivo V80 are decent, bright, and colorful, same as the photos. Whereas the X200T leans toward more natural colors, the Vivo tends to make the overall quality brighter and the colors punchier, which, again, many people might like because of the contrasty colors that are good for social media posting.
Vivo V80 can record up to 4K 60fps from both the front and rear cameras. It also supports several video styles and modes. My favorite is 4K Cinematic Camera mode. Using it, you can produce cinematic-style, color-graded videos.
Fine for Everyday Use, Not for Performance Seekers
Vivo V80 comes with the same Snapdragon 7 Gen 4 used on the Vivo V70. It also comes with downgraded storage, UFS 3.1 compared to UFS 4.1 on the Vivo V70, and LPDDR4X compared to LPDDR5X. Also, the base variant now comes with 128GB instead of 256GB offered on the Vivo V70.
On paper, these are significant downgrades, especially when the Vivo V80 is priced close to flagship territory, where most phones are powered by Snapdragon 8 Elite-class processors.
I understand that most smartphones have recently gone through a price hike, and many smartphones are launching with even 4GB RAM in the budget segment, but those compromises are acceptable in the budget segment; for a phone with this experience, it is harder ot justiy, but considering the rise in memory and component costs, we do not have many choices.
In everyday use, I didn’t notice any big performance drop. Everyday tasks are decently faster. I didn’t have many expectations for the Snapdragon 7 Gen 4, but in gaming and when bumping up the refresh rate, I clearly noticed choppy performance. If performance is your highest priority, this phone clearly isn’t meant for that
Vivo V80 Benchmarks
Easy Two-Day Battery Life With Light Use
Battery life is not really a concern on the Vivo V80. Most smartphones today already come with fairly large batteries and support ultra-fast charging. Vivo also packed a dense 7200 mAh battery in the Vivo V80, and it also supports 90W super-fast charging. It can fully charge the device in under 1.5 hours.
Also, because of the less power-hungry Snapdragon 7 Gen 4, the battery can easily last up to two days with light usage and a full day with heavier use, which includes gaming and everyday tasks like browsing, watching videos, taking calls, and more.
Loud Stereo Speakers With Good Separation
Vivo V80 comes with stereo speakers. Both speakers are equally loud and offer very good stereo separation. There is no 3.5 mm headphone jack, which is pretty much the norm on most phones right now.
OriginOS 7 Is Good, but the V80 Misses Some Features
Vivo V80 is the first phone in India to ship with Origin OS 7 out of the box. OriginOS 7 has plenty of new customization features, including new themes, better lock screen customization options, a new liquid glass design, and a new workbench feature that lets you run five apps at once and switch between them easily. It also comes with useful AI features. Unfortunately, not all of those made it into the Vivo V80.
Vivo V80 lacks both the liquid glass design and the workbench feature because of RAM limitations (Workbench features require devices with 12GB RAM or more). OriginOS 7 still offers plenty of customization features on the Vivo V80. I already covered some of my favorite features in a different post. Adding custom stickers and the new pet pal wallpapers are a few of my favorites.
Vivo Origin OS 7 also brings plenty of AI features to the Vivo V80. After a very long time, I found very few of them useful beyond the AI image editing tools that we initially saw in many phones.
One of the favorite features is Snapshot. You can point the camera at a whiteboard, documents, or any text, and it can extract all the text. In the Notes app, it can arrange the text into tables, lists, and more.
The AI recorder is also useful. It allows you to create transcripts of your recordings, generate summaries, and pull useful insights. There are also plenty of AI camera features as well, letting you generate various AI-generated styles and effects.
Another feature I particularly liked is the Redirect Audio. It lets you play multiple audio tracks through different outputs without interfering with each other. For instance, if your phone is connected to Bluetooth and playing music, you can still watch a YouTube video at the same time using your phone’s speakers without affecting the music playing on your Bluetooth speaker.
Vivo also promised to roll out 4 years of major OS updates and six years of security updates for the Vivo V80, which is a very good software commitment
Vivo V80 Review Verdict: Great Cameras, but Vivo Has Pushed the V80 Too Far
For the asking price of Rs 62,999/-, Vivo has pushed the Vivo V80 a little too far this time. It now sits in the flagship territory, where you start getting phones with much stronger hardware.
It also competes with its own peers like the Vivo X200T, which at least for now feels like an overall better deal if value for your money is your highest priority. However, we are not sure whether the Vivo X200T will continue to exist as a competitor.
Vivo V80 is still a compelling device, especially for the cameras and also the new design. But if you’re open to other options or care about performance, Vivo V80 is harder to recommend. Of course,we all know that smartphone prices have gone up significantly over the past few months, and Vivo V80 is clearly another victim trying to justify its higher price.
