Inside the £1-an-hour official football shirt factories
- Published
Workers are being paid a basic wage of less than £1 an hour to make official football shirts for some of the world's biggest clubs, BBC Sport can reveal.
Our investigation traced authentic replica shirts to two factories in Cambodia, where conditions were described as "grim".
We followed the supply chain behind official shirts after fans told us they were frustrated by rising prices, with many turning to cheaper counterfeits instead.
Images obtained from inside Bowker Garment Factory and Trax Apparel show kits being made for clubs including Arsenal, Celtic, Liverpool and Real Madrid.
Employees there told us they struggled to make ends meet and worked on up to 700 items a day as part of a production line.
In rare interviews, supported by documentary evidence and published anonymously, workers also described:
- Factory temperatures above 35C.
- Verbal abuse when targets were missed.
- Safety concerns about electrical equipment.
The Clean Clothes Campaign, external - a global workers' rights network - said our findings painted a "very grim picture".
"These are issues that many garment workers around the world face every day," added spokesperson Emma Vogt.
Similar issues, such as low pay and high temperatures, have been reported across Cambodia's garment industry.
Research published last year suggested that, of a typical £85 shirt, £8.50 covers fabric, sewing and shipping, £37.45 goes to the retailer, £16.25 to the manufacturer, £9.50 on marketing and £13.60 in VAT.
Shirt prices have increased significantly over the past decade, though industry experts argue advances in technology and expensive kit deals with elite clubs have contributed to the rise.
Adidas does not own either factory, but both are primary suppliers subject to its workplace standards., external
The sportswear giant supplies eight of the 20 Premier League teams.
Adidas said: "We have taken a variety of measures to ensure fair and safe working conditions for workers across our supply chain for more than 25 years.
"Through around 1,200 factory audits per year, we review and evaluate supplier conduct, work with suppliers to address issues and make improvements where necessary."
Life on the production line
Six thousand miles from the club shops where these shirts will be sold, a meeting is taking place inside Bowker Garment Factory.
In a photograph obtained by BBC Sport, mannequins display Benfica, Aston Villa and Celtic kits beneath an Adidas logo on the wall.
About 3,400 people - most of them women - work here on the outskirts of Phnom Penh. Another 3,200 work 10 miles east at Trax Apparel.
Fabric is imported from Thailand and Vietnam before a specialist tailor makes a sample for other employees to follow.
Much of the shirt-making process then takes place at these factories, including sewing, ironing and packaging.
'These shirts contain the sweat of Cambodian workers'
Staff typically work six eight-hour shifts a week and, according to five payslips seen by the BBC, receive basic monthly salaries of $210-$220 (£158-£166).
The salaries comply with local minimum-wage laws, and three of the payslips indicate total monthly earnings of about $300 (£226) once overtime and allowances are included, albeit with significant extra hours worked.
"It's hard to live with this amount," said a Bowker worker, who explained she had little left after rent, food and utilities.
"I want international customers to hear that one shirt they buy costs more than two weeks' salary for a worker," said another worker at Trax.
"Every one of these shirts contains the sweat of Cambodian workers."
Trax told us its average monthly employee earnings range from $305-$342 (£230-£258) this year.
Adidas said average net wages across a sample of its Cambodian suppliers were 34% above the Anker Research Institute's living-wage benchmark,, external adding staff were "usually paid considerably higher than the local minimum wage".
Bowker did not respond to our request for comment.
'One shirt sells for $120. How much are they pulling in from 600 of them?'
In another photograph taken inside Bowker, a thermometer shows 35.2C and humidity of 57.6%.
"The heat stress is really taking a toll on our health," said an employee on the ironing line.
Workers at both factories described pressure to meet group production targets of between 300 and 700 items a day.
"Just think about that," they added. "If one shirt sells for $120 (£90) in the store, how much are they pulling in from 600 of them? They make a ton of money but give almost nothing to the workers."
Others described verbal abuse when targets were missed.
"When we can't complete the quota they scold and yell at us and tell us to resign," said a third worker at Bowker.
The same employee said they received two electric shocks from an exposed wire.
"I tried to report it multiple times, but they only took action after the second time I got shocked," they said.
Adidas told us both factories had "heat-management measures", that its standards "do not permit any form of harassment", and that "no electrical-related accidents" had been found in Bowker's records.
Trax acknowledged "periods of elevated temperature" but said cooling systems were in place and insisted its approach "is not based on enforcing output targets".
Such concerns are widespread across Cambodia's garment industry, with a 2024 International Labour Organization report, external finding 69% of factories had issues with heat and 84% with worker protection.
From Cambodia to the club shop
It's August Bank Holiday in England and two of the Premier League's top sides - Aston Villa and Arsenal - are about to meet.
Tens of thousands of people are at Villa Park - many wearing shirts made in Cambodia.
Arsenal's latest home design was released in May, but we were sent photographs showing it inside Trax months earlier.
Fans of both clubs told us official shirts have become overpriced.
One Villa supporter has just paid £95 for his, complete with a Champions League badge.
"You buy your season ticket. Three shirts, that's around £300 on top. It's ridiculous," he said.
An Arsenal fan is struggling with the outlay for his whole family.
"I've got young kids now and I've started getting them kits, so it's started getting expensive," he said. "They're not cheap if you get the official ones."
Various studies estimate the global market for official football teamwear is worth several billion pounds.
"The mark-up on football jerseys... it's hard to imagine a more lucrative brand market," said Dave Welsh from The Solidarity Center, external - a US-based workers' rights organisation.
But former Puma and Umbro kit designer Rob Warner told BBC Sport last year that the economics behind shirt prices are more complex.
"A lot of the profit margin is made by the retailer because they're so dependent on the success of the team... it's a risk," he said.
"Then you factor in the cost of the kit deals going up, and the brands having to try to recover some of the money they're paying to the elite clubs."
Adidas supplies eight of the 20 Premier League clubs, plus Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales.
Fellow sportswear giant Nike supplies three, as well as England. Its football shirts have been produced in Thailand and Vietnam, and more recently Georgia.
Nike does not publish salary data by country, but told us 71% of its key suppliers pay at or above living-wage benchmarks relevant to their location.
Hummel, which also provides kit to three Premier League sides, did not respond to our enquiry.
'Respect has got to be a baseline in sport'
The average price of an adult replica Premier League shirt has risen by 50.7% over the past decade, helping fuel demand for counterfeits sold for as little as £12.
Many of those counterfeit shirts originate from China.
Fans have been warned against buying fakes, with police saying, external they can be "manufactured without regard for safety standards or workers' rights" and Trading Standards warning that "counterfeiters have no morals and no standards".
The Premier League expects clubs to carry out appropriate due diligence on their kit manufacturers and supply chains.
None of the clubs named in this article responded to our request for comment.
"Respect has got to be a baseline in sport," said Anna Bryher, from UK campaign group Labour Behind the Label., external
"Clubs need to send a really strong message that they won't put their name on a shirt if workers are not treated with respect."

Cardiac rehabilitation, a multidisciplinary approach to recovery and risk-reduction, is an important addition to medications, interventional and surgical procedures in heart patients. A cardiac rehab programme usually includes medical assessments, supervised exercise, nutritional guidance, psychosocial counselling and health education tailored to the clinical, cultural and behavioural needs of the patient.
Cardiac rehab has been incorporated into the routine care of patients in developed countries, while it is just now gaining inroads in low- and middle- income countries like India. The primary benefits of attending a cardiac rehab programme are faster recovery from cardiac procedures, reduced risk of future complications, improvement in blood sugar, blood pressure and lipid levels, increased cardiorespiratory fitness, adherence to a heart healthy diet, better weight management, abstinence from tobacco and excessive alcohol consumption, better emotional health and health-related quality of life, and decreased mortality.
The scenario in India
There is now a growing prevalence of heart diseases in the young Indian population, both in urban and rural parts of the country. According to the Global Burden of Disease, 2021, heart disease is the most common cause of death in India, accounting for 28.6 lakh deaths. Estimates indicate that nearly 27% of all deaths in India are due to heart disease, while 62% of all deaths due to cardiovascular disease in the country are premature, between the ages of 40 and 69 years. Among those who survive, the effects can linger for years, affecting productivity and quality of life. This has brought to the fore, the urgent need for more widespread and accessible cardiac rehab facilities. There is a wide gap in the number of heart patients requiring cardiac rehab and the actual numbers being referred for these services.
Barriers to rehab
Even among those who access and enrol in cardiac rehab programmes, not everyone completes the programme. The main barriers to completing the cardiac rehab program after enrolling include patients’ work commitments, family responsibilities, financial constraints, and medical complications. Programmes that can offer personalised solutions including flexible scheduling, return-to-work counselling, sliding scale payment options and close collaborations with the referring cardiologist to identify and treat complications early, could help decrease drop-outs. Programme facilitators must also be able to proactively identify cues for potential non-adherence and work with patients and their families to circumvent challenges and complete the programme.
What works
A ‘TRACK and CARE’ policy could help in improving patient engagement in cardiac rehab programmes. TRACK denotes establishing Trust, involving the patient’s Relatives, helping them set clear Aims for the programme, Checking on the progress made on a daily, weekly and monthly basis and finally remembering to say Kudos to every single positive behaviour change made by the patient. The CARE refers to multidisciplinary care, comorbidity care and holistic care, where various specialists work together to address the different medical and psychological needs of the patient.
Young people are increasingly contracting heart disease. Getting them back to be productive, healthy and happy members of society is vital. While prevention remains the most important goal, cardiac rehabilitation must become an important part of treatment, not just an add-on that is optional. And to do that, we have to proactively address the potential barriers to access, adherence and programme completion.
(Dr. Priya Chockalingam is the clinical director, Cardiac Wellness Institute, Chennai. drpriya@cardiacwellnessinstitute.com)

The Jan Swasthya Abhiyan (JSA) and the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatment have called for regulation of charges levied by private hospitals and ceilings on trade margins for medicines, medical devices and medical consumables, amid renewed scrutiny by the Supreme Court of pricing practices in hospital pharmacies.
The groups, in a statement issued on Monday (October 5, 2026), said patients continued to face high and arbitrary charges for treatment, medicines and consumables, with limited avenues to challenge hospital bills.
The Supreme Court has recently questioned steep markups on medicines sold through hospital pharmacies and practices that require patients to purchase medicines from hospital-linked pharmacies. The court has also asked the government to examine regulation of trade margins.
Pricing vs determining charge
“The problem extended beyond the pricing of individual medicines to the broader question of how private hospitals determine charges for procedures, services and consumables. Private healthcare has expanded enormously in India, but regulation has simply not kept pace,” said Abhay Shukla, co-convener, JSA. He added that patients often had little bargaining power at healthcare facilities.
The Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010 provides a framework for registration and regulation of clinical establishments and envisages standardisation of services and charges. However, its implementation is not uniform across the country, and several States have their own legislation or regulatory arrangements.
The groups said the absence of a uniform mechanism to regulate hospital charges had left patients vulnerable to hefty bills, particularly for prolonged hospitalisation and procedures involving multiple medicines, devices and consumables.
They are now demanding that the Centre and States introduce ceilings on charges levied by private hospitals for procedures, services and treatment and establish accessible, time-bound mechanisms through which patients can challenge excessive or unjustified bills.
The groups have also called for regulation of trade margins on medicines, medical devices and other medical consumables.
K.M. Gopakumar, co-convener, Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatment, said that the maximum retail price (MRP) cannot become a licence to charge patients many times the procurement price.
The group has also cited earlier concerns raised by the Competition Commission of India (CCI) regarding margins in pharmaceutical sales and incentives created when hospitals or hospital pharmacies control the products patients are required to purchase.
Financial incentives for doctors
Raising concern over the effect of financial incentives on clinical decision-making, Gayatri Sharma, a community health physician and researcher, said revenue-linked incentives could put pressure on doctors to increase investigations or procedures.
“Doctors should be able to make treatment decisions solely on the basis of what is medically necessary for the patient,” she said, calling for the National Medical Commission (NMC) to examine incentive-linked remuneration practices for doctors.
The group, in its statement, has called for a stronger public healthcare system alongside regulation of private providers, including increased public health spending and strengthening of government hospitals to provide accessible care. The demands include immediate regulation of trade margins on medicines, medical devices and consumables; ceilings on private hospital charges; a competition-law review of potentially anti-competitive practices; and an independent and time-bound grievance redress mechanism for patients.

Reusable water bottles are a matter of personal taste, and WIRED reviewers have strong opinions on which jug reigns supreme. We’ve spent years testing, sipping, and spilling our way through the best water bottles to round up our favorites.
A note to remember: You only need one reusable bottle (though I won’t judge if you rotate between two). More than that defeats the environmental purpose of purchasing a reusable bottle in the first place. Also, be aware that some insulated bottles use lead solder. We’ve removed those from our list. We have some standards, after all.
Does your water need to be even cleaner? Check out our guide to the Best Backpacking Water Filters. Then get one of our Best Travel Mugs or Best Tote Bags.
Updated October 2026: We’ve added the Owala FreeSip Sway and Path Water Bottle as picks and the Bentgo Lift Chug as an honorable mention. We also moved the Owala FreeSip Twist to honorable mentions and ensured up-to-date prices and information throughout.
Featured in this Article
A PSA on Lead
Some water bottle companies use lead soldering to manufacture their vacuum-sealed bottles. The Stanley Quencher tumbler is one of them. No amount of lead exposure is safe, but it poses particular risk for children and pregnant people. The company has confirmed that some pellets used to seal the bottom of the cup use lead, but unless you remove or damage the bottom of the cup, the lead will not come into contact with your beverage or skin.
The risk of exposure might be very low, but it should be zero. Given that many brands practice lead-free manufacturing, we think the proximity to exposure is unnecessary.
Best Overall
A longtime favorite of outdoorsy folks and anyone else who wants a water bottle that’s not easily damaged, Hydro Flask has staying power. That may be due in part to its customization capability: Pick your preferred type of bottle, cap, and color, and if you buy from Hydro Flask, you can also engrave many styles. You can choose one color for the bottle, another for the lid, and depending on those choices, yet another for the strap or straw. —Boutayna Chokrane
Best for Straw Lovers
Owala perfected its FreeSip design with the Sway, which includes familiar features of other bottles in the line, like fun colors, triple-layer insulation, and a multifunctional mouthpiece that lets you sip through its straw or tilt the bottle upward to swig through its spout. Details that lift the Sway above its FreeSip cousins include its convenient top-carry handle that’s easy to hold, contoured side edges that let you get a comfortable grip while you drink, and its attached push-button opening with a locking mechanism that both lets you drink one-handed and also saves you from unfortunate spills.
Its materials are durable, it comes in four sizes (the 30-ounce option is plenty big for me without being too cumbersome), and the lid is dishwasher-safe. Even so, because the lid has a lot of edges and ridges where gunk can get trapped, I like to clean it by hand, which is a bit of a pain.
The wider top lid screws off completely, letting you add ice or easily pour in any other beverage, but it’s important to close it tightly before throwing it in your bag. The same warning applies to ensuring you’ve toggled on the mouthpiece lock. While the Sway is indeed leakproof when used as directed, the bottle is ripe for user-error spills, as I’ve learned the hard way. But if you look over to your passenger seat while you’re driving and see water pooling around your bottle because you forgot to close it correctly, at least you can snatch it up easily and plop it into a cup holder—a win that some other FreeSip models don’t offer. —Alexis Berger
Best BPA-Free Plastic
Today’s youths love their wide-leg jeans and Nirvana T-shirts, but ask any ’90s kid, and they’ll tell you that the look is incomplete without the water bottle of our times: the classic Nalgene. Originally made of bulletproof (and BPA-rich) Lexan, the Nalgene was the original name-brand water bottle, a symbol of good taste and outdoorsy vibes to be toted between Planet Hollywood and Blockbuster. The Nalgene had a complete chokehold on the premillennial culture, propping up water at a time when Surge and Josta were at such ready supply that human beings may well have stopped consuming plain water entirely were it not for the Nalgene. The brand has since replaced the chemical plastic with modern materials like Tritan, which is BPA-free and made of half-recycled plastic, but it otherwise remains the same: a perfect bottle, carrying a reasonable supply of fluid for the day with a secure screw-top lid, handy measurement lines, and a wide mouth for ice cubes and easy cleaning—unlike the bacteria-teeming straws on those adult sippy cups. —Martin Cizmar

Frequently Asked Questions
How Much Water Do I Need?
The eight-glasses rule isn’t exactly accurate, but it’s a solid starting point. Since water intake is highly individualized (kind of like the bottle itself), it’s best to consult your doctor about the right amount for you. Several lifestyle factors can influence your hydration needs. If you’re active or sweat a lot, for example, you generally should increase your intake to make up for losses. Remember that while warmer temperatures can make us thirstier, drinking too much water can cause overhydration and sodium levels to drop to dangerous levels in a condition called hyponatremia.
Certain medications can lead to water retention, which is another reason why it can’t hurt to ask your physician about your personal ideal water intake during your next check-up. In the meantime, if you’re not thirsty and your urine is colorless or light yellow, you’re likely doing great, sweetie.
How Do Insulated Water Bottles Work?
An insulated water bottle consists of a double-wall construction with insulating materials that prevent heat transfer. Insulated bottles are heavier and can typically hold less water compared to their uninsulated counterparts, given similar exterior dimensions. However, the advantage is that insulated models are typically vacuum-sealed, allowing them to better maintain the temperature of the liquid inside for far longer periods.
Condensation is typical in non-insulated water bottles, where beads of water form on the exterior of the bottle. In this case, you may end up avoiding packing the bottle inside your bag to protect your personal items from your sweating water bottle.
Insulated bottles are made of stainless steel and other similar durable, damage-resistant materials. While they’re typically more expensive because of the higher-quality materials, advanced technology, and complex manufacturing process, insulated water bottles may also have a longer lifespan than their noninsulated counterparts. This can minimize waste and also save you money in the long run as a result of needing to buy fewer replacement water bottles over time.
For hiking and outdoor climbing trips, you may prefer uninsulated bottles because they are lighter weight, and your concern is likely having enough water rather than cold water. For most other purposes, insulated options work just fine.
How Should I Wash My Water Bottle?
Even if they never hold anything but water, bottles get gross. Mold can grow quickly, especially if you leave the cap on. Straws and mouthpieces accumulate bacteria, oils, and grime from your mouth, and any dirt and dust they pick up in your backpack.
Some bottles can go right in the dishwasher, but be sure to take everything fully apart first, like any silicone pieces that can trap bacteria. For lids that have more nooks and crannies, I recommend hand-washing by soaking them in soapy water and then scrubbing.
Get yourself a bottle brush and straw brush—many kits are available that include both. Even if you don’t use straws, the smaller brush is a helpful tool for getting into any crevices. There are special bottle-cleaning tablets around, but cleaning with regular dish soap works perfectly fine.
Plastic bottles tend to trap odors over time. You can fix this by putting a teaspoon of bleach and a teaspoon of baking soda in the bottle, filling it up with water, and letting it sit overnight. Rinse it out well the next day.
How We Test Reusable Water Bottles
We test every new water bottle for at least two weeks; however, most top picks are ones that members of the WIRED team have loved and carried for months or years. Here’s what we look for:
- Design: First and foremost, we note which materials are used and evaluate whether they feel safe, sustainable, and durable. Because taste can also make or break a bottle, we evaluate whether materials retain odors or leave water tasting metallic or plasticky. We also consider how simple it is to replace parts like lids and straws.
- Portability: We consider the size, weight, cup holder compatibility, and whether it’s designed with ergonomic features like a carry loop.
- Durability: We drop bottles, toss them in totes, and use them daily to see if they dent, crack, or leak. We’ll also twist lids aggressively and test whether the hinges hold up after dozens of openings.
- Ease of use and cleaning: Overall, we’ll judge how intuitive the bottle is to drink from and refill. Each bottle also goes through several rounds of hand-washing and dishwasher cycles (when safe) to evaluate how easy it is to clean and whether odors or stains linger.
- Insulation: For insulated bottles, we’ll fill them with hot and ice-cold water for the advertised time to track how well they maintain temperature.

Fired OpenAI safety researchers dispute their dismissals in open letter
They said company communications around the firing may have made colleagues 'afraid to speak.'
Three OpenAI safety researchers have posted an open letter to OpenAI disputing their dismissals. Jasmine Wang, Mikita Balesni and Tomek Korbak wrote that the "very public manner" of the company's communications around the firings could have a "chilling" effect on employees at a time when "the world's safety depends on them."
Last week, OpenAI dismissed three employees who allegedly shared information with an external AI safety organization. The company said in a statement that the employees "violat[ed] our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information... breaking the trust essential to our work." In the face of recent serious and potentially illegal OpenAI agent hacks of Hugging Face and other organizations, though, the firing of safety employees raised awkward questions and caught the attention of lawmakers.
"We have become concerned that internal and external communications around our firing have
made our former colleagues afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an
integral part of working at OpenAI," the joint letter from the dismissed employees states. "We could raise safety concerns and disagree openly [before], and were encouraged to draw on the expertise of independent safety organizations. This is part of what made OpenAI special, and why we are immensely proud to have been part of the team."
The researchers stated that they "acted in line with OpenAI's mission and within the working norms of the time," and that the firing "leaves us worried that the norms inside OpenAI are shifting and that employees are now unclear on where they stand."
Addressing other rumors, Wang, Belsni and Korbak also said they were not the leak source for a The Information article involving OpenAI's new, less monitorable architectures and don't believe they engaged with external parties outside their mandate. They added that communication with external parties was done "in coordination and discussion with board members and the C-suite," and that Wang notified an executive when she accidentally clicked on a sensitive email.
In parting, the former employees made several recommendations to OpenAI. They said that the company should adhere to its public commitments to embed third-party safety auditors and not use their firing as a "pretext for stepping away from those partnerships." They added that OpenAI must preserve the monitorability of frontier models and maintain an "open and transparent culture of dialogue between its safety researchers and the rest of the safety ecosystem."
In a thread on X, Jasmine Wang wrote that OpenAI leadership "is saying that they strongly agree with our letter," while expressing concern about OpenAI's, well, openness. "We were not the first to be pushed out of OpenAI under suspicious circumstances," she wrote. "Unless employees take a stand now against this kind of maneuver, I am concerned we will not be the last. The message to everyone still at OpenAI is clear: raise concerns or work closely with outside safety groups, and you could be next, without being told why."

WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.

US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condems as 'assault on rule of law'
- Published
The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it sees as a "rogue" institution.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.
The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.
The announcement came just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law.
The US has already sanctioned 17 of the ICC's judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution, and is intended to collapse its ability to operate financially.
The US has though provided a six month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar".
The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support" for the ICC.
The ICC was founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide and counts 125 countries as member states.
But the Trump administration argues the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty.
It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan which the court has since closed, and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions however do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted.
However, Rubio said Trump would not allow the ICC to prosecute Americans, adding: "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC."
The US sanctions will stop US companies from providing goods or services to the ICC, such as banking or software.
Rubio said Washington had delayed imposing the sanctions in the hope that the ICC and its member countries would address US concerns. He said the measures had been structured to allow other countries to negotiate a possible solution.
He also called on US allies that were ICC signatories, including the UK, to "rein in" the institution.
The Netherlands, which hosts the court in The Hague and is also a Nato ally of the US, faces particular pressure. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has said the sanctions would seriously affect the court's ability to function.
The ICC said that the sanctions were aimed at disrupting its work and intimidating those who co-operate with it - but that it "will not be deterred".
It called the measures "an assault on the rule of law" and said no one should be punished for serving the cause of justice, adding: "History will judge this moment."
This showdown potentially marks the gravest crisis in the court's 24-year history. Rather than targeting individual ICC judges and prosecutors, the US is now sanctioning the court itself.

NASA has just released about 800 gigabytes of scientific data generated by the Artemis II mission. The archive documenting the astronauts’ return to the far side of the moon includes 11,000 full-resolution images and videos, 8.5 hours of spoken observations, notes taken by the astronauts, transcripts, and photographs from the cameras aboard the Orion capsule.
The space agency describes this effort as the first set of planetary science data obtained outside Earth and—for the most part—directly by humans in more than half a century. The closest comparable precedent dates back to the Apollo era and its missions to the lunar surface.
In addition to the public database, NASA released three reports summarizing what was learned during the first crewed spacecraft mission to approach the moon in five decades. These are the Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report, the Artemis II Lunar Science Operations Report, and the Artemis II Lunar Science Data User Guide.
Anyone can access the near terabyte of data, though the release is primarily intended for the scientific community. While the astronauts capture and collect the data during the mission, it’s the researchers on Earth who will be able to analyze it and produce new findings about the moon. The information may be particularly useful for planetary geologists, flight engineers, heliophysicists, experts in telecommunications and remote sensing, as well as specialists in meteoroid impacts.
For space and astronomy enthusiasts, some of the most accessible materials include mission transcripts and lunar photographs annotated by the astronauts themselves. NASA has centralized access through its Planetary Data System, the public repository where it stores data from its planetary missions. In the section dedicated to the moon, users can access Artemis II and browse the various available collections, documents, and files.
For a less technical exploration, the agency has also set up an Artemis II science page where you can download the three reports, view a selection of photographs, and access the mission’s audio library. Anyone wishing to work directly with the raw data can visit the Planetary Data System, where the scientific files and their metadata are available for individual download and analysis.
Initial analyses of some of the Artemis II data have already yielded several concrete results. The most clear-cut finding is the detection of five small meteoroid impacts on the lunar surface during the 54-minute eclipse observed by the Orion crew. Recording these flashes will improve estimates of how often fragments just a few centimeters in size strike the moon—a key factor in calculating the risks future bases, vehicles, and astronauts will face.
The observations also documented differences in color, brightness, and texture among various lunar regions, which scientists can compare with composition maps previously obtained from orbit. In addition, photographs taken near the terminator—the boundary between lunar day and night—show in great detail how the terrain and visibility change when the sun is very low on the horizon. These conditions will be common near the south pole, where NASA plans to conduct the next Artemis missions. These data can therefore help the astronauts anticipate challenges related to navigation, lighting, and terrain recognition.

Medical debt is crushing hospital patients in LA. Health officials may have a fix
LOS ANGELES — Every Tuesday, Naman Shah sees tuberculosis patients at a small public clinic in Los Angeles' San Fernando Valley. Shah, a physician and epidemiologist at the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health, pores over images of battered lungs, listens to labored breathing and checks medications.
It's part of an initiative dating to the early 20th century to control infections so tuberculosis doesn't spread. "We like doing things upstream," Shah said, "meaning before they happen, not after the damage is done."
Today, Shah and his colleagues are applying the same principle to medical debt. A key part of that effort is a new system to allow every hospital in LA County to easily screen patients for financial aid. The goal: to stop low-income families from getting a bill that buries them in debt.
Shah estimates this system could prevent several hundred million dollars of medical debt every year.
Vicious cycle
In the U.S., an estimated 100 million adults have some form of healthcare debt. In LA County, the nation's most populous, public health officials calculate that about 800,000 residents have medical bills they can't pay.
"The impacts of medical debt were staggering," said Shah, who used to staff a rural health clinic in India and, since 2023, has led a county initiative in LA to tackle the debt problem.
"People end up with credit card debt and then a vicious cycle of high interest rates and poverty," he said. "People forgo their prescriptions. People forgo appointments. And then you get into worse health."
Hospitals typically offer financial aid to patients with low incomes. But information about assistance is often hard for patients to get. Applying can be cumbersome. And many eligible patients never seek aid, research shows.
"Most people walk into the hospital and walk out without any knowledge of financial assistance," said Jared Walker, founder of Dollar For, a nonprofit that helps patients nationwide apply for aid, often called charity care.
That's fueling debt. It's also driving costly collection efforts that even hospital officials acknowledge pointlessly target low-income patients who are unlikely to be able to pay.
"They're turning their wheels trying to collect on debt that isn't collectable," said Adena Tessler, regional vice president for the Hospital Association of Southern California.
Presumptive eligibility
One potential solution is a system that automatically screens and qualifies low-income patients for financial aid without requiring an application. This is called presumptive eligibility.
Some hospitals already use such systems, which rely on software that checks patient eligibility based on publicly available information such as credit history.
The strategy can be very effective. Shah said hospitals that have deployed presumptive eligibility systems have reported as much as a 50% increase in the amount of financial aid they give patients.
Under a state law passed last year, all California hospitals will have to start doing presumptive eligibility screening by next July.
But the systems can be expensive and difficult for smaller hospitals to implement. Only about 1 in 5 hospitals in LA County currently use them, Shah said.
Public health officials wondered whether they could help more hospitals set up the systems.
The county, which, like many local governments, faces major fiscal challenges, couldn't pay for this, Shah said. But the public health department could bring together healthcare and hospital officials in the county to figure out another solution.
"The beauty of government is not when it always has to do the work," Shah said. "We have the ability to make sure that people cooperate."
The Hospital Association of Southern California, initially wary of the county initiative, came to see improving hospital financial aid programs as beneficial to hospitals, many of which were wasting money on collections. "The billing process is cumbersome and costly," said Paul Young, a senior vice president with the association.
The association agreed to procure a digital presumptive eligibility system and make it available to its members. This bulk-purchasing approach, which Young compared to "a Costco model," would lower the cost for individual hospitals, he said.
At the same time, L.A. Care, a nonprofit health plan that administers Medicaid coverage for more than 2.5 million low-income county residents, committed $2 million to set up the system.
The investment reflected the safety net insurer's mission to make medical care accessible to more people, said Melanie Fontes Rainer, who leads strategic planning for L.A. Care. "It's going to make Los Angeles County better," she said.
Making it work
Getting the new system up and running by January, as the partners hope, faces challenges.
Hospital officials are figuring out how the system will be funded in the long term. And it's unclear how many of the county's 88 acute care hospitals will ultimately use it, even if it's cheaper and easier to access.
The partners are also working to improve the data that the system relies on to screen patients. One goal is to link the system to tax records maintained by the state of California. This would provide hospitals with more accurate information on patients' income than current systems, which often rely on estimated income.
Walker, the patient advocate at Dollar For, said he's heartened by the county's effort. "I'm optimistic that we can make a better charity care system," he said. "And the fact that hospitals in LA County are willing to be innovative and creative about ways we can do that is super encouraging."
For his part, Shah said county public health officials recognize that a better screening system at hospitals won't by itself eliminate medical debt. But he said the public health department couldn't ignore a problem that affects more county residents than asthma or tobacco use.
"Prevention is our bread and butter," he said.

Powerful 7.7 magnitude earthquake rocks Panama
Country appears to have escaped widespread destruction or deaths
A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck southern Panama on Friday, damaging buildings and sending thousands into the streets, but the country appeared to escape widespread destruction or deaths.
The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) said the earthquake hit at a depth of 12.6 kilometres, with an epicentre in a sparsely populated area about 200 kilometres from the capital, and that some casualties were possible.
In the following hours, even as more than 40 aftershocks rattled the isthmus nation, the Panama Canal and Cobre Panama copper mine reported normal operations and the Tocumen International Airport lifted a suspension on flights.
Office workers in the upscale business hub of downtown Panama City fretted about how to get home in the snarl of traffic, after the quake sent thousands into the streets.
Juan Sanchez, a 37-year-old Economy Ministry employee, waited for a bus he said he doubted would arrive.
"They evacuated all of these buildings. Everyone is outside. Now the problem is, how do we get home?"
President Raul Mulino travelled to Penonome, a city about halfway between the epicentre and Panama City, where some buildings collapsed and a church was damaged.
Despite the force of Friday's tremor, the country appeared to have been spared the destruction of other recent powerful quakes in the region, with no deaths or injuries immediately reported.
Back-to-back quakes in Venezuela in June killed several thousand people, while a quake in Colombia in August killed more than 300.
Cars are seen crushed under a collapsed building after an earthquake in Penonome, Panama, on Friday. (Martin Bernetti/AFP/Getty Images)
An exposure report by the USGS estimated about 43,000 Panamanians lived in areas with at least severe exposure to the quake. This compares with nearly 1.4 million in the area of the twin quakes in Venezuela and over 1.6 million in the quake-hit zone of western Colombia.
Nestor Luque, director of Panama's geosciences institute, attributed the quake to the Azuero Sona Fault System that he said contained a massive buildup of pressure that is occasionally released.
"The seismic signals have travelled throughout the national territory and that is why it could be felt everywhere."
People gather on a street in Panama City after an earthquake on Friday. (Enea Lebrun/Reuters)
In Panama City, Luque said he counted 40 seconds of vibrations, though other areas may have felt even longer tremors.
Sabina Rios, who was on the sixth floor of an old U.S. military-era building in Panama City, said the shaking was unusually strong and prolonged.
"The quake felt strong and lasted a long time, the longest I've felt in years," Rios said.
People look at a damaged government building in Penonome on Friday. (Martin Bernetti/AFP/Getty Images)
Victor Pinzon, a 48-year-old maintenance worker, told Reuters he had watched high-rise window cleaners ride out the shaking. "It's a miracle they didn't get killed," he said. "They looked like they were swinging in a hammock."
Strong earthquakes are not common in Panama, and some elderly residents were in tears as they evacuated into the streets.
"We're scared. It's just the two of us old folks here. The house has cracked, and we're afraid it could fall on us," said Ricardo Brown, 74, in Herrera province in southern Panama, where he said he saw a number of damaged homes.
A statue is seen by the earthquake in Penonome on Friday. (Martin Bernetti/AFP/Getty Images)
Omar Smith, who heads Panama's civil protection agency, told news outlet Telemetro Reporta that impacts had also been reported in Chitre, the capital of Herrera, and along the coast in Los Santos province.
The USGS estimated economic losses could amount to 1 to 10 per cent of Panama's gross domestic product, and electricity provider Naturgy reported power outages in six provinces.
Panama was due to hold a national evacuation drill on Monday of next week to test the country's emergency response.

Arunachal Pradesh is set to forfeit its Ranji Trophy Plate group opener against Nagaland, beginning Sunday at the Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad, amid an ongoing legal dispute between two factions of the Arunachal Cricket Association (ACA).
According to the rules, the State team could potentially face suspension for the rest of the season if it forfeits its game.
While Nagaland has already reached Ahmedabad for the fixture, Arunachal’s players are still awaiting clarity on their participation. With the season hanging in the balance, they have appealed to the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) to find a solution and allow them to play.
“We do not know much about the legalities of the matter, but if we cannot play this season, a lot of careers will be affected,” Kamsha Yangfo, who has captained Arunachal earlier, told Sportstar.
“This is the first time we have faced such an issue, so we do not know what to do next or whom to approach. For now, all we know is that we are not playing the first match at least,” Yangfo added.
Earlier on Thursday, Arunachal Pradesh failed to field an Under-19 team for its Vinoo Mankad Trophy opener against Sikkim in Bhubaneswar. Sportstar understands that the senior men’s team is also unlikely to take the field, with the dispute leaving the state association unable to conduct player selection or organise preparations for the season.
For players who spend the year preparing for the domestic season, the uncertainty has raised concerns not just about their immediate prospects but also about their long-term careers.
A huge blow
Mibom Mosu, a young fast-bowling all-rounder and a former trainee at the MRF Pace Foundation, said missing a season would be a significant setback for players who depend on cricket for their livelihood.
“Coming from the northeastern corner of the country, our biggest dream is to see a boy from our region play in the IPL or for India. For that to happen, we need our state association to provide us with the right platform,” Mosu said.
“We have had that platform for the past seven years, and many of us have worked very hard to make the most of it. Every January, I start the year thinking about how I can perform better. A disappointing season does not mean I lack the ability to bounce back,” Mosu said, adding: “But this time, I really don’t know what to do…”
ALSO READ | Siddhesh Lad will ‘respect’ decision to omit Suryakumar Yadav from Mumbai Ranji squad
Having spent the past five years training outside Arunachal Pradesh during the off-season, Mosu has travelled to Punjab, Bengaluru, Gurugram, Noida and Chennai to work on his game. This year, he spent the entire summer in Arunachal Pradesh for the first time, getting a closer look at the challenges facing cricketers in the state.
“There is no proper rehabilitation centre for injured players either. As a fast bowler, I know how important these facilities are. We need the right support to prolong our careers,” he said.
For Mosu, the prospect of missing the Ranji Trophy is particularly worrying. An entire season without competitive cricket would mean losing valuable match practice and an opportunity to establish himself. It could also affect his form, fitness and future prospects.
“I live in rented accommodation in Itanagar, and all my earnings come from cricket. I do not have a job. I have to pay for accommodation, gym membership, travel and other living expenses. If I do not play this season, I do not know how I will manage financially or what my future will look like,” he said.
Mosu maintained that he was not aligned with either faction involved in the dispute and had faith in the legal process. “I respect the legal process and have complete faith that justice will be delivered and that the outcome will be good for cricket. We are cricketers, and our only concern is to play the game.
“If we miss out this year, what guarantee do we have that things will be better next year? There is no guarantee that we will return in the same physical condition or with the same opportunities. Many players could face serious financial difficulties, too. We spend all 365 days thinking about cricket, but we also need the opportunity to play,” he said.
Legal impasse
The BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia had earlier told Sportstar that the dispute between two factions within the ACA had stalled cricketing operations, leaving the state unable to select its teams or prepare for the domestic season.
“Because of the internal bickering between the two factions, there is litigation and a stay order regarding the functioning of the association. As a result, nobody could take up the matter of team selection or preparation,” Saikia said.
Six district cricket associations — Lower Siang, Upper Subansiri, Kamle, Tawang, West Siang and Papum Pare — have alleged violations of rules and procedures in the conduct of the ACA executive elections and demanded a re-election. The matter is being heard by the Gauhati High Court’s Itanagar Bench.
The BCCI has previously appointed committees to oversee cricketing operations in state associations, including those in Bihar, Rajasthan and Jammu and Kashmir, following court directions. In Arunachal’s case, however, the ongoing litigation and the absence of a court-appointed administrator have left the governing body unable to intervene.
Nagaland, meanwhile, is set to receive a walkover if Arunachal fails to turn up. Section 16.2.1.2 of the BCCI’s playing conditions, under the provision relating to the match referee awarding a match, states: “A match shall be lost by a side which, in the opinion of the BCCI Match Referee, refuses to play, and the BCCI Match Referee shall award the match to the other side.”
Arunachal Pradesh, along with other northeastern states, entered BCCI-affiliated tournaments in 2018 after being granted full membership following the intervention of the Supreme Court-appointed Committee of Administrators. Since then, however, the state has been embroiled in several controversies, including allegations of corruption against office-bearers.
ALSO READ | Saurashtra Ranji Trophy 2026/27 squad: Jaydev Unadkat to lead, Ravindra Jadeja included
With the legal dispute still unresolved, the immediate concern is whether Arunachal’s cricketers will lose the opportunity to compete this season and what that could mean for their careers.
Players to write to the BCCI
The players are now considering approaching the BCCI formally, although their financial constraints make it difficult to travel to meet officials in person.
“We will discuss our next steps among ourselves. All the players are facing financial difficulties, and travelling to Delhi or even to Guwahati to meet the BCCI secretary (Devajit Saikia) would be difficult for us at the moment. We are considering holding a press briefing and reaching out through social media. We will write to the BCCI by email as soon as possible and hope to receive a response quickly. An early resolution is very important,” said left-arm fast bowler Yorjum Sera, a first-class player.
According to him, the uncertainty had left players struggling both professionally and financially. “All the players are upset, which is why we have made a small effort to appeal to the BCCI. The legal process could take a long time, but we cannot afford to wait indefinitely. We could not field an Under-19 team for the Vinoo Mankad Trophy, and now we are facing the same situation with our senior Ranji Trophy team,” Sera said.
For players who depend on cricket for their livelihood, the prospect of missing an entire season has added to their financial worries. Sera said several players had borrowed money to meet their expenses and were struggling to make ends meet.
“Not everyone comes from a financially secure family. The players are in a crisis and are under tremendous pressure. We have had to take loans to meet our expenses, including payments to coaches and costs related to practice matches. If we do not find a solution soon, our financial burden will continue to grow. We do not even know how much interest we will have to pay over the course of a year,” he said.
Sera urged the authorities to find a way out of the impasse before the players’ careers suffered further damage. “We are not asking the two factions to accept each other overnight, but we hope there will be an intervention as soon as possible. That would be better than allowing the players’ careers to come to an end. Our parents keep asking us when we will get to play cricket. It is painful for us to be in this position,” he said.
Dado Tachung, who led Arunachal in the U-23 CK Nayudu Trophy last year and also featured in the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy, echoed similar sentiments. “We just want the BCCI to intervene and allow us to play. As cricketers, all we have is hope, and if we can’t play this season, I really don’t know what awaits us,” he said.

The Trump administration announced Thursday that it is investigating nine universities for alleged fraud related to visas commonly used by postdoctoral researchers, a core part of the nation’s biomedical workforce.
Vice President JD Vance announced during a press briefing that Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Brown, the California Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the University of Pittsburgh, and UC Davis are under investigation by the Department of Labor. During the briefing, Vance asserted that these schools are improperly using J-1 visas, the main class of visa used by international postdocs, to bring in cheap labor rather than relying on domestic researchers.
“They’re using these visas way too much,” he said. “They’re using them to undercut the wages of American grad students and American researchers, and it simply has to stop.”
Vance asserted that these schools employ researchers on J-1 visas for work connected to federal grants at a rate of 61% compared to a national average of 38%. STAT contacted the White House and the Vice President’s office for clarification on where these figures came from but did not receive immediate replies. National Science Foundation data show that nearly 60% of postdocs in science, engineering, and health are temporary visa holders; most of these researchers would be on J-1 visas.
The labor department’s inspector general, Anthony D’Esposito, said during the briefing that his office has already issued subpoenas to the schools under scrutiny. He added that he will investigate whether “foreign influence, improper financial relationships, or visa abuse are compromising federally funded research.”
“If an American university is breaking the law to save a dollar while exposing American research to a foreign adversary, that is not academic excellence. It’s institutional betrayal,” he said. “I don’t care how prestigious a university thinks it is. Break the law and screw the American people, and I will personally cuff you in the university square.”
Kimberly Allen, an MIT spokesperson, confirmed in an email to STAT that the university received a “very broad subpoena” on Thursday morning that it is now reviewing. She did not elaborate on the details of the subpoena or what kinds of information had been requested.
“Each J-1 visa holder at MIT has been vetted and authorized to come here by the U.S. government, and we take seriously our obligations to follow U.S. law,” Allen wrote.
Spokespersons for Stanford, Yale, and Harvard did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
It’s unclear how much evidence the administration has to support its visa fraud concerns, and D’Esposito’s office didn’t immediately respond to questions about the investigation’s scope or expected timeline. But Thursday’s announcement fits into a series of moves by the Trump administration to more tightly restrict the entry of international students and scholars into the U.S.
The Department of Homeland Security has attempted to place a four-year cap on how long foreign graduate students and postdocs can stay in the country, alleging that the current system allows these scholars to remain indefinitely and incentivizes fraud. On Wednesday, the Trump administration announced a proposed $70,000 fee for a popular work authorization program used by international students seeking professional experience. And DHS is attempting to revive plans to institute a $100,000 fee for H1-B visas, which are used by foreign workers in high-skill fields such as engineering and biotech.
These proposed restrictions have yet to take effect and have in some cases been temporarily blocked by lawsuits. But Elizabeth Goss, an immigration attorney in Boston, warned that these efforts send a clear sign to international scientists that their contributions are no longer valued, a message she worries could compromise U.S. scientific leadership.
“This is an incredible series of self-owns,” she said. “The government also knows that none of this will stand up in court. They just want to send a message: Don’t come here. But we will lose [out] on so much. It’s going to take decades for us to repair the damage when this is over.”

Lhuan-dre Pretorius has broken Chris Gayle's record for the highest score in a men's T20 match with an unbeaten 188 in a domestic fixture in South Africa.
The 20-year-old South African's knock off 79 deliveries, including 13 sixes and 15 fours, helped Titans post 267-3 against Knights in the CSA T20 Challenge.
It eclipsed the 175 made by Gayle for Royal Challengers Bangalore (now Bengaluru) against Pune Warriors in the 2013 Indian Premier League.
Pretorius, who has played 17 T20s, three one-dayers and two Tests for South Africa, finished with a strike rate of 237.97.
He made his half-century off 24 balls but only required 16 more balls to get to three figures and then got to 150 off just 58 deliveries.
Titans then bowled out Knights for 143 to wrap up an emphatic 124-run victory at the Mangaung Oval in Bloemfontein.

Jammu, Oct 9: The National Investigation Agency (NIA) on Friday filed a chargesheet before the NIA Special Court Jammu against an arrested accused and three killed Pakistani terrorists in the Kishtwar terror attack case.
In a statement, NIA said it filed the 535-page chargesheet against arrested accused Maneer Ahmed, son of Mohammad Yousuf Koli, resident of Naidgam Chatroo, Inderwal, Kishtwar and three killed terrorists including Saifullah @ Saifullah Kashmiri @ Atiq Nazir @ Atiq Ur Rehman. The chargesheet pertains to the terror attack on 22nd February 2026 at Chatroo, Wani Mohalla, Passer Kote in Kishtwar (RC-03/2026/NIA/JMU).
The chargesheet details the conspiracy, the role of the three killed terrorists including Saifullah, a resident of Pakistan and commander of proscribed outfit Jaish-e-Mohammad (JeM), and of arrested accused Maneer Ahmed, along with supporting evidence. It charges Maneer Ahmed with voluntarily harbouring and concealing terrorists involved in attacks on security forces and civilians in hilly district Kishtwar under relevant provisions of UA(P) Act, 1967. NIA has also invoked penal section against the accused terrorists for waging war against India and hatching conspiracy from across the border.
As per NIA, the attack involved three terrorists led by terror commander Saifullah, affiliated to Kashmir Tigers (Azrael Group), which acts under the proscribed outfit JeM. Retaliatory fire from security forces led to killing of all three. The group, which was active in upper reaches of Kishtwar, was found to have conducted several attacks that resulted in killing of security forces personnel and locals. Arrested accused Maneer Ahmed has been found to be involved in providing support to the group.
NIA’s investigation, spanning almost 5 months, has traced the conspiracy to Pakistan. Further investigation in the case is continuing, the agency in a statement said.

Donald Trump was on a fresh collision course with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and European allies on Friday after a stunning agreement to buy Russian diesel, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its four-and-a-half year war against Ukraine.
Zelenskyy reacted furiously to Trump’s announcement of the deal with President Vladimir Putin of Russia, calling it “absolutely terrible” and “not fair and not honest”.
In a move likely to create a fresh crisis with Washington’s Nato allies, Trump announced the deal with Putin on his Truth Social network, saying it was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared as a result of his decision to go to war with Iran.
“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” Trump wrote.
“Based on the condition of their diesel refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 tons of diesel fuel.”
He added: “Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority.”
Fuel prices have rocketed due to Iran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz, a strategically sensitive choke point that was the passageway for 20% of the global oil supplies before the war. While costs have risen for motorists – with a gallon of fuel now averaging $4.20 – it is the soaring price of diesel, which last month rose to a record high of $6.52, that has inflicted the most political damage to Trump and the Republicans as November’s midterm approach.
Diesel is the main supply chain fuel, and a rise in its costs feeds into consumer prices and also hurts US farmers, who need to operate machinery.
The agreement was criticized by Democrats, who said it undercut a law Trump signed last month allowing for a broad range of sanctions on Russian banks, officials and tankers, as well as directing him to impose steep tariffs on the top five importers of oil or natural gas from Russia. The law gave Trump wide discretion to make exceptions to its provisions.
“This is what failure looks like. Failure for President Trump to live up to his promises to lower costs for Americans. Failure to protect America from its adversaries,” the Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, joined by Senator Jeanne Shaheen, who is the top Democrat on the Foreign Relations Committee, and Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the Banking Committee, said in a statement. “Failure to follow the law and the bipartisan will of Congress that only weeks ago passed legislation aimed at cutting off revenue for Russia’s war machine and curbing purchases of Russian oil and gas.”
Some Republicans were also critical of the agreement.
“Propping up Putin’s war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities,” congressman Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican, wrote on X. “The President’s policies towards Russia and Ukraine are failures. We need moral clarity not moral ambiguity.”
Perhaps the fiercest response came from Zelenskyy, who told Axios that it “looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible.” The Russian leader turned 74 earlier this week.
In a long social media post, Zelenskyy, who has had an uneasy relationship with Trump, said the deal amounted to “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged”. Russia was likely to repay it with “further terror and perfidy”.
“It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said.
Trump announced the oil deal as his envoys, Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, met with Ukrainian and European officials in Miami to discuss proposals to end the war.
Zelenskyy, in a separate statement released by Ukraine’s embassy in Washington on Friday, said the Ukrainian negotiators had been “used as a smokescreen for the deal”, which he called “a weak decision by strong partners”.
“That is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” he said.
Trump has recently criticized Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries, calling on Zelenskyy to choose alternative targets. The Ukrainian leader rejected the request unless Russia accepted a reciprocal de-escalation plan that would stop Moscow attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
The agreement also comes on the heels of rising tensions between Russia and Washington’s Nato allies in Europe, amid speculation that Moscow might be preparing military action intended to test the alliance’s resolve.
The latest development is likely to lead to a further deterioration of Zelenskyy’s relationship with the Trump administration. He was infamously ambushed by Trump and the vice-president, JD Vance, last year in an explosive White House encounter when the president told him: “You don’t have the cards.”
But Trump has since reportedly grown disenchanted with Putin, expressing disappointment in his failure to reach a deal.
Trump’s willingness to reach an agreement with Putin that will lower fuel costs comes despite Russia’s support for Iran in its war with the US. Russia is believed to have given Iran satellite intelligence and overhead surveillance data detailing the locations of American forces, ships, aircraft and military bases. It has also provided drone components and ammunition.

The State informed the Kerala High Court that in-principle approval had not been granted to Keralam for establishing an All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS).
The Division Bench of Chief Justice Soumen Sen and Justice V.M. Syam Kumar enquired into the reason why Keralam was not prioritised for building an AIIMS, even though the matter had been pending for almost 10 years. The Bench was considering a petition seeking establishment of an AIIMS under the Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY).
The court observed that the matter was presently at the stage of inter-ministerial consultation and any decision for setting up an AIIMS could be taken only after the continuation of the PMSSY scheme for the next five financial years, FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31, was approved.
In a previous order, the court noted that the idea of having an AIIMS in Keralam was raised in June 2016 and four locations were identified for this purpose. The court opined that Keralam should be considered on a priority basis considering the density of population, and asked the Union government to take a conscious decision concerning the proposal for the institute.
Prioritising other States
The Deputy Solicitor General of India, O.M. Shalina, informed the court that since Keralam had better health-care conditions than other States, the Union government was prioritising those States with a weaker health sector. At this point the court enquired whether the Union government’s stand was that Keralam did not require an AIIMS. The court orally asked whether the hospitals in the State were a disqualification or a ‘handicap’ to consider the establishment of the institute. The court orally remarked that Keralam had the highest density of population in the country, and that the existing hospitals would not be sufficient to provide medical facilities to the needy and poor.
The Union government responded that while considering all other States and Union Territories, Keralam’s status was much better, and that was the reason for the delay in approval. The court then enquired why there was an AIIMS in Delhi and two or three institutes in some other States, if the criteria was availability of medical facilities.
