Life-threatening Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida
- Published
Hurricane Isaias has made landfall in the US state of Florida and is expected to bring life-threatening flooding and winds that have forced thousands to evacuate.
The storm weakened slightly to a category 2 hurricane, with 110 mph (175 kph) winds, before ramming into Florida's western panhandle on Friday evening.
Florida, Alabama, and Georgia have each issued states of emergency as meteorologists warned of life-threatening storm surge that could cause up to 9 feet (2.7m) of flooding in some areas.
Isaias is one of three storm systems affecting North America this weekend, with the two others hitting Mexico and Southern California in the El-Niño fuelled warm waters of the Pacific Ocean.
Both Florida and Alabama instituted mandatory evacuations due to the storm.
In Florida, those evacuations includes coastal communities in direct aim of the powerful storm. Florida Senator Rick Scott encouraged residents in designated areas to evacuate as soon as possible, as he warned in a social media post: "DO NOT WAIT! Get out NOW!"
Governor of Alabama Kay Ivey issued a mandatory evacuation for all non-residents, tourists and visitors in key counties likely to be heavily affected by the storm.
Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane in the Atlantic's hurricane season, which largely has been delayed due to El Niño conditions in the Pacific.
It marks the first time in more than 30 years that a hurricane did not form till October.
The storm is likely to bring "life-threatening storm surge" to the US Gulf Coast, the National Hurricane Center warned.
After hitting Florida, the centre of Isaias is forecast to move across Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley on Saturday and Sunday, the National Weather Service said late on Friday.
As of Friday evening, hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 35 miles (55 km) from Isaias' centre, and tropical storm-force winds extended as far as 205 miles (335 km).
The Florida Panhandle and the rest of the US Gulf Coast are facing fierce winds and heavy rain as the hurricane barrels down. There is also the potential for accompanying tornadoes, Melissa Watson, a Florida-based meteorologist at the National Weather Service told the BBC.
For those who have not evacuated, "the main thing will be having multiple ways to receive warnings" about tornadoes and storm surges, Watson said. "If you are near the coast, being able to move to higher ground," is also essential in the event of storm surges.
"We want people to be safe, so don't go out there trying to look for damage ... to post on social media," she added. "We want people to remain inside and safe while the hurricane is moving through."
Even before the storm made landfall, hundreds of thousands were without power in the country's southeast - and Alabama, Florida and Georgia have issued states of emergency as they brace for heavy rains and flooding.
More than 350,000 were in the dark in Florida and another 170,000 in Alabama saw outages, according to PowerOutage.us.
The hurricane's winds are expected to be felt further inland in Georgia, albeit at a lesser intensity, where already about 8,000 customers were without power.
People on the coast of the Florida panhandle have been told to seek immediate shelter under an "Extreme Wind Warning".
Some Florida officials have ordered residents to "Get out NOW!", urging people to follow evacuation orders.
John Guoth, a resident of Navarre, Florida, told the BBC that he and his wife will remain in their home despite the rest of his street having already left.
"It's a hurricane, we get them all the time... we kind of knew that when we moved here," he said.
"Pretty much everything that can fly and will fly is battened down, and everything that cannot fly is really, really secured," he said,
Guoth said he put his ducks and chickens in the bathroom and weighed down his boats and trailers so "nothing flips over".
A few households have remained in the area, describing them as "long-term locals" who are "going to protect our homes".
Pensacola resident Brandin Ruth told the BBC that they have been turning the gas off to the buildings, icing down product and trying to get team members home.
People in the Florida city have "seen bad storms before" but are "bunkering up", he said, adding: "You don't want to underestimate a storm like this".
One indicator of a storm's severity to communities in the southern US is whether the stalwart restaurant chain The Waffle House would close its doors to customers. On Friday, it did.
A Waffle House spokesperson confirmed to the BBC that the chain had already closed a number of locations in the hurricane's path and "will continue monitoring conditions".
US President Donald Trump said he will no longer attend a major American football college game in Tuscaloosa, Alabama because of the hurricane, shifting plans to attend a rally in Tennessee instead.
Two other storms are also forecast to batter North America this weekend.
Hurricane Simon is bearing down on the Pacific coast of Mexico as a category one hurricane. It is set to pick up speed and become category four by Saturday, eventually making landfall near Puerto Vallarta on Sunday, according to Reuters.
Further north, Tropical Storm Rachel, a downgraded hurricane, is heading toward landfall around the US-Mexico border, along the Pacific.
While, Rachel is expected to reach the coast late on Saturday, the impact of the storm is already being felt due to high tides in southern California.
Video footage and photos show several streets under water in Newport Beach, California, through a combination of the tropical storm swells at sea and high tide.
Posting on its account on X, the City of Newport Beach advised people to "avoid the Balboa Peninsula due to street flooding caused by recent storm conditions and elevated tides".
It also urged people not to drive through flooded streets. Bulldozers have been shoring up the beach to try and prevent further flooding.

In late September, two images circulated online purportedly showing ancient Egyptian sculptures depicting cats walking and resting on their owners.
One of the images shows a sculpture, possibly a wood carving, of a cat in a museum display as either standing or walking on a person at rest. The other image features a cat sitting right up against the chin of a person whose eyes appear to be open.
For example, on Sept. 29, a Facebook user posted a graphic (archived) featuring the two images, with text reading, "4,000-year-old statues prove cats have always ignored personal space." The post's caption adds, "Cats Have Been Sitting on Their Humans for 4,000 Years." The pair of images also spread on Threads and X (archived, archived).
(Nathanistic via Facebook)
Reverse image searches uncovered examples of the standing cat image on Facebook, Instagram and Threads, as well as the resting cat image on Instagram, Threads and X.
Cats prominently feature in ancient Egyptian artifacts, including in mummification. That may be one reason why some commenters under posts have posted remarks indicating they believe the images are authentic. Others mention artificial intelligence, saying they are skeptical about whether the images show actual artifacts that truly exist.
In sum, the images are fake and appear to be AI-generated — as do other images of Egyptian sculptures depicting cats interacting with people.
The aforementioned reverse image searches indicate that the earliest posts featuring the image of the cat standing or walking on top of the person first appeared on Soft Cat Memes (@softcatmemes) accounts on Facebook, Instagram and Threads on Sept. 25, as well as on the possibly-affiliated @hardcatmemes X account. The image contains overlaid text, reading, "Cats have been bothering their humans since the dawn of time."
(@softcatmemes via Facebook)
The image of the cat sitting on a person also first appeared on the same accounts on Sept. 26, receiving more engagement. That second image also features overlaid text, reading, "Evidence suggests cats have never understood personal space."
(@softcatmemes via Facebook)
Snopes contacted the manager of the accounts to confirm the user created the images with an AI tool. We also asked for the name of the tool and the exact text prompts submitted to create the content. We will update this article if we receive further information.
How we know images are fake
Reverse image searches failed to locate any posts or websites containing the same two images prior to late September. With the ongoing popularity of internet cat content, the idea that no one, until recently, would share supposedly real photos of ancient Egyptian sculptures depicting cats acting silly is unlikely.
As one Reddit user has noted, scans of the images with OpenAI's free tool, that verifies content generated using the company's chatbot, display the results, "This content was generated using OpenAI tools," and, "We found a SynthID watermark that originated from OpenAI." For example, a scan of the image of the cat sitting displays the information shown below.
(via OpenAI)
There is also an inconsistency with one of the shadows in that image. The faint shadow nearest where the photographer is meant to be standing (running from left to right along the long edge of the bed) indicates there is a light source on the other side of the display. However, only a shadow of the bed is cast. If the image were authentic, the angle of the shadow suggests the viewer would also be able to see a faint shadow of the human and cat sculptures. That is not the case in this image.
A scan of the other image of the cat standing or walking displays the same result using OpenAI's tool. The absence of a shadow of the cat's tail also further suggests this image is fake.
For further reading, we previously reported about another feline rumor that wild cheetahs have never killed humans.

Trump administration hits International Criminal Court with sweeping sanctions
ICC denounces the move as an 'assault on the rule of law'
The Trump administration has imposed sweeping new sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal that the United States believes has become politicized and attempted to unfairly and illegally prosecute Americans and Israelis on war crimes charges.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the sanctions on Friday, after the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to South African prosecutor Navi Pillay, a former judge at the ICC and other international courts.
U.S. President Donald Trump has coveted that prize for himself. The move, however, long predated the Nobel Prize announcement.
"We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate against us," Rubio said in a video address posted to social media. "The United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC."
The sanctions block any assets that the ICC as an institution might have in U.S. jurisdictions and set a six-month timeline for U.S. companies and individuals that have business with the court to wind that business down.
Rubio said both Republicans and Democrats have deep reservations about the court, which was established to prosecute war crimes and crimes against humanity that might not otherwise be handled by the parties involved.

But he said that only Trump was willing to move against the court.
"Both parties agree on this, but only President Trump has the resolve to take the action needed to end this threat once and for all," Rubio said. "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC."
ICC denounces 'assault on rule of law'
The ICC denounced the step as an attack on the rule of law and the foundations of international order, themes that Rubio had appeared to embrace only two days ago in a speech in front of the Acropolis in Athens.
"It is an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do," the court said in a statement. "It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law."
ICC President Tomoko Akane, a citizen of U.S. ally Japan, said the court would "continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes."
She also appealed to other ICC members for support. "This is not just about defending a single institution, but about safeguarding the international order grounded upon the rule of law."
Rubio had said that the U.S. expects its allies to join in the actions against the ICC. Those include many NATO members in Europe and Japan.
"If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, piece by piece, until Americans are threatened no longer," he said.
Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen, posting on X, called the sanctions announcement "a deeply regrettable step. We stand firm in defence of the court."
He said the six-month window before the sanctions take effect "creates scope for dialogue."
As host state of the court, the Netherlands is a strong defender of the ICC.

Thieves steal 30,000 bottles of wine worth €5m in Italy, reports say
- Published
Thieves have stolen 30,000 bottles of wine collectively worth about €5m (£4.2m) from a prestigious Italian winery, Italian media report.
Marchesi Antinori, one of Italy's biggest family-owned wineries, said the theft at its storage facility in Tuscany took place on Saturday as the company was preparing to ship a consignment to customers abroad.
At least seven masked men are believed to have deactivated the alarms, disabled the cameras and used company forklifts to load two large trucks of the company's prized Tignanello, Solaia and Guado al Tasso Tuscan reds.
Renzo Cotarella, the chief executive, told Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera this was the largest theft of its kind in Italy.
"A theft of this scale and value has certainly never occurred in Italy," he said.
He added that he was hopeful the authorities would be able to trace the stolen wine.
"Two trucks full of merchandise can't just disappear into thin air. The Tuscan roads are full of cameras - perhaps with a bit of luck we'll be able to recover at least some of the bottles stolen from us."
He told the Financial Times: "These wines have a great value and I don't know how they can sell all this wine around the world without being seen."
The company believes the selection of bottles, which usually sell for between €150 and €500 each, suggests the thieves were wine connoisseurs and had inside knowledge.
The theft was only discovered on Monday morning as staff arrived on site. No arrests have been made.
Marchesi Antinori was founded in 1385 and exports to 170 countries. It had a revenue of €263m (£223m) last year.
There has been a spate of wine thefts in Italy this year, including two in the northern Piedmont region where hundreds of thousands of euros worth of bottles were reportedly taken.

Man named Hitler Mussolini elected mayor in Peru
- Published
A man named Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores has secured a narrow victory in Peru's local elections, exit polls show.
The candidate for the centre-left Ahora Nación party was elected mayor of Queropalca, a remote district in the Peruvian Andes.
Some 229 residents voted for the 45-year-old, putting him ahead of the second-place candidate from right-wing Renovación Popular Perú by just 25 votes.
Despite being elected to represent fewer than 1,000 people, his forenames being those of two notorious fascist dictators has drawn outsized international attention to the small corner of the country.
Data from Peru's elections office showed a little over 700 people had participated in the election, with Simeon securing around 34% of the vote.
He was born in the district in the central department of Huánuco, some 360km (224 miles) from the capital, Lima, according to his candidate profile.
That he shares his name with Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini - "two of the most well-known figures of 20th-Century European totalitarian regimes" - has made his candidacy a "striking event", local outlet Peru21 reported.
Despite the curiosity generated by his name, local media noted that Hitler Guesclin Alba Sánchez had been elected mayor of Yúngar in 2018.
He reportedly beat rival candidate Lenin Vladimir Rodríguez Valverde after campaigning on the slogan "I'm the good Hitler".
A politician named Adolf Hitler Uunona attracted similar attention in 2020 after winning local elections in Namibia - a former German colony where Adolf and other Germanic first names are not uncommon.

OpenAI’s latest math release has some academics celebrating breakthroughs and others wondering what happens to the researchers who were still working toward them.
Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematics professor at New York University, told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Thursday that the company’s release had upended work by early-career mathematicians.
“So we've had whole research programs wiped out on Tuesday by their dump,” Buckmaster said.
OpenAI released over 700 mathematical manuscripts on GitHub on Tuesday, describing them in an announcement as the results of an internal frontier model. The company also shared computer-checkable versions of many proofs.
Questions about data and academic norms
For some mathematicians, the concern extends beyond being beaten to a solution.
Bryna Kra, a mathematics professor at Northwestern University, told Business Insider that AI could advance research, but she warned that releasing so much work at once could undermine the collaborative culture that helped make those advances possible.
“Mathematics is an extraordinarily collaborative field,” Kra said. “There is nobody at this company who could possibly give a talk or answer technical questions about any of these results."
Researchers routinely share unfinished ideas in talks and conversations, Kra said, and she worries that the fear that those ideas could be absorbed by AI before they are made public could make mathematicians more secretive.
Buckmaster also raised concerns about whether unpublished work submitted to AI tools could have contributed to OpenAI's math results.
OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment.
"You have to understand, they have access to all our research proposals," Buckmaster said. "So if you submit a research proposal, a panelist will look at that research proposal, and they have to write a summary, and often, how they write the summaries, they put it into the [LLM]," Buckmaster said.
OpenAI said in its announcement that the math results included protocols for revisions and citations, and that it planned to improve the papers’ presentation and fund workshops to help researchers understand AI-generated results.
Alex Kontorovich, a distinguished mathematics professor at Rutgers University, sees reasons for optimism. Kontorovich told Business Insider that mathematical training could become more valuable as AI forces academia to rethink hiring and prizes.
“I don't think we have any interest in giving prizes to someone who pressed the button,” Kontorovich said.
"Mathematics first and foremost teaches people to think clearly and deeply and for extended periods of time on big problems,” Kontorovich added. “And I think in the future there will be even more demand for such skills, which are difficult to attain and take a lot of training.”

Antarctica’s penguins are sending us a distress signal
Something is breaking in the world’s wildest ecosystem.
The world’s largest penguin colony has declined by two-thirds since 2011, most likely because of the climate crisis, a study has revealed. Scientists said the rapid demise of chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski, the northernmost of the South Sandwich Islands in Antarctica, increased the risk of a wider ecosystem collapse.
“It is an enormous population crash, equivalent to half a million breeding individuals being lost from that island,” said the leader of the research, professor Norman Ratcliffe, a penguin ecologist at the British Antarctic Survey.
The Guardian reported in 2020 that chinstrap penguin populations were decreasing on Low in the South Shetland Islands, prompting concerns among scientists that “something is broken” in the world’s wildest ecosystem. The new study, published on Wednesday in the journal Current Biology, indicates that the speed of collapse may be accelerating so rapidly that the distinctive bird — which gets its name from a black line that runs below the beak from cheek to cheek — may need to be classified as an endangered species.
Zavodovski Island had by far the biggest penguin colony in the world, with about 600,000 chinstraps and 90,000 macaroni penguins when the population was measured in 2011. Given the decline between then and 2025, it is likely to have lost that title to Cape Adare in the Ross Sea.
Scientists believe the most likely cause is climate disruption. Human-driven heating has pushed up winter temperatures on and around the Antarctic Peninsula to 5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, one of the fastest rises in the world. On 6 June, the Argentinian Esperanza base on the Trinity Peninsula registered a record winter high of 15.4°C, about 20°C above normal for the time of year — a margin that scientists described as “absolutely crazy.”
Chinstrap penguins are struggling to adapt because they have special diets and specific ocean temperature preferences. Tracking data shows they prefer to forage in cooler waters to the northwest of the island, where they would expect to find Antarctic krill, which make up the bulk of their diet. But as the waters warm, the krill have moved south into the Weddell Sea.
Macaroni penguins, by contrast, are less fussy eaters and their numbers rose 30 percent — though not nearly enough to make up for the loss of chinstraps. Ratcliffe said this was only small comfort because if current trends continued, all penguins would run out of space.
He said the loss of chinstrap penguins would have wider repercussions for food webs. “Each ecosystem could be regarded as like a giant Jenga set, and every component that you remove increases the risk of ecosystems collapsing completely.”
The scientists ruled out several other possible causes of decline. There was no sign that chinstrap and macaroni penguins were in competition for food. The nearest humans lived thousands of miles away.
Although the island is volcanic and had a major eruption in 2016, prompting a “Penguin Pompeii hypothesis” of a sudden population fall, this theory was not borne out either by the data, which showed a steady linear decline, or by observations that showed the chinstraps avoided the main “asphyxia plain” area where the ash and lava were deposited.

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is among the most widespread of human viruses. More than 90% of adults are estimated to have been infected during their lifetime. Most people acquire the infection during childhood without developing symptoms. In some, particularly those infected during adolescence or adulthood, it can cause infectious mononucleosis. The virus then remains in the body for life.
A new analysis by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), the cancer agency of the World Health Organization (WHO), estimates that about 2.3 million new cancer cases worldwide in 2024 were attributable to infections. The analysis incorporates recent evidence linking EBV with gastric cancer and places EBV among the infectious agents responsible for a substantial cancer burden worldwide.
What is Epstein-Barr virus?
EBV, also known as human herpesvirus 4, belongs to the herpesvirus family. It spreads mainly through saliva, including through kissing or sharing drinks, food, eating utensils and toothbrushes.
According to WHO, many people infected with EBV have no symptoms. When illness occurs, symptoms can include fever, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes and marked fatigue. Infectious mononucleosis generally improves within a few weeks, although fatigue can last longer.
After the initial infection, EBV remains in the body in a dormant state. In most healthy people, the immune system keeps the infection under control.
EBV is classified by IARC as a Group 1 carcinogen. It has established causal links with several cancers, including nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Burkitt lymphoma and Hodgkin lymphoma. The latest IARC analysis also incorporates evidence linking EBV with gastric cancer.
Who is at risk?
Most people infected with EBV do not develop cancer. The infection is therefore not, by itself, an indication that a person will develop cancer.
People with weakened immune systems are at greater risk of serious EBV-related disease. This includes some people who have undergone organ or stem-cell transplantation and those receiving treatments that suppress the immune system.
The cancers associated with EBV also vary geographically. Nasopharyngeal cancer, for instance, is particularly prevalent in parts of eastern and southeastern Asia. The development of EBV-associated cancer is thought to involve factors beyond the infection itself.
How is it diagnosed?
A person does not normally need to be tested simply because EBV is common.
When infectious mononucleosis is suspected, doctors may make a diagnosis based on the symptoms and clinical examination. Blood tests can provide supporting evidence. These include tests for heterophile antibodies and EBV-specific antibodies, which can help determine whether an infection is recent or occurred in the past.
In suspected EBV-related cancers or serious disease in people with compromised immunity, more specialised tests may be needed. These can include testing for EBV genetic material in blood or other samples and examination of tumour tissue for the presence of the virus.
A positive EBV antibody test does not mean that a person has cancer. Since infection is so common, evidence of past infection is expected in most adults.
What are the treatment options?
There is no treatment that removes latent EBV from the body and there is currently no vaccine against the virus.
According to WHO, treatment for uncomplicated infectious mononucleosis is mainly supportive. Rest, adequate fluids and medicines to control fever and pain may be advised. Antibiotics do not treat EBV because it is a virus.
People with mononucleosis may also be advised to avoid strenuous activity and contact sports for a period, particularly if the spleen is enlarged, because of the risk of splenic injury.
When EBV is associated with cancer, treatment depends on the type and stage of cancer and may include chemotherapy, radiotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted treatment or a combination of these.
Can EBV be prevented?
There is currently no vaccine against EBV. Preventing transmission can also be difficult because infected people may spread the virus without knowing that they have it.
WHO advises avoiding the sharing of drinks, utensils, toothbrushes and other items that come into contact with saliva.
The development of an EBV vaccine is an important area of research. The latest IARC analysis adds to the evidence on the virus’s contribution to cancer and highlights the need for continued research into prevention.

For years, enterprises hired thousands of human executives to sell loans, answer customer queries and recover abandoned sales. Yet, even with massive teams, many high-value client interactions would slip through the cracks every single day. While some prospects were lost due to poor agent training, others were lost to long support queues. As a result, businesses consistently struggled to reach every lead on their lists. The common assumption was that companies simply needed better training for human agents or simply more calling executives. However, Arrowhead’s founders saw things differently. According to them, the core issue was that human-driven phone processes struggle to function effectively at enterprise scale. The realisation could not have come at a more opportune time. With rapid improvements in AI voice technology, they saw the future clearly – improving human-led call centres would soon matter far less than automating them entirely. This single realisation changed the direction of the startup. Founded in 2022 by Devyani Gupta and Vengadanathan Srinivasan, Arrowhead is building voice AI agents primarily for enterprises. It claims to power autonomous voice systems for many leading banks, NBFCs, ecommerce platforms and healthcare providers. The startup claims that its conversational agents automate everything, from loan sales and customer queries to abandoned cart recovery and collections. In January 2026, the startup raised $3 Mn in its seed funding round led by Stellaris Venture Partners. It claims to work with over 50 BFSI clients, including Tata 1mg, Bank of Baroda Cards, IndiaMART, Aditya Birla Capital, Paytm, Turtlemint, Kissht, InsuranceDekho and others. Yet, Arrowhead did not start with the technology it uses today. The startup’s pivot to enterprise voice AI was the result of a calculated gamble, which forced its team to rethink everything they had built. When Analysing Human Calls Was No Longer Enough Arrowhead didn't start in voice automation. The startup’s initial product was a conversation intelligence tool. Drawing on her experience at BCG across continents, cofounder and CEO Gupta initially built Arrowhead to identify mis-selling and compliance violations on recorded sales calls. Early clients, such as edtech platform upGrad, used the tool to pinpoint bad sales pitches that resulted in refunds. Then came the GenAI boom of 2023 and 2024, and the founders reached an uncomfortable conclusion. “We quickly realised that if we continued analysing just human sales calls, we would soon be analysing something that would potentially go extinct,” Gupta told Inc42. Recognising that human-driven call centres were on borrowed time, Arrowhead pivoted sharply to AI in late 2024. Rather than competing on building another chatbot, the startup focused almost entirely on voice-first enterprise workflows. Arrowhead initially targeted banks and financial institutions, where large calling operations remain critical for loan sales, collections and customer engagement. But, in a stroke of fate, many enterprises that originally bought Arrowhead's analytics software returned as buyers for its autonomous voice agents – this time, to replace their manual calling queues altogether. To scale its voice stack, Arrowhead quickly realised that off-the-shelf software simply would not cut it. The founders needed to control every layer of its underlying engine. Building A Voice AI Stack From Ground Up Instead of relying entirely on third-party API providers, Arrowhead has gradually built much of its voice AI infrastructure in-house. The startup recently launched internally fine-tuned small language models (SLMs), engineered specifically for live enterprise conversations. Rather than optimising purely for lower inference costs, the founders claim that the platform prioritises latency and conversational quality. According to the startup, its latest deployments have achieved response latency below 500 milliseconds, allowing conversations to feel significantly more natural during live phone calls. For context, even small delays in voice interactions can disrupt the flow of conversation, making latency a much bigger challenge than traditional text-based AI systems. To complement its language models, Arrowhead has also developed its own text-to-speech (TTS) models, powered by thousands of hours of custom speech recordings. The startup hired voice artists across specialised agencies to record speech across multiple Indian languages and emotional contexts. This primary data, instead of generic public datasets, enables Arrowhead’s AI models to master subtle human nuances, such as empathy, hesitation, filler words and natural speech rhythms, which generic TTS systems typically miss. Overall, its underlying AI stack also includes: Fine-tuned SLMs built on open-source foundation models such as Gemma and Qwen Proprietary TTS models trained using custom primary speech datasets Emotion-aware speech synthesis systems capable of responding with empathy and contextual tone Optimised inference infrastructure for sub-500 millisecond voice responses Support for multiple Indian languages, including Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam Enterprise deployments designed around data residency, privacy and single-tenant architecture for regulated industries Voice orchestration systems capable of integrating with multiple enterprise APIs during live conversations Speaking with Inc42, cofounder and CTO Srinivasan said that hosting proprietary language models provides cost savings, predictable latency and superior conversational quality while ensuring sensitive customer data stays safely within India for regulated industries such as banking. On the back of its in-house AI stack, the founders claim that over 90% of users cannot distinguish Arrowhead's voice agents from human representatives unless explicitly told that they are speaking with an AI agent. This conversational fluidity has enabled the startup to move beyond pilots to deploying its agents directly into critical, revenue-generating operations. Arrowhead’s BFSI Strength On the business front, financial services remain Arrowhead's biggest market. Around 80% of the company's revenue comes from banks, NBFCs and fintech companies, although it has also started expanding into sectors such as healthcare, ecommerce and edtech. Overall, Arrowhead’s voice AI platform is currently being deployed across three major enterprise workflows. The first is outbound loan sales, where its AI agents move far beyond basic lead qualification to complete much of the loan application journey. During a live call, the agent addresses customer objections, collects required documents, runs OCR-based verification and hands over fully completed files straight to underwriting. The second core area for Arrowhead is inbound customer support. Here, its AI agents first determine customer intent before tapping into the enterprise database to answer complex policy questions, fetch real-time loan statuses and retrieve account-specific records. This drastically cuts manual workload for enterprises that handle tens of thousands of support hours each month. The third area is abandoned cart recovery. For ecommerce platforms, Arrowhead’s AI agents contact customers shortly after they leave without completing a purchase. During the conversation, the system can modify cart items, apply discount codes, update shipping details, and process transactions without ever transferring to a human representative. The startup recently disclosed that its deployment with Tata 1mg generated conversion rates around 15% higher than human agents during abandoned cart recovery campaigns. But with healthy market traction and product-market-fit (PMF) in its kitty, how is Arrowhead monetising its customer base? How Arrowhead Makes Money Arrowhead employs a hybrid pricing strategy that blends traditional SaaS usage with performance-based monetisation. A portion of revenue is generated through per-minute billing, while another component depends on business outcomes delivered through AI deployments. The founders believe that outcome-based pricing creates stronger alignment with enterprise customers while reducing the long-term impact of declining AI infrastructure costs. While the founders did not disclose Arrowhead’s revenue figures, they said that usage-based contracts drive the majority of revenue and yield gross margins between 25% and 30%. They added that profitability varies depending on customer scale and committed call volumes. That said, the startup, despite operating with a lean team, has scaled rapidly to partner with most of the country's top banks, NBFCs, and fintechs. For the founders, replacing traditional call centres is just the opening move. Their bigger bet is that enterprise voice AI platforms will become completely autonomous, capable of completing entire business workflows on their own. But the road ahead may not be easy. The voice AI space in India is peppered with deep-pocketed homegrown startups such as Observe AI, Bolna, and Gnani.ai, among others. On top of this, unit economics also remains a real challenge, as LLM reasoning and TTS together can be an expensive purchase for early stage startups. Infrastructure and UX challenges also persist, particularly around mobile voice navigation and integration with existing enterprise systems. So, as India’s AI ecosystem matures and voice AI infrastructure turns into a commodity, Arrowhead is tasked with maintaining its tech edge to thrive in the long haul.

What are emotions, really? And why do we have them?
Simply put, emotions are intangible responses to what we see happening around us. They arise spontaneously, without conscious thought.
Emotions allowed early humans to efficiently dodge dangers as they explored the world around them. While the world and our lives in it are very different today than the way they were for our ancestors, our emotions haven’t changed.
Despite being so fundamental to our survival as a species, however, scientists are still piecing together how emotions arise in our brains. In a study recently published in Science, in fact, scientists have just reported mapping the brain-wide activity patterns that trigger emotions.
The team found that once an emotion was set off, it outlasted the trigger that sparked it in the first place. If this sounds familiar, it’s because this is what you feel when you accidentally stub your toe, burn your hand, and even when you enjoy your favourite flavour of ice cream.
In all these examples, there is incoming sensory information that prompts an emotional response while the good or bad feeling lasts even after the body part has been reflexively pulled back or after the ice cream is finished.
Stories hidden in blinks
In the new study, scientists led by Karl Deisseroth at Stanford University examined how emotions emerged in response to unpleasant (but not painful) sensory stimuli.
The participants were subjected to an eye puff assay: a machine called a tonometer blew light puffs of air into their left eye in specific sequences. Each puff lasted about 60 ms, the gap between puffs was 3-8 s long, and the entire session lasted 5 minutes. The scientists varied the gap between puffs so that participants didn’t reflexively tense up for the next puff they knew was coming.
Also read: Making the brain transparent
During the entire duration, a high-speed camera recorded the way participants closed their eyes and their behavioral and subjective responses.
As expected, repeated puffs of air to the eye elicited reflexive blinking as participants instinctively pulled back from the tonometer. They also kept the eye closed for certain durations or squinted or blinked rapidly during the gaps. As part of their subjective reports, the participants said this experience was “unpleasant” and “annoying”.
The scientists recruited a separate group of participants who were, at the time of the study, inpatients at the Stanford university hospital and had electrodes planted in their brains to check for epileptic seizures. Members of this group who consented to participate underwent the same eyepuff assay. The scientists found that these participants’ behavioural responses were consistent with those of the previous group. They also blinked reflexively and kept their eyes closed for (relatively) long periods.
The real story emerged in the brain activity patterns.
Enter: ketamine
Each puff causes a signal to be broadcast throughout the brain, like a “breaking news” alert, followed by a slower, more persistent signal. In this second phase, based on data from the electrodes in the brains of participants, scientists found that specific circuits in the brain were activated, which were linked to the generation of an emotional response in the individual.
To confirm this possibility, the scientists administered ketamine to some of these participants and had them redo the eye puff assay. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved ketamine’s use as an anaesthetic and at lower doses as an antidepressant. Ketamine also induces short-term dissociation: i.e. for a brief period, it alters subjective perceptions. By injecting it, the team could separate a person’s reflexive response from the emotional one.
The scientists found that being subjected to air puffs in the eye when a person was on ketamine changed neither the initial reflexive behaviour nor the initial burst of neural activity in the brain. However, it caused the subsequent slower brain response to dissipate much faster, so much so that the volunteers no longer described the experience as annoying but as a “tickling of the eyeball”.
Consistent with this ‘weaker’ subjective experience from ketamine, the participants’ behaviour also changed. They didn’t blink or close their eyes between consecutive air puffs. Instead, they held their eyes open even though they knew more puffs were in the offing.
Ketamine is known to block a sensor in the brain whose job it is to integrate signals coming from different corners. This means in the participants injected with ketamine, the brain may not have integrated the various signals into a coherent emotional response.
Of mice and men
Even though vertebrates have brains of vastly different sizes and complexity, the overall ‘brain plan’ is highly conserved. (The brain plan is akin to the building plan of a house or apartment.) To zero in on those systems responsible for emotions and which have survived evolution, Deisseroth’s team repeated their experiments with lab mice. The mice went through the eyepuff assay, had their brain activity measured with surgically planted electrodes, and had ketamine injected.
The team noticed the same patterns in mice as they had in humans. Injecting ketamine substantially changed the spiking activity in some neurons but not others. Only those neurons (or brain regions) coordinating the second phase — the slower response after the burst — were affected by ketamine. The initial burst didn’t change in any way, just as with the human participants.
The scientists could also study the neural activity following a puff in greater detail in the mouse model. They found that the fast/reflexive responses corresponded with a sharp rise in activity in some of the midbrain regions. This included the thalamus, where incoming sensory signals converge before being relayed onward, and the periaqueductal grey, which is involved in emotional behaviours.
They also found that the second phase of neural activity corresponded with activity in the brain’s emotional centres (described by the umbrella term ‘limbic regions’) and the frontal cortex. Again, as expected.
Then they dissected the brain activity patterns by stages, focusing on how quickly activity in brain regions shot up after the eyepuff and how long it took to fade away. They noticed that activity patterns in most of the pertinent regions increased at an explosive pace right after the eyepuff — but the rate of decrease was more interesting.
A pattern appears
The patterns in different regions slowed at different rates, fading first in the midbrain regions and last in the frontal cortex. The thalamus was active both in the first and the second phase. Considering the thalamus is the brain’s coordinating centre for all sensory signals, it makes sense that it would be active in the first phase. Incoming sensory signals go on to higher brain regions from the cortex. So it also served the role of handing off the baton, so to speak, and thus essayed a sort of bridging role across timescales.
The new study is the first to report this sort of differential pattern across different parts of the brain vis-à-vis emotions. At this point, it is not possible to say with any certainty what the implications are for the brain’s cortical and mid-brain areas.
With computational models of neuron firing activity in the mouse and the mouse’s behaviour following the eye puff assay, the team found that the timescale of neural activity was an important factor that shaped the emotional response.
Indeed, if the sensory signals dissipate before the brain has a chance to integrate the information, the person won’t be able to learn the lesson: “protect yourself from that obnoxious thing”. On the other hand, if brain activity is more strongly coupled to the fast and slow phases that Deisseroth & co. observed, such activity also lasts longer than normal, causing its own problems. Over-stabilised brain states have been correlated with depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder, all of which cause people to experience uninterrupted or mistimed thoughts and emotions.
Beyond the binary of health and disease, the fast and slow phases of brain activity highlighted in the study could reveal the fundamentals of information processing in the brain. People differ in how their brains process information about their environment — in turn a product of their genetic makeup and their upbringing in their formative years.
First steps
Why do we have emotions? For now it may be more gainful to flip the question: what would happen if we didn’t have them?
In the absence of an instinctive reaction that our emotions afford us, the brain’s response would be based entirely on risk-benefit analyses, which can be very time consuming. Over time we’d struggle to make decisions both big and small. What should I wear today? What should I make for dinner tonight? What should I study? Whom should I marry? Purely rational thought would turn such questions into never-ending decision-making exercises with no final answer.
The new study has revealed what happens in the brain in the first seconds when an emotion takes root. One hopes future studies will reveal the specific information encoded by this primal circuitry, how they encode different emotions, and how they evolve with time.
Dr. Reeteka Sud is a neuroscientist by training and senior scientist at the Center for Brain and Mind, Department of Psychiatry, NIMHANS, Bengaluru.

How to split travel costs with friends – without ruining the trip
Money can turn a dream holiday into an awkward one. Here’s how to talk budgets, divide expenses and chase unpaid IOUs without damaging a friendship.
In February 2024, Stasia Maltseva went on a trip through Thailand and Cambodia with a group of six friends, everyone paying in cash and with no system to record expenses.
The cost of street food, souvenirs, group massages and tuk-tuk rides disappeared into an untraceable pit of paper money. They assumed they’d figure out the IOUs when the two-week trip ended. But when it came time to even out the books, “no one had the slightest idea” how much each person had spent, said Maltseva, a 36-year-old content manager from Amsterdam.
A huge argument unfolded, she said. One friend was under the impression he was owed well over US$200 (S$256), but with no receipts and differing recollections, the friend went unpaid.
“It was a battle,” Maltseva said. “We joke about it now.”
Not all friendships are as forgiving. From bachelorette trips to family vacations and bucket-list trips with friends, group travel can easily give rise to contentious situations, especially over finances.
In a 2026 survey of 2,001 US adults, commissioned by PayPal, 46 per cent said money disagreements created tension or “ruined the vibe” on a trip. Another survey from Zelle, the payments platform, of 1,000 US adults, found that consumers often aren’t fully repaid for group expenses. This can cause friendship-altering drama, with about a fifth of millennials saying they ended a relationship because of repayment disputes, according to the Zelle survey.
Here’s what experts say about why friends get themselves into these uncomfortable situations, and how to de-escalate the drama before it turns into a full-fledged fight.
WHY FRIENDS AVOID THE ‘MONEY TALK’
The most common mistake? Not having a candid conversation about spending limits and repayment plans before they start filling out their itinerary, multiple finance and friendship experts said.
“It starts people off on the back foot because it forces them to have a vulnerable moment about not being able to afford something,” said Aja Evans, a New York financial therapist and licensed mental health counsellor.
Danielle Bayard Jackson, a friendship coach and the author of Fighting for Our Friendships, said clients have frequently booked sessions with her specifically about navigating the “complexities of the group trip.”
Close friends often skip the detailed planning process, Jackson said, because of what she called a “relationship-killing myth”: Friends feel they shouldn’t have to explain what they find fun, because they fear that would be evidence that they’re not as close as they thought.
That fear of misperception intensifies when it comes to money. If someone makes more or less than their friends, they don’t want to be viewed differently because of it, Jackson said. That can introduce friction into a friend group.
“We’re not as honest and direct as we ought to be before we get into these situations,” she said.
STARTING THE CONVERSATION
For the trip to make it out of the group chat as smoothly as possible, experts suggest finding consensus about total costs, who’s willing to pay what and the repayment process.
For those struggling to start, Jackson said to think about the one reason you want to avoid the discussion. Then, use that as the opening sentence and tie it to a goal for the conversation.
One example? Jackson said: “Hey, I don’t want to make things awkward, but I feel like we should have a conversation about money, to avoid any misunderstandings or disappointment.”
For those with a strict budget, it might help to tell the other travellers about the other financial goals or responsibilities you have, Evans said.
“That will help them understand that you’re not trying to be difficult, but you have other things going on that require you to handle your finances in a particular way,” Evans added.
UNDERSTANDING YOUR TRAVEL PARTNERS
On a trip to Japan with three friends last November, Malvina Abbott described a balancing act between one friend with a limited budget and a wealthier friend who required five-star hotels with precise square footage.
It took two months to compromise on the hotel, and they didn’t have a clear plan for how to handle uneven spending habits before the nine-day trip started, said Abbott, an 83-year-old retired public defender from San Diego. The wealthier friend ended up spending a lot of time on her own.
“Our failure to talk about money issues made for some uncomfortable situations,” Abbott said.
When planning a group trip, Jackson said she thinks about advice in The Art of Gathering by Priya Parker: Start by asking, what’s the point?
“That helps inform where you should go, how much you should spend and, most importantly, who should come,” Jackson said.
Once the invite list is set, it can be helpful to suss out each person’s spending habits during planning. For example, Jackson said she has a friend who enjoys footing a group bill at a restaurant and gets genuinely insulted when others try to pay their portion.
If you know someone isn’t as reliable at repaying what others fronted, ask yourself if you’re willing to potentially lose that money, said Dr Traci Williams, a clinical psychologist and certified financial therapist. For some people, the loss is worth it for their friend to join the trip.
Frugal travellers should set a financial limit for when to opt out, experts said. If the total others are willing to spend on the trip is going to ruin the experience for you, don’t go, Evans said. It’s better to deal with the fear of missing out than to get upset with yourself or others over how much you’re spending, she added.
IF SOMEONE DOESN’T PAY
The trip has ended and the Venmo requests have been sent. An uncomfortable amount of time has passed. Perhaps you’ve even sent a gentle reminder. And yet some people still haven’t paid up. How do you confront them without triggering a fight?
Dr Williams recommends starting with something positive, so that the friend is less likely to feel defensive. That can be as simple as saying, “I really enjoyed our time together.”
From there, let them know why it’s important for you to be repaid. That could be a bill that’s coming due or upcoming plans you need to save for. Rather than a slap on the wrist, this gives your friend an opportunity to help you out, Dr Williams said.
Resist the temptation to just let it go, Jackson warned. While it might seem like the easiest option, it could cause resentment.
“Too often people stay silent and make the assumption that this person intentionally has not paid back yet,” MJackson said. “Then we start to conflate that action or inaction with their character.”
A FEW USEFUL TOOLS
There are plenty of tools and apps to help travellers make sense of group spending. Reader-recommended apps include Tab, Splitwise, TravelSpend, Splid, Tricount and KittySplit. Some travellers told The New York Times that they use a couple in tandem.
Lauren Downey, a project manager from Hoboken, NJ, recently embarked on an 11-person group trip to Italy. She said she used an app called Tab to take pictures of restaurant receipts and track each person’s spending. She then added those “tabbed” meals to Splitwise, which can be used to equally split payments after users log expenses.
“Some people think it’s petty to settle a bill this way, but ultimately it causes a lot less stress,” Downey, 30, said. “We can’t all afford the same lifestyles, but that doesn’t mean we can’t hang out.”

A Mexican judge has convicted three men of the 2024 murders of two Australian surfers and their American friend in a case that sparked international outrage.
Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33 respectively, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California state in a suspected robbery.
The deaths of the trio sparked an outpouring of grief and condemnation in Australia and the United States.
Jesus Gerardo – known as “El Kekas” – was accused of leading the attack. His surname has not been disclosed for legal reasons. He and two other defendants, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were found guilty on Friday local time.
Martin and Debra Robinson, the brothers’ parents, traveled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 7 September.
“They took our sons from our lives forever,” said Debra Robinson, who testified on the final day of the trial. “What hurts us most is that, in their final hours, they were treated with such cruelty.”
Addressing the court at the start of the trial, Martin Robinson described his sons’ murders as “hell”.
“It’s hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons,” he said.
Rhoad’s mother, Page, and his fiance, Natalie Weirtz, also participated in the hearing in a video call from the United States.
“The accused are guilty and must be punished so that no other family suffers the same pain,” Weirtz said. “Since Carter’s death, I feel paranoid and isolated.”
The surfers were camping in a remote beachside area when they were attacked in April 2024. Their bodies were found in a clifftop shaft, with gunshot wounds to their heads.
Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.
Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were killed in 2015 while traveling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.

Trump talks to Putin, then announces diesel deal with Russia, in sharp reversal of U.S. policy
Ukraine's Zelenskyy slams 'weak decision' for U.S. to do business with Russia
U.S. President Donald Trump said he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal after years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
Trump said on social media on Friday that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he was expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia.
Instead, Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and one million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver another three million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.
Trump had signed sweeping sanctions law
Trump's shocking announcement was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month that aimed to clamp down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel Russia's war against Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it "a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners," according to a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington.
Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were meeting with Ukrainian officials in Miami to discuss a proposal to end the Russia-Ukraine war.
"I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other," Zelenskyy said.
Trump's move casts doubt on the likelihood of the White House imposing new sanctions on Russia, given that the law that passed overwhelmingly by Congress directs the administration to target countries that purchase Russian oil and gas. Lawmakers this week had urged the Trump administration to act quickly to use the tools available to help Ukraine.
'Enough is enough,' Democrats say
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, along with Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, who is the top Democrat on the foreign relations committee, and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the banking committtee, called Trump's announcement a betrayal of Ukraine, the European allies and U.S. national security.
"Enough is enough," the senators wrote. "The President must end his war with Iran instead of funding Russia's war machine."
Residents of a neighbourhood in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, are seen walking Friday outside a building that was damaged by a Russian strike. (Kateryna Klochko/The Associated Press)
Gas prices globally have surged as the war in Iran upends the energy sector. While diesel future prices dipped on the news on Friday, the national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. remained high at $6.28 US, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22.
Trump did not address the sanctions or Russia's war but said, "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority."
The president said later as he left the White House for a campaign rally that he was thankful for the deal.
"I want to thank President Putin. To be honest with you, we have massive amounts of oil coming into our country, and it's diesel, which is what we want. So, thank you," Trump said.
He did not answer shouted questions about the criticism from Zelenskyy.
Details not immediately clear
The White House did not immediately respond to questions about who was paying for the Russian diesel or when it would become available.
Trump said on social media that he'd struck the diesel-related deal after speaking to Russian President Vladimir Putin. (Gavriil Grigorov/Sputnik/The Associated Press)
A statement from Putin, released by the Kremlin on Friday, said that during their call, he and Trump dedicated "significant attention to the prospects of resolving the Ukrainian crisis" and also discussed "the situation around Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations."
Russia "confirmed its readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and global markets," Putin said. "I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy."
Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov, speaking later to reporters, wouldn't say whether the U.S. made any concessions in exchange for the supplies or what, if anything, was promised to Russia in exchange.
Deal 'plays into Russia's hands': Zelenskyy
Zelenskyy, in a lengthy online post reacting to the deal, said Russia would repay it "with further terror and perfidy." He cast it as an investment in the war, allowing it to be prolonged.
"It plays into Russia's hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," he said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, pictured during a recent interview in Kyiv, said in a social media post that Putin is trying to strike 'backroom deals' to buy time in the war. (Alina Smutko/Reuters)
Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who co-sponsored the Russia sanctions law, said Trump's decision "makes us complicit in Putin's war against Ukraine." In his scathing statement, he invoked the memory of the late senator Lindsey Graham, a Trump ally and Russia hawk, for whom the sanctions law is named after.
"This agreement with a murdering dictator is a stain on our nation's character, an insult to Lindsey Graham's memory and directly contrary to Congress's intent in our bipartisan sanctions bill," he said.
Rep. Don Beyer, the senior Democrat on the House of Representatives joint economic committee, called Trump's announcement "infuriating."
"This is what we warned anyone who would listen: Trump isn't the slightest bit trustworthy when it comes to Russia," Beyer said in a statement on X.
The law Trump signed last month envisions sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers, and bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and the handling of sovereign debt.
It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15 per cent of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
Bans began under Biden
The U.S. has not imported Russian oil or gas since 2022, when the Biden administration banned them because of Moscow's invasion of Ukraine, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
Shortly after Trump made the announcement, the U.S. Treasury Department said it was immediately issuing a temporary licence allowing Russian diesel to be supplied to the global market.
This is the latest in several licences the U.S. Treasury has issued regarding Russian fuel shipments since the start of the Iran war earlier this year. But it is the first to ease sanctions on diesel for longer than the standard 30-day window since the start of the Ukraine war in February 2022.
- Russian strike devastates apartment block in northern Ukraine, at least 25 killed across the country
The licence means U.S. sanctions will not apply until April 2027 on deliveries of Russian diesel that has been loaded onto tankers as of Friday.
The extensions underscore how the fallout from the Iran war has boosted Moscow's ability to profit from its energy exports.
'Great benefit' to Russia, Putin: analyst
"What does this do to prices? I think probably not much," said Clayton Seigle, an energy strategist and expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
But Seigle said the new deal is a "great benefit to Russia and to Putin," who are currently trying to offload their summer-grade diesel for the heavier winter and Arctic grades that they will need in the coming months.
"It's kind of shuffling deck chairs on the Titanic," said Michael Lynch of the Energy Policy Research Foundation, a non-partisan research institution focused on energy and economics.
"If we get diesel from Russia, basically it means that their existing customers are not going to get it and they'll have to go somewhere else, and that will keep the price basically where it is now," Lynch said.
Russia, once a major exporter of diesel, has banned exports since July as it has struggled to meet demand inside the country because of Ukraine's repeated attacks on Russian oil refineries. The International Energy Agency says Russian diesel output has fallen by about 30 per cent.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told state news agency Tass that Russia is "immediately starting to lift restrictions on diesel exports ahead of schedule." He said Moscow could start supplies to the U.S. this month and Russia's domestic market will be "fully supplied" with diesel as well.

South Korea will take legal action if it finds that shipments of fuel from its ports to Russia broke domestic law, the government has said, responding to a Guardian report on the trade.
The government, in a statement issued by the foreign and trade ministries and the customs service, said that it is “checking additional information concerning the loading cases reported by the Guardian” and “if the verification establishes that our laws and regulations have been violated, it plans to act in accordance with the law”.
Guardian analysis of port records and ship-tracking data found that in July and August over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, was loaded at several South Korean ports on to seven tankers that made 14 voyages to Russia’s far east.
Three of the tankers were under UK and EU sanctions. One of them took on about 26,000 tonnes through a ship-to-ship transfer at an anchorage off the southern port of Yeosu.
Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finnish thinktank, said the trade “undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea’s support for Ukraine.”
Russia’s capacity to refine oil has been severely disrupted by Ukrainian drone strikes. Its refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, and diesel output is down nearly 30% on last year, according to the International Energy Agency.
Thursday’s statement from Seoul said the refined petroleum products involved were not covered by South Korea’s export controls on Russia, which apply mainly to industrial machinery, electronics and vehicles.
“As reported by the Guardian, the loading of refined petroleum products at our ports does not constitute a violation of our domestic law”, it said.
The government said whether fuel of South Korean origin, such as diesel, had been exported “has not been confirmed”, adding that no diesel, aviation fuel or motor petrol had been “exported” from South Korea to Russia through customs clearance.
It is unclear who owned or sold the fuel, which South Korean port records do not show publicly.
The government also cautioned that the “mere fact that a vessel did not proceed directly to the final destination country stated on its declaration and instead moved to another country makes it difficult to conclude that there is a suspicion of false declaration of destination”.
It said it would examine the tankers’ actual routes, any divergence from their declared destinations and the reasons for them, before judging whether the law had been broken.
The three sanctioned tankers told South Korean authorities they were bound for Japan or Singapore before sailing to Vladivostok.
The Russian-flagged Aram Khachaturian, which is not under western sanctions, loaded at Ulsan three times in July and August and on each occasion gave a destination other than Russia before sailing there.
An adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this week that the shipments stood in “sharp contrast” to South Korea’s sanctions policies.
On Wednesday South Korea’s presidential office said those remarks were “contrary to fact and inappropriate”, and asked Ukraine to refrain from public comment that could damage South Korea’s international credibility.
Ukraine’s foreign ministry reportedly said on Wednesday that it had raised the fuel shipments with Seoul through closed diplomatic channels and asked for an explanation.
Its spokesperson, Heorhii Tykhyi, said Kyiv also had “our own data on such activity”.

Majority of people in Myanmar are living in poverty or at risk, UN report says
More than two-thirds of the population of Myanmar is either living in poverty or at risk of falling into it, according to a United Nations report
BANGKOK -- More than two in three people living in Myanmar are either in poverty or at risk of falling into it, as armed conflict, limited access to basic services and economic instability deepen deprivation across the country, a United Nations report published on Thursday said.
Almost 18 million people, or 32.6% of the population, are poor, while another 19.5 million are vulnerable to poverty, according to the U.N. Development Program (UNDP). That brings the total number of people in or at risk of poverty to over 37 million people, or 68% of the population.
Myanmar has been in turmoil since the military seized power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021, triggering widespread opposition. After security forces suppressed peaceful protests with lethal force, many opponents of military rule took up arms, plunging large parts of the country into conflict.
Kanni Wignaraja, U.N. assistant secretary-general and UNDP regional director for Asia and the Pacific, said: “We are seeing a depth of poverty in Myanmar that is eroding human development itself. This is a no-win war. Everyone is losing. The core muscle of the country is being systematically eroded.”
The UNDP report was based on a nationwide telephone survey of 7,463 households. It used an adapted Multidimensional Poverty Index that captures deprivation beyond income, including overlapping gaps in health, education and living standards.
Deficits in health and living standards account for more than 80% of measured poverty, the report said, reflecting difficulties accessing health care, adequate housing, clean water, sanitation and other essential services, particularly in conflict zones.
Poverty is especially widespread and severe in states facing heightened insecurity and restricted access, particularly Rakhine in the west and Kayah in the east, it said.
Low levels of education, insecure employment and low incomes compound pressures from conflict, displacement, disrupted markets and fragmented services, driving deprivation across Myanmar, the report found.
Repeated economic and natural hazard shocks further deepen poverty, with El Niño expected to intensify those pressures. The naturally occurring climatic pattern can disrupt rainfall and raise global temperatures.
The UNDP also warned of a growing loss of human capital, saying at least 1 million young people may have left Myanmar since 2021 due to a lack of opportunities and growing uncertainty that limits the future prospects for education, jobs and mobility.
Min Aung Hlaing, the leader of the military-backed government, told a Cabinet meeting this week that instability and a lack of peace had slowed the country’s economic growth. He attributed the slowdown to political instability, sanctions, a lack of financial assistance, limited access to international markets, declining trade and increased worker migration, according to state media reports Monday.

A Mexican judge is expected to hand down his verdict in the high-profile murder trial of three men accused of killing two Australian surfers and their American friend in 2024.
Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33 respectively, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California state in an alleged robbery.
The deaths of the trio sparked an outpouring of grief and condemnation in Australia and the United States. The prosecution is seeking 150 years in prison for each of the accused.
The prosecution and defence were expected to present their closing arguments from 1pm Thursday (6am AEDT on Friday), after which the judge was expected to announce his verdict.
If convicted, the three will be sentenced on Friday.
Martin and Debra Robinson, the brothers’ parents, will address the court. Both travelled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 8 September.
Rhoad’s mother, Page, and his widow, Natalie Weirtz, will also participate in the hearing in a video call from the United States.
The surfers were camping in a remote beachside area when they were allegedly attacked in April 2024. Their bodies were found in a clifftop shaft, with gunshot wounds to their heads.
Addressing the court at the start of the trial, Martin Robinson described his sons’ alleged murders as “hell”.
“It’s hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons,” he said.
Authorities allege the men were killed during an attempt to steal their pickup truck, which was later found burned near their bodies.
Jesus Gerardo is accused of leading the alleged attack. His surname has not been disclosed for legal reasons. His girlfriend was sentenced at a separate trial in November to two decades in prison after admitting that she instigated the robbery.
Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.
Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were killed in 2015 while traveling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.

CHENNAI/KOLKATA/PUDUCHERRY/GUWAHATI: TVK cleared its first test barely five months after forming govt in Tamil Nadu, winning the bypolls in two assembly constituencies, while in West Bengal, BJP retained Nandigram - CM Suvendu Adhikari's backyard - and wrested Rejinagar from AJUP (Aam Janata Unnayan Party), winning both assembly bypolls in its first electoral test since coming to office in state.All-India NR Congress, an NDA ally, retained Thattanchavady assembly segment, with Ashok Anand defeating his nearest Congress rival by over 8,400 votes. BJP regained Assam's Nagaon Lok Sabha constituency, with ex-IAS officer Devasish Sharma securing about 50% of the vote. AIUDF chief Badruddin Ajmal finished second, followed by Congress's Sibamoni Bora. Sharma, who was Nagaon district commissioner when he took VRS and had joined BJP last month, led Ajmal by over 1.5 lakh votes, while Bora trailed by over 1.2 lakh votes. A victory for political decorum and personal decency, says VijayThough Madurantakam and Dharapuram in Tamil Nadu presented different political terrain, TVK won both seats with comfortable margins by fielding former AIADMK MLAs Maragatham Kumaravel and P Sathyabama, who had joined the governing party barely 20 days after the assembly election results in May.
