In Rejinagar, BJP candidate Shankharavh Sarkar won by 75,816 votes, pushing AJUP, which won the seat in the April poll, to second place. Muslims constitute 72% of the electorate in Rejinagar, in Murshidabad.

The British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal has been released from a Delhi prison after the Indian high court warned the government it would be found in contempt of court if it continued to attempt to keep him in jail despite an 18 September court order releasing him on bail. Johal has been incarcerated for nine years without any full trial.
The court order was issued after Johal’s lawyers issued a writ of habeas corpus alleging he was being detained against the express direction of the court.
Johal’s nine-year detention on alleged terrorist offences, has been a cause of diplomatic tension between the UK and India, but campaigners have claimed the British government has not been active enough to secure his release or, alternatively, a full trial.
The campaign group Reprieve says his case has never come to full trial largely because of the inability of the Indian government to assemble credible witnesses to back their claim that Johal transported £3,000 to France to fund a multinational extremist plot involving targeted killings in the Punjab in 2016-17.
On Thursday morning, the high court in Delhi instructed the Indian government to release Johal by 2.30pm Indian time, giving government officials three hours to comply or find themselves risking contempt proceedings. In the end, he was released in the late afternoon wearing a red T-shirt to be greeted by friends, family and flowers.
Documents shown to the court by Johal’s lawyers on behalf of his father-in-law as petitioner revealed that messages from the prison to the Ministry of Home Affairs seeking permission for his release had been left unanswered.
His lawyers in their petition stated he had met all the bail conditions yet “the detainee has nevertheless not been released, and is being held in custody without the authority of any court, pending a ‘clarification’ sought by the jail from the Ministry of Home Affairs”.
The petition added that no clarification from the ministry had been forthcoming, explaining: “Every day of such detention is a continuing violation of the detainee’s fundamental rights under article 21 of the constitution of India.”
Johal has been detained by Indian authorities since 4 November 2017. He is facing eight charges of terrorism in the federal court, but had been cleared of largely similar charges by a Punjab court. He claims any initial confessions he gave were extracted under torture.
The bail terms last week imposed 11 conditions, including surrender of passport, a personal bond of 500,000 Indian rupees (£3,930) with two sureties, fortnightly reporting to the investigating officer, prior intimation of any change of residence and a ban on travelling to the Punjab. He was also restricted from talking to media about the case directly or indirectly.
The Indian government has alleged the Khalistan Liberation Force undertook the killings and Johal had “complete knowledge of the conspiracy” and was a KLF member.
His Dumbarton-based brother Gurpreet Singh Johal said: “There have been so many setbacks and disappointments in the last nine years that I didn’t dare to believe it until I saw Jagtar walking out of the prison gates with my own eyes. The last two weeks have been torture – knowing that Jagtar had been granted bail, but the authorities were refusing to let him out. I’ll sleep well tonight, knowing that he’s not behind bars.
“Tomorrow morning, the fight continues, because he’s still on trial and facing the death penalty for something he didn’t do, trapped in a sham legal process designed to punish him for standing up for human rights”.
Reprieve’s deputy executive director, Dan Dolan, said: “While tonight is the first night in almost nine years that Jagtar Singh Johal is not caged in a prison cell, he still has the threat of a death sentence hanging over him. It should also be noted that, despite bail being ordered, the prison refused to release Jagtar until his family brought a habeas corpus petition and a judge warned the jail they’d be found in contempt of court”.
The UK Foreign Office is understood to have been supporting recent calls for his release on bail after last week’s court order, as have two campaign groups in the UK Redress and Reprieve.

Saudi authorities say 3 killed in attacks on Riyadh airport claimed by Houthi rebels
Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation reports that three Saudi citizens were killed and several other people wounded in two attacks Thursday
CAIRO -- Three Saudi citizens were killed and several other people were wounded in two attacks Thursday targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and a Saudia Airlines aircraft, Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation said Friday.
It marked the deadliest attack in the country since Saudi Arabia and allied forces in neighboring Yemen launched a major military offensive last weekend against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in that country.
The first attack on Thursday targeted airport facilities, while the second struck the aircraft, the statement said. It did not identify those responsible, though the Houthis claimed to have targeted the airport with a ballistic missile.
The airport has come under multiple attacks, with a Sudanese national killed there earlier this week.
The new statement noted “injuries to a number of citizens and residents of different nationalities. Their injuries ranged from minor to serious.”
It also indicated that operational activities had returned to normal.

Is Amazon making a smartphone? A Reuters report from earlier this year revealed details about a device codenamed Transformer under development, with Amazon's Alexa+ AI assistant as the focus of the experience.
With Amazon announcing a complete rebrand of its tablet line on Thursday—killing the cheap Fire Tablets and replacing them with premium Alexa Tablets that finally run Android with access to the Google Play Store—we now have a blueprint for what an Android-powered Amazon phone could look like.
Amazon's souped-up Alexa+ assistant is front and center on the tablets. There's a persistent “Ask Alexa” widget on the home screen that lets you call on the assistant to ask it questions—you can say “Alexa” to trigger it, too. But Alexa+ now finally has what Amazon calls On-Screen Intelligence. Like Google's Gemini on Android phones or Apple's Siri on iPhones, which can read your screen and answer contextual questions, Alexa now has the same functionality (if you opt in).
That can be for simple things like summarizing a web page, but it can be used for more complex tasks. Watching a YouTube video about a new product? Ask Alexa whether the product is on Amazon, and if so, add it to your Amazon shopping cart. Perusing an Infatuation article about new restaurants in your area? Ask Alexa to highlight the ones closest to your office.
Alexa also supports “live sessions,” just like Gemini Live or ChatGPT's Voice Mode—it lets you have a free-form back-and-forth conversation with the assistant. Maybe you're focused on a DIY project and want Alexa to spell out instructions slowly at your own pace. It also supports visual intelligence: Point the tablet's camera at anything, and Alexa can identify the object and offer helpful advice. Got a water leak? Point the camera and ask Alexa how to fix it.
These are completely new experiences for Alexa. Amazon's vice president of devices, Kevin Keith, tells WIRED the company “didn't really have the right product to be able to use” these capabilities, but that's now solved with its Android tablets.
But these features would fit right in on a smartphone, where they’d perhaps be even more useful. When I mentioned this to Keith, he laughed and said: “We have nothing to share on that. Interesting idea.”
Amazon notoriously tried to make a smartphone in 2014—the Fire Phone—a massive flop discontinued shortly after launch due to a limited app ecosystem, dismal sales, and an over-reliance on gimmicky features. (Even its designer recently said he was embarrassed by it.) That may partly be why Amazon is retiring the “Fire” branding and killing its budget tablets. People may forget the disaster and won't be reminded of the “Fire Phone” name when the company eventually introduces a new handset.
Switching its tablets over to Google's Android (rather than the forked version the Fire tablets ran) and adding the Google Play Store is a silent admission that it's hard to thrive without a healthy app ecosystem. It also sets the phone up for success, as it won't feel app-limited out of the gate like the original Fire Phone.
Alexa+ is right now a paid service that requires an Alexa+ subscription or Amazon Prime. However, Amazon says anyone with its new Alexa tablet gets Alexa+ for free, and this would likely also be the case with an Amazon phone. Amazon’s devices, after all, are vehicles used to drive users to buy stuff on Amazon.com. A 2022 Pew Research Center survey showed that 76 percent of Americans purchase products using a smartphone. It makes sense that Amazon would want more direct control over the hardware people use to make those purchases, especially if it paints Alexa as a helpful assistant that can shop for you.
Recently, Amazon has been on a mission to make its hardware more premium. This crusade seems to have ramped up after Microsoft Surface creator Panos Panay joined the company as head of Devices & Services in 2023. These upscaling efforts include the slew of Echo speakers it introduced in 2025, which saw marked price increases over their predecessors thanks to upgraded hardware. The Kindles announced at the start of October now come in sleek aluminum variants and are thinner and lighter than ever. The latest Alexa Tablets are more powerful, made from aluminum, and feel very iPad-esque.
Panay spent his final few years at Microsoft on the failed Microsoft Duo folding smartphone. When it launched, he was adamant it wasn't a phone but rather a productivity-focused device that belonged in a new category.
The Reuters report suggests Amazon's phone may feature an “AI interface,” what the industry often refers to as a generative user interface, that eliminates the need for traditional app stores. It could be that when Panay eventually steps on a stage to reveal an Amazon “Alexa” Phone, he'll once again claim it's not a phone, but a helpful AI assistant in your pocket that conforms to your demands—marking a clear departure from every other Android slab on the market.
The smartphone market is in a bit of a predicament right now. Devices are getting more expensive because of the memory crisis, shipments have declined for several quarters in a row, and the duopoly in the US market between Samsung and Apple makes it hard for other players to break through. Established smartphone companies have given up and left the market, like OnePlus this summer or HMD last year.
There isn't much choice left in for American buyers. However, an Amazon phone, made by a company that isn't based in China and backed by Amazon's retail dominance, could quickly swallow the slice of the pie Motorola and Google are fighting over.

How the oil industry is preparing for Hurricane Isaias
Hurricane Isaias, the first Atlantic hurricane of the season, is expected to make landfall on Friday evening near the Alabama Gulf Coast and Florida panhandle.
Days ago, the oil industry around the U.S. Gulf Coast started preparing. A segment of the nation's oil infrastructure — like oil rigs and platforms — operates in the region, although the majority of it is further west, towards western Louisiana and Texas.
Although oil experts are not anticipating major disruptions, oil companies have been taking precautions. Shell and BP have evacuated personnel from offshore facilities close to the storm's path, mainly deepwater platforms. Chevron has evacuated offshore drilling rigs close to the storm's path, and plans to redeploy them once the storm has passed.
In an emailed statement, Exxon told NPR they are "closely monitoring the weather. Operations are normal."
But so far, the storm seems like it will skirt most facilities. The storm's path "could be worse," said Debnil Chowdhury, head of Americas refining at S&P Global Energy. After all, the storm is heading east, and not west, toward where the bulk of oil operations — like refineries — are located.
The storm is "making a swooping turn, almost just to the east of where the most significant infrastructure is," said Bryan Domangue, the Gulf of America region director for the federal Marine Minerals Administration, who oversees offshore oil and natural gas production. "At this point, it's swept just a little south of some of our major deepwater oil and gas facilities, and then it's hugging the eastern boundary of where the infrastructure is."
He added that in addition to evacuating people who work on oil rigs and platforms, which are normal storm precautions, oil operators are doing things like shutting off safety valves below the ocean floor, and moving mobile drilling facilities when possible.
Of course, it's not unprecedented for the oil industry to face hurricanes. Hurricanes Katrina and Rita, in 2005, remain some of the most destructive in the oil and gas industry's history. Nearly 3,000 platforms were in the path of the storms and Katrina destroyed 47 platforms. Other, more recent, hurricanes have not been as destructive but have halted production or reduced capacity — such as Hurricane Francine in 2024, Hurricane Ida in 2021, and Hurricane Harvey in 2017.
Another risk is what would happen if the storm became severe enough to make refineries — which are on land — go offline, analysts told NPR. If a hurricane knocks out the power, or if a refinery floods, it can take a while to get running again. It's more complicated than restarting an oil rig or mobile drilling operations.
"Restarting these things is like starting up an old car," said Carl Larry, a manager at Enverus, an energy data and research provider, even if the shutdown is short. "If you did anything in the world, anything in your life, 24/7, stop doing it for one day," he continued, "you're going to have the shakes."
He says, this is because refineries are vast and complex. They boil oil down into molecules that are turned into diesel, gasoline, or natural gas liquids like propane. Pipelines carry crude oil in and refined products out. And they have to be heated. "Every one of those little steps is built on power that's generated through the facility on a constant 24/7 basis," Larry said. If that power is switched off, the process takes time to restart.
There are two significant refineries on the hurricane's path — the Chevron Pascagoula location and the Vertex Alabama refinery. Representatives of these refineries did not return requests for comment about their storm preparations, but Ross Allen, a spokesperson for Chevron, told NPR that generally speaking, refineries prepare for storms by trying to mitigate flood risk.
Chowdhury of S&P Global Energy said these two refineries "account for about 2.5% of total U.S. refining capacity and about 5% the Gulf Coast refining capacity. And Pascagoula specifically is very important to supplying airports throughout the southeast."
While those numbers may not sound big, the global supply of diesel and gas is short, due to the wars in Iran and Ukraine. So every little bit counts. American refineries are operating at 92.7% capacity, refining about 17 million barrels of crude a day.
With the midterms weeks away, fuel prices are a sensitive political issue: The national average for a gallon of gasoline is $4.37 and $6.27 for diesel, according to AAA.

Argenx disclosed that its blockbuster drug Vyvgart failed to outperform placebo in a Phase 3 trial of patients with Sjögren’s disease, a chronic autoimmune disorder, marking an unusual setback for the company, STAT says. Argenx has racked up a series of wins in autoimmune disorders en route to becoming one of the world’s largest biotechs based on market cap. William Blair analysts had projected $1.4 billion in peak sales from Vyvgart in Sjögren’s disease but described the trial as high risk, in part because Sjögren’s patients often have high placebo responses. The trial was supposed to be completed next year, but it was stopped early after a data monitoring committee determined the primary endpoint would not be met.
The Food and Drug Administration flagged a potential safety signal after four deaths were reported among patients with treatment-resistant schizophrenia who received investigational evenamide in clinical trials, MedPage Today informs us. In April, the agency halted patient enrollment in a Phase 3 trial for the Newron Pharmaceuticals medicine after the sudden death of a participant. That hold remains in place at U.S. study centers but enrollment continues in other countries, and additional clinical sites are being added. The FDA concern relates to the risk that some sodium channel blockers may trigger arrhythmias that can lead to serious cardiovascular events or seizures.

Four medical establishments in Hyderabad were issued show-cause notices after joint inspections by the EAGLE Force and TG SAFE found discrepancies in records concerning the purchase and sale of habit-forming medicines.
The inspections, carried out following inputs from Central intelligence, covered pharmacies in Masab Tank, Mallepally and Tolichowki. Officials checked compliance with requirements governing the purchase, storage and sale of regulated medicines, including Schedule H and H1 drugs.
At Al-Hamra Medical & General Store in Masab Tank, officials found that prescribed schedule registers had not been maintained and sale bills concerning certain habit-forming medicines, including Tapentadol, Alprazolam and others, were either not maintained or produced for verification.
At MM Medical and General Store in Mallepally, operating as MED24 Pharmacy and General Store, officials found deficiencies in prescribed registers and non-production of sale bills relating to Pregalyv 75. The Schedule H1 drugs register and sale bill book were also not produced.
A surprise inspection was conducted at First Step Drug Mart in Tolichowki following information about the indiscriminate sale and distribution of habit-forming medicines. Officials found several such medicines at the establishment, while the pharmacist was not present during the inspection. The Schedule H1 drugs register was also not produced, and discrepancies were noticed in records concerning the purchase and sale of the medicines.
At Hayat Pharmacy in Tolichowki, the prescribed Schedule H1 records and prescription register for habit-forming medicines were not produced. Officials also found deficiencies in the maintenance and production of sale bills for certain medicines.
Show-cause notices were subsequently issued to all four establishments, with further regulatory action to be taken under the applicable provisions and norms of the Drugs Control Administration.

Ukrainian drone strikes have knocked out two of five data centers belonging to the Russian tech giant Yandex. The damage has left Yandex, known as “Russia’s Google” because it operates the country’s most popular search engine, struggling to maintain its AI chatbot and other online services.
The Ukrainian drones struck Yandex data centers in the Sasovo and Kaluga regions of Russia on October 8 and October 9, according to Reuters. Those actions came as a direct response to a Russian drone strike campaign targeting Ukraine’s data centers, which has disrupted mobile phone and Internet services for thousands of Ukrainians since late September.
“We continue to respond to Russia’s attacks on Ukraine, and we’re doing so with high precision,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a post on X. “Another data center was hit as well—our symmetrical response.”
The Ukrainian company Firepoint said its FP-1 one-way attack drones were involved in the latest strike on the Kaluga data center that is Yandex’s largest such facility, Reuters reported. The first Ukrainian attack targeted Yandex’s Sasovo data center that houses two of the company’s three supercomputers used for training the company’s YandexGPT AI model.
Yandex said no employees were hurt but acknowledged disruptions to some services. Russian users reported problems accessing media websites and popular apps for the Ivi video streaming platform, the digital banking service T-Bank and the state-owned Russian Railways, according to the independent Russian news publication Meduza.

Paytm began as a digital wallet, became a payments behemoth on the back of that and then built up the momentum with UPI. But two years ago it had to slow it all down and become a lending company. turn to profitability and the revival of topline after the Paytm Payments Bank bruising was down to this transition from payments to loans and distribution of credit products. But now, the company finds itself at another crossroads as the MDR rules for UPI could once again turn Paytm towards payments as a growth engine. How will that change the fintech platform’s revenue structure and how does the major focus on artificial intelligence (AI) play a role in this? Five years ago, Paytm was almost entirely a payments company. Payment services brought in ₹1,981 Cr of its ₹2,802 Cr operating revenue in FY21, about 71%. Financial services distribution contributed just ₹128 Cr, under 5%. That mix has since been turned on its head. According to the company’s FY26 annual report, financial services distribution, mostly loan distribution, grew at an 83% CAGR to ₹2,594 Cr, more than 20X its FY21 base. It now makes up 31% of the ₹8,437 Cr topline. Payment services is still the largest piece at 58%, but grew at a much slower 19% CAGR over the same period. More importantly, in FY26, the company reported a net profit of ₹552 Cr against a ₹663 Cr loss in FY25. In Q1 FY27, operating revenue rose 28% to ₹2,448 Cr YoY, so the company is on pace to stretch its profitability in FY27 too. Along the way, Paytm throttled its super app ambitions to a certain extent. It has exited businesses such as entertainment ticketing, scaled back its ecommerce ambitions and sharpened its focus on payments and financial services. But look closely, and Paytm’s super app playbook is still very much alive, but it is a focussed effort around its active payments users and merchants, not for just about every consumer out there. The fintech giant is increasingly looking to make more money from the financial relationships it already owns. Merchants Drive Paytm’s Payments Business One may see shades of PhonePe’s revenue model in Paytm’s payments business. The stakeholders are the same and the rules of the business are also the same. But Paytm had a different GTM strategy compared to PhonePe. The latter went for a user acquisition blitz on the UPI consumer side, which is reflected in its lead among consumers, while Paytm looked for deeper penetration on the merchants side. Paytm’s biggest contribution in that regard is the Soundbox, which was then emulated by every other player in the market. That itself makes it clear how Paytm approaches the payments business. It’s a merchants-first approach that set the company apart from other players, save for the likes of BharatPe, which also adopted a similar approach. But as with any other UPI app — in the zero MDR regime — a customer scanning a merchant’s UPI QR code does not generate any meaningful fee for Paytm. The zero-MDR framework has historically prevented direct merchant charges on UPI and Rupay. Paytm banked on its merchants base to monetise even as UPI monetisation remained a problem. This included merchant loans, insurance, point-of-sales device subscriptions and more. A similar playbook was adopted on the consumer side. UPI became the top of the funnel and other services down the funnel monetised this base. Even today, the MDR problem has not been solved as the government’s plans to implement a 0.4% MDR fee on certain high value transactions has now been deferred, as per reports. But merchant GMV rose 31% year on year to ₹7.1 Lakh Cr in Q1 FY27. Subscription merchant deployments reached 1.57 Cr storefronts, while payment processing margins remained above four basis points. Payment Services revenue grew 33% to ₹1,384 Cr in the quarter. The merchants-centric stack generated ₹4,891 Cr in FY26, 58% of Paytm’s operating revenue. The business grew by 21% from ₹4,039 Cr in FY25, when regulatory disruption disrupted parts of Paytm's payments ecosystem. While this is still 27.4% below Paytm’s peak ₹6,236 Cr payments revenue in FY24, this middle ground proves that Paytm has recovered to a large extent after the RBI crackdown in January 2024. Similarly, consumer activity also matters, even when individual UPI transactions are hard to monetise directly. In Q1 FY27, Paytm reported consumer UPI transaction value growth of 45% to ₹5.9 Lakh Cr, compared with industry growth of roughly 20%, and monthly transacting users of 8 Cr. Paytm's management describes the recovery as broader than a single payment product. It spans offline small merchants, large merchants, online checkout and consumer payments. That breadth matters because the company can use the same acquiring infrastructure to sell devices and, eventually, distribute financial products. “GMV growth is accelerating not just because MTUs (monthly transacting users) grew, but because usage per customer did. We focus on customer quality, product quality, and engagement, not just volume,” CEO and founder Vijay Shekhar Sharma said in the Q4 FY26 earnings call. However, in Paytm’s filings, one key disclosure is missing. The company does not separately report how much Payment Services revenue comes from Soundbox and POS subscriptions versus transaction processing. Without that split, investors cannot isolate how much of the recovery is recurring subscription income, or whether the incremental revenue is being generated more efficiently. This will also enable investors to track the expenses trajectory. Paytm incurred ₹2,573 Cr in payment processing charges in FY26, compared with ₹2,125 Cr a year earlier. Plus sales workforce reached 40,512 in Q4 FY26, up from 36,724. This is a particularly important figure because the company hinted in early 2024 that it would have to shrink its workforce to recover from the revenue drop as described above. Plus, quarterly sales employee costs increased 30% year-on-year to ₹317 Cr. So is the payments business still not seeing operating leverage? The next three to four quarters will be critical to understand this. Why Financial Services Could Change The Equation? That’s the payments side of things. On the other side sits the distribution of financial services. This is another way of saying Paytm is a channel for insurance providers, lenders such as banks and NBFCs as well as digital gold investments. But in the post-payments bank world, this is the fastest-growing part of Paytm’s business. Revenue climbed 52% in FY26 to approximately ₹2,594 Cr. and in Q1 FY27, financial services grew another 45% to ₹814 Cr. According to the company’s FY26 annual report, financial services distribution, mostly loan distribution, grew at an 83% CAGR to ₹2,594 Cr, more than 20X its FY21 base. It now makes up 31% of the ₹8,437 Cr topline. Payment services is still the largest piece at 58%, but grew at a much slower 19% CAGR over the same period. On the lending side, instead of disbursing loans from its own books, Paytm helps banks and NBFCs reach customers, distribute credit and support servicing. The partner lenders provide capital and bear the principal lending exposure, while Paytm earns distribution-related fees and commissions under its partner arrangements. The economics depend not only on disbursement volumes but also on repeat borrowing, credit performance and the terms offered by partners. In Q1 FY27, Paytm said more than half of merchant loan disbursements went to repeat borrowers, so it is increasingly capitalising on its existing base. But the lending business only covers about 7% of its subscription merchant base in Q4 FY26, compared with roughly 6% a year earlier. This needs to grow significantly for Paytm’s thesis to hold. After Q1, Sharma suggested that capital capacity with lending partners is not a constraint, but getting the right kind of demand for profitable credit growth is important. Interest rate movements, because of RBI riskweight changes or repo rates add another layer of dependence, but Paytm is hoping that by being a distributor only, it is able to distance itself from the higher costs here. After all, the company is just a channel now, and as such it shouldn’t bear a significant amount of the higher cost of capital under a higher repo rate as announced by RBI recently. But high costs can make NBFCs more selective about new loans. This is also why Paytm needs to focus on monetising its more active merchants which are not covered under its lending distribution business. Incidentally, while distribution of financial services goes beyond lending, the focus is always on loan distribution rather than insurance or digital gold investments, both of which follow the same model of distribution commission. Can AI Make A Difference? The competitive reality for Paytm is exactly the same as it is for PhonePe or CRED or any other UPI app that looks to scale into other areas. While the nature of revenue differs, the operating segments are all overlapping. And Paytm has to compete on multiple fronts like any other payments plus lending app. In consumer UPI, Paytm is well behind PhonePe and Google Pay. In August 2026, Paytm had a volume share of 8.03% compared to 45.64% for PhonePe and 32.26% for Google Pay PhonePe, Google Pay, BharatPe, CRED, Pine Labs, Razorpay are all competing with Paytm when it comes to merchants services, and investments is the core focus for Groww, Zerodha and Angel One, where Paytm Money is not a major player any more. These are different competitive battles, but they converge on the question of how much of a merchant’s or consumer’s financial activity can Paytm capture profitably? That’s where Sharma’s biggest new bet comes in. Software and AI-led services is the new focus. Paytm envisions the Soundbox evolving from a payment confirmation device to a small business engagement and management platform, which brings commerce tools, customer notifications and support in Indian languages. At its September 2026 AGM, it discussed the idea of Paytm Intelligence, or PI, as a potential offering. The company disclosed then that AI is already deployed in product, engineering and merchant sales, as well as loan collections and consumer acquisition and retention. On the software side, the company is looking to make software that can help enterprises create an “agentic workforce” for running workflows and business processes. Importantly, Sharma added that by FY28, Paytm shareholders will see AI revenue reflected in disclosures under the commerce and cloud verticals. Whether this helps reduce Paytm’s dependency on cross-selling to its consumers and merchants is not clear. How the AI business might connect to this vast user base is also not clear. And with the UPI MDR debate far from settled, Paytm is likely to find itself waiting at the current crossroads for some time. In fact, one could argue that given Paytm’s profitability right now, it can afford to wait for the transition to MDR. This allows Paytm to build up more profitability in the next 12-15 months by continuing its current approach, and by then, if Vijay Shekhar Sharma’s words hold true, it may well be a fintech and an AI company.

Political disagreement over US President Donald Trump at a dog park in Ohio took a violent turn. It happened at Bainbridge Township, when an altercation broke out between two men, both of whom had guns in their cars, according to a report by The New York Times. All of this took place while both men were out with their pet dogs at a dog park. The incident began with a conversation about the president’s decision and resulted in criminal cases against both men. Reportedly, one of them is now facing possible jail time. According to The New York Times, the argument went on for about 20 minutes. The incident dates back to April when David Mattai, 55, arrived at the dog park with his spaniel, Bob. Mattai, who worked as a forklift mechanic, reportedly had the week off from work. It is believed that he ended up in the dog park after he tried taking his dog on a hiking trail, but failed. As a result, Mattai drove to the park in Bainbridge Township, northeast Ohio. At the park, Mattai met Emmanuel Mathews. The 80-year-old Mathews was a retired meat distributor who was said to be a regular at the dog park with his corgi, Frankie. Mathews, alias Mike, was believed to be sitting at a picnic table with a copy of The Wall Street Journal whose headline read, “Trump Grapples With Fears on War”, added the report. Amid this, Jamie Jedlinsky, 70, who was at the park with his pit mix, Willow, unknowingly became the eyewitness of the confrontation. The New York Times reported that Jedlinsky had become somewhat friendly with Mathews over the years. Upon noticing the newspaper, he gestured towards the headline about the Iran war and remarked, “That sucks, don’t it.” However, Mathews disagreed. As a supporter of Trump, Mathews reportedly began defending the President's decisions. Mattai, who had arrived shortly before the exchange, was listening to their conversation. Mattai reportedly considered himself a democratic socialist and had a collection of political bumper stickers which read, “Trump Is a Felon” and “Hicks Don’t Mix With Politics”. In the predominantly Republican area of northeast Ohio where he lived, he considered it his moral duty to “comfort the afflicted and afflict the comfortable”, reported The New York Times. The political disagreement between the two men subsequently escalated into an argument and turned into a shouting match. Both men carried firearms in their cars, and the simple confrontation became a criminal matter. Citing details from the confrontation through interviews, records and body-camera footage, the report said that both men face the possibility of imprisonment. Jedlinsky is likely to testify in both cases as a key witness in the matter. The report described him as someone who generally avoided discussing politics as advised by his mother. Reportedly, Mattai struggled with alcoholism in his life and would later say that he was drinking on the day of the incident. According to cleveland19, Emmanuel John Matthews shot David Mattai in the back while he attempted to leave the dog park. Later, the matter reached Chardon Municipal Court, where Matthews pleaded not guilty on April 22 and posted bond, as per the news outlet. It is reported that the victim went through multiple surgeries after the shooting incident. “He (Mattai) saw the guy’s gun. He did not reach for his. He had the door open and was trying to get Bob situated when the man shot him in the back. At that point, he did fall, but reached in and grabbed his weapon and returned fire at the man’s car,” said Sally Mattai, the victim’s wife. The defence attorney reportedly claimed that Matthews was in danger and acted in self-defence. Bainbridge Township Officer Friedrich Kaufmann testified in court. Later, the case was transferred to Geauga County Common Pleas Court. 'Ran through me' & 'good value in pub' - ex-NFL star Kelce tries rugby
- Published
Amateur rugby union players from Hackney had a shock when they turned up for a training match - to see a former Super Bowl champion among the opposition.
Hackney RFC's players rocked up on Wednesday for a 30-minute friendly, only to find former NFL star Jason Kelce playing for local rivals Old Streetonians.
Kelce - older brother of Travis, the three-time Super Bowl winning Kansas City Chiefs tight end married to global pop superstar Taylor Swift - played 13 seasons with the Philadelphia Eagles.
The 38-year-old is now learning to play different sports for his YouTube channel, and had a rugby lesson from former Harlequins and England prop Joe Marler.
"It's a nice little story being able to say we played rugby against Taylor Swift's brother-in-law, which I'm sure he loves as a title," Hackney full-back Peter Scott joked to BBC Sport.
"It's amazing that the sporting community, not even just the rugby community, can make these sorts of things happen. It was pretty surreal and it's pretty cool."
Kelce was part of Philadelphia's 2018 Super Bowl winning side and earned seven selections to the Pro Bowl - the annual NFL game featuring the league's top players - before retiring in 2024.
He was joined by former Philadelphia team-mate Beau Allen, also a member of that Eagles championship side of eight years ago, at Hackney Marshes in London this week.
- Eagles stun Patriots in Super Bowl LII 
  - Published5 February 2018
'I put him on his back - then he ran through me'
Hackney prop Dave Lewis told BBC Sport it took Kelce - a former center, an offensive lineman, whose main role is to snap the ball to the quarterback and then protect him, each play - a while to get used to rugby's rules.
"We got a message from our club captain saying our local rivals were coming down with two ex-NFL players, but we didn't know anything else about it," Lewis said.
"With the rules, he got there. At the very start, he sort of went round the back of a ruck and picked the ball up, which he obviously was then penalised for.
"I handed him off at one point and put him on his back in front of his team-mates and all of our fans as well. I hope they release that footage because I'll be dining out on it forever if they do.
"He just got back up and absolutely smashed me later on when he had the ball, running through me. So, I don't think he has an ego. I think he's just up for the physicality of it all."
Lewis' team-mate Scott said he thought Kelce picked the game up pretty quickly.
"He's a pretty intimidating figure," Scott added. "Very broad shoulders, powerful legs. They were using him as a number 8, which, I think, is the perfect position for him.
"There were a few intricacies, like how he was carrying the ball and where he was in the scrum, but he clearly knew what he was. He didn't look out of place at all.
"In rugby you are taught to tackle at an angle, and go at people's shoulders. He was a lot more front on, like 'OK, route one, I'm just gonna go straight at anyone that came out'."
'Good value in the pub afterwards'
Kelce is in England this week to commentate on Sunday's NFL overseas game between his former club Philadelphia and the Jacksonville Jaguars at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium (14:30 BST).
Old Street chairman Will Gilgrass said both Kelce and Allen really embraced the whole opportunity.
"They were very good value in the pub afterwards," he said. "We took them to one of our locals, and they put their cards behind the bar, chatting with the lads for a few hours after the game and really getting involved.
"They even did our initiation, singing a song and downing a pint."
The Hackney players also had their 15 minutes of fame after the match, with Kelce's American film crew interviewing some of them.
"They were asking how he got on, and what were the major differences to translate to an NFL audience," said Scott.
"The one I picked up on was the amount of power that he was able to generate after he would get tackled. His leg drives were sensational. It felt like three people would hit him and then he would go for another 20 metres.
"American football seems to be all about short, sharp, explosive power and he had that in spades - like he was rapid, very powerful, and then would take a backseat for a little while and then come back and do it again."

NEW DELHI: Keeping in mind its estimates on turnout, 
Delhi Police
 has drawn up a security plan involving road blockades, preventive detentions and restrictions on movement for the protest against SIR and CEC Gyanesh Kumar.
As many as 600 buses, 25 cranes have been put in place to aid detentions in New Delhi. Metro services, markets and transport will also be affected.
Security plan
30+ blockade points Checkpoints identified across city to stop protesters from reaching Jantar Mantar. A DCP-rank officer and personnel from the same district to be deployed at each point; across Delhi, nearly 35,000 security personnel, including Delhi Police and paramilitary forces; women cops requisitioned from outside the city, including 25 from UP.
Three layers of barricades
Roads leading to Jantar Mantar to be closed. Police have also mapped locations where violence, stone-pelting or clashes occurred during the previous protest on July 20, including Ashoka Road, Tolstoy Marg and Jantar Mantar Lane. These stretches have been barricaded as part of the preventive measures.
The placement of barricades has been kept in a zigzag pattern to slow down protesters in case they breach the initial security cordon and attempt to move further towards the restricted areas.
30–35 detention centres Stadiums, community centres and police stations being readied to accommodate protesters detained at borders and checkpoints.
Leave cancelled Leave of Delhi Police personnel of all ranks have been cancelled from Oct 8 until further orders. Central Armed Police Forces deployed to assist with security and crowd contro.
Social media surveillance Three posts showing old violence as recent incidents flagged so far. During the previous protest, police fact-checked 56 such posts.
Hotels and PGs under watch
Curbs across the capital
Roads and transport Traffic restrictions on roads along the Delhi borders with UP and Haryana and also those leading to Jantar Mantar and across New Delhi.
Police coordinating with cab aggregators to regulate movement. Several trains reportedly cancelled.
Internet restrictions
Mobile internet services to be suspended in 4km radius of Jantar Mantar.
Liquor shops shut Liquor outlets across the city ordered shut on Oct 9 and 10.
Markets and offices Curbs proposed for markets, offices, restaurants and otheroffices, restaurants and other commercial establishments in Connaught Place.
Market associations in CP, Sadar Bazar and parts of Karol Bagh and Chandni Chowk have confirmed closure on Oct 10.
Markets in Green Park, Sarojini Nagar and GK to stay open.
Metro services to be hit
45 metro stations shut
Following a request from Delhi Police, 
DMRC
 announced the closure of entry and exit gates at 57 stations from 9pm on Oct 9, along with reduced train frequency.
Later, the list was curtailed to 45 stations. This coincided with Supreme Court’s direction to Centre to reconsider the sweeping curbs. The restrictions are likely to stay till Oct 10 6pm.
Key stations on the list-Central Delhi-
 Rajiv Chowk, Janpath, Patel Chowk, Central Secretariat, New Delhi, Mandi House, Barakhamba Road, ITO, Supreme Court, Khan Market, Lok Kalyan Marg, Shivaji Stadium, Seva Teerth, Delhi Gate, Ramkrishna Ashram Marg, Jhandewalan
North and northwest Delhi
- Kashmere Gate, Vishwavidyalaya, GTB Nagar, Azadpur, Jahangirpuri, Majlis Park, Haiderpur Badli Mor, Rithala
East and northeast Delhi
- Shahdara, Welcome, Seelampur, Jafrabad, Maujpur, Yamuna Vihar, Khajuri Khas
South Delhi
- INA, Hauz Khas, Lajpat Nagar, Jangpura, Ashram, Jamia Millia Islamia, Hauz Khas
Other major stations-
 Karol Bagh, Chawri Bazar, Jama Masjid, Inderlok, Netaji Subhash Place, Rajendra Place, Indraprastha, Sarai Kale Khan Nizammuddin.
Traffic movement
- DMRC had temporarily closed nearly 20 stations

 16 stations were shut after protesting farmers entered the city and clashes erupted near the Red Fort and ITO
Feb 2024-
 Multiple gates at nine metro stations across Delhi were shut in view of the farmers’ protest

Verstappen on sprint pole after another settings issue
- Published
Red Bull's Max Verstappen beat Mercedes driver George Russell to sprint pole at the Singapore Grand Prix.
Verstappen, fresh from his and Red Bull's first victory of the season in Malaysia last weekend, was 0.12 seconds quicker than the Briton, with Ferrari's Charles Leclerc third.
McLaren's Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris were fourth and fifth ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, who went early in final qualifying and fell down the order from initially being second behind Leclerc.
Championship leader Kimi Antonelli, using the Mercedes upgrade that underperformed in Malaysia while Russell is on the previous specification, could manage only seventh.
And there were further glitches with the engine settings provided by governing body the FIA five days after the formation laps in the wet in Malaysia saw cars reduced to crawling speed as a result of a software bug.

  - Published2 hours ago
What went wrong this time?
The settings issue in Singapore, which was combined with a glitch in the F1 timing system that delayed the start of second qualifying, affected all cars but had a bigger impact on some drivers than others, depending on the timing of their runs.
The problem involved the settings being different before and after a red flag caused by a crash for Sergio Perez's Cadillac and left drivers complaining of reduced power.
It involved overtake mode - which allows an extra 0.5MJ of energy to be harvested - being switched on and off again in the space of 28 seconds.
Williams driver Carlos Sainz was knocked out in the first session after what we described as a "really poor lap", but added: "On top of that, half the cars did the lap with half a second quicker engine than the others.
"There was another software issue and we were on the bad end of it, and for whatever reason, the FIA, like in Malaysia, again didn't decide to do sporting equity and were happy to do half of the quali with cars with higher power than the other half of the cars.
"A bit confused why the sport keeps doing different things depending on who is out in Q1 or who is out in lap one."
Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad and Aston Martin's Lance Stroll were also affected and were knocked out in the first session.
The FIA said in a statement: "During the first period of sprint qualifying there was a human error in race control unrelated to the timing issue also encountered in SQ1.
"This issue in question meant overtake mode was not available after the red flag period during SQ1.
"When it became apparent that overtake mode was not active after the restart, it was then activated for a period of 27 seconds before being deactivated again.
"The FIA acknowledges that this unfortunate human error had an impact on the performance of certain cars based on the timing of their run and their position around the lap.
"The second and third periods of sprint qualifying were not affected."
The FIA system automatically disables overtake mode when there is a red flag. A pop-up then appears on the screen asking whether officials want to re-enable it.
This was ignored, then overtake mode was reactivated before being disabled again, on the basis that it was fairer to do so than leave it enabled.

Upgraded Mercedes 'very difficult, very unpredictable'
Verstappen's pole lap appeared to be further confirmation of Red Bull's resurgence after his dominant win in Malaysia but he faces an investigation for overtaking under yellow flags shown before the first session was stopped for the Perez incident.
The four-time champion said he had not believed pole was possible before qualifying.
"We have some difficulties with the car in ride, as we know," he said, "but at least when we went to the soft tyres (in the final session), it made the car a bit more stable in places where before you were a bit unsure.
"I did not expect this but you take it, I'm happy for sure. Qualifying tomorrow is still the main goal and for us the start is always a critical point but at least a positive end to our day."
Russell's performance compared with that of Antonelli raises further doubts about the efficacy of the Mercedes upgrade introduced in Malaysia.
It was their biggest car update since the Canadian Grand Prix in May but team boss Toto Wolff said at Sepang that it had appeared to take them backwards rather than forwards.
Mercedes split the car spec here in Singapore in an attempt to better understand its performance but Antonelli ended the session 0.573secs behind Russell.
The Briton said: "As a team there is still nothing telling us it isn't working but it's all driven by the stopwatch and, yeah, the stopwatch hasn't been great for the upgrade yet. Maybe tomorrow's a different day."
Antonelli, who leads the championship by 84 points going into the weekend, said: "Already FP1 I was struggling and there is still a lot to understand about this package. Really the car is very difficult, very unpredictable, very difficult to put a lap together. It's a shame. I was coming with high hopes but so far it has been very difficult.
"It's going to be a difficult weekend unless we can pull something out tomorrow. Other than that it is going very tricky. I don't really see where we can find 0.7secs but you never know."
Wolff said before sprint qualifying: "The new car seems to be a little more tricky to drive. Not saying it's necessarily slower, because there will be goodness in it, but maybe we haven't just found a way of putting it all together and tuning it. The older car is a bit more stable, grippy, but that is really just one data point."
Leclerc was 0.243secs off pole, and ruing what he said was Ferrari "losing a little bit of our raw performance" in the past three or four races.
However, he added: "Still I feel there is potential in the car and maybe tomorrow we can be there or thereabouts in fighting for pole."
Hamilton said: "We did a slightly different run plan to the others. It was my choice, but I think we got that wrong. But ultimately, the car was very oversteery on that lap. If the rears [tyres] are not ready or they are overheating, it's difficult to say. But it was very snappy and oversteery in the lap overall."

Sally Schultz thought she had struck gold when she purchased land in Rio Rancho Estates, an unincorporated, census-designated community just outside the city of Rio Rancho, New Mexico. A single mother of four, Schultz came there following a divorce to build a homestead of her own and finally gain some stability in her life.
For $3,500, she was able to purchase half an acre for her trailer in a rural area located close to numerous elementary schools and parks. In a relatively short time, she was able to coax crops like corn, squash, and green chile from the ground. This cheap land became Schultz’s haven, giving her a second chance at life.
Then a missile company showed up next door.
“We’ve already been through so much,” she says, “and now we have to leave. It is the unknowing that is scariest.”
Castelion, a startup founded in November 2022 by three former SpaceX executives, is building Project Ranger, which it claims will be America’s “largest dedicated hypersonic manufacturing production facility.” Construction is set to be complete by the end of the year.
The company’s chosen site for its mega-campus is, in some cases, it appears, a little more than 1,000 yards away from roughly 450 properties in Rio Rancho Estates, including Schultz’s. That puts the homes squarely within a danger zone should any explosive chemicals stored onsite catch fire.
A year into Castelion’s relationship with the state of New Mexico, the company—which declined to speak with WIRED for this story—still hasn’t answered basic safety questions, even as an official hazard assessment found buildings would simply be left to burn in the case of fire, releasing hydrochloric acid gas into the air. Emails between the company and Rio Rancho officials reviewed by WIRED also show Castelion was negotiating fire safety standards even after construction was well underway.
“I live next door to where World War III will be manufactured,” says local resident Laura Lundberg.
Big Plans
Castelion has become a bit of a darling among the new wave of defense tech startups. The company has recently hit a valuation of $13 billion—more than four times its Series B valuation of $2.8 billion from last year.
It has received over $500 million in US military contracts in just 18 months, swiftly securing its spot as one of the “Arsenal of Freedom” suppliers.
The firm touts its ability to make hypersonic missiles—a label for any missile flying at five times the speed of sound or higher—at a lower cost than its competitors. The US Army’s Dark Eagle is the most mature domestic hypersonic weapon, and it costs an estimated $41 million per missile, according to a 2023 Congressional Budget Office study. Castelion’s main product, Blackbeard, is a solid-rocket-powered missile that was set to sell for $384,000 per unit.
In reality, the missiles are looking as if they will turn out pricier than initially advertised.
Castelion kicked off the year with a nearly $50 million Navy contract to build full-scale prototypes of its Blackbeard missile. By June, the Navy expanded the effort, adding another $23.4 million to supply the first 50 operational Blackbeard prototypes. Then, in August, the Navy doubled down with another $90 million contract to cover manufacturing services for the same 50 Blackbeards—pushing the total to $163.4 million for 50 missiles, or $3.3 million per unit.
And most recently, in September, the Navy awarded Castelion the company’s largest contract yet—up to $200 million.
Recently, Castelion released the first photo of its Blackbeard hypersonic strike missile, but concrete performance figures for Blackbeard remain hidden. Castelion has not publicly released any test data to verify its weapon’s efficacy.
Project Ranger will become Castelion’s biggest manufacturing and testing hub. The company broke ground on the 1,000-acre facility on January 21, and it’s targeting mass production as early as next year.
The facility wasn’t always supposed to be in New Mexico, though.
Unredacted
In August 2023, the company applied to build a rocket factory in Churchill County, Nevada, under a different name—Pallas Industrials. Chief financial officer Andrew Kreitz signed a special use application, which disclosed the company’s plans to build rocket motors and ground-test them up to eight days a month at the site.
In response to the application, Churchill County officials provided eight pages of staff analysis and required the company to provide testing conditions and safety protocols. Not long afterward, Pallas Industrials pulled out of Nevada under the new name: Castelion. A few months later, the company began testing the soil in western Rio Rancho.
Rio Rancho Estates residents say that by the time they started noticing soil-probing trucks in the spring of 2025, Castelion was already in a conversation with New Mexico officials about using the land for the missile factory.
In June 2025, Sandia National Labs delivered a hazard report as part of the New Mexico Small Business Assistance Program, originally intended to help local small businesses access the expertise of Los Alamos and Sandia National Laboratories at absolutely no cost.
Under the Freedom of Information Act, Sandia later released a heavily redacted version of the report. Instead of scrubbing the underlying data layer of the file, the lab simply put black ink highlight over black text, leaving the full unredacted report accessible via copying and pasting.
The report alleges Castelion’s plans to build and operate the missile factory present significant risks.
It identifies a massive “storage facility fire” as the worst-case scenario. Castelion is set to store colossal stockpiles of propellants on Project Ranger’s site. The company has publicly stated its plans of working with at least one heat-sensitive chemical oxidizer—ammonium perchlorate—and storing up to 250,000 pounds inside covered magazines and bunkers, according to the Sandia report. But outside those bunkers, the report notes, Castelion is allowed to keep up to 81,000 pounds of active explosive material at a time inside the hazardous integration facilities during the assembly process.
A detonation of the facility’s largest allowed stockpile of explosive material would require a buffer from the nearest inhabited building of almost nine football fields in length. Sandia calculated that a worst-case explosion could shatter large windows as far as almost four miles away and have a 3.2 percent chance of causing minor eardrum damage to people 400 yards from the detonation.
Sandia declined to provide comment for WIRED. One of the hazard reports authors, Meg Davidson, has since left Sandia Labs and is now a senior manager of strategic partnerships at Castelion. She did not respond to requests for comment.
The report identifies a fire at the test stand as “the most probable foreseeable hazardous event.” A chemical fire would release a toxic haze containing byproducts like hydrogen chloride and chlorine. In gas form, both are highly corrosive and can cause severe eye, skin, and respiratory tract burns. Even short-term inhalation at high concentrations can cause chemical lung damage and asphyxiation.
Emails obtained through public records requests reveal that the Rio Rancho Fire Department determined 17 of the 26 buildings at the Project Ranger site would be left to burn if a fire ignited, due to the risks a chemical blaze would pose first responders. Firefighters would be barred from even entering the high-risk facilities.
Such events are hardly unheard of. WIRED reported on a June incident at Anduril’s Mississippi facility where a test run of an ammonium perchlorate–based rocket motor ended in an explosion. The blast—which didn’t cause any casualties—underscored the technical risks of scaling solid propellant production.
In May, a storage tank holding approximately 7,000 gallons of methyl methacrylate, a flammable liquid used to manufacture acrylic plastics and resins for military and commercial aircraft, began to overheat at a GKN Aerospace plant in Garden Grove, California, leading local authorities to evacuate more than 40,000 residents.
Despite these warnings, internal emails obtained through public records requests reveal that Castelion was still negotiating critical fire-response requirements between March and May—even as construction had already started.
Castelion’s site developer, Bryce Barlow, wrote to the city on March 23 that the company had not yet finalized the fire-flow response, offering to discuss the question by phone or in person instead.
After a few weeks, the requirements were replaced by city manager Matt Geisel with a statement that hard numbers would appear in the plans later on. Castelion only needed a signed memorandum of understanding to proceed—backed by the governing body’s resolution and a serviceability letter.
“Great news! Saves all of us both legal bills and headaches,” Kreitz wrote in response.
‘A Done Deal’
In August 2025, prior to Castelion’s formal announcement that it had selected New Mexico, Republican state senator Jay Block appeared before the Sandoval County Commission to speak in support of financing Project Ranger. Before becoming state senator, Block was a county commissioner.
The county had approved $125 million in industrial revenue bonds and had passed a resolution giving itself control over the state land picked for the site. The commissioners granted an astounding 95 percent discount on what Castelion would normally owe in property taxes. Finally, the county agreed to abate compensating taxes on out-of-state equipment, lowering the upfront costs for the incoming missile manufacturer to relocate to New Mexico.
Block’s district includes Rio Rancho as of January.
“I strongly supported Project Ranger as it moved through the local approval process, because I believed Rio Rancho and Sandoval County had the workforce, infrastructure, and defense heritage to help Castelion succeed,” Block tells WIRED.
Castelion held its first public information meeting on Project Ranger in October 2025.
“All of this happened behind the scenes. By the time it was public, it was already a done deal,” says Zachary Darden, a Rio Rancho resident who ran an unsuccessful bid for mayor on a platform opposing the development.
In November, emails show Alberto Solís, Rio Rancho’s economic development manager, coordinated Castelion CFO Kreitz’s four-day trip to New Mexico—part of the outreach process required by the state. The CFO asked to attend a Chamber of Commerce “Jingle Mingle” mixer and an event with the Sandoval Economic Alliance, a local nonprofit tasked with recruiting new business to the county.
More than a month after Kreitz’s networking trip, Castelion held its groundbreaking ceremony. Local residents weren’t invited, but many of the state’s most prominent political and business figures were. Block was there as well as US senator Martin Heinrich. So were Gregg Hull, Rio Rancho’s then mayor and Republican candidate for governor, as well as Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham. County and state economic development officials were also in attendance.
“Castelion's Project Ranger shows what a strong public-private partnership can deliver for a local community,” Rob Black, New Mexico’s secretary of economic development, tells WIRED.
Residents living next to the site, though, are contemplating whether the risks are too high to stay. But for most living in Rio Rancho Estates—a low-income neighborhood—the costs of relocation might be too high.
“This land is affordable for people who need it,” says community member Jason Clifford. “We were sold out by our local officials.”

The gifts and payments that doctors receive from drugmakers increased inappropriate prescribing and the number of prescriptions written, likely leading to rising health care costs, according to a Cochrane review of dozens of previous studies that have explored the influence the pharmaceutical industry has on medical practice.
In addition, pharmaceutical advertising or education aimed at doctors may also increase inappropriate prescribing, probably increases the number of prescriptions written, and may increase the costs of prescriptions. But conflict-of-interest policies that restrict or manage interactions between companies and doctors probably improved prescribing practices, the analysis found.
However, there was not enough evidence to draw clear conclusions on whether free drug samples and other promotions affect decisions to place specific drugs on hospital formularies. These are the list of medicines approved for use and routinely stocked in a hospital or health system.

U.S. working to reverse an Egyptian man's third-country deportation to Africa
The Trump administration on Friday said it has started to facilitate the return to the U.S. of an Egyptian man who was deported to Equatorial Guinea, in a rare case of the government working to reverse a third-country deportation.
A federal judge in Arizona earlier this week ordered the Department of Homeland Security to return Ahmed Soliman to the U.S. from the country in central Africa where he has no ties, and respond how it plans to do so.
The administration said it is working "collaboratively" with Soliman's lawyers to find and contact him, and is "beginning the process to facilitate" his return, according to Friday's filings in the case from Timothy Courchaine, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Arizona.
Soliman, who is a gay, had been able to get an order from a U.S. immigration judge to prevent him from being deported to his home country, Egypt, where he could be persecuted for his sexuality.
Instead, the Trump administration deported him earlier this year to Equatorial Guinea, which ranks as one of the least free countries in the world, according to Freedom House, a nonprofit devoted to protecting and growing democracy, and human rights across the globe.
Arizona District Court Judge John Hinderaker, an appointee of President Trump, said that DHS violated the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment when it removed Soliman to a third country.
"It is unrebutted that he has since been held under armed guard; threatened at gunpoint; and arrested, beaten, and held incommunicado by Equatorial Guinean authorities," Hinderaker wrote in his Oct. 6 order.
The ruling comes even as the U.S. Supreme Court last week allowed the Trump administration to resume deportations of migrants to countries where they have no ties, at least for now, while agreeing to take the case up for full oral argument in December.
DHS told NPR in a statement this week that it would comply with lawful court orders and that Soliman would continue to receive due process.
"But the end result will be the same — he will not remain in the U.S. This administration will not ignore the rule of law," the DHS spokesperson added.
Facilitating Soliman's return
Dana Camilleri, one of Soliman's lawyers, said compliance means diplomats in Equatorial Guinea must work to facilitate Soliman's release. She is working to get a similar outcome for another client in the central African country, a gay Brazilian man.
" We're all just really hopeful that this could be the beginning of getting them home," Camilleri said. "Because they're in an awful situation, and our government put them there."
The office of the U.S. ambassador to Equatorial Guinea did not respond to a request for comment.
Soliman has been held under armed guard at a decommissioned hotel where he has been threatened at gunpoint, arrested, beaten and been unable to communicate with his family or lawyers, according to court filings.
Soliman emigrated to the U.S. from Egypt when he was a child, grew up in Arizona and became a green card holder. He lost his immigration status after a 2023 drug possession and aggravated assault led to a prison sentence.
That's when an immigration judge ruled he could not be sent to Egypt, where he would most likely be tortured.
The harm Soliman is alleged to have suffered in Equatorial Guinea could put the U.S. in violation of international law, according to Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, a senior fellow at the American Immigration Council. The council advocates for a fair process for immigrants in the U.S.
" We are signatories of the UN convention against torture, and domestic law makes it illegal to send someone to a place where they will be persecuted," Reichlin-Melnick said. " All of this really violates a lot of the basic principles of due process and human rights that Americans support," and serves as "a direct rebuke to the Trump administration's broader strategy of third country removals."
The Trump administration has made deals with over 30 countries to deport migrants to places where they have no ties or connections as part of the president's immigration crackdown.
Hinderaker's order to return Soliman marks the second time a judge has forced the government to return a third-country migrant from an African nation. A Colorado judge also ordered the return of Brayan Omar Sanchez Servellon, originally from Honduras, who was sent to the Central African Republic earlier this year.
