The Trump administration is facing growing questions over its decision to abandon a fraud and bribery case against the Indian billionaire Gautam Adani after he promised to invest $10bn in the US.
For the second time this year, two Democratic senators have demanded attorney general Todd Blanche answer questions about the US Department of Justice department’s handling of the case – and raised concerns over its judgment under Donald Trump.
In August, a federal judge in New York agreed to drop the fraud case against Adani, one of the richest people in the world, at the request of prosecutors, despite having concerns about “irregularities” in the “highly unusual” decision. It has become the latest example of judges raising eyebrows at Trump administration prosecutors for pushing to dismiss criminal cases.
Now, more than a month later, senators Elizabeth Warren and Richard Blumenthal are asking Blanche to clarify whether people close to Donald Trump were involved in that decision.
It comes aftera New York Times report revealed that Adani, represented by one of Trump’s personal lawyers, admitted to offering a $10bn investment in the US to resolve the criminal case. The federal judge overseeing the case determined the investment played no role in the DoJ’s decision to abandon the case.
“These fresh details continue to raise concerns about the judgment of the DoJ, and the extent to which the DoJ is willing and able to prosecute white-collar criminals under President Trump,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in a letter sent on Wednesday, and seen by the Guardian.
Adani was indicted in 2024 in New York for allegedly participating in a bribery and fraud scheme in which he paid Indian officials to secure a contract for one of his companies. He denied the allegations.
Prosecutors suddenly moved to dismiss the case against Adani in May after he hired a new legal team, led by Robert Giuffra Jr, and offered to invest $10bn into the US.
Following the news, Warren and Blumenthal sent a letter to Blanche in June requesting information about the fraud case and raising concerns about whether the justice department dismissed the case in exchange for Adani’s investment.
However, the senators did not receive a response. Since then, new details about the case have emerged, including allegations that Boris Epshteyn, a member of Trump’s personal legal team who also served as an informal adviser, helped Adani.
Another report claimed Donald Trump Jr, the president’s son, met with Adani in November 2025, before the case was dropped. A spokesperson for Trump Jr said earlier this year that the conversation “had zero to do with DoJ’s actions in this case”.
A spokesperson for Epshteyn denied being involved in Adani’s “arguments, advocacy or efforts” to the Wall Street Journal in June. Epshteyn was never hired by Adani or his company, the Adani Group, nor did he maintain a relationship with Adani, the spokesperson added.
The Guardian has asked Epshteyn for comment.
The Democratic lawmakers are now asking the DoJ for more information about Adani’s alleged investment offer, including a list of employees who were present when the offer was made, the terms of the offer, when the offer was made and where.
They also want to know whether the DoJ employees knew Epshteyn was allegedly working on behalf of Adani, or if Epshteyn had any contact with DoJ employees regarding Adani, among other questions.
“We are also concerned about the involvement of two of President Trump’s personal lawyers in this case, and the extent to which they reveal potential political influence and special treatment for well-connected insiders at the DoJ,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in their letter.
The Democrats also want to know if Trump Jr, or any person working on behalf of Trump Jr., had contact with a DoJ employee regarding Adani.
Warren and Blumenthal requested responses no later than 5 October. The Guardian has asked Blanche’s office for comment.

- Fans are calling the new Street Fighter movie collab Chun-Li and Ryu skins "downgraded" versions of the original.
- The bulk of the backlash is focused on the new Ryu skin in Fortnite, which looks very different than the video game version of the character.
- Both the Street Fighter Movie skins release in the Fortnite Item Shop on October 10, 2026 with the Item Shop reset.
Fortnite fans are quite critical when it comes to their favorite characters being turned into in-game skins, and the latest topic of discussion is the new Street Fighter Movie skins. The official Street Fighter Movie X account teased Ryu and Chun-Li skins on October 9, 2026, and fans were quick to spot some drastic changes made to the beloved video game characters, which they slammed as “massive downgrades.”
The video featured Andrew Koji (who plays Ryu) and Callina Liang (who plays Chun-Li) from the movie showcasing their in-game skins. However, fans who already know that Fortnite has Chun-Li and Ryu skins in the game, but the design is closer to the Street Fighter games, has caused an upset in the community.
Of course, it’s not just Chun-Li’s assets that players have their eyes on; it’s Ryu’s muscular structure from the original skins vs. the more “realistic” version of Koji’s Ryu that has them all turnt up. According to one fan, when comparing the older Ryu Street Fighter Fortnite skin to the newer one, it’s the “downgrade of the century.”
His overtly large, muscular body has been reduced to normal proportions, which takes away his flair. It’s the equivalent of giving the Peely skins in Fortnite more human-like proportions. Despite the newer version of Ryu being more lifelike, it’s clear that fans prefer the video game aesthetics.
Furthermore, Chun-Li fans like EvrythingsJake wrote on X: “New Chun-Li looks like she’d come in 20th place at a Chun-Li cosplay contest.” Popular Fortnite leaker HYPEX even chimed in on X, saying: “The realism in these ones specifically makes them look like PUBG skins and I can’t unsee it.”
Epic could only hope that this won’t stop everyone from purchasing the new Street Fighter movie collab skins from the Fortnite Item Shop. However, the reception is not what Epic Games expected, especially considering one of the skins is Chun-Li, who is one of the fan-favorite Fortnite skins yet.

Alberta woman, 61, breaks her own world record by planking for 5 hours
DonnaJean Wilde, a grandmother of 12, says she multitasks to pass the time
You can accomplish a lot in five hours.
Fly direct from Toronto to Vancouver, for instance. Or play an entire 18-hole round of golf. Run a full marathon at an average pace. Smoke a rack of ribs.
It's an objectively long stretch of time. Now, imagine holding a plank, one of the most notoriously challenging core exercises, for the amount of time it takes to cook a Thanksgiving turkey?
"I just love it," laughed DonnaJean Wilde, who at age 61 just broke her own world record for the longest time holding an abdominal plank position (female) during the Huntsman World Senior Games in Utah this week.
Wilde is a grandmother of 12 and retired teacher from Welling, Alta. And on Tuesday, in front of a cheering crowd and several judges, she held an abdominal plank for five straight hours, shattering her previous 2024 world record of four hours, 30 minutes and 11 seconds.
On Friday, she told CBC News Network she was "feeling good" and waiting for Guinness to make the record official.
"It just becomes easier to do the more repeated times you do it," Wilde said.
An abdominal plank is an isometric core exercise where you hold your body straight like a plank of wood. Most adults can hold a plank for 20 to 60 seconds, according to Health magazine.
Guinness World Records notes that to successfully achieve the record, the challenger's forearms and toes must touch the ground at all times. "The remainder of the body must be lifted off the ground and be kept straight throughout."
Not her only world record
Wilde says she started planking about 15 years ago when she broke her arm and was looking for a way to stay fit.
"I love to work out. I love fitness, and I discovered I could plank with a cast on," she said.

"And when the cast came off, it became a habit that I actually embraced and fell in love with."
When she first started, she says she could hold a plank for about a minute or minute and a half, but she kept practicing. With her family's encouragement, she kept going and minutes became hours. By 2024, she broke the Guinness World Record.
Wilde, seen in the midst of achieving her latest world record, says that while she holds her hours-long planks she likes to multitask: reading, writing and earning her master's. (Submitted by DonnaJean Wilde)
And, for good measure, she broke a second one that year by completing 1,575 pushups in one hour — the most push ups in one hour (female). She told the Guinness World Records she fell in love with doing pushups while doing 500 every day as training for her planks.
Now, she planks every day for at least a few hours. But it doesn't eat into her time, she says. She multitasks.
"Just read, do texts, whatever, do schoolwork. I did a master's degree while I was planking. Wrote a book," she said.
The book, From Minutes To Hours: I Wrote This Book While Planking, came out last year.
CBC News did not attempt to write this story while planking.

The Keralam government has constituted a high-level task force to develop an evidence-based road map for a phased prevention and early detection framework, along with appropriate treatment and rehabilitation plan, and an action plan for healthy ageing, with the broader objective of establishing a “Kerala Holistic Model for Health, Wellness and Longevity”.
According to the government order issued by the Health and Family Welfare department on Wednesday, the task force will be headed by the Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan, with Health Minister K. Muraleedharan as vice-chairman. Sharmila Mary Joseph, Principal Secretary (Health and Family Welfare and AYUSH), will be the member-coordinator.
The 16-member task force includes K.R. Jyothilal, Additional Chief Secretary (Finance); Ratan Kelkar, Secretary to the Chief Minister; Deepak Singhal, former Uttar Pradesh Chief Secretary; Shiv Kumar Sarin, Director of Institute of Liver and Biliary Sciences, New Delhi; Faizal E Kottikolon, chairman, KEF Holdings; C. Devidas Varier, managing director of AVP Coimbatore; Harsh Mahajan, chairman of Mahajan Imaging and Labs; Pratap Chauhan, chairman Jive Ayurva; Kancherioa Ravindranath, chairman, Global Hospital, Hyderabad; S.S. Lal, Director ReAct Asia Pacific; P.M. Varier, chief physician, Arya Vaidya Sala Kottakkal; M.V. Pillai, chairman International Cancer Care Network, USA, and Nisha Nigil, President-elect, Association of Kerala Medical Graduates in North America.
The task force has been asked first to assess Keralam’s disease burden, ageing trends, healthcare service capacity and gaps in access, and identify priority populations, diseases and districts.
Path forward
It will then design a phased prevention and early-detection framework covering risk assessment, screening protocols, referral pathways, follow-up and measurable coverage targets, aligned with existing State and national programmes.
A significant component of its mandate is to explore and identify evidence-based models for coordination among modern medicine, Ayurveda and other recognised systems of medicine. The order specifically calls for clearly defined scopes of practice, clinical governance, consent, contraindications, referral mechanisms and adverse-event reporting.
The task force will also examine the creation of a network of diagnostic, hospital, rehabilitation and wellness services, including criteria for pilot projects, accreditation, quality assurance and independent evaluation.
Another proposed component is the implementation of a Keralam Health Intelligence and Longevity Grid, with emphasis on interoperability with existing health systems, consent, privacy, cybersecurity and data stewardship.
Its mandate extends to workforce development in nursing, allied health, public health and relevant systems of medicine. It will also set uop research partnerships in health economics and financing.
The task force has been asked to examine possible investment and public-private partnership (PPP) models for diagnostics and wellness infrastructure, specifying fiscal exposure, procurement safeguards and public benefit.
It will also examine standards and opportunities for health and wellness tourism and identify the legal, regulatory and institutional changes required to implement its recommendations.
The order also recommends facilitation and support of the proposed World Holistic Health Forum, “a global NGO”, after assessing its purpose, financial commitment and expected outcomes so that Kerala’s positioning as a “cradle and destination” for holistic health, wellness and longevity can be explored.
Action-oriented report
The task force is required to submit an action-oriented report within two months of its first meeting.
The report is expected to contain a baseline assessment and priorities, two or three defined pilot projects with details; a three-year phased roadmap, indicative costs and funding sources and fiscal risks.
The task force is also expected to draft institutional and regulatory measures, and an implementation dashboard specifying milestones and accountable departments.
The Health and Family Welfare department will function as the nodal department, with support from AYUSH, Finance and other departments. Research, analytical, financial, technical and secretarial personnel will be deputed from the Health Department and its attached organisations.

Original| October 8, 2026, 14:05 IST Shares of fintech companies Paytm, Pine Labs and MobiKwik came under pressure today following reports that the proposed merchant discount rate (MDR) on select UPI transactions could be deferred. Paytm’s stock fell as much as 10% to an intraday low of ₹1,560.60 apiece on the BSE. As of 13:30 PM IST, the stock was trading 5.21% lower at ₹1,643 apiece, giving the company a market capitalisation of ₹1,05,416.1 Cr ($10.8 Bn). Pine Labs was trading 4.3% lower at ₹169.90 apiece, with a market capitalisation of ₹19,619.18 Cr ($2 Bn). MobiKwik, meanwhile, was trading 5.7% lower at ₹241.25 apiece, with a market capitalisation of ₹1,899.7 Cr ($196.3 Mn). The sell-off comes amid reports that the rollout of MDR on select UPI transactions may be deferred from October 15, to January 1, 2027. As per a report by Business Standard, a proposal to defer the MDR rollout is under consideration, with a final decision expected in the coming days. The delay, if approved, would keep eligible merchant UPI payments free of MDR through the festive season. The UPI and Services Steering Committee, headed by NPCI, met on Wednesday to discuss the proposed rollout among various other aspects of the framework. The committee is also considering increasing the exemption threshold to businesses with an annual turnover of up to ₹40 Lakh. Under the earlier proposal, merchants receiving up to ₹1 Lakh a month through UPI QR codes directly into their bank accounts would be exempt from the fee. Meanwhile, the RBI governor Sanjay Malhotra said on Wednesday that a “small fee” in the form of MDR is unlikely to have a major impact on UPI transaction volumes. “As of now, we do not see any drop in volumes. And I don't personally think that a small fee will have a major impact on the volumes,” Malhotra told reporters at the central bank headquarters. Meanwhile, UPI transactions continued to grow, with the platform processing 24.07 Bn transactions worth ₹29.37 Tn in September, up 22.6% YoY in volume and 18% YoY in value.

September marked 50 years since my colleagues and I published a paper describing what became known as interleukin-2, or IL-2, one of the first cytokines to be discovered and a protein essential to the growth and regulation of T cells. Science marked that anniversary with a perspective by renowned immunologists Rafi Ahmed and Steven Rosenberg examining the discovery. Their perspective prompted me to reflect on a question I’ve been asked many times over the years: What has been IL-2’s greatest legacy?
My answer depends on how you define importance.
From my perspective, IL-2 made possible the discovery of the first human retroviruses, including one that is the only known cause of a human leukemia, and ultimately, HIV. From that came the evidence that HIV causes AIDS and the development of the blood test that helped protect the blood supply.
That said, many of my immunology colleagues may answer differently. They may say that IL-2’s greatest contribution was making it possible to grow human T cells and opening the door to modern cellular immunology and cancer immunotherapy.
IL-2 has led to many important milestones, but to me, its larger lesson is about the nature of scientific discovery. We could not have known at the outset where this work would lead or its broader impact on the field, as is often the case with basic science. Many people who say they support science don’t understand the process and expect immediate results. But some of medicine’s greatest advances began with a question whose ultimate impact no one could have predicted.
In the case of IL-2, we didn’t set out to treat cancer. We were hunting for growth factors, the signals that would let different kinds of human blood cells grow in a cell culture system so we could study them. Then we got human T cells to grow, and I knew we had reached a turning point. For the first time, we could watch these cells up close. T cells were not supposed to grow (cell division) for more than one cycle. What I couldn’t have told you was where it would lead.
At the time, many scientists believed human retroviruses did not exist and that they existed only in animals. As noted, others believed T cells simply could not be grown continuously in culture. In fact, the very week our paper was accepted, a leading expert gave a lecture stating that everyone knew T cells could not be grown in culture.
But we showed that they could. That is how science advances. One discovery makes the next one possible.
For us, the next step led to the discovery of human T-cell leukemia virus-1 (HTLV-1), the first human retrovirus, followed by HTLV-2.
HTLV-1 also provided the first proven demonstration that a virus could cause human leukemia and directly cause a normal cell to become a malignant cell. Without IL-2, those discoveries would have taken much longer and could not have been characterized nearly as well.
Who could have imagined that an even more deadly infectious threat was literally right around the corner? That threat, of course, was AIDS. Our years of work with human T cells meant we weren’t starting completely from scratch to learn about and how to treat it. We already had the tools needed to identify a new human retrovirus, HIV, and establish it as the cause of AIDS.
We could never have imagined what IL-2 would do years later.
The ability to grow human T cells transformed cellular immunology. Steve Rosenberg recognized early that IL-2 could help harness the immune system against cancer, and he pioneered the field of cancer immunotherapy. His work, together with that of some others, launched modern cancer immunotherapy.
Rafi Ahmed, one of the great immunologists of our time, went on to help define our understanding of T-cell memory and how the immune system responds over time to infection and vaccination. The field continued to grow in directions we never envisioned.
We also could not have imagined that IL-2 would be the first of what became a vast field of interleukins and other cytokines derived from lymphocytes and regulating much of our immune responses as well as inflammation. The experimental approach we described in our original Science paper became a model for studying other human cytokines. Looking back, that may be as important as anything that came directly from our own work. Other scientists could use the same approach to pursue their own questions.
None of this was what we set out to do. We were trying to answer a basic biological question. Basic studies led to clinical and translational advances that no one could have predicted.
I worry about calls to direct research funding primarily toward work with immediate and obvious applications. You can’t just fund the obvious. The most consequential research is often about what is not obvious. If scientists must know the practical outcome before asking the question, they’ll never ask some of the most important questions.
Science rarely moves in a straight line. Discoveries come from right field, left field, and sometimes way out in center field. If we support only what appears immediately useful, we risk overlooking the discoveries that will become the foundation for tomorrow’s medicine.
I learned that lesson long before IL-2. As a boy, I visited my sister while she was dying of leukemia. I remember watching physicians take bone marrow biopsies and asking why they were putting her through them when they could not save her. Her doctors answered simply, “For the future.” I have never forgotten those words.
I was young then. It took me years to understand what those words really meant. Only later did I see those doctors were saying that research does not always help patients right away. Sometimes years pass before anyone knows what a discovery will mean or where it will lead.
IL-2 was like that. We knew it was important, but we couldn’t have pictured everything that came next, or how many other scientists would pick it up and run with it.
Fifty years on, the lesson holds. The discoveries that will change medicine a generation from now are probably being chased today by people asking questions no one else sees the value of yet.
Robert C. Gallo, M.D., is founding director of the University of South Florida’s Institute for Translational Virology & Innovation, director of the microbial oncology program at the Tampa General Hospital Cancer Institute, and co-founder and international scientific director of the Global Virus Network. He is best known for his pioneering discovery of human retroviruses, including HIV as the cause of AIDS.

Early backer Peak XV Partners has sold 12.2 Lakh shares of coworking space provider Awfis in a bulk deal worth ₹29.8 Cr. According to NSE data, the VC giant, via its affiliate entity Peak XV Partners Investment V, offloaded the shares at ₹245 apiece to rake in the amount. The investor sold the shares at a discount of 0.9% to the stock’s last closing price on Friday. With this, Peak XV has diluted more than half of its shareholding in the coworking space provider. At the end of June 2026, the VC major held a 3.24% stake, or 23.2 Lakh shares, in Awfis. As the shares flooded the market, Kritagyata Trust lapped up 11.5 Lakh shares at ₹244.97 apiece for a cumulative sum of ₹28.2 Cr. There was no clarity on who picked up the rest of the shares. The bulk deal comes as Peak XV looks to pare some of the losses amid a downward spiral in Awfis shares. While the stock has jumped 5% in the past week, it has tanked more than 58.6% in the past year and is hovering close to its 52-week low of ₹229.55. On a year-to-date (YTD) basis, shares of the listed company are down 49.87%. Awfis shares have tanked amid broader market pressure, institutional selling and valuation adjustments. Nevertheless, the listed company continues to put up a healthy show on the financial front, The coworking space provider’s net profit zoomed 140% to ₹24 Cr in the first quarter (Q1) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27) compared to ₹10 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Meanwhile, operating revenue also jumped nearly 27% to ₹424.9 Cr in the quarter under review from ₹334.7 Cr in Q1 FY26. Founded in 2015 by Amit Ramani, Awfis is a tech-enabled workspace solutions platform, catering to enterprises, freelancers, startups, and SMEs. At the end of June 2026, the company operated 251 centres, around 1.7 Lakh seats and about 84 Lakh square feet of chargeable area. It also caters to 100+ global capability centres (GCCs), which contributed 24% of its rental revenue in Q1 FY27. Shares of Awfis closed Friday’s trading session 3.7% higher at ₹247.15 on the BSE.

As authorities gear up to tackle Saturday’s (October 10, 2026) protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar at Jantar Mantar, the capital is set to face stringent curbs on communication.
The Delhi Police have imposed a 24-hour Internet shutdown around the protest site from 10 p.m. on Friday (October 9), while the Information Technology Ministry has urged social media platforms to quickly take down content referred to them by government Ministries and departments.
The Internet shutdown order will be in effect in a four-kilometre radius of the Janpath-Kartavya Path intersection, according to a notification by the Special Cell. The shutdown, an extraordinary measure in the national capital, was also imposed during the Gen-Z protests in July.
The IT Ministry’s advisory, on the other hand, urges social media platforms to limit the reach of content “likely to cause public disorder or incite the commission of a cognisable offence relating to public order”. The order further told them to “accord priority to reports/complaints received from authorised government agencies regarding content having potential implications for public order, and take appropriate action in accordance with applicable law.”
The advisory indicates a further ramping up of censorship of posts on Meta’s Instagram and Facebook, both of which have been complying automatically with non-binding takedown notices under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 over the last few months.
Censorship of anti-establishment content, including satirical posts and dissenting videos, has been increasing since February, when the IT Ministry reduced the time limit to lose the so-called safe harbour against legal action for keeping such posts online, from over a day to just one to three hours.

The U.S. last held a public execution in the 1930s. The Pentagon wants to change that
The Pentagon says it will livestream the planned military execution of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people and wounded 32 at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009.
Hasan, 56, has been on military death row since his conviction and sentencing in 2013. His case returned to the public spotlight this week when the Pentagon announced that President Trump had approved his death by firing squad — a first for the military since World War II.
The Pentagon says Hasan's execution will take place on the afternoon of Dec. 3 at Fort Hood, the site of his shooting rampage. On Thursday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the proceedings would be available for public viewing.
"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public, because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said in a video interview with Real America's Voice, a right-wing streaming network.
The Pentagon confirmed to NPR in a statement Friday that the execution "will be livestreamed," saying details would follow.
But much remains uncertain. Legal experts have said Hasan could delay his execution by years if he decides to file a habeas corpus appeal in federal court. Michael Radelet, a professor emeritus at the University of Colorado Boulder who studies capital punishment, says outside groups could potentially challenge the livestream plans too.
"Hegseth is a rather controversial person," Radelet told NPR. "If he says, 'Do it this way,' it's not at all clear that it will actually be done that way."
If it does come to pass, it would be the first public execution in the U.S. in nearly a century — and the first ever to be livestreamed.
"Public executions have typically been held in authoritarian countries to instill fear in the population and to show the power and control of the government," Robin Maher, the executive director of the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center, told NPR. "We're not aware of any regulation or historical precedent for a [U.S.] military execution to be livestreamed on the internet or otherwise made widely available to the public."
The last high-profile public execution in the U.S. was 90 years ago
The last high-profile public execution in the U.S. was the hanging of Rainey Bethea — a Black man convicted of raping a white woman — in 1936. The case drew national attention.
Roughly 20,000 people gathered in the western Kentucky city of Owensboro, where workers had built a gallows near the riverfront, according to NPR station WKMS. People celebrated with "necktie" parties the night before and sipped soft drinks at the scene in what attendees and historians describe as a festive atmosphere.
"They sold sandwiches and they sold Coca-Colas, and you'd have thought it was a big picnic or something," attendee Bill Shelton recalled in a 2013 oral history interview with the Daviess County Public Library.
The spectacle prompted a public backlash over the perceived barbarity of executions. Kentucky held a "semipublic" hanging in a prison yard the following year, Radelet said, before outlawing public executions altogether in 1938. There haven't been any in the U.S. since.
He said the closest example was the lethal injection of Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh in 2001. The Justice Department made a closed-circuit telecast available for designated survivors and victims' loved ones to watch remotely; 232 of them gathered in a viewing room in Oklahoma City to do so.
"It's like getting rid of the guillotine — when it's gone, it's gone," Radelet said. "There was no serious discussion about bringing it back."
He said public executions fell out of favor for two main reasons: They are no longer widely believed to be a crime deterrent, and authorities became worried that public executions — especially those that went wrong — would turn people against the death penalty.
In fact, as part of that shift, executions have become less visible over time, Maher said. Initially, she said, states would conduct them in the middle of the night. Now, she said, some states that still carry out the death penalty have limited access for media witnesses.
"We moved away from public executions quite deliberately because they had turned into spectacles. That was not sitting comfortably with people anymore," said Maher. "And I think there was a move away from that sort of circus environment to inside prisons in the middle of the night."
Tennessee's recent botched lethal injection of Christa Pike has reignited debate over the death penalty. Radelet thinks a firing squad execution — especially if it's livestreamed — could further diminish public support for capital punishment, already at a five-decade low.
"There probably wouldn't be too much blood, but enough to make people talk about it over their morning coffee, if they're not sick," Radelet said. "And that discussion might be yet another step towards abolishing the death penalty."
Justin Mazzola, deputy research director at Amnesty International USA, said in a statement that Hegseth's announcement "adds to the display of cruelty" seen recently with Pike's botched execution.
"The U.S. death penalty is irredeemably broken," he said. "It is high time that the U.S. authorities, at all levels, use their power to show human rights leadership and end this ultimate cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment once and for all."
Leaders call for Hegseth to reverse course
Hegseth's comments were met immediately with questions, concerns and calls for reconsideration. On Friday, Vice President Vance told reporters, "If it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."
Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, released a statement saying a public execution "will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people."
"In no way can Hassan's [sic] actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," he wrote.
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., wrote on X that he supports Hasan's death sentence but called a livestream "beyond disgusting."
"Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do," he wrote. "It should not be happening in America."
Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, similarly mused on CNN about whether Hegseth is "mimicking ISIS executions." He called public executions "medieval" regardless of people's feelings about the death penalty itself.
The top Democrats on both the House and Senate Armed Services committees issued statements condemning the Pentagon's plan. Sen. Jack Reed, D-R.I., the ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, called it "another stunt by Secretary Hegseth to distract from his tenure's repeated failings" and "a gift to anti-American terrorist recruiters."
"The Trump Administration should reconsider this abhorrent move, which only gives the shooter what he wants: more attention and more control," Reed wrote.
Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., also called on the Pentagon to revoke its decision, saying, "A country cannot condone livestreaming a man's death for entertainment."
"We are long past the days of public hangings in the town square," she wrote on X. "Kids watch what our leaders do and say, is this kind of bloodshed really what we want them seeing?"

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Gautam Dev, a 61-year-old job seeker in Dallas. He previously worked as a software engineer before resigning in 2024. The following has been edited for length and clarity.
In 2024, while working as a software engineer for an IT company in Dallas, I was told I'd have to relocate to another state to keep my job.
That September, I decided to quit my job, stay in Dallas, and look for a new role. That decision became a disaster.
I didn't realize how difficult finding another job would be
I'd worked in the IT industry for more than two decades and had gaps of a few months between jobs before, but I was always able to find another one.
This time has been completely different. I never expected to still be without full-time work nearly two years later.
After I resigned, I didn't immediately start seriously searching for another job, but I soon began applying, mostly to jobs through LinkedIn.
I also tried networking, but it wasn't much help. Most of the people I talked to said their companies weren't hiring. Some told me their jobs had gotten tougher, but that they were afraid to quit because they might not find another one.
Still, I've managed to land some interviews over the course of my search, including multiple with the same company. I thought some went well, but I never received an offer.
I thought my significant experience in the IT industry would help me find a job. However, I think being in my 60s could be working against me. And after being out of work for so long, I also think the employment gap is making things even more difficult.
It seems like AI can do some of the things software engineers used to do manually. I've seen job postings for AI engineering positions, but I don't have much of an AI background, so I'm not sure they're a good fit.
Between my age, the long gap, and the state of the IT industry, my expectations for finding another job have fallen.
I've largely stopped applying for jobs
For a while, I kept applying and applying, but most applications received no response.
Eventually, I reached a point where I didn't see much use in continuing to spend so much time applying. I've largely stopped now. I need to spend that time earning money instead.
For a while, I tried day trading to earn some income. It was going well for a while, but then my luck turned.
Earlier this year, I started doing gig work through platforms like Uber, DoorDash, and Walmart Spark. I wish I'd started doing it earlier, though I haven't been able to make as much as I'd hoped.
Still, it's some money. It's not zero.
My options are also limited. I can't carry heavy items, which rules out some gig work options.
Read more about people who've found themselves at a corporate crossroads
My long job search has drained my finances
Even with gig work, it's become difficult to keep paying the bills. I've had to drain my savings and take on a lot of credit card debt.
My rent in Dallas is high, and I'd like to move somewhere cheaper. Right now, though, I feel stuck.
I worry that if I tried to rent another apartment, a landlord would ask for proof of employment and income. Without a full-time job, I don't know whether I'd qualify. Even if I could move, the process would take time away from doing deliveries and earning money.
In January, I started a GoFundMe and received more than $9,000. It's all gone toward paying my bills. It was hard to ask people for money, and not everyone has been supportive. But some people have been really nice and generous.
For now, my plan is to keep doing gig work. I'm eligible to start receiving Social Security when I turn 62 in January. Once that begins, I'm hoping it, combined with whatever I can earn through gig work, will make my situation a little easier. Until then, it'll be tough.
I've also strongly considered moving back to India, where I lived before moving to the US more than two decades ago and eventually becoming a citizen. But I'm not in a rush to do so, and it would take some time to make the move happen.
I never imagined I'd end up in this situation, but here I am.

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

Making politics 'fun, trendy, sexy': How Gen Z could shape Kenya's next election
- Published
Ademba Allans is making it "cool" to vote in Kenya.
The student journalist turned civic mobiliser launched a voter registration drive on social media earlier this year, using snappy selfies infused with music and humour to target young people.
The result astonished him and many observers of Kenyan politics – by the time the registration period ended, 2.6 million new voters across the country had signed up. He is aiming to get another 2.3 million on board in the next round.
"It was the Gen Z way of doing politics," he tells me. "Fun, trendy, sexy, fashionable. Because of how we created the hype around it, people had the fear of missing out. Everybody wanted to be involved."
Gen Z, the term used to describe people born in the late 1990s and early 2000s, burst onto the scene two years ago with mass protests that forced the government to retreat on a widely unpopular tax bill. But their victory was followed by a police crackdown that killed and injured dozens of demonstrators.
Now many young Kenyans are planning to move from the street to the ballot box, angry with a political establishment they accuse of corruption and police brutality.
And they have the numbers to make a difference - more than 30% of voting-age Kenyans are younger than 35.
Polls suggest President William Ruto is looking vulnerable.
[The youth] just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created"
But can Gen Z convert a decentralized digital-led rebellion into organised political power?
"These youth-led movements are a wild card, in that they are unpredictable," says political analyst Tom Mboya.
"They don't require much in the way of resources and can pop up at any time. The finance bill protests were political in nature, but the movement has not been tested at an overtly political level. So if they decide to support a candidate, then he's likely to do fairly well."
One of the strengths of the digitally savvy Gen Z activists is that they have been able to mobilise outside the party structures and ethnic allegiances that anchor Kenyan politics.
Allans has been careful not to advocate a particular candidate or party – emphasising leadership rather than politicians, marshalling a new force, he says, outside traditional tribal voting blocs.
"There has never been a case where there is a bloc that is not affiliated to any person or any party. They just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created," he says.
"It's more of a swing vote because you cannot tell who we are going to vote for."
Ruto and his United Democratic Alliance (UDA) are facing strong head winds with less than a year to go before the August 2027 vote.
More than three-quarters of respondents to a survey conducted in June felt the country was moving in the wrong direction, with two-thirds saying their personal economic situation had worsened since Ruto was elected in 2022.
But analysts argue that the president does not necessarily have to be popular to win. He is a master political organiser with the resources of the state, they say.
Ruto's political rivals are also fragmented, and it is not yet clear whether they can form a united opposition to take him on.
One man who has captured the attention of many Gen Zs is Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna. He has emerged as the leader of a movement called Linda Mwananchi (Protect the Citizen), which is getting strong support from disaffected young people.
Sifuna first caught their attention when he tried to stop police from shooting at protesters who were storming parliament during the 2024 demonstrations.
- 'They aimed to kill' - BBC identifies security forces who shot Kenya anti-tax protesters 
  - Published28 April 2025
Now he is championing a "people-led" movement that promotes the protection of human rights and rule of law as enshrined in the constitution.
He has yet to officially declare a run for the presidency, but is already on the road rallying support. The BBC caught up with him on a recent trip to Meru county in central Kenya, a region that voted strongly for Ruto in the last election.
"Young people want us to create an environment where everybody feels that they can compete fairly," he told me before starting out on his raucous road show.
"We need to absolutely dismantle the system so that everybody has a fair chance at life, a fair chance at education, a fair chance at employment, and the opportunities to grow themselves.
"This election in 2027 is when this theory that the young people are advancing will be put to the test," he said. "Our challenge as a leadership is to ensure you have a compelling message that then encourages people to come out, let them see the vision for the new country."
Ruto also had a compelling vision for the country when he came to power in 2022.
He promised to transform the economy from the bottom up, with a focus on lifting the marginalised. His government has since introduced changes including landmark reforms that widen access to public healthcare, but many young people felt betrayed by his austerity measures and tax hikes.
"I'm here to participate in a revolution change that we want a new Kenyan youth leader who knows the common problems that are facing the young people," 23-year-old Brandon Muremi told the BBC.
I found him in a relatively quiet corner of the final stop in a hectic day of a "rolling rally" – Sifuna's convoy visited four locations, sometimes blocking traffic as he and local politicians climbed on top of their vehicles and delivered rousing speeches at ear-splitting volumes.
They promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths"
"We are looking for a leader who sticks to his plans, not just talking the promises that he makes," agreed Conrad Mutangili, a 19-year-old mechanical engineering student who had come out of curiosity.
"We are looking for somebody who can actually accomplish and actually bring to the people what they are talking about," he said. "Because they promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths."
"We want immediate results," said a 22-year-old computer science student, Yvonne Kileme, acknowledging that the results of government projects may be more long-term. "And one thing that we want as youths is employment, employment, employment, employment."
Ruto argues strongly that his government is delivering jobs, and says the high rate of youth unemployment is a problem that predates his presidency.
He has reached out to Gen Z with various programmes that offer grants and loans to small business and youth-led enterprises, technology hubs and digital work opportunities.
The national youth leader of Ruto's UDA, Kariuki Ngunjiri, told the BBC he was confident of winning the election with an overwhelming majority.
"The president is a listening president and he's been able to now come down to the youth, get what their concerns are, give them jobs, and that has absolutely, even for the party, given us a head start," he said.
"We are not worried about the social media buzz because we are people who actually engage the young people on real, actual, tangible development. What you see mostly on sponsored hashtags and sponsored headlines does not really concern us."
He was speaking as a senior sports official promised to expand the stadium-building programme with another venue, at a packed UDA town hall meeting in Kangema, about 100km (60 miles) north of the capital, Nairobi.
Like so many others, 23-year-old Shintah Mutahi was job hunting.
"I came to listen to what they were saying," she said, "maybe find an opportunity for a job. I think they can give me a chance, they should just be given some time to do that."
John Kiragu, a local UDA youth leader, said he understood the grievances that had driven young people to protest.
"There have been challenges," he said, "but now the government is really trying hard to consolidate the youth. The government is implementing programmes that will really uplift their lives."
Kiragu told me he was involved in a programme to deal with youth alcoholism – a real problem in this region. Many of the young men who attended the morning town hall meeting were already drunk on a cheap local liquor.
The captain of the local football team, Calvin Ware, also turned up to hear the stadium announcement. He said he had heard similar promises many times before, especially before elections, and this one was not going to influence his vote.
"We have already made our mind," he said. "The whole government should go home. We want to build a new Kenya, new youth, new people, fresh people from all over the country, and we are not basing on tribal [allegiances] or anything else. We just want a change, a change, and a change. Nothing else."
As we were speaking, we heard a loud cheer – the event had ended and people were lining up to receive cash handouts – 350 Kenyan shillings, about $3 (£2.20).
It is common practice to pay people to attend political meetings in Kenya, and politicians can use much larger sums to try and influence votes.
"More so than many other parts of the world, money talks in an election here," says political analyst Mboya. "The cost of politics is significantly higher than in other parts of the world."
Less than a year to Kenya's election, it does feel like politics might be changing, that the race could be shaped by youth disillusionment with the political establishment. But while the Gen Z movement has rejected the "old politics" based on ethnic group and money, those have been the building blocks that win elections in Kenya.
Nobody yet knows what the energy of Gen Z voters will mean at the ballot box.

Malaysia PM Anwar’s 2027 budget spreads the goodies, but will it win over voters?
While some experts said that Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s 2027 budget preserves fiscal discipline and the country's investor appeal, others say its lack of a “wow factor” may limit its impact with voters.
JOHOR BAHRU: Four years into his administration, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim is pitching his fifth budget as an opportunity to turn the country’s economic gains and earlier reforms into more tangible benefits for ordinary Malaysians.
“As we press ahead with reforms, the fruits of growth and every saving achieved through reform must be returned to the people in the form of greater benefits,” Anwar, who is also finance minister, told parliament on Friday (Oct 9).
Budget 2027 attempts to make good on that promise, with a broad range of measures aimed at easing cost-of-living pressures and raising disposable incomes, while continuing to channel investment into industries that Anwar hopes will propel Malaysia further up the economic value chain.
But the budget was delivered against an increasingly significant political backdrop. Malaysia must hold its next general election by early 2028, making this potentially Anwar’s final budget before seeking a fresh mandate, should he choose to call the polls early.
That heightened expectations that the 2027 budget would carry the hallmarks of an “election budget” - putting more money into voters’ pockets after several years in which Anwar’s government pursued politically difficult reforms, including the rationalisation of subsidies.
Economists who spoke to CNA were divided over whether Anwar has done enough to reap a political dividend. Some pointed to the unusually broad range of beneficiaries, while noting that the government has resisted abandoning fiscal consolidation and continued to court international investment.
Others, however, said the budget lacked a standout “wow factor”, arguing that the government may have missed an opportunity to unveil bolder measures capable of significantly shifting public sentiment ahead of the next election.
Economist Sedek Jantan of IPP, a Malaysian financial planning group, said the key to Anwar translating the budget into political capital would be whether its measures produce “measurable and lasting improvements” for households.
“Voters will ultimately judge the Madani agenda not by the number of reforms announced, but by whether they can feel the economic benefits in their daily lives,” he told CNA, referring to the slogan of the Anwar government based on a Malay acronym that stands for sustainability, care and compassion, respect, innovation, prosperity, and trust.
WAS THIS AN “ELECTION BUDGET”?
Budget 2027 certainly offers something for almost everyone.
Lower-income households will receive more cash assistance, middle-income taxpayers get tax cuts, while additional support has been extended to civil servants, pensioners, students, gig workers, farmers, fishermen and small businesses.
Azmi Hassan, a senior fellow at the Nusantara Academy for Strategic Research, pointed to the wide “breadth of beneficiaries”, saying the government had sought to reach groups that previously fell through the cracks.
Gig workers, for instance, have long grappled with stagnant incomes and gaps in social protection, he said. Budget 2027 includes measures to raise their earnings and subsidise social security and retirement contributions.
“Anwar is pushing for better wages for them, as well as everyone else in the lower- and middle-income groups,” Azmi told CNA.
The most widely distributed benefits come through the government’s STR and SARA financial assistance programmes. Their allocation will rise from RM15 billion (US$3.67 billion) this year to RM16 billion in 2027, with up to nine million STR recipients eligible for as much as RM150 a month in SARA assistance.
These two initiatives are direct cash aid programmes introduced under the Madani government framework to help Malaysians manage the cost of living.
Workers will also see Malaysia’s minimum wage rise from RM1,700 to RM2,000 a month from June, although smaller businesses are exempted.
Not all economists were convinced, however, that spreading the benefits widely would translate into a significant political boost.
Geoffrey Williams, director of Williams Business Consultancy, described the announcements as “rather lacklustre” given the possibility of an early general election.
“Overall this is not a populist budget ahead of GE16 and looks like a missed opportunity in terms of gaining voter support,” Williams told CNA.
He argued that some of the headline measures had already been anticipated, including the increase in the minimum wage, while the RM1 billion increase in STR and SARA funding was unlikely to make a substantial difference to individual households.
“It was a rather ordinary work-a-day budget with no ‘wow factor’,” he said.
Williams argued that Anwar could have gone considerably further if his objective was to make a decisive pitch to voters. He cited the possibility of writing off student-loan repayments from the National Higher Education Fund Corporation (PTPTN) rather than merely deferring them for borrowers earning up to RM2,500 a month, as announced in the budget.
PTPTN is an authority responsible for giving study loans to students pursuing tertiary education in Malaysia.
Williams also pointed to the possibility of introducing a universal basic pension rather than relying on more targeted assistance for retirees.
Economist Sedek similarly said that while the budget could help narrow the gap between the government’s reform narrative and Malaysians’ lived economic experience, it was unlikely to close it altogether.
“What is important is that some announcements have a strong feel factor, with tangible benefits and implementation starting as early as next week,” Sedek said.
He pointed to the RM1,000 one-off payment for 38,000 taxi and hire-car drivers and 15,000 school bus drivers, which Anwar said would be distributed in the week following the budget.
FISCAL DISCIPLINE NOT ABANDONED
For all the additional assistance, Anwar has stopped short of opening the fiscal taps ahead of an anticipated general election.
Malaysia is projected to spend more next year while simultaneously reducing its budget deficit – a combination the government will point to in rebutting accusations that the 2027 budget amounts to fiscal populism, economists said.
The fiscal deficit is projected to narrow to 3.3 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2027, from an estimated 3.6 per cent this year. That continues a downward trajectory from 5.5 per cent when Anwar's government came to power in 2022, and puts Malaysia closer to its target of bringing the deficit down to 3 per cent by 2028.
The government also expects federal debt as a share of the economy to decline, from 65.2 per cent of GDP in 2025 to 64 per cent this year and 63.7 per cent in 2027.
Azmi said that Anwar's decision to increase spending without projecting a wider deficit was “sensible”.
“He has managed to dish out election goodies without going overboard (with the spending),” he said.
He added that part of the government's calculation rests on higher revenue. Federal revenue is projected to increase from RM363.6 billion in 2026 to RM380.8 billion next year, providing additional room for spending even as the deficit narrows.
Lee Heng Guie, executive director of the Socio-Economic Research Centre, said the figures showed that the government had maintained its commitment to fiscal consolidation even as it increased assistance to households and spending intended to support economic growth.
“We are reassured by the government's continued commitment to fiscal discipline without sacrificing social and growth priorities,” he told CNA.
Lee noted that 2027 would mark the sixth consecutive year in which the deficit has narrowed. A steady reduction in the deficit and a stable debt trajectory would help strengthen confidence among international investors and credit rating agencies, he stressed, while rebuilding the fiscal buffers Malaysia may need to respond to future economic shocks.
MALAYSIA TO CONTINUE COURTING INTERNATIONAL INVESTORS
Analysts were also encouraged that despite the budget’s focus on domestic concerns, Anwar devoted part of his speech to signalling that Malaysia remains open to investment and is focused on moving into higher-value industries.
Central to that strategy is the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ), which Anwar said recorded RM132 billion in investments between 2025 and June this year. Anwar and Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong are expected to launch its master plan and blueprint by year-end, as both countries deepen cross-border economic ties.
Beyond the JS-SEZ, Anwar announced initiatives aimed at strengthening industries including semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI), aerospace, renewable energy and advanced manufacturing, as Malaysia seeks to create more highly skilled and better-paying jobs.
Sedek said the measures collectively “strengthen Malaysia’s appeal to multinationals”.
“A sovereign AI cloud could support domestic AI capabilities, while the JS-SEZ could combine Singapore’s capital and business networks with Johor’s industrial capacity,” he said.
“Semiconductor investment could also help Malaysia capture more value from its existing manufacturing base.”
Azmi said the announcements showed that Anwar recognised foreign investment as an important part of improving Malaysians’ living standards over the longer term.
“He recognises that it means better-paying jobs, and more disposable income for Malaysians,” he said.
“It’s a two-pronged approach – give Malaysians more assistance, but at the same time offer more higher-paying jobs.”

Last month, Tamil Nadu Health Minister K.G. Arunraj said Tamil Nadu would soon create a stem cell/bone marrow registry to facilitate bone marrow transplantation. At present, 50 patients are on the waitlist for bone marrow transplantation in T.N., he said.
A stem-cell donor registry is a database of people who have voluntarily agreed to potentially donate their blood-forming stem cells to a patient in need. Their human leukocyte antigen (HLA) profile is recorded for comparison with patients looking for a suitable donor.
For people living with blood cancers such as leukaemia and lymphoma, and disorders such as thalassaemia and aplastic anaemia, a stem-cell transplant can be a potentially curative treatment. But finding a suitable donor can be the first challenge. Only about 25% to 30% of patients have a fully HLA-matched sibling donor. For those without a suitable family donor, an unrelated donor registry can provide another route to finding a match.
What is a donor registry?
A bone marrow registry allows eligible people to register as potential donors. Registration usually involves providing a cheek or buccal swab for HLA typing.
Although these are commonly called bone marrow registries, they are essentially stem-cell donor registries, says Jeyasankar S., consultant, medical oncology, haematology, haemato-oncology and bone marrow transplant, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai.
If a patient does not have a suitable family donor, the transplant team can search the registry for an unrelated donor. The search can also extend to international donor networks.
How is a match found?
The key factor in matching is HLA, rather than the blood group. HLA markers are proteins that help the immune system distinguish the body’s own cells from foreign cells. They are inherited, and a closer HLA match can improve the chances of a successful transplant and reduce complications such as graft-versus-host disease.
The patient’s HLA profile is compared with those of registered donors. If a potential match is identified, the donor is contacted and further testing is done before donation.
A.R. Jaswanthini, haematologist, haemato-oncologist and bone marrow transplant physician, VS Hospitals, Chennai, says a patient without a matched family donor can be searched against potentially large numbers of registered donors. A donor in one part of India, or another country, may eventually be found to be a suitable match for a patient they have never met.
What is the situation in India?
India does not have a single national stem-cell donor registry. The World Marrow Donor Association currently lists five donor registries in the country, DATRI Blood Stem Cell Donors Registry, DKMS Foundation India, Marrow Donor Registry India (MDRI), GeneBandhu and The Arjan Vir Foundation. Together, these registries have several lakh registered donors, although the numbers vary between registries and are updated at different intervals.
The registries are linked to international donor networks, allowing transplant centres to look beyond India when a suitable donor is not found locally.
Increasing the number of registered donors is important, but the composition of the donor pool matters too. HLA characteristics are inherited and vary across populations. India has substantial genetic diversity across regions, communities and ancestral groups. Therefore, a patient may have a better chance of finding a suitable unrelated donor when people from similar backgrounds are represented in the registry.
“The importance of registries is particularly high for patients from communities that are under-represented in existing donor databases,” Dr. Jeyasankar says. “A registry can only help if it has donors who reflect the genetic diversity of the population. If certain communities have very few registered donors, patients belonging to those groups may face greater difficulty finding a suitable donor,” he adds.
G. Vimal Kumar, senior consultant, paediatric haematology, oncology, blood and marrow Transplantation, MGM Cancer Institute, Chennai, says India needs more healthy young adults to register as potential donors, particularly from diverse communities.
What happens after registration?
Registration does not involve donating stem cells. If a person is identified as a potential match, the registry contacts the donor and further HLA testing and medical assessments are carried out. The donor can then decide whether to proceed.
If the donor proceeds, stem cells can often be collected from the bloodstream through a process similar to platelet donation. In some cases, stem cells may instead be collected directly from the bone marrow.
This distinction is important because some potential donors associate the term ‘bone marrow donation’ with a major operation. In many cases, however, blood stem-cell collection is performed through the bloodstream.
Dr. Vimal Kumar says misconceptions about pain, weakness and the donation process can discourage people from registering. He also stresses that registration should be an informed commitment, as a person may be identified as a match months or years later.
What we need
Experts say India needs sustained awareness campaigns, particularly through colleges, workplaces and community organisations, along with better representation of different regions and communities. Stronger coordination between registries and transplant centres and reliable donor follow-up are also important.
The challenge is not simply to create a larger registry, but one that better represents India’s population and improves the chances of finding a suitable donor when a patient needs one.

Homeowners gassed up generators, filled bathtubs with water and bought last-minute supplies along the U.S. Gulf Coast on Friday (October 9, 2026) while Hurricane Isaias gained strength as it charged toward the beaches of Alabama and the Florida Panhandle.
The Category 3 storm has grown into a major hurricane — the first of an unusually quiet Atlantic season — and is expected to make landfall Friday (October 9, 2026) night.
Forecasters warned of a significant storm surge, damaging winds, flooding and possibly even tornadoes before the storm loses steam as it moves inland and delivers strong winds and rain well north into Atlanta.
Tropical storm-force winds began to lash the Gulf shoreline around midday, hours before Isaias was expected to make landfall between Mobile Bay on the Alabama coast and the city of Destin in the Florida Panhandle. The low-lying coastal area is known for its powdery white sand beaches dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars and seafood shacks.
Residents in Panama City, Florida, braved the rain while filling sandbags Friday to protect their houses.
“I mean, it's just the nature of the beast. It's Florida," said Corliss Stone, who works for the fire department.
Many will brave Isaias at home
One of the biggest concerns is a storm surge that could be as high as 6 to 9 feet (1.8 to 2.7 meters), according to the National Hurricane Center. Places most at risk include Florida's Pensacola Beach and the Gulf Islands National Seashore.
Anne Petzold, who lives with her husband in the Florida beach community of Gulf Breeze, said everyone in their neighborhood planned to ride out the storm. The couple installed hurricane shutters, picked up anything in their yard that could turn into a projectile and have two generators ready if they lose power.
“Everybody does what they can do, everybody asks if they need help — they ask for help, they offer help. All good,” she said. “It's just another adventure.”
Neighbor Jay Brazzell said he went through a checklist of things to do, including stocking up on ice and gasoline. He decided to stay put because Isaias isn't as powerful as other hurricanes he's experienced.
“I mean I'm not boarding up,” said Brazzell, 69. “I've been through, this being, the ninth hurricane.”
Dangerous conditions are expected throughout the western panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi, the National Hurricane Center said. Rain began falling along the coast Friday morning, and tropical storm conditions were picking up in the early afternoon.
In a sign of how serious the warnings are, dozens of Waffle Houses in the Florida Panhandle were closed, according to the company's website. The beloved Southern breakfast chain is known for staying open through severe weather and often is a measuring stick of a storm's severity.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis warned residents to expect power outages, gasoline shortages and closures of bridges and highways.
As of early afternoon, the storm was centered about 90 miles (145 kilometers) south of Pensacola and moving to the north-northeast, the center said. It was packing 120 mph (193 kph) sustained winds Friday morning and picking up speed. Category 3 storms are considered major hurricanes and are capable of causing devastation.
The whole region could get soaked
Once Isaias comes ashore, it is expected to weaken until it is downgraded to a tropical storm by Saturday afternoon, the hurricane center said.
Still, heavy rain is forecast as it moves inland, with 4 to 8 inches (10 to 20 centimeters) or even more expected through the weekend from southern Alabama to southwestern Georgia.
Isaias, which will be the first hurricane to hit the eastern U.S. since Milton tore up the Gulf Coast of Florida in 2024, also is expected to bring heavy rain and potential flooding to much of the Southeast over the weekend, and then to parts of the Midwest and Northeast into Monday.

Hurricane Polo is barreling towards the Baja California region of Mexico, the latest system in a Pacific hurricane season that has been notably active in recent months. On 22 September, a measurement of 892 millibars was registered for Hurricane Polo, making it the second-most intense hurricane on record in the east Pacific. It is fuelled by exceptionally warm waters across the Pacific Ocean, providing favourable conditions for the system to maintain its considerable strength.
Polo is expected to turn towards the west-north-west, before taking a more north-westerly trajectory on Saturday. It has maximum sustained winds of around 150mph, with even stronger gusts occurring within the most intense parts of the hurricane. Hurricane-force winds extend outward for approximately 40 miles from the centre, while tropical storm-force winds reach as far as 125 miles. These powerful winds, combined with torrential rainfall and dangerous seas, could have significant impacts. Although some fluctuations in intensity are possible over the coming days, Polo is expected to remain powerful as it tracks north-westwards.
In India, a deep 988-millibar low-pressure system – a tropical storm in this case – is centred along the east coast, bringing widespread and potentially disruptive weather conditions to Odisha and surrounding areas. The system is producing heavy rainfall across the region, with the latest forecast models suggesting totals could exceed 200mm in some locations over a 24-hour period. Rainfall rates are expected to be particularly intense at times, with hourly totals potentially exceeding 30mm in the heaviest downpours. Such intense rainfall could cause significant surface water and localised flooding, particularly in low-lying areas and places with poor drainage. Strong and gusty winds are also affecting coastal parts of Odisha. Winds are forecast to reach around 50-60mph, creating hazardous conditions in exposed areas and potentially causing disruption to travel, infrastructure and power supplies. Authorities have closed numerous schools across the affected districts for safety reasons.
Meanwhile, in Iberia, the relentless heat of summer is extending into meteorological autumn, with temperatures rising into the high 30s celsius on 23 September. Alvega, in Portugal, recorded a maximum temperature of 41.7C, smashing many July records from previous decades.

The Indian juggernaut has finally been halted.
Chasing may be the preferred template in modern T20Is, but not when you have to hunt down 250. That was the tall order in front of the West Indies at the JSCA Stadium here on Friday.
Conventional wisdom would’ve predicted an easy win for the defending team, but not against a marauding West Indian batting order.
The Men in Maroon made light work of what looked like an insurmountable task, gunning down the target in 18.3 overs and pulling off a stunning six-wicket victory in the second T20I.
IND vs WI, 2nd T20I - As it happened
After Mayank Yadav’s fiery opening burst (three for 36), Shai Hope (102 n.o., 45b, 6x4, 9x6) and Sherfane Rutherford (84, 37b, 7x4, 7x6) kept up with the asking rate, and then some.
Kuldeep Yadav could have removed Rutherford just before the halfway stage had Mayank held on to a regulation catch. The left-arm wrist-spinner got his man when the southpaw was caught behind in the 15th over, but not before he added 46 more from 18 balls.
At that point, after the breathtaking 120-run stand, West Indies still needed 72 off 35 balls.
Hope and Romario Shepherd (34 n.o., 13b, 3x4, 3x6) then went on to seal the win, a memorable one at that.
The two final sixes that Hope hit off Axar Patel not only brought up his century but also signalled West Indies’ highest successful run chase in T20Is.
Earlier, the Indian willow-wielders sent the visitors on a leather hunt to amass 249 for five, with Sanju Samson (82, 41b, 9x4, 4x6) being the protagonist.
Kamil Pooran dropping a straightforward catch straightaway unshackled Samson, who was batting on six.
After getting smashed off a free-hit right after the lost opportunity, Akeal Hosein bore the brunt of Samson’s brilliant strokeplay.
Though Samson’s trigger movement was almost always to the leg-side, the shots he hit covered the entire ground.
Roston Chase — who had earlier dismissed Abhishek Sharma — castled Ishan Kishan (43, 22b, 6x4, 2x6) to break the 97-run stand before removing another left-hander, No. 4 Shivam Dube.
India lost momentum as well as Samson, who holed out to Kamil at third-man off Shamar Springer.
Shreyas Iyer (40, 18b, 3x4, 3x6) and Tilak Varma (44 n.o., 18b, 3x4, 3x6), however, built on the foundation set by Samson & Co.
Tilak was particularly ruthless against Springer after getting a life caught off a no-ball. Springer’s 23-run 20th over took India to 249, which proved nowhere near enough once Hope’s men took strike.

Conagra Brands has stopped producing Celeste frozen pizzas, bringing an end to a brand that has occupied a place in American grocery freezers for nearly six decades. The decision is part of a wider effort to simplify the company's product portfolio and prioritise businesses with stronger growth prospects. The announcement has prompted nostalgic reactions from longtime customers, many of whom associate the affordable frozen pizzas with childhood meals, family kitchens and quick dinners on a budget. According to TODAY.com, a Conagra representative confirmed that production had stopped as part of the company's SKU rationalisation process, which involves reviewing individual products and removing those that no longer fit its business priorities. The company had also discussed the decision during its earnings call in September. The move comes as Conagra seeks to streamline its operations and improve profitability. Chief executive John Brase has indicated that the company is prepared to discontinue smaller brands that offer limited financial returns. “There are certain brands and categories where we simply just don't see a future,” Brase said, according to Food Dive. Conagra's review extends beyond Celeste. The company is examining its wider range of products, including individual stock-keeping units, to reduce complexity and direct investment towards businesses with greater potential. Brase has pointed to the company's range of more than 400 single-serve meal products as an area where a more focused assortment could improve performance. The company plans to increase investment in categories such as meat snacks and popcorn, while seeking opportunities to strengthen its core businesses. The benefits of its portfolio review are expected to build over the next 12 to 18 months, Food Dive reported. Although production has ended, shoppers may still find Celeste pizzas in some supermarkets while existing stocks last. A Conagra spokesperson told Fox Business that the company would continue selling its remaining inventory, but there would be no further Celeste products once those supplies were exhausted. For consumers who have relied on the brand as an inexpensive meal option, the distinction offers little long-term comfort. Availability will depend on how quickly retailers sell through their remaining stock. The brand traces its origins to Celeste “Mama” Lizio, who built a food business in the Chicago area before selling it to Quaker Oats in 1969, according to Fox Business, which cited a 1988 Los Angeles Times obituary. Over the decades, Celeste became familiar to generations of shoppers looking for convenient, affordable pizza. Its departure has revived memories of supermarket promotions and family members who regularly kept the pizzas in their freezers. The discontinuation is therefore more than a portfolio decision for some customers. It marks the disappearance of a familiar product whose place in everyday life extended well beyond the freezer aisle.
