Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Friday (October 9) that it had struck a liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) carrier attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz via what Tehran described as an “illegal route”, as maritime authorities separately reported a projectile strike that triggered a fire aboard a vessel off the United Arab Emirates (UAE) coast.
The two reports identified different vessels, and it was not immediately clear whether the incidents were connected.
In a statement carried by Iranian state media, the Revolutionary Guards said Iranian forces had “taken control of the administration of the strait”, reiterating Tehran's efforts to regulate shipping through the strategic waterway amid the ongoing Middle East war.
“In carrying out this mission, a few hours ago, a giant LPG carrier named NV Sunshine, owned by NatWit, which was attempting to transit via the illegal route south of the Strait of Hormuz, was struck,” the IRGC said.
Iran has sought to impose control over the Strait of Hormuz since the conflict began in late February, insisting that vessels obtain its permission to cross through routes designated by Tehran. However, some ships have increasingly attempted to transit through an alternative route along the strait's southern coast.
Separately, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said a vessel had been struck by a projectile approximately 13 nautical miles (24 kilometres) off Al Jazeera Al Hamra in the UAE, southwest of the Strait of Hormuz.
The incident caused a fire aboard the ship, UKMTO said in a statement on Friday.
“The status of the crew, damage assessment and environmental impact are unknown at present. Authorities are investigating,” the agency said.
British maritime security firm Vanguard also reported the incident, identifying the vessel as the Panama-flagged crude oil tanker GEM NO.2.
The available reports did not establish a connection between the reported strike on the NV Sunshine LPG carrier claimed by Iran and the projectile incident involving GEM NO.2 off the UAE coast.
The latest reports come days after another tanker was struck off Qatar, approximately 500 kilometres (300 miles) west of the Strait of Hormuz.
Ships operating in the Gulf and those attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz have faced repeated attacks since the United States and Israel launched military action against Iran in late February.
The strait is the only maritime passage into and out of the Gulf and serves as a critical route for global energy supplies. Before the war, approximately one-fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas shipments passed through the waterway.
Iran has sought to restrict traffic through the strait, although some vessels have continued to cross. US media reports have also described American military efforts to protect ships using the southern route.
The United States, meanwhile, has imposed a counter-blockade on Iranian ports and has occasionally fired on vessels linked to Tehran, further intensifying the confrontation over maritime access.
The competing efforts to control shipping through the waterway have heightened risks for commercial vessels and added to concerns over the security of global energy supplies.

Firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed, Pentagon says
Trump’s defense secretary wants to ‘make sure that people are able to watch’ the ‘public’ killing of Nidal Malik Hasan

Donald Trump’s administration has announced that the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan by firing squad will be livestreamed, an unprecedented broadcast for a state-sanctioned killing by one of the world’s most powerful democracies.
In an interview with right-wing activist Jack Posobiec on Thursday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution of Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, was a “no brainer.”
“He’s gonna get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be,” Hegseth said. “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”
A Pentagon official clarified to The Independent that the event will be livestreamed, and details will follow.
Hasan is scheduled to be killed December 3, marking the U.S. military’s first execution by firing squad since 1945, part of a renewed push by the president to restart federal executions and turn to methods such as firing squads as well as nitrogen gas and electrocution to carry out sentences quicker.
“Judgment day for Hasan has finally come,” Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell wrote on X earlier this week following Trump’s approval of the killing.
Asked on Thursday whether Hasan made any final requests or reached out to the Trump administration, Hegseth said: “Don’t care.”
“We’ll see him on December 3,” he said.
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, was convicted by a military jury on 45 counts of murder and sentenced to death in 2013.
Hasan, who was scheduled to be deployed to Afghanistan at the end of 2009, admitted responsibility for the shooting.
He was left partially paralyzed after he was shot by police during his arrest.
Under the Uniform Code of Military Justice, a death sentence imposed by court-martial may not be carried out “until approved by the president.”
If the Pentagon carries out the killing, Hasan will be the first person killed by a military firing squad since January 31, 1945, when Army Private Eddie Slovik faced 12 riflemen from his own unit armed with M1 Garands. Four shots were fatal.
The last military execution took place April 13, 1961, when Army Private John Bennett was hanged.
Bloody public spectacles of government-sanctioned deaths and lynchings by mob violence began to disappear in the U.S. over the last century as states and the federal government moved towards what they considered more “humane” ways of killing people being closed doors through the expanded use of gas, electrocution and drugs.
Executions are typically carried out privately within correctional facilities, away from cameras and the general public, except for a small audience of officials, families and members of the press.
During Trump’s first term, the federal government executed 13 people, the most under any president in more than 120 years, and a streak that resumed after a 17-year hiatus.
Before he left office, Joe Biden commuted the sentences of 37 people awaiting executions on federal death row, leaving death sentences in place for only three men. Hours after he returned to the White House, Trump signed an executive order directing the attorney general to seek the death penalty in future cases “for all crimes of a severity demanding its use.”
Earlier this year, the Department of Justice also unveiled a plan to “strengthen the death penalty” by directing the Bureau of Prisons to use pentobarbital for lethal injections and consider other execution methods — including firing squads and even electrocution — to expedite death sentences of federal death row inmates.
Two dozen states do not carry out capital punishment, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Deterrence is “one of the most commonly expressed reasons” for using the death penalty. But despite Trump’s claims, evidence shows that “states that impose the death penalty are not safer than states that do not use the death penalty,” according to the center.
At least five states allow firing squads as a method of execution. Last year, South Carolina carried out three killings by firing squad, the first in more than a decade.
In April 2025, a three-person firing squad in South Carolina shot Mikal Mahdi, who cried out as the bullets struck him, according to witnesses. He groaned twice before taking one final breath.
An autopsy report later revealed two wounds on his chest, and none of the bullets directly hit his heart, which is where the gunmen are supposed to aim. Mahdi, 42, endured “excruciating conscious pain and suffering” for up to one minute and suffered a prolonged death, according to his attorneys.

South Korea test-flies its first domestically developed hypersonic weapon
SEOUL, South Korea — South Korea flight-tested on Thursday its first domestically developed hypersonic weapon, designed to fly at least five times the speed of sound and evade missile defense systems, bringing Seoul closer to what it says could be game-changing weapons capabilities.
There was no immediate response from North Korea, which last week tested its own hypersonic missile that landed in the waters near Japan.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung attended the test, saying it's a major step in strengthening the country's conventional defense capabilities, according to a statement. It did not elaborate where the test took place.
The statement said the weapon separated from its booster rocket at the planned altitude, then descended and maneuvered both vertically and horizontally before hitting a test target. It said once developed, the weapon would be able to strike key targets by surprise in the "Korean Peninsula theater of operations."
Lee stressed that South Korea "must secure our security through our own strength," and also inspected the country's most powerful Hyunmoo-5 ballistic missile on Thursday, his office said. It did not mention any direct comments by Lee on the North.
Tensions between the Koreas have increased in recent weeks after three South Korean soldiers were injured in land mine explosions last month near the heavily armed inter-Korean border.
The South's military and the U.S.-led United Nations Command concluded the blasts were caused by devices planted by North Korea, which has denied responsibility and ridiculed the South's demands for an apology.
North Korea has also stepped up weapons testing activity as its leader Kim Jong Un expands his military nuclear program while taking an increasingly hard line toward Seoul.
Kim has so far rebuffed U.S. President Donald Trump's calls to revive their diplomacy that broke down in 2019, with his government demanding that Washington abandon its "hostile" policy toward Pyongyang and drop demands for its denuclearization as a precondition for talks.
The tensions have been a setback for Lee, who favors engagement with North Korea and has tempered his rhetoric toward the North even as public anger grows over the mine blasts.
Lee has also called for strengthening South Korea's conventional defense capabilities while reducing its reliance on the United States, which unilaterally decided to scale back a major military exercise with the South in August, with Trump citing his "very good relationship" with Kim.
In its latest weapons test on Oct. 3, North Korea launched what it described as a hypersonic intermediate-range missile that it said flew more than 1,000 kilometers (621 miles). Japan said the missile landed in waters outside of its exclusive economic zone.
South Korea said it detected the missile flying more than 700 kilometers (435 miles), while Japan's Defense Ministry said it assessed that the missile flew about 680 kilometers (422 miles).
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of the North Korean leader, claimed the differing flight estimates by the two U.S. allies showed they are incapable of properly tracking such a missile during its flight and would therefore not be able to intercept it.

Man City titles 'absolutely not' tainted - Maresca
- Published
Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca says the club's titles are "absolutely not" tainted after they were found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges brought against them by the Premier League.
Maresca reiterated his faith in the club's owners and belief that they will win their appeal against the verdict during a news conference on Friday dominated by questions on the matter.
The Italian, notably relaxed as he offered his responses, rejected the suggestion City's titles have been tainted by the ruling, as he knows "exactly the effort that the club put in to achieve" them.
An independent commission found Manchester City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.
The club have appealed against the verdict and claimed in a statement the commission's ruling contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe".
Preparing to play their first match since that verdict was announced, away to rivals Liverpool on Sunday, Maresca said in an in-house interview on Thursday the "feeling is fantastic" among his players and they are not affected by "the noise" surrounding the club.
He added on Friday: "The reason I joined this club is that I completely trust, 100%, the owner, the CEO, the sporting director, all the organisation. So I don't have doubt about that.
"I spoke with the club for sure. We all trust, and probably the right moment to speak about that is when we are going to win this appeal."
He added: "For me, the players - we can control just the pitch side, the football side. So we are focused on that. This is what we can do and what we can control."

Trump Mobile apparently failed to obtain necessary authorizations to operate the international calling portion of its phone service, Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) wrote in a letter to the company today.
Her letter said Trump Mobile also doesn’t appear to have submitted a required plan for fighting robocalls. Trump Mobile’s key business partner, Liberty Mobile Wireless, did make a robocall database filing, but it was not complete, Hassan said.
Hassan’s letter raised questions about Trump Mobile’s security related to a report that hackers stole personal data of 3,615 customers and Trump Mobile’s previous confirmation that a vendor it uses exposed customers’ personal data on the Internet. Hassan alleged that Trump Mobile failed to follow multiple FCC filing rules that are supposed to help ensure the security of mobile services.
“The apparent absence of authorization for Trump Mobile international services raises questions about who is providing or reselling the international telecommunications services advertised by Trump Mobile, the authority under which those services are being provided, and the company’s commitment to complying with requirements designed to safeguard national security,” Hassan told Trump Mobile CEO Patrick O’Brien.
Referring to the recent data breach, Hassan said it’s worrisome that a ransomware group “claimed that when it notified Trump Mobile of the breach, the company responded that ‘[w]e have no team to handle this.’” Trump Mobile also seems to lack a robust customer authentication process and offers “streamlined service activation that can make it easier for scammers to obtain US numbers,” Hassan wrote.
Trump Mobile, which has a trademark and name licensing deal with the Trump family, advertises that its customers can call more than 230 countries and territories. “Yet a search of the FCC’s International Communications Filing System suggests that Trump Mobile does not hold the necessary authorization for these services under Section 214 of the Communications Act of 1934,” wrote Hassan, the top Democrat on the US Congress Joint Economic Committee.

What it's like to spend a night in a Pebble Flow EV RV
Staying in the tech-infused trailer can kind of feel like being in a spaceship — in a good way.
There's something oddly thrilling (and a little terrifying) about steering a 6,000-pound trailer around a parking lot with nothing more than touchscreen controls on an iPad. It's also the perfect encapsulation of what makes the Pebble Flow electric trailer unlike any other RV out there.
With integrated solar panels, electric motors and automated hitching, the tech-forward trailer is meant to simplify many of the complexities and annoyances that often come with RV ownership. That's Pebble's promise, anyway.
I've been intrigued by the Pebble Flow since my colleagues first saw it on the CES showfloor in 2024. The futuristic-looking RV has a sleek, minimalist interior, a dedicated workspace and full bathroom. But like any CES veteran will tell you, a carefully orchestrated demo is about as far from real-world conditions as you can get. So when Pebble gave me the opportunity to spend a day (and night) in one of their trailers at an actual campsite, I was very curious to see if the $159,000 RV would feel as luxe as it seemed.
After spending nearly 24 hours in a Pebble Flow, I can confirm that the RV is indeed an incredibly comfy space to work and sleep in. But I was even more impressed with how much tech the company has infused into it.
My husband and I stayed in a Flow set up with the same layout we've seen previously from Pebble. There's a dinette at the front end, which can convert into a bed, and a queen-sized Murphy bed in the back that doubles as a desk.
I was worried it might feel cramped with two people working in such a compact space, but we both had plenty of room to stretch out. I spent a few hours with my laptop at both the dinette table and the dedicated desk. I liked the extra comfort of the cushioned bench seats in the kitchen area better, but the table was just wobbly enough to be distracting. The dedicated desk is simple but functional. I don't think it's quite wide enough to set up an external monitor comfortably, but I had plenty of room for my laptop, phones, camera and their respective chargers. The desk also has the advantage of being right next to the back window that can fully open up for fresh air and views.
Speaking of the windows, one of the coolest features is that all of the exterior windows are made of electrochromic "smart glass" that can change from clear to frosted with the touch of a button. It's a nice privacy feature, especially if you're in a shared campsite like I was. However, the combination of the interior LED lights and the frosted, light-blocking windows can also give the inside of a Pebble a slightly disorienting feel since you can't easily tell what time of day it is. It wasn't unpleasant, but it felt a bit like being in a bright, if pleasantly lit, spaceship.
Most of the time, though, my time in the Pebble Flow felt less like a trailer and more like a micro-hotel suite. The bathroom is equipped with a flushing toilet and a separate shower stall. It was easily the nicest bathroom setup I've ever used while camping. The shower was small, but heated up quickly and had good water pressure. The only downside was that the water pump was quite loud while using the sink or shower. If you get up in the middle of the night, the *thud thud thud* of the pump will probably wake up anyone else in the space.
Even so, I slept so much better than I expected. The Murphy bed was surprisingly comfortable, and I appreciated that there were outlets easily accessible on both sides of it.
As comfortable as the inside setup was, I was even more impressed with how the Pebble Flow's tech has simplified so many aspects of RV camping and towing. Each trailer comes with its own iPad Mini that functions as the main controller and hub for the vehicle. It's where you adjust the climate control, lights and other functions. It's also a controller for the trailer's automated hitching and remote control features.
The hitch on the Pebble Flow is equipped with a camera that's able to detect the position of the ball on the hitch of a towing vehicle. As long as the tow vehicle is within four feet of the front of the trailer, you can engage what's essentially a self-hitching mode, even if the two vehicles aren't perfectly lined up.
I watched this in action several times; the whole process took about 45 seconds. As someone with no prior RV experience, I can't speak to how this compares to the typical setup, but I can say that I was able to guide the trailer onto the hitch of a Rivian parked a couple feet away without doing anything other than pressing a couple buttons on an iPad. I also used the same iPad to maneuver the unhitched trailer around its parking spot. I only felt comfortable moving it a foot or so in either direction, but I watched Pebble reps use the remote to parallel park it and move it around the mulch-covered ground of the campsite.
One of Pebble's goals is to streamline the more tedious tasks that can be part of camping with an RV. It has an "instacamp" feature that deploys hydraulic lifts to automatically level and stabilize the trailer when you reach your destination.
Besides being able to remotely control your trailer, the in-wheel motors also help with towing. They provide some added power to help save your gas mileage or EV range a bit. Obviously, I wasn't able to simulate an actual roadtrip, but I was able to experience what it's like to tow a Pebble Flow.
I've never hauled anything bigger than a ski rack, so I was a bit nervous to tow a giant trailer around the campground parking lot and onto Highway 1, but it was actually pretty foolproof. While I was driving, another person held the iPad controller for the trailer — the company advises owners to keep the tablet inside the tow vehicle while you're on the move — and turned the motors on and off. It was an incredibly subtle difference, but it felt stable the whole time.
Pebble also brought out one of its new 2027 models, which come with some notable updates like a new floorplan option. Instead of a queen-sized Murphy bed it comes with dual twin beds. Unlike the Flow I stayed in, this configuration leaves the beds stationary for additional under-bed storage, though the two mattresses can also be pushed together to form a single king-sized bed.
The other big upgrade is that Pebble has partnered with solar panel maker Jackery to offer additional solar capabilities. Existing models come with 1.1 KW of rooftop solar panel capacity, but the 2027 models can support up to four additional 500-watt external panels, if you opt for the "self-powered" add-on. This brings the trailer's total input capacity to 3.1 KW, which Pebble says is more than enough to power a "typical day's" energy needs and help juice up the trailer's 45kWH battery. You might not need all that extra solar if you're mostly planning to stay at campgrounds or close to power sources, but it could really push the Pebble Flow's off-grid potential.
With a starting price of $159,000 (an upgraded "founder's edition" will run $193,000 with the self-powered upgrade) a Pebble Flow is a pretty massive investment. And it's one that won't fit into my life financially or literally (my garage is tiny). But after spending a day staying in one and trying out every feature I could, it feels just as innovative as we hoped it would be when we first saw it two years ago.

Zydus Lifesciences has launched in the U.S. market Riociguat tablets, in multiple strengths, developed and manufactured by MSN Laboratories.

I remember the birth of the iPod, 25 years ago this month. I was working at Newsweek. It was October 23, little more than a month after the attacks on the twin towers of the World Trade Center, and everybody was focused on the aftermath. I didn’t go to Cupertino for the launch, where Steve Jobs pulled the gadget from his jeans pocket and boasted that it contained a whole music library. Apple couriers hand-delivered the device to me in New York, and Jobs got on the phone with me. “iPod,” he told me, “will be a landmark product.”
He was right. By 2004, I was writing a cover story called “iPod Nation,” and later I published a book about the iPod called The Perfect Thing.
The death of the iPod wasn’t as memorable. It’s not even clear when it happened. Officially, one might date the time of death as occurring on May 10, 2022, when Apple discontinued the iPod Touch, the last product to use that name. But I never considered the Touch a real iPod; it was simply an iPhone without cellular connectivity. Maybe the appropriate death call might have been July 27, 2017, when Apple killed the Nano—the last traditional iPod with a screen—and the iPod Shuffle, a postage-stamp-sized player that clipped to your shirt. (Apple had quietly discontinued the classic iPod, with a hard drive and click wheel, in 2014.)
All these final dates were an inevitable consequence of what Steve Jobs put in motion on January 11, 2007. That’s when he announced three new products—a phone, an internet device, and “the best iPod ever,” all integrated into a new thing called the iPhone. From that moment on, the iPod as a separate device was living on borrowed time.
Still, for years, Apple sold millions more of the beloved devices before the iPod went silent. But even as we love our smartphones, the iPod scratched an itch that still lingers, and I’m sticking to my claim that the iPod was The Perfect Thing. It was a one-function device that superbly executed its function. It made people unconditionally happy. In contrast, our relationships with our iPhones (and Android phones) are more complicated. Yes, the device that superseded the iPod is galaxies more impactful than its predecessor. Financially, of course, it is the engine of a $4 trillion company. I can’t imagine any other contender for the mantle of best product of the century.
But I would not call the iPhone perfect. It gobbles our attention, sometimes with toxic social media apps. Countless cars have been totaled because drivers were more interested in its touch screen than what was happening on the other side of the windshield. iPhone doomscrolling can result in depression. Whereas that perky iPod brought nothing but joy.
Adding to the excitement was Steve Jobs’ willingness to redesign the iPod every year. Apple could have maintained its original iPod for a long spell, but almost immediately the company began a series of significant reinventions. Every cycle yielded an iPod with a different size and shape. With each iteration, the iPod seemed to grow smaller and cooler. First came the mini, then came multiple variations of nanos and shuffles in crazy colors and configurations. iPhone updates have kept people buying, but without the fun of a total reshaping of the product.
Is there an alternate universe where Apple continued making the iPod as a dedicated digital music player? I called Tony Fadell to discuss. Fadell is often referred to as the father of the iPod; he headed its hardware team and delivered the product in an amazing sprint of less than a year. He later was deeply involved in developing the iPhone, and his post-Apple career includes cofounding Nest, becoming a successful tech investor, and writing a well-received book.
Fadell resigned from Apple in 2008 and consulted for two years after that, when Apple was still supporting the iPod. But he recalls Jobs and other execs agreeing that the device was on a course to oblivion, despite being a great product with an enthusiastic user base. With the iPhone proving to be a monster success that also helped boost the Macintosh, and Apple pursuing potentially mass-market innovations like the iPad, iPod sales were becoming less relevant to the company’s bottom line. Jobs was a relentless prioritizer, and his successor Tim Cook felt the same way.
Fadell says that there was very little hand-wringing about the iPod’s fate. “The discussion was about Apple [not] doing lower-value things,” he says. Yet he agrees with me that the iPod’s disappearance created a hole that hasn’t been filled.
In retrospect, he says, what made the iPod invaluable is what it didn’t do—connect with the internet. “Because the iPod wasn't connected, you didn’t have all these other things going on to distract you. Today, you get all the annoyance of being connected without being able to get the same listening experience. You can always be distracted and go somewhere else.”
“This thing should still exist,” he says.
A lot of people seem to agree. There are multiple active communities on Facebook and Reddit of refuseniks who go to great lengths to mod old iPods—putting in large flash drives, installing Bluetooth. There’s even an app that makes your iPhone look and play like an iPod Classic. It works great, but you’re still one swipe away from your feeds, your mail, and everything else in your life that isn’t as fun as music.
I ask Fadell how he regards the iPod’s legacy. Tellingly, his answer speaks to Apple’s history more than exhilaration for the product itself. “The iPhone never would have existed without it,” he says. “That means that the Apple we know of would never have existed without the iPod.” It helped turn a computer company with a limited user base into a consumer electronics giant.
“And the crazy thing is that it was exactly 25 years ago—which is half the years that Apple has existed. There was the Apple II, and then the Mac, and then, boom,” he adds.
I prefer to remember the iPod for what it was, not what it led to. Not long ago, I exhumed my iPod Classic. I have an old boombox with a cradle designed for the iPod, with the old 30-pin connector. I put it in shuffle mode and blissed out.
I suspect a lot of others might like to return to iPod Nation. New CEO John Ternus has no incentive to revive the product, of course. I do find it sad, however, that a generation exists that doesn’t know what it’s like to have a dedicated music device that will never interrupt a tune with calls, texts, and notifications. They don’t know what they’re missing.

Shai Hope has been a beacon of Hope for Caribbean cricket.
The West Indian’s batting graph has gone north ever since landing in India. After five outings against the Men in Blue across three ODIs and two T20Is, Hope has added 432 golden runs to his international tally.
It’s tough to pick out his best knock from the last two weeks. He has three centuries and a half-century to choose from. Perhaps he will narrow it down to the unbeaten ones: 162 in the New Chandigarh ODI and 102 in the Ranchi T20I. He did hit the winning runs in both, each sealing the Windies’ highest successful run-chase in that particular format (352 and 250, respectively).
What may tip the balance towards his exploits at the JSCA Stadium would be that it was his first T20I century (always special).
“I think people underrate Hope a lot. He is a guy who can block out noise and just focus on what he has to do. Because when everything seems to be going wrong, he’s still up there giving his best and performing for the team,” West Indies all-rounder Roston Chase said after the visitors’ record chase on Friday (October 9, 2026).
Hope is not one to use brute force — a trait popular among the West Indian willow-wielders — and he has often had to face critiques about his strike-rate. That has been taken care of for now with his ball-striking against India (SR of 112.10 in ODIs and 187.80 in T20Is).
“People play down his stats and record in T20 cricket. They always say he either bats too slowly or he bats for himself. I’m always happy when I see him do well. I know he’s an ultimate professional who tries to tick every box and do the right things all the time,” Chase added.
And Hope’s upgrade wasn’t just built on hope. “He’s done a lot of gym work to make himself stronger in terms of hitting the ball over the ropes. He also practises a lot of range hitting to get in those strong positions,” Chase explained.
Hope’s heroics even drew praise from the opposition camp.
“We know Shai is a world-class cricketer. We respect him for what he has done in white-ball cricket,” head coach Gautam Gambhir said after India’s six-wicket loss.
Hope — as the famous Shawshank Redemption dialogue goes — is a good thing, maybe the best of things. Now, Shai Hope’s best is here, ready for some redemption!

Man City whistleblower to remain in witness protection
- Published
The Portuguese computer hacker who released documents which helped trigger the Premier League investigation into Manchester City will remain in witness protection after authorities in the country suspended the decision to end it.
Football Leaks founder Rui Pinto had been scheduled to leave the protection programme on Saturday, a ruling he previously said had put him in a "life-threatening situation".
Pinto, 37, disclosed a tranche of confidential football documents, including emails and financial records relating to the English Premier League side.
In 2018, he shared documents with German magazine Der Spiegel, which used them for investigations into City's finances and alleged breaches of financial fair play rules.
City were recently found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. They have appealed against the decision.
Pinto became part of Portugal's witness protection programme in 2020 after agreeing to co-operate with authorities and provide information obtained through the Football Leaks operation.
However, in a statement on Friday,, external Portugal's Ministry of Justice said a decision to remove Pinto from witness protection had been reversed for the time being, with the body responsible for it - the special security programmes commission - having not adequately "notified" Pinto of grounds for its termination or given him the opportunity to challenge the decision.
Pinto will now be given 10 days to assess a risk assessment conducted by the special security programmes commission that indicates a low threat to his safety.
He posted on X, external thanking Portugal's Minister of Justice, Rita Alarcao Judice and saying the commission's initial decision had clearly violated the law and amounted to a "manifest abuse of power".
Pinto has described himself as a whistleblower, but was convicted in Portugal of offences including illegal access to data and attempted extortion and given a four-year suspended sentence.
He wore a bulletproof vest during his first trial in 2020, which was also subject to heightened security measures.
Earlier this year, he was acquitted of 241 counts of illegally accessing email accounts belonging to a number of sports bodies in Portugal, including Benfica.

Throughout 2025 and 2026, YouTube channels posted videos online (archived) claiming that Buzz Aldrin, one of the first two astronauts to land on the moon, broke down in tears during an interview and said, "The moon is not what you think."
At least three other popular videos (archived) on YouTube (archived) make the same claim (archived). Snopes readers sent emails asking if the claim was true.
Snopes could not find evidence that Aldrin ever said this in any interview he has ever participated in. Therefore, we've rated this claim as an incorrect attribution.
We reached out to Aldrin through his website's inquiry form to ask if he has ever said such a quote, or anything akin to it. We'll update this story if we receive a reply.
Searches for the "The moon is not what you think" quote and Aldrin's name on Google, DuckDuckGo, Bing and Yahoo did not find any videos or transcripts of the interview in which Aldrin supposedly said the quote, or the full interview in writing. The searches did not reveal any credible news reports that quoted Aldrin saying these words. Considering one YouTube video claims Aldrin said the moon quote in interviews and another referred to the quote as Aldrin's "famous warning," it's unlikely that there'd be no credible references to this quote outside of these YouTube videos.
Each of the four videos linked above tells a different story, and three of the four center the story around the moon quote Aldrin allegedly said. The fourth video, despite having a title about Aldrin apparently saying "The moon is not what you think," is not about Aldrin. That video focuses on Michael Collins, another astronaut on the Apollo 11 mission alongside Neil Armstrong and Aldrin, and does not even include the quote "The moon is not what you think."
The three videos that actually focus on Aldrin use the same commonplace artificial intelligence-generated voice for narration. In fact, two of these videos include YouTube's "AI" label just under the videos' titles.
The narrator, instead of Aldrin himself, says the quote in all three videos. None of the videos use footage from the interview in which Aldrin supposedly said it, even though one of the videos claims the interview took place in a television studio. One of the other videos changes Aldrin's quote to "You are mistaken about the moon" in the middle of the video.
Each video assigns a different meaning to the quote in its conclusion. One video says Aldrin's apparent quote was referring to the moon as the beginning of humanity's exploration. Another video refers to the quote as a reference to the moon's earthly origins. The third video suggests the quote means that no amount of data or knowledge of the moon can replicate the experience of being on the moon itself.
A search for the quote itself does show it has been used as a title for YouTube videos and social media posts. Snopes could not find any evidence the quote has ever been associated with Aldrin or any other astronaut.
This claim may have originated with an older video also narrated by an AI voice. A 2023 YouTube video titled "Apollo Astronaut Breaks In Tears: 'The Moon Is NOT What You Think!'" (archived) focuses on Michael Collins. The quote "The moon is not what you think" does not appear anywhere in the actual contents of the video.
None of the channels that posted the videos included publicly available contact information on their YouTube channels.

Trump licks his Nobel-snub wounds by sharing nasty post after Peace Prize winner’s swipe at him
Trump has spent much of the last two years openly campaigning for the prize that has been awarded to two prior American presidents

President Donald Trump responded to being passed over for the Nobel Peace Prize for a second straight year by amplifying a post from his former impeachment lawyer blasting the winner, the South African jurist and former UN human rights chief Navi Pillay, “an unabashed hater of America and Israel” who “has never done a thing to foster peace.”
The post, written by David Schoen — who defended Trump in his 2021 Senate impeachment trial over the Jan. 6 attack — went up on Truth Social at 7:58 a.m. Friday, within hours of the Norwegian Nobel Committee’s announcement in Oslo, and was reposted by the president to his 10 million followers shortly afterward.
“Today the Nobel Committee shamed itself beyond repair and demeaned the once great Nobel Peace Prize by giving it to the UN’s Navi Pillay,” Schoen wrote. “Pillay is an unabashed hater of America and Israel. In her position she celebrated terrorists and rewarded Hamas. She conducted a phony ‘investigation’ claiming to find that Israel committed genocide and urging prosecution. She has no credibility in any normal sphere and has never done a thing to foster peace. Just the opposite. But what could be expected from a committee that previously gave the once-coveted peace prize to Yasser Arafat?”
The post, which neglected to note that Arafat, the late Palestine Liberation Organization leader and former terrorist, had been awarded the prize jointly in 1994 along with Israeli leaders Yitzhak Rabin and Shimon Peres for their work together on the Oslo Accords, then pivoted to the man Schoen believed should have won — his former client.
“President Trump gave us the Abraham Accords, which the world said would be impossible and is now expanding them!” the post went on. “He brought home the hostages when all seemed hopeless! He is making best efforts to end the Russia/Ukraine war, to stop Iran, the number one sponsor of international terrorism, and he is trying to rebuild Gaza despite the terrorists’ best efforts to control it. The list goes on and on. These are the kinds of things the Nobel Peace Prize was intended to recognize and reward!!!” The post closed by tagging the president’s account.
Pillay, 85, had by then already gotten in a shot of her own. Arriving to applause at a legal conference at the Nuremberg courthouse — the site of the postwar trials of Nazi leaders — she told the room: “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.”
The committee’s citation did not mention Trump, but it did not need to. Committee chair Jørgen Watne Frydnes said Pillay was being honored for being “instrumental in ensuring war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted,” at a moment when “the system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack.”
The committee’s statement went further: “We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respects for law and justice. Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful coexistence.” It ended with three words: “Peace requires justice.”
Pillay defended Nelson Mandela and other anti-apartheid activists before serving as a judge and later president of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, then as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2008 to 2014. The “phony investigation” Schoen referred to was the independent UN commission of inquiry she chaired, which concluded that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza — a finding Israel rejects, and one the Trump administration has treated as further proof that the UN’s human rights machinery is, in the words of White House deputy press secretary Anna Kelly last month, a body that has “accomplished nothing for human rights while spouting unserious nonsense for decades.”
Trump had spent the week making the case for himself, telling reporters on Wednesday that he’d “done stuff that nobody else has ever done” and claiming that “no president has probably ever settled any wars” while boasting of having supposedly brought eight to a close.
The figure was seven when he addressed the UN General Assembly last September; the United States has been at war with Iran, one of the seven, since February. And his assertion that none of his predecessors had “settled any wars” appeared to betray his ignorance of the fact that Theodore Roosevelt, the 26th President of the United States, was awarded a Nobel Peace Prize (which is displayed in the West Wing’s Roosevelt Room) for negotiating an end to the Russo-Japanese War in 1905.
Trump’s repost of Schoen’s rant was a far more muted reaction to this year’s snub compared to what happened when he was passed over last year.
When the 2025 prize went to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, the White House accused the committee of placing “politics over peace.” Machado later presented her medal to Trump as what she called “recognition for his unique commitment with our freedom.” As of Friday afternoon, Pillay had made no comparable offer

Washington – U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel prices, and his administration temporarily lifted U.S. sanctions on Russian fuel that were designed to deprive Moscow of revenues for its war on Ukraine.
Prices for diesel, used for agriculture, heating homes and trucking, are near a record and have put Trump’s fellow Republicans at risk ahead of the Nov. 3 congressional elections that will determine whether they maintain thin control of Congress. Diesel prices fell after the announcement, but analysts said the deal may not be enough to keep them down.
Trump said on social media he had a “highly successful” discussion with President Vladimir Putin in which they agreed that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to U.S. and global markets, equal to about 2.25 million barrels of fuel. The U.S. exports about 1.5 million barrels of diesel per day.

Trump, elected chairman of the Kennedy Center board after installing loyalists, has tried to remake the DC landmark in his image

A federal judge ordered the Kennedy Center to turn over more financial records as part of the ongoing lawsuit involving President Donald Trump role in the operations - but has yet to decide on an ‘executive privilege” claim.
On Friday, a judge told the center to turn over some records but gave the Department of Justice more time to respond to its executive privilege claims, according to the Washington Post.
The DOJ invoked executive privilege to keep Trump’s role in the operations of the John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts secret.
Trump, who was elected chairman of the Kennedy Center board after installing loyalists to oversee the D.C. arts institution, has tried to remake the landmark in his image by attempting to slap his name on the building's facade and close it for repairs.
Representative Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat, has sued the center in her capacity as an ex officio board member to stop the renaming of the center and its planned two-year closure. While Beatty was successful in getting a federal judge to order Trump’s name to be removed from the building, she’s hit a snag in her fight to keep the Kennedy Center open.
On Monday, Beatty’s lawyers objected to the DOJ’s attempt to use executive privilege to limit what evidence the Kennedy Center has to turn over as part of her case, The New York Times reported, citing court records.
During depositions this week, DOJ lawyers instructed Kennedy Center’s executive director, Matt Floca, to not answer questions about his conversations with Trump and his advisers, according to court records reviewed by The Washington Post.
When asked by one of Beatty’s lawyers about what Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said when he first contacted Floca about helping the Kennedy Center, a DOJ lawyer told Floca, “Executive privilege on that. Don’t answer that,” a transcript of the deposition showed.
Executive privilege typically allows presidents to keep certain conversations related to their official responsibilities private, so that they can speak candidly with aides.
But the DOJ’s use of executive privilege in this case is unusual, given that Trump has two jobs — president and Kennedy Center chairman.
Jonathan Shaub, a University of Kentucky law professor who previously worked in the DOJ, told the Post, “If the president is not acting in his capacity as president, it doesn’t apply.”
“Donald Trump is the chair of a nonprofit corporation’s board, and his decisions and directions lie at the heart of that board’s actions which, in turn, are the subject matter of this case,” Beatty’s lawyers wrote in Monday’s filing.
The lawyers argued that using executive privilege in this context would “obstruct the search for the truth.”

A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.
It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.
At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots.
Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.”
Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?”
Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants in Guinea-Bissau in the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life.
An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said was suspended after international uproar earlier this year.
Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study.
“You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”.
Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reportedly set aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation.
The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial.
The news that the trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee was first reported on Thursday by CIDRAP News. This is the first time details of the updated protocol have been disclosed.
The Guinea-Bissau study protocol has changed since it was posted in January, according to details shared with the Guardian. The researchers will now test mothers for hepatitis B before they give birth. The babies of mothers who test positive will be given the vaccine and will not be included in the trial. But the babies of mothers whose tests are negative may be enrolled. The new protocol has not been shared publicly.
In previous research, half of children who contracted hepatitis B did so after birth, through community exposures. “This virus can be transmitted casually,” Offit said. It can live on surfaces for up to seven days, and it can be acquired by sharing washcloths, toothbrushes and fingernail clippers. In addition, the hepatitis B test has a 5% false negative rate, which could provide false assurance that a birthing parent does not have the virus.
Decades of research make it clear that the vaccine would be beneficial, which means it would be unfair to place some children in the vaccinated group and some children in the unvaccinated group, said Henrik Støvring, a professor of statistics and pharmacometrics at Aarhus University in Denmark.
According to the Helsinki declaration, international medical research must be approved by ethics committees in both the host and sponsor countries.
The Danish research ethics committee at the University of Southern Denmark had never considered medical studies before, but it changed the rules in order to vote on this one. While committee members with expertise argued against approving it, the majority ruled to move forward.
“It’s very unusual to bring this into a committee like that,” Støvring said. The national ethics committee in Denmark oversees medical research, but this study was outside of their purview because it won’t take place in Denmark.
Yet “I don’t see why you couldn’t do it in Denmark,” Støvring said of the trial. In fact, several conditions make it a better location. The hepatitis B vaccine is not usually given to newborns in Denmark unless the mother is positive for the virus, for which all pregnant people are tested in Denmark.
Guinea-Bissau has some of the highest rates of hepatitis B in the world, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. While it may be transmitted from mother to child during birth, it could also be transmitted from another parent, relatives, siblings or caregivers. Children who are infected with hepatitis B in the first year of life are significantly more likely to develop severe outcomes, including chronic infection and liver cancer.
The Bandim Health Project, run by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, has operated in Guinea-Bissau for decades and is closely enmeshed in the country’s health system. At least one top official, the current director of public health, held a dual appointment with Bandim as recently as December.
Kennedy praised the Danish researchers at a recent anti-vaccine conference, calling them “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy claimed that a prior study they conducted indicated that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.” He did not mention that another follow-up study from the same researchers found no effects at all.
This study will focus on vaccination and mortality, as well as outcomes such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. “The main problem of this trial is that you have some very well-known bad diseases that you can protect with this vaccine,” Støvring said. “And what they then want to study is something highly speculative – in a situation where WHO and others are saying that you should give this vaccine at birth, period.”
When asked about the study in a Thursday briefing, an official with the Africa CDC, which has opposed the trial, said there were “ongoing discussions” between the US and Guinea-Bissau and more details would be shared shortly. Guinea-Bissau planned to begin vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B in 2027, but they pushed the campaign back to 2028.
Kennedy and the Danish researchers were “taking advantage of that delay in practicing standard care to put these children at risk unnecessarily”, Offit said. “What a terrible thing to do. What a horribly unethical and cruel thing to do.”

The Karolinska Institute awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Medicine to researchers Karl Deisseroth of Stanford University, Peter Hegemann of Humboldt University in Berlin, and Georg Nagel of the University of Würzburg. Their discoveries led to the development of optogenetics, a technique where scientists can turn individual nerve cells on or off using beams of light.
According to Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Medicine, “Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of.” No other technique allows for such precise study of a living brain, helping researchers better understand the functions of our nervous systems as well as various neurological diseases and disorders.
But this prize is not just a celebration of neuroscience. It also serves as a triumphant example of what can happen when different disciplines of biology converge, as the findings that served as the basis for the development of optogenetics emerged from research in microbiology.
At the end of the last century, Peter Hegemann began a series of studies to understand how the single-celled alga Chlamydomonas is able to detect and react to light. Previous research documented that Chlamydomonas has an “eye spot,” a small orange dot on its surface that contains a light-sensing molecule called retinal.
Hegemann used tiny electrodes to measure the electrical signals generated by the alga and to expand our understanding of this structure’s rapid response. The scientist discovered that the organism was capable of producing an electrical impulse about 0.5 milliseconds after receiving light. This response time is 20 times faster than that of the human eye, whose light detection process takes at least 10 milliseconds.
Hegemann suggested that light detection in the alga must be the result of a much simpler process than that identified in the human eye. In the early 1990s, he proposed that the eye spots contained a protein that both detected the light and responded to it, likely opening as a channel to let ions through. At the time, this hypothesis sparked controversy. Many ion channels had been documented up to that point, but none could respond to light on their own.
To test his theory, the scientist attempted to isolate the light-sensitive proteins from the eye spot. However, when removed from their natural environment, these proteins became unstable. Later, a group of Japanese researchers sequenced the complete DNA of Chlamydomonas, which allowed Hegemann’s team to identify two genes that would create proteins with the expected characteristics of a possible light-sensing channel.
Georg Nagel took the next step of verifying the function of the genes. He introduced copies of each of the identified genes separately into different groups of frog eggs. The eggs began to produce the corresponding proteins, which eventually localized to the cell membranes. Nagel then turned on the lights.
Both proteins functioned as ion channels that opened when exposed to light. He named the genes channelrhodopsin-1 and channelrhodopsin-2. Further experiments showed the protein produced by this second gene—called ChR2 for short—opened especially quickly, the flow of ions occurring in just 0.2 milliseconds. It explained the extraordinary speed of the light reaction originally observed in Chlamydomonas.
When the researchers introduced the gene into mammalian cells—which do not normally respond to light—the cells generated an electrical signal when illuminated. This is what got the neuroscientists particularly excited.
Ion channels are important across many types of cells, but they do some especially heavy lifting in our nervous systems. The electrical impulses that neurons use to communicate with one another, as well as other tissues in our body, are mediated by the flow of ions in and out of the cell. If you can control the ion channels, you can control the neuron.
This is where Karl Deisseroth comes in. Deisseroth was searching for a method that would allow him to toggle the activity of specific nerve cells in a living brain. In his view, this tool could expand our understanding of brain functions and open new avenues for treating conditions such as depression and schizophrenia.
Following the discovery of ChR2, he asked Nagel for the DNA sequence so he could introduce it into rat nerve cells. The neurons, growing in dishes, produced ChR2 and, when illuminated with blue light, reacted immediately—sending an electrical impulse that propagated to other neurons. This result, obtained in 2005, was decisive in establishing ChR2 as a tool for neuroscience.
In the following years, Deisseroth, Hegemann, and Nagel collaborated to identify other proteins capable of activating or deactivating neurons using different wavelengths of light. With this toolkit, researchers can now design experiments where one group of neurons is turned on by one wavelength of light and another set of neurons is controlled by a different wavelength.
The term optogenetics was coined in 2006 and has since been implemented in a variety of studies. “Using optogenetics, researchers have been able to reveal neural circuits governing specific memories, feelings, and behaviors relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders. In clinical medicine, researchers are using the method in attempts to restore sight in people with visual impairment,” the Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute stated in a press release.

At the United Nations High Level Meeting (UN HLM), in New York in September 2026, India made official remarks on the Political Declaration on Pandemic Prevention Preparedness and Response (PPPR). The Declaration is part of the emerging global legal regime on pandemics led by the WHO-Pandemic agreement (PA).
Shaping the framework
The PA was adopted by 124 member-states in 2025, including India. No country voted against it, while 11 abstained, reflecting alignment across high-, middle- and low-income countries (HICs/LICs/LMICs). The negotiations hinged on how to balance national sovereignty with international cooperation and solidarity, exposing the fault lines between the Global North and the Global South. Key issues included whether a global treaty can set binding targets for measures such as ‘One Health’ without securing funding for countries with fragile health systems. Or whether national pandemic regulations can be harmonised through global frameworks. And whether private manufacturers can be required to share vaccines in real time at affordable prices.
The PA is not yet open for ratification because negotiations are still ongoing for an annex concerning the Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing (PABS) system. PABS could help ensure that, during a pandemic, LICs and LMICs receive a fair share of vaccines, medicines and other therapeutics.
Even without ratification, the PA has created a first-of-its-kind global legal regime for the PPPR. Operationalisation requires countries such as India to balance interests of the HICs, LICs and LMICs. This will determine whether the PA will further entrench the inequities of the COVID-19 pandemic or make global health governance truly inclusive.
Editorial | Landmark agreement: On the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement
At the UN HLM, India succeeded in enshrining the multilateral components of the PA within the principle of national sovereignty. India reiterated its commitment to strengthen global pandemic preparedness but stressed that effective pandemic management requires that international coordination is demonstrated. The first is equitable access to drugs, vaccines and therapeutics and the creation of global public goods, such as digital infrastructure (which admittedly align with its own national priorities).
The second is a respect for national sovereignty and the primacy of member-states in shaping global policy interventions according to national circumstance. As a contrast, the United States rejected the Declaration, calling the PABS and WHO’s role in declaring pandemics as a challenge to its national interests.
India’s line
In its remarks, India has acknowledged the concerns of the Global North and the South. Both sides have upheld national sovereignty as paramount in several provisions. The African countries did not give consent to commitments to monitor the human-animal-environment interface, a key source of pandemic outbreaks, without significant funding, which was not guaranteed by the Global North. Similarly, countries in the Global North did not want binding targets with regard to technology transfer (and other similar provisions).
But as India said at the UN HLM, ‘Global Solidarity must be demonstrated through action’; India must be an active player in the finalisation of the global PPPR regime. India is already actively engaged in the PABS negotiations and must lead the Global South in the post-PABS context. India can consider three options. First, developing partnerships on technical areas of the PA (One Health, surveillance, health workforce strengthening) to build trust with other countries in the Global South, and a ‘store’ of operational solutions to tricky national sovereignty problems.
Second, leveraging its leadership role within existing global political groupings. For example, the H20 summit (a health and development G-7 and G-20 partnership) will take place under the United Kingdom’s G-20 leadership at the end of 2027; pandemic preparedness is one of the core health agendas. During India’s G-20 presidency in 2023, India launched the Global Initiative for Digital Health and holds considerable influence within the platform’s health initiatives. Another is ‘Partners for Multilateralism’, which was launched in 2026 by the European Union (co-sponsors are Australia, Barbados, Brazil, Canada, India and Kenya).
Third, strengthening and aligning domestic policy and regulatory architecture around its own priorities for the PA. Global leadership always rests on domestic strengths. India must ensure that its national policies on PPPR such as regulation of access to biological material and distribution of the benefits uphold the highest standards of equity which India can then demand at the global level.
A South-South health role
An equitable global regime on PPPR is in India’s interests as much as a responsibility towards the Global South. India is the pharmacy of the world, manufacturing one of the largest shares of vaccines in the world in terms of volume. Yet, it needs an equitable global vaccine distribution regime. The patents for the vaccines that India manufactures are held by global pharmaceuticals. India is also import-dependent for Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs).
India needs access to the latest technology from the Global North to strengthen the manufacturing of high-grade personal protective equipment and medical devices. At the same time, India needs to lead South-South Cooperation and share its technological strength with other countries in the Global South.
India’s health system has a continental scale, and as India’s Health Secretary stated at the UN HLM, its interventions in digital health infrastructure, laboratories networks and One Health are valuable as global public goods. An effective PA needs an engaged India, and a strong PA will strengthen India’s own pandemic management.
Priyadarshini Singh is a Research Fellow at the Centre for Social and Economic Progress (CSEP). This article is based on a forthcoming CSEP working paper on the Pandemic Agreement.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

FIFA’s Social Media Protection Service (SMPS) has found that more than half of the 1,606 players, coaches and officials at the 2026 FIFA World Cup received abuse online.
Over half of the individuals received at least one message which could be classified as abusive, while racism accounted for one in five of the abusive messages. Messages threatening violence and xenophobia were recorded at 14 percent and 12 percent respectively.
SMPS says that the individual who was the most targeted received around 10,000 abusive posts, of which 40 percent were racist.
SMPS analysed 17.1 million posts and comments and, after human review, discovered that about 2,40,000 were abusive. Their AI moderation tool filtered through 60.7 million comments on official FIFA and member association channels and hid 9.2 million of them, including spam. After this, FIFA escalated 2,905 accounts for investigation and even sent 786 of them to law enforcement for review
“Ahead of World Mental Health Day, we are reinforcing FIFA’s commitment to protecting the football community from online hate through optimised technology that tackles not only manually created content, but also AI-generated imagery. We remain resolute. FIFA’s SMPS is at the disposal of football stakeholders with a view to supporting all 211 FIFA Member Associations and the confederations alike, because we need to unite to tackle this abhorrent behaviour that causes distress and affects emotional well-being,” FIFA President Gianni Infantino said in a statement.

The Trump administration has long been hostile to the court and has previously imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges. Friday’s move would go far further, by potentially punishing companies that provide services to the court itself.
“President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement reviewed by Reuters ahead of the official announcement.

Amid a rain deficit of 35% between June and September in Karnataka, the prices of rice and toor dal have increased. The price of rice had already increased twice in two months between August and October.
This has impacted household budgets, while hotels are now weighing their options of increasing their rates.
For instance, the price of the Sona Masuri variety which was ₹75 per kg, has now increased to about ₹80, Basmati has gone up from ₹110 to ₹140 per kg, bullet rice from ₹80 to ₹100, Kolam rice from ₹75 to ₹100, and Rajamudi rice from ₹125 to ₹150, on an average, as per traders The Hindu spoke to.
The price of toor dal varieties have also increased by ₹10 to ₹15 per kg from what it was 10 days ago. The Gulbarga fatkar variety is priced at ₹145 per kg, from ₹125.
According to the Department of Agriculture, the target area for paddy cultivation for the kharif season was 10 lakh hectares while the sown area was only 6.2 lakh hectares. Last kharif season, it was 10.43 lakh hectares. The target area for toor dal this kharif was 16 lakh hectares while the sown area was 13.35 lakh hectares. Last year, the sown area was 14.16 lakh hectares.
Chamarasa Malipatil, president of Karnataka Rajya Raitha Sangha (KRRS), said: “The government did not release water from reservoirs in major paddy cultivation areas of Karnataka, including Ballari, Raichur, Gangavati, Mandya and a few districts of Malnad region, at the right time. It is the same with toor dal cultivating districts mainly in Kalaburagi. Hence, there is crop failure, no stock in market, and demand surge leading to hike in price.”
Mr. Malipatil pointed out that not all farmers benefit from price hike. Those who have stored the harvest from the rabi season will benefit as they can now sell it in the market, he said.
G.R. Denesh, Professor of Agronomy and Scheme Head at All India Coordinated Research Projects (Rice) run by Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), explained: “According to our estimation, more than 50% crop loss is likely to be recorded in paddy cultivating districts of Karnataka. It is a water-intensive crop and needs sufficient water and rains. Both were not available this year. If we get good rains by the end of October and November, then the price of rice and toor dal might stabilise or it will only increase.”
Shivakumar, general secretary, Karnataka State Rice Mills Association, said: “There are 700 rice mills operating across the State, but the stock of rice is low in the market. Two months ago, mill owners procured paddy at ₹3,500 per quintal which has increased to ₹4,600 to ₹4,700 per quintal. Neither the State nor the Union governments can regulate the price of rice here because they cannot ask farmers to decrease the price of their harvested crops.”
Muniswamy S., scientific officer, Directorate of Research, University of Agriculture in Raichur, said that Maharashtra and Karnataka are the leading producers of toor dal in India. “Even though there is toor dal yield in the State, the quality is not as expected because of less moisture in the atmosphere and infertile soil. Flowering is also delayed because of extreme heat in Kalaburagi.”
Mr. Muniswamy pointed out that floods in Kalaburagi last year was another reason for the price hike. “Floods impacted the production of toor dal in approximately 1.7 lakh hectares,” he said.
