Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky has accused the US of being unwilling to help Ukraine defend itself after a Russian bomb attack on two passenger buses killed at least 35 people.
The attack, which struck public buses in the embattled city of Kramatorsk, came amid a wave of Russian strikes across Ukraine that killed 78 people and injured 215 over two days, according to Zelensky.
Speaking to reporters in Pryluky, the Ukrainian leader criticised Washington for pursuing economic ties with Moscow while attempting to broker an end to the war, now in its fifth year.
He urged the US to expand Ukraine’s access to the Starlink satellite service to help its forces target Russian ballistic missile launchers.
“Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran ... I’ve said quite openly – give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table,” he said.
It comes as Ukrainian negotiators will travel to the US on Friday and Saturday for talks, Zelensky added, urging Donald Trump to increase sanction pressure on Russia.
Russian air strike kills one, injures two in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia, official says
A Russian air strike has killed one person and injured two others in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, acting governor Mykhailo Semikin said on Telegram on Friday.
Ed Miliband says UK 'will not relent in its support for Ukraine'
UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband visited the site of the Russian strike in Pryluky along with Volodymyr Zelensky, where he condemned Vladimir Putin's "evil intent and evil strategy".
He announced "more sanctions on Russia, on the war machine of Putin, on the shadow fleet, on the oil companies, on the crypto, on the financing of the war".
“My message to Putin is clear – you cannot wait us out. Until you choose the path of peace, the UK will not relent in its support for Ukraine, our values, or our national security. You will remain a pariah,” he said.
They visited a site where 22 people, including five children, were killed in a single strike on a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky on Wednesday.
The sanctions package, which includes around 40 targets across Russia’s financial, oil and technology sectors, is designed to disrupt Russia’s supply chain and cut off financing streams.
Zelensky calls for US to expand Starlink access after deadly bus strikes
Volodymyr Zelensky urged the US to accede to his request to expand Ukraine’s access to its Starlink satellite service in order to better target Russian ballistic missile launchers, after Moscow launched one of the deadliest single aerial attacks of the war so far.
Speaking to reporters in Pryluky in the east of Kyiv, he said: “Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran ... I’ve said quite openly – give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table.”
At least 30 people were killed in a Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk, rescue officials said.
Three others were killed in the nearby village of Bilenke, while 18 people were wounded, according to Donetsk regional governor Vadym Filashkin, who accused Russia of deliberately targeting passenger buses to maximise civilian casualties.
Two dead in drone strikes in Russia's Belgorod region, officials say
Two people were killed in Ukrainian drone strikes on Thursday in Russia's border region of Belgorod, regional officials said.
The regional operational headquarters reported one person died when a drone struck a car.
A later evening strike killed one person and injured three.
Reuters could not independently verify the reports.
Belgorod region has been a frequent target of Ukraine's forces.
Indian imports of Russian oil sink to lowest level since 2022
Indian imports of Russian oil have their lowest level since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022, according to a report.
In the four weeks up to 4 October, shipments of Russian rude averaged just 310,000 barrels a day, Bloomberg data showed. This is the lowest level since March 2022.
India has gradually reduced its dependence on Russian oil since the US threatened punitive sanctions earlier this year.
Zelensky says Ukraine expects Europeans to join talks with US
Volodymyr Zelensky said that Ukraine expected Kyiv's European partners to join talks with the US in coming days.
Zelenskiy earlier said that Ukraine's negotiators would hold talks in the United States on Friday and Saturday as part of efforts led by the United States to seek a settlement of the war with Russia.
The president, speaking to reporters in Kyiv, said Ukrainian negotiators would raise the issue of air defences in light of near-constant Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities. More than 70 have been killed in strikes over the past two days.
Zelenskiy also said Ukraine had "mirrored" Russian attacks on data centres, referring to a strike on a centre operated by Russian technology company Yandex.
"We always respond in mirror-like fashion," Zelenskiy said. "You all know, they have been hitting and continue to hit our data centres. We are responding. I can't share all the details."
Russian technology and AI company Yandex said on Thursday it could not yet determine whether equipment at a data centre hit by a Ukrainian drone attack could be restored.
Russian drone strike on Kramatorsk kills two, local authorities say
A new evening drone strike on the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk killed two people on Thursday, local authorities said.
The Kramatorsk city council, in a post on Telegram, said the drone struck a car, killing two people inside. It said a total of 35 people had been killed in the city after a bomb attack tore through two buses.
Russia agrees with Rubio that Ukraine conflict is in a stalemate
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted as saying on Thursday that Russia agreed with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that the Ukraine conflict was in a stalemate.
"Yes, we agree with him," Russian news agencies quoted Peskov as saying on the sidelines of a meeting of leaders of ex-Soviet states in Turkmenistan.
State news agency RIA quoted Peskov as saying it was up to diplomats to find ways of moving towards peace.
"The art of diplomacy precisely involves finding some way out that would allow moving onto a peaceful track," Peskov was quoted as saying.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will meet Ukrainian representatives on Friday in Miami to discuss new ideas and try to produce a unified proposal for resolving the war, an American source familiar with the plan said on Thursday.
Peskov was quoted as saying he saw no immediate prospect for a three-way summit between Putin, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky and US President Donald Trump.
He restated the Kremlin's position that Russia wanted an overall solution to the conflict and was not interested in temporary measures, like a limited ceasefire.
"We are not for a fragmented solution, we are for a comprehensive solution that will allow for sustainable settlement for many, many years, for decades," the agencies quoted him as saying.
The crippling effect we’re all feeling from the deadlock in Ukraine’s war with Russia
Two of the world’s largest exporters of grain, locked in war for more than four years, have seen exports plunge even further over the last year. Prolonged conflict around the Black Sea threatens both economies - and those most in need, writes James C. Reynolds.
The crippling effect we’re all feeling from the deadlock in Ukraine’s war with Russia
Rubio claims war in Ukraine is 'at dangerous stalemate'
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Thursday that Russia's war in Ukraine is at a dangerous stalemate and the United States will continue to try to facilitate a settlement to end the conflict.
"We'd love to see a negotiated settlement to this war that is permanent, enduring, and fair," Rubio told reporters during a visit to Portugal.

Boosting US oil supplies with Russian diesel unlikely to have much impact on prices, experts say
A new pact that calls for Russia to boost the U.S. supply of diesel over the next few months is unlikely to make a dent in painfully high prices at the pump or elsewhere, energy policy experts say

A new pact that calls for Russia to boost the U.S. supply of diesel over the next few months is unlikely to make a dent in painfully high prices at the pump or elsewhere, energy policy experts say.
President Donald Trump announced Friday that he had struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to immediately supply the U.S. more than 300,000 tons of diesel. That would be followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November, then 4 million more tons at some point after that.
The deal marks a stark reversal of policy by the U.S., which from the start of Russia’s war with Ukraine had banned imports of Russian oil, and comes at a time when the U.S. economy and consumers are being squeezed by a global rise in oil prices due to the eight-month-long U.S. war with Iran.
The price of diesel has shattered records in recent weeks, ratcheting up inflation for a broad swath of consumer goods.
The national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. hit a record high of $6.53 on Sept. 22, according to motor club AAA. It averaged nearly $6.28 a gallon on Friday, up from almost $3.68 this time last year. Diesel prices have hit records in Europe, too.
Higher diesel prices mean more expensive transportation for a long list of everyday goods. That’s because diesel is used for many freight and delivery networks. And some businesses have already passed along steeper costs to consumers in the form of added fees on online orders and packages in the mail.
Shoppers may feel more and more sticker shock, particularly in the grocery aisle. Perishable foods, like meat and produce, face one of the most immediate strains of expensive diesel because they need to be hauled in and restocked frequently — or may be harvested using farm equipment powered by the fuel.
That’s turned up the heat on Trump and the Republican Party to address surging prices ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections. The president’s approval ratings on the economy have hit a new low, according to an AP-NORC poll released last week, as the Iran war and his trade battles have increased U.S. prices for oil and other goods.
A limited impact, at best
Energy policy experts on Friday expressed doubts that a boost in diesel supply from Russia will have a significant impact on oil prices, whether in the U.S. or globally.
“It’s kind of shuffling deck chairs on the Titanic,” said Michael Lynch, distinguished fellow at Energy Policy Research Foundation, a nonpartisan research institution focused on energy and economics.
“If we get diesel from Russia, basically it means that their existing customers are not going to get it and they’ll have to go somewhere else, and that will keep the price basically where it is now,” Lynch said.
And while the White House may be counting on this move to give some relief at the pump for U.S. truckers, ranchers and farmers who have been hit hard by rising diesel prices, that’s not a given.
“The best you could hope for is a tiny dip in prices locally in places like the New York-New Jersey area, Philadelphia maybe,” Lynch said. “It just means that the oil is just going to be shuffled around and it’s not really going to change the price globally or across the U.S.”
If Russia, which in July moved to ban diesel exports due to Ukrainian drone strikes on its refineries, now believes it is able to resume exports of diesel, then that will help stabilize global diesel prices, said Daniel Sternoff, senior fellow at the Columbia Center on Global Energy Policy.
However, prices are likely to remain elevated overall because a lot of refining capacity in the Middle East isn’t available to the world market due to the disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz from the ongoing U.S.-Iran war.
“Refined products like diesel are still barely half of prewar levels,” Sternoff said. “So, even if there were to be some follow-through from the Russians to put a little extra diesel into the world markets, it might take the edge off of prices, but it will not substantially lower them.”
While the deal between Trump and Putin probably won’t have much of an impact on prices for diesel consumers in the U.S., it will benefit Russia, said Clayton Seigle, an energy strategist and expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
That’s because Russia is trying to offload its summer-grade diesel for the heavier winter and arctic grades that they will need in the coming months, Seigle noted.
“I don’t think it’ll be enough to materially lower prices in the United States or Europe, but it does certainly let Moscow off the hook in terms of revenue squeeze,” he said.

NEW DELHI: Following a long period of strained India-US ties, the gloves came off finally as India hit out at US Vice President JD Vance for labelling H-1B visa holders and foreign tech professionals as foreign indentured servants, a characterisation New Delhi slammed as deeply offensive and unwarranted.The scathing response followed the US announcement about the suspension of many tech companies, including several from India, from PERM Green Card programme. Govt acknowledged the development may impact the permanent residency process of eligible employees even though the validity of existing H-1B visas or the status of those visa holders and dependants will remain unaffected.Vance had reinforced the announcement by declaring that American workers cannot be laid off and then replaced with foreign indentured servants. He also insisted that only top-tier, elite foreign talent not available domestically should be brought into US.MEA countered Vance's comments as it said in a statement that such descriptions were unwarranted.
MEA: Use of colonial legacy terminology deeply offensive
MEA said US Vice President JD Vance’s comments also ignored the fact that Indian professionals in US are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem.“Indeed, the history of the US itself has been shaped by generations of immigrants whose labour, enterprise and innovation have contributed to its growth and prosperity.
Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive,” said the ministry, adding it will continue to follow developments related to the issue.The unusually blunt pushback suggests India’s patience is wearing thin after a series of bilateral setbacks, ranging from trade and tariffs, immigration and talent mobility to India’s ties with Russia and Washington’s Pakistan outreach. External affairs minister S Jaishankar had recently warned that the US’ growing ties with Pakistan would hurt the India-US relationship.The ministry also cautioned in its response that the steps announced by the US do not advance the shared ambitions of both countries. It said talent mobility adds value to both economies, creating opportunities for Indians and helping US companies equally with cutting-edge talent, innovation, research, productivity, competitiveness and job creation, besides creating shareholder wealth in the US.
“This is therefore an area of tremendous mutual benefit for the two countries and our expectation is that all stakeholders in this process can appreciate this fact,” said Indian govt.While the America First signalling through the announcement seems designed for an electoral boost in the upcoming midterm polls, it’s unlikely to help the already rocky state of India-US ties. The timing is also problematic as it creates poor optics for PM Narendra Modi’s visit to the US in Dec for the G20 summit. It also comes just ahead of Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to India this month, during which India will look to raise its concerns related to the issue.

‘If a sibling uses a skin-lightening product, you may be more likely to use one too’. This was among the findings from behavioural research cited by the World Health Organisation (WHO) during a discussion on colourism in Hyderabad on Wednesday (October 7, 2026).
The discussion was part of ‘Complexion of Change: Challenging Colorism Through Policy, Art, and Science’, held at Goethe-Zentrum in Hyderabad. A documentary exploring global skin colour bias and the deep-rooted societal association of fair skin with higher status, beauty and success was also screened as part of the programme.
“Skin-lightening product use was not a single behaviour but was influenced by psychological, cultural and environmental factors,” said Ammaarah Martinus, Behavioural Insights consultant at the WHO.
The psychological dimension includes motivations such as wanting to appear fairer, younger or to fit into society. The cultural dimension includes the influence of families, communities and social networks. Mr. Martinus said research had found that people were more likely to use a skin-lightening product if a sibling used one. She also spoke about access to such products . In India, skin-lightening products could be easily purchased in local markets and supermarkets. “Interventions to address skin-lightening therefore need to work across all three levels rather than focus on only one aspect of the behaviour,” she added.
Psychologist and researcher Bharti Upparu said children begin receiving messages about skin colour at a very young age, often without anyone explicitly telling them that one skin tone is preferable to another. They observe who is complimented, who is bullied and who is teased, and gradually learn which physical characteristics society values. “A person perceived as fair and attractive may unconsciously be associated with other positive characteristics such as competence, goodness and trustworthiness. Such biases can compound into an overall perception of a person’s character and affect how others interact with them,” she said.
The discussion also highlighted that colourism is not restricted to women. Arpit Bhutani, co-founder of Circular Innovation Lab and moderator of the session, pointed to products marketed specifically towards men and noted that the pressure to conform to lighter-skin beauty standards also affects men.
Former Miss America Nina Davuluri recalled an incident involving a friend’s baby, when an older family member cautioned against taking the child into the sun because the child could become darker. “Such comments are not necessarily made with malicious intent but can come from a desire to see children succeed in a society where lighter skin is perceived to offer advantages,” she added.
Mercury in skin-lightening products
In remarks before the documentary screening, Monika Stankiewicz, executive secretary of the Minamata Convention on Mercury, said mercury was among the chemicals of highest public concern according to the WHO and that cosmetics were one pathway through which people could be exposed. “Mercury-containing skin-lightening products can damage the skin and may also contaminate households, potentially exposing other family members,” she added.
Ms. Stankiewicz stressed that the issue was not solely a chemical problem but also a social one linked to beauty standards and the pressure to conform to them. She said meaningful change could not come through regulations alone and that activism, art, culture and storytelling also had important roles to play.

Eradicating Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection early could become an important strategy for preventing gastric cancer, Nobel laureate and gastroenterologist Dr. Barry Marshall said, stressing the need for wider testing, appropriate treatment and confirmation that the infection has been cleared.
Dr. Marshall, who shared the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Robin Warren for their discovery of H. pylori and its role in gastritis and peptic ulcer disease, said the bacterium should no longer be regarded only as a cause of ulcers.
“H. pylori is much more than an ulcer organism. If the infection persists for many years, it can cause chronic inflammation in the stomach and increase the risk of gastric cancer. That gives us an opportunity because this is a potentially preventable cause of cancer," Dr. Marshall told PTI.
Dr. Marshall was in India to attend the World Congress of Gastroenterology (WCOG 2026) in the national capital.
Held in India for the first time, the four-day event, which concluded on October 3, brought together around 3,000 delegates from 61 countries to discuss the changing global burden of gastrointestinal and liver diseases, including H. pylori infection, gastric cancer prevention, early diagnosis and treatment.
His comments come amid renewed global focus on population-based H. pylori "screen-and-treat" programmes for gastric cancer prevention.
The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) working group has recommended such programmes in populations where the benefits are expected to outweigh potential harms.
Dr. Marshall said the priority should be to identify infected individuals and ensure they receive effective eradication therapy.
"If we can find the infection before there has been extensive damage to the stomach, we have a much better chance of preventing the chain of events that can eventually lead to cancer," he said.
However, rising antibiotic resistance is emerging as a major challenge to this approach, he highlighted.
A 2026 review in Gastroenterology noted that increasing antimicrobial resistance is threatening the success of established H. pylori treatment regimens, while concerns also remain about the effects of repeated antibiotic exposure on the microbiome.
"We cannot simply keep giving the same antibiotics and expect the same results. Resistance varies between countries and even between regions, so treatment needs to take local resistance patterns into account," Dr. Marshall said.
The IARC guidance similarly emphasises antibiotic stewardship, treatment based on local resistance patterns and follow-up testing to determine whether eradication has been successful.
Dr. Marshall said India, where H. pylori infection is common, has an important role to play in generating evidence on local bacterial strains and antibiotic resistance.
"India has a very large population with H. pylori, so it is an important setting for research. We need to understand which strains are circulating, what antibiotics are still effective and how we can make testing and treatment accessible," he said.
According to the IARC guidance, Indian recommendations have included bismuth-containing quadruple therapy in areas with high clarithromycin resistance, highlighting the importance of regional resistance patterns in treatment decisions.
Dr. Marshall also stressed that successful treatment should not be assumed simply because symptoms improve.
"Treating the patient is only half the job. We should confirm that the bacterium has actually been eradicated. Otherwise, the patient may continue to carry the infection and remain at risk," he said.
He said non-invasive testing could make detection easier and help expand screening.
Dr. Marshall has also invented PYtest, a C14 urea breath test that provides a 15-minute, non-invasive and quantitative method for detecting current H. pylori infection using a breath sample from the patient.
The patient-friendly test could help Indian doctors detect active H. pylori infection through a quick diagnostic procedure.
PYtest is available in India through Pylorium Diagnostics, part of Trimed Australia, founded by Dr. Marshall and headed by Bhanu Rahoni in India.
The need for prevention has gained urgency as gastric cancer remains a major global health burden, with the highest incidence concentrated in several Asian regions.

Thousands of security personnel deployed as Delhi braces for ‘cockroach’ protest
- Published
Parts of the Indian capital, Delhi, have been turned into a fortress, with tens of thousands of security forces deployed, as the influential Gen Z-led "cockroach" movement has called for a major protest on Saturday.
The protesters are seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists.
The Election Commission has denied this and Kumar is yet to comment on the resignation demand.
Police say they have denied permission for the gathering and all roads leading to Jantar Mantar, the main protest venue, have been closed with huge metal barricades.
Several trains to Delhi have been cancelled and police have ordered dozens of metro stations shut to prevent protesters from gathering.
But Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) - the online satirical movement that is spearheading the protests - has said the CJP will march to Jantar Mantar on Saturday morning "come what may".
"If you want to jail us or even shoot us we are prepared," he added, addressing Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a post on X.
The CJP's weeks-long protest in the summer seeking education reforms was its first major challenge to Modi's government. The CJP scored a major victory when it forced education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign in July.
The CJP protesters returned to streets last week with a rally in Mumbai city to press for CEC Kumar's resignation. On Thursday, they held a huge rally in the southern city of Bengaluru (formerly Bangalore).
Student groups and opposition parties have also protested in the capital over the past few days.
Saturday's protests are being billed as the biggest in recent times as they are also being supported by several opposition parties, farmer organisations and student groups.
CJP leaders allege the authorities have been preventing many of their supporters from reaching Delhi.
In the capital, more than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel have been deployed and authorities have appealed to citizens to stay away from protests.
Police official Nupur Prasad told a press conference, external that one of the reasons for denying permission to protest at Jantar Mantar was the "short notice" given by the CJP.
"Under current guidelines, an application to organise an event at Jantar Mantar must be submitted at least 10 days prior to the scheduled date," she said.
Also, she added that in the past, the CJP had not followed "lawful directions" given to them.
"In light of the non-compliance with prescribed procedures, the failure to adhere to past legal directions, and the current state of public safety, law and order, and traffic regulation, permission for the proposed protest at Jantar Mantar is hereby denied."
The CJP have questioned police denying them permission for the protest - they say that legally they only have to inform the police and do not need their approval to gather.
At the centre of the row is a controversial revision of the country's electoral rolls known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, which began last year.
The Election Commission says it is to remove duplicate and ineligible entries - and so far, 130 million names have been struck off the voters' list.
But opposition parties and activists have alleged that many of those are eligible voters and that the process is being manipulated by CEC Kumar to favour Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations.
The past few days have also seen a major escalation in the opposition's standoff with the Election Commission.
For three days in a row starting Tuesday, Delhi witnessed dramatic scenes with police breaking up protests by opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and other MPs over the issue.
Videos showing police forcing Gandhi on to a bus and preventing him from climbing out of the bus window subsequently went viral on social media.

Australian shark attack survivor says he hit at the predator's eye in an effort to fight it off
Shark attack survivor Mel Ismail jabbed at the eye of the predator that severed his leg in an effort to fight it off before struggling back to shore, the surfer and professional firefighter said in an interview that revealed new details of his near-dea...
MELBOURNE, Australia -- MELBOURNE, Australia (AP) — Shark attack survivor Mel Ismail jabbed at the eye of the predator that severed his leg in an effort to fight it off before struggling back to shore, the surfer and professional firefighter said in an interview that revealed new details of his near-death encounter.
The professional firefighter was surfing at Glenfield Beach near Geraldton on Australia's west coast when he was attacked on Sept. 14. He lost his right leg below the knee.
Ismail recalled in an Australian Broadcasting Corp. interview broadcast on Thursday that he was sitting out the back of the surf break and spotted a pod of about 20 dolphins before being hit by something big. It was the first time he has spoken publicly about the attack.
“I thought I got hit by a dolphin, initially,” Ismail said.
“And suddenly — bang — something grabbed me and dragged me down into the water. And I knew it was a shark,” Ismail added.
Ismail said it looked like the shark winked at him before it bit his leg.
“I got to a point where I saw its eye … a big black eye,” Ismail said.
“But it was winking back at me — I was trying to get my fingers in its eye and just pushing its eye as I was being dragged,” Ismail added.
Many sharks, including the white shark and mako shark, do not have eyelids, but when attacking prey, they roll their eyeballs backward into their sockets as a protective measure, exposing a tough layer of white cartilage. Authorities have yet to determine the species of shark that attacked Ismail.
Alone and bleeding at the back of the surf break, Ismail caught a wave that took him about 20 meters (66 feet) closer to shore.
Ismail said he was out of breath and losing strength when he spotted surfer Shannan Dunn coming down the dunes on to the beach.
Dunn went to Ismail’s rescue, helping the shark victim on to Dunn’s board.
Ismail described Dunn having “eyes like saucers.”

“The first thing he (Dunn) said to me is, ‘Where’s the shark?'” Ismail said.
“I said ‘I don’t know. I've got a bit going on here,'” Ismail added.
Once they returned to the beach, an onlooker crafted a tourniquet for Ismail using a leg rope and another onlooker phoned for an ambulance.
A pair of teenagers helped Ismail climb into Dunn's SUV and they drove along the beach to meet an ambulance.
“I had a heap of people laughing, keeping me alive, keeping me positive in the back,” Ismail said.
“I gave a few knuckles to the people there, because I was feeling good,” Ismail added. “I started to feel like I (was) going to make it.”
Four days after Ismail was attacked, 63-year-old swimmer Greg O’Neill was fatally mauled by a large white shark. O’Neill was attacked off Sorrento Beach in Perth’s northern suburbs, around 400 kilometers (250 miles) south of Geraldton.
Ismail said he intends to return to the surf as a bodyboarder.
There have been five fatal shark attacks in Australia this year.
Three spearfishing divers were killed by sharks off the Australian coast in four weeks over May and June. In January, a 12-year-old boy died in a hospital days after he was mauled by a bull shark in Sydney Harbor.
Australia has averaged between two and three fatal shark attacks a year since 2000, according to the Australian Shark Incident Database, a partnership including Taronga Conservation Society Australia, Flinders University and the New South Wales state government.

- The claim that Matthew Ingalls, one of seven Cornell University students accused of rape in a September lawsuit, fled to Dubai is still under investigation.
- The rumor stems from an article in the Daily Mail, a British tabloid, which cited an anonymous neighbor of Ingalls' uncle, who said they believed the accused man is in Dubai.
- Using old yearbook photographs and searches of public records, Snopes was able to determine Matthew Ingalls also was known as Umar Matthew Ingalls, an alumnus of Dubai International Academy. While we know Ingalls lived in Dubai at some point, we cannot confirm his current whereabouts.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We have reached out to Ingalls, the Dubai International Academy, Ingalls' former school in Washington state and the person tabloids identify as Ingalls' father in Dubai and are waiting for responses.
In October, several weeks after a lawsuit was filed accusing seven male students at Cornell University of drugging and raping a female student in 2024, a rumor spread about the whereabouts of one of the accused men. According to the claim, Matthew Ingalls — who reportedly initiated the encounter with the accuser, named in court documents only as Jane Doe — fled to Dubai, where he previously lived.
Posts on Facebook (archived) and Instagram claimed Ingalls, who the posts said also goes by Umar Matthew Ingalls, was in Dubai with his family:
Umar Matthew Ingalls, one of the "Cornell 7" accused in the alleged 2024 gang rape at the Chi Phi house, is now reportedly in Dubai, where he grew up. Neighbors of his relatives in Connecticut told the Daily Mail they believe he's back in the Middle East with his dad. How convenient.
Quick refresher on Mr. Ingalls. He's the one Jane Doe says invited her to the house that night. He's also the one who, according to messages filed in her lawsuit, shared a photo of her in the frat's Snapchat group chat and wrote "Like you can walk in and whip it out." The New York Post reports he added "Boys come whip it out." Truly the words of a gentleman.
(Facebook user Feminist News)
The rumor originated from a report in the Daily Mail, a British tabliod, that relied on anonymous sources. Snopes is unable to verify Ingalls' whereabouts as of this writing, so we have left this claim unrated. We have, however, found records of an Umar Ingalls who studied at the Dubai International Academy in Emirates Hills, Dubai, whose appearance matches that of Matthew Ingalls.
We have reached out to Ingalls — whom The New York Times reported had been expelled from Cornell — via his old college email address, to a person believed to be his father, to the Dubai International Academy and also to the Annie Wright School in Tacoma, Washington, where Ingalls reportedly studied as a child. We will update this story as we learn more.
The Daily Mail identified Ingalls as Umar Matthew Ingalls and spoke to an anonymous neighbor of Ingalls' uncle in Connecticut, where Ingalls' address was listed in court records. That neighbor reportedly told the tabloid Ingalls hadn't been seen at the home in some time and that they thought he was in Dubai.
Our public records search for Umar Matthew Ingalls found his name appeared connected to an address in South Dartmouth, Massachusetts, that also was linked to the name Matthew B. Ingalls.
The Daily Mail identified Ingalls' father as a Yale-educated professor at the American University in Dubai. We found a Matthew B. Ingalls listed as an associate professor of Middle Eastern studies at the American University in Dubai. Snopes reached out to him to verify his identity and relationship to Ingalls and will update this story as we get more information.
Several purported photographs of Matthew Ingalls have circulated, including one showing him wearing a Cornell rugby T-shirt and another from what appears to be his now-deleted LinkedIn account. According to the university's student newspaper, The Cornell Daily Sun, the school's rugby club confirmed Ingalls was previously a part of its roster.
We found that Ingalls' image from his deleted LinkedIn account had SynthID markers — which are inserted into images created with some generative artificial intelligence platforms — and was thus likely edited with AI. However, the photograph of Ingalls in his rugby shirt did not. We then compared that photograph to other images we found of him and found several matches.
Dubai International Academy's 2022-23 yearbook identifies Umar Ingalls as a member of the class of 2023 and part of the athletics team. The person in the yearbook photo appears to be the same person wearing the Cornell rugby shirt.
(Dubai International Academy)
Umar Ingalls also was mentioned in a 2022 story in the Khaleej Times, a Dubai newspaper. The article reported on a group of students who created their own version of a lunar rover. The accompanying photograph is blurry, but the student in the back right has a strong resemblance to Ingalls.
A 2020 blog post on the website for Annie Wright Schools, an elite private school in Tacoma, Washington, identified Umar Ingalls as half-American. He appeared to have studied at the Lower School until 2016 and lived in Dubai at the time the article was written. He commented on how Americans were perceived in Dubai after the election victory of U.S. President Donald Trump.

The Union Health Ministry has proposed extending restrictions on advertisements of prescription medicines to drug retailers, wholesalers and distributors, seeking to close a regulatory gap in the Drugs Rules, 1945.
A draft amendment notified through Gazette notification G.S.R. 861(E) on September 28 proposes inserting a new sub-rule under Rule 65 to prohibit holders of licences to sell, stock, exhibit, offer for sale or distribute drugs listed under Schedules H, H1 and X from advertising these medicines without prior sanction of the Central government.
Under the existing framework, pharmaceutical manufacturers are prohibited from advertising drugs covered under these schedules without prior government approval. However, the corresponding restriction does not explicitly cover entities involved in the retail and wholesale sale and distribution of medicines.
The proposed amendment seeks to extend the requirement across the drug supply chain, strengthening oversight of the promotion of prescription medicines and reducing the risk of inappropriate self-medication.
Misuse of prescription drugs
The medicines covered by these schedules include drugs that require medical supervision, including certain antibiotics and psychotropic medicines. Unauthorised promotion of such medicines can encourage their use without appropriate medical advice, raising concerns over patient safety and the misuse of prescription drugs.
The proposal follows recommendations made at the 93rd meeting of the Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB) on February 16, 2026, which examined the need for provisions regulating advertisements by holders of drug sale and distribution licences.
The Ministry has invited objections and suggestions from stakeholders and members of the public within 30 days of the date on which copies of the Gazette notification containing the draft rules are made available to the public.
The submissions received within the prescribed period will be considered by the Central government before the amendment is finalised.

Railways cite congestion, cancel Delhi-bound trains ahead of Jantar Mantar protest
West Central Railway and Western Railway cancelled several Delhi-bound trains before Saturday's Jantar Mantar protest. The move hit key services as officials cited anticipated congestion and operational reasons, not the rally.
West Central Railway and Western Railway cancelled several Delhi-bound trains on Friday, citing anticipated heavy traffic congestion in the national capital and other operational reasons. The cancellations came a day before the Cockroach Janta Party's planned protest at Jantar Mantar on Saturday, where it is set to demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
Asked whether the cancellations were linked to the planned protest, West Central Railway chief public relations officer Madhur Verma told PTI Videos, "There is no message regarding protests with us." Replying to another query, he said the trains were cancelled because heavy traffic congestion was anticipated in the Delhi area.
Verma said the five cancelled trains were the Mahakaushal Express, Jabalpur-Nizamuddin Sampark Kranti, Jabalpur-Nizamuddin Superfast, Bhopal-Nizamuddin and Kota-Nizamuddin services.
In a separate release, the public relations officer of West Central Railway, Bhopal said, "Due to operational reasons, the railway administration has cancelled Train No. 22221 Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (Mumbai)-Hazrat Nizamuddin Rajdhani Express via Bhopal from its originating station on October 9." The release added that the railway administration regretted the inconvenience caused to passengers.
Western Railway, meanwhile, said eight trains passing through the Ratlam division had been cancelled due to operational reasons, while two trains had been rescheduled. Ratlam divisional public relations officer Mukesh Kumar told PTI that the division had not received any information about the planned protest in Delhi, and that the decision was taken due to operational reasons.
The cancelled trains scheduled to depart on October 9 were the Dr Ambedkar Nagar-New Delhi Express, Indore-Hazrat Nizamuddin Express, Indore-New Delhi Intercity Express, and Bandra Terminus-Hazrat Nizamuddin Yuva Express. Their return services on October 10 were also cancelled. In addition, the Mumbai Central-New Delhi Rajdhani Express and the Mumbai Central-Hazrat Nizamuddin August Kranti Rajdhani Express were rescheduled by five hours on October 9. Overall, the railways said the cancellations and changes were made because of anticipated congestion in Delhi and other operational reasons.

Union minister Chirag Paswan on Friday said “nothing” could stop India’s youth from reaching Delhi for the planned October 10 protests against chief election commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.

The Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) has announced a protest march to Jantar Mantar in New Delhi on 10 October 2026, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. The party’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, announced the protest after demonstrations in Mumbai on 02 October and in Delhi in the days that followed. CJP leaders have said they will continue the protest even if the police stop them from reaching Jantar Mantar. As of 09 October 2026, Delhi Police had not granted permission for the proposed gathering and had tightened security ahead of the demonstration. CJP has also alleged that authorities were detaining its members and volunteers across the country to prevent them from participating in the protest, with party leaders vowing to continue the agitation (here, here, and here).
In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows women police personnel assaulting students during the CJP protest in Delhi on 04 October 2026. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows women police personnel assaulting students during the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest in Delhi on 04 October 2026.
Fact: The video predates the October 2026 Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest and shows a confrontation between the family of a man found dead under suspicious circumstances and the police in Budh Vihar, Rohini, Delhi, in July 2026. Although clashes between protesters and police were reported in Delhi during the first week of October amid demonstrations demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation, the viral video is unrelated to those protests. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to several social media posts (here, here, and here) dated 01 August 2026 featuring the same video, confirming that it predates the October 2026 CJP protest. According to these posts, the video shows an incident in Budh Vihar, Rohini, Delhi, where a young man named Ganesh was found dead in a rented apartment. Following the incident, his family staged a protest by blocking the road and making serious allegations against the landlord. The posts also describe a clash between women and police personnel during the protest.
We also found news reports (here, here) published around the same time covering the incident. According to these reports, tensions erupted in Budh Vihar, Rohini, Delhi, after the body of a 30-year-old man named Ganesh was found under suspicious circumstances at his rented house on 31 July 2026. His family accused the landlord of murder and staged a roadblock, during which they alleged that the police assaulted them. The reports also state that a woman dressed in black, identified as the deceased’s aunt, alleged that a police officer had snatched her mangalsutra and pulled her hair. These findings confirm that the viral video shows a confrontation between the family and police in July 2026, unrelated to the CJP protest in October 2026.
Meanwhile, during the first week of October 2026, clashes broke out between protesters and police in Delhi during demonstrations demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Police detained several protesters and stopped groups from reaching protest sites, while some demonstrators alleged that police personnel pushed, dragged, and assaulted them (here, here, and here). However, the viral video predates these demonstrations and shows an unrelated incident in Budh Vihar, Rohini, in July 2026.
To sum up, an unrelated video is shared as showing women police personnel assaulting students during the CJP protest in Delhi.

AI emerged as the defining theme in the Indian startup ecosystem in the July-September quarter, with startups in the segment raising their highest-ever-recorded quarterly funding. According to Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026, AI startup funding surged 265% year-on-year to $438 Mn. The number of deals rose 35% to 35 from 26 in Q3 2025. The momentum builds on a strong first half of the year. Indian AI startups raised $676 Mn across 57 deals in H1 2026, more than four times the $162 Mn raised in the corresponding period last year. With another $438 Mn raised in Q3, the sector’s funding for the first nine months of 2026 stood at $1.1 Bn+. The surge stands out against a relatively subdued funding environment. Indian startups collectively raised $2.2 Bn across 210 deals in Q3, up just 5% YoY, even as the deal count fell 13%. Quarterly funding also remained below the $3.4 Bn raised in Q3 2024 and the eight-quarter average of about $2.7 Bn. AI was not the only segment to record a significant increase in investor interest during Q3. Cleantech startups raised $433 Mn, up 267% YoY, while funding for advanced hardware and technology startups, including robotics, semiconductors and aerial vehicles, rose 176% to $290 Mn. Meanwhile, fintech funding fell 11% YoY to $249 Mn, while ecommerce funding declined 31% to $245 Mn. The divergence suggests that AI is attracting a growing share of investor capital even as funding across the wider startup ecosystem remains under pressure. But with valuations under scrutiny and large funding rounds driving the headline numbers, the question is whether AI can sustain its momentum in the coming quarters. Investors Want More Than AI Exposure Inc42’s Indian Investor Ranking & Sentiment Survey, based on responses from more than 85 institutional investors, found that about 63% of investors see some degree of froth in Indian AI startup valuations. About half of the investors who see valuation froth expect a correction within the next 18 months. Another 31% see mild froth but believe valuations are supported by real revenue. Pranav Obhrai, founding and managing partner at Atrium Ventures, said the rise in AI valuations is part of a global trend, particularly in the US. At the pre-seed stage, he said, valuations are often shaped more by capital requirements, future potential and acceptable founder dilution than by revenue or profitability multiples. For instance, a startup raising $3 Mn at 20% dilution would imply a $15 Mn post-money valuation, assuming the investor agrees to that price. Beyond valuations, investors are also becoming more selective about the AI applications they expect to create the most value. Vertical AI applications across sectors such as BFSI, healthcare, defence and agriculture emerged as the top choice in Inc42’s survey, with 39% of investors expecting this segment to capture the most value over the next five years. AI hardware and semiconductors followed at 23%, while AI-led IT and business services accounted for 18%. Indian-language and sovereign foundation models received 14% of investor votes. Data, tooling and evaluation, and AI infrastructure and compute received 3% each. Obhrai said foundation models and AI infrastructure typically have longer gestation periods than venture investors prefer. Vertical AI, by contrast, offers a clearer path towards building a defensible business through distribution. “Distribution becomes the moat, especially in India, where technology alone offers limited protection against global competition,” he said. An investor who requested anonymity made a similar distinction, pointing to the capital required to scale foundation models and model-routing infrastructure. Such businesses may have to operate at nil or negative gross margins for extended periods, a commitment that Indian venture capital firms find difficult to sustain given their smaller asset bases compared with their US counterparts. The investor added that application-layer businesses could offer more durable revenue opportunities than model-routing or foundation-model companies. While some investors are backing small language models and task-specific model developers, the capital required to build and scale the underlying technology remains a constraint. The findings suggest that rising AI funding is not translating into an indiscriminate appetite for the sector. Investors are increasingly distinguishing between businesses that can use AI to solve specific problems and those that need substantial capital to develop the underlying technology. Can AI Sustain The Funding Momentum? The scale of the funding increase raises questions about how much of the momentum reflects a broad-based expansion in investor activity and how much is attributable to large growth-stage rounds. The investor who requested anonymity said funding figures need to be assessed after accounting for sizable Series B and Series C transactions, including rounds raised by companies such as Emergent. “One would have to normalise by excluding large Series B or Series C cheques,” the investor said, adding that, in their assessment, absolute AI funding had not moved significantly after accounting for these larger rounds. This distinction matters because a small number of large transactions can lift aggregate funding without necessarily signalling that more investors are deploying capital across the sector. Obhrai expects AI to retain a strong share of startup funding, even if capital flows fluctuate between quarters. However, he warned that a broader global AI bubble bursting could trigger a correction, given what he described as arguably inflated valuations of companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Several structural factors could continue to support investment in Indian AI startups. In its H1 report, Inc42 highlighted the transition of enterprise AI adoption from pilots to production, global hyperscalers’ investments in Indian AI infrastructure, and efforts to build sovereign AI infrastructure and foundation models as drivers of the sector. However, India's AI funding pool remains much smaller than the capital being deployed globally. The H1 report noted that Indian AI startup funding was still a fraction of global investment, even as companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic raised multi-billion-dollar rounds during the same period. For Indian startups, this gap presents both an opportunity and a constraint. Growing enterprise adoption and demand for specialised applications could support further investment, but businesses requiring substantial capital to develop foundational technology may find it harder to compete with better-funded global peers. The Q3 numbers establish AI as one of the biggest drivers of Indian startup funding in 2026. Whether that momentum continues will depend on more than the size of the next funding round: investors will be watching for sustainable revenue, defensible applications and valuations that can withstand a potential correction in the global AI market. It was getting late, and the movers still hadn't arrived with the beds or the crib, so I tucked my three kids (5, 2, and 11 months) into bed on an air mattress on the floor of an otherwise empty bedroom.
I wanted to tell the kids that, once everything was set up, their room wouldn't look so bland. But the truth was, even with all of our belongings moved in, we'd only have the essentials.
I'd sold a lot of furniture and decor ahead of the move (both to get some extra cash and make the moving process less strenuous). Plus, my ex was keeping some of our shared possessions. When all was said and done, I was down to the basics.
After the kids fell asleep, I stood in my new empty living room. I realized this: At 34, I was starting over.
I met my husband when we were 17
My husband and I met when we were 17 and were together for the next 17 years. We always used to say we were lucky to have met so early and grown up together. We thought we'd be together forever.
But somewhere along the way, things changed. It wasn't that we argued all the time or didn't love each other. It was just that we'd become different people. The 17-year-old versions of ourselves were a perfect match. But I guess the 34-year-old versions weren't. It seemed smarter to just focus on being good parents and great friends.
But there was still so much to figure out. I had to decide how I was going to transition from stay-at-home mom to breadwinner. I needed to learn how to manage all household to-do lists on my own. Plus, I wanted to focus on the kids and help them through this massive change.
It was daunting and emotional. But I could take it day by day. My first task was figuring out a landing zone.
I wanted to start fresh
I could've stayed in the townhome my ex and I bought four years before, but I wanted to start fresh in a new place where I could make new memories. A blank slate.
So we put the place on the market, and I moved closer to my mom, where I could lean on her as both a babysitter and a shoulder to cry on. I focused on my first big project: making my new home feel like a warm, nurturing place for my kids and me.
We had what we needed: beds, a couch, a small dining table from one friend, and a living room rug from another. I got my blank slate — but maybe it was too blank.
We had a lot of clothes with no drawers to put them in, books with no bookshelves, and a lot of empty walls.
The walls bothered me the most. Our old place was covered in wedding pictures and smiling family photos, and while I'll admit they made me sad as my marriage was unraveling, they were still reminders of happy times. At the very least, they brought color to the rooms.
Meanwhile, these new, empty walls felt sterile and a little intimidating.
So I started hanging things up.
I wanted our place to feel like home
My daughter's preschool art pieces skipped the fridge and were lovingly affixed above the couch with painter's tape. I went to thrift stores and sifted through all the frames and paintings, finding some gems for around $10 each. I also collected mirrors to make the rooms look bigger and brighter.
Then my mom offered up a box of old art pieces I'd done in elementary school and high school, and even some oils I'd made in a college class.
I'll admit: they aren't masterpieces. But they were both free and cute. I was glad to display the watercolor of a cat I made when I was 10, among others. Why not? I wasn't trying to impress anyone with a magazine-ready "grown-up house." I just wanted it to feel homey. Plus, it was nice to connect with a younger, pre-relationship version of me. It was nice to remember who she was.
Pictures of the kids were also easy wall decorations, but I swapped framed snaps of me and my ex with a silly picture of me with Pooh Bear at Disneyland and a treasured shot of me meeting Hollywood icon Dick Van Dyke. "Look," I told a friend when she came to visit, "it's the men in my life."
Furniture was the next project.
With the walls covered, I went online for some secondhand furniture. I was tired of sitting on the laminate floor whenever I played with the kids, so I searched mainly for chairs and rugs.
I thought this would be an easy task, but after browsing listings on Facebook Marketplace, I was confused. I didn't know what I wanted.
The problem was that my husband had such a great sense of style, so I always let him pick our furniture and decor. And it worked out: I loved his clean, midcentury vibe. But was it what I'd pick if left to my own devices? I wasn't sure.
At first, I tried to search for the clean lines and angles I was used to, but after a few days of searching, I found more whimsical stuff caught my eye. I ended up driving 20 minutes to pick up a pink velvety chair. There was a green bookshelf I simply had to have. It was stuff I never would've looked at before the move, but now, I was leaning into more girly, softer styles.
I used my cat watercolor as my guide. Whenever I looked at it, with its earthy tones and cozy, soft vibe, I felt a warm sense of pride and familiarity. Maybe this was my style. Or at least a small version of it.
It's a work in progress
Now, it's only been eight months since we moved, since the reset, and the place is finally starting to feel like home. There are pictures on the wall, furniture I love, and a lot of noise and activity. My kids seem comfortable and happy. And I do too. There's something great about starting over, starting from nearly scratch, and ending up with something good.
But of course, the place isn't perfect. Some corners still feel sparse, and I've got some fixes and changes on my to-do list. It's a work in progress; I think it might be for years. And maybe right now I'm a work in progress, too. That's OK.
Recently, my mom came over after a long weekend of hanging pictures and arranging furniture. "Wow, you're really moved in now!" she said. "It looks good."
I thanked her but said I wanted to hang some floating shelves and swap some paintings around. She interrupted and wrapped an arm around me.
"Really, you've done a good job," she said. "I love it."
I looked around, feeling proud, "I do too."

Alejandro Hidalgo, director of “The Exorcism of God,” is set to make “The Hungry One,” a supernatural horror film unfolding over Malaysia’s Hungry Ghost Festival.
Kuala Lumpur-based Abnormal Studios is handling worldwide sales and is introducing the project at the Busan International Film Festival‘s Asian Contents & Film Market. Singapore-based Clover Films has already picked up rights for Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia.
The story follows Emily, an American woman who travels with Simon, her Chinese Malaysian husband, and their son Louis to spend the summer at his family’s mansion. Their stay coincides with the 15-day festival, when the underworld is believed to open and the dead mingle with the living. Emily becomes the target of escalating encounters with a vengeful presence trying to cross over, and must dig into the house’s hidden past before it takes her family.
Popular on Variety
Filmmaker and entrepreneur Justin Leong is driving the project through Los Angeles-based Lightning Pictures.
“Growing up in Asia, I always felt the Hungry Ghost Festival was incredibly rich visually, from the fire and offerings to the rituals and mythology behind it. When you capture that and shoot it cinematically, it’s movie gold. It gives us a world that audiences may not have seen before, but one that feels immediately atmospheric, mysterious and made for horror,” Leong said.
Leong, who has deep ties to Malaysian-Chinese culture, drew on his own family’s traditions to shape the story.
Hidalgo’s first feature, “The House at the End of Time,” remains Venezuela’s biggest horror hit at the box office. It earned strong notices on the festival circuit and has since gathered a cult audience for mixing the supernatural with science fiction. His 2021 follow-up, “The Exorcism of God,” bowed at Fantastic Fest and went on to sell to more than 150 countries, with Saban Films handling its U.S. theatrical release. It ended 2022 as the highest-grossing Latin American film worldwide.
Producer Harrison Allen, who won the live action short Oscar at this year’s Academy Awards for Netflix title “The Singers,” is also on board. His latest feature, “Anima,” screened at SXSW this year.
Also attached is Thomas Percy Kim, a Sundance and Toronto fellow whose debut feature “Isle Child,” based on his own short that HBO Max acquired, premiered in Toronto. Screenwriter Justin Parker worked on the development of HBO’s Emmy-nominated limited series “Station Eleven” and was a writer on docuseries “Religion of Sports.”
“The Hungry One” is in pre-production, with its producers working to lock the last portion of its financing.
Abnormal Studios, a subsidiary of Westec Media Limited, has been acquiring and releasing films since 2020 and has handled more than 400 titles to date. It now brings around 100 films a year to Southeast Asia, Australia, New Zealand, Taiwan, Mongolia and Nepal. Recent releases include “How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies” and “Twilight of the Warriors: Walled In.”

Thieves pull off Italy's biggest-ever wine heist, stealing 30,000 bottles worth 5 million euros
Thieves have stolen about 30,000 bottles of premium wine worth an estimated 5 million euros from a Marchesi Antinori winery in Tuscany in what the company says is the largest wine theft in Italy’s history
ROME -- Thieves stole about 30,000 bottles of some of Italy’s most prized wines worth an estimated 5 million euros ($5.8 million) from a winery in Tuscany, in what the producer described Friday as the country's largest wine theft on record.
The theft targeted Marchesi Antinori’s facility near Cortona, in the province of Arezzo, where a group of at least seven thieves on Saturday night made off with bottles of some of Italy's most sought-after wines, including Solaia, Tignanello and Guado al Tasso. The theft was discovered Monday, but the company made it public on Friday to avoid interfering with the investigation.
Chief Executive Renzo Cotarella said the thieves disabled the winery’s alarm system and surveillance cameras before entering with two large trucks. Using the company’s forklifts, they loaded the vehicles with wine and fled during the night.
“It is certainly a very well-prepared gang,” Cotarella said, adding that it may be the same group that has targeted other Italian wineries in recent months. “A theft of this size and value has never occurred in Italy.”
The stolen bottles were all from the 2023 vintage and are typically sold at a retail price of between 150 euros and 500 euros each. They included about 10,000 bottles of Solaia, one of Antinori’s flagship wines, from what Cotarella described as an exceptional year.
The company, founded in 1385 and run by the Antinori family for 26 generations, said it was alerting customers worldwide to be wary of offers outside official sales channels.
“We are informing our clients around the world and asking them to pay attention to any offers outside the official channels,” Cotarella said.
Authorities are investigating how the stolen wine may be sold. Police and Carabinieri officers are examining surveillance footage and other evidence. Cotarella said he remained confident investigators could trace the shipment, noting that two truckloads of wine would be difficult to move without attracting attention.
The theft eclipses previous high-profile wine robberies in Italy. In 2017, thieves stole about 2,000 bottles of rare wines valued at 750,000 euros from a warehouse near the Adriatic resort town of Cervia.

New Delhi, Oct 9: Indian telecom giant Jio is gearing up for the 6G era. The company says India could be among the first countries to roll out 6G when global standards are finalised in 2030. Jio has already developed its pre-6G stack and Giga MIMO Radio, both of which are on display at the ongoing India Mobile Congress (IMC) 2026 in New Delhi.
According to Jio, 6G networks could offer up to five times the capacity of current 5G networks, with a target to reduce latency by nearly 10 times. In simple terms, networks could handle much more data and many more users simultaneously, while responding to commands significantly faster. Data speeds are also expected to improve. These advances could unlock new possibilities for real-time AI, holographic video, healthcare, education and other next-generation digital services.
A major highlight of Jio's IMC showcase is its Giga MIMO Radio, which the company describes as India's first. Jio has also unveiled a common baseband unit that can support both 5G and 6G.
But the race to 6G isn't just about greater capacity or faster response times. It's also about helping shape the technology and global standards that will define the next generation of connectivity. Jio says it has filed more than 8,000 patents, including hundreds related to 6G. The company also claims to have made over 934 contributions to global standards.
Jio expects 6G to make AI-powered services more responsive, particularly in situations where instant information or quick answers matter. At IMC, the company highlighted potential AI applications for farmers, doctors and students. Jio is also working towards AI-native and quantum-safe networks, aiming to combine faster connectivity with stronger security.
Jio's 6G ambitions go beyond simply operating the next generation of mobile networks. The company wants to build a stronger presence across four key areas: hardware, software, patents and global standards.
Jio describes its vision through two themes: 'India's 6G in the Making' and 'From India to the World'.

Cyberpunk 2077 is the latest video game to get the movie treatment
Paramount Pictures will develop the film and CD Projekt Red will produce.
Movie adaptations of video games are currently doing a brisk business, and today brings a new title into the fold. Deadline reports that Paramount Pictures is working on a live-action film set in the world of Cyberpunk 2077, a narrative-driven RPG from CD Projekt Red. The game developer is attached to produce the movie along with Lorenzo di Bonaventura, whose past producer credits on action movies run the gamut from Red and Shooter to The Meg and several Michael Bay Transformers flicks.
It's unclear whether this is a separate endeavor from the early-stage news of a production deal with Anonymous Content announced back in 2023. Today's report is also very preliminary, with no suggestions of a plot or cast.
CD Projekt Red's Cyberpunk 2077 is already itself an adaptation of a tabletop game, so it's perhaps not a surprise that it would continue to inspire a ripple effect of retellings. The video game world of Night City has already provided fodder for the anime series Cyberpunk: Edgerunners on Netflix, which is about to return for a second season.

(Bloomberg) -- Panama was struck by its strongest earthquake in more than seven decades on Friday, prompting the evacuation of the capital’s international airport and sending people fleeing buildings as powerful aftershocks rattled the country.
The 7.7-magnitude quake struck Herrera Province, more than 120 miles (193 kilometers) southwest of the Panama Canal, according to the US Geological Survey. Economic losses in the region are likely to exceed $1 billion, according to an early USGS estimate.
The earthquake was the strongest to hit that part of Panama since at least 1951, according to the US National Earthquake Information Center. It struck at a depth of 12.6 kilometers, the USGS said.
A magnitude-6.6 aftershock hit west of the initial quake late Friday afternoon, according to preliminary USGS readings. Another eight aftershocks have been recorded at magnitude 4.8 strength or higher.
The first earthquake was caused by a rupture along a major plate boundary on the Ring of Fire, the seismically active zone that encircles the Pacific Ocean. The mechanism resembled a strike-slip event, in which tectonic plates grind past each other horizontally, according to Jonathan Tytell, a geophysicist at the US National Earthquake Information Center.
“It was a very messy event, and shallow, which is not good,” Tytell said. “The energy is right there at the surface and it doesn’t really have time or distance to dissipate.”
The USGS initially registered an 8.0 magnitude before revising it. Panama’s geological institute reported the quake as a 7.2-magnitude.
Immediately following the quake, the Pacific Tsunami Warning Center said waves of one to three meters (3.3 to 9.8 feet) above tide level were possible along parts of Panama’s coast. As of 2:42 p.m. local time, all warnings had been lifted.
The Panama Canal said operations were continuing normally, with emergency protocols activated and technical teams inspecting facilities for possible damage.
The quake was felt as far away as several Colombian cities, including Medellín, according to local media. In Panama, people evacuated buildings, businesses, schools and homes across several regions, local newspaper La Prensa said.
President José Raúl Mulino said the government was mobilizing personnel, resources and aid for people affected by the quake, and ordered ministries and public agencies to respond immediately and take preventive measures. Emergency officials were expected to hold a news conference to provide an update on the impact.
People stood barefoot or shirtless in the streets as aftershocks continued, said Cibeles De Freitas, a communications representative for the local unit of First Quantum Minerals Ltd.
“There’s a lot of fear because we’re not used to earthquakes in Panama,” she said. “We’re OK, just very scared.”
First Quantum Minerals didn’t immediately provide a comment when asked about any impact on its partially idled copper mine, located about 140 kilometers north of the epicenter.
Tocumen International Airport temporarily suspended air operations and evacuated passengers and administrative areas as a precaution while officials assessed the safety of the airport and its control tower. Some flights are being diverted to Colombia and Costa Rica, according to flight-tracking website Flightradar.
Panama City’s Metro said lines 1 and 2 were temporarily shut down because of the earthquake.
Panama’s firefighters said there were no reports of deaths or injuries in the immediate aftermath of the quake. AES Panama, a unit of AES Corp., the country’s top electricity supplier, said through a spokesperson that its hydroelectric, gas-fired and renewable power plants were operational.
Activities at the Trans-Panama oil pipeline were continuing normally after the quake, according to a statement from its operator.
Friday’s quake was the latest to hit Latin America in recent months.
Venezuela was struck by twin earthquakes in late June that killed nearly 6,500 people and caused widespread destruction along its northern coast. In Colombia, an Aug. 10 quake killed more than 330 and prompted an economic emergency as damage was estimated at roughly $10 billion.
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella expressed solidarity with Panama and offered assistance following Friday’s earthquake.
“Panama is not alone,” De la Espriella said in a post on X, adding that Colombia was ready to provide whatever assistance was needed.

Kalshi taps former FBI agent to fight against money laundering
Kalshi, a leading prediction market company, has hired a former FBI agent to run its first anti-money laundering team as prediction markets come under increasing legal scrutiny by state and federal regulators.
Sean Fern will work closely with law enforcement and regulators and senior staff at Kalshi to keep an eye on suspicious and potentially criminal activity on the platform, which has exploded in growth in the past year.
According to the firm TickerTracker, Kalshi has crossed $260 billion in bets so far this year, already triple the amount traded in all of 2025.
In an interview with NPR, Fern, who worked as a federal prosecutor in Brooklyn before his time at the FBI, said his aim is to build defenses against people trying to use the platform to commit financial crimes.
"I want to make sure it's a hard place to launder money or evade sanctions and commit fraud," Fern told NPR on Friday. "On a day-to-day basis, that involves knowing who our customers are, knowing where their money comes from, and making sure we aren't doing business with sanctioned entities or parties," he said. "And when something looks off or looks suspicious, we can catch it and make referrals to law enforcement."
The announcement echoes what cryptocurrency companies did during that sector's boom times in the early 2020s. The cryptocurrency exchange Binance, for instance, hired former federal prosecutors and FBI agents to beef up its compliance and anti-money laundering divisions. Several years later, Binance's founder Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty to money laundering charges.
Avoiding its own money laundering scandal, Fern said, is the reason Kalshi tapped him.
At the FBI, Fern was a special agent in the bureau's international corruption squad, where he helped lead the investigation into the multibillion-dollar bribery scheme tied to Malaysia's sovereign wealth fund, a scandal that became known as 1MDB.
Kalshi hopes adding Fern will lend credibility to the surging platform as it faces mounting scrutiny over insider trading and market manipulation.
Prediction market bettors can place wagers on everything from sports to what politicians say at public events to the outcome of elections. Experts have warned that introducing betting into domains like voting and policy decisions encourages people to monetize insider information.
Federal regulators and law enforcement in Washington have launched criminal investigations into alleged abuse on prediction market platforms. Earlier this year, regulators settled with former U.S. Rep. George Santos over market manipulation. Federal prosecutors have also indicted a former U.S. Army soldier and a former Google employee for allegedly using non-public information to cash out on Polymarket, Kalshi's main rival. In August, President Trump's former teleprompter operator was fined by regulators for using advance notice of the president's speeches to profit on Kalshi's so-called "mention markets."
Elisabeth Diana, a Kalshi spokeswoman, said that as banks, hedge funds and other financial institutions use Kalshi, the need to shore up financial crime safeguards has become apparent. "We are growing up," Diana said.
The company, which PitchBook estimates to be worth around $40 billion, has 250 employees, and it plans to double its headcount over the next six months.
During his time in federal law enforcement, Fern was one of the lead prosecutors in the trial of OneTaste, an "orgasmic meditation" wellness company whose founders were sentenced to prison following convictions for forced labor conspiracy.

A student hated reading for years. Her podcast explores finding the right diagnosis
LONG ISLAND, N.Y. — Cora Walsh walks home from middle school every day. It's only a few tree-lined blocks in Rockville Centre on Long Island, but the movement helps clear her head of the school day. She probably thinks about how the brain works more than most seventh-graders.
"I want to be a doctor," she says. "And I want to go to Princeton and major in neuroscience."
Her fascination started a few years ago when she was struggling to figure out what was happening in her own head.
"It's kind of confusing what it is like in my brain," she says. All she knew back then was that reading was hard. Even when she spent more time working on it than her friends, she could never reach their level.
Like millions of Americans, Cora has dyslexia, but it took her almost five years to get the correct diagnosis.
Her podcast about the journey to understanding her own mind is the grand prize winner for middle school in this year's NPR Student Podcast Challenge. "Dyslexia and MEE" was chosen from nearly 1,500 submissions from 42 states and the District of Columbia.
"I feel really excited," Cora says about her victory. Her parents, who spent the whole journey right by her side, are thrilled too.
"This is a kid that works so hard and has such a good attitude," says her mom, Emily Johnson. "I'm so proud of her."
Finding the right learning style
Cora has come a long way. She has received tutoring for her dyslexia for two years now.
Her podcast takes the listener along to one of her lessons. She sounds out words over Zoom, and her tutor gives her feedback and tips. They don't move too fast, making sure Cora really understands something before moving on.
It can be tedious, but her hard work outside the classroom is starting to pay off.
"I think I'm a better reader now, and I enjoy it a lot more," she says. "I feel more comfortable reading bigger books, but not too big!"
Her mom says that this summer marked a turning point: She saw her daughter reading the first book in the Hunger Games series.
"She would pick it up for fun, and she would go read to [her pet] rabbit. Or we were traveling this summer, and she read on the train," Johnson says. "I mean, it's the first time that's ever happened."
It was a winding road to get to this point, but Cora and her parents are excited to see where it goes. Winning NPR's national competition is another bright spot.
"I'm kind of just proud of myself that I overcame this hard, annoying thing," she says. "And proud of myself that I created something really cool and interesting that everyone can listen to."
Cora hopes that her podcast might help dyslexia feel a little less scary for listeners and maybe even reach younger students who are still trying to figure out their own learning styles.
"I would say: Always try your hardest, and don't sell yourself short," she says. "I think trying is … the best thing you can do."
Cora Walsh is still trying: She just checked out that second Hunger Games book from the library.
