Before the 2017 ODI World Cup, journalist-turned-broadcaster Gaurav Kalra led a media training session for the women’s cricket team in Mumbai. In an ecosystem rife with clichés like ‘trust the process’ and ‘control the controllables’, Kalra was tasked with helping the women get comfortable with media engagements, pushing them to be honest about their stories and journeys so their own lives inspire at least one other.
Kalra remembers Harmanpreet eagerly raising her hand to say, “ Sir, aap bol to rahe ho ki apni story bataon, par koi sunna hi nahin chahta” (Sir, you’re asking us to tell our stories, but no one wants to listen).
Life for the ecosystem nine years on looks starkly different. India has become a force to reckon with, taking its place among the game’s competitive (and not just monetary) elite. It enters tournaments among the favourites. Its players are household names now, not just in India, but also in pockets abroad where some feature regularly on the franchise circuit.
The roots of this new era of the women’s game can be traced back to this eager 28-year-old (relatively) newly appointed full-time T20I captain. She forced people to stop and listen, eventually becoming the protagonist of the vertical’s most cherished chapter (so far).
Taking space
“ Sardaran hai. Ladne ki thaakat toh uski khoon mein hai” (She’s a sardarni, that fighting spirit is in her blood) - this is former chief selector of the Indian national team Neetu David’s first adjective for Harmanpreet. Fighting is a three-act phenomenon in the life of this maverick from Moga, Punjab.
First, there was the fight to play.
Young Harmanpreet was a sports buff, playing anything and everything she could. She even tried hockey, where the stick and ball ultimately became part of a game of cricket, much to her school teacher’s chagrin. “ Bohot mushkil se bacchon ko cricket se hockey tak le aaye hai hum. Aap yeh na karein (It’s taken a lot to get kids to pivot from cricket to hockey. Don’t do this now),” she once cheekily recalled.
“ Pehle hi dekha ki jo log six marte hain, unki bohot value hai (It was evident to me very early on that those who hit sixes, their value is a lot higher),” Harmanpreet said of her formative days in the sport. Her coach Kamaldeesh Pal Singh Sodhi spotted heroics of the sort watching her smack the ball while playing with a group of boys. He didn’t know if she was a boy or a girl, given her long locks were tied up in the trademark sikh high bun.
Young Harman only knew the bat and ball in her hands. She knew not of any pathways of progress, or what would come of her life should she stick with cricket and nothing else. The 80s and 90s had no women’s cricket on television, so there were no ambitions for her to soak off a screen.
But Sodhi did and he saw what Harmanpreet would mean for the sport if she could extrapolate the raw spunk he saw into enduring legend. So did her father Harmandar Singh Bhullar. Given his own sporting success at state level, he wanted his daughter to go past him and clinch the honour of donning an India jersey some day. All when his daughter did not even know of the existence of the women’s side.
Sodhi built a women’s team around Harmanpreet and she repaid the faith by eventually building a new culture of excellence which ultimately led her and her pack to the sport’s biggest podium.
Simple pleasures
Former India international Soniya Dabir’s earliest memory of Harmanpreet is one from the manual - a six she hit in the U-19 inter-zonal match in Pune. She was the local manager then.
“That was the first time I saw a player at that level hit such a long six. She could smack sixes at will and the difference was immediately apparent in the stance, the backlift… She decides ki abhi aane wala hai and we prepare,” Soniya says.
In a domestic Challenger series, the pair were teammates and eventually even became roommates during the 2010 T20 World Cup in the West Indies.
That Harmanpreet was naive, untouched by the burdens of spotlight and just grateful to make cricket her life’s fulcrum. She would happily eat the same food regularly, diligently follow workout regimes on repeat and also, unfortunately for Soniya, play the same song on loop for days on end.
“I would keep a lot of songs loaded on my phone, but hers had just one song called Tere Liye. For almost 12-16 hours, she would play it. I had enough eventually. There were no Hindi channels in the Windies at the time.”
“She had a routine she followed strictly. She prayed everyday, she did her things a certain way. It stopped for nothing, no one and no result. She used to be able to switch off really well. Kuch carry forward nahi hota tha pichle match ka (Nothing carried forward from one match to another) . That was a good thing, to take each day for what it is.” Fifteen years later, that very trait would help Harmanpreet bhangra her way towards the ODI World Cup trophy before a manic crowd at the D.Y. Patil Stadium in Navi Mumbai on a dewy November night.
Legendary Indian legspinner Neetu David, who was the chair of selectors when India reached the One-Day zenith, fondly remembers the Punjaban who took on Railways in the domestic circuit.
“Back then, the Indian Railways was as good as the Indian national side,” Neetu says. “The way she fearlessly tackled out bowlers and as good as led the batting effort made us feel like this girl would go places and maybe even captain India someday.”
After getting employed by the Western Railways, Harmanpreet – who now can’t venture out into any street in India without being mobbed – would sprint through streets to catch the Mumbai local, shuttling between work and training at Bandra Kurla Complex. She unabashedly admits to sitting on Diana Edulji’s head to get exemptions sanctioned so her stomach wouldn’t kill her heart’s desires.
Diana’s condition was clear: help Railways win the domestic tournament first. The rest eventually fell into place.
Unending hunger
From here, Harmanpreet realised just how much ‘change’ would come to define her chapter in Indian cricket. She moved from the Railways to Punjab Police to be able to be closer to home. The Women’s Big Bash League came calling in 2016 when she became the first Indian to feature in an overseas league, having signed with Sydney Thunder.
It reinforced a love affair with the systems Down Under that began in the late 2000s when she and M.D. Thirushkamini were sent for an exposure trip there.
Former India captain Purnima Rau, who had selected her for that tour in 2007, took charge as head coach in 2014, two years after Harmanpreet had stepped up in the absence of an injured Mithali Raj and Jhulan Goswami to lead India to the first of what would eventually be four Asia Cup triumphs.
“She was a very raw, energetic kid who was very hungry for knowledge. That ambition was evident in her eyes,” she says.

Bring up Harman and her thoughts go back to an earnest 26-year-old who stayed back for advice after the dressing room had cleared post a series win against New Zealand.
“I am usually the last one to get out of the dressing room or the team bus so I can check if players have left anything behind. One such day, I found Harman standing there. She held my hand and said, “Ma’am, I want to do much better than what I’ve done. What should I do?”” Purnima remembers being asked.
She recalls copious notes on technique, on how she urged Harman to be audacious on the front foot and tweak her elbow placement to extend her field of strokemaking.
In Purnima, the evangelist Harmanpreet would eventually become for Indian cricket found her first believer. Both agreed on one fundamental element - India was talented enough and gutsy enough to win not one ICC title, but three. This was without the Women’s Premier League, little to no media attention and a system that made it a point to tell the girls they were good, but just not good enough.
A disappointing home T20 World Cup campaign, where India sank in the group stage, meant India found itself increasingly jaded by Mithali’s steady, risk-free brand of leadership. Harmanpreet’s aggressive, unbending style of batting was already turning heads. It wasn’t long before Mithali made way for her deputy in the shortest format.
But all of that would be eclipsed by a superhuman effort in Derby in the 2017 ODI World Cup, a monstrous knock that would lay the foundations of ‘Harmonster’ as she would come to be called, and a particular penchant for treating the world’s most decorated and dangerous side - Australia - like a puppy slinging around a rope toy.
Harman vs the odds
That unbeaten 171, which both made and, many times, broke Harmanpreet has to be among the most documented knocks in the history of the game. Like a raging Spanish bull, a red-faced and hungry Harmanpreet hacked Australia down.
For Purnima, however, it was Harman’s effort 149 days prior to that knock that has her respect.
“Everytime I’ve coached a side, I gave my captains a book when they won a series. Mithali got seven books from me. Harman got one, for the ICC qualifier before the 2017 World Cup. One by Shiv Khera,” she remembers.
Chasing 245 for victory against South Africa in the final, India needed eight runs off the last two balls. Harmanpreet, the stand-in skipper, smacked the ball over the midwicket ropes and then ran two to send her dugout into a tizzy at the P. Sara Oval in the heart of Colombo.
“She fought with the last wicket (Rajeshwari Gayakwad). That six she hit sums up everything about her. Forget her captaincy. She did well, that’s a given. But for me, as a player, tagda thi wahan pe (She was tough),” Purnima declares.
2017’s big high and equally ravenous low came and went, but what remained was the adulation and then fascination of the general public, all waiting for the next big news from this bunch.
Unfortunately, the squad served rotten meat to vultures waiting to feast and from singlehandedly sculpting a memorable pièce de résistance, Harman suddenly became the face of one of the biggest controversies to rock the system. A bitter tussle for power which involved leaks and snide comments and much in between saw Harmanpreet and Mithali on two sides of what looked like an irreparably torn national side.
The 2018 T20 World Cup became the battleground.
Facing England in the semifinal, skipper Harman made a temerarious decision to drop Mithali for the knockout fixture. Mithali had batted in just two games in that campaign, scoring 50s on both occasions. She picked up a knee injury and didn’t feature in India’s 48-run group stage win against Australia. Harman defended her decision saying she wanted to stick to a winning combination.
Things, however, didn’t go as planned, with India folding for 112 in 19.2 overs, its last eight wickets falling for just 23 runs. England didn’t blink as it sealed an eight-wicket win.
“Whatever we decided, we decided for the team. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn’t, no regrets. I’m proud of the way my girls played through the tournament,” she said defiantly then. But the apple cart had been blown to smithereens.
The fallout of this incident added to an already tumultuous time for the side, with two coaches – Purnima and Tushar Arothe – finding themselves out of the scheme of things rather unceremoniously, documented to be at the behest of the players. Ramesh Powar, earlier an ally to Harmanpreet, was also shown the door, not once but twice. W.V. Raman, too, was not retained, and with no explanation.
Team first
Raman unenviably walked into a broken dressing room masquerading as a team.
“Harmanpreet was obviously hurt, and she felt she was blamed for no fault of hers about a lot of things that happened before. It’s very easy for us to live in the past. I sat them both down and said I didn’t intend to go back there. Let’s try and start with a clean slate.”
He pushed Harman to be large-hearted and focus on the time she has to leave her imprint behind as captain and player.
“I told her that she needed to try and make an identity for herself. Of course, she had been doing that as a player but for her to make an impact as captain, she couldn’t afford to be distracted by the past or by how people outside were trying to box her in. At some point, I even read an interview where she said she contemplated leaving the game. Fortunately, she carried on,” he says.
Harman was not one for diplomacy and Raman cites that as one of her attributes he values the most.
“A lot of things have been said about her for the simple reason she just spoke her mind. She did not have the finesse like some of her predecessors to try and convey things in such a manner. No matter what the implications were, no matter what people might think about her decisions, she came across as somebody who did things the way she felt she needed to do. Perhaps, that’s not something people always look at kindly. But that is Harman for you. It’s always good for people to be different, or the world would be a very boring place,” he shrugs.
The musical chairs in leadership positions is an Indian cricket staple, particularly in the women’s game. Purnima remembers how friends quickly became foes as selectors rolled in and rolled out ‘one series captains’ in their blind quest for results, which is why she underlines that permanence as the enduring legacy of both these players.
“Stability is important for any captain,” Mithali says. “But a long tenure also has to come with accountability. You have to keep assessing whether the team is progressing and whether the captain is still the right person for the next phase.”
“Harman had that time, and there were different phases to her tenure, good and difficult. But that continuity allowed her to shape the team in her own way. That is ultimately the value of giving a captain a long rope,” she adds.
Breeding belief
In the eight years that passed, Harmanpreet first defined her (in capital letters) side as one that could enter tournaments as favourites, that could give Australia and England a run for their money.
India’s march to the final in the 2020 T20 World Cup was imperious. The campaign was propped on the captain’s unflinching faith in the prodigious abilities of a 16-year-old Shafali Verma. However, like it had many times before, India’s ambitious castles were watered down by the mighty Aussies, with nearly 90,000 people watching at the Melbourne Cricket Ground.

“It would have been the perfect gift if we were to win on that day because it was played on her birthday. That was not to be, unfortunately. It would have kept the side going through the COVID-19 pandemic which followed for a year and a half right after. That was a challenging phase,” Raman reminisces.
“Maybe it was the early stages of her captaincy or the fact that India was so near yet so far all the time… That victory could have perhaps proved to the world that they’re capable of winning a World Cup, that she is capable of winning a World Cup. And that’s something that she wanted for the team to do because India was always looked upon as an entity that didn’t have the wherewithal to win the World Cup. She wanted to change that. A lot of things were riding on that particular final. So it was a bit frustrating.”
This was around the time calls for a women’s Indian Premier League were growing increasingly louder. Losses saw even board officials lament about not having sufficient talent to stage a league. Harman credits former BCCI secretary Jay Shah for breaking that cycle, breaking the unending chase the women’s team was set on to first achieve before having the guts to ask for foundational sporting architecture.
Another opportunity presented itself in 2023. Once again, Australia stood in India’s way and would eventually push India back like a bully cordoning off privileged territory. An unfortunate run out involving Harmanpreet and some stinging yet nonchalant criticism from new captain Alyssa Healy triggered the makings of a memorable rivalry to spice up a vertical bedrotting in the lull of Meg Lanning – its most decorated commander – shockingly calling time on her international career.
The group stage exit in the 2024 T20 World Cup, by their own admission, hurt the side the most. Systems were changing. The Women’s Premier League had turned two. Harmanpreet and Smriti Mandhana, her eventual successor, had won the first two editions. With new coach Amol Muzumdar, experiments and fresh perspectives were the Women in Blue’s oxygen. But the side returned from the arid Emirati deserts with their tails tucked between their legs.
A desolate Harmanpreet, spacing out at the post-match presentation after yet another gutsy fight against Australia, became the image of that dismal campaign. That perhaps explains why the tears were so unaesthetically raw in 2025, when India overcame the mighty Aussies before a raucous home crowd in the semifinal in Navi Mumbai.
When Jemimah Rodrigues and Amanjot Kaur brought India home, Harmanpreet sat with trenches for creaselines on her forehead in the dugout, Smriti hugging her as they saw victory inch closer. As Smriti led the entourage out to embrace a tired and emotionally broken Jemimah, Harmanpreet roared away into the dugout, with Deepti Sharma and Muzumdar enveloping her from either side.
“I would actually say the World Cup victory. For me, that will define her captaincy more than anything else. Indian women’s cricket had waited a long time for that ODI World Cup, and Harman was the captain when it finally happened. There were different phases to her tenure, but that achievement will naturally stand out. That is a significant part of what she leaves behind as captain.”Mithali Raj
She might have enjoyed one single song on loop for days on end all those years ago in the West Indies, but she was tired of taunts, disbelief, “go back to the kitchen” jibes. History repeated herself. Once, Harman validated the aspirations her father and coach saw for her. On October 30, 2025, Harman’s team realised hers. The coronation a few days later, the unquestionable cementing of her legacy, may have taken some doing, but was a mere formality.
India’s own angry, young woman
Amitabh Bachchan popularised the trope of the angry, young man in Indian cinema, allegorical of the mood of the nation then. Harman became that symbol for the women’s game. Remember how she rained down on poor 19-year-old Deepti when she almost ran Harman, then on 98, out. Evidently, Harman was not hunting the ton, but the win. The pair hugged and made up soon after and India clinched that epochal win.
That same Deepti she reduced to tears in Derby had Harman’s complete backing at Lord’s in 2022, when she ran out Charlie Dean at the non-striker’s end which helped India seal 3-0 ODI series sweep.
When asked, Harman snapped back at why the other nine wickets weren’t as interesting to talk about before unequivocally stating, “I will back my player. She’s not done something which isn’t in the rules. It shows our awareness.”
Little under a year later, Bangladesh faced Harmanpreet’s wrath enough for her to become a yardstick for bad behaviour for the system there. Stumps were smashed, nasty things were said, umpires were accused of favouring the home side and a prompt two-match ban was slapped on the Indian skipper too.
Harman, consistency personified, quietly served the ban without an ounce of regret. “I don’t think I said anything wrong to any player or any person. I just said what happened on the field. I don’t regret anything,” she said later.
That unbridled anger is something Raman remembers from his early days with the mercurial (now) former Indian skipper.
“In the run-up to the 2020 World Cup, there was a murmur in the side. The girls were a little scared, a bit peeved by Harman giving everyone a piece of her mind. One of our warm-up games was rained out, so I sat her down and began talking about a couple of other captains. Harman knows me to be direct and was a little puzzled by why I was beating around the bush and asked me in so many words.
“I then told her that different captains have different methodologies but this cannot be a system of top-down management all the time. It might not always work. She needed to do what was possible to get the best out of her teammates.
“I suggested that if she wanted to let loose, we could nominate a player for every game to be her punching bag (not literally, of course) and we’ll get on with it. She slept over it and came back back and said there was merit in what I said. Things then suddenly changed. She hardly said anything on the field.”
“Players came raising issues with that too and all I said was, ‘You can’t complain about everything.’ Harman controlled was better than her letting loose,” he quips.
Legacy and a wheel that refuses to break
A year is a long time. India soaked in the hysteria of a World title far too many thought would never arrive. Soon, it was time for another World Cup, but a disastrous campaign in 2026 and another group stage exit followed.
Harmanpreet Kaur’s captaincy record: 211 games across formats
A now 37-year-old Harman, with diminishing returns with the bat, could not fight the pendulum swinging towards Smriti, long understood to be India’s captain-in-waiting and in the form of her life. The 30-year-old growing increasingly vocal of her ability and willingness to lead the nation only fanned a flame that needed no help spreading.
That image from 2025, the camaraderie from the ones before that, all seemingly made way for subtle distances that rabid fanbases of both players frothed at the mouth to blow up online.
In early October, images emerged on an Assamese news portal of Harman and Smriti in Guwahati with BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia. A day later, Harmanpreet announced her decision to step down from Indian captaincy.
This is a woman who jumped up for the World Cup-sealing match with an injury in her left knee. The same woman who played that 171 knock with a dislocated finger had to be held back by the team doctor from venturing out for the second innings despite severe dehydration. Somehow, though, the words of her resignation felt loaded with far more pain.

There is an interview with Harmanpreetwhere she describes how the balance and make of the bat doesn’t matter, but the grip does. If it doesn’t feel like she has full control, it ruins the full experience. Now, the grip has been yanked away.
For a Punjabi girl growing up on a sporting diet, the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics was the perfect carrot to push her ageing and hurting body through a few summers for that one coveted gold medal. She comes from a hockey and athletics hotbed and a State that values Olympic golds like divinity. She still has a shot at it, but not as the bird leading the migration. She won the fight to play and the fight for collective belief. But she couldn’t prolong the fight to lead.
Paisa and pyaar
Harmanpreet’s journey cannot be detached from the financial whirlwind that has embraced the women’s ecosystem. Noopur Kashyap, her manager, has seen Harman’s “value’ grow into a bankable commercial face for big brands.
“In 2017, women’s cricket was still emerging. Viewership was still quite limited. We began with digital campaigns so she could at least be seen,” Noopur explains.
Harman got a lot of webinars around the lockdowns and that gave her team the confidence that people want to hear what she has to say. That translated to on-ground events and activations and eventually to big brand deals, the arc hitting its peak right after the 2025 ODI World Cup. When Navi Mumbai woke up to continue ringing in India’s triumph barely five hours after the final, Harman had already been named brand ambassador for real estate firm Omaxe Ltd.
Harman loves a photoshoot but the larger world of brand engagements was alien territory for her for quite a while.
“For her to be at a shoot for eight hours would be draining, with the lights, arrangement and people. But send her to a cricket field for as long and she’d be totally fine. That shift came about with the WPL. It taught players to balance training and matches with shoots thanks to how advertising and appearances are coded into franchise operations,” she explains.
Noopur stepped in for Harman at a time when the math involved in being a ‘brand’ in sports left her utterly confused. The fear of being misled or cheated was there too and since then, Noopur has been Harman’s firewall. Over the years, a girl who was once mistaken for a boy now loved seeing herself on posters, cover shoots and ad films.
Noopur sees this next phase of her career as an opportunity for Harman to finally make her life’s favourite thing – cricket – about herself.
“Harman’s never been one to have a big circle. You won’t see her doing dinners, outings etc very often. She has missed out on all this and wants to experience it all. She’s drawn her legacy. She also wants to be more socially available. Captaincy and its responsibilities came with several personal restrictions. Even going home was a challenge. She lives away from her parents to be close to an airport so she can report for duty anytime. Those are things she will be able to address now,” she says.
In the 2025 final, after a job well done, Harmanpreet running to her father and Bhullar lifting her up like she was five again was among the unforgettable frames of that triumph. It was anything but just the adrenaline from the night, Noopur suggests.
“Harman comes from a very simple, non-city background. She wants time with her family. Her parents are getting older. She watched her sister’s wedding on video call. Both her siblings stay abroad. She doesn’t talk about all this but it really matters. It’s why that hug with her dad after the final means so much. That’s what she misses.”
Epilogue
This exercise of documenting Harman the captain might seem like an end-of-career tribute piece. It’s perhaps inevitable considering how much of Harman’s life in this sport has gone into taking the lead in some form.
“Captaincy suited her. She wanted things to happen all the time and wanted the team to win. It suited her personality and her mindset. She’s been a captain all along. She now has a chance to show what kind of a leader she can be. It’s time to create an ever bigger legacy,” Raman says.
“Captaincy does add pressure, because you are thinking about the team even when you are batting. But I wouldn’t put Harman’s batting inconsistency entirely down to captaincy. She has always had periods of outstanding batting and periods when she hasn’t been as consistent, even before she became the all-format captain,” Mithali explains.
“What captaincy does is add another layer to that. When you are not scoring, you are answering questions about both your batting and your leadership. Now she doesn’t have that additional responsibility. So she has the opportunity to concentrate on her batting and let her performances speak for her,” she adds.
Harman has been the genesis of the rule of fitness and form in this ecosystem and now stands consumed by the very frameworks she cemented in place.
She was part of a side that is infamously reported to have pushed for a male coach – which led to Purnima’s sacking. But she is now part of a franchise setup that has always championed women in the coaching staff, from Charlotte Edwards and Lisa Keightley to India’s own Jhulan Goswami and Devika Palshikar.
It’s been a long vigil for an unapologetic servant of the game, who now finally has the space and reason to fire up this next chapter just for herself. As one of her early coaches told Harman (as documented in Sidhanta Patnaik and Karunya Keshav’s “T he Fire Burns Blue”), “No bowler can get you out unless you want to get out. Everything is in the mind.”
Chardi Kala, Harmanpreet.
“Apart from the World Cup title, she’s won so many Test matches for India as captain. That’s an equally good record. India, for the longest time, didn’t play Tests. It’s not easy to win these against England and Australia when you’re leading a side in all three formats. Winning that Test match at Lord’s after exiting the T20 World Cup, where they had to sit and watch other teams get through the end and push for a win in the Lord’s Test, was incredible. Credit to her for that record too!”Soniya Dabir

Below, we look back at the celebrities we lost in 2026, listed in alphabetical order.
Scott Adams, 68
Scott Adams worked at a telephone company in the 1980s. The experience inspired his beloved comic strip, "Dilbert."
By the end of the decade, the character and his satirical office humor began appearing in comic strips.
At its peak, "Dilbert" was syndicated in over 2,000 newspapers. A cartoon series debuted in 1999, running for two seasons.
Adams gained notoriety when he began writing blog posts praising Donald Trump during his 2016 presidential run. In 2023, "Dilbert" was pulled from newspapers across the US following racist comments made by Adams.
Adams died on January 13 from metastatic prostate cancer.
Brad Arnold, 47
The lead singer of 3 Doors Down, Brad Arnold launched the group into fame with the 2000 rock anthem "Kryptonite," which peaked at No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 that year.
The success led to other hits like "Loser," "Here Without You," and "When I'm Gone." Arnold's vocal range and lyrics focused on love and love lost, which fueled the group to stardom.
Arnold died on February 7 from a type of kidney cancer.
Afrika Bambaataa, 68
A hip-hop pioneer during the 1970s and 1980s, Lance Taylor, known professionally as Afrika Bambaataa, first gained attention as a DJ in the Bronx.
He signed with Tommy Boy Records in 1981 and released landmark songs like "Jazzy Sensation" and "Planet Rock." He would go on to influence the likes of Queen Latifah and A Tribe Called Quest throughout his career.
Bambaataa founded the hip-hop awareness group, Universal Zulu Nation, in the 1970s to steer kids away from gang life. Bambaataa stepped down as the head of the organization in 2016 after accusations of sexual abuse.
Bambaataa denied all claims.
He died on April 9 due to prostate cancer.
Rob Bass, 59
One of the icons responsible for bringing hip-hop to the mainstream, Rob Bass crafted the iconic track "It Takes Two" alongside DJ E-Z Rock.
The track, released in 1988, reached No. 3 on the Billboard Hot Dance/Club Songs chart and later went certified platinum. In 1989, it was voted the greatest single of all time by Spin magazine.
Bass died on May 22 following cancer.
Nicholas Brendon, 54
Nicholas Brendon was a television actor, best known for playing Xander Harris in all seven seasons of "Buffy the Vampire Slayer."
He also starred in "Criminal Minds" and "Kitchen Confidential."
Brendon died in his sleep on March 20 due to natural causes, according to his family's statement.
In 2023, Brendon suffered a heart attack and was diagnosed with a congenital heart defect. He also had cauda equina syndrome, which led to several spinal surgeries.
"While it's no secret that Nicholas had struggles in the past, he was on medications and treatment to manage his diagnosis, and he was optimistic about the future at the time of his passing," the statement to The Hollywood Reporter read. "Our family asks for privacy during this time as we grieve his loss and celebrate the life of a man who lived with intensity, imagination, and heart."
Peabo Bryson, 75
Two-time Grammy winner Peabo Bryson is best known for his classic love ballads.
Bryson began releasing music in the late 1970s, but one of his first major hits was opposite Roberta Flack on the 1983 duet, "Tonight, I Celebrate My Love." He continued hit-making a year later with the smash "If Ever You're in My Arms Again," and in 1991, he topped the R&B charts with "Can You Stop the Rain."
Bryson found global stardom with his renditions of two Disney classics. In 1991, he released the pop version of "Beauty and the Beast," alongside Céline Dion, and a year later, he duetted with Regina Belle on "A Whole New World" from the 1992 release of "Aladdin."
Bryson died on June 2. No cause was given.
James Burrows, 85
An 11-time Emmy winner and co-creator of "Cheers," director James Burrows helped shape modern TV comedy through his work on iconic sitcoms including "Will & Grace," "Friends," and "Frasier."
Known for his comedic timing and elaborate blocking, Burrows got his start directing episodes of "The Mary Tyler Moore Show." Throughout his career, he directed episodes of "Frasier" (winning an Emmy for the pilot episode), "Will & Grace," "Friends," and "The Big Bang Theory." He directed over 50 pilot episodes.
Burrows died on June 19. No cause was given.
Kyle Busch, 41
Two-time NASCAR Cup Series champion Busch was considered one of the greatest racers of all time.
Busch was hospitalized on May 21, before two upcoming races. Hours later, he was pronounced dead.
Busch died from severe pneumonia that progressed into sepsis.
Robert Carradine, 71
Robert Carradine was best known for his roles as Lizzie McGuire's dad and as the iconic geek Lewis Skolnick in the 1980s franchise "Revenge of the Nerds."
As a member of Hollywood's famed Carradine family, Robert was destined for an onscreen career.
He received one of his first screen credits starring in his brother David Carradine's popular 1970s TV series "Kung Fu" and went on to land roles in everything from Samuel Fuller's World War II classic "The Big Red One" to the "Lizzie McGuire" series.
Carradine's family shared statements with Deadline that emphasized being open about his struggles with mental illness.
"We are bereft at the loss of this beautiful soul and want to acknowledge Bobby's valiant struggle against his nearly two-decade battle with Bipolar Disorder," Carradine's family said. "We hope his journey can shine a light and encourage addressing the stigma that attaches to mental illness."
Carradine died by suicide on February 23.
If you or someone you know is experiencing depression or has had thoughts of harming themself or taking their own life, get help. In the US, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. Help is also available through the Crisis Text Line — just text "HOME" to 741741. The International Association for Suicide Prevention offers resources for those outside the US.
Bud Cort, 77
Most famous for his role as Harold in the 1971 cult-classic "Harold and Maude," Bud Cort became the epitome of 1970s counterculture thanks to his baby-faced looks, wit, and sophisticated persona.
The dark comedy starred Cort as Harold, a man in his 20s who is obsessed with suicide until he meets 79-year-old eccentric Maude (Ruth Gordon).
Before that, Cort scored bit parts in Robert Altman's "M*A*S*H*" (1970) and "Brewster McCloud" (1970).
After "Harold and Maude," Cort worked steadily for the rest of his life, occasionally showing up in hit movies like Michael Mann's "Heat" (1995) and Wes Anderson's "The Life Aquatic with Steve Zissou" (2004).
Cort died on February 11 following a long illness.
Tim Curry, 80
Curry is best known for playing Dr. Frank-N-Furter in the cult-classic musical "The Rocky Horror Picture Show," after originating the role in the original stage production.
Over six decades, Curry carved out a niche playing outlandish villains like Rooster Hannigan in the 1982 film "Annie" and Pennywise in the 1990 miniseries "It." Other notable roles include Wadsworth the Butler in "Clue" (1985) and Mr. Hector in "Home Alone 2: Escape from New York."
Curry suffered a major stroke in 2012, which required brain surgery. He said in 2025 that he was "still recovering."
Curry died at his Los Angeles home on August 26. No cause was given.
Eric Dane, 53
Long before becoming one of TV's most recognizable heartthrobs, Eric Dane was building his career with guest roles on series like "Saved by the Bell" and "Married… with Children."
He later gained wider attention with appearances on "Charmed" before landing his breakout role as Dr. Mark "McSteamy" Sloan on "Grey's Anatomy." He most recently starred in HBO's "Euphoria," where he played Cal Jacobs, the father of Jacob Elordi's character, Nate Jacobs.
Dane has two children with his wife, Rebecca Gayheart. In April 2025, the actor said that he was diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS.
Dane died on February 19 at age 53, his publicist confirmed in a statement to Business Insider.
"He spent his final days surrounded by dear friends, his devoted wife, and his two beautiful daughters, Billie and Georgia, who were the center of his world," his publicist said.
Clive Davis, 94
A legend in the music world, Davis was responsible for elevating pop music to unthinkable heights by discovering talents like Aretha Franklin, Barry Manilow, Bruce Springsteen, Billy Joel, Whitney Houston, and Alicia Keys, to name a few.
Over his 50-year career, along with being an executive behind millions of album sales, he also won five Grammys, including two for Album of the Year ("The Bodyguard" soundtrack and "Supernatural" by Santana).
Davis died on June 22. No cause was given.
Mike Ditka, 86
Mike Ditka was the first tight end ever inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame. As a coach for the Chicago Bears, he led the team to its only Super Bowl win to date in 1986.
Ditka's success turned him into a celebrity who showed up in commercials, TV shows, and movies in cameo roles.
One of his most famous was starring opposite Will Ferrell in the 2005 comedy "Kicking and Screaming."
His persona became the long-running "Saturday Night Live" sketch called "Bill Swerski's Superfans," in which cast members dressed up as Ditka and spoke about their love for "Da Bears."
Ditka died on October 9; no cause was given.
Robert Duvall, 95
Robert Duvall starred in a plethora of timeless classics, including "The Godfather," "The Godfather Part II," "Apocalypse Now," "THX 1138," "The Natural," "Days of Thunder," and "The Apostle."
Duvall will be best remembered for starring in three of director Francis Ford Coppola's iconic films: playing Tom Hagen in the first two "Godfather" movies and Lieutenant Colonel Bill Kilgore in "Apocalypse Now," in which he delivers one of the most memorable lines in movie history: "I love the smell of napalm in the morning."
Duvall was lauded for his acting talent, from not saying a word while playing Boo Radley in his first big screen role in the 1962 classic "To Kill a Mockingbird" to his portrayal of a country singer dealing with alcoholism in 1983's "Tender Mercies," which earned him an Oscar.
He died on his ranch in Virginia on February 15. No cause was given.
Brenda Fricker, 81
This Irish actress was a fixture on the stage and screen for six decades. But she's most known for showing up in the "Home Alone" sequel.
As The Pigeon Lady in 1992's "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York," Fricker has become a fixture for families during the holiday season for decades (and in 2020 became the subject of a popular meme).
But Fricker's acting talents go beyond playing a spooky wanderer of Central Park.
In 1990, she became the first Irish actress to win an Academy Award, as she was given the best supporting actress Oscar that year for her performance in "My Left Foot."
Fricker died on July 16; no cause was given.
Mark Fuhrman, 74
Fuhrman cemented his place in popular culture as one of the lead LAPD detectives on the 1995 murder case of O.J. Simpson's ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend Ronald Goldman.
Fuhrman found the famed bloody glove on the Simpson estate, and during the trial, he gained infamy when Simpson's defense team used his past racist language to discredit him as a witness.
Fuhrman retired from the LAPD after the Simpson trial and moved to Idaho, where he wrote true crime books.
Fuhrman died on May 12 of throat cancer.
Valentino Garavani, 93
For over six decades, one name has been synonymous with women's high fashion: Valentino.
The Italian designer launched his fashion business in Rome in 1960 and never looked back. Soon, every star wanted to be seen in his creations. They've been worn by icons like Elizabeth Taylor, Joan Collins, Jackie Kennedy, Princess Diana, Sharon Stone, and more.
Though Garavani retired from designing in 2008, his label is still a red carpet staple, as is his famous shade of bright red dubbed "Valentino Red."
Garavani died on January 19. No cause was given.
Donald Gibb, 71
No one defined a bully for a generation more than Gibb's hulking fraternity character Ogre in the "Revenge of the Nerds" movies of the 1980s.
Since the original raunchy comedy was released in 1984, Gibb's intimidating size and loud yells of "NERDS!" have become as memorable as the pocket protectors worn by the movie's geeks.
Gibb went on to star opposite Jean-Claude Van Damme in his classic 1988 action movie "Bloodsport." He also landed guest star roles through his career on shows like "Quantum Leap," "Magnum P.I.," "MacGyver," "Night Court," and "Cheers."
Gibb died on May 12 following health complications.
Chad Gilbert, 45
Gilbert was the guitarist and backing vocalist for the punk band New Found Glory.
The band's hit albums include 2002's "Sticks And Stones" and 2004's "Catalyst." Both showed up in the top 10 on the Billboard 200 chart.
Gilbert died on September 20; no cause was given, but Gilbert told People in April he was battling stage 4 adrenal cancer.
Glen Hansard, 56
Irish singer-songwriter Hansard was the frontman of the rock band The Frames and one-half of the band The Swell Season. But he was perhaps best known for writing and starring in the hit 2007 indie film "Once," in which he and his Swell Season bandmate Markéta Irglová play two struggling musicians who fall in love. The duo won an Oscar for best original song for the film's standout track, "Falling Slowly."
Hansard also embarked on a solo career; his 2015 album, "Didn't He Ramble," was nominated for a Grammy for best folk album.
Hansard died on July 29 in a motorcycle crash in Dublin.
Dennis Haskins, 75
For those who grew up in the '90s, Dennis Haskins was your favorite high school principal, Mr. Belding.
Starring in the hit TV series "Saved By The Bell," Haskins' Belding character traveled the halls trying to be a step ahead of the hijinks inflicted by Zack Morris (Mark-Paul Gosselaar) and his friends. But unlike many school principals in pop culture who were mean and seemed to hate kids, Haskins played his authority role with a playful, good-natured style.
He was on the show's full four-season run from 1989 to 1993, and also starred in the spin-off, "Saved By The Bell: The New Class," from 1993 to 2000.
Haskins' other credits include "The Bold and the Beautiful," "Mad Men," "It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia," and "New Girl."
Haskins died on September 27; no cause was given.
Anthony Head, 72
Rising up through the UK stage scene in the 1980s, Head found fame when he was cast as Rupert Giles, who became a father figure to Sarah Michelle Gellar's Buffy Summers in all seven seasons of "Buffy the Vampire Slayer."
Most recently, he played the bitter former owner of AFC Richmond on "Ted Lasso."
Head's death was announced by his family on June 5. They stated the cause was "complications due to pneumonia."
David Hockney, 88
British painter David Hockney was renowned for his striking portraits and figurative pop art. Many of his best-known paintings, including 1966's "The Splash" and 1972's "Portrait of an Artist (Pool with Two Figures)," were inspired by the bright colors and sun-dappled pools of Los Angeles.
Hockney moved to Los Angeles in the late '60s, and his work became synonymous with the warmth and leisure of Southern California. He was also one of the few popular artists at the time to depict openly gay scenes, and Hockney was outspoken about anti-gay censorship.
Throughout his career, Hockney split time between California, England, and France. He died at his home in London on June 12 at age 88, his publicist confirmed to The New York Times. No cause of death was given.
Jesse Jackson, 84
The Rev. Jesse Jackson was a leader of the Civil Rights Movement, a minister, and an activist icon who twice ran for president.
Born on October 8, 1941, in Greenville, South Carolina, Jackson experienced Jim Crow segregation on public buses and at school firsthand. It would shape the rest of his life.
His fight for civil rights began in the 1960s, when he helped organize protests and demonstrations across the US and worked closely alongside civil rights icon Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.
His decadeslong career as a leading civil rights activist included support for modern national movements, such as the push for voting rights, the fight against racism, and a higher minimum wage.
Jackson ran for president twice, both times as a democrat. He placed third for the party's nomination in 1984 and second in 1988. This marked the most successful presidential runs of any Black candidate prior to Barack Obama.
Jackson announced in 2017 that he'd been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease. In November 2025, Jackson was treated in a Chicago hospital after complications from progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), a rare neurodegenerative condition.
Jackson died on February 17.
Yayoi Kusama, 97
Kusama was a famed Japanese pop artist who often used polka-dot motifs in her work, initially rising to prominence in Japan in the 1950s.
In 1959, Kusama presented her first solo exhibition in New York: a collection of abstract paintings that an ARTnews review praised as "strong, advanced in concept and realized."
Kusama later branched into sculptures, performances, and immersive installations. She continued to expand her influence and relevance into the social media era, when her mirrored "Infinity Room" installations became Instagram-friendly attractions that inspired many copycats.
Kusama died on August 14 in Tokyo. She was 97.
Bob Mackie, 87
As one of Hollywood's most renowned costume designers, Bob Mackie's eye set the style for decades.
Known as the Sultan of Sequins, the Rajah of Rhinestones, or the Guru of Glitter, a signature of Mackie's work was its use of sparkle, which made everyone from Cher to Elton John to Dolly Parton to Sabrina Carpenter shine on stage.
He also was the costume designer on "The Carol Burnett Show" for all eleven seasons through the 1970s. He won nine Emmys, a Tony Award, and was nominated for three Academy Awards for his work.
Mackie died on September 14; no cause was given.
Patrick Muldoon, 57
In the 1990s, you couldn't escape the piercing eyes of Patrick Muldoon.
He played Austin Reed on "Days of Our Lives" for most of the decade, and when he wasn't on the soap, he was over on "Melrose Place" playing the villain role of Richard Hart.
If being on two iconic shows wasn't enough, he also showed up on "Saved by the Bell" and had a role in the cult classic movie "Starship Troopers."
Muldoon died on April 19 after a heart attack.
Sam Neill, 78
With a career spanning more than five decades and including countless memorable performances in movies and television, Sam Neill was one of the most versatile actors of his generation,
The New Zealand actor starred opposite Nicole Kidman in the 1989 thriller "Dead Calm," played the loyal first officer opposite Sean Connery in 1990's "The Hunt for Red October," played the lead in John Carpenter's 1994 horror "In the Mouth of Madness," and most recently starred in the hit series "Peaky Blinders."
But Neill is best known for playing the brave and all-dinosaur-knowing Dr. Alan Grant in the "Jurassic Park" franchise.
Neill died on July 13; no cause was given. Neill was battling a rare and aggressive form of blood cancer, but was cancer-free at the time of his death, according to a post on his Instagram account announcing his passing.
Tom Noonan, 74
Standing at a towering 6' 5", Tom Noonan was born to play the bad guy. And he did just that, starring as the villain in movies like "Manhunter," "RoboCop 2," and "Last Action Hero."
But this actor had more to show off. He showcased his comedy chops as Rodney Dangerfield's degenerate gambling friend in the 1983 comedy "Easy Money," and set up the heist for Robert De Niro in Michael Mann's 1995 classic "Heat."
His knack for storytelling also translated behind the camera. Noonan wrote, directed, and starred in the drama "What Happened Was," which won the grand prize at the 1994 Sundance Film Festival.
Noonan died on February 14; no cause was given.
Chuck Norris, 86
Few action stars have Chuck Norris' credentials.
Before he ever stepped in front of a camera, he was a martial arts champion and a black belt in Karate, judo, Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, Taekwondo, and Tang Soo Do.
His talents would become known the world over in 1972, when he faced off against Bruce Lee in "The Way of the Dragon."
Through the 1980s, Norris became one of the biggest action stars in the world thanks to movies like "A Force of One," "The Octagon," and the "Delta Force" and "Missing in Action" franchises.
In the 1990s, he took over the small screen, playing the lead in the "Walker, Texas Ranger" TV show, which aired in over 100 countries during its run from 1993 to 2001.
Norris was hospitalized on March 19 in Hawaii and died the following day, according to his family. No cause was given.
Catherine O'Hara, 71
O'Hara, who was best known for her roles in "Beetlejuice" and "Home Alone," got her start in the Canadian comedy scene, appearing in the now-legendary cast of "SCTV."
It would mark the beginning of a fruitful partnership with fellow actor Eugene Levy, who became her frequent costar and collaborator in memorable appearances in Christopher Guest films like "A Mighty Wind" and "Best in Show" and television series like "Schitt's Creek," which earned her an Emmy Award for outstanding lead actress in 2020.
O'Hara's representative confirmed her death to Business Insider on January 30. The Los Angeles County Department of Public Health confirmed in a death certificate viewed by People that O'Hara died of a pulmonary embolism, with rectal cancer listed as an underlying cause.
Hayden Panettiere, 36
Panettiere began acting as a child, landing one of her earliest major roles as Sarah Roberts on the ABC soap opera "One Life to Live," on which she appeared from 1994 to 1997.
As her career progressed, she became best known for portraying Claire Bennet on "Heroes" and Juliette Barnes on "Nashville."
Over the years, Panettiere had spoken openly about her struggles with alcoholism and postpartum depression. She detailed those experiences in her memoir, "This Is Me: A Reckoning," which was released in May.
Panettiere died on August 16. A final autopsy report by the Greenville County Coroner's Office ruled her death an accident caused by the toxic effects of fentanyl and other drugs.
Dolly Parton, 80
Parton released her debut album, "Hello, I'm Dolly," in 1967 and went on to pen country hits like "I Will Always Love You" and "Jolene," both of which were released as singles in 1974.
In addition to her music, Parton was beloved for her flamboyant style and her philanthropy. She founded the Dollywood Foundation in 1988, a charitable organization focused on education and community initiatives in her home state of Tennessee. She continued to fund scholarship programs and donate to hospitals, public health initiatives, and disaster relief programs throughout her life.
Parton is known as the best-selling female country music artist of all time. She was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1999, the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2001, and the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022.
Parton's 49th and final solo studio album, "Rockstar," was released in 2023. The tracklist included both original material and covers of classic rock songs, featuring an array of guests like Paul McCartney, Ringo Starr, Sting, Joan Jett, and Parton's goddaughter, Miley Cyrus.
News broke on August 25 that Parton died following unspecified health issues. She was 80.
Vincent Pastore, 80
This character actor found fame appearing in a string of mob movies in the 1990s, like "Goodfellas," "Carlito's Way," and "Men of Respect." But Pastore truly became a star when he was cast in the hit HBO series "The Sopranos."
As Salvatore "Big Pussy" Bonpensiero, Pastore was part of the main cast for the first two seasons of the show, playing Tony Soprano's mob enforcer-turned-FBI informant. Bonpensiero's shocking death was one of the most famous in the show's history and proved that no one was safe from getting whacked.
Pastore died on August 1. No cause was given.
Valerie Perrine, 82
Perrine found herself cast alongside the biggest stars of the 1970s.
She played the love interest opposite Jeff Bridges in 1973's "The Last American Hero" and Robert Redford in 1979's "The Electric Horseman." She earned an Oscar nomination for starring alongside Dustin Hoffman in 1974's "Lenny."
For most, she'll be remembered best for sharing the screen with Gene Hackman as the secretary to his evil Lex Luthor in 1978's "Superman." She also starred in the sequel. As Ms. Teschmacher, her loyalty to Luthor is questioned when she rescues Superman (Christopher Reeve) after he's chained with Kryptonite.
Perrine died in her home in Beverly Hills on March 23. She was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease in 2015.
Sonny Rollins, 95
One of the most influential jazz musicians in history, Rollins recorded more than 60 albums over his seven-decade career.
His live album, "A Night at the Village Vanguard," is considered one of the greatest jazz albums ever made.
Rollins died on May 25; no cause was given.
Eva Marie Saint, 102
An Oscar and Emmy winner, Eva Marie Saint appeared in classic movies in Hollywood history.
She made her film debut starring opposite Marlon Brando in Elia Kazan's 1954 classic "On the Waterfront," which won her the Oscar for best supporting actress. In 1959, she heated up the screen with Cary Grant in Alfred Hitchcock's defining thriller "North by Northwest."
In 1990, she won an Emmy for her work in the miniseries "People Like Us."
Saint died on October 6 of natural causes.
Neil Sedaka, 86
Sedaka is responsible for some of the biggest pop songs of the 1960s and 1970s.
The Brooklyn native wrote over 500 songs, including classic hits like "Laughter in the Rain," "Breaking Up Is Hard to Do," "Bad Blood" and the Captain & Tennille song, "Love Will Keep Us Together."
Sedaka died on February 27; no cause was given.
Gene Shalit, 100
Before there was Rotten Tomatoes or even Siskel & Ebert, movie lovers got their recommendations from Gene Shalit.
The iconic movie critic could be seen sporting his signature look of glasses, bushy hair, and big mustache as a staple on the "Today" show from 1973 to 2010. If he wasn't interviewing the biggest movie stars, he was reviewing movies with incredible puns ("'Ishtar' is Ish-terrible.")
His larger-than-life presence left a mark on pop culture: he was parodied as a Muppet and on countless episodes of "SCTV" and "Saturday Night Live."
Shalit died on June 12; no cause was given.
Duncan Sheik, 56
Sheik found success in the late 1990s with his hit song "Barely Breathing." He later pivoted from alt-rock to a career on Broadway, composing the music for the Tony-winning musical "Spring Awakening." His other stage credits include "American Psycho" (2013) and "The Secret Life of Bees" (2019).
Sheik died on September 17 after a cardiac arrest.
Kiki Shepard, 74
In her 15-year tenure as a co-host on "Showtime at the Apollo," Kiki Shepard was considered royalty at Harlem's famed Apollo Theater.
Known in the building as "Apollo Queen of Fashion" thanks to her dazzling outfits, Shepherd was a fixture on the show from 1987 to 2002.
Throughout her career, Shepard also appeared on TV shows like "Baywatch," "A Different World," "NYPD Blue," and "Grey's Anatomy."
Shepard died on March 16 after suffering a heart attack.
Gloria Steinem, 92
An icon in the women's liberation movement of the 1970s, Steinem dedicated most of her life to fighting sexism.
Starting her career as a journalist, she became a columnist for the newly founded New York Magazine in 1968. She cofounded Ms. magazine in 1971, which focused on women's issues. She also helped launch the Women's Action Alliance, which focused on tackling sexism.
Steinem was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2013.
Steinem died on September 2, according to a post on her social media. No cause was given.
Béla Tarr, 70
Hungarian filmmaker Béla Tarr became a legend in the arthouse world for his unflinching work featuring several-minute-long takes.
With movies like "Family Nest" (1979) and "The Turin Horse" (2011), Tarr showcased his slow cinema style while focusing on marginalized characters living bleak lives. Tarr pushed the envelope with his style when he made "Sátántangó" in 1994, which had a run time of 450 minutes.
His work influenced several arthouse filmmakers, including Jim Jarmusch and Gus Van Sant's "Death Trilogy" ("Gerry," "Elephant," and "Last Days").
Tarr died on January 6 following a battle with a "long and serious illness."
James Tolkan, 94
You might not recognize the name, but if you're a movie fan, you know the face.
Tolkan's tough-guy persona made a mark on movie history in films like "Top Gun" and the "Back to the Future" franchise.
In "Top Gun," he played Commander Tom "Stinger" Jardian, who famously gives Tom Cruise's character a tongue lashing, saying, "Your ego is writing checks your body can't cash."
In "Back to the Future" and its sequels, he played Principal Strickland, who had zero tolerance for "slackers."
Other credits include "Serpico," "WarGames," "Masters of the Universe," and "Dick Tracy."
Tolkan died on March 26; no cause was given.
Ted Turner, 87
Ted Turner changed the television landscape thanks to his maverick maneuvers to harness the 24-hour news cycle.
After taking over his father's advertising company in the 1960s at the age of 24, Turner embarked on a path to change the media landscape by buying up radio and TV stations around the South. He even bought sports teams including the Atlanta Braves MLB team and the Atlanta Hawks NBA team.
All of that programming would eventually become part of TBS, a "super station" that showed old movies, reruns, and Braves and Hawks games.
Turner then set his sights on the news. He founded CNN, the first 24-hour news channel, in June of 1980.
Over the decades, Turner gained celebrity status, particularly after marrying Jane Fonda, a union that lasted from 1991 to 2001. In 1991, he was named Time's "Man of the Year." He sold his networks to Time Warner for $7.5 billion in 1996.
Turner died on May 6; no cause was given.
Bonnie Tyler, 75
Welsh singer Bonnie Tyler became one of the biggest artists of the 1980s thanks to her legendary power ballads.
Tyler was behind hits like "Total Eclipse of the Heart" and "Holding Out for a Hero," which was also featured on the 1984 "Footloose" soundtrack. Both songs were chart-toppers that have since become two of the best-selling singles of all time.
Over her career, Tyler was nominated for three Grammys and was appointed a Member of the Order of the British Empire (MBE) by Queen Elizabeth II in 2022.
Tyler died on July 8 in Portugal, where she was being treated for an illness, according to a statement posted on her social media.
James Van Der Beek, 48
Van Der Beek was beloved all over the world for his role as the titular teen Dawson Leery on the WB series "Dawson's Creek."
The series, which ran from 1998 to 2002, turned Van Der Beek into a star and a teen heartthrob. While "Dawson's Creek" was still airing, he'd cement his stardom playing the lead role of high school quarterback "Mox" Moxon in the 1999 coming-of-age drama "Varsity Blues."
Van Der Beek found steady work the rest of his career in movies like "Texas Rangers" and "The Rules of Attraction, and memorably played a fictional version of himself on the TV series "Don't Trust the B---- in Apartment 23," and performed on "Dancing with the Stars" in 2019.
Van Der Beek learned he had stage 3 colon cancer in 2023, and publicly announced his diagnosis in late 2024.
Van Der Beek previously told Business Insider that the news came as a shock, given the subtleness of his symptoms and his efforts to stay as healthy as possible.
"I was doing everything," he said. "I was doing sauna, cold plunge, weightlifting, Pilates. I would dance and also do football training."
Van Der Beek died on February 11.
Bob Weir, 78
Weir was one of the founding members of the Grateful Dead.
The singer-songwriter wrote and/or sang on songs like "Sugar Magnolia," "Playing in the Band," "Truckin,'" "I Need a Miracle," and "The Other One."
After the Grateful Dead disbanded in 1995, Weir went on to form several other bands, including Kingfish, Bobby and the Midnites, RatDog, The Other Ones, and, alongside John Mayer, Dead & Company.
In the summer of 2025, Weir was diagnosed with cancer.
Weir died on January 10.
Victor Willis, 74
Willis was the lead singer of the iconic disco band the Village People.
Along with being the lead vocalist and dressing as the police officer (and sometimes naval officer), Willis was also the cowriter on many of the band's hits, including "In the Navy," "Macho Man," and the song that will keep the Village People in pop culture lore until the end of time, "Y.M.C.A."
Willis left the band to embark on a solo career in 1979, then re-formed the Village People in 2017.
Willis died on June 30 following a "short but aggressive illness," according to the Village People Facebook page.
Frederick Wiseman, 96
For over five decades, Wiseman's brand of non-fiction storytelling put a spotlight on everyday people.
From high schoolers to hospital workers to Air Force cadets training for nuclear war, Wiseman's close to 50-film catalogue is an unvarnished reflection of America over the last half century.
Wiseman died on February 16. No cause was given.

The visuals in the footage have an authentic origin, but the audio has been edited to significantly change the meaning of the prayer.
On Oct. 4, a social media user posted a video purportedly depicting a man leading a group of Arkansas farmers in prayer, asking "baby Jesus" for "more Mexicans" to replace the "Mexicans we had deported" to save their farms.
The user posted the footage to Facebook (archived) and Instagram (archived). The audio seemingly shows the man leading the prayer saying:
Dear Baby Jesus, please help us. We're losing our farms. We know we sent all the Mexicans away. Dear Lord, please send us some more Mexicans to replace the Mexicans we had deported. We're going to lose our farms; please, Baby Jesus and all things holy. Amen.
The clip spread amid numerous reports of rising prices and trade wars impacting U.S. farmers.
In short, the visuals in the video have an authentic origin, but the audio has been edited to significantly change the meaning of the prayer. Therefore, we rate the audio as fake.
The authentic footage originates from a broadcast by KATV 7, a TV news station in Little Rock, Arkansas. The channel posted the segment to YouTube on Sept. 2, 2025 (archived), more than a year earlier than when the edited clip was circulating. It shows hundreds of Arkansas farmers in a school gymnasium seeking the federal government's help regarding their financial struggles.
At about 2:24, the video cuts to a man leading the farmers in prayer. He can be heard saying:
Farmers, in my opinion, dear Lord, and it's only my opinion, are closer to you than anyone else on this Earth because we deal with your Earth every day. Dear Lord, we're hurting, dear Lord. We can't help what's happened to us.
According to KATV 7's article about the event, also published on Sept. 2, 2025, the farmer then said, "We need help, dear Lord."
Another piece of evidence that the "more Mexicans" iteration of the clip is edited is the quality of its audio. The prayer in the edited version is sharp, clear and lacking an echo. Inside a school gymnasium, the audio of the farmers praying should, in reality, feature an echo, like the man's voice does in the original footage.
Both Facebook and Instagram identified the audio as original to Aaron Beltrán, the person who appeared to first post the edited clip on both platforms.
Snopes reached out to Beltrán to ask whether he originally edited and posted the manipulated video, if the voice is his own and if the content was meant to be satirical. We will update this story if we receive a reply.

The era of Amazon's Fire tablets—cheap slate computers ranging from $60 to $280—is over.
All of the Fire tablets are being replaced by the all-aluminum Amazon Alexa Tablet. These tablets will, in a first for Amazon, run official Android and have full access to the Google Play Store. The lack of proper app support was always a sticking point for the Fire tablets, which ran a custom version of Android and had a much more limited app library.
The new Alexa Tablet series comes in three models: the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro ($500), Alexa Tablet 11 ($330), and Alexa Tablet 8 ($230), with the numbers corresponding to the display size. Amazon is also offering kids' editions of the latter two devices at the same prices. These include bumper cases for extra protection, a one-year, worry-free guarantee to replace the device if it breaks, and a year of Amazon Kids+ service to fill the tablet with age-appropriate content.
As for Fire tablets, Amazon says it will stop shipping the devices in the next month or two. It will support them for four years from the last ship date. Amazon is committing to at least four years of software updates for the new Alexa tablets, which will launch with Android 16 and will receive Android 17 early in 2027. Preorders for the new Alexa Tablets are open now, and they'll begin shipping on October 14.
Premium Tablets
The experience is largely the same on all three tablets, with aluminum builds designed to mimic the new aluminum Kindles. The MediaTek Dimensity 8189 chip powers the two smaller tablets, whereas the 12-inch device gets a little more power from the MediaTek Dimensity 8400.
The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is the outlier of the trio, as it's the only one with two display variants: a standard 12-inch LCD screen or a 12-inch Nanomatte display with anti-glare and anti-reflective properties. Upgrade to the Nanomatte—starting at $550—for a matte, paperlike look and feel. With a peak brightness of 500 nits, it should still be bright enough to view in sunlight.

Amazon says it developed this screen in partnership with Corning (the company that makes most of the glass that protects smartphone displays). It's similar to the matte displays found on devices like TCL's Nxtpaper series, though Amazon's vice president of devices, Kevin Keith, says the hexagon-shaped imprint on the Nanomatte display can push out vivid colors and crisp blacks while still retaining those matte properties.
The screen also offers a “really good” writing experience, according to Keith. He says the same engineers who worked on the Kindle Scribe worked with Corning to get that paperlike feel. The screen works with Amazon's new Alexa Tablet Pro Pen ($90), which has 4,096 levels of pressure sensitivity, plus tilt detection. The pen can magnetically dock to the top of the slate for charging and pairing. Amazon also sells a Pro Keyboard ($150) for the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, which attaches to the device via the pogo pins on the bottom edge—no Bluetooth needed.
Now that Android has recently gained multiwindowing features, attaching the keyboard turns the largest Alexa tablet into a productivity machine: split apps across the screen, resize them into various windows, and “save” several desktop arrangements so you can pick up where you left off.
For the kids’ versions of the Alexa Tablet 11 and Alexa Tablet 8, Amazon says the software is still Android with a heavily customized interface for kid-friendly content and built-in parental controls. Keith says one in five kids in the US has an Amazon tablet, so it'll be interesting to see how that changes now that these devices start at a higher price.
Alexa Front and Center
It may look and feel like Android, but Amazon has tweaked the interface to make these Alexa Tablets feel like Amazon hardware.
The top-left corner of the home screen features a persistent widget called the Dynamic Tab. This scrollable widget lets you dive into Amazon content you may have been consuming on another device—say, if you were reading on your Kindle, watching a movie on Prime Video on your iPhone, or snapped some photos and you want to view them on Amazon Photos.
Swipe right, and instead of Google's Discover feed, you're instead greeted with Amazon's For You experience. Amazon's Fire tablets were a vehicle to put Amazon content in front of your eyeballs, and that hasn't changed with the Alexa Tablets. Again, you can continue consuming content here, with tabs for movies and TV, games, and Kindle. There's also a news feed, and you can tap Alexa prompts for more information on a story.
Uniquely, opening the Kindle app triggers “Kindle mode,” which disables all notifications, turns on the blue light filter, and extends battery life to 20 hours (less on the smaller tablets). You can also choose one of three display treatments in this mode: subtle warmth with natural color, a softened paper tone, or monochrome. There's even a fun page-turn effect that mimics turning a page in a book. As soon as you exit the app, notifications turn back on, and the screen returns to normal. Annotations you make with the stylus will sync with Kindle apps on pen-supported devices, like the Kindle Scribe.
As the tablets’ names suggests, Alexa+ is front and center. So far, Amazon has restricted Alexa+ access to paid subscribers or Amazon Prime customers, but Keith says you don't need to subscribe to anything to use Alexa+ on these devices.
In the bottom-right corner, a persistent “Ask Alexa” chat box lets you call up the virtual assistant immediately. You can also trigger it by saying, “Alexa,” just like an Echo device. It can control your smart home devices, but the marquee addition is Alexa's On-Screen Intelligence. It's opt-in—with an on-screen indicator whenever it's active—allowing the assistant to see what you're looking at and answer contextual questions.
For example, if you're traveling to a new city and are looking at a guide filled with restaurant recommendations, you can ask Alexa, “Which of these is closest to my hotel?” and it can filter the list. Got a schedule for your kid's soccer games? Bring up Alexa and ask it to add all the events to your calendar.
Alexa+ also supports live sessions—much like Google's Gemini Live or ChatGPT's Voice Mode, you can have a real-time back-and-forth conversation with the assistant without speaking the wake word at every turn. Watching a TikTok and wondering whether a product in the video is available on Amazon? Naturally, you can ask Alexa, and the assistant can even add it to your shopping cart.
The hardware may finally have the look and feel of other premium Android tablets, but these slates are still built to keep you hooked on Amazon's retail empire.

Ethiopia warns Eritrea it will defend itself after troops cross border
- Published
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of an "all-out invasion" of its northern Tigray region and warned it will defend itself, days after residents told the BBC Eritrean troops had crossed into the country.
In a letter to the UN Security Council, Ethiopia's foreign minister called it a "blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia's inherent right to self-defence", following reported strikes on Eritrean troops in Tigray.
Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel responded by saying it was facing "an unprovoked war of aggression" from its neighbour.
Fighting broke out between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), two weeks ago.
Both blame each other for violating a 2022 deal that ended its civil war. Ethiopia says Eritrea backs the TPLF, which it denies.
During the two-year civil war, Eritrea was a key ally of the Ethiopian government, having fought alongside them against the TPLF.
But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated - largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports - leading to the severing of diplomatic ties last week.
Accusing Eritrea of violating its sovereignty, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said Eritrean forces had advanced up to 60km (37 miles) into Tigray.
Ethiopian drone strikes reportedly targeted Eritrean forces in the Tigrayan town of Adigrat on Wednesday and Thursday, amid fears of a wider regional war.
US-based conflict monitor Acled said "Eritrean troops and ammunition" in Adigrat were hit by "multiple drone strikes" overnight.
One resident told AFP news agency "there were many, many drone strikes", and that some Eritrean lorries had been destroyed.
Another witness said Eritrean forces appeared to be retreating north after the strikes, AFP reported.
Dated 8 October, Ethiopia's letter to UN Security Council members read: "In this time of difficulty, when Ethiopia is left with no other option but to defend itself, we count on your understanding, support, and solidarity."
But while Ethiopia accuses its neighbour of supporting the TPLF, Eritrea has blamed the conflict on Ethiopia's leaders, and accused them looking for a reason to seize Eritrean territory.
On Friday, Eritrea's information minister called the accusations levelled against Asmara as "duplicity in their most extreme forms".
In a post on X, he said Ethiopia was "openly working to bring about regime change in Eritrea by providing shelter and support to certain mercenaries who claim to be opposition".
Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, but ties were only normalised in 2018, when Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power.
This latest unrest follows months of tension and the launch of new alliance of armed groups in Ethiopia - including the TPLF - in September.
Last week, TPLF forces withdrew from Tigray's main city of Mekelle, which is 115km (71 miles) south of Adigrat and is now under army control.

Mercedes critics think I'm Satan - Wolff
- Published
Mercedes Formula 1 boss Toto Wolff says critics who accuse the team of bias against George Russell are "brainless".
The British driver's championship hopes were all but extinguished by an engine failure while he was running third at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia last Sunday.
Russell enters this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix 86 points behind team-mate Kimi Antonelli, and will start from the back because of a grid penalty for using too many engine parts.
Wolff described accusations of favouritism towards Antonelli as "completely nonsensical".
He added: "We've had it in the past with Lewis (Hamilton) fans.
"I mean, literally, I don't know what's going on. Do they think I have a button that says, 'George engine failure now', or disadvantaging one driver against the other when we are fighting for a Constructors' Championship, when we have always had the mindset of providing everybody equal material?
"But I guess this is maybe where social media goes today. People hide behind their screens and then they lash out.
"There's a lot of polarisation going on, and sometimes I read what people write. I find it hilarious. These people really contribute to my own entertainment when they are abusing the team or myself. I'm Satan, I've heard."
Wolff emphasised that he had always pursued a policy of equality between drivers since he took over the leadership of Mercedes in 2013.
He underlined his close personal relationship with Russell and Antonelli, who are both long-time proteges of the team and Wolff personally.
"We have had Kimi since he was 11," Wolff said. "He is an integral part of the team.
"It is very nice to see him grow, be in a position now that he is fighting for a championship at such a young age, the talent he has.
"And then on the other side, George, who has been with us since he was 17, someone that I feel a lot of, how can I say, emotions for and compassion. We are very close."
He said he and his wife Susie socialise with Russell and his fiancee Carmen Montero Mundt.
"We are spending time with Carmen and Susie off the track with each other," he said. "If people would see that we're travelling together, we're having coffee in the same coffee shop, we're going to the gym.
"That's why it's pretty annoying to have some lunatics that have no understanding really about how relationships work coming up with these kinds of accusations.
"So, I don't pay any attention to this. Most important is that George knows how the team is and Kimi knows, and we will always try to give them equal opportunity."
He said a "good example" of the equal treatment of both drivers was this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix.
The team has decided to split the specification of its cars at Marina Bay after an upgrade in Malaysia last weekend failed to provide the expected step forward in performance.
Russell is using the previous spec car and Antonelli the new one.
Wolff said: "We don't know which one is going to be quicker."
He said initial indications were that the "new car seems to be a little more tricky to drive - not saying it's necessarily slower, because there will be goodness in it, but maybe we haven't just found a way of putting it all together and tuning it.
"The older car is a bit more stable, grippy, but that is really just one data point. That is one free practice session, and it will be needing more time to really come to more conclusive information."
He said the success or otherwise of the upgrade, Mercedes' first significant change to the car's design since June, could have significant ramifications on Mercedes' preparations for 2027.
"We've put a few months of upgrades into the car, clearly pointing in a direction that we think is advantageous," Wolff said, "and maybe we just need to calibrate it a little bit in order to find the right way forward for 2027."
