A claim that retired professional U.S. soccer star Megan Rapinoe called for Super Bowl champion and ESPN analyst Jason Kelce's firing began circulating online this week.
Snopes readers searched for references to Rapinoe and Kelce on this website, which led us to consult search engines DuckDuckGo and Google for basic details about why the two names were making the rounds together. We located a popular Facebook post (archived) that appeared on the Empire Sports Facebook page on Oct. 5, reading in part:
MEGAN RAPINOE: Calls for Jason Kelce to be FIRED..
Megan Rapinoe criticized Jason Kelce after he used Washington's former team name during a live broadcast.
"I know Jason Kelce said that racist name on purpose to create division. He should be fired immediately."
— Megan Rapinoe
The comments under Empire Sports' post indicated some people believed Rapinoe truly called for Kelce's firing.
Other users shared the rumor on Facebook (archived) and Threads (archived), though the original Empire Sports Facebook post earned far more likes, comments and shares than other examples.
In sum, while it's true Kelce mentioned the old Washington Redskins' team name during a TV broadcast, Rapinoe did not call for his firing.
The Empire Sports page displays a disclaimer acknowledging it publishes fabricated content of a parodical and satirical nature, reading, "Delivering the Finest of Sports Parodies / Satire / Updates / Insider News & much MORE." In other words, Empire Sports does not publish authentic news reports.
The aforementioned searches of DuckDuckGo and Google located no news media outlets credibly reporting Rapinoe said any such things about Kelce. Rapinoe's active Instagram page also did not feature any content about him.
Snopes emailed representatives for Rapinoe and Kelce to ask if either wished to address the popular made-up story. The Empire Sports page didn't display a Messenger button or any other contact methods.
Purveyors of misinformation and fabricated stories — whether labeled as parody and satire or not — have long wielded Rapinoe's name and image as politically-fueled engagement bait, whether for social media posts or website traffic, sometimes thinly disguised as satire. Part of the reason for the firestorm of controversy in this instance stems from U.S. President Donald Trump's comments about Rapinoe, and vice versa.
What Kelce said
On Oct. 4, Kelce served as an analyst during the ESPN-owned NFL Network TV broadcast of the Indianapolis Colts' 30-13 victory over the Washington Commanders, which took place in London.
A video from that broadcast shows Kelce apologizing to the Washington Commanders after he used the team's former name. In the clip, Kelce breaks down the Commanders' defensive coverage, saying, "The Redskins right now are doing a great job of not only staying tight but making the play when the ball is in the receiver's hand and keeping it short of the sticks."
Announcer Dave Pasch laughs, telling Kelce he accidentally said Redskins, to which Kelce responds, "Oh my gosh! I almost made it out." Pasch then says he, Kelce and former Super Bowl MVP Kurt Warner, also working as an analyst, all had a "gentleman's bet" regarding who would slip up first. Kelce replies, "Well, sorry Washington."
Snopes has debunked similar pieces of media before, including past satire-labeled rumors suggesting Rapinoe was leaving the U.S. due to a "massive red wave," going bankrupt and was banned from the Olympic sports.

WASHINGTON — The Food and Drug Administration says its ongoing safety review of the nation’s main abortion pill will continue into next year, a timeline that was quickly condemned by abortion opponents hoping to see the drug’s use curtailed.
The FDA gave a court-ordered update on its progress in a legal filing late Wednesday, providing the first substantive information about the controversial reevaluation ordered by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
Mifepristone was first approved by the FDA in 2000. The agency has repeatedly reaffirmed the pill’s safety and effectiveness over the years, in addition to easing a number of restrictions on the drug, including dropping a requirement that it be dispensed in person.
But since President Donald Trump returned to the White House, anti-abortion groups and their allies in Congress have pushed the administration to revisit the pill, in the hopes of restricting its use.
The FDA said in its filing that it expects to complete a safety study of the pill by mid-December this year. A report on the findings is expected “no later than March 2027,” after which the agency will decide whether to impose new restrictions or other changes on the drug’s use.
Gavin Oxley of Americans United for Life, an anti-abortion group, criticized the move as a lack of “true leadership” by Trump administration officials.
“The administration continues to find itself on the wrong side of women’s health, clearly uninterested in mitigating the ongoing harms caused by the abortion pill,” Oxley said.
The two-drug regimen of mifepristone, combined with a second drug misoprostol, is the most common form of abortion in the U.S.
The FDA was directed to provide the latest update by a federal judge in a case brought by the state of Louisiana alleging that mail-delivery of mifepristone undermines the state’s abortion ban. It’s one of several state lawsuits related to mifepristone winding their way through the courts.
Last month a three-judge panel for the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals questioned the merits of Louisiana’s case, including whether the state had the legal standing to challenge FDA’s oversight of mifepristone.
Any ruling from the 5th Circuit on the Louisiana case would not immediately change the landscape because the Supreme Court has blocked changes to the drug until it sees the case again.
The FDA said Wednesday it is using a “statistical data mining method” to discover “unknown safety concerns,” that may exist with the drug. The data comes from an electronic database that collects reports of medical injuries and drug side effects from major health networks and insurers.
In addition to the safety study, the agency said it is considering a number of petitions proposing changes to how mifepristone is prescribed and distributed.
Abortion opponents have focused most of their efforts on a 2021 decision allowing doctors to prescribe the drug online and send it through the mail during COVID-19. That decision, made permanent under President Joe Biden in 2023, had the effect of undermining a number of state abortion bans, since women can receive the drug through the mail.
— Matthew Perrone

Winning a Nobel Prize is a matter of great prestige. Winning a Nobel Prize also means the award going to a small number of people while a large number are left out, even if they really deserved to win.
This is partly because of the prizes’ rules. Alfred Nobel’s will said nothing about the number of people that can be awarded at one time but the Nobel Foundation’s statutes limit each prize to at most three people at a time, and no one that has died by the time a prize is announced. Also, scientists need to have been nominated by nominators who have their own eligibility criteria.
A big-picture view of the science Nobel Prizes through history brings another pattern into view: a preference for singular breakthroughs rather than lifetime achievements.
Boyden, Bamberg, and beyond
Start with the Nobel Prize this year for physiology/medicine, to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel, for their work on optogenetics. In 2002, Austrian scientist Gero Miessenböck & co. had first sensitised to light some neurons that were not naturally light-sensitive. Miessenböck is now at the University of Oxford, where his profile page describes him as an ‘inventor’ of optogenetics.
Hegemann and Nagel have been feted for identifying and characterising the protein channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2). The next step was to show that it could control neurons. The first author of the paper that did was Edward Boyden, who helped pioneer the application of ChR2 to neuroscience. Boyden is now a professor of neurotechnology at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and the Broad Institute.
Another author of this paper, Ernst Bamberg, had supervised Nagel’s PhD and was part of the team that established the importance of ChR2. A page on the website of the Max Planck Institute of Biophysics, Germany, where Bamberg is now an emeritus professor, says he was instrumental in translating the ChR2 finding into practical applications.
Yet another author, Feng Zhang, is also at MIT now, and in 2007, he was a member of one of two teams that adapted another protein, called halorhodopsin, to silence neurons with light instead of activating them. The other team, consisting of Xue Han and Boyden, had demonstrated the same capability.
These contributions together — rather than only those that the laureates led — turned the ability to control neurons with light into a tool of neuroscience with real-world applications, including in medicine.
No lone wolf
Next, the physics prize — which this year demonstrated the brokenness of the Nobel Prizes on a whole other level. Francis Halzen won the prize all by himself “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin”. But IceCube is an international collaboration involving around 450 experts from 58 institutions in 14 countries.
Crucially, the prize-giving committee was not constrained to give the prize to one person here. The Nobel Foundation statutes allow the committee to decide whether its prizes can be awarded to associations or organisations. But the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, which awards the physics, chemistry, and economics prizes, does not seem to have adopted this option. If it had, the physics prize could have recognised the IceCube collaboration as a whole.
But even if this rule did not exist, it is hard to say why the committee picked Halzen alone. In 1988, Halzen and (today) University of Hawai’i physics and astronomy professor John G. Learned reported the idea of using Antarctica’s ice mass as the target in which neutrinos from outer space could interact with atoms together. Learned then focused on an underwater neutrino experiment called DUMAND while Halzen pursued a project that eventually became IceCube.
Also, in 2012, while searching IceCube data for neutrinos coming from outer space with very high energies, scientists found two candidate events. The data quickly snowballed into evidence proving that neutrinos could be energised significantly by natural phenomena in space — and the prize citation credits this feat to Halzen alone.
But in real-life (as opposed to Nobel-life), the IceCube collaboration had credited Japanese physicist Aya Ishihara with finding those two candidate events, and for which she received an International Union of Pure and Applied Physics award in 2013. This particular oversight is oddly reminiscent of the infamous Jocelyn Bell Burnell story. Ishihara is currently a professor at Chiba University, where she continues to study high-energy neutrinos and develop the next generation of neutrino detectors.
Furthermore, the 2013 Science paper that reported the high-energy neutrinos also named three scientists named Claudio Kopper, Naoko Kurahashi, and Nathan Whitehorn as its corresponding authors.
The physics prize for Halzen is not misplaced. Halzen was very good — but the point is so were very many others. Aside from the scientists named here, it also required engineers and technicians who could build it in one of the most hostile locations on our planet. And all these people had to work together to make the project and its subsequent achievements possible. Halzen alone could never have done it.
Drawing difficult lines
Finally, the chemistry Nobel Prize this year illustrates the problem with the rule that it cannot be given to people who have died by the time the prize is announced. In 1953, the British physicist Frederick Charles Frank came up with a mathematical way to explain how a small chemical imbalance in a specific kind of reaction could force the reaction to make that imbalance the norm. This way required the reaction to have three properties, called autocatalysis, enantioselective catalysis, and mutual inhibition.
Between 1986 and 1995, Henri Kagan in France and Kenso Soai in Japan had reported evidence of all the conditions of Frank’s model, providing experimental evidence that it could work in the real world. However, Frank died in 1998, aged 87.
That said, the 1995 paper by Soai et al. included Takanori Shibata, who made essential contributions to this branch of chemistry (and was second author on the paper). And whereas Kagan and Soai had demonstrated different aspects of Frank’s model, Shibata was the first author of a 1999 paper that extended the work of Soai et al. to demonstrate the reaction Frank had tried to model. Shibata is currently at Waseda University. And again, it is not easy to rationalise the prize-giving committee’s decision to not include him among this year’s chemistry laureates.
On the other hand, the committee’s decision to exclude U.S. chemical engineer Donna Blackmond throws light on one possible line of reasoning. A technical statement accompanying the chemistry prize credited her with extending Kagan’s attempts to use mathematics to understand non-linear effects in chemical reactions. Blackmond and her team later also took big strides in making sense of the mechanism of the so-called Soai reaction.
And yet, the committee elected to reward the discovery of the validity of Frank’s model rather than work that explained and further extended it.
The S.N. Bose example
In the final analysis, the citations for the Nobel Prizes should not be mistaken for the history of science. Scientists build on the work of others and science advances in these slow but steady increments. When Peter Higgs and François Englert were awarded the Nobel Prize for physics in 2013 for predicting the Higgs boson, there was some clamour in India for not recognising the work of Satyendra Nath Bose. The objection was fair to the extent that you can’t have a fruit without the whole tree and yet petty because it is not reasonable to expect one prize to laud the entire history of a field.
This is why each Nobel Prize award can be a chance to reflect on its limitations, and remember that it is not an ultimate recognition. No prize is.
In that vein, we should also not confuse the number of winners every year with the number of people it takes to do excellent science — from grad students who perform simple experiments to senior colleagues to discuss complicated ideas with. In fact, depending on where in the world you are and your socio-economic standing, your ability to be a good scientist may turn on something as deceptively simple as having someone to help with household chores.
Perhaps most of all, while the Nobel Prizes recognise good science, not all good science wins Nobel Prizes.

The Union Health Ministry is engaging with youth volunteers to find people with tuberculosis (TB) who may be missing from the health system. JOSH teams of the National Cadet Corps (NCC) and MY Bharat volunteers are deploying for household-level outreach in 55 districts across 11 States and Union Territories.
Health Minister J.P. Nadda launched the JOSH (Joint Squad for Health) teams under the TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan on Thursday. The teams will work at block and ward levels to identify people with symptoms, encourage testing, and support patients so they can complete treatment.
Each team will comprise five NCC cadets and five MY Bharat volunteers and will function under a designated Class-I officer. The initiative is being implemented jointly by the Ministries of Health and Family Welfare, Youth Affairs and Sports and Defence.
The government’s emphasis is on active case finding, with the Health Minister stating that people could be living with TB without recognising their symptoms and therefore remain outside the formal healthcare system. “Awareness is important, screening is important, but our responsibility does not end there,” he said, stressing the need to ensure diagnosis and completion of treatment.
The Centre also felicitated 67,933 Panchayats across 697 districts that were declared TB Mukt in 2026. The JOSH initiative is expected to be expanded to other districts after orientation and mobilisation of volunteers.

Singapore GP: FIA admits 'human error' created power disparity in Sprint Qualifying at Marina Bay Street Circuit
Formula 1's governing body, the FIA, has revealed a "human error" caused a power disparity in the first part of Sprint Qualifying on Friday; watch the Singapore Sprint on Saturday at 10am (build-up from 9am) ahead of Qualifying at 2pm, live on Sky Sports F1 and Main Event
Friday 9 October 2026 16:04, UK
The FIA has admitted "human error" caused a power disparity during Sprint Qualifying in Singapore.
Following a red flag for debris in SQ1 caused by Cadillac's Sergio Perez, the FIA did not activate Overtake Mode - an extra power boost that is normally active throughout qualifying and used in races to aid overtaking.
The FIA reactivated Overtake Mode for 27 seconds before deactivating it again, thus causing an unfair advantage in the first part of Sprint Qualifying.

Sky Sports F1 understands the brief re-activation of Overtake Mode happened in the last minute of SQ1 when several drivers were on flying laps before being turned off.
It is also understood Williams petitioned for all teams to progress to SQ2, which was declined, and no protests are expected.
Williams' Carlos Sainz was one of the six drivers to miss out on SQ2 and says the drivers who had Overtake Mode for those 27 seconds gained around half a second.
There was also a timing issue during Sprint Qualifying, which the FIA says was "unrelated" to the "human error".
"This issue in question meant Overtake Mode was not available after the red flag period during SQ1," read an FIA statement.
"When it became apparent that Overtake Mode was not active after the restart, it was then activated for a period of 27 seconds before being deactivated again.
"The FIA acknowledges that this unfortunate human error had an impact on the performance of certain cars based on the timing of their run and their position around the lap. The second and third periods of Sprint Qualifying were not affected."
The human error comes just five days after an "unprecedented" software glitch at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia caused several cars to grind to a crawl or a halt.
Sainz, who qualified last for Saturday's Singapore Sprint at 10am (build-up from 9am), live on Sky Sports F1 and Main Event, claimed half of the field had an advantage in SQ1.
"Half of the cars did their laps with half a second quicker engine than the others," said Sainz.
"There was another software issue with the cars this time around, and we were on the bad end of it.
"For whatever reason the FIA, like in Malaysia, at the end decide to do sporting equity and were happy to do half of the cars in qualy with higher power than the other half of the cars.
"A bit confused why the sport keeps doing different things depending on who is out in Q1 or who is out in lap one."
All of the main contenders progressed to SQ2 although Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad and Aston Martin's Lance Stroll would have fancied their chances of getting through.
Max Verstappen went on to take Sprint pole from Mercedes' George Russell and Ferrari's Charles Leclerc.
Teams keen to understand what happened in SQ1
Sky Sports F1's Ted Kravitz:
"Unfortunate human error from the FIA, not the first time we've heard that.
"As far as Aston Martin are confirmed, their sporting director Andy Stephenson is still up with race control. They just want to understand what happened here today.
"They don't believe that anyone was doing their qualifying lap and then didn't have the extra half a megajoule available, what it's concerned about is the tyre preparation on the out-lap.
"Most of the drivers were on the radio saying they didn't have power, so they couldn't do the out-lap they wanted to do. That skews everything else, the rest of the computations they've done.
"While Aston Martin aren't making a protest, they do want to understand what's going on.
"They say the easiest thing would have been to stop the session and do it all again, but you've used your tyres by that time and that's not going to be possible."

How Brighton attract and develop the best young players ahead of their rivals
- Published
Brighton & Hove Albion sit third in the Premier League, with one of the highest-scoring teams in Europe.
To the uninitiated it might seem logical that the Seagulls must have spent big, investing in players ready for the first team.
Yet Brighton are, along with Everton, one of only two clubs to record a profit in transfer spending over the past five years.
It is a team full of young players, testament to the club's data-led recruitment and development strategy.
But how do they do it?
"We have a really clear philosophy around how we can be competitive in arguably the most challenging league in the world," Brighton sporting director Mike Cave told BBC Sport.
But Brighton are more than just competitive. They went into the international break with a 3-0 home win over champions Arsenal.
From identifying players, to providing pathways, integrating them into the team and then selling at the right time, it is a strategy which has worked, year after year.
This is how the the club identify, attract and grow talent - and make them into first-team players.
Data-led approach, but a character is crucial
Brighton use analytics and data as their primary method of tracking and identifying players.
Through club owner Tony Bloom's Jamestown Analytics, the performance of pretty much any player - or coach - who is in a professional league can be monitored.
"It helps us to identify talent from around the world in quite an efficient way," Cave said. "That allows us then to move quite quickly in what is a really competitive transfer market."
Just how Brighton's analytics set works is a closely guarded secret. But it does involve assessing a number of characteristics to identify signings who fit the club's model.
"There's no single attribute or a single metric that we particularly go after," Cave explained. "It's more trying to assess a player's performance and potential.
"It'd be great to break it down into one or two things but we're dealing with human beings playing a really complex game - sometimes in different parts of the world, in different leagues."
Over time, there is a constant re-evaluation. Success and failure help to refine how the data is interpreted.
The Seagulls, along with Brentford and more recently Bournemouth, are widely considered to be the best operators in this sector.
Many clubs have tried to copy it without achieving the same level of success.
But it is not about data alone.
"What's as important is the information we try to gather around the player's character, their background and their suitability for our environment," added Cave, who has been at Brighton since 2022 and was promoted to sporting director in the summer.
"Not every player would be right for Brighton and Brighton won't be right for every player either.
"We invest a good amount of time in trying to understand the individual, the person, the human being. Ultimately, this is a people industry.
"That's where the subjective and the non-football data really plays a huge part in our decision-making processes."
Buy-to-loan market gives players key experience
The use of the loan market, both domestically and in Europe, is crucial for the planned career development of many of Brighton's signings.
Since 2018-19, the Seagulls have agreed well over 20 loan deals in each campaign, with 27 last season. This summer, Brighton loaned out 16 players. More will follow in January.
"We've had over a period of time now a really productive and successful loan pathway," Cave explained.
"So we might identify players that we think have good potential, but maybe aren't quite ready for the Premier League.
"We believe we can offer one of the best developmental pathways, be it through the loans strategy that we have, or through our own under-21s programme."
Take Alexis Mac Allister, who was signed by Brighton for £6.8m in January 2019 but immediately loaned back to former club Argentinos Juniors, and then to Boca Juniors for 2019-20.
Only in the summer of 2020 did Mac Allister become a first-team player at the Amex.
The Argentina international, who won the World Cup in 2022, went on to make 112 appearances for the Seagulls before being sold to Liverpool for £35m. It would likely have been a higher transfer fee if the player's contract did not have a release clause.
Most recently, there is Jan Paul van Hecke. The defender was signed from NAC Breda for £6m as a 20-year-old in 2020, and spent two seasons on loan with Heerenveen and Blackburn Rovers.
The Netherlands international then became a first-team player and, after 131 matches for the Seagulls, was sold to Tottenham for £52m in the summer.
The fruits of the policy this season can be seen this season, with two players signed in the summer of 2024.
Malick Yalcouye, a £6m signing from Gothenburg, spent the past two years out on loan, first with Sturm Graz in Austria and then with Swansea City in the Championship.
The 20-year-old has two Premier League goals in his first five appearances.
Ibrahim Osman, a £17m capture from Danish side Nordsjaelland, was with Feyenoord in the Netherlands, Auxerre in France and Championship side Birmingham City.
The 21-year-old winger has made three substitute appearances so far.
"Malik's had a really good start to the season," Cave said. "Osman is another young player who has had three loans now and then has come back into the squad for this season.
"They're good examples and role models of a commitment to their own development, having an attitude and a desire to want to get better.
"Now we're starting to see them delivering in the Premier League for us which is a fantastic success story but real testament to them and their hard work."
One to watch this season is Matias Orozco, an 18-year-old who cost £3.75m from Deportivo Calli. He is with Castellon, who sit second in the Spanish second division.
The defensive midfielder was handed his first senior caps for Colombia during the current international break.
"We do a lot of work in analysing the right clubs, coaches, leagues, understanding how complex it is, to find the right destination," Cave added.
"Depending on where that player is in their career, what areas of their game we're looking to help develop, or as just part of their maturity and experience."
Brighton have shown - from Mac Allister to Carlos Baleba, who was sold to Manchester United in the summer - that they can be a stepping stone for an ambitious player. And that reputation is crucial in a competitive market.
"The key thing is being able to demonstrate to young players that we have a plan," Cave said.
"Depending on the age, that can be over one year, or several years. Hopefully, that leads to playing in our senior team.
"That track record of being able to nurture young talent in different ways plays a big part in why a number of players agree to come to Brighton."
For Cave, "arguably the most critical part" is integrating players into the city and the culture of English life.
"We can have all the data, all the character backgrounds, context and information that's available," Cave added.
"But ultimately when that individual and their family arrives in Brighton, how we onboard them, how we embed them, how we make them feel like it's their home all contributes to them being the best version of themselves on the football pitch.
"We want players to come to Brighton and thrive and enjoy the city, enjoy the football club."
Brighton do not 'set out thinking about how we're going to sell'
Brighton have a reputation as one of the most savvy operators, but they are also one of the most prolific.
Over the past five seasons, the Seagulls have made 62 permanent signings. Only Chelsea, on 72, have made more of clubs to be in the Premier League throughout.
"It offers the opportunity to recruit a wider base of talent and that's probably why you've seen the scale of our recruitment over a period of time," Cave said.
"We try to have a longer-term view on how we can build the squad over a period of time."
There is one stark difference between the two clubs. Brighton recorded a transfer profit of £10m, while Chelsea show a deficit of £721m.
Though player trading is clearly important when it comes to the financial regulations, Cave insists the club do not "ever set out thinking about how we're going to sell a player".
"Ultimately, we recruit them to come and perform and develop for Brighton," Cave added.
"Like nearly every club in in the world, at some point players choose to leave or depart a football club. That's just a natural cycle."
Moises Caicedo, Marc Cucurella, Mac Allister and Joao Pedro were all sold for a profit in excess of £25m each. In Caicedo's case, it was £77.5m.
"The important thing is to maximise the sale of that player, because that goes back into the football club to reinvest, to hopefully, again, improve the squad," Cave added.
Alongside the emergence of Yalcouye and Osman has been the rise of Charalampos Kostoulas, who was signed from Olympiakos for £30m in the summer of 2025, just after his 18th birthday.
When Danny Welbeck was sold to Chelsea the loss of his goals - he scored 13 in the Premier League last season - could have been a concern.
Kostoulas was bedded in last season and now has four goals from six starts across all competitions this term.
Luka Vuskovic, the 19-year-old club record transfer from Spurs, has seamlessly replaced Van Hecke.
Chema Andres, 21, looks to be another astute summer purchase in midfield after Baleba's departure.
Signed from Stuttgart for £18m, Andres is a Spain Under-21 international who came through the Real Madrid academy. His one season in the German Bundesliga feels like the kind of loan Brighton would have done had they signed him directly.
Three hugely promising young players signed to replace key stars.
"It's fundamentally around having had a consistent strategy over a period of time that we can then try to improve," Cave said.
"Over a period of time now we've had real faith and confidence in the potential of young players to come into the league and perform at the highest level"
They knocked Manchester United out of the EFL Cup, coming from two goals down to win 3-2.
Next week, Brighton begin their Conference League campaign at home to Lithuanian outfit FK Kauno Zalgiris.
The club are the clear favourites to win the competition, which would be the first major trophy in the club's 125-year history.
The club does not really need vindication of their vision and long-term plan, but some silverware would be nice.

The Trump administration will no longer allow Microsoft and other tech companies to participate in a program that allows H-1B visa holders to apply for green cards, one of the most common pathways for skilled foreign workers seeking permanent residency in the United States.
In addition to Microsoft, administration officials said on Thursday that software giant Adobe and IT companies including Cognizant, Infosys, and Tata will be suspended from the PERM program, the Labor Department's permanent labor certification program. PERM is a key step for H-1B visa holders to gain permanent residency, requiring employers to prove that there are no American workers who would be suitable for the applicant's permanent job opportunity.
Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said that the agency is investigating whether these companies committed fraud, undercutting American workers by hiring foreign employees.
Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, singled out Microsoft. “There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft,” Vance said during a press conference.
In a statement provided by Microsoft representative Kaitlin Haskins, the company said it “only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category," adding that it develops its workforce by "strengthening this country’s talent pipeline, hiring American workers, and attracting the best talent from around the world."
Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, and Tata did not immediately respond to WIRED's request for comment.
The suspension marks a victory for tech workers who have complained about unfairly losing out on jobs to immigrant workers.
Jobs Now, an advocacy group composed of US citizens working in big tech, celebrated Vance’s announcement on its X account with a video of dancing crabs. The group publicizes otherwise difficult-to-find PERM job postings and says it helped Americans apply to nearly 500,000 jobs across 7,000 employers between last January and this past July.
The organization and its members have also filed complaints against tech companies about alleged abuse of the PERM system, and have called for a number of changes to the employment immigration system. “Every job in America should be offered to an American first, no exceptions,” the group told WIRED in an unsigned statement.
This isn't the first time tech companies have been targeted over PERM. Earlier this year, OpenAI and a company it acquired agreed to settle accusations from the Trump administration about violating rules for the program. Apple reached a similar deal in 2023.
The administration's disparagement of H-1B visas—one of the most common work visas in the US—has sent waves of panic through Silicon Valley since Trump's reelection. Tech companies are some of the H1-B program's biggest users: So far in the fiscal year 2026, the top three employers with the most visas approved are Amazon, Tata, and Infosys.
Microsoft is No. 5, with 3,688 visas approved in 2026; in 2025, 6,258 visas were approved. According to the company, 80 percent of last year's visas were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees, not to hire new people.
"The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our US workforce," Microsoft’s statement said.
It's unclear if Thursday’s announcement would affect the ability of employees at these companies to apply for H1-B visas themselves. The Office of the Vice President and the Department of Labor did not immediately respond to WIRED's request for clarity on if the suspension would impact those seeking H-1B visas.
"It's one thing if you want to bring in someone like Elon Musk" who aims to "build something great in America," Vance said on Thursday. He equated the current state of the H-1B program to bringing "indentured servants" into the US, taking jobs away from American workers. (Musk, who was born in South Africa, came to the US via Canada to pursue a bachelor's degree at the University of Pennsylvania.)
The announcement came shortly before Trump was set to award Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. When asked about the upcoming event, Vance said, "We’re going to continue to support Microsoft and have a great relationship with Microsoft, but we’re also going to deny them the ability to apply for these permanent residencies until they show that they are going to get serious about putting American workers first.”
Vance also said that the administration is investigating nine universities to see if they might be committing fraud with the J-1 visa program, which allows international candidates to study and conduct research in the US.
“I don’t care how prestigious a university thinks it is, break the law and screw the American people, and I will personally cuff you in the university square," Department of Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said.

In the 53rd episode of The Health Wrap by The Hindu, Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, and Athira Elssa Johnson, Senior Reporter, discuss medicine pricing, drug safety and dengue surveillance.
The episode examines the Supreme Court’s concerns over the difference between the supply price and maximum retail price of essential cancer medicines. In one instance, the court was told that a cancer drug with a price to retailer of about ₹2,700 carried a maximum retail price of ₹27,000. The Bench described the difference as “broad daylight dacoity”.
The discussion also covers the court’s concerns about hospitals requiring patients to buy medicines from their own pharmacies, its suggestion of a uniform 16% margin and questions around generic prescriptions and the implementation of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order.
The episode also covers the risks of indiscriminate painkiller and antibiotic use, including kidney disease and antimicrobial resistance. While prolonged or inappropriate use of painkillers can cause kidney-related complications, unnecessary or incorrect antibiotic use can make infections harder to treat. The discussion highlights the importance of appropriate prescribing and responsible medicine use.
The final segment focuses on a Dengue Early Warning System being developed by researchers at the Institute of Advanced Virology in Keralam. The system combines disease surveillance data with rainfall, temperature and humidity to generate weekly, district-level forecasts using machine learning.
Trained on six years of data, from March 2020 to February 2026, the system aims to help health authorities anticipate increases in dengue transmission. If validated, the forecasts could support earlier surveillance, mosquito-control measures, healthcare preparedness and public alerts. The system is still under development and evaluation.
The episode ends with a fun fact about dengue mosquito eggs, which can remain dormant for months in dry conditions and hatch when water becomes available. Even seemingly dry containers can harbour eggs that may contribute to future mosquito populations.

Brazilian police have killed a suspect who held at least 13 children at knifepoint in a school of the city of Curitiba, in the country’s south
SAO PAULO -- Brazilian police killed on Thursday a suspect who held at least 13 children at knifepoint in a school of the city of Curitiba, in the country's south. None of them were injured.
Parana state police spokeswoman Leticia Martins told journalists outside school CMEI Sao Braz that the man broke into one of the classrooms and kept children and staffers as hostages for two hours.

"(The suspect) also threatened to pour gasoline onto himself and others, our negotiating teams were in place, but saw no alternative but to neutralize him,” said Martins, who did not say whether the suspect had expressed a specific reason for his actions.
The incident took place in the middle class region of Sao Braz in Curitiba, a city of 1.8 million residents 400 kilometers (248 miles) south of metropolis Sao Paulo.
Local media showed footage of tearful parents outside the school waiting for information as the negotiations between the suspect and police were ongoing. Minutes after two explosions, policemen emerged carrying some of the children outside.
Curitiba city hall said in a statement that the children and the staffers of the school will receive psychological support after the incident.

In a bid to make cancer treatment more affordable and reduce patients’ out-of-pocket expenditure, the Union government has decided to cap trade margins at 30% of the maximum retail price (MRP) for all non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs.
Also read | Bitter pills: on Court’s intervention, drug pricing
The measure will cover branded and generic drugs, domestically manufactured and imported medicines, and patented and non-patented products. An expert committee under the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) will finalise the list of medicines to be brought under the measure.
Current mark-ups up to 700%
The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA), which analysed market data, found that the average trade mark-up on non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines was around 170%, with mark-ups reaching up to 700% in some cases. It also found substantial differences between prices charged through retail, hospital, and online pharmacies.
The government said the decision was prompted by the high financial burden of cancer treatment. Around 75% of cancer treatment expenditure is estimated to be borne out of pocket.
The anti-cancer medicines market comprises around 225 drugs and 500 formulations, with an annual turnover of approximately ₹12,500 crore. Scheduled cancer medicines account for about ₹2,250 crore.
Massive savings
A senior official said that the government is drawing on the experience of a similar intervention in 2019, when the NPPA capped trade margins on 42 selected non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs by invoking its extraordinary powers under Paragraph 19 of the Drug Price Control Order, 2013. The exercise had reportedly resulted in price reductions of up to 91%, with annual savings of ₹984 crore across 526 brands.
The latest intervention is expected to result in price reductions of up to 70% of MRP and annual savings of around ₹2,500 crore, the government said.
‘Production must be maintained’
Under the new framework, the trade margin will be capped at 30% of MRP, equivalent to 42.86% of the price to stockist.
“To ensure availability, manufacturers will be required to maintain their existing production level,” said the official.
The government said the measure would regulate trade margins rather than manufacturers’ selling prices or revenue, with the intervention aimed at reducing the margins retained across the distribution chain.

The setting for perhaps the country’s biggest exercise in public debate was quintessential rural India: fields of green paddy, a pond, a temple. On a normal day, as dusk falls in the village of Ajgara, in Uttar Pradesh, people gather beside the pond to chat about the price of crops, the weather, or the theft of a goat.
But for more than a month, metaphysics and ethical dilemmas replaced the usual topics. Is it permissible to use deceit to defeat an evil enemy? Is a lie justified to save a life? What is the nature of reality?
The debating tournament was the brainchild of Abhishek Pandey, district magistrate of Pratapgarh district in Uttar Pradesh. When he took up the post two years ago, he knew the area was rich in archaeological treasures connected to the ancient Indian epic, the Mahabharata.
Throughout the text, Yudhishthira, one of the central characters, debates the nature of human existence. In Ajgara he answers a string of philosophical questions to save the lives of his four brothers.
Pandey, 35, like most Indians, grew up on this story and was proud of the intellectual depth of the dialogues. When he attended Oxford University on a fellowship, he admired the debating society, which has a 200-year-long history. But India’s tradition of sophisticated public debate is much older, going back more than 3,000 years.
Pandey started to question why the tradition had not survived. “Indians have celebrated certain traditions for centuries,” Pandey says. “Why have we ceased to celebrate the legacy of debate and questioning?” Was it possible to revive this noble tradition, particularly when it was a vital component of a democracy?
He decided that the annual fair held in Ajgara in September would be a good time to stage the event. In the run-up to the fair, Pandey and his team arranged 1,500 debates across the district.
Age and education were no bar. The youngest participant was a 10-year-old schoolboy, the oldest an 80-year-old farmer. In debating for and against a motion, participants were judged on reasoning and moral clarity.
The overwhelming public response dumbfounded Pandey. Thousands of people participated in multiple rounds, and were whittled down to eight finalists – two women and six men.
While villagers milled around, enjoying the food, watching folk theatre, buying local crafts and taking a ride on a ferris wheel, a silence descended inside the debating tent.
The finale of the Great Ajgara Debate 2026 on 17 September lasted about six hours.
One topic was women’s rights. A finalist, Vivek Singh, argued that women might have equality on paper but society’s expectations of them impeded the exercise of these rights.
Another, Prajjwal Shukla, 24, argued that the real question was not what role society assigned to women but who had the authority to make those choices. Whether a woman chose a career, household responsibilities, or both, should be her choice and hers alone, he said.
“What amazed me the most was not the intellectual quality of the debates (which was great), but the atmosphere. Everyone listened respectfully, patiently, without interrupting. No one got personal. People sat for hours,” says Pandey.
Marx’s adage that history repeats itself, first as tragedy and then as farce, is a perfect description of how debate in India has descended from the sublime to the farcical.
In television studio debates everyone shouts at the same time. No one can finish a point. Personal abuse and gibes fly while the anchor whips them into ever greater frenzies.
Sadhana Dwivedi, one of the two women to progress into the last round of the Great Ajgara Debate, despises this new format.
“People need to learn to listen, to understand there may be value in another person’s point of view,” she says. “In a democracy, it is crucial for all opinions to be aired so that we can get to the truth.”
The turnout was a good demonstration of the thesis posited in economist Amartya Sen’s book The Argumentative Indian that India had a rich tradition of questioning authority and entertaining heterodoxy.
It is only in recent years that dissent has been suppressed, notably by the ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party, which values conformity.
“It’s ironic, because the BJP wants to recreate a Hindu state but is not even acquainted with the traditions of ancient Hindu civilisation, such as that of debate and being open to different ideas,” says author and commentator Parsa Venkateshwar Rao Jnr.
At the end of the tournament, the eight finalists were garlanded and driven around in an open-top car to much cheering, feted as “intellectual heroes”. The winner was Shukla, who is preparing to sit exams to enter the civil service.
“I can’t believe I am the winner of a debate that took place at the exact same spot as in the Mahabharata all those centuries ago. I participated just because I wanted to hear other people’s thoughts,” he says.
Pandey is still processing the public enthusiasm. “My deputy asked me if we should get some police deployment because the turnout everywhere was so big, but I laughed and said no. That would be a sad affair.”
He hopes to spread the event across other Indian states and perhaps nationwide. “We have to inculcate a culture of debate. It’s the hallmark of a democracy.”
Meanwhile, he has planted his flag. The inscription on the stone slab he has installed at the site reads: “The Great Ajgara Debate. First Debate 3152 BC: Yudhishthira. Second Debate 2026: Prajjwal Shukla.”

The MRP debate, which has been recently triggered where a hospital purchased a product for ₹11 and billed it for ₹325, is misplaced and lacks the context we need to understand the issue properly.
Hospitals rightly point out that the gap between procurement and billing is not all profit: storing supplies, maintaining sterility and ensuring availability carry costs. But patients are entitled to ask a more basic question. How did ‘maximum’ become the price they routinely pay?
Understanding maximum retail price
MRP was designed as a ceiling to protect consumers. In healthcare, it can, however, also conceal how a price is built. The printed figure tells a family little about the manufacturer’s returns, the margins taken along the supply chain, or whether the product offers any advantage over a cheaper alternative. A patient in an emergency cannot shop around. When choice disappears, a ceiling risks becoming the default charge.
This is a serious problem, and price controls can help. In 2019, the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority applied trade-margin rationalisation to 42 non-scheduled cancer medicines. The government estimated that this could save patients 200 crore annually. But the wider lesson is not that every medicine and device should have the same permitted margin. It is that India needs to decide what each margin is paying for.
Different products, therapies
A standard syringe sold by multiple suppliers does not justify the same return as a therapy developed for a rare disease after years of research and clinical trials. Nor should a familiar medicine acquire an innovation premium simply because it has a new brand name and a large marketing budget.
India needs a differential profit and margin strategy. Routine, high-volume products should have modest, transparent distribution and hospital margins, informed by comparable procurement prices. Bulk purchasing should benefit patients, insurers and public programmes. Genuine costs of stocking, safe handling, wastage and round-the-clock availability should be recognised openly, rather than recovered through an inflated price for the item itself.
Companies that take substantial scientific risks deserve a different approach. Those investing in original research, rare and neglected diseases, or products that demonstrably improve outcomes while reducing hospitalisations and total care costs should be able to earn higher profits. Fair returns give investors a reason to fund difficult work. But the premium should go to the organisation creating the clinical value, not automatically to every intermediary between the factory and the patient.
Science must earn
‘Novel’ must not be a label a company awards itself. A claim for a higher return should be tested against existing treatments: Does the product help patients live longer or better? Does it prevent complications? Is it safer or easier to use? Does it lower the total cost of treatment, even if its purchase price is higher? A product that costs more upfront but prevents repeated admissions may be better value than the cheapest item on the shelf.
Societal impact should count too. Research into diseases affecting small or neglected patient groups, reliable supply in underserved areas, and meaningful differential pricing for vulnerable patients merit consideration. These commitments must be specific and measurable. A patient-assistance scheme that reaches a handful of people cannot excuse a price that excludes everyone else.
India has an institution on which to build: Health Technology Assessment already evaluates clinical effectiveness, costs and equity to inform public decisions. Its evidence could help distinguish genuine advances from claims designed to justify a higher price.
Margins under microscopes
The government should establish an independent Healthcare Pricing and Value Panel with clinicians, scientists, health economists, patient representatives and pricing regulators. It should assess products against published criteria: clinical benefit, research risk, development investment, disease burden, total health-system cost and access for those least able to pay. Its members should disclose conflicts of interest, explain decisions and provide an appeal process.
A higher return would come with obligations. Companies seeking one should submit evidence and relevant costs for independent review. Premiums should be reconsidered as products mature or competitors enter the market. Where promised benefits remain uncertain, agreements could link part of the payment to observed outcomes. Concessional access for eligible patients and public programmes should be enforceable, rather than left to goodwill.
The panel must also separate manufacturer profits from trade and hospital margins. Otherwise, a policy intended to reward research could simply enlarge the amount captured downstream. Regulators need visibility into invoice prices, rebates and patient charges. Patients need itemised bills showing the product charge and any separate handling fee. Small and rural pharmacies, meanwhile, need viable returns to keep essential products available. A pricing policy that closes the last-mile supplier has failed its patients.
Profit, but not profiteering
MRP should remain a shield against overcharging, but it cannot be our entire definition of fair price. Companies should be able to make a profit, but not profiteer. India can protect a family buying an IV set and reward a company developing a breakthrough for a child with a rare disease. To do both, we must ask what the price rewards, what benefit the patient receives, and who can actually afford it. In healthcare, margin should follow proven value and access, and not bargaining power over a captive patient.
(Dr. Rajendra Pratap Gupta is the chairman of Health Parliament, a global executive think tank on healthcare, and former advisor to the Health Minister, government of India. founder@parliament.health)

NAMSCON 2026, the 66th annual conference and convocation of the National Academy of Medical Sciences (India), will bring together medical professionals, researchers and academicians from across the country in Chennai from October 8 to 11.
Hosted by SRM Medical College Hospital and Research Centre, SRM Institute of Science and Technology, Kattankulathur, the conference will focus on the theme ‘Synergy of Science and Technology in Healthcare for a Healthier Tomorrow’.
Tamil Nadu Governor Rajendra Vishwanath Arlekar will inaugurate the conference as the chief guest.
The four-day programme will include pre-conference workshops, symposia, keynote addresses, National CME sessions, and oral and poster presentations.
The scientific sessions will cover antimicrobial resistance, CAR-T cell therapy, biosimilars and biologics, senolytic therapies, rare genetic disorders, emerging infections, pandemic preparedness and the Indian diabetes phenotype. Discussions will also focus on medical education, robotics in surgery, organ donation and transplantation, and evolving approaches to tuberculosis management.
Eight workshops on October 8 will cover trauma care, neonatal resuscitation, AI in clinical research, spine surgery, endoscopic gastroenterology, palliative care, diagnostic reasoning, and physician entrepreneurship.
Among the speakers are Shekar C. Mande, president, Indian National Science Academy; Abhijat Sheth, Chairman, National Medical Commission; Mohan V., Chairman, Dr. Mohan’s Diabetes Specialities Centre, Chennai; Mohan Kameswaran, Managing Director and Senior Consultant, Madras ENT Research Foundation; Vivekanand Jha, Executive Director, The George Institute of Global Health, India; and Gobardhan Das, Member, NITI Aayog.
M. Srinivas, member (Health), NITI Aayog, will deliver a plenary lecture on ‘Good Governance for Transforming Medical Institutions in India and Quality Research during Residency’. He will also interact with undergraduate and postgraduate students on research during residency.
Founded in 1961, NAMS is a non-statutory body that advises the Government of India on health policy and planning. NAMSCON 2026 will be the first annual conference of NAMS to be hosted by SRM Medical College Hospital and Research Centre.
The conference is being organised under the leadership of R. Jayanthi, Organising Chairperson and Dean, SRM MCH&RC, and Melvin George, Organising Secretary and Head, Centre for Clinical Pharmacology and Clinical Trials Research, with Rajarajan Swaminathan as State Convenor.

Elon Musk’s America PAC is focusing its war chest on the most consequential Senate races this midterm cycle—and doing so by financing attack ads on Democrats, as voters nationwide sour on the Trump administration’s agenda.
The trend of political parties and outside groups focusing on trashing their opponents is not a new phenomenon. But America PAC's approach has been unusual: for every dollar it has spent supporting GOP Senate candidates, it has spent almost three dollars attacking Democrats.
To monitor America PAC's spending on digital ads and mailers this cycle, our ace team at WIRED has created a live tracker that updates daily and highlights where Musk's political contributions are heading as we enter the waning years of Trump’s second term.
The political stakes are especially high for Republicans this midterms cycle because of the possibility of Democrats taking the majority in the US Senate, should the party flip four battleground races and retain three of the Senate seats it currently holds.
For Musk, the implications of a Democratic-controlled Senate would also be far-reaching, as he personally could become the target of congressional investigations, while his companies might be affected by bills related to tech and AI regulation.
Texas Senate Race
For the critical Texas Senate race, America PAC has poured more than $9.4 million into ads opposing Democratic candidate James Talarico and roughly $1.8 million into ads backing Republican candidate and state attorney general Ken Paxton.
The lopsided spending here is perhaps the least surprising of all of the close Senate contests. Paxton comes with so much personal baggage—from facing impeachment charges that were eventually dropped to having his wife (who has since endorsed him with an ad that doesn’t mention him by name) file for divorce on “biblical grounds”—that trying to boost him with ads highlighting his background is tough.
Republicans in Texas also cannot realistically do positive ads of President Donald Trump and Paxton together, since both men have terrible approval ratings.
The largest single expenditures by America PAC have been two $1.3 million digital media buys opposing Talarico. America PAC has not put any money into television ads, which is being handled by other groups, like MAGA Inc., the Trump-affiliated super PAC.
Meanwhile, the Senate Republican Conference–affiliated Texas PAC has so far booked the lion's share of television ads. Punchbowl News reported last month that Texas PAC has booked around $120 million and was looking to buy $100 million in ad slots before November 3.
Ohio Senate Race
In Ohio’s Senate race, America PAC has spent $3.3 million against Democrat Sherrod Brown compared to $1.6 million supporting Republican candidate Jon Husted.
Husted has been struggling to distance himself from supporting data centers at a time when voters in the state have become fed up with rising costs associated with the projects. Husted has been tagged as "the face of data centers" because of a planned Nvidia data center project in Ohio that will be leased by OpenAI, and for his past support for data centers when he served in the state government.
The effort by Brown to cast Husted as the champion of data centers has in fact been so effective that a memo by the Senate Republicans' campaign arm in August said it was tying an anchor around the neck of Husted's public polling.
At a rally this week in Ohio, despite the cratering public support for data centers, Trump could not help himself and declared to the crowd: “We want them.” Husted’s campaign quickly replied that it should be a “local decision.”
Iowa Senate Race
In Iowa, America PAC has spent $1.5 million hitting Democratic candidate Josh Turek, while only spending roughly $100,000 supporting the Republican candidate Ashley Hinson—the biggest disparity, according to the WIRED tracker.
To put that another way: To date, Musk's political operation has spent a staggering 14 times more attacking Turek than supporting Hinson.
This could be because Hinson has taken great pains to distance herself from Trump's agenda. She recently called on Trump to ban diesel exports and end the Iran war (after previously voting six times against the House resolution to end the conflict), after Turek called for both of those measures.
To illustrate the upside-down nature of this race, Hinson recently launched attack ads against Turek, accusing him without evidence of having “received tens of millions in support from men in the Epstein files,” a remarkable situation given that Trump has sought to tamp down any mention of the files because of the negative blowback on him personally.
Once again, pro-Republican ads are likely not helpful when the candidate is trying to run a race apart from Trump and is barely ahead in the polls in what should be a safe Republican seat. In the most recent New York Times/Siena poll, Hinson was just one single, solitary point ahead of Turek.

In a country where cricket eclipses every other sport, the recently concluded Asian Games offered a much-needed reminder of India’s breadth of sporting talent. In this edition of the games, in Japan, India won 85 medals: 21 golds, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals. I admit I did not know many of the players competing, or even some of the sports they play before putting this piece together. Learning about the stories, I wonder why not.
There were individual breakthroughs, records broken and history made. There were also hard-fought team victories, including the Indian women’s hockey team gold medal after a 44-year wait.
Sports broadcaster Siddharth Pandey cited an old saying in the world of sport: “You cannot be what you cannot see.” For Pandey, one of the most heartening sights was families and communities rallying around the four female players from the north-eastern states. (The region has endured decades of conflict and is often overlooked in the national conversation.) “We simply cannot underestimate the impact these games and medals have on future generations taking up non-cricketing sport and wanting to excel in it,” he told me.
Recognition is also important. Vidya Pillai, the first Indian woman to win a snooker world championship has spoken about her sport not getting the attention or respect it deserves. She felt unacknowledged following her 2023 feat, despite the fact that it came after six unsuccessful world finals and she beat two former world champions along the way.
Behind India’s medal glory are dozens of athletes and families who have struggled financially, trained with limited facilities, and often without much institutional support.
So this week, I am sharing a sample of the many extraordinary stories from different parts of the country. These are only a fraction of the champions to emerge from the games, yet they provide a glimpse of the possibilities that can open up when a country sees and celebrates sporting talent across the spectrum.
Neeru Dhanda (gold in trap shooting): Dhanda’s family in Haryana’s Jind relies on the government’s food subsidy programme and she began her sporting journey using a borrowed shotgun with tin cans as targets. Right before the games began, the 26-year-old spent a few days in a hospital recovering from an illness instead of training. But last week, as rain lashed the shooting range in Urenocho, she became the first Indian woman to win an individual gold in trap shooting at Asian games. She won a second gold in mixed team trap event as well as a silver in the women’s team trap event.
Vithya Ramraj (gold in 4x400m): Ramraj was one of the breakout stars of the event with a three-medal haul. NDTV reported that her father had to borrow money to support Ramraj and her twin sister’s athletic careers. Alongside the team gold in 4x400m, she won a silver in the mixed 4x400m relay. She also broke Indian legend PT Usha’s long-held national record in 400m hurdles which won her a bronze medal.
Sahil Jadhav (gold in compound mixed archery team and men’s compound team): Not long ago, Jadhav contemplated quitting archery, frustrated by not making the progress he had hoped for. He had been forced to compete with borrowed arrows for selection trials, the New Indian Express reported, adding that his mother sold her jewellery to buy him professional compound bows. Now, the 25-year-old has two gold medals and an automatic entry to the 2028 LA Olympics.
Lalremsiami Hmarzote (member of the gold-winning women’s hockey team): The women’s hockey team forward once had to travel about 100 miles from her home to reach the only hockey academy in Mizoram. When she was growing up, her parents had no idea about what hockey and she played barefoot on dirt pitches. This month, playing her 200th international appearance, the 26-year-old struck gold. She scored the lone goal of the final against China, which Hockey India described as a “stunning reverse-stick strike”.
Ancy Sojan (silver in long jump): With colourful beads glistening in her hair, Sojan flung herself 6.53 metres in long jump, to win the silver medal. Earlier this year, the 25-year-old broke the national record set in 2004. Her journey, from a village in Kerala’s Thrissur district to the international stage, has not been straightforward. Last year, she was diagnosed with polycystic ovarian syndrome, forcing her to drastically change her diet and manage the medication-related weight gain she had before the tournament.
Aslam Inamdar (a member of the gold-winning men’s kabaddi team): Inamdar came to kabaddi, a south Asian contact sport combining elements of tag and wrestling, from humble beginnings – he was partly drawn to it because it was affordable and didn’t require expensive equipment. Coming from a village in Maharashtra’s Ahilyanagar, he worked odd jobs – from cleaning washrooms to working in the fields – so he could spend evenings training. “It still feels like a dream to me,” Inamdar told the Indian Express. “I often think about how someone who didn’t even have food at home now holds two international medals.” The 26-year-old was instrumental in helping India win their gold-medal match against Iran.
I would love to hear from you: which sportsperson from the Asian Games did you find most inspiring and why?
What else we’re reading about
Flydubai incident | Indian pilot Smit Machchar is being hailed as a hero for helping to save 174 passengers on the flydubai flight to Israel last week, after his co-pilot made an apparent effort to crash the plane. After being stabbed, Machchar opened the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to enter and overpower the attacker. He is recovering in a hospital in Saudi Arabia, where the plane eventually landed.
Datacentres | Protests against water-guzzling datacentres erupting from the US to Australia are gathering momentum in India. South Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen travelled to the small village of Tarluvada, in Andhra Pradesh, where the state government has been accused of fast-tracking plans for a $15bn AI datacentre for Google, allegedly to avoid stringent environmental scrutiny.
Art and design | Designer Vikram Goyal, celebrated for his signature repoussé brass work, brings his installation Wings and Tales to a Georgian townhouse in London’s Mayfair from 12 to 16 October. The exhibition includes furniture designs inspired by landscapes from the Indian epic Ramayana.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Shireen Gandhy, director of Mumbai’s pioneering Chemould Prescott Road Gallery, founded in 1963, recommends the work of artist Al-Qawi Nanavati. “[She] is a young artist from Bombay whose practice is rooted in printmaking and making her own paper. Her mother’s passing left her with a void,” says Gandhy. Nanavati created Letters to My Mother, an epistolary artwork crafted in, as Gandhy puts it, “a deeply personal language that is not known to anybody but her. Using fabrics and saris that belonged to her mother, she creates this tactile imagery for these letters. I find it very moving and like alchemy.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
13,626
This is the number of students from disadvantaged communities who dropped out of some of India’s most prestigious institutions: central universities, Indian Institutes of Technology and Indian Institutes of Management between 2018 and 2023, according to Anubhuti Vishnoi of the Economic Times. The figure comes from an interim report by a committee set up by the supreme court last year to examine mental health and suicide prevention in higher education.
Vibe check
Nitesh Shetty’s sketches find absurdity in everyday life, turning familiar characters and social interactions into unexpected punchlines. This is what makes his work powerful: you’re laughing one moment and moved the next. There is a reel for every character imaginable: the person perpetually trapped in the limbo of land disputes, the man who is strangely knowledgeable about funerals, or the friend who has a unique dressing sense.
The 35-year-old from Mumbai didn’t plan on a career in comedy. “When you don’t know what to do, you try anything,” he told me. Now, Shetty rejects more conventional formats such as television in favour of challenging himself creatively. His advice for those who look up to him? “It’s a great time to build something. The [online] audience is ready-made for you. Be original and don’t follow trends.”

Bay Area lettering artist Jesscia Hische knew that when she took a freelance gig to design the M logo for Meta’s new AI assistant Muse, it was bound to make some people angry. “AI is such a third rail, and Meta is such a third rail,” she tells me.
Still, as a small business owner who relies on client work to keep her two brick-and-mortar art and stationary shops in Oakland afloat, she says she needed the money. “New Work! (Don’t be mad at me),” Hische wrote in her newsletter last month. “I worked with Meta on an icon and logotype for their latest release: Muse, which just launched! It’s Meta’s foray into the AI agent / personal assistant world. I know folks have big feelings about both AI and Meta, but this has been a really fun project for so many reasons.”
The news quickly went viral on Threads, where dozens of fellow designers criticized Hische for selling out. She responded to the haters by trying to explain the decision:
“For the past year, I pretty much have 2-4 payrolls in my account at any given time, which if you own a small business, you know is pretty precarious,” she wrote. She added that she had also invested $100,000 in Studioworks, an admin platform she runs for creatives, and $30,000 in Drawling, her art shop for kids in Oakland, where she hosts classes and workshops. “I have 4 people on payroll including myself, my mom, and two shop employees,” she added. Nothing she said seemed to help.
“Disgusted,” wrote one user. “It’s not about money, it’s about ethics.”
Another person responded saying, “Doing this job is like doing a hit for the mob, and being surprised later when the mob takes you out too.” Other users posted photos of Hische’s house and speculated about her wealth and finances.
Hische had expected some pushback from the artist community, but the level of vitriol caught her off guard. Even if people didn’t like Meta, she felt the company should be commended for hiring an independent artist rather than using generative AI. But the backlash made it clear just how unpopular generative AI has become in some circles, to the point that working for one in any capacity is seen as a betrayal.
We spoke on the phone last week about the backlash, her design process, and whether she was instructed to not make the Muse logo look like a butthole.
This interview has been edited for clarity and length.
Zoë Schiffer: In your newsletter, you acknowledge that people have complicated feelings about Meta and about AI. Did that make it hard for you to take this job?
Jesscia Hische: The last year or two, my client work has been really slow, and my client work is what supports the other things I do, because the brick-and-mortar businesses are not hugely profitable. My margins are razor thin. I think between the two shops, I had like $10,000 in profit last year. I can't sustain myself on $10,000 a year.
So when the Meta project came around, it was like, alright! Let's get some money in the account so I can pay my staff and I don't have to feel so stressed out every time I have to run a pay cycle.
What were you hired to do, specifically?
I specialize in logo refreshes. I did the redesign of Squier from Fender, I redesigned Jeni’s Ice Cream a few years ago and did Southern Living magazine. When I work on logos, I want them to look like they went to the spa for a weekend—not that they went and got a ton of plastic surgery, you know? Just fresh and new, where you're like, “Oh, something's different. I can't tell what, but I like it.”
The [Meta] team had done an exploration of the M internally. They knew it wasn't quite right. It’s just a bunch of product designers and engineers designing type. Some of them are very skilled at typography, but it's just such a super unique thing to be able to draw letterforms. They wanted to refine what they had already done in terms of the M.
It was a huge sprint for that M. I did the work in two days. There were 32 different versions. The logotype took another two weeks.
What did the team tell you they wanted to change?
They had drawn the M as a single stroke, a vector stroke. It was the same width all the way around. When something is just a mono-weight stroke with no adjustments, there's not a lot of subtlety around the shape. This is where the fun happens with type design. As strokes touch each other and join, it creates this heavier pocket, visually. You get these little inky moments. And what type designers often do is sort of play with subtracting and adding bits of weight.
Their big ask was, “We want this thing to feel inspiring and creative and to get people thinking that Muse is a fun thing you can play with, not that it's like this very rigid, engineered, cold thing.”
How much do you get paid for a project like this?
I charged what I thought was an amazing fee for a two-day sprint for a big company, which was like $12,500. That’s an amazing amount of money to make in two days, but it’s not life-changing.
Meta chief AI officer Alexandr Wang has been talking about the logo recently, noting he’s happy it doesn’t look like a butthole, unlike some of Meta’s competitors.
I do think the “don't make it a butthole logo” thing was probably something they had top of mind internally. But for me, the discussions were more about looking at the Meta infinity loop logo and wanting the Muse logo to look like it was part of the same universe.
How did you decide to start talking about the work publicly?
I wanted to share it because I like sharing about my work. Within my newsletter group, everybody knows that my husband worked for Meta for ages, so they know that I have an association with the company.
I also wanted to acknowledge that AI is a very sensitive topic for people, but acknowledge it to an audience that understands my relationship to both Meta and AI.
I noticed that you responded to a bunch of the people criticizing you. Why?
Generally, if something happens online where there's a misunderstanding, I've been able to just come at [whoever is posting about me] and say “Hey, I hear you,” in an open and conversational way. I’m not trying to persuade them, I’m trying to say, “I agree with this part, but have you considered this?” That's always kind of worked for me in the past to help de-escalate stuff.
But with this, I made a comment about how hopefully, because of this job, I won't have to carry $50,000 in credit card debt through the holidays for my shop, because I have to do a bunch of inventory purchasing. Then that got taken out of context by someone being like, “This rich girl spends $50,000 on Christmas.” And I was just like, OK, wait, someone will see that and not the original post, and then all of a sudden it spins into this story about me being like a kajillionaire sitting on like a pile of emeralds, yelling at poor suffering artists, which is the opposite of my whole vibe.
How did it feel to you, when all this was happening?
The first day when I was like replying to people, I was not torn up about it at all, because I was like, “Oh, these people just don't understand that I'm a small-business owner, that I want to pay my employees. This helps me offer a health plan to like one of my employees. This is good!” And also, this company isn’t hiring me to use AI, I didn’t use AI at all in the process. Isn't this ultimately the future that we want? Large companies hiring independent artists to do things?
But then, as it started to escalate, it just blew up way bigger than I could have ever anticipated. It wasn't just a handful of people talking about it online. It felt like the entirety of Threads, you know? One of the things I have the hardest time with is feeling really misunderstood. I love teaching, but I'm not a guru that's making a predatory $1,500 course or whatever. I tend to charge $35 for a five-hour workshop.
I’m very intentional about things, and I don't just flippantly say yes to things that I obviously feel conflicted about, but I'm also like, this didn't feel like one of those conflicts just because they were paying me as an artist, and I wasn't using AI at all, you know?
So I felt deeply sad. I felt like I had been hit by a truck. For the two days following it, I sat in my bed and sobbed. It just made me feel so awful, like everything I have done up to this point, all the good decisions I tried to make, the free resources I've put out, have been for nothing.
Did it make you regret taking the job?
Not exactly. There was one camp of people who were like, “Of course, do the work if you need to, but just don't talk about it.” But I felt like I was doing a good thing for artists by commending a company that is hiring artists instead of making generative work.
Where do you think the reaction comes from, for designers in particular? Is it fear?
I mean, the fear is real. There’s real fears about AI's impact on commercial art. My husband and I really got into it at one point, because he was working on AI and really excited about it, and I was vehemently anti-AI. Eventually I started seeing the infrastructure, low-level data-processing side of it and how useful it is for things outside of creativity. Then I was like, OK, well, there are silver linings to using this thing. I think that softened the edges for me. My husband also came around to AI’s impact on commercial art, which helped.
Most of the folks in AI are like, “AI helps creativity because it makes human-made things more valuable!” Maybe in fine art, but that's not how commercial art works. Of course, there’s anti-AI purists, and their whole thing is that AI is built on theft, which is true. I think I’m going to benefit from the Anthropic settlement, because they've definitely scraped my books.
I don't use AI for generative art or anything like that. I just use it for admin and for help with coding and web building. But anytime that AI takes the place of a person or does the heavy lifting on stuff that requires human creativity, that's when it becomes problematic.
