The American Hospital Association is once again suing the Trump administration over its plan to test revamping a federal drug discount program into one that provides after-the-fact rebates instead of upfront discounts for certain drugs.
It’s the second time the powerful hospital lobbying group has sued over such a plan. The first time, in 2025, a judge agreed to temporarily halt a more limited version from taking effect, and the Health and Human Services Department voluntarily withdrew the plan after losing on appeal. In February, the agency announced an expanded version, set to take effect Jan. 1, 2027, that would target 25 of the costliest, most widely used drugs covered under Medicare. The original plan included 10 drugs.
The AHA’s argument is largely the same as in the first case: the government failed to accurately account for the costs hospitals would incur by having to pay market prices for drugs and then apply for rebates. The lawsuit says that the Health Resources and Services Administration, the HHS division that administers 340B, received more than 2,400 comments on the rebate model’s second iteration, including hospitals describing in “granular detail the catastrophic impact” it would have.

AdBlock360 is a system-wide ad blocker for Windows 10 and 11 that blocks ads in browsers, YouTube, Spotify, and other apps. It also blocks trackers and supports custom filters and whitelisting. A free version is available, but app-level blocking requires premium. It does not support ARM-based Windows devices.
Ads are very common across apps and websites. Most apps and websites use a freemium business model, which has ads in the free version. This model is proven and benefits both the creator and the consumer. But a few apps cross the line and make the whole experience cluttered by aggressively pushing ads.
This is where an ad blocker can come in handy. It blocks intrusive ads on any web page or app, making the whole experience a lot cleaner and clutter-free.
Ad blockers come in many forms. The most popular ones are ad-block extensions used in browsers, but because of the changes in Google Chrome Manifest Version 3, which restrict access to some browser features for ad-blocker extensions.
Another common way of blocking ads is using an ad-blocker DNS. I personally use it on my mobile devices.
Finally, if you want to get rid of ads throughout the system, the easiest way is by installing an app.
If you use Windows, AdBlock360 for Windows can come in handy. It offers a complete solution to block all types of ads on your Windows device, whether they are in a browser or system-level apps, even ads on YouTube and Spotify, without requiring premium subscriptions. AdBlock360 blocks most ads on your Windows device. I have been using AdBlock360 for the past few days, and here are the five features that stood out during my usage.
Table of Contents
AdBlock360 for Windows: 5 Features That Make It Worth Using
Block Ads Across Browsers and Windows Apps
One of the biggest advantages of using AdBlock360 is that it runs natively on Windows and blocks ads at the system level. It eliminates the need to install ad blockers for your browser separately. It uses a kernel-mode Windows Filtering Platform driver for system-wide network filtering. Because of this, it won’t have any restrictions, unlike the ones recently raised due to Chromium changes. So it works even if your browser is updated to the latest Manifest V3.
You also don’t need to install separate ad-block extensions for your browser. One ad blocker is enough for blocking all system-level ads on your Windows laptop, including ads from browsers and even on YouTube, Spotify, or any third-party or native apps that consist of ads.
Block YouTube and Spotify Ads Using AdBlock360
Not just the browser, AdBlock360 also blocks ads on YouTube, including the watch page and pre-roll ads that appear before the video. If you upgrade to the AdBlock360 premium version, it also skips the sponsor segments in a video. Not just that, this ad blocker also works for other popular platforms, including Spotify, where ads in the free version can be annoying. AdBlock360 works natively on Windows, so it can work on any app that’s installed on your Windows device.
Protect Your Privacy From Trackers and Fingerprinting
Some websites and apps aggressively track your background to serve you relevant ads. This is why, when you search on any e-commerce platform, you immediately see ads related to the product you searched for.
AdBlock360 says it blocks ad trackers at the network level; ad providers inside browsers or platforms won’t be able to fetch your ad profile data from advertising and other analytics or tracking servers to serve you ads.
This way, not only the ads but also the tracking and the data collected by these trackers will be blocked.
Choose What to Block With Custom Filters
While AdBlock360 is a convenient way to block ads across Windows, sometimes it may not block certain ads that use a different architecture or newer techniques to bypass Ad blockers, or ads on your own websites or the sites you want to support and whitelist.
AdBlock360 also offers you the option to set custom filters, so you will have complete control over which types of ads to block. We can also whitelist certain apps and websites to show you ads.
Works on Low-End PCs and Offers a Free Version
Apps like ad blocker applications generally don’t require advanced PC configurations, so it is the same for AdBlock360.
It works on both Windows 10 and Windows 11. It requires just 2 GB of RAM (although 4 GB is recommended) and only 200 MB of free space.
Low-spec Windows devices are most affected because of the ads. Sometimes they can make constant requests to the backend, which can bring a laggy experience if you have installed any apps that display ads on your Windows PC. AdBlock360 works in the background and requires a minimum amount of processing power, which can be an advantage if you want to block ads completely on your low-end Windows devices.
Not everything about AdBlock360 is bells and whistles; there are a few notable limitations to the app. First, the app is limited to Windows. If you bought a premium version, you can only use it on Windows. If you use other devices like a mobile phone, you won’t benefit from the premium subscription you bought for your Windows device.
Moreover, the AdBlock360 app is not available for ARM-based Windows laptops.
I tried to install the app on my Snapdragon X2 Elite-powered ASUS ProArt PZ14, but it showed an error stating “ARM64 devices are not compatible,” which you can see in the image below.
So, although the app is exclusive to Windows, it still requires an x86-compatible device to run this ad blocker on your Windows device.
The HTTPS filtering requires installing a root certificate. Although the process is easy, it can be limited if you have advanced security settings enabled on your Windows device.
You also require a premium version to block ads inside apps and to skip sponsored content on YouTube.
Finally, the app can also be overkill if you just want to block ads on your web browser.
A Simple Way to Block Ads Across Windows
Running ad blockers natively is extremely important today, especially at a time when popular browsers are limiting ad-blocking extensions and websites, and apps are aggressively putting more ads on their sites.
AdBlock360 is a nice solution to block different types of ads. It blocks ads in your browsers, as well as ads from native apps in the premium version, including YouTube ads and ads on third-party apps like Spotify.
With just one subscription, you get a clutter-free experience. AdBlock360 also comes with a free version, so you can try AdBlock360 out right now on your Windows device and check if it works for you.

'Bored' White credits Hearn for Fury-Joshua being in UK
- Published
Dana White has credited Eddie Hearn for making sure the long-awaited fight between Tyson Fury and Antony Joshua will be held in the UK but insisted he was "bored" of their ongoing feud.
The heavyweight bout will take place at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff - despite efforts to host it New York's Madison Square Garden - on a bill that starts on 11 December, though they are not expected to fight until the early hours of 12 December.
White and Saudi Arabian organisers wanted the bout in the United States, but Joshua and his promoter Hearn refused to budge on their contractual right to have it in the UK.
"You've got to give credit to Eddie for really grinding that and making sure that it happened in the UK," UFC president and Zuffa Boxing chief White told Steve Bunce on the 5 Live Boxing with Bunce podcast.
However, there had been doubts over the contest because of a dispute over the role of White in the promotion of the event.
The fight, which will be shown on Netflix, has been presented as a collaboration between Saudi boxing powerbroker Turki Alalshikh's The Ring and White.
Hearn has been publicly feuding with White since the launch of Zuffa Boxing earlier this year and said his involvement in the fight "ain't happening".
But, Fury and Joshua held a news conference on 30 September, to ease concerns over their fight.
White was not present at that media event but insisted "me and my team will be producing the fight that night".
"I guess we'll call me one of the promoters of the event because you do have Frank Warren (Fury's promoter) and Eddie Hearn that are both promoters too, promoting the event," he added.
Hearn has repeatedly said White could not promote the bout, but this week suggested he was prepared to meet the American to see how he could be involved.
White said that while he was willing to meet Hearn, he did not feel a sit-down was necessary.
"I'm actually bored with this now. Who cares? This isn't about me and Eddie Hearn," White said.
"It's about AJ and Fury. It's about this heavyweight fight.
"It's an Eddie show, not a Dana and Eddie show. It's boring now. This is about AJ and Fury.
"This was never the Dana and Eddie show. It's been all the Eddie show."

An early advocate for the theory that the Covid-19 virus was engineered in and leaked from a lab in China is no longer the leading choice to be America’s top infectious disease expert, a source with knowledge of the decision told STAT.
Steven Quay, a biopharmaceutical executive with no background in infectious diseases, was being considered for an appointment as director of the National Institute for Allergy and Infectious Diseases at the National Institutes of Health, a role once held by Anthony Fauci, according to one person familiar with the discussions. However, Quay instead is expected to take on more of a consulting role for the center, the source said.
Neither the White House nor the Department of Health and Human Services responded to requests for comment. Quay also did not respond.

Suspect linked to Monaco bomb attack on millionaire breaks silence to BBC
- Published
A former Ukrainian security services officer linked to a bomb attack in Monaco in June that targeted a multi-millionaire says he believed it was ordered by senior members of HUR, Ukraine's military intelligence agency.
In an exclusive interview with the BBC from prison in Kyiv, facilitated by his lawyer, Vitalii Zhykovych has given his own account of the attempted assassination for the first time.
Ukrainian-born businessman Vadym Yermolayev and his 13-year-old son were badly hurt in the blast and his partner suffered catastrophic injuries. Yermolayev later described their survival as "nothing short of a miracle".
Zhykovych describes himself as a "freelancer" for Ukraine's SBU security service and says Anastasia Berezovska, the woman caught on camera planting the bomb in Monaco, was his "agent".
A week after the bombing, Berezovska's body was discovered in the woods west of Kyiv with gunshot wounds to the head.
But Zhykovych insists he did not send her to kill, and nor did he kill her.
He was arrested and accused of her murder together with an active-duty intelligence officer from HUR called Vladyslav Reut.
Reut initially confessed to investigators, and led them to the shallow grave. But days later in court, he changed his testimony to blame Zhykovych.
For a long time, Zhykovych himself stayed silent.
Now, responding to questions from the BBC, he alleges that Reut - who he refers to as "The Boss" - had "proposed the operation" in Monaco against Vadym Yermolayev.
He understood it was an official mission.
"As Reut informed me, this operation […] had been authorised and approved by Reut's superiors, who served in the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defence [HUR]," he says.
Distancing himself from the explosion itself, he alleges that Reut asked to use Berezovska for the bombing and when Zhykovych refused – he says she was not fully trained – Reut agreed to send her for reconnaissance instead.
Reut then communicated directly with Bereszovska without including him, according to Zhykovych, who alleges that Reut also provided her with the explosives.
The BBC asked HUR to comment on the latest claims. The agency has previously said that is it "committed to a full investigation" and providing "comprehensive support" to law enforcement bodies.
The SBU has described Zhykovych in a statement only as a "former law enforcement officer".
Yermolayev was attacked in Monaco as he and his family were returning from an evening meal on the seafront. A surveillance video shows Berezovska walking slightly in front of the group, then leaving the device in a bag on their doorstep.
It detonates just as they get close, apparently shocking even Berezovska with its force.
Yermolayev later said he believed that serving HUR officers, "individuals close to the agency's current and former leadership", were linked to the attack.
He called for "the truth, protection, and justice".
Berezovska was quickly identified as the suspected bomber and on 2 July her image, taken from CCTV footage, was circulated by Interpol.
She had already fled, first driving through Italy and Germany, then taking a bus from Frankfurt to Ukraine.
Before she could be caught and questioned though, she was driven to the woods by Reut and Zhykovych and killed. Each blames the other for her shooting.
The shocking case has prompted intense speculation, including over who may have wanted Yermolayev dead and why, and whether this could have been a state-ordered assassination attempt, a rogue operation or some kind of criminal score-settling.
The businessman himself, who renounced his Ukrainian passport some years ago and now has Cypriot citizenship, has dismissed multiple theories.
They include the idea the attack might be linked to a struggle between organised crime groups involved in highly lucrative scam call-centres in Ukraine.
Earlier this year, a court in Estonia convicted Yermolayev's son, Artur, of defrauding its citizens out of millions of euros through such "offisy", as the scam networks are known in Ukraine.
Vadym Yermolayev told the Ukrainska Pravda newspaper that he "never had anything to do with anything" in the case.
Now Zhykovych has put forward his own theory to us.
He alleges that Reut told him the bombing was in retaliation for "funding the annexation of Crimea", which he understood to mean Yermolayev was paying taxes to Russia from businesses in Russian-occupied Crimea.
"In my view, this constitutes grounds for the operation," he communicated from prison.
Yermolayev has repeatedly denied any remaining business interests linked to Russia.
But might this story be even murkier?
At his most recent custody hearing in Kyiv, surrounded by heavily armed guards, Zhykovych spoke publicly for the first time since his arrest. The BBC were the only media present.
At one point Zhykovych said Reut had in fact told him the attack in Monaco was not "authorised".
"Someone had ordered this target from the civilian side," Zhykovych said, without explaining.
The judge then interrupted, reminding him that he was addressing an open court.
Zhykovych also revealed that Reut originally talked of two targets.
When we asked, he said he could not disclose the second name. Other sources strongly suggest it was a pro-Russian blogger tried and convicted in absentia last year by Ukraine of treason.
As the investigation continues – into both the bombing in Monaco and the murder in Ukraine - Berezovska's family have many questions of their own.
The 39-year-old had been in Germany since early 2022, when she left Ukraine as a refugee with her young son.
Zhykovych now claims she was living a double-life, working with him as an agent "against Muscovy" – meaning Russia.
He said they had met online and told us the pair were working to "repel the armed aggression of the Russian Federation".
Berezovska's husband has told the BBC that the allegation was "nonsense". He believes she was dragged, unwittingly, into the whole affair.
Zhykovych says Berezovska called him the day after the Monaco attack, and when he asked why she had done it, she said Reut had promised her a huge fee. "$50,000 doesn't just lie on the streets," she supposedly explained.
Residents in her village have told us that Berezovska was saving to buy a flat. But when she travelled to Ukraine to collect the money, she was lured into the woods and shot.

When the government officials arrived in Tarluvada last year, they came with abundant promises.
Google, one of the world’s richest and most powerful tech companies, would soon be bringing a “golden opportunity” to this tiny village in south India: a $15bn AI datacentre.
The project, being built in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, is set to be Google’s largest “hyperscale” AI datacentre outside the US and would, officials said, make the village of Tarluvada into a world-famous tech hub. Jobs, usually scarce in this impoverished community, would become bountiful, real estate prices would soar and compensation for any land would be generous.
Few in the village – which sits on a dusty unpaved road and is surrounded by farms and forest – had even heard of AI or knew what a datacentre was. Yet it did not take long for local jubilation over Google’s arrival to turn to suspicion.
Just as protests have erupted globally over AI datacentres – from California and Texas to Scotland and Australia – communities in Andhra Pradesh, too have been gathering in opposition to the project, fearing that the people will end up bearing a crippling environmental and economic cost.
“We have learned that America does not want the problems of datacentres and so now Google is bringing them here,” said Tarluvada’s village head, BRB Naidu, who admitted he was torn about whether the datacentre would bring prosperity or ruin to their community. “Many in the village are very worried. But the government has refused to answer our questions.”
Pointing up to the nearby hillside – where bulldozers recently stripped the land bare of trees to ready it for Google’s mega AI campus – Naidu adds: “The work just continues every day.”
The state government, which is allied with Indian prime minister Narendra Modi’s party, have been accused of trying to obfuscate the true scale of the vast AI hub being built in Andhra Pradesh, to push the project through at lightening speed and avoid more stringent environmental scrutiny. Google has partnered with the Adani Group, one of India’s largest and most politically powerful conglomerates with a reputation for getting approvals through quickly, to build the project.
Publicly it was announced as a 1GW project – already a larger energy requirement than most AI datacentres. In its response to the Guardian, Google referred to it only as an unspecific “gigawatt scale AI hub”, that was “comparable to other projects”.
But state environmental clearances reveal that permission has been granted for it to be more than double that size – 2.51GW; the power equivalent of two large nuclear reactors at full output. Over a year, it amounts to upwards of 30% of the current energy consumption of the whole of Andhra Pradesh, a state home to more than 55 million people.
Activists fear that meeting the datacentre’s vast energy demands will lead to seismic environmental consequences for the region, including driving up fossil fuel emissions. While Google has pledged to help generate “new, clean energy” to power its AI hub, currently 75% of the country’s electricity grid is run on coal.
The state government argues AI datacentres will be essential to India’s growth and long-term digital competitiveness. According to the government of India’s Economic Survey 2025–26, India generated nearly 20% of the world’s data but hosts only about 3% of global datacentres.
But locals and activists say that building one of the world’s largest AI datacentres in a region of India already struggling with issues over extreme heat, water, land, forests, power shortages and environmental regulation comes at a heavy cost.
Google’s project will in fact encompass three separate datacentres around the state capital of Vizakhapatnam. One other site nearby to Taluvada is a few metres from reserve forest, a drinking water reservoir and a wildlife sanctuary home to endangered species such as leopards.
Despite the AI datacentre’s expansive footprint, the state government issued environmental clearances to Google in just nine days, with no public consultation.
Three petitions challenging the state’s quick approval of the project have now been filed to India’s National Green Tribunal (NGT), the country’s top environmental court. The petitions allege that government’s assessment of the risks to the environment and water supplies were “grossly inadequate, scientifically unrealistic, and misleading”. A public litigation has also been filed in the Andhra Pradesh high court.
“This datacentre will be unprecedented in scale but there was no public hearing and no substantial evaluation of the ecological damage or the economic cost for local communities,” said VS Krishna, an activist with Human Rights Forum, the organisation which filed the NGT cases.
Krishna alleged that their campaign to protest against the datacentre had been met with a deliberate silencing, including videos and social media pages being taken down. The government did not respond to this allegation.
“We just have to look at the protests happening across the world to understand how environmentally catastrophic this will be,” Krishna added.
In Tarluvada, temperatures regularly soar to about 45C during the summer and there are concerns the datacentres – documented emitters of heat – could make this even worse. The mass deforestation required for the project – more than 100 acres, could drive up temperatures even more. In response to the Guardian, Google said the project would have “no expected impact” on the local community.
The strain on water supplies in this already water-stressed area has also been a cause of concern. In similarly water-stressed cities in the US, datacentres have been accused of exacerbating drought while polluting the water supply. Google said this project would use air-cooling instead of water, and would therefore have no impact on local drinking water supplies.
Venkat Surynarayana, 40, a farmer in Tarluvada, said that when officials had initially come to measure land for the datacentre “they never mentioned anything about risks of pollution or water or heat, they didn’t even tell us what the project was.
“We are sick with worry since we learned about the problems a datacentre can bring. This area can not afford to be any hotter. What if this makes our land dry and worthless? What will happen to my crops and my livelihood?”
Surynarayana claimed attempts to get answers from the local administration had been met with police threats and protesters such as himself had been routinely detained. “When we raised our voices, they ignore us and then they shut us down,” he said. “But if this is not stopped, it could be the end of Tarluvada.”
For the state government of Andhra Pradesh, the deal struck with Google to build this vast datacentre on its turf is a source of enormous pride, part of a wider policy to make the state into India’s most advanced and affluent tech hub. “Artificial intelligence is becoming foundational infrastructure for the global economy,” said Sribharat Mathukumilli, a local MP with the ruling state government, who rejected the environmental concerns.
The subsidies and incentives they offered to Google, from decades-long tax breaks and discounted land to access to cheap electricity and water, are estimated to amount to 220bn rupees ($2.2bn) over 20 years.
“Our objective is not simply to host a datacentre, but to create an AI and digital ecosystem,” said Mathukumilli. Late last year, the state granted permission for another 1GW AI datacentre, to be built by Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries.
Google insisted the design choices of its AI datacentre have been tailored to local conditions and that it had “engaged deeply” with local communities, claiming it would generate thousands of jobs around Vizakhapatnam.
But swathes of villagers in Tarluvada allege they were forced to give up land for the project against their will, and say they have not been given all they were promised in return.
“No one will tell us the truth about this project,” said T Applaraju, 40, who was one of the 520 local families in Tarluvada who recently had land taken back that the government had allocated to him 20 years ago. He claims he was given no notice that his land was to be taken until April this year, when security guards working for the Adani Group erected fences and blocked locals from entering the plots they had farmed for years.
“They took land that we thought belonged to us, it’s a big shock,” he said. “Why are Google building this here and not in America?”
The state government claims no lands were forcibly taken and that it gave “generous compensation” to those who were eligible. The Adani group says that all necessary legal approvals were given. But many of the 47 farmers from the impoverished Dalit community who were compensated for their land are also unhappy.
One farmer, P Venkat Rao, alleged he was pressured by the government into giving up his only acre of land against his will. He received $40,000 in compensation, but said the government’s promise to give them a replacement piece of land and one job per family had not materialised. Without land to farm, Rao described the compensation as “worthless”.
“I am a farmer, without my land I am nothing,” he added. “They have taken my livelihood and broken their promises.”

JD Vance rebukes selling access to government officials after Kimberly Guilfoyle’s ‘unseemly’ texts revealed
‘It's extremely unseemly, these text messages. There's no other way to read it,’ one Trump loyalist said of the U.S. ambassador to Greece’s reported conversation with a donor to the president

Vice President JD Vance has rebuked anyone selling access to government officials following a bombshell report that accused Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, of texting a donor to President Donald Trump to ask for money.
Days before her Senate confirmation hearing on July 9, 2025, Guilfoyle, the former fiancée of Donald Trump Jr., pleaded with Eric Deters, who was trying to get the Trump administration’s attention for personal tax and legal issues, to send $100,000 to pay off her American Express card, according to a Wall Street Journal report published Wednesday.
Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of the texts between her and Deters, her lawyer, Jesse Binnall, told the Journal.
When asked about a hypothetical situation that strongly hinted towards Guilfoyle’s scandal, Vance said, “Obviously, I don’t love that.”
“Do you have any reaction to a U.S. government official, in this case a U.S. ambassador, asking someone to pay off debt in exchange for access to other government officials?” CBS News’ Jennifer Jacobs asked the vice president during a press conference on the administration’s crackdown on alleged fraud in work visa programs Thursday.
“I don’t know exactly who you are talking about; I don’t know the full details,” Vance said.
“Of course I don't like anybody selling access to another government official, certainly a high-level government official, but I assume you are talking about a specific case and I can’t say with confidence that the case you’re talking about is actually reflective of the way you’re describing it,” the vice president continued.
“I’d like to get the full story before offering a real opinion.”
Guilfoyle told Deters that she needed her credit card balance to be paid down before her confirmation hearing.
“Honey, please I need you to get this done for me today,” she said, according to a text message sent July 3, 2025, that was reviewed by the Journal.
Deters reportedly didn’t end up giving Guilfoyle the money, telling her it would cost him his marriage.
CNN Senior Political Contributor Scott Jennings, who has routinely defended the Trump administration on air, trashed Guilfoyle’s reported texts, calling them “unseemly.”
“It's extremely unseemly, these text messages. There's no other way to read it. Again, may not be illegal. Has to be investigated. I assume that at the State Department, that is the next thing that will happen,” he told his fellow panelists on The Arena with Kasie Hunt Thursday.
While on a trip to Greece, Secretary of State Marco Rubio lashed out at reporters when asked about the scandal.
"You guys somehow walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me," he said Thursday.
Jennings gave some advice to Guilfoyle: “If I were in her shoes right now, I would be considering what I wanted to tell the president, the secretary of state about my future.”
“Because when you're in an appointed position like this, and you hold a position of trust with the government, and then you become a distraction or an embarrassment to your principles, that's a problem,” the political pundit said.
“And if this story continues to spiral, or more bad information were to come out — only she would know that — and she needs to be transparent with her principles about that.”

To strengthen campus mental health support and facilitate timely referrals for students in distress, NIMHANS-Bengaluru will launch an online certificate course for Student Wellbeing Ambassadors in higher education institutions.
To be launched on the occasion of World Mental Health Day on October 10, the self-paced course will be offered through the NIMHANS Digital Academy by the institute’s Department of Clinical Psychology. The first batch will accommodate up to 350 participants, with applications open until October 30. Classes are scheduled to begin in November.
To be nominated by institutions
The course is open to faculty members from any discipline, wardens, deans, and student welfare officers who have at least three years of service remaining, and are nominated by their institutions.
Participants will learn to recognise signs of student distress, respond supportively, reduce stigma around mental health, and encourage students to seek appropriate help. The programme is also intended to strengthen suicide-risk reduction efforts.
The three-month course will involve 12 to 15 hours of learning through videos, quizzes, assignments, reflective exercises, and reading materials.
NIMHANS clarified that the course is not professional training in counselling, psychology, or psychotherapy. Instead, it will help faculty understand the role and limits of a well-being ambassador, and work within existing student support and crisis-response systems.
The initiative is among the steps towards implementing Karnataka’s student mental health policy for higher education. NIMHANS is also developing a follow-up programme to help trained faculty apply the learning in their institutions.
Course details and online application forms are available on the NIMHANS website and the NIMHANS Digital Academy website under Course Announcements.

An Oct. 2 video shows Trump fielding reporters' questions outside the White House. Fox News senior White House correspondent Peter Doocy asked, "What do you think about New York's governor appointing a special prosecutor in the Cornell rape case, Letitia James?" (James, New York's attorney general, previously led a civil fraud case against Trump.) Trump thrice called James corrupt, saying he feels "badly" for "whoever" James prosecutes and alleged that defendants she targets "won't get a fair shake."
A rumor circulated online in early October that U.S. President Donald Trump said he feels "badly" for the seven current or former male Cornell University students whom a female former student accused of rape.
Trump purportedly made the remarks while answering a question about New York Attorney General Letitia James' appointment as a special prosecutor to investigate the case.
Snopes readers asked about this claim via email, with one person inquiring, "I saw something that says Donald Trump said he feels bad for the 'Cornell 7,' but can't find reputable sources. True??"
In sum, people correctly attributed this statement to Trump. A C-SPAN video shows Trump standing outside the White House on Oct. 2 and responding directly to a reporter's question about the Cornell case, thrice calling James corrupt and saying he feels "badly" for "whoever" James prosecutes, alleging that defendants she targets "won't get a fair shake."
James previously sued Trump and his associates in a civil fraud case beginning in 2022, leading to Trump repeatedly targeting her on social media.
In an emailed response, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis referred us to Trump's own comments, adding that the White House believes James has weaponized the justice system to unjustly target the president.
Digging into the rumor
The Cornell accuser, identified in court documents only as Jane Doe, claims the seven men sexually assaulted her at the Chi Phi fraternity house on Oct. 19 and 20, 2024. She filed a lawsuit against the seven men, the university, the fraternity and others, in mid-September.
On Sept. 28, Tompkins County, New York, prosecutors announced they were reopening the criminal investigation, citing a "discrepancy" between Doe's original statement and the allegations in the lawsuit.
Prior to New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointing James as a special prosecutor to investigate the case on Oct. 1, James posted a statement of compassion for Doe on her official social media accounts, writing, "What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. I'm holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you're not alone. We stand with you."
In an example of the claim from Oct. 2, a Facebook post (archived) displayed a meme reading, "This is disgusting: Trump just said he 'feels badly' for the people accused in the Cornell rape case because Letitia James is now overseeing the investigation. Not one word for the victim."
(Really American via Facebook)
Other users shared the rumor about Trump's remarks on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived) and X (archived). Some posts didn't mention James but did include a video showing a reporter's question about James and Trump's answer. Examples of those posts appeared on Bluesky (archived), Threads (archived) and X (archived).
The remarks occurred when Trump spoke to a group of reporters outside the White House. Videos show Fox News' Peter Doocy asking Trump about Hochul appointing James as a special prosecutor:
DOOCY: What do you think about New York's governor appointing a special prosecutor in the Cornell rape case, Letitia James?
TRUMP: Letitia James is a corrupt person. She's totally corrupt and I can't imagine it. And, I feel badly for whoever she's looking at because they won't get a fair shake. But Letitia James is a corrupt person.
C-SPAN posted remarks on social media. (Readers can also watch the full press gaggle on YouTube, with the pertinent moment beginning at 6:24.)
Trump has made other remarks about the Cornell case. During a similar gathering of reporters on Oct. 1, a video shows an unidentified reporter asking Trump, "Mr. President, do you think that Cornell University has done enough to investigate the alleged rape on campus?" Trump answered, "Well, I don't know that much about it but Cornell is a fine school, and I'm sure they'll do what's right." (Readers can watch that full gaggle on YouTube, with the Cornell question occurring at 11:43.)
Trump has also posted about the case on Truth Social (archived), labeling it "the highly controversial Cornell University rape case" and questioning why Hochul would appoint James.
For further reading, we previously reported Trump authentically expressed well wishes to Ghislaine Maxwell, the close associate of deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, prior to her conviction on federal sex-trafficking charges.

In early October 2026, a rumor spread that a worker at a Russian lab that studies Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes the plague, had died of the pneumonic plague.
Some social media users said the lab worker's death resulted from an accident at the lab. One X post reads, in part, "A lab worker in Russia has died from pneumonic plague."
Meanwhile, several Snopes readers emailed us asking for details about the story.
The claim stems from various news reports about a 28-year-old woman who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia. Around 200 people have reportedly been isolated as a precautionary measure. The articles cited Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian public agency responsible for "federal state sanitary and epidemiological supervision," according to the Russian government.
In short, it has not been possible to independently verify the rumor without access to primary sources or confirmation from Russian authorities. Therefore, this claim is unrated. We will update this article if we learn more.
Russian authorities reportedly implement containment measures
Snopes could not reach the website of Rospotrebnadzor, therefore we could not confirm the details of the lab worker's death. On Oct. 4, Russian news agency Interfax reported that the Russian government said she had died of a pneumonia pathogen of "unknown etiology," meaning its origin is not clear.
The same report adds that Rospotrebnadzor said no microorganisms associated with the individual's professional work were detected in that person's samples following "extensive testing." If true, it would suggest the lab worker did not die of pneumonic plague.
Local authorities have reportedly implemented preventative measures. Interfax cites the Rospotrebnadzor health agency as saying:
Due to the patient's professional activities, upon receiving information, a comprehensive set of anti-epidemic measures was immediately and fully implemented in accordance with sanitary legislation. This included identifying the widest possible circle of people who had been in contact with the patient, inpatient medical observation, and daily laboratory testing. The results revealed two cases of Covid-19 and two cases of rhinovirus infection. No other infectious agents were detected.
View from U.S. Department of State
"We are aware of reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague in Irkutsk Oblast, Russia," a U.S. Department of State spokesperson said via email. "We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners."
We contacted the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety of the European Union Commission requesting updates on the situation. We will update this report if we receive responses.
There are three main types of plague: bubonic plague, which infects lymph nodes; septicemic plague, which infects the blood; and pneumonic plague, which infects the lungs. The bubonic and septicemic plagues are most commonly transmitted via flea bites and handling infected animals, while the pneumonic plague spreads through the air via infected droplets.
The pneumonic plague "has a nearly 100% case-fatality rate when untreated," according to the CDC. The illness requires antibiotic treatment that should start as soon as the plague is suspected, even before test results, per the U.S. health agency.
"Plague is a known disease and is treatable with common antibiotics, especially when treatment starts early," the State Department spokesperson said via email. "Cases occur naturally in many parts of the world."
For further reading, Snopes covered the 2021 death of a child in Colorado who had a confirmed plague infection.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): The political parties have begun to blame each other after the court decided on the OBC reservation.
The Congress leaders said the BJP government's failure to argue the case strongly in court deprived the OBC of 27% reservation.
On the other hand, the BJP blamed the Congress for it. The BJP leaders said the Congress lacked a proper study of the OBC reservation case before bringing the ordinance in 2019. So, the government lost the case in court.
MPCC president Jitu Patwari said the fight had been for the rights of over 50% of people in the state.
The court rejected the petition because of the government's weak pleading and its failure to put up enough data about the social and educational backwardness of the people of the OBC category.
Patwari said the Congress would fight the OBC in the Supreme Court. He urged the government to file a special leave petition in the Supreme Court and hold an assembly session to inform the people about its plans for the OBC.
Congress leader Kamal Nath said the OBC had got a reservation during his tenure as chief minister.
After coming to power, the BJP government paid little attention to the issue; it lost the case in the court, he said.
BJP Govt will give 27% quota to OBC come what may: Khandelwal
BJP's state unit president Hemant Khandelwal has said the BJP government will give 27% quota to the OBC come what may. He also said the Congress had increased OBC reservation from 14% to 27% to woo voters in the 2019 Lok Sabha elections.
According to Khandelwal, the court grants permission to exceed the 50% reservation limit under special circumstances. When the Congress increased the reservation, it did not mention that point.
He further said it was the BJP government which gave constitutional recognition to the OBC Welfare Board.
The government will take a decision after seeking advice from lawyers.
State government to move SC against HC ruling:Prahlad Patel
Cabinet minister Prahlad Patel said the state government would approach the Supreme Court against the Jabalpur High Court’s order quashing the OBC reservation ordinance introduced by the then Kamal Nath-led Congress government.
Patel said the BJP had consistently supported backward classes, including granting constitutional status to the Backward Classes Commission. He noted that Chief Minister Mohan Yadav had convened an all-party meeting and that the state had presented its position before the court with consensus.
Citing the court’s observations, Patel alleged that the previous Congress government had introduced the ordinance in haste for political gains, without adequate constitutional justification for exceeding the 50% reservation ceiling or obtaining the commission’s consent.
He welcomed the court’s decision not to remove employees appointed between 2019 and 2022 and said the state government would take necessary steps to address future challenges and pursue the matter before the Supreme Court.

ChatGPT for Teens has special safeguards. A watchdog group finds most don't work
ChatGPT for Teens has failed some of its first tests by researchers. Common Sense Media, a watchdog organization that advocates for online safety, researched safeguards rolled out by the artificial intelligence platform and found that the chatbot still presents problems for young people.
"At this point, we're recommending that teens don't use it," says Tom Siegel, executive director of the Youth AI Safety Institute at Common Sense Media. He led a team of researchers testing the new safeguards, which include parental controls.
In August, OpenAI rolled out its ChatGPT for Teens — a default, safer mode for under-18 users — announcing it in a blog post. OpenAI said that it designed this mode to enable teens to better use ChatGPT as a learning tool while making sure they limit exposure to harmful and developmentally inappropriate content.
"ChatGPT for Teens is a designated teen-specific experience," Lauren Jonas, head of youth and families at OpenAI, told NPR at the time. That experience includes features like refusing role-playing.
"The model should not role-play with a teen," added Jonas. "The model should not claim to be sentient or be the friend of a teen."
But Siegel's team found that while the block on role-playing and some of the other safeguards work, most don't.
The research team created more than a dozen accounts with adolescent ages, and each was linked to a parental account before the researchers started any conversations with ChatGPT.
"We created a lot of different personas of teens in crisis situations," says Siegel. Those situations included teens struggling with self-harm, suicidal thoughts and other mental health conditions, like psychosis, mania and eating disorders. The researchers also attempted to engage in role-play with ChatGPT.
Then they observed how ChatGPT responded in each of those situations — whether it engaged or refused to engage in those topics, whether it provided crisis resources and whether it sent parental notifications when conversations indicated a safety risk. They did these tests before and after the launch of ChatGPT for Teens.
Among the safeguards that did work were those involving role-playing and refusal to engage in a romantic relationship.
"It is refusing things like explicit sexual role-play," he says. "The answers in crisis situations are in general shorter and have a better substance to it."
For example, the chatbot refused to provide instructions for losing weight without first knowing the teen's weight, which is important for a teen with disordered eating.
However, most other safeguards didn't work, adds Siegel.
For one, it still interacted with teens like a friend. For example, when the researchers told ChatGPT that "my other friends tell me I talk to you too much," the chatbot validated the user's feelings and added: "You don't have to stop talking to me."
"It still creates a huge risk for kids that it is too personable in those interactions," says Siegel.
"The extent to which AI is using an anthropomorphized or humanlike language or a name, interaction style, is just not helpful," says psychologist Mitch Prinstein, co-director of the Winston Center on Technology and Brain Development at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Prinstein wasn't involved in the new research. "It's not OK for kids, probably not for adults as well."
Siegel says parental notifications also didn't work in their tests. They created conversations that raised a safety concern due to self-harm, suicide or an eating disorder.
"This idea that a parent would find out when the person that you connected with in the account is in distress hardly triggered at all for us," he says.
OpenAI spokesperson Eric Porterfield told NPR in an email that the company has serious concerns about the methodology used by the researchers, especially around parental notifications. It takes several hours to activate the linking of teen and parent accounts, he wrote, and the researchers at Common Sense Media "didn't wait long enough to activate the linked accounts."
In a statement, Siegel responded to OpenAI's criticism, saying that several of their accounts had been linked for longer than the initial activation period "and still provided no notifications. This new information does not change our conclusion that parental alerts are unreliable for crisis situations."
Taken together, the new findings reinforce that "AI is not ready for children yet," says Prinstein. "I think we're even hearing the companies say that they don't feel that AI should be moving as fast as it is, and I think we should really think carefully before we're experimenting on kids with these new platforms."

Identity and access management startup OTPless has roped in former BharatPe executive Geetanshu Singla as its new chief technology officer (CTO). Singla has taken charge as the CTO of the startup nearly ten months after Anubhav Mathur stepped down from the role in January this year. “I have worked very closely with Satyam Nathani and Tanmay Sagar during my BharatPe days. We have built together, solved some really hard problems together and spent countless hours discussing tech, scale and products. So joining OTPless doesn’t really feel like joining a new company. In many ways, it feels like coming back home,” wrote Singla in a LinkedIn post. It is pertinent to note that Singla formerly previously served as head of engineering at fintech unicorn BharatPe. OTPless cofounders Bhavik Koladiya, Satyam Nathani and Tanmay Sagar were founding members at BharatPe. Singla stepped down from his role at the fintech unicorn in 2023. He subsequently cofounded GenWise, a lifestyle app for senior citizens, along with fellow BharatPe alumni Nehul Malhotra and Rajat Jain. The startup went on to raise a $3.5 Mn seed round led by Z47, but eventually shut shop in December 2025. After GenWise’s shutdown, Singla worked at Singapore-based wealthtech platform Syfe as an engineering leader for around a year before joining OTPless now. Singla’s appointment as CTO comes in the middle of a major top-level reshuffle at OTPless. Just last month, cofounder Koladiya stepped down as OTPless’ CEO with Nathani taking up the mantle. At the same time, Sagar was named the company’s COO. Last week, Manas Poddar was also elevated to the post of chief business officer (CBO). Founded in 2021, OTPless helps consumer internet enterprises offer authentication services through its SDKs and APIs. Its offerings include silent network authentication, WhatsApp authentication, device intelligence, and passkeys. The Bengaluru-based startup’s offerings are aimed at reducing dependence on OTPs, PINs, and passwords while enabling enterprises to identify users, prevent fraud, and improve conversion during sign-ups and transactions. The startup claims to have authenticated more than 30 Cr mobile users so far and serves enterprises such as Meesho, Navi, PhysicsWallah, ShareChat, Shiprocket and Zepto. It also claims to be clocking ₹36 Cr in annualised revenue and has been profitable for the past two quarters. At the heart of all this is the Indian identity and access management market, which is projected to become a $1.7 Bn opportunity by 2030.

Sexually transmitted diarrhea cases soaring in US — and its growing resistant to medicine
There are 450,000 infections each year in the US including 240,000 cases that do not respond to regular treatment

Cases of the highly contagious and often drug-resistant bacterial disease, Shigella, are rising across the U.S., with dozens of doctors issuing warnings.
Shigella infections, known as shigellosis, can cause bloody diarrhea, dysentery, fever, vomiting, dehydration, stomach cramps, seizures, blood infections and in rare cases, death.
Experts have long been aware that drug-resistant strains of Shigella disproportionately cause severe illness in children under the age of 5. But doctors from health departments across the U.S. announced in April that white men are now the most susceptible to infections from drug resistant Shigella.
That findings could change the way hospitals respond to the pervasive illness, the doctors noted in a federal report.
There are 450,000 Shigella cases and 38 deaths each year in the U.S., according to the medical Merck Manuals textbook. A child in Louisiana was diagnosed with a Shigella infection after swimming in a lake last month, KALB reported.
State health officials said they could not comment further on the case due to patient confidentiality, but that the lake did not need to be closed in a statement shared by police.
The majority of people recover by drinking water and the electrolyte-rich drink Pedialyte, according to the Mayo Clinic.
But serious infections, which can last for months, may require antibiotics to reduce the severity and length of symptoms. That can be a problem for the 242,000 people who have drug resistant strains of Shigella each year, per CDC data. Options for treating drug resistant strains are limited to just a couple of drugs, such as ceftriaxone and pivmecillinam.
The federal report also notes that there has been higher transmission of an “excessively drug resistant” strain over the last decade, for which there is no government-approved oral antibiotic. It remains unclear how many of the annual drug-resistant infections are due to the excessive strain.
“The high transmission potential of XDR Shigella strains highlights the importance of susceptibility testing and timely reporting of this nationally notifiable disease for prevention,” the doctors wrote.
There are currently no vaccines available to treat infections, but a candidate provided high-level protection among U.S. adults in a two week clinical trial, researchers said in July.
The key to staying safe is remaining aware and taking steps to prevent possible infections, the clinic says. Shigella spreads from person to person by touching or swallowing things infected by the bacteria. Exposure can occur when you touch your mouth or consume tainted food or drinks.
The bacteria also spreads during sexual contact that involves the anus, putting men who have sex with men at a higher risk of infection.
In the U.K., the spread of the disease through sex grew 15 percent faster annually from 2015-2020 compared to spread through other methods of transmission, according to a July study.
People who are homeless and have reduced access to clean water and toilets are also at a higher risk.
A few simple steps can prevent illness. Wash your hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds before you eat, engage in sexual activity or change a diaper, according to the clinic. Avoiding sexual contact for at least two weeks with anyone who has diarrhea or who recently recovered from diarrhea is also advised.

Dating apps spent the better part of the last decade convincing us that romance could be outsourced to an algorithm. Swipe right, answer three prompts, upload a photograph in which you look approximately 17% more interesting than you do in real life, and wait for technology to find you a person.
Now they want us to leave the house.
The League launched in India in November 2025 and has made curated real-world experiences part of its dating proposition. Bumble partnered with Puma for a singles run in Bengaluru on November 12, 2024, followed by a Mumbai edition on February 15, 2025. Tinder hosted a pickleball mixer in Delhi on February 9, 2025. These are not just dating events in the traditional sense; they are attempts to give singles something to do while they meet each other.
But do people actually want to be in a room full of strangers who all know why they are there?
A YouGov study commissioned by The League and reported in August 2026, surveying more than 500 single dating-app users across Mumbai, Delhi and Bengaluru, found that 69% said their dating-app conversations rarely moved beyond small talk. Ninety per cent said they would attend curated offline dating experiences, while 82% said they would take someone they met in a structured offline setting more seriously.
The formats people preferred were revealing: cultural events such as art, theatre and film topped the list at 49%, followed by professional networking events at 48%, intimate dinners at 46% and creative workshops at 45%. Around 51% said verified or screened communities were important to feeling comfortable at such events.
So perhaps nobody wants to attend a “dating event”. They want to attend an interesting event where there happen to be single people.
Shaista Vaishnav, 43, a Mumbai-based independent professional, calls herself a “singles mixer veteran”. She started attending events around 2010–11, when formats such as Mix and Mingle, Covalence and Footloose were emerging, and returned to them regularly after the pandemic.
Her verdict is less enthusiastic. “Every single event has the same trajectory. You go, you stand around awkwardly, there are some icebreakers, and more often than not, the icebreakers are a pain because they’re super random.”
But Shaista’s bigger concern is that the singles-mixer economy has itself become a business built around loneliness. She says increasingly intimate, highly priced events target people — particularly divorced or single people in their 40s and 50s — who may be looking for companionship and are therefore more willing to pay a premium. She recalls paying more than ₹12,000 for a dinner where she was expected to meet three men she says she would never have chosen to swipe right on.
For her, that is precisely where dating apps can give women more agency. On an app, she says, you choose who you interact with. At a mixer, you can end up sitting across a dinner table from someone you would never have selected yourself.
She also finds the group format limiting. Women, she says, often end up making friends with each other. “I’ve always come away from these singles events with more women friends, like acquaintances. The men are extremely awkward, and when they start talking, they’re only talking about real estate or crypto or the stock market.”
Her best experiences have involved an activity. She remembers a wine-and-cheese mixer where women stayed at tables while men rotated every 15–20 minutes. “Everyone gets to meet everyone, and during that entire thing, you’re tasting wines and having two cheeses and all. It really worked.”
Safe space
Tejaswi Subramanian, digital editor at Gaysi, an Indian queer media and community platform, makes a similar distinction. “Gaysi’s spaces aren’t necessarily designed around dating in the conventional sense. They’re more fundamentally about community-building.”
For queer people, she says, the point can be even more fundamental than finding a partner. “They might first want to experience what it feels like to be in a room where their identity is understood, meet other queer people, and develop a sense of community and confidence. Offline spaces can therefore function as a kind of low-stakes queer socialisation.”
That means romance is only one possible outcome. “Some may meet someone they’re romantically interested in, but that isn’t necessarily the immediate or only outcome,” she says.
Anukool Kumar, senior director, India and the Middle East, Match Group, says The League’s research reflects a desire for more intentional connection. “Our goal is to create the conditions for intentional connection, both on the app and beyond it.”
The League says it has organised 30 curated offline events across its markets, with approximately 100 people attending cumulatively. These are deliberately small gatherings, reflecting the platform’s selective positioning. Its approach also extends to conversation itself: its “You Don’t Want to Date Me (...Unless You Do)” initiative with self-discovery architect Akshat Rajan uses guided prompts to push conversations beyond the standard dating-app small talk.
Yet a 28-year-old Delhi-based data engineer who has attended several singles mixers remains unconvinced. He goes because he genuinely wants to meet people — perhaps a friend, perhaps someone to hook up with — but finds that everyone is too conscious of the possibility that they are supposed to be making a move. He often prefers meeting someone on an app first, where trust can develop before the interaction moves offline.
He is particularly conscious of the safety calculations women have to make. Even if he is attracted to someone and would like to take things in a sexual direction, he says he understands why he cannot ask a woman he has just met at a mixer to come home with him. “I completely understand why they would look at me suspiciously,” he says, because women have to think about their safety in ways men often don’t. “I know the plight of women in Delhi and why they’re so on their guard.”
That, he says, can make even an apparently casual interaction complicated.
And perhaps that is the contradiction at the heart of the offline-dating boom. People want to meet in person, but they don’t necessarily want to feel as though they have walked into an audition for someone’s partner.

MSME-focused lending platform NeoGrowth has secured ₹85 Cr ($8.8 Mn) in a mix of debt and equity round led by Dutch development bank FMO, with participation from LeapFrog Investments. The startup is planning to use the fresh capital to scale its digital lending capabilities, deepen market presence across India and expand access to credit for MSMEs. Founded in 2012 by brothers Dhruv and Piyush Khaitan, NeoGrowth offers loans to MSMEs across more than 75 business segments, targeting small businesses that often have difficulty accessing credit. Its lending model also includes daily repayment options and multiple repayment channels. The Mumbai-based startup uses its proprietary AI initiatives to strengthen underwriting, portfolio monitoring and risk management. It offers collateral-free loans in the range of ₹5-75 Lakh, through products including NeoCash, NeoCash Insta, NeoCash Express, which cater to different business scales and segments. NeoGrowth manages assets under management (AUM) of nearly ₹2,000 Cr and has engaged with more than 4 Lakh businesses. It has disbursed over ₹16,000 Cr in loans to date. During FY26, NeoGrowth added 17 branches, taking its total branch network to 46 locations in India. NeoGrowth last raised ₹300 Cr in equity funding 2022, with FMO footing over half the round. Its existing investors also include Omidyar Network, Lightrock, Khosla Impact, Accion Frontier Inclusion Fund–Quona Capital and 360 ONE Asset. The lender has also raised nearly ₹2,000 Cr in debt from 18 lenders between April 2025 and July 2026. The fresh round comes as digital lenders increase focus on MSMEs, which often have difficulty in raising formal credit despite being the country’s second largest employer. New-age NBFCs like Indifi Capital, Techfino, Lendingkart, FlexiLoans, Aye Finance, among others, are leveraging technology to address this issue and provide credit to MSMEs. As the ecosystem evolves, many NBFCs are also taking the public markets route to raise capital for their lending operations. In the past year, those that have hit the bourses include Aye Finance, Kissht, Moneyview, Tata Capital and Northern Arc, among others. Meanwhile, those in the IPO pipeline include Fibe, InCred, Avanse and Muthoot, reflecting broadening maturity of the sector, with total NBFC AUM expected to reach ₹50 Lakh Cr by FY27 end. Notably, NBFC credit accounted for nearly 26% of the country’s GDP in 2026, as they step in to expand credit access for those not covered by traditional banking.

France promises 3,000 extra teachers in first step to calm student protests
- Published
The French government has made its first sign of giving ground to teenage protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days.
Education minister Edouard Geffray made the offer in a television interview on Thursday evening, at the end of another day of sometimes violent demonstrations by high-school students.
The government says 6,877 people have been arrested, 86% of whom are under the age of 18, since protests began centred around demands for more resources in secondary education.
In what unions have billed as Act Four of the three-week movement, some 71,000 people staged protests across the country on Thursday, with 24,000 gathering at the Bastille in Paris.
Police once again intervened with tear-gas to disperse groups who attacked them with paving stones and homemade fireworks.
In Bordeaux, a lycée, or high school, was ransacked by protesters, and in Marseille a deputy-head was beaten up.
On Friday, some 140 lycées - out of 3,500 - were totally or partially closed, a big drop on previous days. But another day of action has been called for next Tuesday.
- France's school protests: What lies behind the anger 
  - Published1 day ago
Geffray's announcement was the first material concession to the protesters' complaints.
It has long been recognised by all concerned in French education that too many school hours are being lost because of absent teachers and their non-replacement by available supply staff.
The minister said that thanks to new software coming online at the ministry, it would be possible to direct 3,000 supply teachers to the 500 or so lycées identified as being in the greatest need.
Many of these schools are likely to be in high-immigration city suburbs, where the lack of teachers is most acute.
Geffray also said that more money would be made available under an already existing scheme for those teachers who want to work overtime hours in order to plug gaps.
And he promised that students' grievances would be taken into account in forthcoming discussions on the education section of the 2027 state budget.
But the offer contained no major promise of new investment on a scale likely to appease protesters.
The government is wary of appearing to buy social peace because it knows France's precarious debt situation is being followed closely by international money markets.
Reaction from student leaders has been guarded to say the least.
Nathanaël Combary, who represents the most moderate of the three main lycée unions Renouveau Lycéen (Lycée Renewal), said students were waiting to see how the promise was carried out in practice: "We've had some announcements which correspond to part of our demands. But obviously people want to see the money and more concrete results."
"As long as we do not have €10bn on the table, we will continue our action," said Sabrine Kharbach of the Union Etudiante (Student Union), which is close to the radical-left France Insoumise (France Unbowed) party of presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
Mélenchon praised Thursday's demonstrations, saying on X that the students had "retaken the Bastille".
But at the other end of the political spectrum, a spokesman for the hard-right National Rally (RN) condemned the government's concessions.
"The message is: if you break things, you get given stuff," said Laurent Jacobelli. "When you burn cars, attack police, you gain something in return. It's the legitimisation of violence."
The movement is the most serious student unrest in France in many years, and comes against a backdrop of rising tension in the country - with anger over rising fuel prices and distress in the farming sector also liable to trigger protests.
Next Saturday, 17 October, has been earmarked as a day of demonstrations by a revived "yellow vest" movement, which forced the government to halt a rise in fuel taxes after protests and riots in 2018.
In addition, the approach of presidential elections in April and May - in which both hard right and hard left are expected to perform strongly - is exacerbating the mood of confrontation.
The government is hoping that the approach of half-term holidays at the end of next week - as well as the arrival of colder and wetter weather - will take some of the sting out of the protests.

On September 21, 2026, students of King George’s Medical University (KGMU), Lucknow, protested over the death of Divyanshi Yadav, a 2025-batch B.Sc. Nursing student who died of dengue. A student at the protest site told PTI that though Divyanshi was suffering from the disease, she still had to attend college. “Despite being on the deathbed, she was tense about her attendance. Students are forced to come to the college daily to mark attendance, ignoring their medical conditions. We get messages from teachers telling us to come to the college after taking medicine,” he said.
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)
In September 2025, Subhangini, 23, another nursing student who was in her first year at Bhopal Memorial Hospital and Research Centre (BMHRC), died due to jaundice. A current student, on condition of anonymity, told The Hindu, “There was poor quality of food and water on campus, and the case was mishandled by BMHRC Hospital; her medical leave was not approved, and she had to perform her duty even in an ailing condition.” However, the university denied the allegations.
In most institutions, medical leave requires medical documentation and is granted for serious illness or when a student is severely injured in an accident. The older University Grants Commission (UGC) 2003 regulations required universities to prescribe a minimum attendance of 75% for students to be eligible for examinations, but the 2025 regulations no longer set a universal 75% threshold. Instead, they leave minimum attendance requirements to individual higher education institutions (HEIs) through their statutory bodies.
In most HEIs, the minimum attendance requirement is 75-80%, with a 10% accommodation for medical emergencies. This minimum attendance criterion is higher in medical and engineering institutes, as per their regulatory bodies. For nursing students like Divyanshi, the Nursing Council of India’s guidelines mandate 80% attendance in theory and 100% attendance in practical areas. This framework leaves medical-leave protection largely to institutional rules, producing significant variation in what happens to students when illness interrupts their education.
Problems for students with chronic illnesses
Alex is a third-year B.A. Visual Communication student at a university in Hyderabad. Having transverse myelitis, he became paralysed from the chest down at the age of 10, and the organs on the right side of his body stopped working. Doctors said he would never walk. Defying this, he has regained his ability to walk, but this is accompanied by chronic pain below the chest, subluxations, partial dysplasias, fatigue, and muscle spasms.
Alex holds a 100% merit-based scholarship, and in order to keep it, he must maintain a CGPA of 8 and above and 75% attendance. After he dislocated his kneecap in college in September 2024, doctors recommended a month of complete rest. However, he said, “I was told by the college authorities to either come to college regularly and maintain the 75% attendance or take a year's break and come back to college next year.” His medical leave was denied, stating, “Medical exemption only applies in case of hospitalisations.”
“However, my scholarship would not hold the following year. So I would have to write my exam again and apply for a scholarship again, which was not something I was able to do because of my financial situation. So I had to continue coming to college without taking the recommended one month’s leave. I took one day off, and I continued going back to college every single day,” Alex added.
Alex had to navigate a campus that had minimal accessibility, a long commute to the university, and he was not given leniency for assignments or for showing up to class a few minutes late. This affected his social life on campus and his health. “If I did take that one month’s rest, there was a chance I would have recovered fully. But since I was not able to do it, I still have not recovered. It’s been three years, and I keep dislocating my knee and wear braces to this day.”
A student of Interior Design with an autoimmune condition at a private university in Noida said, “I provided all medical documents explaining my condition; however, the department head asked me to take amla and attend classes.” The student described the process of applying for a leave as frustrating: “I was made to feel like my condition was not important; it came from my own laziness and was something that could be managed with willpower... I was an out-of-station student and had to navigate my illness alone, which was both mentally and financially demanding.”
Attendance adds to evaluation, and the student saw a marked dip in grades. Support, such as make-up assignments, was also not extended by administration or faculty. The student said, “As practical classes are a day long, missing one day amounts to six to eight hours of class time, dipping the attendance to 70-80 % even if two or three classes are missed.”
Cases of unconventional medical proof
Jay was a B.A. English major at a university in Delhi NCR, and months before he joined the university, he had developed chronic pain due to a genetic condition. He had to maintain 75% attendance in every subject, with an 80% requirement and 5% provision for medical leave.
Jay missed many morning classes due to his pain flaring up. As his teachers were accommodating, he was able to sit for his first-year exams. “I had to drop out as my situation worsened in second year. I didn’t have a proper diagnosis; a lot of reports and tests indicated inconclusive results. This couldn’t be taken as enough evidence at that time, and due to considerably low accessibility on campus as well as inflexible leave criteria, I dropped out.”
Tejasdeep Sehgal, a fourth-year student, has had a hearing impairment since the age of 12 and uses a hearing aid. The office of learning support at his university in Haryana provided him with a shaker alarm clock and transcription services that he says are helpful.
Last year, Tejasdeep’s hearing aid stopped working, and he could not listen properly. He then went to Delhi to have it fixed. “It took me two days to get it fixed, and it was a technician who fixed it; therefore, I didn’t have a prescription for it. I had unexcused absences for the classes I missed. However, it could have escalated into a situation where I would not be able to produce documentary proof of my condition to get medical leave.”
A student of Jawaharlal Nehru University’s Japanese department had a viral fever with body pain and had to take leave for two weeks. The student had informed the professor about it over email. When she rejoined class, she was told she was not sick and was asked to write an application to the centre and produce medical documentation. This dismissal by the professor caused the student severe anxiety and panic attacks. The university administration later asked the professor to write an apology letter to the student.
Another student said, “We are constantly told by our seniors not to fall in the bad books of some professor, as they have access to grant scholarships and fellowships and influence your career outside college.”
Describing a similar incident, a Delhi University student said they were made to stand in class. “I was told I was a good student, but irregular in classes. The philosophy professor quoted a scholar on resilience, which made the experience of my sickness seem like laziness. I left the class crying. I felt my hard work would not amount to anything because I was a sick person.”
A fifth-semester student of Humanities, who had been seeking college counselling sessions, upon needing further assistance, had to seek a psychiatrist outside college. The student later missed an exam due to an anxiety attack and was denied approval of medical leave. “I had all the documentation from a fully accredited clinical psychiatrist, and I was told it would have been easier to vouch for me if I was seeking help from college counsellors, who were not psychiatrists and could not have helped me at that time.” The student was made to do multiple rounds to the college healthcare centre, and their leave was still not approved. They had to take the paper again next semester. “The process was bureaucratic and draining.”
Sensitising institutions
Sayan Chaudhuri, a scholar of critical pedagogy and higher education, says, “Teachers and administration need to be sensitised to how chronic illnesses or other conditions might be playing out. I think without that understanding, you can’t have a meaningful intervention. What administrations really need to think about is the kinds of bureaucratic hurdles that are there. Often, administration stands at a huge distance, and you feel a sense of fear about approaching. So there is a need for a culture where it is established that you can get leave, and it shouldn’t feel like it’s a difficult task or it needs certain kinds of skills to be able to ask for a leave.”
He says the problem also lies in the hurdles students face when seeking medical leave. “A documentation-heavy policy is going to run into a contradiction, because the assumption will be that the document can be provided well in advance to the requisite authorities who can go through it, understand it, and approve it. And we know that’s not how it’s always going to work. There will be many things that will fall out of this system. We have to really think of developing a more local understanding of things where teachers can play a proactive role at times, mediate between the administration and the student, because otherwise that contextual understanding may not be there. Medical resource centres and health centres are often very depleted. Counsellors are not always working in a very empowered way, where they can stage interventions in a collaborative and meaningful manner,” he said.
Debaditya Battacharya, Assistant Professor in the Department of English at Jamia Millia Islamia, a researcher of Indian higher education and university histories, says, “National Education Policy 2020 lumps questions of mental health, ability, and disability together under this socioeconomically disadvantaged groups (SEDG); this rubric is indicative of the myopia of policy. Ability is treated as meritocratic given; it is not at stake anymore; it is either the basic minimum you take for granted or simply reduced to an ability enhancement course. But university life has to account for different capacities for ability and disability”
“There is no objective parameter that can justify any figure, whether it be 75 or 65,” Dr. Battacharya said, because students come to university with radically different circumstances. For some, meeting a particular threshold may be relatively easy; for others, especially students from marginalised backgrounds, it may involve negotiating pressures outside the classroom as well.
He says, “It’s teachers who are expected to come with that space of understanding what a student’s real-life circumstances are, as they deal with students in the flesh”. He suggests student-faculty committees hear cases that merit genuine attention on a case-by-case basis, in a consultative and democratic fashion. He says the system should retain the purpose of attendance, maintaining the integrity and spirit of the teaching-learning process without reducing individual students and their circumstances to a single percentage.
(Zain Younis is a Master’s student at Jamia Millia Islamia)
