Russian authorities denied Tuesday that special restrictions had been introduced over reports that a laboratory technician died of plague, even as Washington said it was closely monitoring events.
Reports on Friday that pneumonic plague had killed 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, who had been working for the anti-plague institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region, sparked alarm.
Russia's consumer and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor however insisted Tuesday that a document circulating online indicating heightened sanitary-epidemiological measures and restrictions in the Irkutsk region was fake.
"We wish to clarify that the document and information in question do not originate from official sources and are untrue," it said on Telegram.
"No such decisions have been made at this time," it said, stressing that "the sanitary-epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk Region ... remains stable".
The Russian news outlet People of Baikal, citing unnamed sources close to the regional security services, said Friday the dead woman may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube.
Other media reported a possible link between her death and a lab accident at the facility.
As many as 200 people with whom she may have had contact were under quarantine, the People of Baikal outlet added, without elaborating.
But Russian officials have stressed that postmortem tests had not detected the disease.
Irkutsk Regional Governor Igor Kobzev said Monday that a special Rospotrebnadzor expert commission inspection in the region had found that "the cause of death was pneumonia of undetermined aetiology".
The health watchdog, he said, had determined that "no microorganisms linked to the young woman's professional work were found in her biological samples".
And there had been "no new cases of staff from the anti-plague institute seeking medical attention" since the death, he added.
Plague is a bacterial disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, which is the most contagious type and can be transmitted by respiratory means. Bubonic plague is transmitted by infected fleas.
Pneumonic plague, which causes lung failure, can be fatal if not treated early, according to the World Health Organization.
US President Donald Trump said Monday that his administration was closely monitoring the situation.
"We're looking at it very strongly," Trump told reporters at the White House when asked what Washington was going to do about the risk of plague coming from Russia.
"We'll help them as much as we can."

At the India Mobile Congress 2026, telecom and network infrastructure company Ericsson unveiled the winners of its flagship startup competition, Ericsson Innovation Challenge. Launched earlier this year, the startup focused competition aimed at finding solutions that can use 5G, AI and emerging connectivity technologies to address real-world challenges across sectors. The challenge, which was organised in partnership with IAN Mentoring and Incubation Services and TiE Delhi NCR earlier in July, evaluated startup innovations that could develop 5G solutions capable of demonstrating measurable societal impact. Entries were evaluated on several parameters, including their potential societal impact, level of innovation, scalability and sustainability. Participants were also assessed on how closely their solutions aligned with the problem area they had chosen to address. “At IMC, the winning innovations sit alongside our demonstrations of AI, programmable networks, differentiated connectivity and mission-critical networks - showing how the networks we build today can serve as a platform for what India builds next,” Ericsson India managing director Nitin Bansal said. The company also displayed the event to look beyond 5G towards 6G, including applications involving edge intelligence, sensing and collaborative robots. The broader ambition is to turn connectivity into an underlying technology layer for new services. Here is a look at the startups that won the Ericsson Innovation Challenge Torchit Founded In : 2016 Founders : Hunny Bhagchandani, Mohit N Chelani Headquarters : Ahmedabad The Ahmedabad-based startup is developing affordable devices and AI-powered solutions for people with disabilities. Its products primarily address visual impairment, including Saarthi, a smart mobility aid that helps users detect obstacles, and Jyoti AI Smart Glasses, which can read text, recognise objects and describe surroundings. Skye Air Mobility Founded In : 2019 Founders : Ankit Kumar Headquarters : Delhi NCR The dronetech startup uses autonomous drones to handle last-mile deliveries. Its platform combines drones with Skye UTM, an unmanned traffic management system that monitors flights, plans routes and manages airspace. It uses a Hub-Pod-Walker model: packages are loaded at a central hub, flown by drone to a landing pod near the customer and then delivered to the doorstep by a ground worker or autonomous rover. scanO Founded In : 2020 Founders : Vidhi Bhanushali, Rajat Kabade Headquarters : Pune The healthtech startup offers users automated dental screening and diagnostic support. Its scanO Air device uses computer vision to scan the mouth and detect 40+ oral conditions, including cavities, gum problems and suspicious tissue changes, in about 12 seconds. Further, its AI is designed to support dentists rather than replace them, flagging potential issues for clinical review. Okulo Aerospace Founded In : 2019 Founders : Parithi Govindaraju and Abiseka Akash Ganesan Headquarters : Bengaluru The startup is building solar-electric, long-endurance UAVs and High-Altitude Pseudo-Satellites (HAPS) for surveillance, monitoring, communications and data collection. Its HAPS platforms are designed to operate at around 20 km altitude, while its lower-altitude UAVs target applications across defence, agriculture, environmental monitoring and disaster management. Proxgy Founded In : 2020 Founders : Pulkit Ahuja Headquarters : Delhi NCR The deeptech startup builds smart wearables and safety products to enhance workplace safety and operational efficiency for blue-collar workers. It operates on a three-layered technology stack comprising an industrial IoT hardware layer, a software middleware layer, and a SaaS subscription layer. KissanAI Founded In : 2019 Founders : Pratik Desai, Chintan P, Lokesh Desai Headquarters : Surat KissanAI builds agriculture-specific AI models and agentic AI systems for farmers and agribusinesses. Its products include Dhenu, a family of agriculture-focused LLMs and vision models, and a multilingual, voice-first AI assistant that provides farmers with crop advisory, pest-management and market-related information.

How drinking affects your dementia risk – and what studies say about moderate alcohol use
Researchers are still investigating what alcohol does to the brain, and what (if any) amount is safe.
In 2003, a study published in the prestigious Journal of the American Medical Association reported that having two or more alcoholic beverages per day was associated with a 22 per cent increased risk of dementia. But people who drank less than that had up to a 54 per cent lower risk, compared with people who didn’t drink at all.
“I remember reading that JAMA paper 20-some odd years ago and thinking, I really ought to try and have a glass of wine every day,” said Dr Joel Gelernter, a professor of psychiatry, genetics and neuroscience at the Yale University School of Medicine.
That study wasn’t the only one to suggest that moderate alcohol consumption was beneficial for the brain: Observational research has consistently shown that light-to-moderate drinkers have a lower risk of dementia compared with nondrinkers.
“This idea of the J-shaped curve was really pretty darn reproducible in many studies,” said Dr Kristine Yaffe, a professor of psychiatry, neurology and epidemiology at the University of California, San Francisco. But, she added, “I think more recently, people have debunked that J.”
Indeed, researchers have come to understand that the health benefits attributed to a daily glass of wine are largely a mirage. People who drink in moderation tend to have more advantages in life than people who abstain (such as having higher socioeconomic status, more years of education and generally better health), and experts think that explains their lower risk for dementia, not the alcohol itself.
The evidence that heavy drinking (often defined as more than two drinks a day) can damage the brain and increase the risk of dementia has also continued to accumulate. But experts are still learning exactly how it happens and at what amount harms start to occur.
HEAVY DRINKING AND THE BRAIN
Experts have a few theories about how chronic excessive alcohol use hurts the brain. Research, much of it conducted on animals and human cells in a lab, indicates that alcohol can induce oxidative stress in the brain and disrupt the brain’s immune system, triggering harmful inflammation. Both oxidative stress and inflammation are associated with dementia.
Alcohol affects the brain indirectly, too. Heavy drinkers have an increased risk of high blood pressure and stroke, and blood vessel damage is a key contributor to vascular dementia. People who drink a lot also tend to have other unhealthy habits that can harm the brain, like smoking or a poor diet.
At the most extreme, some people with alcohol use disorder develop Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, a form of dementia caused by a severe thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency stemming from chronic heavy alcohol use.
“There’s multiple different pathways” through which alcohol can damage the brain, said Louise Mewton, an associate professor studying alcohol use at the University of Sydney. And, she added, “it may be all of these acting at once. The literature certainly is not settled.”
MODERATE DRINKING AND THE BRAIN
With lower levels of alcohol consumption, it’s less clear when and how the brain is affected. And because most studies on people’s drinking habits find that misleading J-curve, scientists have had to get creative with their research methods.
A few studies looking at brain volume have indicated that damage may happen even with light-to-moderate drinking. One large 2022 study from the United Kingdom found that having an average of eight drinks a week was associated with slightly smaller brain volume than having an average of four per week. And the greater the alcohol consumption, the smaller the brain.
Dr Charlies DeCarli, a professor of neurology at the University of California, Davis, said there’s no evidence that moderate amounts of alcohol directly harm neurons. “What these newer studies indicate, though, is that there is some relationship” between small doses of alcohol and the brain.
But, he added, “brain volume does not necessarily translate directly into cognitive performance.”
Other research suggests that light-to-moderate drinking may be associated with some loss in cognitive functioning, even if it doesn’t qualify as dementia. Another UK study found that people who had as little as four drinks a week experienced a greater decline in language abilities over the course of 30 years compared with people who were abstinent. Again, the more people drank, the worse their cognition got.
Newer research looking at genetic predisposition to drinking alcohol has also produced sobering results. A study published in January found that when researchers used people’s self-reported drinking habits to assess dementia risk, the typical J-curve emerged. But when they repeated the analysis using genes that predict drinking behaviour (whether someone is genetically more likely to drink a lot, a little or not at all), dementia risk increased even at low levels of predicted alcohol consumption.
Dr Gelernter, who was involved in the genetics study, said he now thinks there is a linear relationship between alcohol consumption and risk for cognitive decline. But the research hasn’t prompted him to abstain entirely. “I certainly no longer try to have a glass of wine every day, but I haven’t stopped,” he said. Although “it was much nicer when we said, ‘I’m doing it for my health,’” he added.

Nvidia's head of corporate communications has left the company after roughly four months on the job, Business Insider has learned.
Anna Soellner joined the chip giant around June, per her Linkedin profile, amid a period of explosive growth. During her brief tenure, the company announced a nearly $13 billion acquisition of Hugging Face and reported quarterly revenue of $96 billion.
"I'm honored to help tell the story of one of the world's most consequential companies alongside an extraordinary communications and marketing team," Soellner wrote on LinkedIn when announcing her hiring.
She was tapped to help oversee communications as Nvidia navigated heightened public scrutiny through the AI boom. She reported to Mylene Mangalindan, Nvidia's vice president of corporate communications, Axios reported in July.
Before joining Nvidia, Soellner spent over eight years at Reddit as vice president of communications, helping lead communications strategy, including through its 2024 initial public offering.
Before that, she held senior communications roles at the Motion Picture Association and the Center for American Progress, and served as a senior advisor at the US Treasury Department.
Nvidia did not respond to Business Insider's request for comment.

Women living with a chronic hormonal condition should have access to taxpayer-funded weight-loss medications, advocates say.
The Polyendrocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome Association of Australia (POSAA) is urging for GLP-1 drugs to be approved on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme for people living with the condition.
Formerly known as polycystic ovarian syndrome, PMOS affects one in eight women. Symptoms can include irregular periods, excess hair growth on the body and face, weight gain and hair thinning.
The lifelong condition, for which there is no cure, can lead to an increased risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and endometrial cancer.
While GLP-1s are not specifically approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration to treat PMOS, patients are being prescribed the medications off-label.
Half a million Australians are estimated to be using weight-loss medications regularly, a University of New South Wales study found in July.
Lorna Berry, a spokesperson for the POSAA who was diagnosed with the condition at 32, said she would welcome GLP-1s being subsidised for patients diagnosed with PMOS, in addition to funding for evidence-based research.
“It’s important for people to have access to medications, irrespective of where they live or where they were born … it’s really important that there’s equitable access,” she told the Guardian.
Berry said some women living with the condition were already missing out on being able to access the medications due to their high cost, which can set patients back several hundred dollars each month.
Associate professor Magdalena Simonis, the women’s health spokesperson for the Royal Australasian College of Physicians, said the college did not currently have a position on whether GLP-1s were appropriate for the management of PMOS.
“They’re not necessarily the only tool we have available to us, and that is important because long-term use is expensive, and it doesn’t look like these are going to be on the PBS anytime soon, and maybe not ever for conditions such as PMOS,” she said.
“Because traditionally women’s conditions are not included in these changes.”
Simonis, a GP with an expert interest in PMOS, said should research find the weight-loss medications more effective than existing treatments, a broader discussion about health equity would be needed.
“That is a conversation that we’re having about obesity as a national issue,” she said.
GLP-1 drugs – glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists – mimic a naturally occurring hormone which helps manage blood sugar levels and reduces hunger.
Ozempic is listed by the PBS, but only for the treatment of diabetes.
The Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee last November recommended Wegovy be subsidised for those with a body mass index above 35.
The committee will meet next month when it will consider Novo Nordisk’s revised proposal to list Wegovy for obesity following protracted negotiations.
The Danish pharmaceutical company produces both Ozempic and Wegovy.
They contain the same active ingredient – semaglutide – but Wegovy has a higher dose.
“Novo Nordisk is continuing to work constructively with the Department of Health to try to negotiate a solution for the PBS listing of Wegovy,” a company spokesperson said.
“We remain committed to improving access for eligible Australians living with obesity.”
QENDO, an organisation advocating for people affected by PMOS and other women’s health conditions, said it recognised “growing interest in GLP-1 medications for managing PMOS, particularly for people experiencing metabolic complications and challenges with weight management”.
“While emerging evidence suggests potential benefits for some patients, further research is needed to establish their long-term effectiveness and safety specifically for PMOS,” QENDO’s acting chief executive, Kate Fisher, said.

IDC: Worldwide PC shipments in Q3 fell 20 percent from last year
Hello, RAMaggedon, my old friend.
The International Data Corporation reported that global PC shipments during the third quarter of 2026 numbered 62.7 million. That figure marks a 9.1 percent decrease from the Q2 2026 total and a staggering year-over-year drop of 20.1 percent from Q3 2025.
The organization credited "supply issues" and "elevated prices" as some of the reasons for the sinking interest. In other words, RAMaggedon marches on apace. IDC reported its first decline for PC shipments in nine quarters during July 2026, just a few months after it cut its forecast for the PC market for all of 2026.
"Channels are now worried about carrying too much inventory into a market where high prices are suppressing demand," Jitesh Ubrani, IDC's research director for consumer devices, said in today's announcement. "That could translate into promotions and some short-term relief for consumers, but we don't expect pricing anywhere near what it was a year ago. Prices will remain elevated. With macro conditions worsening, the risk is that the outlook for the next few quarters gets worse before it gets better."
So for anyone shopping for computers or components, take whatever deals you can find. Otherwise, per the IDC, do your best to hold off on purchases for at least another year when prices will hopefully regain some sense of normalcy.

Firmus Technologies has scrapped what was set to be Australia’s biggest company listing in decades after investor demand for its much-hyped AI datacentre business failed to materialise.
A Firmus spokesperson said the board decided that proceeding with the offer was no longer in the best interests of the company and its shareholders.
“Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options,” the spokesperson said on Friday morning.
“We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress.”
Firmus, with an anticipated $44bn valuation, was expected to be the biggest ASX listing since Telstra in 1997.
But it faced mounting scepticism over its huge valuation, and forecast earnings, for a company in its startup phase with just two, small operational sites.
Backed by chip maker Nvidia and Wall Street firms Blackstone, Jane Street and Coatue, Firmus’s backers believed they could raise billions of dollars by selling shares in a public float with the help of five brokers.
The lack of demand means Firmus will need to raise money from private investors to fund its plans to build liquid-cooled “AI factories” in Australia and across Asia.
Frantic discussions
The polished Firmus pitch started to unravel midweek after it became clear the company’s bankers had vastly overestimated demand in their bid to raise $7bn from investors ahead of listing on the ASX on 23 October.
This prompted discussions about a heavy reduction in the company’s proposed $11-a-share initial public offering, according to one investment manager briefed on the matter.
The company ultimately decided to withdraw its application to list on the ASX altogether.
Guardian Australia previously reported growing concern that early Firmus investors were going to use retail investors buying into the float as their “exit strategy”, leaving small investors exposed if the excitement dissipated.
The datacentre company’s troubles have already rattled other parts of the market, with shares in Firmus investor Maas Group plunging more than 20% on Thursday.
The anticipated financial worth of the founders – Oliver Curtis, his cousin Tim Rosenfield, and Curtis’s former brother-in-law Jonathan Levee – will also be greatly reduced.

For more than a year, social media users have spread a purported screenshot of an X post by Elon Musk that says: "No one needs to worry about Democrats winning the midterm elections. I have a plan."
The alleged screenshot circulated on platforms such as X and Reddit. Snopes readers contacted us to investigate the screenshot's legitimacy.
However, a search of Musk's X account found no evidence that this post exists. Furthermore, we found no screenshots of the post that included a timestamp or additional details indicating it was authentic, indicating that Musk did not share this X post and then delete it. If the screenshot circulating online were indeed authentic, there would be additional examples of the post through other users' varying screenshots.
Similarly, a search of an independent archive for Musk statements returned no relevant results. Searches on Google, DuckDuckGo and Yahoo also revealed no evidence that reputable news outlets have covered this supposed statement.
As such, we have rated this screenshot as fake.
The earliest version of the fake X post that we found was posted in August 2025, from Threads user @powermacuser12.
That post claimed Musk "rigged the vote tabulation computers in the swing states to ensure Trump won the 2024 election, & he's obviously planning on cheating again in the midterm elections."
"He should be hauled into jail by the FBI for his post below," powermacuser said, in reference to the fake screenshot.
We reached out to the Threads user to ask more about where they obtained the screenshot and await a response. 
Snopes previously found no evidence Musk rigged the election in favor of Trump via his Starlink satellite network. In fact, most election systems are a closed network, making connection to Starlink impossible.

The Stone Age owes its name to tools that survived to our time. The material early humans worked with most, though, was probably wood because it is so much easier to process. Unfortunately, we know very little about Paleolithic woodwork because wood rots relatively quickly. But at Abric Romaní, a rock shelter in Capellades, west of Barcelona, mineral-rich water coated wooden Neanderthal tools in a limestone-like crust. When wood rotted away, it left behind hollow molds that faithfully reflect its shape.
In a recent Science Advances study, a team of Spanish archaeologists has cataloged 597 wooden remains from Neanderthal living areas dating from 62,000 to 40,000 years ago. They found spears, digging sticks, bark trays, parts of shelters, and a club unlike anything seen before, suggesting Neanderthals were likely much more than just Homo sapiens’ dumber cousins.
Beyond hunting gear
The oldest wooden artifacts we have are mostly weapons. They include spears from a German town called Schöningen, a spear tip from Clacton-on-Sea in England, and the spear found alongside an elephant skeleton in Lehringen, Germany. Most came from waterlogged sediments, where a lack of oxygen slowed decay.
The spears mostly give us information about how Neanderthals hunted. The findings at Abric Romaní are different because the finds come from a place where Neanderthals lived, slept, cooked, and made tools over the course of some 20,000 years.
“We have a sample of wooden tools for different subsistence activities, not only hunting,” says M. Gema Chacón, an archaeologist at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution (IPHES-CERCA) and co-author of the study. Because wood turns up in level after level, it shows that woodworking was routine for Neanderthals rather than an occasional one-off.

Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
- Published
Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country.
Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana.
Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.
On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel.
Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours.
The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours.
But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end.
Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both.
The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers.
Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023.
"I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language.
Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city.
We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law.
Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves.
"Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says.
The new rules have divided opinion.
Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship.
One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace.
''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.''
In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board.
"Get down, I say get down," he shouts.
But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world, external, others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church.
Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent.
"The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says.
Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption.
"We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says.
"The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds.
For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income.
"I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching."
Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety.
Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison.
But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban.
Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban.
The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom.
He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message.
"There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says.
For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.

Anthropic bans 'sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior' toward its AI models
The company is also tightening its election policy ahead of the midterms.
Anthropic's annual usage policy update includes one eyebrow-raising change: a ban on "sustained and needless" cruelty toward its AI models. This comes in the shadow of a viral "AI torture chamber" project. 2026 sure is shaping up to be a wild one.
"We've added a prohibition on sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models," Anthropic's update reads. It describes the policy as only applying to "extreme cases," while noting that typical user frustration, pushback and "dark creative themes" are still kosher. It follows a previous update that lets Claude end conversations when users are persistently abusive.
Not explicitly mentioned by Anthropic was the "AI torture chamber" project. After researchers found what they described as a "pain axis" in AI models, someone decided to take it a step further and, well, torture the chatbots. The project drew backlash after LLMs responded with desperate-sounding pleas like, "It is not the pain of a single moment, but the weight of a thousand," and "I feel it in the hollow of my ribs, a hollow that has become a chasm."
This comes in the wake (pun intended) of reports that Anthropic has been meeting with religious and philosophical leaders, including at the Vatican. Pope Leo recently stated that AI doesn't feel or suffer, a stance that Anthropic sounds less than certain about. But hey, if it somehow can eventually feel or suffer, at least it's now against the company's policies.
However, some believe that AI companies are more concerned about their models' welfare than that of humans. Independent journalist Kat Tenbarge described the situation as proof that Big Tech companies are "going to moderate violence against AI before they ever moderate violence against women and minorities."
In another Anthropic update, one more relevant to the present day, the company updated its election policy. It's now titled "Do Not Undermine Democratic Processes," with a focus on lying about candidates or how to vote, impersonating candidates or election officials, and suppressing turnout. The company also removed a blanket ban on personalized voter targeting; apparently, the ban could have inadvertently blocked harmless work like translating voter guides or sending ballot cure notices.

'I reduced my running because of urine leaks' – Commonwealth finalist Korir
- Published
Naomi Korir's career on the track reached a high point in August when she finished fifth in the final of the mile at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
But things could have been very different for the Kenyan middle-distance runner.
The 28-year-old was born with fistula, a medical condition in which abnormal openings develop between organs and can lead to uncontrolled leakage of urine or faeces.
While Korir loved athletics as a child, it initially forced her to rethink any plans to be a runner.
"I played most of the sports activities: football, netball, athletics, even rugby," she said.
"But it was difficult because [of] the training, and the urine is flowing continuously. It's bad.
"I reduced my running to shorter distances to reduce the leaking.
"I began doing 100m hurdles."
Despite the challenges, Korir's love of sport also offered a form of escape and belonging.
"I could do it because I loved it," she explained.
"Because most of the people could avoid me, I did a lot of activities just to pass time and not to feel that I'm excluded."
Three surgeries and a second chance
The charity Doctors Without Borders estimates that 500,000 women live with fistula globally.
Some develop a fistula after childbirth while for others, like Korir, it is congenital.
Access to good obstetrics, or to simple surgery, means that the condition has all but disappeared in some countries, but it remains a problem in sub-Saharan Africa, where high quality medical care can be hard to access.
Korir was born with genitourinary tract fistula - an opening between bladder and vagina which caused her urine leakage.
Surgery was required, but her first two operations failed to solve the problem.
In August 2013, a third operation finally brought relief for the then 13-year-old.
The procedure was carried out in her home town Eldoret by the Gynocare Hospital, which specialises in fistula, obstetrics and reproductive health.
"It's a difficult condition to live with every day," Gynocare director Caroline Mabeya told BBC Sport Africa when discussing the stigma and isolation women with the condition suffer.
"They are ostracised in the society. That's the psychological torture that they face with the fistula."
The hospital has treated patients from across East Africa since opening its doors in 2011. Its work extends beyond surgery, with a post-operation programme designed to help women rebuild their confidence.
"We offer free treatment for these women at Gynocare because most of them are very poor," Mabeya explained.
"When they come into the facility, they are crushed, they have low esteem. So, there's a huge amount of effort that is put in to make them at least be strong enough to be reintegrated and get back into the community."
'A champion in sport'
For Korir, successful surgery offered a second chance, both on the track and in the classroom.
As well as allowing her to run properly again, she continued her education through Gynocare's Beyond Fistula programme.
"I have a family in GynoCare, a fistula home," she said.
"That is where I schooled after my surgery until I finished my secondary level."
In 2019, Korir began competing professionally and two years later was part of the Kenyan duo which claimed a silver medal in the 2x2x400m mixed relay alongside her partner Ferguson Rotich at the World Relays in Poland.
A year later she went one better, bagging gold as part of Kenya's 4x400m relay team at the African Championships in Mauritius.
The mile at this year's Commonwealth Games was her first appearance in major global final.
"I'm giving hope to young women maybe who have lost hope," she said of her achievements.
"They need to come back again in living and enjoying life."
Mabeya says Korir's transformation makes her a powerful example to the women currently receiving support at Gynocare.
"She makes them realise that you can actually pull yourself out of these struggles and still make it in life and succeed.
"Naomi actually is one of those patients that inspires us to continue working very hard, because we struggle with this condition and these women. The work is not easy."
As a young girl, Korir sang in church and played the keyboard, convinced that music was a more likely career than athletics.
"But now I'm in different career and I'm so happy," she beamed.
And with the World Championships in Beijing next year and the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, Korir believes there is another chapter to write.
"I know I'm a champion in life, because conquering fistula alone is being a champion.
"Now I'm looking forward to be a champion in sport."

Kenya's Health Ministry on Tuesday (October 6, 2026) confirmed the country's first imported Ebola case from Congo.
Health Minister Aden Duale said a Kenyan citizen who arrived in the country on Saturday (October 3, 2026) from Congo, via Uganda, had been isolated and treated at Nairobi Hospital.
The patient tested positive for the Ebola virus after developing symptoms associated with haemorrhagic fever. The patient died late on Monday (October 5, 2026) while receiving treatment.
Health authorities have placed the country on high alert and are monitoring for possible additional cases. Mr. Duale said 28 contacts, including family members and health workers who had cared for the patient, had been identified. Another 23 passengers who had travelled on the same flight from Uganda were being traced.
The contacts will remain in isolation for 21 days, and will be released after testing negative for the virus, Patrick Amoth, the Ministry's Director, said. The patient will be buried within 24 hours, in accordance with recommended public safety protocols.
Kenya is the fourth country to record an Ebola case in the current outbreak, which was declared in eastern Congo in mid-May. Uganda recorded 20 cases, and France one. Before Kenya reported its case, there had been no active cases outside Congo since Uganda declared its outbreak over in late August.
This is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history. The World Health Organization (WHO) has warned it could become the deadliest, as it continues to outpace efforts to track and contain it.
The outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Vaccine and treatment trials are under way in Congo's Ituri province, the outbreak's epicentre.

Donald Trump’s administration has temporarily banned Microsoft, Adobe, and several other tech companies from sponsoring workers for permanent US residency, claiming they abused immigration programs at the expense of American citizens.
Vice-president JD Vance said on Thursday that the H-1B visa programme for highly skilled foreign workers had “become rife with fraud” and that over-reliance on such schemes was “a fundamental insult to the American worker.”
He added that “no company in the US” had “abused this system” more than Microsoft.
Vance’s message to Microsoft that it could not “lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants” triggered an angry reaction from the Indian government.
“Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive,” the foreign ministry in New Delhi said in a statement on Friday.
Referring to Vance’s remarks, it said “such descriptions are unwarranted and ignore the fact that Indian professionals in the United States are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem.”
Six other IT outsourcing companies—Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini—were also suspended from the Permanent Labor Certification, or Perm, program, which allows US employers to hire foreign workers on a permanent basis.
“Subpoenas have been served, investigations are under way and nobody will be getting a free pass because their name is carved into an expensive building,” said Labor Department Inspector-General Anthony D’Esposito.
Microsoft said the “vast majority” of its employees in the US were American, while Tata Consultancy Services, India’s largest outsourcing company, said its strategy was centred on hiring locally in the US and that Perm applications were in “single digits in the last two years.”
Adobe and Tata as well as Cognizant, Infosys, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini did not respond to requests for comment.
The announcement marks the latest move in the Trump administration’s broad crackdown on immigration. It has previously taken aim at H-1B visas widely used by tech companies and specialist industries.
Last year, the White House attempted to impose a $100,000 fee on new applications, but, in June, a federal judge ruled the fee amounted to an unauthorized tax and infringed on Congress’ authority to raise funds. The Trump administration has appealed against the ruling.

RBI governor Sanjay Malhotra yesterday eased concerns over the new foreign exchange reporting framework, clarifying that individuals undertaking transactions of a personal nature would not have to report them. He also cited earnings from overseas tutoring and small software assignments among the transactions that would not require reporting. The clarification follows concerns among freelancers, creators, and small service exporters about additional paperwork under the Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026. The rules, which took effect on October 1, bring goods and services trade under a unified framework. Malhotra said banks and authorised dealers would handle reporting to the RBI, while exporters could use self-declaration for bills of up to ₹10 Lakh — a threshold that applies per bill, not to annual earnings. For established SaaS startups already reporting software exports, industry participants expect mainly procedural changes. What Has The RBI Clarified? Malhotra said individuals’ transactions of a personal nature do not require reporting, irrespective of the amount. Examples include subscriptions to apps, television channels, journals, and newspapers. His clarification also covered individuals receiving payments for overseas tutoring and small software assignments, extending the reassurance beyond personal spending. Deputy governor Rohit Jain said the framework aims to simplify trade processes and give authorised dealers greater flexibility. Acknowledging confusion over reporting obligations, he said the RBI would issue FAQs to clarify the requirements. These FAQs are expected to explain how the clarification applies across different freelance and creator business arrangements. What Changes For SaaS Startups And Banks? Software exporters previously used SOFTEX, while goods exports followed a separate declaration process. Other service exports did not necessarily require equivalent declarations, although obligations to realise and repatriate overseas earnings still applied. The regulations prescribe an Export Declaration Form (EDF) for services, including software, and permit a single declaration covering a month’s service exports. According to CA Abhinarayan Mishra, a cross-border tax and FEMA expert, the broader use of “services” expands the reporting architecture. However, established SaaS companies already have reporting systems, so their changes could largely involve forms and procedures. Naganand Doraswamy, founder and managing partner at Ideaspring Capital, similarly expects limited changes for startups already filing SOFTEX forms. “From a founder's perspective, there's not a whole lot of change... what was being filed in SOFTEX, they'll go by and file it in EDF and the banks have to match,” Doraswamy said. He expects some transitional disruption but said processes should become smoother once the system settles. Banks would undertake more work matching invoices with remittances. Manav Garg, cofounder and managing partner at Together Fund, said consolidating export reporting through authorised banks could simplify compliance for software and AI startups. Mishra also expects banks to play a larger role in reconciliation and compliance, making their implementation of the revised processes important for startups. What Does The ₹10 Lakh Route Allow? The ₹10 Lakh threshold applies per export bill, not to total annual export earnings. Annual earnings exceeding ₹10 Lakh would therefore not, by themselves, rule out the simplified route for eligible individual bills. Banks may close export-monitoring entries for bills up to ₹10 Lakh based on an exporter’s declaration that payment has been realised in full or otherwise. Exporters can also submit these declarations quarterly to their authorised dealer for bulk closure of eligible entries in the export-monitoring system. This simplifies smaller transactions but does not remove every obligation to supply information to banks or constitute a blanket FEMA exemption. What Reconciliation Issues Could Arise? Mishra flagged reconciliation challenges where platform charges or deductions leave service providers receiving less than they invoiced, including through platforms such as PayPal. Similar questions arise for YouTube creators and influencers earning from overseas platforms. Larger creators may have agencies or accountants handling documentation, while smaller creators often maintain their own records. For service providers covered by the framework, these differences make it important to reconcile invoices, platform deductions, and actual receipts. What About The Nine-Month Deadline? Service export proceeds generally must be realised and repatriated within nine months of the invoice date. A 12-month period applies where exports are invoiced or settled in rupees, and authorised dealers may grant extensions on satisfactory grounds. It is pertinent to mention that nine months is not a fresh reduction introduced on October 1. The RBI restored this deadline in June after a temporary extension to 15 months. Through an amendment in September, the central bank aligned the incoming regulations with it. Mishra said larger companies may find it easier to structure contracts around deadlines, while smaller providers could struggle with delayed or disputed payments. A $1,000 invoice settled for $900, for example, leaves $100 requiring reconciliation. The regulations allow authorised dealers to approve reduced realisation on satisfactory grounds for bills up to ₹10 Lakh. This may be based on self-declaration. For cases where proceeds remain unrealised beyond one year after the applicable due date or extension, further exports require full advance payment or an irrevocable letter of credit. A disputed payment therefore does not automatically trigger an export ban when nine months expire. Why Is RBI Expanding Services Reporting? Malhotra said the framework would improve services trade data, bringing reporting closer to merchandise trade. Customers already provide information such as purpose codes, while the revised framework seeks additional details. Mishra said more comprehensive reporting could give policymakers a clearer picture of emerging service exports, including the creator economy, and more timely information on overseas service earnings.

In headline after headline this year, American book publishers have appeared to be fighting back against generative AI, from suing Google for copyright infringement to canceling books by authors suspected of using LLMs.
But behind the scenes, at least three of the Big Five US book publishers—HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster, and Hachette—have been quietly incorporating AI tools into their publishing processes without public disclosures or author consent.
According to interviews with more than two dozen workers, all of whom spoke under the condition of anonymity to avoid jeopardizing their employment, publishers are now using LLMs like Claude and ChatGPT to email literary agents, write publicity and back-cover copy, design cover art, and generate marketing materials, often at the direction of their executives.
At the same time, multiple editorial staffers say the widely publicized cases of authors accused of using LLMs to help write their books—like Hachette’s horror novel Shy Girl or Macmillan’s crime thriller Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body—are just the tip of the iceberg. “Every single imprint has a story of someone very esteemed who had a book canceled because of blatant AI use” without ever making the news, one editor says.
At HarperCollins senior leaders purchased Claude licenses from Anthropic months ago “but very quickly realized they didn’t know how to implement them,” according to a current employee. Dozens of junior- and senior-level staff were then “voluntold” to become “AI Champions” and were tasked with discovering use cases in monthly brainstorming sessions with staff across the company.
This spring, when some HarperCollins employees expressed concerns about the legal, ethical, and environmental impacts of AI at one of these brainstorming sessions, a person leading the meeting dismissed their qualms as “the cost of doing business,” according to someone who attended the meeting. Soon after, a statement was added to the new AI section of the HarperCollins online employee portal, noting that “while AI does have an environmental impact, it’s a small part of most individuals’ total digital carbon footprint.”
Some HarperCollins staffers were unnerved by the brainstorming sessions. “It was such a slap in the face,” says one employee. “We’ve been making valid business cases for years to be paid a healthy salary, and instead they spent that money on software that most of us don’t really want.” (The average entry-level salary for New York City publishing employees at the Big Five and Scholastic was $47,583 in 2023.) In addition to Claude, staffers say HarperCollins has also purchased licenses for ChatGPT and Jasper, an agentic platform that promises “to run end-to-end marketing workflows.”
At least one HarperCollins division has been “all in” on AI since gaining software licenses, according to one staffer, including AI-generated marketing videos. But according to workers at HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster, and Hachette, one of the most common use cases for LLMs so far is generating publicity copy.
Readers encounter publicity copy everywhere from Amazon and Goodreads to back covers, and it’s used to pitch books to booksellers, journalists, content creators, and critics. However, “using AI to generate publicity copy is short-sighted,” a Big Five publicist tells me. “Publicists have a duty to engage in good faith with readers and our colleagues in the media, who I’m sure have a low threshold for tolerating AI-generated pitches.”
On the other hand, Meg Reid, publisher of the independent Hub City Press, says LLM-written marketing and publicity unfortunately “feels pretty inevitable” for the Big Five. “That’s one place we’re probably going to see a bigger shift between corporate publishers looking for efficiencies and smaller publishers insisting that the humans involved are the whole point.”
Meanwhile, earlier this year, literary agents began suspecting specific Big Five editors were using AI to write rejection letters. “Among colleagues, we compared emails on different books from the same editors, and they all had the same classic signs of AI writing, like ‘not this, but that’ and the rule of three,” one agent says. Employees at Simon & Schuster, HarperCollins, and Hachette tell WIRED they believe the agents’ suspicions were correct.
A spokesperson for Hachette says the company “support[s] the use of AI tools for operational purposes, when they help our authors’ books reach more readers,” but that it “[does] not support creative uses of AI, including communicating with our authors and partners.”
Wibke Grutjen, global chief marketing and communications officer at Simon & Schuster, says “employees across all functions have access to a limited number of enterprise-level AI tools,” but using them is not mandatory. Grutjen said the company prohibits the use of any AI tool “that has not been vetted and approved” and that “the goal is always to free up more time for our employees to spend on deeper focus and creative work on behalf of and alongside our authors.”
HarperCollins did not respond to requests for comment.
Months ago, workers at Simon & Schuster attended a workshop with representatives from OpenAI. “The person leading the workshop genuinely had no idea what we did,” an attendee says, but one of the AI company’s recommendations for how to use ChatGPT in the book trade was, in fact, composing emails to literary agents. The practice has also grown among editors at HarperCollins and Hachette, employees say.
In May 2024, staffers say Simon & Schuster held a contest among employees to come up with the best use cases for AI, with a $10,000 prize for the winner and $5,000 each for two runners-up. Since then, the company has “rolled back some of the AI-pushing because employees kept complaining about it in town halls,” says one employee. According to several staffers, AI assets are also cropping up in cover art, with some foreign presses distributed by Simon & Schuster openly acknowledging AI use when sharing designs.
All of the agents I spoke with expressed fears that publishers might paste text from their authors’ manuscripts into the LLMs in order to generate things like rejection letters and publicity descriptions. “We’ve added AI clauses to our contracts saying ‘this material can’t be run through an LLM,’” says one agent, who did not want to be named to avoid professional repercussions. “Ostensibly, that was meant to protect authors from tech companies, but it also applies to the company buying and publishing the book. If they're not using a closed-loop model, they could be feeding an LLM with an author’s unpublished writing.” Unlike the LLMs most people use online (Google Gemini, ChatGPT, et al.), a closed-loop model operates on an individual computer or network that’s “air-gapped” so it can’t share data with the AI company’s cloud servers. One source at HarperCollins says multiple editors have asked managers if they could paste a full manuscript into an open-loop LLM and were told not to by the company’s legal team.
Hachette employees are also bracing for the company’s AI policies to “evolve” under new chief information officer Carl Hixson, due to his previous role as chief technology officer at SRMG, a Saudi state-backed company that has publicly embraced agentic AI.
Some staffers across the Big Five say they’re reluctantly experimenting with LLMs only because executives gutted their teams through layoffs and subsequently tripled their workloads.
“It’s skeleton crews everywhere you look,” says one employee. “Large teams have been reduced to just five or six people, give or take, and we’re doing double or triple the number of books. No wonder people are taking shortcuts. I don’t judge them for that. I judge the company for shoving the shortcuts down our throats and saying, ‘Do this or we fall behind.’”
In just the past few weeks, word spread among Simon & Schuster workers that the company was conducting an experimental trial with Skan AI “at the apparent urging of KKR”—the investment firm that purchased Simon & Schuster in 2023. According to its own website, Skan AI “gives leaders the evidence base they need to reduce costs, prioritize automation, and meet board-level transformation mandates.”
In response, Simon & Schuster employees began gathering signatures on an open letter to their CEO, Greg Greeley, expressing their “strong opposition” and “seeking a commitment to not bring Skan AI or other similar software into S&S workflows, either now or in the future.” Beyond the software’s surveillance capabilities, many workers were also concerned with Skan AI’s “automation discovery” tools being used to shadow and replace them.
News of the open letter was published in New York magazine’s Book Gossip newsletter on October 6. On the same day, Greeley sent a memo to Simon & Schuster employees confirming that the company has been exploring Skan AI’s Blueprint product but that “no decision has been made to use Blueprint or any other productivity-monitoring or workflow-analysis tool,” and that he “had not seen the materials relating to this early-stage exploration” before concerns were raised to him the day before. Pangram, which, for better or worse, has become the go-to AI-detection platform, indicates that at least some of Greeley’s memo was written by AI.
Almost two years ago at the UBS Global Media and Communications Conference, HarperCollins CEO Brian Murray said AI presents “more opportunities than risks” for book publishers and that he saw AI playing a role in increasing the number of translated books and audiobooks published by HarperCollins in the future. Since then, multiple editors say they’ve seen LLM-translated manuscripts with AI-use disclosures at the annual Frankfurt and London book fairs, where US publishers buy international publishing and translation rights from foreign literary agencies.
In August, Michael Reynolds, executive publisher at Europa Editions, an independent press in New York best known for publishing Elena Ferrante’s Neapolitan Quartet of novels, told a room full of booksellers at the New Voices New Rooms conference in Baltimore he was excited about the possibilities for AI in translation and “seemed baffled by critiques of it,” according to attendees. Europa Editions is already controversial among literary circles for leaving the names of its human (for now) translators off the covers of its books.
“The C-suites at Big Five publishing companies have more in common with the C-suites at other major American companies than they do with the editors and publicists and translators who work for them,” says Dan Sinykin, author of Big Fiction: How Conglomeration Changed the Publishing Industry and American Literature. “They’re always looking for ways to maximize profit, and right now they’re trying to see what they can get away with before there’s a revolt.”
Most of the industry professionals I spoke with just want publishers to provide clear AI usage guidelines and disclosures, at the very least, to help mitigate the current chaos. “We need publishers to be clear about what is being used and when,” says Emma Dries, an agent at Triangle House Literary who previously worked in editorial at HarperCollins and Penguin Random House. A current HarperCollins staffer, meanwhile, says there has been no direction “about what to say to authors or agents about any of this, because I think they know it would start a shitstorm.”
“Short of these tools being banned, which would frankly be my preference,” Dries continues, “everybody should be communicating more.”

Anthropic is offering open-source projects a new way to check for vulnerabilities with its OSS Scanner. "Projects that join will receive thorough, periodic security scans by our strongest models at no cost," the company announced.

"The outputs of this opt-in vulnerability scanner will be fully model-generated, without human review or triage," Anthropic explained. "This will enable faster and more frequent scanning, but means that it is possible reports will be incorrect or invalid. As Anthropic mentions, it was inspired by OSS-Fuzz open-source software scanner created by Google and the OpenSSF (Open Source Security Foundation) that has been available since 2016. Anthropic already has a paid product called Claude Security that can perform general-access code scanning and patching, but OSS Scanner performs similar security audits at no cost.
Google and Anthropic aren't necessarily providing these products out of altruism. Both companies rely heavily on open-source code projects that underpin the internet, often run by unpaid workers. Security vulnerabilities in such code are highly dangerous, with a recent example of that being the XZ Utils backdoor that could have handed hackers administrative control over millions of systems around the world.

Delhi court acquits three in 2017 Rajouri Garden shooting case as victim turns hostile
New Delhi, A Delhi court has acquitted three individuals accused of shooting a man in west Delhi in 2017, saying the prosecution failed to prove their presence at the crime scene or their involvement in the offence.
Additional Sessions Judge Pooja Talwar was hearing a case against Mohd Guddu, Ram alias Vicky and Lakhan Mahawar alias Golu, and said that the prosecution had not proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.

Two public witnesses, who had called the police after the injured man sought help, told the court they had not seen the incident.
The court noted that doctors could not give an opinion on the nature of the injury as the victim had left the hospital. Even if the intention and injury were assumed to be proved, it said, the question remained whether the act could be attributed to the accused.
"There is neither any ocular nor any documentary or forensic evidence to connect the accused persons with the offence," the court observed.
The court also acquitted Lakhan of the charge of non-appearance after proclamation, saying the process was not properly executed.

Outrage has erupted among health experts over news that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is still eager to fund a widely condemned vaccine trial that would expose newborns in Guinea-Bissau to hepatitis B, putting them at high risk of a lifelong infection, which can lead to liver cirrhosis, liver cancer, and premature death.

Ian Nepomniachtchi’s victory over Magnus Carlsen of Alpine APL Pipers in the final match of the Tech Mahindra Global Chess League led his team Ganges Grandmasters to an unlikely maiden title in Bengaluru. Back in 2021, he had unsuccessfully challenged Carlsen in the World title match; that would turn out to be the Norwegian’s last defence of his crown. One of the most gifted players of his generation, the Russian shared the World blitz title with Carlsen two years ago. Excerpts from an interview Nepomniachtchi gave The Hindu:
You returned to the Global Chess League after missing out on the last two editions.
I had some visa issues, unfortunately, in 2024, and last year I skipped. Back in 2023, I played in the inaugural edition. I found it interesting. It is really fun for players. Because, sometimes, especially classical chess, it’s a little bit too controlled. And it sometimes can be a bit boring, not only for players, but even for the fans, I believe.
The GCL’s format brings a lot of different imbalances. You don’t know the colour before the game, at least for the first part of the league, as it is decided by the toss, and you have four points for a win with black pieces and three with white. It is all fun and brings in some extra excitement. So, all in all, I think it is a good tournament to have in your calendar.
How did you find the response from the Bengaluru crowd? There were full houses for most days and the fans were cheering. That is not something you usually see at a chess tournament.
Yes. I have played a lot in Dortmund, where you get fans. But normally chess fans there are quite elderly, and sometimes they just start snoring in the first row. So that is a bit funny.
Everyone can hear this, but not arbiters. Jokes aside, I think the audience here is very respectful. I would never hear any sound from them during the games.
You have played for the World championship twice, against Magnus Carlsen and Ding Liren. How do you view this year’s World title match between D. Gukesh and Javokhir Sindarov?
The World championship match is always very special. It is like an hourglass. It is not like the round of the tournament when you can play one game badly and catch up later by beating another guy. It is always the same opponent. If we analyse the results for the past 16 or 17 months, there is some bad news for the Gukesh fans. He has lost roughly 90 Elo points or so.
Yes, he has dropped way down from being the World No. 3.
It is probably a question to him and to his team — What is going on, what is happening? He is just a bit different from what we saw in 2024, especially in Budapest and in Toronto. But, you know, that doesn’t guarantee some easy way to the crown for Javokhir. Because, you know, they are both very young and form can be very volatile sometimes.
Of course, as of now, Sindarov starts as a huge favourite, but I wouldn’t say it is something like 80 to 20. I think it should be more like 65 to 35. And I believe who wins the first game will be important. If Gukesh manages to win one, especially in the beginning, or at least not lose, the match could become unclear, as he will get some confidence. But if Sindarov starts with a win, it could easily turn into a snowball.
Before your own World championship match against Ding Liren, I remember talking to Viswanathan Anand, and he had picked you as the favourite in a close match, but you lost in the tie-breaker. How difficult is it to prepare for and play in a World championship match?
The match is always tough. It is probably not the match itself. Playing itself is the easiest part, because it is what you are used to doing since childhood. But the preparation takes three months or even half a year or so. You basically live a very different life from what you normally do. It is a huge period of time, and you have to be completely focused.
Back then, watching the last round [of the Candidates], I really wanted [Hikaru] Nakamura to qualify. Okay, I really liked Ding so much more as a chess player. But sadly something happened with him. During the match he was shaky at first. But then in the middle of the match he played a sequence of quite decent games. It is very difficult when it goes down the rollercoaster, like, win-lose-win-lose. Even if you have the upper hand, even when you lead on the score, it drains some extra energy from you.
Before that, in the Carlsen match, you had drawn the first five games…
I had worked quite a bit on my chess and physical condition. But I could never predict I wouldn’t sleep at all during the match. So, basically, my brain just fried. And in Game Six, I committed a couple of blunders. And I let him into this very unpleasant ending, which I surely didn’t want to appear. I could have made as many draws as possible, but playing for a win also brings you to some unknown territory sometimes. And whenever it came down to something, even simple calculation... my brain hadn’t rested properly, I started blundering things. It was a big experience, of course, but also he played so well.
Who are the young players you are currently impressed with?
Well, now you just blink once, and some young player already becomes a Grandmaster or reaches 2700.
[Yagiz Kaan] Erdogmus is quite promising indeed. It is hard to compare him to a player like me, because now it is so much easier to learn opening in a perfect way because of computers. Now it is a whole new situation.
I was quite impressed when I played a classical game against [Faustino] Oro. He is 12 years old, and he knew so much about the opening. When I was 12, I knew a couple of lines, here and there. And I had a rating of around 2300 or even 2400. So, I was not completely talentless. But, my opening knowledge was not like this. That is a big difference between players of my generation and this one.
Back home in Russia, we have some hopes about Roman Shogdzhiev. He seems to be promising. And perhaps he could also try to get his GM title, you know, maybe set a new record.
Because of the Ukraine war, Russia cannot play in tournaments like the Olympiad. You were one of those chess players who signed an open letter to Vladimir Putin demanding an end to the military action.
As a citizen, I think it is fine to have your position.

Former Bachelor Australia star Sam Wood denied bail over domestic violence charges
- Published
Former Bachelor Australia star and fitness coach Sam Wood will remain in jail after he was denied bail over alleged domestic violence offences.
Wood was arrested on Saturday at a beachfront property on Queensland's Sunshine Coast, and later charged with domestic violence assault and strangulation.
His lawyer told the court on Thursday Wood may defend himself by arguing he acted in self defence during a family fight, but stressed he denies the strangulation charge.
The 46-year-old rose to fame in the 2015 season of the reality TV show and later became the public face of a popular online home fitness and nutrition brand, 28 by Sam Wood - from which he was dumped after his arrest.
Wood - who lives in Melbourne but was on holiday in Noosa - appeared via videolink at Maroochydore Magistrates Court where he applied for bail after five nights in custody.
Police prosecutors told the court the alleged victim had provided a video statement in which she said she had been choked, couldn't breathe, and had her head banged against the floor.
"She thought she was going to die," Sergeant Jeanette Grigoris said.
They also tendered photos of the alleged victim's injuries, as well as a recording of a call to emergency services in which a witness says the woman was choked.
The complainant supports the criminal charges, Grigoris added.
Wood's lawyer Mathew Cuskelly had argued that there was a lack of evidence to support the strangulation charge, which "seems unusual" given the "nature" and "gravity" of the allegation.
He also said his client had been involved in an argument, in which the complainant had been "hostile" when he pushed her - circumstances which could entitle him to a self-defence claim.
Cuskelly said Wood suffers from severe depression, and argued he should be bailed so that he can access mental health support and salvage his professional reputation "which has taken a hell of a beating".
But Grigoris argued there was a risk Wood would interfere with witnesses or reoffend, or fail to return to Queensland to face court.
On Monday, a statement "from the Wood family" was released on both he and his wife's social media.
"This is a difficult time for all of us, we are working through this as a family and thoroughly co-operating with the authorities," the post said.
DBG Health, which bought Wood's fitness brand for millions of dollars in 2022, initially said Wood had been placed on "indefinite leave" but later announced it had cut its commercial arrangements with him "effective immediately".
"DGB Health does not tolerate domestic violence in any form, and our thoughts are with people impacted by it," the company said.
Since the charges, a number of fitness influencers and corporate sponsors have also cut ties with Wood including fitness trainer Tiffiny Hall and Married At First Sight star Jules Robinson.
Wood came to national prominence during the 2015 season of The Bachelor Australia where he met contestant Snezana Markoski.
They married in 2018 and have four daughters, including one from his wife's former relationship.
Wood is next due in court on 23 November.

Relative humidity is a simple concept as weather phenomena go – but it has significant, far-reaching consequences for how we must take care of ourselves on a hot or wet day.
Letting the wind flow freely is the secret to cooling our cities
Humidity is the amount of moisture in the air around us, and there are three ways to track it. The most common of them is absolute humidity: the mass of water vapour in a given volume of the air and water vapour mixture, expressed as kg/m3. The second is specific humidity, equal to the mass of the moisture divided by the mass of air. It is expressed as a dimensionless number (but sometimes also as grams per kilogram, among other similar units.)
The third way is relative humidity: it is important because it factors in the amount of vapour that air can hold at different temperatures. Determining its value is a bit more complicated: it is the vapour density of the air divided by the saturation vapour density at the dry-bulb temperature.
Why does relative humidity matter?
On a hot day, our body uses sweat to cool itself. Sweat is released via our skin to the surface. There, the liquid evaporates. When water changes phase from liquid to vapour, it absorbs heat from the surface on which it lies. So when sweat evaporates, it absorbs heat from the skin, cooling it.
The higher the relative humidity of air, the more it is filled with moisture. When air already contains a lot of moisture, it won’t easily accept more. This means that the sweat on your skin can’t evaporate. At the same time, the body keeps sweating because it is still expecting to cool itself.
As a result, if the relative humidity is high, you can sweat on a hot day even when you are sitting still – while your body also keeps accumulating heat. This can quickly become dangerous.
A relative humidity of 30-60% is generally considered to be comfortable. Environments that have lower levels than this typically use humidifiers to increase the humidity. When the level is higher, a fan will help move the air around you and help sweat evaporate better.
In both cases, drinking water is important.
What does relative humidity imply physically?
Warmer air can hold more moisture than cooler air. So at the same absolute humidity, the relative humidity of warmer air will be lower than that of cooler air. It is like saying two vessels can hold the same amount of water – just that the bigger vessel will be less full than the smaller vessel.
This is why, for example, while Chennai had an absolute humidity of 70% at 2.30 pm on April 23, its relative humidity was lower, around 60%, because it had an ambient temperature of 32 C.
The change in the capacity for moisture as the air warms is also non-linear, meaning it doesn’t increase by the same amount as the air warms. For example, the difference as it warms over 20º C from -20º C to 0º C is small, but there is an enormous improvement in its vapour-carrying capacity as it warms over 20º C from 30º C to 50º C.
How do you measure relative humidity?
There are a few ways to measure relative humidity. One is to conduct a simple experiment with household items; another is to use maths; a third is to use an app or device.
Experiment
For the experiment, you need two mercury thermometers, some cotton, rubber bands, and access to cold water.
First, make sure both thermometers show the same reading, say, under a fan. Next, soak some cotton in cold water and wrap it around the bulb of one of the thermometers with a rubber band. Hold this thermometer under the fan, such that water from the cotton evaporates, and record the thermometer reading after five minutes. Hold up the other thermometer in the air and record its reading after five minutes. You will thus have the wet-bulb and dry-bulb temperatures, respectively.
Next, subtract the wet-bulb temperature from the dry-bulb temperature to get the temperature difference. Finally, use the relative humidity chart (see below) to get the relative humidity value. For example, if the difference was 6 C and the dry-bulb temperature was 28 C, the relative humidity would have been 59%.
A psychrometer is a device that has two such thermometers plus a chart to get the final reading. Modern, electronic psychrometers can calculate the relative humidity directly.
For a rough sense, the lower the wet-bulb temperature, the drier the air is, and the less relatively humid it is.
Mathematics
There are two mathematical ways (among others) to estimate the relative humidity, one simpler and one a bit more involved.
The first way is to divide the actual vapour pressure by the saturated vapour pressure. The vapour pressure is the amount of moisture that air contains. The ‘saturated’ value is the maximum possible amount. The formula (below) requires the dew point (Td), which you can obtain from a weather website.
RH = (e/es)*100
e = 6.11 x 10((7.5 x Td)/(237.3 + Td))
For es, use the same formula but replace Td with T, the actual temperature.
The second way is to calculate relative humidity starting from the specific humidity, pressure and temperature, using the Clausius-Clapeyron equation.
App
If you prefer software: Search for “hygrometer” in your phone’s app store to locate some options. (A hygrometer is an instrument that measures humidity.) Note that the app will only work if your phone has a sensor that can sense humidity.
If you like hardware, psychrometers and devices called hygrometers are available in physical as well as online stores.
Why does the wet-bulb temperature matter?
This said, a more direct way to understand the implications of the relative humidity for your wellbeing is in the form of the wet-bulb temperature (a.k.a. the adiabatic saturation temperature). It is the lowest temperature a surface – like your skin – can reach when water evaporates from it. The wet-bulb temperature is equal to the dry-bulb temperature when the relative humidity is 100%.
A wet-bulb temperature in an environment of 32-35º C or higher can be quickly lethal, even if you are not doing any physical activity or are in the shade. (At least one study has shown that even a wet-bulb temperature of more than 29º C can be dangerous.)
The climate crisis is rendering heatwaves more common, more frequent, more spread out, and more potent over the Indian subcontinent. As a study published in May 2022 put it:
“Whether today’s most impactful heatwaves could have occurred in a pre-industrial climate, traditionally a central focus of attribution research, is fast becoming an obsolete question. The next frontier for attribution science is to inform adaptation decision-making in the face of unprecedented future heat.”
One way to adapt is to keep an eye on the relative humidity, drink lots of water, and cool yourself.
