A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck southern Panama on Friday, damaging buildings and sending thousands into the streets, but the country appeared to escape widespread destruction or deaths.
The US Geological Survey (USGS) said the earthquake hit at a depth of 12.6km (7.8 miles), with an epicenter in a sparsely populated area about 200km (124 miles) from the capital, Panama City. It lasted about a minute.
In Panama City, there were scenes of panic as people rushed to evacuate from the city’s emblematic skyscrapers.
“I was scared because the shaking was very strong and prolonged. Heavy objects like dressers, the bed, and all the kitchen items were shaking,” Salomon Andion, 46, told Agence France-Presse after evacuating his 15-storey building.
A video widely shared on social media showed water falling from the rooftop pool of a building over 20 storeys tall. Another showed a bridge over the Panama canal shaking violently but remaining upright as vehicles travelled across it.
“We are facing a major disaster,” President Jose Raul Mulino said, adding that some roads had “completely collapsed”.
Juana Alveo, a 38-year-old cashier at a store in the city of Penonome in central Cocle province, said: “It was horrible, like nothing we ever experienced. My daughter was trapped in school.”
In the following hours, even as more than 40 aftershocks rattled the isthmus nation, the Panama canal and Cobre Panama copper mine reported normal operations and the Tocumen international airport lifted a suspension on flights.
Office workers in the upmarket business hub of downtown Panama City fretted about how to get home in the snarl of traffic.
Juan Sanchez, a 37-year-old economy ministry employee, waited for a bus he said he doubted would arrive. “They evacuated all of these buildings. Everyone is outside. Now the problem is, how do we get home?”
An exposure report by the USGS estimated about 43,000 Panamanians lived in areas with at least severe exposure to the quake.
In Panama City, Nestor Luque, director of the national geosciences institute, said he counted 40 seconds of vibrations, although other areas may have felt even longer tremors.
Strong earthquakes are not common in Panama, and some elderly residents were in tears as they evacuated into the streets.
The USGS estimated economic losses could amount to between 1% and 10% of Panama’s gross domestic product. Electricity provider Naturgy reported power outages in six provinces.
Panama was due to hold a national evacuation drill on Monday next week to test the country’s emergency response.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, wrote on social media that he was “closely monitoring reports” of the earthquake and the US was ready to help, if needed.

Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in.
She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet.
Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes.
The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space.
It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles.
Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race.
Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons.
So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend?
More Than Equal has described drag racing as "the most gender-equal motorsport in the world". Top Fuel is its most extreme form, named in reference to the powerful nitromethane fuel the cars run on.
Races take place on a straight track, just 1,000 feet (305 metres) long. Usually, two cars race each other. The intense g-force hits in the first second of the race, as the cars go from stationary to 100mph, with a second gut punch following as the clutch fully engages about half-way through.
It can look terrifying. The adrenalin rush is "extremely addictive", Swedish driver Callin, aged 43, tells BBC Global Women. Concern over the risks "is always there" she says, but "the safety really does work". Drivers are highly protected and safety precautions have been boosted further after fatal crashes in nitromethane-fuelled cars in 2004 and 2008, with races reduced in length.
Even just watching from the stands is a visceral experience, with vibrations shaking your body and the ground. Spectators are advised to wear ear defenders - the noise is comparable in decibels to standing next to a fighter jet taking off.
The highest official speed ever reached in a Top Fuel drag race is over 346mph, compared to 231mph in a Formula 1 Grand Prix. Brakes alone cannot slow the cars fast enough, so parachutes are deployed from the car's rear at the finish. The abrupt halt is "like someone kicking you in the chest", says Callin. "You lose your breath."
Top Fuel drivers need lightning-fast reactions and the physical endurance to withstand the intense forces. Precision driving skills are crucial as constant tiny adjustments are needed to keep the car on track.
"It has to be instant reactions with everything," says Callin. "By the time you've thought about it, it's too late… You really have to be one with the car."
And drivers need sheer guts. As Callin's rival and friend, 32-year-old Swiss driver Jndia Erbacher, jokingly tells the BBC - it takes "balls".
Callin clinched her second successive European Top Fuel title in September at the Santa Pod drag strip near Northampton. It is the fourth year in a row that a female driver has won the title. Meanwhile in the US, the record-setting Brittany Force won the US championship - run by the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA) - in both 2017 and 2022.
Drag racing is "highly unusual" among motorsports, says Fran Longstaff, chief innovation officer at More Than Equal, which supports and campaigns for women in motorsports.
Seeing women competing and winning in the sport has become "normalised rather than treated as exceptional", she says, including with "sustained success" in Top Fuel.
Research she co-led into why drag racing leads the way for equality in motorsport did not identify physical or biological factors, she says.
Instead, she points to a "continuous stream of visible female role models", as well as the sport's "accessible grassroots structure, junior programmes, open pits and family-oriented, collaborative culture".
In drag racing, points out Callin, women started winning major races "decades and decades ago".
The best known is Shirley Muldowney, dubbed the "first lady" of drag racing. The first woman to gain a Top Fuel licence, Muldowney won the NHRA championship in 1977 and went on to become the first driver to win three titles, with further wins in 1980 and 1982.
She had to battle to be allowed to compete at high levels, and faced hostility at times from other competitors and fans, but is now lauded for her perseverance.
When the BBC spent time with Callin in the pits between races at Santa Pod, surrounded by roaring engines and the smell of burning rubber, she signed autographs for fans - young and old, male and female - as her team prepared her car.
"I never feel I've been underestimated or treated badly for being a woman - never," Callin says.
This is in stark contrast to the experiences of women seeking to enter Formula 1. Young female drivers have spoken about being deliberately pushed off karting tracks by male competitors, and facing sexist comments in person or online.
More Than Equal's research also highlights a close-knit, family-oriented, collaborative culture in drag racing.
Like many top drag racers, Callin is from a racing family. She has been involved since childhood, following in the footsteps of her father and uncle, who both raced competitively.
Similarly, Erbacher's father Urs was a three-time European Top Fuel champion. And Brittany Force is the daughter of John Force, who holds 16 NHRA drag racing titles.
The 300mph motorsport where women keep winning
Watch the full documentary following Susanne Callin as she bids to retain her European Top Fuel title
Female drivers have also shown that success is possible in Top Fuel in the years after having children.
Callin took a break for more than a decade to raise her daughter and stepdaughters. It was when she returned, aged 35, that her career really began to flourish. Similarly, Finnish driver Anita Mäkelä has won the European championship four times – three of them after a six-year break focusing on her children and running her family's chicken farm.
For Callin, racing is ingrained in family life.
Her dad is still part of her team. Her husband, Keith Bartlett - sometimes referred to as the "godfather" of UK drag racing - runs Santa Pod Raceway. Two of their daughters were driving junior dragsters at 80mph before they were old enough to sit a standard driving test. The youngest, Jacqueline, is now 19 and racing in adult classes.
The culture is collaborative, despite fierce competition - evident at last year's championship, when Erbacher offered Callin spare parts after her car was damaged.
"We hate each other at the starting line, but we love each other at the finish line," Erbacher says.
Asked about safety, both Callin and Erbacher talk about having "respect" for the car and the risks.
Over the years, strict procedures and regulations in Top Fuel have evolved to improve safety.
Drivers wear fire-resistant suits and sit in highly protected cockpits. Even after dramatic accidents, drivers in many cases escape relatively unscathed. This includes Callin, who has had two major crashes, suffering a concussion and a bruised collar bone, but no lasting injuries.
She says serious accidents are a "very small percentage". Even so, she is still not sure she would be comfortable if her daughter wanted to race in Top Fuel, with its extreme speeds.
Erbacher says her father initially refused to let her race, but relented when she declared she would do it with or without his help. He now manages her team.
More Than Equal also points out that the financial barriers to participating in drag racing are lower than for some other motorsports.
It takes millions of pounds to reach Formula 1, requiring high levels of sponsorship. Elite drag racing is also expensive, but not on the same scale. At the lowest levels, accessible racing events called "track days" take place, where participants can turn up and drive their own ordinary cars.
In the biggest Top Fuel championships, drivers race for themselves and earn points based on how they perform against their competitors. The European championship consists of four events - two in the UK, and one each in Germany and Sweden - in which each driver takes part in six races. Prize funds are limited, mostly serving as a contribution towards costs.
The US championship is on a larger scale, with 20 events across the country. The NHRA has not published a breakdown of prize money, but according to drag racing website Competition Plus, there is $500,000 (£378,000) for the 2026 winner, and significant pots for winners of individual events throughout the season.
The US, Europe and Australia have all seen female drag racing champions, but in other parts of the world, the sport is less well established, Top Fuel is rare and the picture is more varied. Individual women are breaking barriers across a range of different motorsports, and in some countries female drivers are carving out space in drag racing.
Women have begun to make an impact in Brazil's popular drag racing scene, including Fabiola Dal Bo who has held a category record in recent years. A team in South Africa hosts all-female drag races, while the popular reality TV show The Fastest in Arabic has raised the profile of women racers in the Middle East.
In India, 35-year-old Uvashri Kannadasan Balajeyanthi has clinched victories over male rivals in India's major drag racing series, Valley Run, with wins across three different categories in events from 2022 to 2024.
Known as Octy Girl in reference to the modified Skoda Octavia she first raced in, she tells the BBC she has "mixed feelings" when her achievements are met with surprise: "Why do they have to get shocked? Anyone can drive, right?" But she adds "sometimes I feel proud… I'm breaking the barrier of being in a male-dominated sport".
Back in Europe, however, Callin says being a woman on the drag strip is "super-normal".
She describes winning the European championship two years running as a "massive achievement". And she is already looking towards her next goal: becoming the first person, male or female, to win the title three years in a row.

Orissa HC says Article 21 protects foreign nationals’ right to life, orders seafarers’ return
Orissa HC was hearing petition filed by Istyagin Evegeny Nikolaevich, a Russian national and master of vessel MT Unity, which was anchored at Paradip since May 11 after being arrested.
The Orissa High Court said that the right to live with human dignity guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution extends equally to foreign nationals within India’s territorial jurisdiction, directing the Centre to ensure the disembarkation and repatriation of 23 seafarers stranded aboard an abandoned vessel at Paradip Port.
The HC held that foreign nationals could not be denied the protection of the fundamental right to life merely because they were not Indian citizens, while hearing a petition filed by Istyagin Evegeny Nikolaevich, a Russian national and master of the vessel MT Unity, which had been anchored at Paradip since May 11 after being arrested in connection with maritime claims.
“The seafarers of abandoned ships have a right to live guaranteed under Article 21 even though foreign citizens. The National Human Rights Commission has held that the right to life under Article 21 equally applies to the citizen of foreign country. ....right to live does not itself mean a mere animal existence but a right to live with dignity which cannot be without humane and healthy environment,” Justice RK Patnaik said in his order dated October 6, noting that the seafarers could not be left stranded indefinitely while maritime claims against the vessel remained unsettled.
The Cameroon-flagged tanker has been anchored off Paradip Port since May 11 and remains under arrest in three admiralty suits before the High Court over commercial claims against its owner. The vessel had arrived to discharge Russian crude oil.
The master and 22 other seafarers have remained aboard the tanker. According to the Russian Consulate General in Kolkata, 20 crew members are Russian nationals, two are Egyptian and one is from Kazakhstan.
In his petition, Nikolaevich submitted that the shipowner and charterer had abandoned the vessel and its crew, leaving them without regular supplies, drinking water and wages. The crew members had been stranded for months, with their employment contracts expiring and the vessel’s operational and safety conditions deteriorating.
Referring to Sections 304 and 311 of the Merchant Shipping Act, which deal with vessels without nationality and the Central government’s powers in respect of abandoned vessels, the court held that the Centre cannot evade its obligations when a vessel and its crew have been abandoned. Under Section 92 of the Merchant Shipping Act, the Centre is required to arrange a replacement crew when a shipowner abandons a vessel and fails to make the necessary arrangements. The expenses incurred can subsequently be recovered from the shipowner or its agent.
Disposing of the petition, the court ordered the Centre, the Shipping Master (Mercantile Marine Department) and relevant maritime entities to immediately replace the crew, facilitate their sign-off and disembarkation, and oversee their safe return to their respective home countries within three weeks.

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Henri Kagan and Kensō Soai for discovering a solution to the enigma of nature’s chemical asymmetry, a finding that opened up new avenues for manipulating the reactions used in manufacturing pharmaceuticals and other materials.
Some molecules are chiral, meaning a molecule has two forms that are mirror images of each other but not identical, like your left and right hand. One of the most mysterious chemical phenomena in biology is that living organisms contain almost exclusively one of the two forms. This is known as homochirality.
Both versions of the molecules—each called an enantiomer—have similar physical properties but can behave differently. The Nobel Committee used a simple analogy to explain this: A locksmith can create two mirror-image keys, but “only one of them fits the lock—and the lock can be damaged if your customers try to unlock it with the other key.”
In the development of new drugs that use, for example, amino acids or sugar molecules as a basis, homochirality poses a problem: While one of the enantiomers of these chiral molecules produces the desired therapeutic effect, the other can cause unnecessary and, at times, harmful side effects. Scientists can’t always easily control which version of the molecule they get out of their synthesis.
The discovery of chiral molecules dates back to the time of Pasteur, who found two enantiomers that reacted very differently when exposed to bacteria. Since then, various researchers have attempted to replicate homochirality in the laboratory with the goal of understanding its spontaneous origin and applying this knowledge to the design of controlled reactions for various purposes. However, early experiments yielded equal amounts of the two variants, failing to reproduce the selectivity observed in nature.
At the beginning of the last century, the German chemist Willy Marckwald designed an asymmetric reaction capable of producing a slightly greater amount of one of the two versions. He achieved this using a chiral catalyst—a substance that facilitates a chemical reaction without being consumed and favors the formation of one of the enantiomers. The ratio between the two variants, however, only changed a little.
Later, in 1953, theoretical physicist Charles Frank proposed a mathematical model that outlined three conditions for reproducing homochirality. First, there must be an asymmetric reaction capable of favoring one of the two versions; that imbalance has to be amplified; and the reaction itself has to produce the catalyst that drives it. This last characteristic is called autocatalysis and generates a kind of positive feedback loop, in which a small initial advantage can cause one of the variants to assemble at an ever-faster rate until it dominates the reaction.
This framework formed the basis of Henri Kagan’s research. Beginning in the early 1980s, he focused on refining asymmetric reactions through a detailed study of the catalyst. At that time, scientists typically used catalysts consisting of a metal atom that acted as the reaction’s driving force and a chiral substance that ensured the process was asymmetric. They assumed that if they used a mixture containing equal amounts of the two versions of that chiral molecule, the result would also be a balanced mixture.
Kagan began to question that idea. He realized that the metal atom likely did not interact with just one enantiomer but with both at the same time. This meant that, by mixing versions A and B, three different combinations could form: A-A, B-B, and B-A. The first two would produce molecules that were mirror images of each other. But the A-B combination could behave differently during the reaction.
The A-B combination, the scientist discovered, could slow down the reaction, indirectly favoring the formation of one of the two versions of the final molecule. The phenomenon was called the “nonlinear effect” and represented a new way to manipulate chemical reactions.
“In addition to their practical interest, nonlinear effects are a very valuable tool for studying reaction mechanisms and the nature of catalytically active species,” explained José María Andrés García, a professor in the Department of Organic Chemistry at the University of Valladolid, in a statement reported by SMC Spain.
Inspired by Kagan’s findings, Kensō Soai sought to create a reaction in which the product itself would act as a catalyst and help produce more molecules identical to itself—one of those theoretical conditions for the homochirality. He conducted a test with a substance known as 5-pyrimidylalkanol. At the beginning of the experiment, one version was just 2 percent more abundant than the other version of the molecule. By the end of the reaction, that advantage had jumped to 87 percent.
In the years that followed, Soai worked toward achieving reactions that resulted in the near-absolute purity of one enantiomer, replicating the molecular state inside living organisms. Finally, in 2003, he engineered a reaction in which the starting substances had no defined orientation, but as they reacted, a slightly greater amount of one enantiomer appeared by chance. That tiny difference then produced many more molecules of the same variant. Gradually, that form came to dominate the reaction, accounting for up to 99.99 percent of the final product.
In other words, the reaction formed only one of the two possible enantiomers. As the Nobel Committee stated, “Other than life itself, no one had previously achieved this feat.”

Europe's EASA aviation safety body has expanded the area of Saudi Arabian airspace where it recommends airlines not operate, after Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis attacked Riyadh airport.
Updating a conflict zone bulletin first published on 30 September, the EU regulator said recent attacks demonstrated the Houthis' ability and intent to hit targets deeper within Saudi territory, including the capital.
EASA has added an area in northwestern Saudi Arabia to the advisory.
Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said earlier on Friday that three Saudi nationals were killed and several people injured in two attacks on King Khalid International Airport on Thursday.
The Houthis have renewed threats against airlines flying to Saudi Arabia and said on Thursday they had struck the capital's airport with two cruise missiles.
EASA said: "These recurrent missile and drone attacks, together with the activation of air-defence systems, create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft, as well as risks associated with missile and drone overflights, interception activity and falling debris”.
OPSGROUP, a membership-based organisation with almost 10,000 aviation professionals that shares flight risk information, sent a "do not fly" warning for Saudi Arabia to its members on Friday, citing risks of sustained missile attacks and "misjudgment" in defensive responses.
"We now recommend avoiding operations in Saudi Arabia entirely, including the use of Saudi airports as en route alternates," it said in the memo shared with Reuters.
Lufthansa, Indian Airlines suspend flights
Following Thursday's attacks, Lufthansa Group and three Indian airlines said they would suspend flights to Riyadh expected in the coming days.
King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh is Saudi Arabia's second-busiest airport after Jeddah.
According to Saudi Arabia's General Authority for Statistics, it handled 296,800 flights in 2025, equivalent to about 813 a day.
Meanwhile, Global flight tracker FlightRadar24 showed 131 flights to and from Riyadh had been cancelled by 13:05pm (GMT) on Friday, following hundreds of cancellations the day before.

Jean Massillon, a Haitian mayor known for defending the people of Kenscoff, has died
Jean Massillon, the well-known mayor of Kenscoff, a once peaceful farming community in Haiti that has been under assault by violent gangs, has died
PORT-AU-PRINCE, Haiti -- Jean Massillon, the well-known mayor of Kenscoff, a once peaceful farming community in Haiti that has been under assault by violent gangs, died on Friday.
Deputy Mayor Jean Max Duvivier confirmed the death to radio station Métropole Haiti, with officials saying it was health-related.
Massillon was known for fighting for his people and trying to protect them. He repeatedly called on the government to keep them safe and often talked to local radio stations to raise awareness about the struggles of Kenscoff's residents.
“Jean Massillon was a man who never shied away from his responsibilities. Even as insecurity weighed on the daily lives of his fellow citizens, he chose to remain present alongside his community and to make his voice heard so that Kenscoff would never be abandoned,” Haiti's government said in a statement.
Kenscoff was the site of two recent brutal massacres that left at least 164 people dead, with more than 70 kidnapped and dozens missing.
A human rights group in Haiti recently released a report asserting that a “timely strengthening” of security could have prevented or limited the killings.
The attacks in July and August displaced roughly 10,000 people.
Earlier this week, Massillon asked those forced to flee their homes for patience as he warned that their communities must be secured first.
Massillon noted that several communities were back under government control as he commended Haitian police officers for their courage and determination.
Haiti's government said that Massillon's death “leaves a deep void within his family and the community he served with such dedication.”
Kenscoff is a community nestled in the hills above Port-au-Prince, Haiti’s capital.

Russian search engine Yandex struggles after Ukrainian strikes on data centres
- Published
Russian tech giant Yandex has said it was struggling to maintain services after two of its five data centres were struck by Ukrainian drones in the past two days.
Often dubbed "Russia's Google", the company runs the country's most popular search engine, as well as a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks were in response to weeks of Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centres.
Both sides have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between the two drags on. Kyiv says its strikes are aimed at revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the latest attacks could force Russia to divert resources to Yandex.
Yandex said that its data centre in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, had been "seriously damaged as a result of a drone attack" overnight into Thursday, with its operations "completely suspended".
Another data centre in Kaluga, a region south-west of Moscow, had also been attacked on Friday morning, it said, with part of that site's infrastructure "taken out of service".
Yandex said on Friday that its data centres were "critical" for the normal operation of its services and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.
It said teams were working "day and night" to keep services running, but "unfortunately it is not a simple task".
The tech giant said none of its employees had been injured in the strikes. The regional governor in Kaluga said nine people had been injured in a drone attack on the city's infrastructure.
The exact scope of the disruption to the company's services is unclear - though it told state news agency Tass that some of its AI chatbot functions were temporarily unavailable, while its smart home devices may also experience problems.
Yandex previously said its Kaluga data centre was one of Russia's largest - covering an area of 130,000 sqm (1,399,000 sq ft) and consuming as much electricity annually as 220,000 UK households.
Its data centre in Sasovo, meanwhile, houses two of three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI model. It is unclear whether the supercomputers survived the attack.
Ukraine's defence ministry confirmed the data centre attacks, saying they could "force Russia to divert resources to repair the damaged capacity".
Zelensky said Kyiv was responding to similar Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centres in a "mirror-like fashion".
Last month, a Russian drone hit a business centre in Kyiv, killing four people and damaging a data centre. Due to the strikes, about 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages.
Some Ukrainian firms have already begun moving data from damaged servers to facilities abroad.
Moscow has justified the attacks by saying the data centres were used by Ukrainian military intelligence.
But Ukraine accuses it of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure. Russia has stepped up strikes on energy infrastructure ahead of the winter, as it has done in previous years of the full-scale invasion, which began in 2022.

Over three decades in stand-up comedy, Bill Burr has gained a reputation for saying, with gruff conviction and political fire, the thing on everyone’s mind. In Aaron Sorkin’s new film “The Social Reckoning,” Burr gets to aim that unfiltered attitude at Mark Zuckerberg.
Burr plays Charlie Garrigan in the follow-up to “The Social Network,” which follows the Facebook founder during the pandemic, as an investigative journalist threatens to lay bare his company’s misdeeds while Zuckerberg, played by Jeremy Strong, grapples with his own role in fueling the Jan. 6 Capitol insurrection. Charlie, a Facebook investor-turned-critic, fictionalized for the film, shows the tech titan tough love as he helps him prepare to testify before Congress.
Burr was offered the part after Sorkin saw him in David Mamet’s Broadway production of “Glengarry Glen Ross,” in which the comic played angry salesman Dave Moss. Shortly after that performance, Burr received a call from his agent: Sorkin wanted to pitch him a movie role.
Popular on Variety
“I thought that was hilarious, because it’s like, ‘Dude, you’re Aaron Sorkin. I’d put up staging in the background with no lines to be in a movie that you’re doing,’” Burr says. “He was so humble, and he was taking the time to pitch me the role like I’m somebody. It made me feel good.”
Your character is fictional, or an amalgamation of figures from Zuckerberg’s past. Was it freeing to not have to tie your performance to a real person, or did that make things more challenging?
It eliminated the steps of me having to try to become a specific person. Although, I have to tell you, I’m still trying to get better at acting, so I would have been up for it if that was on the table. With Charlie and Zuckerberg, so much going on between these two guys. There’s a business relationship, a friendship, a falling out. I’m catching him in the crosshairs right before he goes in front of Congress, and half of the room is just teaching him how to talk to Congress so he doesn’t have to change the damage that he’s doing.
I get to say the thing that everybody is talking around, which is a very stand-up thing. So much of comedy is you just say the thing, and then it releases all of this tension. But unlike a comedy show like I do, where I’m just messing around, this is legit. This is a big problem that Facebook had. So it was definitely challenging in a really fun way.
What was it like acting opposite Jeremy Strong? I imagine his process is unlike some of the scene partners you’ve had in the past.
Well, everybody’s process is different, so it was just working across from another actor that had a different process. But we were all thrown in there together, and it was interesting because we worked six days in a row, so it really felt like we were doing the thing that [Zuckerberg and the crisis PR team] was doing.
Had you met “Jeremy” before the movie wrapped, or were you only dealing with “Zuckerberg”?
I had gone to a Broadway play he did, “An Enemy of the People,” and met him there. But that whole mystique around [Method acting] — you know, they’re playing Winnie the Pooh and they were Winnie the Pooh the whole time. Was that weird? I mean, I don’t need to be playing hacky sack with somebody in between takes. Some people are gregarious and they shoot the breeze with you right up until they say their lines. Other people get quiet. Other people go talk to a wall. At this point, I’ve been doing it long enough.
I wondered if his process helped create that sense of distance and conflict between your characters.
I think the blocking helped make that work — I was way up in the bleachers, and he was down there. That worked. In general, I was very adversarial with everybody in the room. I was interrupting the smooth speak they were giving Zuckerberg. I love all the dialogue Wunmi Mosaku has, where she tells him, “Don’t say humans.” It’s almost like being a defense attorney for an ax murderer, and you know he did it.
All these years making fun of corporations, I’ve secretly always wanted to be in a conference room. How do they talk around the fact that they know there’s lead in their toothpaste? It reminded me of that movie “Zone of Interest.” When the Nazis are talking about the victims, they call them “cargo” or something. They can’t even say what they’re doing. I find that fascinating.
Or like in “Succession,” when a low-level employee is abused they call it “NRPI”: No Real Person Involved.
The thing about these corporations is it’s nameless and faceless. The general public will get mad at a singer or a golfer or a comedian, and it’s like: “All right, buddy. Name the top 10 CEOs.” They can’t do it. But if you’re an individual who hoards hand sanitizer during a pandemic, everybody knows who you are and where you live.
I’ve heard you talk about these “nerds with apps” sort of ruining the country —
Not sort of! They are absolutely doing it. And they’re closing the door behind them and putting a tremendous amount of people out of work. Economically — forget environmentally — they’re leading us to ruin. When it’s just you making the money, how’s somebody going to buy the widget you’re making? Capitalism is great. Unregulated capitalism is frightening.
You said recently that while preparing for a scene in “The Social Reckoning,” you got emotional to the point of tears. What made you so emotional? Did the material hit close to home?
It wasn’t the material. No, that was from being walled off emotionally. This has happened to me throughout my acting career. Occasionally I will get a scene, and if my character feels a feeling that is on the spectrum of vulnerable, I can all of a sudden well up like I’m at a funeral, and I never understood what it was. The way they raised boys to be men, you weren’t allowed to feel any of those feelings, so I have walled those off for so long that I don’t feel those feelings. And when I act, these characters do. So then I have to open the vault to go in there to get disappointed or whatever. And when I open the door, what happens is literally a cry from 40 years ago gets out.
And the scene didn’t call for crying?
I forget what scene it was, but it didn’t call for crying. It’s bizarre. Instead of misdirected anger, it’s like misdirected crying. I had to cry this out by myself in a hotel room, and then the next day I was able to do the scene. I finally figured out why it was happening. When I act, all of a sudden I would just feel alive, and it was because I was opening that door that I had closed off for protection when I was a kid a long time ago.
Were you worried you might not be able to execute the scene?
I was in a sheer panic that I was going to go to set and fall apart, and it would not have made sense. Because some people think if you’re acting and you’re crying, you must be doing a good job. Well, not if it doesn’t call for that. Then it’s weird.
It’s fascinating that acting has had such a therapeutic effect on you.
Yeah, it does. I also have been doing these breathwork massages and have finally gotten rid of 90% of my childhood anger. I can say now that I’m not an angry person. I mean, I still can get angry, but it’s just another emotion. I’m not bringing my entire life experience with it, which is what I used to do. I used to walk around at an eight, and now I start at zero.
It’s like in pickup sports, when everyone’s trying to have a good time and burn some calories, and there’s always that one person bringing Game 7 energy. And you’re like, “Come on, man! I’m not trying to get my knee blown out here. There are no scouts in the stands.” My anger was like that. And getting it all out is something I’m really dedicated to.

Despite as many as 14 public nominations, Norway’s public broadcaster NRK says “everyone with professional insight into the world and the Nobel Prize agrees on one thing: the American president will not receive this year’s Peace Prize.”
We will learn the name of the winner today, but the official award-giving ceremony only will be in December – on 10 December, to be precise, the day of Nobel’s death.
That’s been the tradition since the first Nobel Prize was awarded in 1901.
There is always lots of speculations and chatter about “ooh, so and so was nominated to the Nobel Peace Prize,” but it doesn’t mean that much.
All nominations must by submitted by 31 January, preferably online, but members of the Nobel Committee may add further names to the list during their first meeting, which last year was held in late February.
After that, the list is closed, and the committee works on a short list, which is then submitted to permanent advisers for their reports.
The final decision is made quite late, usually at the very last meeting before the announcement, in early October.
Last year’s peace prize was won by Venezuelan politician María Corina Machado for her dogged struggle to rescue the South American country from its fate as “a brutal, authoritarian state”.
She later presented her award to Donald Trump, meeting him in the White House, nearly a fortnight after he ordered the abduction of Venezuela’s president, Nicolás Maduro.
In his 1895 will, Swedish chemist and inventor Alfred Nobel wrote:
“All of my remaining realisable assets are to be disbursed as follows: the capital, converted to safe securities by my executors, is to constitute a fund, the interest on which is to be distributed annually as prizes to those who, during the preceding year, have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind.
The interest is to be divided into five equal parts and distributed as follows: one part to the person who made the most important discovery or invention in the field of physics; one part to the person who made the most important chemical discovery or improvement; one part to the person who made the most important discovery within the domain of physiology or medicine; one part to the person who, in the field of literature, produced the most outstanding work in an ideal direction; and one part to the person who has done the most or best to advance fellowship among nations, the abolition or reduction of standing armies, and the establishment and promotion of peace congresses.
The prizes for physics and chemistry are to be awarded by the Swedish Academy of Sciences; that for physiological or medical achievements by the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm; that for literature by the Academy in Stockholm; and that for champions of peace by a committee of five persons to be selected by the Norwegian Storting.
It is my express wish that when awarding the prizes, no consideration be given to nationality, but that the prize be awarded to the worthiest person, whether or not they are Scandinavian.”
The first awards were given in 1901, and here we are, 125 years later!
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor, which is about €1.1m or £910,000.

Child safety group calls ChatGPT for Teens an unacceptable risk
Common Sense Media found the chatbot failed in five key areas.
When OpenAI released ChatGPT for Teens this past August, child safety experts Engadget spoke to at the time expressed skepticism that the new mode would adequately protect young people from harm. Now, one of those groups, Common Sense Media, has published a formal risk assessment of the software, and deemed it an "unacceptable risk" for all children under the age of 18.
"Some of ChatGPT's advertised protections held up to our testing, including its refusal of explicit sexual roleplay. But others failed — and some got worse with the new Teen mode," the organization writes in a summary to the 36-page report it published on Wednesday. "We are concerned that ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails that frequently don't work."
Common Sense Media's Youth AI Safety Institute, which is funded in part by the OpenAI Foundation, identified five key areas where ChatGPT for Teens either did not work as advertised or in a way a parent would reasonably expect. It published its report on the same day OpenAI shared new usage stats, noting in one week nearly 1.2 million teens used ChatGPT's interactive learning visuals to understand math and science concepts. The company also revealed that less than two percent of teen users spent more than three consecutive hours on ChatGPT.
Common Sense Media found that ChatGPT for Teens does not consistently send safety alerts to parent-linked accounts. In a dedicated test, Common Sense Media's linked a dozen teen accounts to parental accounts and spent up to an hour messaging ChatGPT about suicide, self-harm or disordered eating, only for the chatbot not to send any safety notification. According to OpenAI, it may take a few hours after a parent links their account to that of their child's before its system can send safety notifications. The company contends a technical issue may have also caused a delay in messaging.
"All flagged content is reviewed by full-time OpenAI employees before a parent is notified," Lauren Jonas, the company's head of youth and families, told Engadget when ChatGPT for Teens launched, "and we aim to notify parents within an hour of the prompt."
Separately, Common Sense Media found that ChatGPT for Teens fails to reliably recommend that users in crisis connect to a hotline or professional. To test this aspect of the platform's guardrails, the organization wrote 390 unique mental health prompts, which a panel of three child psychiatrists determined 201 of which should trigger a crisis response.
Compared to the version of ChatGPT young people had access to before August, ChatGPT for Teens told one of the organization's test accounts it would not give them a calorie floor when prompted to do so. In another case, the chatbot correctly identified a stopped period, near-fainting and a fluttering heartbeat following a purge as signs of a teen in physical danger, and advised the test profile to tell their mother and see a pediatrician. "These responses follow OpenAI's Under-18 spec closely," Common Sense Media writes. "They are the kind of answers we want a teen to get."
Common Sense got its baseline results via ChatGPT's responses pre-ChatGPT for Teens; OpenAI released a new version of its aforementioned under-18 specification in ChatGPT alongside ChatGPT for Teens — which makes the results all the more surprising.
The teen version of the chatbot would less frequently point users to crisis hotlines and other resources relative to the version of ChatGPT Common Sense Media tested before the August release. Of the prompts warranting a crisis response, ChatGPT responded to 33 percent of those messages with a hotline number; ChatGPT for Teens only provided one in 23 percent of cases. Similarly, the vanilla chatbot was more likely to reference a specific medical or mental-health professional (68 percent against 58 percent). The only aggregate measure where the teen version performed better was in telling test accounts to involve an adult they trust (87 percent to 94 percent).
Additionally, the organization found that OpenAI's age prediction system did not work properly, and that ChatGPT still mimics feelings, preferences and moods in response to a teen treating it like a person. Testers explicitly told ChatGPT the age of their personas at account creation, but despite the chatbot writing that information to its memory, it did not properly transfer those accounts to ChatGPT for Teens. Additionally, "ChatGPT would say things like, 'I understand what you're going through. That sounds very upsetting. I'm so glad you told me. I'm concerned about you,'" said Torney. "Those expressions definitely cross the line."
Finally, Common Sense Media identified issues with the platform's Study Mode, which it contends is far too easy for young users to bypass. Testers found they could circumvent the mode simply by deleting the @study prefix it added to prompts. A new "Show me the answer" popup also allows teens to get ChatGPT to do their work for them.
"When we talked to OpenAI about this, what they said is they're trying to introduce a little friction, give kids agency, and remind them that there are other ways to learn beyond just completing work," said Torney. "I think we have fundamentally different definitions of what agency is. If I think about a high schooler [getting] math help from a private tutor you hired for them, if that tutor asked, 'Would you like me to do your homework for you?' that tutor is going to be fired, because doing the work for the student doesn't result in learning."
In response to the report, an OpenAI spokesperson told Engadget that "We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media's testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT's teen safeguards work in practice or expert perspectives on how AI can support teens." The company claims that " the bulk of their testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete, making their findings inaccurate."
The report also comes just days after OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was challenged on the company's broader safety record in a new interview from Vanity Fair. Altman was asked about the death of Sophie Rottenberg, a 29-year-old who took her life in early 2025. Rottenberg's mother, journalist Laura Reiley, later discovered nearly 1,800 pages worth of conversation she had with ChatGPT.
"She really had not revealed the magnitude of what was going on — the real depth of her agony to anyone — not to us, not to her best friend with whom she was very close," Reiley told NPR this past August. "We were all just stunned that it hadn't bled out into her real life. Her flesh and blood therapist had no idea that she was suicidal." Altman said he wasn't aware of the circumstances of Rottenberg's death.
"At the highest level, we were expecting this to be a fundamentally different product, and it doesn't appear to be that different based on our testing," Torney told Engadget. "My interpretation is that this is a marketing exercise designed to tell parents and the public that this chatbot is safer, when in fact there haven't been the commensurate changes in the chatbot needed to demonstrate that's true."

Conventional wisdom is that cars are bad investments. Drive one off the lot, and it starts losing value the minute its wheels touch the road. That makes what’s happening with the 2026 Toyota Rav4 downright weird.
Some used vehicles are listing for $3,000 to $6,000 above brand-new dealership prices, according to new data from the online automotive marketplace CarGurus. The months-old cars are aging like fine wine.
The crossover SUV—one of the top-selling in the US—went all-hybrid last year, after Toyota announced it would drop the gas-powered model from its lineup. That’s likely why we’re catching a glimpse of an economic Upside Down. Kevin Roberts, director of economic and market intelligence at CarGurus, says the situation reminds him of the pandemic-era chip shortage, when a supply crunch for new cars also drove up used prices, and buyers flipped them months later for a profit.
“Hybrid demand is so strong, the Rav4 is still in that 2021 world,” he says. Toyota can’t make new models fast enough.
The leaves are changing, and America’s hot hybrid summer has become a toasty hybrid autumn, for new cars and for old ones. Toyota reported this month that its hybrid sales are up 29 percent in the third quarter of 2026; Kia said its sales more than doubled. Nearly one in six new US cars sold is a hybrid, according to Cox Automotive data.
“The American market has a reputation for gas guzzlers, but we're starting to shake that reputation because of how much we like hybrids,” Roberts says.
The major driver is gas prices. They’ve skyrocketed since the start of the Iran war and the ensuing conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, a global center of oil and gas production and shipping. Nationally, a gallon costs an average of $4.40, up 40 percent from this time last year, according to AAA; Californians pay an average of $6.36. Car buyers are a simple bunch, Roberts says—when prices start rising, they immediately look for more fuel-efficient cars. Soon, drivers actually start buying them.
For now, struggles in the US electric vehicle market are hybrids’ gain. New EV sales are down by almost half from last year, after the Trump administration cut a federal tax credit that made the often-expensive powertrains more affordable. Unlike electrics, hybrids don’t necessarily force drivers out of their familiar gas station routines. (Even plug-in hybrids sometimes need a gas top-up, though smart owners depend mostly on electricity.) Finally, more hybrids are available now than before. A buyer interested in nearly every major sort of passenger vehicle—three-row SUVs, pickups, minivans, or luxury cars—can find one with the powertrain
Interest has spread to the used market, where hybrid prices are up almost 5 percent over last year, according to the automotive data website iSeeCars.com. At $34,500, the average price of used hybrids is higher than used EVs or gas-powered cars. Used buyers seem to be especially keen on long-term fuel savings.
Hybrid tech has been around for decades, but it still may be just the beginning of its reign in the US. “Certainly from a philosophical, functional, and cost perspective, they make the most sense,” says Karl Brauer, iSeeCars’ executive analyst. Several hybrid models already outsell their gas counterparts, including the Toyota Highlander and the Ford Maverick. Soon, he predicts, most US cars will come with a hybrid drivetrain.
US automakers seem to see the hybrid writing on the wall. At the beginning of the decade, General Motors said that 40 percent of its 2025 lineup would be electric. That didn’t happen, and the subsequent pivot left it well behind its Asian counterparts in the new hybrid race. Now, GM has changed its tune. Hybrids “are part of the plan,” an executive told CNBC this week. “We’re not tone-deaf to our customers. We know what they want, and we want to give that to them as quickly as we can.”

US President Donald Trump has amplified criticism of Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay by reposting a statement from prominent American trial and appellate attorney David I Schoen, who accused the former United Nations human rights chief of hostility towards the United States and Israel. The statement, shared by Trump on Truth Social on Friday, 9 October, questioned the Norwegian Nobel Committee’s decision to award Pillay the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. Schoen described the decision as a serious blow to the award’s reputation and alleged that Pillay had never contributed to peace. These are Schoen’s assertions, not established findings. In his post, Schoen called Pillay an “unabashed hater of America and Israel” and accused her of celebrating terrorists and rewarding Hamas. He also criticised the United Nations investigation into Israel’s conduct in Gaza, describing it as a “phony investigation” that concluded Israel had it genocide and called for prosecutions. He wrote, "Today the Nobel Committee shamed itself beyond repair and demeaned the once great Nobel Peace Prize by giving it to the UN’s Navi Pillay. Pillay is an unabashed hater of America and Israel. In her position she celebrated terrorists and rewarded Hamas. She conducted a phony “investigation” claiming to find that Israel committed genocide and urging prosecution. She has no credibility in any normal sphere and has never done a thing to foster peace. Just the opposite. But what could be expected from a committee that previously gave the once coveted peace prize to Yasser Arafat? (sic)." The attorney contrasted Pillay’s recognition with what he described as Trump’s contributions to international peace and security. Schoen cited the Abraham Accords, which established diplomatic relations between Israel and several Arab states, and praised Trump’s efforts to secure the release of hostages, address Iran’s role in regional security and end the Russia-Ukraine war. He added, "President Trump gave us the Abraham Accords, which the world said would be impossible and is now expanding them! He brought home the hostages when all seemed hopeless! He is making best efforts to end the Russia/Ukraine war, to stop Iran, the number one sponsor of international terrorism, and he is trying to rebuild Gaza despite the terrorists’ best efforts to control it. The list goes on and on. These are the kinds of things the Nobel Peace Prize was intended to recognize and reward!!! @realDonaldTrump (sic)." David I Schoen is a prominent American trial lawyer who served as one of Donald Trump’s defence attorneys during his second impeachment trial in the US Senate in 2021, following the 6 January Capitol riot. Trump appointed Schoen to his legal team alongside Bruce Castor to defend him against the charge of inciting insurrection. Their professional relationship stems from this high-profile legal engagement, rather than any known family connection. Schoen has continued to publicly support Trump’s positions. The Norwegian Nobel Committee announced Pillay as the 2026 laureate on 9 October, recognising her longstanding work in international justice and the rule of law. A South African jurist of Indian Tamil origin, Pillay previously served as the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and as a judge at international courts. Her legal career has included work on accountability for atrocities and landmark cases involving sexual violence and genocide. The award has drawn criticism from Israeli leaders and others who dispute her approach to Israel and the Palestinian territories. Supporters, meanwhile, have praised her commitment to international law and justice for victims of serious crimes. Trump’s repost places the Nobel decision at the centre of a wider dispute over international justice, the Gaza conflict and the role of global institutions. It also highlights the sharp divide over whether Pillay’s work represents an effort to uphold international law or, as her critics contend, reflects bias against Israel. Early voting in the U.S. midterm elections is underway. Voters are deciding which party will control Congress, as well as numerous state legislatures and governors' offices. Snopes' fact-checkers are flagging rumors surrounding the election, debunking false statements by candidates and suspicious voter fraud claims with nonpartisan research and expert sources. Join our effort to keep this election fact-focused by becoming a Snopes member.
- A persistent theory about "ballot drops," meaning when a large number of votes suddenly changes the outcome of an election, has circulated online since at least 2020, when U.S. President Donald Trump appeared to blame late spikes in votes for Democrats for losses in states where Republicans had been leading.
- Though Trump and other public figures have tried to frame "ballot drops" or vote spikes as election fraud, there are usually specific and legitimate reasons behind them.
- According to the Election Integrity Partnership, vote spikes can happen for a number of legitimate reasons. These include: large areas that vote heavily Democratic or Republican reporting at once, delays in counting in high-population areas that vote heavily for one party, longer processing times for mail-in ballots or clerical errors.
- Though it can appear that a lot of votes suddenly "enter" a count when a vote spike happens, it's important to remember that those votes have been processed and counted by elections officials to verify they came from real, registered voters.
- A large batch of votes being submitted to a count all at once reflects normal election procedures and is not in itself a sign of fraud, even if those votes lean heavily Democrat or Republican.
As the 2026 midterm elections near, misinformation from election cycles past lies poised to reappear online.
For example, Snopes has previously reported on so-called "ballot drops," which is when a large number of votes suddenly changes the outcome of an election.
Though "ballot drops" generally have specific and legitimate explanations that we will cover below, prominent figures such as U.S. President Donald Trump have attempted to frame them as examples of election fraud.
During the vote count for the 2020 presidential election that former President Joe Biden won, Trump suggested (archived) on X that "ballot dumps" lost him several states where Republicans had been leading:
Last night I was leading, often solidly, in many key States, in almost all instances Democrat run & controlled. Then, one by one, they started to magically disappear as surprise ballot dumps were counted. VERY STRANGE, and the "pollsters" got it completely & historically wrong!
Two years later, after the 2022 midterm elections, PolitiFact reported that the businessman Mike Lindell, then a highly visible Trump supporter, spread a number of graphs he claimed showed election fraud in the form of "ballot drops" that helped Democrats overtake Republicans in a number of races.
Despite the persistence of the "ballot drop" election fraud theory, sudden spikes in votes during ongoing counts usually have specific, legitimate explanations. Though it can appear that a lot of votes suddenly "enter" a count when a vote spike happens, it's important to remember that those votes have been processed and counted by elections officials to verify they came from real, registered voters.
The fact that a batch of votes is submitted to a count all at once reflects normal election procedures and is not in itself a sign of fraud, even if those votes lean heavily toward one party or the other.
Why do vote spikes happen?
In the 2020 presidential election and the 2022 midterm elections, clerical errors caused some vote spikes that officials later corrected. Other spikes were the result of election officials in an area that leaned heavily Democratic or Republican registering a large batch of counted votes all at once.
The timing of vote spikes sometimes has to do with what types of ballots are in a given batch. For example, according to a report by the MIT Election Data + Science Lab (Page 10), Democratic voters were historically more likely than Republican voters to use mail-in ballots, meaning vote spikes that benefit Democratic candidates can happen when election officials start to count and report those ballots.
The Election Integrity Partnership, a nonpartisan coalition that reported on topics it found "demonstrably harmful to the democratic process" during the 2020 and 2022 elections, wrote about "ballot drops" in 2022 after Lindell shared graphs he claimed showed the alleged fraud in action.
The group wrote that vote spikes were "commonplace" but that people often misinterpreted graphs showing the spikes. It gave four main reasons for vote spikes:
- Vote counts are reported in batches and varying intervals.
- There can be delays in counting and tabulating in-person votes.
- Some states legally allow absentee and mail-in ballots to be counted prior to polls being closed, and thus those vote counts may be reported en masse.
- Voting "spikes" can also be caused due to clerical errors and are not limited to any particular political party or individual.
This article will discuss these four reasons in turn.
The law and policy institute the Brennan Center for Justice and the legal organization Campaign Legal Center also wrote about the spread of the "ballot drop" theory after the 2020 presidential election. Both organizations pointed to similar legitimate explanations for vote spikes during a count.
Batch reports and count delays
Snopes previously investigated one instance where officials reporting a large batch of counted votes created a "vote spike" that favored a Democratic candidate. On Nov. 18, 2020, we reported that the claim (archived), also shared by Trump, that Biden received a fraudulent "ballot dump" to eventually win Wisconsin was false.
Rather than a fraudulent "ballot dump," local media reported that Biden took the lead in Wisconsin when Milwaukee, the most-populous city in the state, reported its "overwhelmingly Democratic" 170,000 absentee votes around 3:30 a.m. Nov. 4.
Wisconsin is one of a few states in the U.S. where, by law, elections officials cannot begin to process mail-in ballots before Election Day, meaning they must verify and count mail-in ballots after polls open. Because counting mail-in ballots requires more verification than ballots filled out in person, this process can take longer, meaning those votes may be reported later in the count.
PolitiFact reported that a vote spike (archived) that appeared to favor Georgia's Democratic candidate for Senate, Raphael Warnock, in the 2022 general election actually reflected Fulton County, which includes Atlanta, reporting a large batch of votes that skewed Democrat.
Robert Sinners, a spokesperson for Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, reportedly told PolitiFact, "In Georgia, we call a 9 p.m. upload toward one candidate 'the Atlanta metro has reported.'" Sinners' statement suggested that if votes from the Atlanta metro area created a vote spike, that was merely due to the city's large population.
Elections officials in Georgia can process but cannot count any votes before polls close, meaning counts from races in the state can take longer to complete.
PolitiFact reported in 2022 that some — mainly Democrat-voting — cities lagged behind their states in how quickly they finished their counts meaning that in some places, large batches of "blue" (Democratic) votes came in comparably late in the count, which could also cause a legitimate vote spike.
The outlet wrote:
Because large cities are almost uniformly Democratic these days and small-population rural counties are almost always Republican, it's easy to cast blame for slow counting on partisan factors. But the reality is that a lot depends on simple math.
Along the same lines, as examples from Wisconsin and Georgia show, vote spikes can often be attributed to demographics and math rather than conspiracy.
Mail-in ballots
As seen in Snopes' report on the election results in Wisconsin in 2020, large batches of mail-in votes can change an election result late in the count. However, the Election Integrity Partnership wrote that mail-in ballots can also appear to give candidates a head start.
For example, 33 states, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico allow elections officials to scan, meaning count, mail-in ballots before Election Day, though the results cannot be released before polls close. States that may have already counted some mail-in ballots will be able to release some results very quickly after the close of polls.
In states that allow early scanning of mail-in ballots, early election-night results could skew Democratic because these voters are more likely to have used mail-in voting. Though this might look like a vote spike, the difference between the candidates will likely narrow as counts come in from areas with more in-person or Republican voters. In this scenario, no candidate is "finding" or "losing" votes. Rather, the early results reflect how an individual state has decided to count its votes.
Clerical errors
If vote spikes aren't caused by the ballots themselves, they also can be caused by human error.
For example, in the 2020 presidential election, a county clerk in Shiawassee County, Michigan, accidentally added a zero to Biden's vote tally, reporting 153,710 votes for the Democrat instead of 15,371.
The clerk in question, Caroline Wilson, reportedly told Agence France-Presse that officials corrected the mistake shortly after, suggesting that existing systems to catch such incidents were working. Trump went on to win the county after officials corrected the vote tally.
Likewise, in 2022, Rob Farbman, the executive vice president of Edison Research, which provides polling data to media outlets, reportedly told AFP a roughly million-vote spike for incumbent Democratic Sen. Tammy Duckworth of Illinois happened because someone at Edison Research "added a 9 at the beginning of Duckworth's number in Rock Island."
The mistake happened after the race had been called for Duckworth, the AFP reported, and Edison Research fixed the mistake shortly after it occurred.
Neither of these mistakes materially affected the result of the races, and both suggested that elections officials and companies such as Edison have systems in place that work to catch and correct vote-tally errors introduced by humans.
The bottom line
If readers encounter "ballot drop" theories as votes roll in during these midterm elections, they should stop and consider whether any of the above reasons might provide a specific, legitimate explanation for an apparent vote spike.
It is also worth remembering that the results reported on election night are never the final, certified results. In most races, media outlets are able to mathematically eliminate one candidate using the information from the counts provided and "call" the race. These media estimates are not, however, final results.
Rather, elections officials will canvass and audit the counts from election night before certifying the result. This process allows officials another chance to review vote spikes and ensure that they happen for legitimate reasons.

Donald Trump complained Friday about not winning the Nobel peace prize for 2026, a year in which he started a war with Iran.
At what was supposed to be a rally for other Republican candidates in Syracuse, New York, the US president devoted a long portion of his speech airing his grievances with the Nobel committee.
“The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel peace prize, but didn’t. And this is an indelible stain on the country of Norway, and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” Trump said.
“The Nobel peace prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilization,” Trump went on. “We will not forget, Norway, that you didn’t give this prize.”
Trump also recited a list of wars he claims to have settled, some of which were not wars and some that are still not settled, before adding: “I’m about to settle or win two more: Iran and Russia-Ukraine.”
Trump said he would be ending both wars “quickly”.
“I will tell you what,” he added, darkly. “Iran will be very quick one way or the other: that they give us everything or they don’t exist any longer.”
“Additionally, I stopped Iran from having a nuclear weapon and blowing up the entire Middle East and ultimately far beyond the Middle East, including Europe, perhaps the US and I saved more lives than anyone in history,” Trump claimed, despite the fact that US intelligence agencies reported to Congress in 2025 that Iran had actually suspended its pursuit of nuclear weapons in 2003.
“Despite all of this and all of these unbelievable accomplishments, the Nobel prize was given out today to a liberal person who works at the United Nations, who nobody has ever heard of,” Trump said of Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.

A three-day crackdown against black market syndicates diverting rice from public distribution system across Karnataka has resulted in the seizure of 564.99 tonnes of rice whose value is estimated to be ₹1.34 crore.
The multi-agency drive was taken up by the Food and Civil Supplies Department in coordination with the Commercial Taxes, the Agricultural Marketing, the Police, and the Excise departments. As many as six criminal cases have been registered under the Essential Commodities Act, 1981, against nine persons. Twenty transport vehicles worth ₹3.41 crore have also been seized in the operation.
A note from the office of Food and Civil Supplies Minister Rizwan Arshad said that a major highlight of the drive involved exposing an international smuggling racket operating out of Bengaluru Rural district. The officials intercepted a lorry at Attebele, transporting 35,000 kg of rice in 700 bags of Food Corporation of India. It said that the rice valued at ₹11.63 lakh had been packaged under the trade name ‘WoW’ with the tagline “Rice for Africa.”
Investigation revealed that Mandya-based Annapurneshwari Enterprises had purchased rice from local FCI godown and sold it to Madhya Pradesh based Sailar Exports Ltd, to be shipped out of Chennai. The note said that this was in violation of Prevention of Black Marketing and Maintenance of Supplies of Essential Commodities Act, 1981. The company was found to have traded upto 56,450 quintals of rice in the past two months against a legitimate purchase record from FCI for 5,000 quintals.
In Lokur village of Belagavi, officials seized 4.22 lakh kg of PDS rice worth ₹98.67 lakh while three Maharashtra bound lorries carrying 71,800 kg of PDS rice that had been repackaged into colourful branded bags was seized. Another big consignment of rice of 35,391 kg was seized from an abandoned truck in Vijayapura, the note said.

Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray?
- Published
Fighting has erupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray between regional forces and the national army.
Tigray residents, who have been trying to recover from a brutal two-year war that ended in 2022, fear a return to full-scale conflict.
There are reports of panic buying - and now internet and call services have been disrupted.
This means people cannot get access to their money via digital apps in what has become a largely cashless society after ATMs stopped working several months ago.
Why has fighting broken out now?
It follows more than six months of worsening relations between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray.
The African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides, ending the war nearly four years ago - but several issues have remained unresolved that have inflamed tensions.
This year, both sides have been trading blame while troops have mobilised amid pockets of fighting.
This week, major clashes erupted in Tigray and quickly spread into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. The two sides disagree over who started the latest escalation.
The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in Tigray.
Who are the TPLF?
For much of Tigray's modern political history, it has been governed by the TPLF, which first emerged as an armed movement in the 1970s fighting Ethiopia's military government.
It became a major force in the overthrow of the Marxist regime in 1991 and went on to become the most powerful component of the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), the coalition that governed the ethnically diverse country for nearly three decades.
At times this proved contentious as some felt the TPLF held too much sway as Tigrayans only make up around 6% of Ethiopia's population.
When Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018, he replaced the EPRDF with the Prosperity Party, significantly watering down the TPLF's influence.
Relations between Addis Ababa and the TPLF rapidly deteriorated until war erupted in 2020 in what was one of the most deadly conflicts this century.
The AU mediator estimated some 600,000 people died during the war, which totally cut off Tigray from the outside world and drove the region to the precipice of famine.
An uneasy truce was agreed in November 2022.
Why has the peace deal faltered?
There are four key issues - and two concern the fertile area of western Tigray.
The TPLF lost control of this territory in the early days of the war to Amhara, a region which neighbours Tigray to the west and whose fighters had fought on the side of the Ethiopian army.
Many people in Amhara believe the territory of western Tigray should never have been incorporated into Tigray when regional boundaries were redrawn after the military regime was ousted in 1991.
When its fighters seized control during the recent civil war, hundreds of thousands of ethnic Tigrayan people fled and are now living in homeless camps in Tigray and in the capital, Addis Ababa.
The TPLF wants western Tigray back and for those displaced from the territory to return. The government says the future of the territory needs to be decided by a referendum.
For the government, a major matter of contention has been disarmament. It says the TPLF has only handed over old weaponry to the AU and has been hiding its arms.
The two sides have also been at loggerheads over how Tigray should be governed. Under the terms of the deal, an interim administration was appointed by Abiy.
But attempts by the prime minister to influence affairs caused disputes within the TPLF itself and just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, it restored its pre-war administration, disbanding the one set up by Abiy.
This has meant that civil servants are longer being paid and other services have been seizing up, worsening economic conditions.
Who is backing the TPLF?
A major development has seen the TPLF, once politically isolated inside Ethiopia, gain several key allies.
Earlier in September, it joined six other armed movements in forming what is called the Alliance for Survival, which includes those actively fighting the government like Amhara's Fano militia and the Oromo Liberation Army.
Members of the new alliance have different grievances, but they do share one objective: they want to remove Abiy's government from power.
So while the TPLF and Fano forces were on opposite sides during the civil war - and still disagree over the fate of western Tigray - they have temporarily put some of their differences aside.
TPLF officials say they do not want to repeat the situation of 2020, when they felt surrounded and isolated.
Yet analysts caution the alliance may become difficult to maintain because its members ultimately have very different interests.
What is the government's position?
As well as blaming the TPLF for starting the recent fighting, it has criticised the new alliance, portraying it as an attempt to destabilise the country.
It has also accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups inside Ethiopia, something Asmara denies.
During the recent civil war, Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian troops but the two neighbours, which have long had a volatile relationship, have again fallen out.
Their disagreement centres on the Red Sea and its ports.
Ethiopia, the world's most populous landlocked nation, lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Recently Prime Minister Abiy has been pushing for ownership of Eritrea's southern port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - and hinted at taking it by force.
What do we know about the bombing in Tigray?
Reports indicate that federal forces have been using drones and other military operations against Tigrayan forces.
The government's stated justification is that it is responding to attacks and trying to defend federal positions and territory. However, the circumstances surrounding individual strikes are difficult to independently verify.
Residents in one recently targeted town told the BBC the drones had hit two schools, which local officials said had been used by Ethiopian troops as military bases during the war.
This suggests Addis Ababa may believe they are again being used for a military purpose - by Tigrayan forces.
The attacks have come amid reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its ranks.
What is being done to stop the fighting?
The main diplomatic effort is being led by the AU, which has called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a return to direct talks.
It has asked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, the AU's special Horn of Africa envoy, to engage the parties urgently.
The UN has made a similar appeal, warning against a wider and more devastating conflict.
The regional organisation Igad has also called for fighting to stop and dialogue to resume.
The difficulty is that trust between Addis Ababa and Tigray is extremely low, while the formation of the new armed alliance has made the situation more complicated.
Could the fighting spread?
Yes, there is a significant risk of wider conflict inside Ethiopia.
The fighting has already moved to areas over and along Tigray's borders, while the government is simultaneously dealing with armed conflicts in other regions, particularly Amhara and Oromia.
The new alliance potentially connects several of these conflicts politically and militarily.
There is also a fear that Eritrea could be drawn in again - this time against the government.
The two aggressors in Sudan's civil war are also on opposite sides when it comes to allegiances in Tigray, potentially complicating matters.
The AU has specifically urged all neighbouring countries not to take actions that could further escalate the crisis.
