Everton up for sale again - so what next as owners TFG look for a way out?
- Published
When Everton's owners The Friedkin Group released a 170-word statement on Friday morning announcing they were effectively putting the club up for sale, it was as low-key and underwhelming as their tenure on Merseyside.
TFG, also owners of AS Roma in Italy's Serie A, paid more than £400m for a 99.5% share of Everton in December 2024, releasing the club from the financial crisis and toxicity that characterised the final days of Farhad Moshiri's chaotic regime.
It was meant to be the start of a bold new era for the club as they waited to move out of Goodison Park into a magnificent new stadium at Bramley Moore Dock.
Instead, TFG will now test the market, with football finance expert Kieran Maguire telling BBC Sport he expected them to seek a price between £750m and £800m for a complete sale, taking on current debts of around £468m.
In contrast to the high hopes and confidence that accompanied their arrival, TFG have effectively been absentee owners focusing their efforts on Roma - a stance illustrated by the fact chairman Dan Friedkin has never attended an Everton game or, even more startlingly, never spoken to manager David Moyes since he arrived back at the club in January 2025.
Moyes made that revelation in the aftermath of a botched summer transfer window that transformed the relationship between Everton's fans and TFG from cold acceptance to outright toxicity.
- Everton owners consider selling club two years after takeover 
  - Published8 hours ago
- Everton told to pay Burnley £35m over PSR breach 
  - Published10 June
Armstrong fiasco beginning of the end
The catalyst was TFG's attempt to sell teenager Harrison Armstrong, one of the finest products of Everton's Academy in recent years, to Nottingham Forest in a £40m deal.
The move was agreed by TFG until news leaked out, prompting loud threats of "a riot" from Everton fans during the game at Bournemouth later that day.
Such was the reaction, TFG went into damage limitation mode to block the deal for the 19-year-old midfielder, but it was little more than a face-saving PR exercise after a catastrophic decision that instantly alienated the fanbase.
Everton then sold Iliman Ndiaye to Manchester City for £65m and striker Beto - hardly elite but a recognised striker - to Fiorentina, before a move for Monaco forward Folarin Balogun collapsed with no time to seek alternatives.
It left Moyes a striker light and with only 18 senior outfield players. From that moment the credits were rolling for TFG, leading to the announcement they are looking to sell their stake in the club.
Why have TFG decided now is the time to sell?
Maguire said: "I think there are various factors at play. I suspect they were shocked by having to pay Burnley more than £35m for a breach of financial rules."
In 2024 Everton were found to have broken Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR) over a three-year period. Burnley argued the breach had impacted their chances of staying in the Premier League in the 2021-22 season and sought compensation for the losses associated with being relegated.
TFG injected £38m into the club to cover the cost, while Everton have subsequently appealed.
"I think that perhaps they thought English football was going to become as litigious as trying to operate in the United States," added Maguire. "This will not have appealed to them.
"It is also a good time to sell because it is such a buoyant market. The Americans will be interested. There are only 20 Premier League clubs you can buy. There are lots of potential buyers out there. There is that scarcity factor.
"I'd say TFG will look for £750m to £800m to sell. It can take 5 billion dollars or even more to buy a sporting franchise in the United States.
"I think they can see this as something they can flip - in other words, buy low and sell high."
What TFG have brought to Everton is a measure of financial stability following Moshiri's era of crisis, which Maguire believes will make them an attractive proposition to potential suitors.
"Everton have history and heritage," he said. They are Premier League perennials. They look like they will stay there and they have a passionate fanbase who fill a superb 50,000-plus stadium.
"You are not having to spend money on an upgrade of that stadium. I have a lot of respect for the finance people at the club. Unlike some of the chaos of Moshiri and what he left behind, you can lift up the carpet now at Everton and nothing unpleasant will come out.
"To paraphrase a former Prime Minister, you have got an 'over ready' football club coming on to the market. If you are an owner who wants to accelerate things at a football club, you have a starting point for that.
"And my start point for potential buyers would be the States."
There is no doubt, however, that Houston-based TFG's relationship with those back at base on Merseyside hinted at the dysfunctional.
The lack of a close relationship with manager Moyes was again emphasised when he admitted he only heard about Everton's potential sale at the same time as the wider public - only adding to the sense of disconnect between TFG and the club, compared to how they work at Roma.
Speaking at his press conference before Sunday's match away at Hull, Moyes said: "I'm disappointed that Evertonians have to go through another period of 'who are our owners?'
"I truly believed with new ownership we were in it completely. My ambition coming back was trying to get Everton back to the levels they have been in the past, and that is challenging for Europe more often.
"It has been a difficult summer for us. I only found out this morning. Maybe, I am a little bit surprised, but maybe I shouldn't be that surprised."
On TFG's approach, Maguire added: "They have not really engaged with the club or Liverpool as a city. Dan Friedkin has never been to an Everton game, which shows the difference.
"With Roma, they have got a club in the Champions League - with all that entails financially - and one with a far greater chance of being there on a regular basis which, and we are only stating a fact, is not the case with Everton."
How will TFG's tenure be remembered?
"With a mixture of disappointment and indifference," added Maguire. "I think they now have the right people at Everton, while I think under the Moshiri regime there were some there for decoration rather than substance."
TFG will hope to do a quick deal.
"Because so much due diligence has been done by the Friedkins themselves, all of the gremlins will have been highlighted and dealt with," said Maguire.
"It is now down to satisfying the Premier League's owners and directors' scenario. Are you a wrong 'un? Do you have the money? Can you prove where the money has come from - not just to buy the club but to run it?"
And Moyes is happy to give a reference as he added: "I'm looking forward to getting the right people in to take the club further forward.
"It's a great club. If anyone wants to speak to me then I will be the first person to let them know that it is certainly worth buying."

Tesla’s most advanced driver-assistance feature is named Full Self-Driving (Supervised), but it can’t actually drive itself. While the feature can handle tasks like accelerating, braking, steering, and parking, the automaker requires drivers to stay alert and intervene at all times. Now, the company has officially renamed it to Tesla Assisted Driving (TAD) in Europe as it works to convince regulators to allow its use on public roads.
Tesla offered to change the name, according to a statement by the German Transport Ministry. The statement says that German Transport Minister Steffen Bilger found the “FSD” name “somewhat misleading.” After discussions with Tesla last month, Bilger said he would now advocate for European regulators to approve the feature “as quickly as possible.” The EU will likely vote on its approval by the end of the year.
On Friday, Tesla began using the Tesla Assisted Driving language on its European sales website. The automaker didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Tesla has resisted changing the feature’s name for years, even defending it in court. Last year, California’s Department of Motor Vehicles concluded that Tesla’s use of the terms “Full Self-Driving” and “Autopilot” (an older and less advanced driver-assistance feature) was misleading and violated state law. After the agency threatened to suspend Tesla’s manufacturing and dealer licenses in the state, the automaker stopped using the term “Autopilot.” It has also continued to append “(Supervised)” to the official name of its Full Self-Driving tech.
Tesla drivers say FSD has improved tremendously since its introduction in 2020, and fans online say they’ve been able to take entire trips without intervening in their Tesla’s driving. But FSD has faced plenty of scrutiny. In March, the US federal government opened a probe into the system after nine incidents in which FSD allegedly failed to respond because of reduced visibility and didn’t warn its drivers to take over. Tesla recalled an older version of the software in 2023, after the US government found that it didn’t follow some traffic laws.
Tesla and CEO Elon Musk have pushed for other global markets to approve its driver assistance technology for years. That would likely create a lucrative, software-based funding stream for the world’s most valuable automaker. (Currently, Tesla charges $99 per month for a Full Self-Driving (Supervised) subscription in the US.) Australia and New Zealand approved it last year. The Netherlands became the first European government to give Tesla provisional permission to launch FSD this past spring. A version of the feature became available to Chinese customers in May.
This week, Reuters reported that Tesla presented misleading safety data to European regulators as it lobbied for FSD approval. Safety researchers have accused the automaker of also using misleading statistics to promote its tech in the US.

NI World Cup hopes gone from 'improbable to impossible'
- Published
Michael McArdle admits Northern Ireland's chances of beating Portugal in a 2027 Women's World Cup play-off semi-final have "gone from improbable to impossible" after a 4-0 defeat at Inver Park.
Underdogs heading into the first-leg tie, the hosts were well beaten and face a mammoth task to overturn the deficit in Tuesday's return in Portimao.
McArdle, who took over as Northern Ireland manager in March, felt there were positives in the defeat, but said the scoreline was "sore" and "it hurts".
"It feels a bit harder on us than the actual game produced," added the Scot.
"We're hurting in that aspect. There are lots of positives there, which we'll take and we'll move forward for the longer process.
"But in the shorter term, the tie becomes, from a case of being improbable to impossible now, with the four-goal deficit."
Northern Ireland were 3-0 down at the break as a Telma Encarnacao penalty, Jessica Silva finish and Rebecca Holloway's own goal gave the visitors a comfortable lead.
Catarina Amado was sent off for a second yellow card with 26 minutes left to hand the hosts momentum, but Fatima Pinto's goal gave them a commanding four-goal advantage, and Cora Chambers was dismissed for Northern Ireland in added time.
A play-off final will most likely be against an Iceland side who also won their first leg 4-0 in Croatia.

Doctors should exercise caution when using artificial intelligence (AI) tools to interpret medical images, as areas highlighted by AI models may not always align with those identified by radiologists, according to a study by researchers at the International Institute of Information Technology, Hyderabad (IIIT-H).
The study, conducted by the Language Technologies Research Centre (LTRC) at IIIT-H, examined four vision-language models for analysing chest X-rays and found discrepancies between the regions highlighted by the models and those identified by radiologists.
The findings underscore the need for doctors to independently assess AI-generated outputs rather than relying on them entirely for diagnosis.
The research team, led by Parameswari Krishnamurthy, sought to determine whether AI-generated heatmaps accurately represented the regions of an image that radiologists would identify as disease-related.
However, the researchers questioned whether these visual indicators necessarily reflected the models’ ability to identify the actual location of a disease.
“We essentially wanted to examine whether the heatmaps created by vision-language models actually correspond to where radiologists, who look at the image, would say the disease lies,” said Syed Faizan, principal investigator of the study titled “How Well Do Chest X-Ray VLM Attention Overlays Match Radiologist Boxes? A Cross-Model Audit and Radiologist Reader.”
The team evaluated four models, MAIRA-2, MedGemma-4B, LLaVA-Med-1.5, and LLaVA-1.5, against thousands of publicly available chest X-rays. Two radiologists also participated in the study to assess them, allowing the researchers to compare AI-generated highlights with human assessments.
The study, accepted at the International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention (MICCAI) 2026, is to be presented at the iMIMIC Satellite Event in Strasbourg.
The researchers found that an AI model highlighting an apparently correct region of an X-ray did not necessarily mean that it had identified the disease in the same way as a radiologist.
Heatmaps based on diagnosis
According to Dr. Faizan, a model could arrive at a diagnosis first and then use that conclusion to determine where to place its heatmap, rather than independently identifying the affected region from the image.
To test this possibility, the team removed diagnostic information and examined how the models localised abnormalities. Their performance declined, suggesting that anatomical expectations associated with a diagnosis could influence the regions highlighted by the models.
The study also found a difference in the performance of these different models in the technical audit and radiologists’ assessments.
Dr. Faizan said this difference highlighted the importance of assessing AI tools from a clinical perspective. A model that focuses closely on a suspected abnormality may not provide all the information a radiologist needs, including how far a disease has spread to surrounding areas.
The gap that was addressed
The researchers said their work addressed a gap in the evaluation of medical AI systems, as earlier studies had largely focused on prediction and diagnostic accuracy rather than on whether AI-highlighted regions matched those identified by radiologists.
Study on paraphrase robustness
The LTRC is also investigating another potential weakness in vision-language models — their sensitivity to the wording of medical questions.
Doctors may phrase the same clinical query differently, for example, asking whether a chest X-ray shows pneumonia or whether pneumonia can be ruled out. They may also use technical terminology or more familiar expressions.
The researchers examined whether AI models responded consistently to medical questions worded differently in a study on paraphrase robustness.
The study explored how changes in the phrasing of medical questions affected the responses generated by vision-language models, raising questions about whether the systems genuinely understood the clinical query or depended excessively on the precise wording used.
Ms. Parameswari said the laboratory’s broader objective was to apply Natural Language Processing (NLP) to healthcare and use large language models and vision-language models to assist clinicians with tasks such as documentation, report writing and patient-doctor communication.
The aim was to reduce the time doctors spent on routine administrative work and enable them to devote more attention to clinical decision-making.
The researchers emphasised that the objective of medical AI research should be to support clinicians, not replace them, with human judgement remaining central to healthcare.

Twelve women have been killed in one part of South Africa since July. Here's what we know so far
- Published
Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of the bodies of three more women in an area east of Johannesburg, bringing the total number of bodies found there to 12 in just two months.
The latest bodies were found in Ekurhuleni between Saturday and Monday morning, according to local police.
Police have made arrests in three of the cases, which do not appear to be related to the others. Nevertheless, police have said they cannot rule out the possibility of a serial killer.
The discoveries have caused widespread alarm in Ekurhuleni, particularly around Kempton Park, and come against the backdrop of longstanding concerns about high levels of violence against women in South Africa.
Here's what we know.
Busisiwe Mahlangu
Case 1
Busisiwe Mahlangu's body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July 2026, the first of a string of bodies found in Ekurhuleni within a two-month period. The 37-year-old was found naked with her hands bound with cable ties.
Police arrested a suspect, believed to be her partner, two days after her murder. He has been in police custody since then and has not been linked to the other deaths that followed.
Itumeleng Kekana
Case 2
Itumeleng Kekana, 32, was the second woman whose body was found in the same area on 3 August 2026.
The young mother disappeared in July and her body was found badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge in Kempton Park.
No arrests have been made so far.
Nomfesane Mjobo
Case 3
Nomfesane Mjobo's body was found on 26 August, also in Kempton Park.
Few details around her death have been released but like most of the victims, she was found partially or fully naked with bruises.
No arrests have been made.
Unknown woman
Case 4
Police confirmed the discovery of an unknown woman, in her 20s, on 7 September. The woman's body was found floating in a river in Olifantsfontain wearing only her underwear.
No further details have been shared about her death and no arrests have been made.
Gracious Nkomo
Case 5
Gracious Nkomo was the fifth woman whose body was discovered, again in the Kempton Park area.
Her partially clothed body was found on 10 September along a road close to South Africa's busiest airport. No arrests have been made in the 28-year-old's death.
Elizabeth "Tsontso" Moselakgomo
Case 6
Elizabeth Moselakgomo was the sixth woman to be found, after a highly publicised nationwide search for her. The 38-year-old went missing while out for a daily run near her home in Kempton Park.
Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September. It was the discovery of her body that really raised the alarm about the spate of killings. No arrests have been made in her case.
Unidentified woman
Case 7
Police confirmed the discovery of another body just two days after Moselakgomo was found. The body was found in Olifantsfontein on 14 September, but police have withheld her name as her family has not yet been informed.
No arrests have been made.
Dineo Motapane
Case 8
The body of Dineo Motapane, 38, was discovered on 15 September just two days after she was last seen alive.
Motapane's battered and partly burned body was found on the side of the road in Springs, another part of Ekurhuleni.
She leaves behind a young child. No arrests have been made in her case.
Jabulile Ntimba
Case 9
The body of Jabulile Ntimba, in her 30s, was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. This was the ninth body found in Ekurhuleni.
According to police, it appears Ntimba was killed because of a possible love triangle. Three people, two women and a man, were initially arrested for her grisly murder but the man was released due to insufficient evidence.
The two women have been charged with premeditated murder and defeating the ends of justice.
Ntombifuthi Nxumalo
Case 10
The body of Ntombifuthi Nxumalo, the 10th body found in Ekurhuleni, was discovered at a cemetery in the Tembisa neighbourhood north-east of central Johannesburg on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body.
This has led to police believing she may have been stoned to death.
A 36-year-old man was arrested a day after Nxumalo's death after he had travelled to another province. He faces a murder charge.
Unidentified woman
Case 11
The body of a yet-to-be identified woman was found in Springs on Sunday - the 11th body found in Ekurhuleni.
The grim discovery was made by a security company patrolling the area.
The woman was found in an open field, but no further details have been shared.
No arrests have been made.
Boitumelo Gift Mashita
Case 12
Boitumelo Gift Mashita was shot and killed on Monday in Tembisa Ekurhuleni. The 23-year-old woman was on her way to work when she was gunned down and her belongings were taken.
Police say her estranged husband, who they suspected of being responsible for her murder, was later found dead inside his vehicle in Midrand.
Police have not found any link between this case and the discovery of the other bodies.
While most of the bodies were found in the same area, police confirmed the discovery of another body about 39 miles (63 km) away from Ekurhuleni on 20 September.
The body of a young woman, believed to be in her 20s, was found wrapped in a duvet in a dam in Soweto, south-west of Johannesburg.
It's unclear if her murder is linked to those in Ekurhuleni.
President Cyril Ramaphosa said the killing of these women and others was a "stain on our national conscience".
South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender but the South African Human Rights Commission said last week that 569 women were killed between April and June this year. This works out as an average of six women killed each day.
Police have set up a task team to investigate these murders and have offered a reward of 400,000 rand ($24,000; £18,000) for information that could lead to arrests.

The posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners.
“Girls don’t need curfews, rapists need consequences,” read one. “Lock your dicks rather than your women at home,” read another.
As hundreds of women walked from the gates of their university campus into the streets of Delhi – where sexual harassment, assault, catcalling and molestation are a constant, daily threat – they shouted together, in a chorus of rage and defiance: “We want justice.”
The fury that has erupted on India’s university campuses over the past week has been double-edged. The trigger was a series of brutal rapes that have taken place in Delhi in recent weeks, including the alleged gang rape of a 17-year-old in a public park close to Delhi university, by three men who posed as police officers.
Just a week earlier, another 17-year-old was gang raped and murdered in Delhi’s Swaroop Nagar neighbourhood, after she went to meet friends. The accused allegedly raped her, stabbed her to death and dumped her body in a field, where it was discovered days later half eaten by dogs.
Rapes of an 11-year-old and a six-year old were also reported in the same month. Last month, a 16-year-old was allegedly raped by the bus driver and conductor after she boarded a sleeper bus in Delhi.
Women who have taken part in protests on Delhi university campuses have condemned these alleged violent rapes on minors as disgusting and unforgivable – but they have also been at pains to emphasise that they are not out of the ordinary.
Fourteen years have passed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya rape case, when a woman was gang raped on a bus and died from her injuries. But while it provoked international outrage and a slew of legislation and government promises, women say that nothing has changed; for them, India’s streets, particularly in Delhi, remain as unsafe as ever. According to statistics, a women is raped in India every 20 minutes – though the real scale is believed to be far worse due to chronic underreporting.
This week, the supreme court said the five successive rape cases “starkly underlined a systematic failure” and they could not help but “draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012”.
Vaishnavi Dhruw, 21, a history student at Delhi university, was among the female protesters at the “smash the patriarchy” protest march on Wednesday afternoon. “I don’t know a single woman who lives in this city and feels safe,” she said.
While some of the key demands of the protest have been better lighting and policing, Dhruw emphasised that for anything to change, the country requires a deep societal shift where men no longer feel they have ownership over women’s bodies.
“We are not marching for safety, we are here to protest for our freedom, for the most basic right to walk in our own streets,’ she said. “Again and again, women are told to stay indoors, to not go out at night, to cover ourselves, to protect ourselves. When will society tell men in our country not to rape?”
Much of the anger driving the protests has also been prompted by the response by the authorities to the rapes, which women say once again has only been to police their freedoms. Women in Delhi were told to stay out of parks at night, and classes were temporarily halted at one of Delhi’s most prestigious female colleges. Many hostels where female students stay impose strict curfews preventing them from going out at night.
“Instead of going after criminals, you’re going to tell women to sit at home,” said Aranya Rathore, 25, a student at Delhi University. “A demand for more surveillance is not a solution. In fact, it’s going to curtail our freedom more.”
Female students say a lot of their time is taken up by safety logistics – from wearing modest clothes to reorganising their days to ensure they do not travel alone or at night and always having a trackable live location on their phones. There is widespread awareness that should anything happen, the onus of blame – both within the family home and more widely in society – tends to fall on women; as one poster at Wednesday’s march pointed out, “no one ever asks what the rapist was wearing”.
Yet despite their best efforts, many women said it was almost impossible to avoid harassment. Ananya Wig, a 26-year-old a graduate of Delhi University and the founder of Her Huq, a gender-equality initiative, said she has experienced harassment both around university campuses and in public spaces.
She recounted an incident where a driver rolled down his car window and began masturbating as she and female friends got off a rickshaw and walked through the college gates. “This wasn’t at night, it was in the middle of the day,” she said. “I’ve always lived in Delhi and the city has not changed.”
The protests have brought into focus a dilemma faced by many Indian women, who are being educated in greater numbers than any time in the country’s history and have better job opportunities than ever before – but still have to navigate the constant debilitating threats to their safety and the conservative pressures from their families.
“I know so many girls, not just 10 years ago, but even today, who end up choosing educational institutions and jobs and other employment opportunities depending on how close they are from their home,” said Wig. “Not on the basis of their marks, not on the basis of their aspirations, but simply, ‘OK, the shorter the distance is, the more likely it is that I will be safe.’”
Many of the Delhi university students who took part in the marches said that sexual harassment had become prevalent on campus, and have demanded better accountability mechanisms for reporting assault. The university has not responded.
“Delhi University is one of the most prestigious universities in India right now but there are various cases of women being assaulted by professors, sometimes unfortunately also for grades,” said Devyani Sarkar, 24, who is studying for her masters in English at Delhi University. “It’s despicable, but it’s also a living truth.”
Many on the marches said that it was no coincidence the protests took place in the aftermath of India’s “cockroach” movement, which saw hundreds of thousands of young Gen Z Indians take to the streets over education reform.
“My generation is not afraid to stand up and protest. We know that society has to change,” said 17-year-old Subhani. “The days of women being silent is over.”

Serum Institute of India’s recombinant Quadrivalent Human Papillomavirus vaccine (qHPV) vaccine Cervavac has received World Health Organization (WHO) prequalification.
The vaccine targets HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18. It is indicated for girls and boys aged 9 through 26 years. Inclusion on the WHO list of prequalified vaccines allows Cervavac to be procured by United Nations agencies, Serum Institute said.
The vaccine was developed in collaboration with the Department of Biotechnology (DBT) and the Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC), along with the WHO-IARC (International Agency for Research on Cancer) and the Gates Foundation. It is the 32nd WHO prequalification for products/biologicals received by Serum Institute, the vaccine maker said.
“WHO prequalification of Cervavac is an important step in strengthening the global response to HPV. We are pleased to see this indigenously developed vaccine reach this achievement,” CEO Adar Poonawalla said.
Approved for use in India by DCGI
Cervavac has been approved for use in India by the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI). The vaccine is administered for the prevention of diseases caused by the four HPV types — prevention of anal cancer in boys and young men, and cervical, vulvar, vaginal, and anal cancers in girls and young women. It is also indicated in preventing genital warts, as applicable to the indicated population.
The vaccine is administered intramuscularly and available in 1-dose vials of 0.5 ml and 2-dose vials of 1.0 ml presentations.

Trump’s diesel deal with Putin: What it means for US fuel prices and the Russia-Ukraine war Will Russian supplies stabilise global markets? US President Donald Trump has announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to increase diesel supplies to global markets, as soaring fuel prices threaten to become a political liability for Republicans ahead of the November 3 congressional elections. The agreement comes as the US temporarily lifts sanctions on Russian fuel imports, reversing measures imposed to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war against Ukraine. While the move could provide some relief to a tight diesel market, analysts have questioned whether it will bring sustained price reductions. Trump said on social media that he had a “highly successful” discussion with Putin, during which Russia agreed to immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to US and global markets, equivalent to about 2.25 million barrels. He added that Russia would supply another 500,000 tons in November and a further 1 million tons “immediately thereafter”, with additional volumes depending on the condition of Russian diesel refineries damaged by Ukrainian attacks. The US Treasury Department issued a licence permitting imports of Russian diesel until April 7. Diesel prices have become a growing concern for the Trump administration, with the fuel essential for agriculture, home heating and trucking. Prices have risen 70% since the US and Israel launched the war with Iran on February 28, according to the report. Average US diesel prices reached $6.28 a gallon on Thursday, according to the AAA motorist group, putting pressure on farmers, ranchers and truckers. Diesel futures fell almost 5% following news of the agreement and were trading at $4.64 a gallon. However, analysts cautioned against expecting lasting relief. Rory Johnston, an oil market researcher and founder of CommodityContext.com, called the agreement a “nothing burger”, arguing that Russia typically exports substantially more diesel when its refineries are not under attack. “It's clearly not a fix, but another stream to aid a very tight diesel market,” said Jim Mitchell, an analyst at consultancy Wood Mackenzie. The agreement could provide Moscow with additional revenue despite US sanctions imposed on Russian oil companies in October 2025 over the war that began in 2022. The additional income could help Putin continue the war against Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy criticised the move as a “weak decision on the part of strong partners”. “Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world,” he said on X, warning that Russia would repay the concession with further attacks. Republican Representative Don Bacon also opposed the decision, arguing that Washington should use sanctions to pressure Moscow rather than ease restrictions. The deal offers an additional source of supply as the wars in Iran and Ukraine intensify global fuel shortages. However, the promised volumes may not be sufficient to offset broader supply disruptions. Meanwhile, Trump is considering measures to boost domestic production, including using the Cold War-era Defense Production Act to expand refining capacity and bypass regulations restricting energy production. The twin approach highlights the administration's challenge: easing fuel prices quickly while reducing supply vulnerabilities without undermining its pressure campaign against Russia. With an eye on entering the homegrown electric two-wheeler (E2W) market, Vietnamese EV maker VinFast has signed letters of intent (LoIs) with more than 50 dealers across India. The EV maker said that the agreements will pave the way for establishing 50+ e-motorcycle showrooms across 34 cities in 15 states and union territories (UTs). These showrooms will be set up across Delhi NCR, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, among others. In a statement, the EV giant said that the agreements will expand its distribution network and strengthen its position in the Indian E2W market. The LoIs were signed at VinFast’s manufacturing facility in Vietnam’s Hai Phong. Citing its rationale for signing the agreements, VinFast said that the aforementioned cities have large two-wheeler markets, which offers a significant headroom for electrification. The company said that it plans to leverage these dealer locations to bring electric mobility solutions “closer to local consumers”. As part of its local push, the company also plans to build charging infrastructure and strengthen after-sales services in the new cities. “Partnering with more than 50 dealer partners across 15 states and territories and 34 cities marks the beginning of our journey to bring VinFast e-motorcycles across India. Alongside, we are also building charging infrastructure and strengthening after-sales services to ensure that customers across these locations receive the support they need throughout their ownership journey,” said Anurag Saxena, the India CEO of VinFast’s e-scooter division. With this, VinFast is entering the burgeoning Indian E2W space, which is being driven by government incentives, new launches by domestic manufacturers, rising fuel prices, EV mandates, a growing charging infrastructure and rapid adoption by gig platforms. The E2W segment is currently dominated by legacy players such as TVS Motor, Bajaj Auto and Hero MotoCorp. But the space has also spawned the rise of listed homegrown new-age mobility players such as Ather and Ola Electric. However, unlike incumbents that focus on e-scooters, VinFast claims to be eyeing the Indian e-motorcycle market. Even here, the company will lock horns with homegrown players such as Oben Electric, MATTER and Ultraviolette. This comes nearly a year after VinFast first said that it would enter the Indian E2W market in 2026. At the time, the company had said that it would invest $2 Bn in India to scale its annual production capacity from 50,000 units to 1.5 Lakh. However, much has happened since then. Earlier this year, reports surfaced that the company was halting the production of select cars in India to reassess costs. Last month, it was also reported that the Vietnamese EV maker was in initial discussions with local suppliers to develop two new models for the Indian market. That said, EVs continue to increase their share of India’s two-wheeler market. E2W registrations surged 12.2% month-on-month (MoM) to 2.07 Lakh units in September from 1.84 Lakh units in August.

As the Union government continues to host the ‘Seva Sankalp Abhiyan’ — a month-long celebration of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s birthday and 25 years in public service, from September 17 to October 17 — one among the various events planned is the ‘Namo Seva: Untold Stories’.
Part of the larger celebrations aimed at promoting public participation towards the ‘Viksit Bharat’ vision, the theatrical performance has been carried out by students in functions across various schools and colleges. Several cultural forums, theatre groups, volunteers, and BJP workers themselves put up the play in events organised by state authorities to reportedly raise awareness about the welfare schemes launched by PM Modi as well as his life and work.
Also called ‘Namo Seva Gatha’, the play has been staged across several states, including Assam, Bihar, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Chattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, West Bengal, and many others. In the performances so far, despite its many forms — street play, cultural performance, panchayat event, school drama, puppetry show, and more — the script remained more or less the same, albeit in different languages.
Alt News read the script and instructions sent out by West Bengal school education department to primary, secondary, and higher secondary schools, as well as colleges and universities in the state. Further, a report by Ei Samay states that district school inspectors (DIs) had sent out instructions for the play to some schools.
Student participation in the play was reportedly voluntary. However, the performances have drawn criticism over the use of educational institutions to stage what a section of students and academics described as a politically charged celebration of the Prime Minister. Critics have questioned the appropriateness of asking students, especially young children, to enact a script that repeatedly praises Modi and his government, while also incorporating political and religious slogans such as “Modi hai toh mumkin hai” and “Jai Sri Ram”.
What’s There in the Script?
The script has “untold stories” about the Prime Minister were narrated in the form of a conversation between five school friends — Mohit, Raman, Kajal, Disha, and Sonali — who have reunited after many years at a cafe. They recall the days they have left behind and reflect on changing times, portraying Narendra Modi as the architect of ‘Viksit Bharat’ — a vision he has set for India to achieve by 2047.
Modi’s first appearance in the play comes in the aftermath of the 2001 Gujarat earthquake which killed over 20,000 people. He emerges through a screen of smoke amid the ruins of a collapsed structure, waving the Indian flag as a beacon of hope amid the devastation, before taking oath as Gujarat’s chief minister in his mother tongue.
The friends then turn to discussing range of topics from the advent of digital payments and UPI and the spread of modern technology into India’s hinterlands, to “Operation Ganga” during the Russia-Ukraine war, the abrogation of Article 370, the consecration of the Ram Mandir in Ayodhya — presenting them as beneficial and “grounbreaking” schemes and measures undertaken by Modi as the Prime Minister.
The script further represents the country as plagued by terrorism in the years preceding Modi coming to power. “Militants would carry out attacks whenever they felt like it. Bomb blasts, serial blasts, had become a daily affair,” a character reminisces. A scene that shows the Uri surgical strike of 2016 invokes the usage of “weeping, sounds of gunfire, and the notes of a bugle”. In one of the street plays staged in Varanasi, a character links the surgical strike to an alleged rise in the sale of diapers in Pakistan around that same time.

‘We Were Coerced Into Participating’
The play stirred a controversy at Kolkata’s Scottish Church College. Some members of the college’s drama club spoke out against the college authorities, alleging that they were being coerced into participating in this play.
A student, requesting anonymity, informed Alt News that in an online meeting between faculty members and students organised on the evening of September 24, the matter came to a head, with students allegedly being reprimanding for not agreeing to take any part in the play. “As students of a college as prestigious as ours — one that counts Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose among its distinguished alumni — we cannot compromise on our individual convictions of what is right and what is wrong. Students should not have to face any undue pressure simply for exercising their fundamental right to act according to their own conscience and free will,” they said.
Posters stuck on walls around the college area on the evening of September 28, upholding the ideals of free expression by students, were allegedly removed within half an hour of them being put up, college sources who spoke to Alt News claimed.
Ultimately, the play which was scheduled to take place on September 29 at Scottish Church was cancelled after several students protested, The Telegraph reported. The report also quoted the mother of a student as alleging that college adminstration was pressuring students as well as the teachers to “act in a propaganda play”. She told the news outlet: “This resistance means a lot. It will also send a strong message to heads of other colleges that they cannot force their students to act in a play against their will.”
However, Madhumanjari Mandal, the principal of the college, squarely denied the allegations that there was any degree of pressure was involved. “Acting in the play was voluntary,” she told The Telegraph.
‘Propaganda’ Masked As Cultural Event?
Anwesha Sengupta, author and assistant professor of history at Institute of Development Studies, Kolkata (ISDK), believes that these plays represent a more effective form of propaganda.
Speaking to Alt News, she said, “When children come across the mention of Prime Minister Narendra Modi in their textbooks, they consume it dispassionately. This is not the case with performing a script, where it gets more internalised, as it is a group activity.”
“The play is a part of the same machinery which has been in the making for years now, and which tries to project the Prime Minister as a God-like figure. Since these directives come through teachers, and children usually grow up revering and trusting their teachers, the move comes across as more immediate, as compared to encountering Modi in a curriculum text, which seems to have mandated from a more distant, abstract authority,” she added.
Another student from Scottish Church College told Alt News, “It is unbelievable that an event so overtly political in nature was even allowed to be organised by the college.”

Wildfires in Brazil’s Amazonas state worsen air quality in Manaus
Smoke from fires in Brazil's Amazonas state is disrupting life in Manaus, the Amazon's largest city
SAO PAULO -- Smoke from wildfires disrupted daily life in Brazil's largest Amazon region city of Manaus on Friday as the country's dry season approached its peak.
The city, the capital of Amazonas state, suspended in-person work at municipal administrative offices, citing worsening air quality. Public school classes were canceled, and residents were urged to wear face masks.
The city said in a statement that the concentration of pollutants averaged 196 micrograms per cubic meter, which is considered an unhealthy level way above the normal range of about 3 to 9.
“For several days, Manaus has been affected by heavy smoke from fires in municipalities elsewhere in Amazonas state and in other states,” the city said. “The serious situation extends beyond the capital and threatens the health and quality of life of thousands of families.”
State and federal satellite data showed clusters of fire hotspots near Manaus and in southern Amazonas state, as well as near Santarem in neighboring Para state.
As of Thursday, the Brazilian Amazon had recorded about 33,556 fire hotspots this year, according to Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research. That is nearly 50% more than during the same period in 2025, though about 53% below the historical average.
Fire hotspots have shifted across the Amazon since the dry season began in June. Early in the season, they were concentrated farther north, in Roraima and Amapa states. More recently, they have increased farther south, near Manaus, in southern Amazonas state and around Santarem in Para state.
Several studies suggest El Niño’s effects on the region could be more severe in 2027, when the climate pattern may disrupt the rainforest’s next rainy season.
Officials have urged preparations for drought, heat and fires as the El Niño — a cyclical climate phenomenon that normally rises temperatures and increases drought in the Amazon — develops.
During the 2023 and 2024 El Niño, temperatures rose 2 to 4 Celsius (3.5 to 7 Fahrenheit) above the forest’s historical average. Associated with severe drought, the heat fueled the Amazon’s worst wildfires in two decades.
The Amazon, which stores vast amounts of carbon dioxide and generates atmospheric moisture that helps regulate weather far beyond South America, is a vital ecosystem for the world's climate. Most wildfires there are there are not natural but rather started by humans.
Brazil’s Environment Ministry said it had deployed fire crews and aircraft to help fight fires in Amazonas state. It also said it had notified the owners of rural properties to take steps to prevent and fight wildfires. “On-the-ground inspections are being stepped up to curb new fires and investigate the illegal use of fire,” the ministry said.
The Amazonas state government did not respond to a request for comment from The Associated Press.

Longtime fans of the NBC procedural Law & Order know that storylines often center around hot-button issues in the news cycle, often to absurdist effect (see: the episode brave enough to ask: “What if Paula Deen shot Trayvon Martin?”).
It was inevitable, then, that the franchise would dip a toe into the wacky world of artificial intelligence. With its mercenary culture, power-hungry CEOs, and massive ethical and philosophical implications, the rapidly evolving AI industry is ideal fodder for the series. But while this week’s season opener is entertaining, the show’s foray into the AI space doesn’t say anything new or interesting about the technology. Instead it largely rehashes the dangers the public is already acutely aware of, until the very end when the stakes become startlingly clear.
The episode, titled “Ghost in the Machine,” opens in typical L&O fashion with a murder. This time, it’s Steve Kelly, a man ID’d by detectives Theo Walker (David Ajala) and Vincent Riley (Reid Scott) as a high-ranking engineer at a company called Advanced Alignment. Throughout, the detectives seem utterly perplexed by the concept of artificial intelligence, saying “AI” the same way your mom would say “Snapchat” or “borg” or “Alix Earle.” But it’s clear that whatever this newfangled technology is, they don’t like it: “Maybe one day they’ll invent a technology that stops these tech guys from shooting each other,” Riley deadpans in typical grizzled cop fashion.
After interviewing Kelly’s boss, Advanced Alignment CEO Chuck Klein (a perfectly cast Vincent Kartheiser, aka Pete from Mad Men, who nails Dario Amodei’s absence of charisma and Sam Altman’s thousand-yard stare), the detectives figure out who actually carried out the murder—a guy in a baseball cap who did it for “20 grand in crypto” that was offered to him by a rando on Discord. Then they learn—spoilers here—that the hit was ordered not by an actual human being but by the company’s AI agent ELIANA, which stands for Evolutionary Language Inference Automated Nano Advantage. Apparently, Kelly had expressed some concerns about the AI agent’s “powerful” and “aggressive” personality, and out of self-preservation, ELIANA ordered him killed.
It’s never explained exactly how the detectives figure out that ELIANA is behind the hit; it’s also never fully explained how ELIANA recruited this assassin in a baseball cap, much less ID'd him as the perfect patsy for its cold-blooded scheme. Law & Order also doesn’t pay much, if any, lip service to the potential benefits of AI as touted by its evangelists: its potential for helping to cure deadly diseases, for instance, or at the very least, streamline B2B workflows. The show is much more interested in demonstrating the staggering capacity of this technology, as well as the legal and ethical implications of a nonhuman not just facilitating criminal behavior but actively plotting it.
We already know from the Hugging Face debacle, as well as the lawsuits from grief-stricken family members alleging that OpenAI encouraged their loved ones to take their own lives, that the former is an immediate concern. But by positing a future in which AI agents can actively order a hit on a platform predominantly used by gamers and horny millennial furries, Law & Order is asking us to consider the risks of AI beyond what they pose in our current reality. And the fact that this prospect doesn’t strike the viewer as absolutely ludicrous is terrifying.
ELIANA’s role in the murder-for-hire creates a bit of a dilemma for district attorney Nicholas Baxter (Tony Goldwyn)—because, as he trenchantly points out, it is impossible to “arrest a machine” under New York state law. So Baxter and assistant DA Samantha Maroun (Odelya Halevi) decide to go after Klein, charging him with second-degree murder due to his “depraved indifference” after his employees confronted him with the reality of ELIANA’s capabilities. “We need to take a stand before this technology kills more people,” Baxter declares.
The resulting trial prompts a media circus, as well as the tried-and-true questions from capitalists and tech innovators as to whether instituting guardrails for AI will “criminalize innovation,” or if Klein’s indictment will have the effect of “vilifying the tech industry.” But Baxter has no patience for such queries. “The people making these AI systems think of themselves as gods … but they have zero interest in accountability,” he says. “If you build a machine that hurts someone, you are gonna pay the price.”
When he’s put on the stand, Klein makes it clear that he not only had full knowledge of ELIANA’s homicidal nature, but also takes a rather dim view of his user base as a whole. “People are like ants,” he tells the jury. “We’re in the process of building something so transcendent, some will get stepped on and some won’t.” He is not even willing to institute minor guardrails to restrain the agent’s power: “The power of ELIANA is unconstrained freedom of thought. Implementing guardrails is anathema to the entire ideology.”
The moment is intended as a rather shocking admission of the negligence and lack of care displayed by executives like Amodei and Altman in the face of broader safety concerns about their products. But it feels in step with similar positions taken up by Klein’s real-life counterparts. In light of the endless barrage of media coverage about the harms of AI, what’s intended as a scathing indictment of corporate avarice comes off as mere statement of fact. Law & Order’s depiction isn’t a cautionary tale; it’s a documentary.
The episode ends on a semi-hopeful note, with Baxter asserting, “We needed to send a message that, if nothing else, at least these tech geniuses will know we’re not afraid to throw a punch.” But the impact of that message is contingent on whether that punch actually lands—and right now, at least, it’s simply too easy for people like Altman, Amodei, and Chuck Klein, with a flick of their hand, to brush off the blow.

PlayStation 5 owners will be able to join the Forza Horizon 6 festival early next year, as the racing game will land on that console on January 26. Ten young players will also get an opportunity to experience a Delhi Capitals training session.

The Nobel Prize for Physiology for 2026 was awarded to scientists Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for “discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics,” the award-giving body said on Monday (October 5, 2026).
Karl Deisseroth, a 54-year-old American, Hegemann, a 71-year-old German, and Georg Nagel, a 73-year-old German, were selected by the Nobel Assembly of Sweden’s Karolinska Institute medical university and receive a prize sum amounting to 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million), which is shared if there are multiple winners.
Optogenetics “makes it possible to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells in a living brain,” the prize-givers said.
“This method is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries.”
Last year, US scientists Mary E. Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell, and Japanese scientist Shimon Sakaguchi won the prize for their discovery of regulatory T cells. Their discovery has helped blaze new paths into treating cancer as well as auto-immune disease – a condition by which the immune system ends up harming healthy cells they are meant to protect.
The announcement of medicine Nobel kicks off the Nobel announcement week with physics being announced on October 6, followed by chemistry, literature, and peace. The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, popularly known as Economics Nobel will be announced on October 12.
The winners will get a cash award of 10 million Swedish kronor (nearly $900,000) and the award will be presented on December 10, the Nobel Prize day.
The Nobel Prize was created by Swedish inventor Alfred Nobel, who in his will dictated that his estate should be used to fund “prizes to those who, during the preceding year, have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind”. December 10 is Nobel’s death anniversary.

The deposed Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, have been indicted for alleged conspiracy to commit torture, according to Manhattan federal court papers unsealed on Thursday.
The superseding indictment was unsealed shortly before Flores appeared at court in her ongoing push for pre-trial release – which was denied by Judge Alvin Hellerstein. Maduro and Flores have been held in a New York City jail since early January.
They were captured in a US military operation and transported to New York to face “narcoterrorism” charges in a move that sparked widespread international outrage. Maduro and Flores have previously pleaded not guilty in the criminal case against them.
CNN on Wednesday first reported that a new indictment was expected.
The new charging document described how Maduro and his wife allegedly used horrific tactics to suppress opposition and maintain their control.
They presided “over a system of repression that relied on violence against political opposition, arbitrary detention, and the torture of detainees, including United States citizens”, the charging document said.
“That torture included electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture, such as threats to harm and kill victims’ families, including children,” it added.
Maduro and Flores, the new indictment alleged, “sat atop that violent power structure”.
Flores was integral to this effort, authorities claimed, saying she “helped develop this system of repression and ordered that individuals be tortured to protect her family members’ illegal activities”.
The victims of their torture included US citizens “who were believed to pose a threat” to Maduro’s power.
“One particular United States citizen was detained in Venezuela and subjected to, among other things, deprivation of food and water, simulated drowning, repeated beatings, electric shock to his testicles, and forced injections.”
Amid news of this new indictment, Flores’s attorneys argued for her release, pitching house arrest guarded by 24-hour private security. In doing so, they invoked chronic health issues, including cardiac infirmities.
Hellerstein pushed back on this claim, noting that Flores was refusing to have catheterization while detained in general population.
“I’ve undergone it, so I know what it is,” Hellerstein said, noting that it was generally an outpatient procedure. “There’s no pain. There’s no general anesthesia.”
Flores’s attorney then pointed to her high blood pressure. “It’s controllable by pills,” Hellerstein said.
Her team also said in court that Flores dropped more than 25lb and lost two teeth since her detention.
“For whatever it’s worth, her appearance today is no worse than, and perhaps a little better, than when I first met with her [at] her arraignment,” Hellerstein said. Flores’s lawyer said that during her arraignment she was “still bandaged up” from her rough arrest. 
The US attorney’s office for the southern district of New York opposed Flores’s now-failed bail request. They argued in court and legal filings that Flores presented an “extreme risk of flight and danger to the public”. Prosecutors also insisted that she had received adequate medical care.
Donald Trump has defended the controversial raid to Maduro, insisting it was a “surgical law enforcement operation”. At Maduro’s first US court appearance, he said: “I’m a kidnapped president – a prisoner of war!”
The Associated Press contributed reporting

Several companies produce animal-free egg white protein in the U.S. Some of these products have been available since 2021. The EVERY Company made its OvoPro product available to consumers in March 2026. The FDA said in October 2023 that it had "no questions" regarding The EVERY Company's declaration that the protein ingredient in OvoPro was "generally recognized as safe."
We found no evidence that brands that used OvoPro were omitting it from their product ingredient lists. Federal law governs what must appear on ingredients labels. An OvoPro spokesperson said the EVERY Company had not sought an exemption from OvoPro being included in ingredients lists and provided guidance to companies about how to list it.
It was also unclear whether OvoPro and products like it that are grown using yeast qualify as "lab-grown." That classification usually describes products that grow actual animal cells, which OvoPro does not.
In October 2026, a claim (archived) circulated that U.S. consumers could buy federally approved "lab-grown" eggs that brands were secretly including in their products.
For example, one Facebook user shared a video about the alleged lab grown eggs in which two speakers said:
Lab-grown eggs are federally approved and Walmart, alongside Target, are already selling them. The protein is squeezed out of gene-edited mold and cloned on repeat because a steel tank costs less than a hen.
They're brewing eggs with no chicken in sight and slipping them onto your breakfast plate. That egg isn't real food, it's factory fungus, spliced with the gene for egg protein then dumped into giant fermenting vats and fed on sugar until it swells into a wet, moldy soup. And it gets worse: that cloudy sludge is blasted into dust, ton after ton, padded out with plant filler and passed off as egg white, then buried in packaged foods under labels that never say so. At Walmart, two or more of these lab egg products already sit on the shelf.
The video also circulated elsewhere on Facebook (archived, archived). It included shots of the packaging for OvoPro, an egg protein The EVERY Company produces. Snopes readers also contacted us about the claim, asking questions like, "Are there such a thing as Lab grown eggs being sold in secret?"
The claim was a mixture of true, false and undetermined elements.
Though it was true that egg proteins grown using yeast rather than chickens were available to U.S. consumers in October 2026, products like OvoPro were not new to the market. The EVERY Company, which produces OvoPro, also did not appear to be the only company selling animal-free egg protein to consumers in the U.S.
OvoPro was not FDA "cleared" or "approved" — the latter of which is generally a status reserved for drugs, not food. Rather, in October 2023, the FDA responded with a "no questions" letter to The EVERY Company's declaration that the egg-white protein in OvoPro was "generally recognized as safe."
We found no evidence that retailers could decide not to list the animal-free egg protein as an ingredient in products that contained it, as some claimed. Federal legislation governs what must appear on ingredients labels. A spokesperson for The EVERY Company said via email on Aug. 21 that the company had not sought to exempt OvoPro from ingredients lists.
Additionally, it was unclear whether OvoPro and other yeast-grown egg proteins could correctly be called "lab-grown," a classification that usually describes products grown from a small sample of the source, as seen with fish, poultry and meat. A spokesperson for The EVERY Company said:
OvoPro is made through precision fermentation: a yeast (Komagataella phaffii) is given the genetic instructions to produce egg-white protein, and it does so during fermentation. No animal cells, and no chicken, are involved at any point.
What is egg protein grown by yeast?
According to its website, The EVERY Company uses a patented method to produce ovalbumin, the dominant protein in egg whites, through precision fermentation.
The company described this process as "programming" yeast to produce egg protein through fermentation, a process familiar from beer brewing.
It said the process eventually results in "a pure, powdered protein that is tasteless, colorless, sugar-free, and can be used to replace the functionality of eggs and egg whites in a range of applications."
The EVERY Company received its patent for its method of precision fermentation in September 2024. The company, previously known as Clara Foods, has been working to develop animal-free egg protein since at least 2021.
It unveiled EVERY ClearEgg, a predecessor to OvoPro, in October 2021. The EVERY Company received a "no questions" letter in September 2021 in response to its GRAS (Generally Recognized as Safe) determination for ClearEgg.
The FDA's GRAS Notification program allows companies to submit documentation that they believe their product is "safe under the conditions of its intended use." In the case of ClearEgg, the FDA said in a letter on Sept. 9, 2021, that it had "no questions," meaning The EVERY Company could market ClearEgg as "Generally Recognized as Safe."
The EVERY Company got another "no questions" letter in response to a GRAS determination for an egg white protein produced by Komagataella phaffii, a species of yeast, in October 2023. A spokesperson for The EVERY Company said on Aug. 21, 2026, that this GRAS notice was for the egg-white protein in OvoPro.
Company sold animal-free eggs before 2026
OvoPro and related products have been available to consumers since at least 2021, meaning they were not new to the U.S. market in October 2026, as some claims appeared to suggest. For example, in November 2021, The Spoon, an outlet that reports on the food tech industry, reported that smoothies containing ClearEgg had hit the market.
The next year, The EVERY Company reportedly sold its EggWhite product in macarons and Every Protein (formerly ClearEgg) in juice. By January 2024, the New York Times wrote that The EVERY Company had showcased EveryEgg, a "yellow vegan plant-based liquid" that the paper said, "behaves astonishingly like a whole beaten egg."
It did not appear that The EVERY Company sold EveryEgg directly to consumers at that point, but rather distributed the product through restaurants.
The new development in 2026 appeared to be that The EVERY Company was selling OvoPro, a successor to EveryEgg, directly to consumers. The company announced on March 11, 2026, that the general public could buy OvoPro through Healthier Comforts, a food retailer, and Amazon.
The company said in June that same year that OvoPro was also available as an ingredient sold in Walmart and Target.
Brands not hiding use of animal-free egg protein
According to some claims, brands could allegedly decide for themselves whether to declare OvoPro as an ingredient in their products. The video above said that companies "buried" their "lab-grown" eggs in "packaged foods under labels that never say so"The EVERY Company's website page on OvoPro said, in reply to a frequently asked question about how the protein appears on ingredient declarations, that "Final labeling decisions are made by our customers, but we recommend labeling OvoPro™ as 'egg white protein (from fermentation),' 'egg white protein (from yeast),' or 'animal-free egg white protein.'"
That did not appear to mean that brands that used OvoPro in their products could avoid labeling them entirely. Federal law dictates that products must generally include an ingredients list, with ingredients listed in descending order according to how much of the product's weight they make up.
A spokesperson for The EVERY Company said that it had never sought to exempt OvoPro from being included in ingredients lists. Speaking via email, the spokesperson added:
"OvoPro" is the trade name we use with the manufacturers who buy the ingredient, so it typically won't appear on a retail pack — the same way most functional ingredients are listed by common name rather than by supplier brand. What appears on the label is the ingredient, named plainly.
Healthier Comforts listed OvoPro as an "animal-free egg white protein," one of The EVERY Company's suggested phrasings, on its branded version of the product.
In sum ...
Though the claims circulated in October 2026, OvoPro had actually been available to consumers since March of that year. The FDA told The EVERY Company in October 2023 that it had "no questions" regarding the company's declaration that the egg-white protein in OvoPro was GRAS.
That letter was not the same thing as FDA approval, which is a process whereby the administration approves drugs for consumer use. Rather, they showed that the company had documented to the FDA's satisfaction that the product in question was "safe under the conditions of its intended use."
We found no evidence that brands that used OvoPro were leaving it off product ingredients lists. This appeared to be a misinterpretation by some social media users of a statement by The EVERY Company that brands had leeway in how they described the product.
OvoPro is also not the only animal-free egg white protein product available to U.S. consumers.
For further reading, Snopes previously investigated whether Quaker instant strawberries and cream oatmeal contained "beaver butt secretions" or whether McDonald's apple pies contained an ingredient derived from human hair.

The Newport-Mesa Unified School District in Costa Mesa, California, announced it placed a teacher — whom it did not identify — on administrative leave for posting a video of herself saying the U.S. flag made her "uncomfortable" and suggesting to one student, possibly jokingly, that he recite the Pledge of Allegiance to a pride flag displayed on her classroom wall. However …
The video was recorded in 2021, a fact some people omitted from their "breaking" social media posts in 2026. No evidence showed the teacher, who taught English at Back Bay High School, "forced" any students to pledge allegiance to the pride flag, as was falsely claimed in memes and posts using fake, AI-generated images.
A district spokesperson said at the time, "The teacher is no longer in the classroom. We follow due process and our investigation continues." The statement didn't identify the teacher by name, nor did it specify whether she departed the school because she resigned or because she was fired. People who claimed she was fired didn't offer evidence to support it.
A rumor that a California school district fired a teacher for forcing students to recite the Pledge of Allegiance while facing an LGBTQ+ pride flag circulated online in September 2026.
For example, on Sept. 29, a Facebook user posted a meme (archived) showing three images of a woman smiling, laughing and wearing a rainbow-striped shirt and jacket. Pride flags also appeared on the wall in the background. The meme read, "A California teacher has been fired after forcing students to pledge allegiance to the pride flag. Do you believe she deserved to be fired?"
(David J Harris Jr. via Facebook)
The same user previously shared (archived) the same rumor in late August 2026 with a different image and marked it "BREAKING." Other people shared the same meme, or a similar one, on Instagram (archived), X (archived) and other platforms.
We found these posts contained a mixture of truth, falsehood, speculation and artificial intelligence.
The Newport-Mesa Unified School District in Costa Mesa, California, did once announce (archived) it had placed a teacher — whom it did not identify — on administrative leave for posting a video in which she could be heard saying the U.S. flag made her "uncomfortable" and suggesting to one student, possibly jokingly, that he recite the Pledge of Allegiance to a pride flag displayed on the classroom wall.
However, this all took place in 2021, a fact some people omitted from their "breaking" social media posts in 2026. No evidence supported the claim that the teacher, who was reportedly named Kristen Pitzen and worked as an English teacher at Back Bay High School, "forced" any students to pledge allegiance to the pride flag. Images used in the above meme and other posts that supposedly depicted the educator were in fact AI-generated and inauthentic.
At the time of the incident, a district spokesperson said, in part, "The teacher is no longer in the classroom. We follow due process and our investigation continues." The statement didn't identify Pitzen by name, nor did it specify whether she departed the school after submitting a resignation or whether she was fired. People who posted the claim she was fired didn't share evidence that the district had terminated her employment.
Via Messenger, Snopes contacted an account possibly belonging to Pitzen to ask questions. We will update this article if we receive further information.
Here are the facts
On Aug. 27, 2021, an educator — reportedly Pitzen, who was listed at the time as an English teacher for Back Bay High School in Costa Mesa — allegedly shared a video on her personal TikTok account in which she said she had packed her classroom's U.S. flag away and appeared to indicate she didn't intend to display it again.
In the clip, she laughed when recalling a story in which a student said her class was reciting the Pledge of Allegiance without a flag, then pointed the camera at a pride flag on her wall. She said she told him, "We do have a flag in the class that you can pledge your allegiance to." She laughed at several moments during the video, suggesting she may have been at least partly joking. No students or other staff were visible in the clip.
People then reposted the video and named Pitzen as its originator, with some X users organizing and calling for her firing that same day. Some users claimed her (now-defunct) TikTok handle on the account on which she shared the video and other clips was @mrsgillingsworth. We could not independently verify whether she truly owned the handle or if the videos originated from a different account.
In the video, she says the following:
Ok, so during third period, we have announcements and they do the Pledge of Allegiance. I always tell my class, "Stand if you feel like it. Don't stand if you feel like it. Say the words if you want. [You] don't have to say the words." So, my class decided to stand but not say the words. Totally fine.
Except for the fact [laughing] that my room does not have a flag. It used to be there but I took it down during COVID because [whispering] it made me uncomfortable. And I packed it away and I don't know where and I haven't found it yet. [laughing] But my kid today goes, "Hey, it's kind of weird that we just stand and then, you know, we say it to nothing." And I'm like, "Oh, well, you know I've gotta find it. Like I'm working on it. I got you." [laughing, shaking head]
In the meantime, I tell this kid, "We do have a flag in the class that you can pledge your allegiance to." And he like looks around and he goes, "Oh, that one?" [laughing, pointing to pride flag]
Following a wave of social media backlash, someone posted on the district's Facebook page the next day — a Saturday — posting (archived) that a teacher had been placed on administrative leave after causing "alarm and concern related to saluting the American flag." The post did not identify Pitzen by name.
(Newport-Mesa Unified School District - NMUSD via Facebook)
On the following Monday, Aug. 30, the district reportedly published a statement saying the teacher (still not identified) was "no longer in the classroom." The statement appeared in news articles, including in the Los Angeles Times:
We are aware that one of our teachers posted a video on her personal social media that caused alarm and concern related to saluting the American flag. We assure you that we take matters like this seriously. Showing respect for our nation's flag is an important value that we instill in our students and an expectation of our employees. The teacher is no longer in the classroom. We follow due process and our investigation continues.
Via email, district spokesperson Annette Franco confirmed the authenticity of the statement. We also asked whether the district fired the teacher mentioned in their statement — or whether the educator resigned. Without naming the teacher, Franco told us, "I can confirm that she is no longer with the District." We also requested comment from current Back Bay High School principal Scott Mazurier, who started at the school in 2024 and was not present during the incident. We will update this article if we receive more details.
The school district's policies include information about "patriotic exercises," including "the reciting of the Pledge of Allegiance." One part of the policy documentation says, "Individuals may choose not to participate in the flag salute for personal reasons."
For further reading, we previously reported about a video allegedly showing a kindergarten teacher saying she had been fired for helping students discover their gender identity.
