No one wants to be “Data Center Dave”
Voters on both sides of the aisle despise hate data centers. But do they hate them enough to influence the midterms?
As far as political slurs go, this one is pretty tepid: “Meet Data Center Dave Crowley,” intones the stern-voiced narrator of a recent Tom Tiffany campaign ad.
Tiffany, a Republican, and Crowley, a Democrat, are both running for governor of Wisconsin. And in this very tight race, as in dozens of midterm contests across the country, voters’ growing animus toward AI could potentially make a real difference.
In less than four weeks, Americans will head to the polls to decide which party controls Congress, along with a slew of state and local offices. The stakes are arguably, unusually high: Voters will choose whether to check the power of a president who has bulldozed over historical limits and launched an unpopular war that has worsened a cost-of-living crisis.
As we count down to that momentous and potentially messy day, I’m partnering with my colleague Astead Herndon and Vox’s The Midterms, Actually team for weekly editions on the biggest issues shaping the midterms. We’re breaking down one issue each week and suggesting further reading and races to watch in November.
Last week, we tackled the dual identity crises that both parties have suffered since 2024. And this week, we’re digging into the dramatic bipartisan backlash to AI and data centers. One analyst recently told NPR the issue “upended politics as we know it.” But it’s less clear how that’ll play out in November’s contests.
Go a little deeper
There was a time not so long ago when “Data Center Dave” might be a neutral nickname for the well-meaning IT guy at work. Then Americans soured on AI and the hulking, cavernous warehouses that supply its computing power.
The hostility crosses geography and party lines. At first, opponents focused on noise, water use, and energy costs — quality-of-life concerns for nearby residents. But increasingly, even voters far from these projects grew leery of them.
Too often, the public got little say in where data centers were built and on what terms. And as Vox’s Marina Bolotnikova reported over the summer, the construction boom gradually became a stand-in for broader fears about artificial intelligence. Would AI cause mass unemployment (…or worse, mass extinction)? Would it widen the gap between rich and poor? And do politicians cater to business interests over the needs of ordinary people?
Without clear answers to those questions — let alone a rigorous plan to address AI’s fallout — many voters channeled their unease into stopping, or slowing, data center development.
Candidates have reacted by “falling over themselves to sound tough on data centers,” Washington Post data reporter Jeremy Merrill recently told Vox’s Noel King. He analyzed thousands of social media posts and newsletters to see how elected officials are talking about data centers, and the answer is: not positively!
Some candidates in high-profile midterm races have backed policies that would keep data centers from raising household energy bills. Others have called for ending the facilities’ tax breaks and subsidies or requiring public notice before new construction. Strikingly, both Republicans and Democrats have supported these types of proposals … and both Republicans and Democrats have sought to tar their opponents as “Data Center Daves” of one kind or another.
I asked my colleague Andrew Prokop, who covers politics, if many races will actually turn on this. “Data centers have been a major theme in several races, particularly governor’s races where one of the candidates has taken past pro-data center positions,” he said.
But even when voters say they oppose data centers, very few list the issue among the most important concerns determining how they cast their ballots. In Ohio, for instance — a hub for both data-center development and the grassroots movement opposing it — only 3 percent of voters named data centers as the top issue driving their vote. And that’s the highest share in the entire nation.
Andrew points to the Democratic gubernatorial primary in Wisconsin, where “Data Center Dave” triumphed over Francesca Hong, an outspoken data center critic. “That just goes to show that data centers don’t necessarily crowd out everything else,” Andrew said.
Still...that’s just one race. And voters’ hatred of data centers has only grown since.
➨ Races to watch:
- Wisconsin governor’s race, where both candidates have attempted to distance themselves from data centers without embracing an actual ban;
- Texas governor’s race, where Republican Governor Greg Abbott has hastily retreated from his previous, pro-data-center position;
- Ohio Senate race, where Democrat Sherrod Brown has hammered incumbent Republican Jon Husted over his past votes for data center development.

The EU said it has reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.
Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the deal was the first of its kind and the result of “intense” negotiations with China since June to curb a trade deficit of €1.18bn (£1bn) a day, which has caused mounting tensions between the two economic powers.
The deal “opens the prospect of cutting China’s export [of hybrids] by more than a half”, Šefčovič said, adding that this would translate into a reduction in exports of plug-in and battery-powered hybrid cars by “several millions” over the next four years, said Šefčovič said Šefčovič at a press conference in Beijing on Friday.
“It is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tension,” he said, a reference to the usual investigations that must take place before safeguards under WTO trading rules are put in place.
China has been flooding Europe with cars, including hybrids and pure battery electric vehicles (BEVs), threatening European manufacturers. Hybrids combine an internal combustion engine with a small battery. They are sold by carmakers as a transitional step towards BEVs.
Šefčovič said the Chinese had recognised the political pressure building in every member state in Europe with “literally thousands of job losses” at risk because of the flood of cheap imports from China across many sectors including chemicals and textiles.
He said EU leaders were “clearly expecting very fast action” from the European Commission and the Chinese recognised that.
“I am glad to say that the Chinese partners appreciated this very strong political argument, and therefore, we can proceed through the negotiated solution,” he said.
“This is far from the end. It’s a crucial first step, but only a first step,” Šefčovič told reporters in Beijing where he had travelled to hold talks with his Chinese counterpart.
Earlier this week senior EU officials said they were heading to Beijing to seek what they called a “proof of concept” or pilot scheme with one sector which they hoped could then be expanded to other areas under pressure from Chinese competition.
Šefčovič said he put “so much emphasis” on the negotiations because it was “very difficult to stop” a trade war once it was declared.
As part of a 16-point agreement, Beijing and Brussels will continue negotiating on cars, export restrictions on rare earths and access to China for more food and drink from the EU.
China said both sides would adhere to “procedures concerning company price undertakings” for hybrid cars suggesting one method of curbing sales would be to set higher minimum price tags for Chinese cars sold in Europe.
The EU commissioner will brief EU diplomats in Brussels on Sunday ahead of a leaders’ summit on Thursday.
A statement from the Chinese ministry of commerce said China is “willing … to continue facilitating the approval of export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU”.
It added that both sides had “reaffirmed their commitment … to properly handle differences within the framework of WTO rules, and to continuing to stabilise and balance bilateral trade and economic relations”.
While China and the EU acknowledged “differences” between them it appears that China has accepted the EU’s request to create a new model for trade balances starting with a pilot on hybrid cars.

SpaceX wants to become a 'major mobile carrier' with low-band spectrum acquisition
That will allow Starlink’s signal to penetrate walls and reach customers inside buildings.
SpaceX has revealed that it plans to become a major mobile carrier and not just a satellite internet broadband service provider with Starlink. To achieve that goal, it has agreed to acquire 100 percent of Grain Management's nationwide 800 MHz spectrum portfolio. SpaceX says the acquisition is for a "low-band spectrum license portfolio of up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band," though it's still pending FCC approval. Access to the low-band spectrum will address one of the key "technical gaps" remaining to be able to turn Starlink into a major mobile carrier in the US, SpaceX adds.
The company acquired spectrum licenses from EchoStar late last year, including frequencies used in the US for commercial wireless services like mobile and satellite communications. But this particular low-broadband spectrum acquisition will enable Starlink Mobile's signal to penetrate walls and other obstacles. While more established carriers have access to a wider range of bands, this will allow the company to offer a robust and veritable alternative to their offerings. Most mobile devices already support the band, so SpaceX will be able to offer its services to millions of potential customers regardless of their phones.
"With this new low-band spectrum and our Gen2 constellation, Starlink Mobile can now become the first network operator to deploy both satellite and terrestrial spectrum," SpaceX's announcement reads. This new acquisition will allow SpaceX to offer a reliable service indoors, while Starlink's broadband internet will provide customers with a signal even in far-flung places.
The FCC has recently authorized SpaceX to deploy 15,000 Starlink Mobile Gen2 satellites optimized for the 2 GHz spectrum. According to the company, those satellites will be able to deliver more than 100 times the bandwidth of its current satellite generation, giving SpaceX the capability to offer high-speed internet in more regions around the world.

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has brought the promotion of doctors and hospitals and how they attract patients online under the ambit of medical ethics, prohibiting paid rankings, fake reviews, referral fees, misleading claims and the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to create or manipulate patient testimonials.
The Ethics and Medical Registration Board’s Guidelines on Ethical Advertising and Public Communication by Hospitals/Medical Institutions and Registered Medical Practitioners, issued on October 6, apply to communication through websites, social media, messaging platforms, podcasts, sponsored content, influencers and online platforms. The guidelines have come into effect immediately.
The guidelines prohibit registered medical practitioners (RMPs) and hospitals from making claims such as “best”, “No. 1”, “leading”, “most trusted”, “top” or “unmatched”, unless these can be objectively verified through a transparent and independently ascertainable methodology. Any ranking or award used in advertising must also be independently verifiable, with relevant details disclosed where necessary to prevent the public from being misled.
Online promotion targeted
The NMC has specifically addressed online promotion. RMPs and hospitals cannot procure or manipulate fake followers, likes, reviews, ratings, testimonials, comments, views or other digital engagement. They cannot manipulate search rankings, visibility or algorithms to create a misleading impression of their professional standing.
The guidelines also target financial incentives for bringing in patients. An RMP cannot offer, pay, solicit or receive a commission, rebate, bonus, gift, gratuity, referral fee, lead-generation fee or other consideration connected with the referral, recommendation or procurement of patients, specimens or materials for diagnosis or treatment.
Advertising agencies, digital marketing agencies, influencers and online platforms cannot be engaged in a manner in which payment is linked to the procurement or referral of individual patients.
On patient testimonials
Patient testimonials have also come under specific restrictions. An RMP cannot use or permit a celebrity, influencer, patient, employee or other third party to promote professional services through prohibited testimonials, endorsements or recommendations. The guidelines also prohibit RMPs from requesting or sharing patient testimonials, recommendations, endorsements or reviews for professional promotion on social media.
The guidelines prohibit the use of AI to create or manipulate patient testimonials and other promotional material in a manner that misrepresents treatment, outcomes or professional standing. The provisions also cover manipulation of patient images or voices and synthetic endorsements presented as though they came from actual patients or professionals.
The NMC has also specified what doctors and hospitals can communicate. “Hospitals can provide factual information about their location, departments, facilities, equipment, emergency services, accreditation, services and fees. Doctors can provide factual professional information and participate in public-health and educational communication, provided it does not become prohibited promotion,” it said.
Discounts, limited-period offers, contests, coupons, gifts, cashbacks, referral benefits and free procedures are also prohibited where they are likely to encourage unnecessary consultation, diagnostic investigation or treatment. Lawful disclosure of fees and packages can be made if it is factual, transparent and not misleading.
The guidelines prescribe graded disciplinary action against RMPs. A first violation can attract a warning and mandatory ethics training; a second can result in censure and a monetary penalty; and a third can lead to suspension of registration for three to six months. Serious violations can attract suspension for six to 12 months, while repeated violations can result in removal from the medical register for one to three years.
For hospitals and medical institutions, the applicable penalty and appellate mechanism under the Clinical Establishments Act or the relevant State law will apply. Where an RMP has authorised, participated in or endorsed prohibited communication, the doctor’s professional conduct can separately be examined by the appropriate medical regulatory authority.
The guidelines have been issued in the context of a writ petition before the Supreme Court and the existing framework governing professional conduct.

Ecommerce giant Amazon has reportedly laid off at least 100 employees in India as part of its latest global job cuts. Citing sources, ET reported that the affected employees in India were primarily from retail and customer service functions. Globally, fewer than 1,000 employees were affected, Business Insider reported. The cuts spanned customer service, selling partner support, and engineering roles within Amazon’s Stores business, which oversees its main ecommerce operations. Employees in India, the US, and the UK were among those affected. Responding to Inc42’s queries, an Amazon spokesperson confirmed that the company had eliminated roles as part of changes to its Stores business. “We’re always looking at our team structures to ensure we’re best set up to move fast as we innovate for customers. We’ve adjusted parts of our Stores business because we believe this structure will better enable us to deliver on our priorities. As part of these changes, we’ve made the difficult decision to eliminate a small number of roles, and we’re committed to supporting affected employees through their transition,” the spokesperson said. However, Amazon did not disclose how many employees were affected in India or provide details of the support being offered to them. The layoffs coincide with the start of Amazon’s Great Indian Festival sale, which opened to all customers yesterday. Further Cuts After Two Major Rounds The latest layoffs follow two major rounds of workforce reductions that affected Amazon’s India operations. In January 2026, Amazon laid off more than 500 employees across its India offices, with multiple sources estimating the number at 500-700. Technology and human resources teams were among the worst affected, with software development engineer roles accounting for the highest number of layoffs. Those cuts were part of a global restructuring exercise affecting approximately 16,000 roles. Amazon said at the time that it was reducing organisational layers, increasing ownership, and removing bureaucracy. Earlier, in November 2025, more than 1,000 employees were laid off in India, with sources estimating that the total could reach 1,500. Prime Video, people experience and technology, Q&A devices, retail stores, and Amazon Web Services were among the worst-hit divisions. The cuts affected mid-senior and senior employees across Chennai, Hyderabad, and Bengaluru, with sources saying that some verticals had lost entire teams. Alongside these workforce reductions, Amazon is increasing investment in infrastructure. The company plans a record $220 Bn in capital expenditure in 2026, covering data centres, chips, and other infrastructure, with the majority supporting AWS and AI. CEO Andy Jassy said during Amazon’s second-quarter earnings call that higher memory costs had pushed the estimate up from $200 Bn. In India, Amazon announced an additional $13 Bn investment in AI and cloud infrastructure by 2030 in June, taking its total investment commitment across businesses in the country to $48 Bn. The company also reportedly plans to invest $3 Bn in its quick commerce business, Amazon Now, by 2030 to expand its dark store network, strengthen inventory management, deploy AI tools, and widen its product mix.

Australian bishop acknowledges 8-year delay in justice in Indigenous abuse case but defends process
A top Australian Catholic bishop has acknowledged the eight-year delay in bringing a fellow bishop to justice on charges he sexually abused young Indigenous men
VATICAN CITY -- A top Australian Catholic bishop has acknowledged the eight-year delay in bringing a fellow bishop to justice on charges he sexually abused young Indigenous men. But he defended the church’s decision to let police take the lead in the case as a necessary guarantee.
Archbishop Timothy Costelloe, president of the Australian Bishops Conference, said Friday he hoped the church could soon reopen its own in-house legal procedures against former Broome Bishop Christopher Saunders now that he has been sentenced criminally.
“We still have to respect the integrity of the Australian justice system,” Costelloe told The Associated Press on the sidelines of a Vatican conference. “That’s been probably the fundamental reason why it’s stretched out as long as it has.”
Saunders, 76, was sentenced to six years and six months in prison on Wednesday after he was convicted by a District Court of Western Australia state jury of 13 out of 19 charges of sexual abuse that occurred between 2008 and 2019 in his sprawling Broome Diocese on the country’s tropical northwest coast.
Prosecutors alleged Saunders lured young Indigenous men to his church-owned house with alcohol and cigarettes paid for with church funds. He denied wrongdoing. It isn't known yet if he will appeal.
Church and law enforcement officials first learned of the allegations in 2018, and the Vatican in 2021 forced Saunders to retire at age 71, four years early. But the Australian police investigation was twice halted for lack of evidence.
The Vatican typically allows criminal investigations to play out before initiating canonical trials so as not to interfere, and that is especially so now in Australia, after the church's wretched legacy there of abuse and cover-up.
“I understand that some people are very, I’d say, even cynical about this and wonder about the response of the church,” Costelloe said. "It hasn’t been held up in a kind of an obstructionist way. We’ve had no choice but to allow the police to act independently and without interference.”
The Vatican began its own investigation into Saunders in 2022, then handed the Western Australia Police Force a 200-page report on its findings the following year. Police reopened the criminal investigation and finally charged Saunders in 2024.
While the report’s contents were never officially made public, they were leaked to Australia’s Seven Network television news, which reported Saunders likely sexually assaulted four Indigenous youths and potentially groomed another 67 Indigenous youths and men.
“I think people who are ready to think this through understand that in order to safeguard the integrity of the process and make sure that the church didn’t or wasn’t seen to be compromising the integrity of that process, we needed to step back,” Costelloe said.
“So I’m very conscious of how long it’s taken, how distressing it’s been, but I believe that in this particularly complex case, this was the right approach to take,” he said.
Costelloe denied that the delay was due to the fact that the original allegations involved men who were over age 18 when the alleged abuse occurred. The Vatican has long looked the other way when priests were accused of abuse involving adults, especially if the priests were bishops.

The death of a laboratory worker in Siberia on October 2, 2026, and the subsequent quarantine of dozens of people have sparked concerns about a pneumonic plague epidemic, with Russia revealing little information publicly. The incident has revived memories of the COVID-19 pandemic and allegations that the coronavirus may have emerged at a Chinese lab.
What happened at the Siberia lab?
The 28-year-old woman, Darya Shipilova, employed at a research institute in Siberia, fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances, prompting authorities to quarantine dozens of people and dispatch the head of Russia’s health watchdog to the Irkutsk region.
The woman worked at the anti-plague research institute in the city of Irkutsk, where the plague occurs naturally in wild animals. She died at a hospital in nearby Shelekhov that the mayor said had been placed under quarantine. Following the incident, top Russian health officials have travelled to the region.
Russian authorities say the lab worker died of what initially presented as a “typical” acute respiratory viral infection.
Russia dismisses epidemic concerns
Meanwhile, Russia’s health regulator insists there were no risks of an epidemic breaking out in Siberia after the plague institute worker’s death.
Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s health watchdog, said on October 7 that it was winding down precautionary measures it had put in place after concluding there was no risk of an epidemic.
No cases of plague had been detected among anyone who had come into contact with the deceased worker, it said, while adding that 90% of those placed in quarantine had been released after nearly 5,000 lab tests had failed to detect any dangerous pathogens.
When asked about a second person in Siberia allegedly falling ill, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged caution against using media reports as a reference for what was happening.
‘Causative agent behind death not known’
A top official with the World Health Organisation (WHO) said it doesn’t know how the lab worker in Siberia died. Maria Van Kerkhove, WHO director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management, said the UN health agency doesn’t know what the “causative agent’ was behind the woman’s October 2 death.
She has urged Russia to provide more information about the incident that prompted global concerns about suspected pneumonic plague. The WHO initially said it estimated the risk of the Russia case to the public as low, but told a press conference on October 7 it could not make a fuller risk assessment due to insufficient information from the Russian authorities.
What is pneumonic plague, symptoms
Reports blamed the woman’s death on pneumonic plague — a less common but severe form of plague that can spread from person to person.
Pneumonic plague causes a severe form of pneumonia, but recovery rates are high if it is detected and treated in time. The severe disease is less common than the better-known bubonic plague linked to the Black Death in the Middle Ages.
Pneumonic plague and bubonic plague are caused by the same bacteria. The former is spread by respiratory particles while the latter is spread through bites from fleas that have jumped from infected rodents.
Symptoms of pneumonic plague include shortness of breath and coughing-up blood, and they can occur in as little as 24 hours after exposure, according to the WHO. If untreated, the illness can be fatal.
Not linked to a biological weapon
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Wednesday (October 8) that the death of the Russian plague laboratory worker did not appear to be linked to a biological weapon.
Mr. Trump said Russia insisted it had the situation under control, but added that not much information was coming out. He, however, said that the United States will help Russia over the incident.
The European Union has also called on Russia to “share timely and transparent reporting” about the death of the plague laboratory technician.

Intel is reportedly launching new CPUs on old sockets that support DDR4 memory
This is, of course, due to the AI-fueled RAMpocalypse.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
Intel is reportedly releasing new CPUs built on LGA 1700 sockets, according to motherboard manufacturer Gigabyte. The LGA 1700 has been around since 2021, which is a really long time in processor land. Why use relatively ancient technology in brand-new processors that are set to release next year? It all comes down to the price of memory, according to a report by PC Gamer.
LGA 1700 sockets offer support for both DDR5 and DDR4 memory, so the running theory is that upcoming refreshes of Raptor Lake and Alder Lake processors will be configurable to use DDR4 RAM. This is likely to accommodate the ongoing AI-fueled RAMpocalypse, in which memory prices have skyrocketed. Simply put, DDR4 RAM is a lot cheaper than DDR5. Folks can pick up a 32GB DDR4 kit for around $210, but a 32GB DDR5 kit costs upwards of $480.
Intel hasn't confirmed this theory, but VP Robert Hallock recently said that Raptor Lake chips would be sticking around for "years to come." He also suggested that DDR4 integration is one of the primary reasons. "LGA 1700 is still a good socket. Lots of people are still interested in DDR4, so we'll keep offering," he said.
This isn't that surprising, given that many of the company's current line of processors can already be configured to use DDR4 memory. DDR4 isn't as fast as DDR5, but the older memory type is still fine for the vast majority of modern PC games. Testing has revealed that DDR5 sticks deliver a 1 to ten percent FPS improvement. However, this largely depends on the resolution the player chooses and the GPU.

India condemns JD Vance's ‘indentured servants’ remark amid green card curbs
India said the US freeze on permanent labor certification filings by major technology companies undermines shared ambitions.
India on Friday said the US administration’s freeze on green card filings by Indian IT majors such as Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) and Infosys go against shared ambitions of both sides, even as it denounced US vice president JD Vance comparing Indian and other foreign professionals to “indentured servants” as unwarranted and deeply offensive.
The response from the external affairs ministry came hours after the Trump administration froze some Green Card filings by eight IT majors and launched probes into nine elite universities, widening a visa crackdown aimed at curbing fraud and US job losses. The move specifically targeted Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies, Microsoft, Adobe and Capgemini.
The external affairs ministry noted in a statement that talent mobility adds value to the Indian and US economies, creating opportunities for Indians and equally helping US firms with cutting-edge talent, innovation, research, productivity, competitiveness and job creation, besides creating shareholder wealth in the US.
Deep Dive
“This is therefore an area of tremendous mutual benefit for the two countries and our expectation is that all stakeholders in this process can appreciate this fact,” the ministry said. “The steps announced by the US do not advance the shared ambitions of both countries.”
Also Read | ‘US history shaped by immigrants’: India calls out JD Vance over ‘deeply offensive’ H-1B visa remarks
The Trump administration’s action targeted the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM), a key employer-sponsorship mechanism that has allowed skilled foreign workers to gain permanent residency through their employment since 2005. Under PERM, which most employment-based green cards require, employers must show a foreign hire will not hurt US workers’ jobs.
The statement noted that the PERM programme is distinct from the H-1B visa programme, and said the suspension of PERM applications “does not, by itself, affect the validity of existing H-1B visas or the status of H-1B visa holders and their dependents”. However, the new move can have an impact on the permanent-residency or green card process of “eligible employees of the affected companies”, the statement said.
The Indian side also took exception to comments made by Vance at an event where the new curbs were announced. Vance’s remarks suggested that foreign talents were no more than “indentured servants” whose hiring was resulting in the laying off of American workers.
“We believe that such descriptions are unwarranted and ignore the fact that Indian professionals in the United States are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem,” the statement said.
Also Read | 'Opportunities for Indians but also helps US': India on Vance's remarks amid Green Card curbs
The external affairs ministry pointed out that the history of the US itself has been “shaped by generations of immigrants whose labour, enterprise and innovation have contributed to its growth and prosperity”. The statement added, “Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive.”
The developments marked yet another low point in India-US relations during the second term of President Donald Trump. The US administration’s decision last year to hit Indian exports with 50% tariffs sent ties to their lowest point in more than two decades. Though the two sides reached an understanding earlier this year on reducing the tariffs, they have struggled to finalise a bilateral trade deal and recent remarks by Indian and US leaders have suggested an agreement is not imminent.
The twin actions by the Trump administration marked the broadest strike yet against skilled worker immigration programmes, potentially blocking a common path to permanent residency for thousands of foreign tech workers, including Indians.
While announcing the move against the eight tech firms, US labour secretary Keith Sonderling said: “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies.”
Vance added, “I’m sure that everyone here understands the game that is being played. Bring in indentured servants from outside the country, you lay off American workers and if you’re a corporation, you make a ton of money by undercutting the wages of American workers, replacing them with people who probably should not be in the United States of America to begin with.”
During his second term, Trump has widened efforts to reduce the number of foreign-born people in the US and to curtail their pathway to residence and citizenship.
Also Read | ‘Can't replace American workers with foreign servants’: Why Vance's H-1B visa axe fell on Microsoft
The Trump administration has sought to disincentivise US employers from using the H-1B visa programme. In September 2025, Trump announced a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa petitions, though it was subsequently blocked by a US court in June 2026. In August, the Trump administration proposed a fresh $103,265 H-1B visa fee that will apply to all petitions subject to the annual cap of 85,000.
Microsoft is the largest filer of PERM applications, according to Permtrack.app, which compiles US labour department disclosure data.
Nasscom, India’s IT body, said late on Thursday that firms had significantly reduced their dependence on H-1B visas in recent years while expanding local hiring in the US. Relatively few workers move from H-1B visas to permanent residency through PERM, Nasscom added.
Shares on Indian IT firms rose on Friday. The NIfty IT Index rose 3% while the broader market gained 1.3 per cent.

Ex-Marineland beluga whale dies in Chicago aquarium
4 other belugas, 1 dolphin have also died after relocation from closed Canadian theme park
Another whale shipped out of Marineland has died at the Shedd Aquarium in Chicago.
The aquarium says Caspian, a 27-year-old female beluga, died on Wednesday despite efforts to save her.
It's the sixth animal from the closed Niagara Falls, Ont., theme park to die after a massive relocation of whales and dolphins over the summer.
Four other belugas and one dolphin from Marineland have died since they were moved out of the former tourist attraction.

Shedd says Caspian had not been eating properly and blood samples showed abnormalities in her electrolyte levels. The park added that her blood had become "dangerously acidic."
The aquarium says those findings helped the veterinary care team understand how sick the beluga was, but they did not establish a cause of death.
Shedd says Caspian was on life support for nearly four hours before she died.
Shedd recently performed necropsies on Peekachu and Rain, two other Marineland whales that died there, and concluded that they had chronic, pre-existing diseases.
Shedd and four other aquariums in the United States and Spain helped Marineland relocate all 30 of its belugas and four dolphins over the course of six weeks this summer.
Marineland had said it was running out of money and could no longer care for the last captive whales and dolphins in Canada.
A beluga named Jelly Bean and a dolphin named Echo died at Oceanografic Valencia in Spain after the move.

The Trump administration plans a public killing
Pete Hegseth’s “barbaric” plan for a livestreamed execution, briefly explained.
Welcome to The Logoff: The Trump administration is planning a public killing.
What’s happening? On Thursday, the Pentagon announced that it would execute Nidal Hasan, a former Army major sentenced to death for a 2009 mass shooting on a military base, publicly and on livestream.
The execution, if it happens, would be unprecedented: The last widely reported public execution in the US was 90 years ago, in Kentucky, but to stream a death live would be something else entirely. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has promoted the announcement with something approaching glee, telling a reporter that “we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it.”
What’s the context? According to the Pentagon, Hasan will be executed via firing squad on December 3 — the first such execution by the military in more than 80 years.
Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, was sentenced to death in 2013 by a military jury following a court-martial for the 2009 shooting, when he killed 13 people and wounded more than 30 at Fort Hood in Texas. The execution is set to be carried out at the same Army post.
Will the Pentagon go through with this? It’s unclear, for multiple reasons. The Pentagon’s announcement that Hasan’s death will be livestreamed has generated a great deal of bipartisan pushback, as well as condemnation by religious groups, though that is unlikely to stop the execution itself.
The head of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops decried the decision to livestream the execution as “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death,” and retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-NC) called it the decision “beyond disgusting.”
“Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do,” Tillis wrote in a post on X.
On Friday, Vice President JD Vance also said that he was unsure if the livestream would take place.
Hasan’s legal team could also delay the execution substantially — potentially for multiple years — by challenging his detention in federal court, though he has exhausted the military appeals process.

The El Nino that’s upending weather across South America and Asia has intensified to the strongest on record, according to Japan’s national forecaster, threatening widespread economic disruptions that could linger long after the climate pattern dissipates.
The naturally occurring weather pattern warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall.
Sea surface temperatures in a patch of the tropical Pacific Ocean monitored by the Japan Meteorological Agency were 4 degrees Celsius above normal as of September, the highest in records going back to 1949, the forecaster said in a bulletin published Friday. The previous record was set in December 1997, when temperatures were 3.7 C above normal, the bureau said.
El Nino has already disrupted weather patterns worldwide. The climate event has led to the weakest Indian monsoon in more than a decade, exacerbated wildfires in Indonesia that have spewed toxic smoke over neighboring Singapore and Malaysia, and threatened sugar and coffee output in Brazil.
The JMA’s outlook comes a day after the World Meteorological Organization said in its latest seasonal forecast that El Nino is set to be the most intense ever. The WMO’s projection is based on the Nino 3.4 region, which overlaps with but lies west of the Nino 3 region tracked by Japan.
The Japanese bureau predicts a 100% chance that El Nino will persist through the Northern Hemisphere winter, in line with the U.S. Climate Prediction Center’s outlook that the weather-roiling phenomenon is certain to last through the January-March period.
Many record-hot years -- including 1998, 2010, 2016, 2023 and 2024 -- followed major El Nino events or developed alongside them.

The Colorado Republican continues to be haunted by a date gone wrong at a musical in Denver, for which she has apologized

A clean energy Super PAC has targeted Congresswoman Lauren Boebert with a humiliating ad that reminds voters of the time she was kicked out of a Beetlejuice show.
The Colorado Republican, who is a staunch opponent of Biden-era energy policies, was the latest GOP candidate in the midterm elections to be singled out by the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, a group that works to elect politicians who support renewable energy.
Weeks before Halloween, the Super PAC unveiled a new ad, showing security footage of Boebert being escorted out of a musical based on the 1988 horror film Beetlejuice in Denver in September 2023.
“Costs are skyrocketing in Colorado, and politicians are failing us,” the ad, obtained by Politico, said. “If Lauren Boebert can’t be trusted in a room full of kids, then she can’t be trusted in the halls of Congress.”
Boebert and her date were accused of vaping, singing, recording and causing a disturbance in the theater before being kicked out. Video of the two in their theater seats also appeared to show them fondling each other.
Amid backlash from the incident, Boebert issued an apology, saying, “There’s no perfect blueprint for going through a public and difficult divorce, which over the past few months has made for a challenging personal time for me and my entire family.”
“I’ve tried to handle it with strength and grace as best I can, but I simply fell short of my values on Sunday. That’s unacceptable, and I’m sorry,” the congresswoman wrote on social media at the time.
Boebert is running for reelection against Democrat Eileen Laubacher in Colorado’s 4th Congressional District, which local outlet 9News describes as one of the state’s most Republican-leaning seats.
The congresswoman says on her website that she believes in “unleashing America’s God-given resources to create jobs, lower energy costs, and strengthen our economy.”
While she says she supports renewable energy such as solar, wind and hydropower along with oil, gas and coal, she insists that fossil fuels “are the backbone of our energy security.”
Invest in Tomorrow will spend $1.5 million on its campaign against Boebert, according to Politico. This is part of a larger $15 million plan targeting a total of seven Republicans, including Representatives Scott Perry of Pennsylvania and Victoria Spartz of Indiana, who voted to end renewable energy incentives implemented under former President Joe Biden, The New York Times reported.
“When we’re done here, we will have fundamentally reshaped the electoral incentives of congressional energy politics and sent a very clear message to our would-be opponents: No matter how safe you think your seat is, if you politicize our industry, we will come for you and we will win,” Tom Matzzie, a solar company chief executive who is chairman of the super PAC, said in the Times article.

A botched execution and plans for one in public show the US is conflicted about capital punishment
Americans have long been divided over executing the nation’s worst criminals

Americans have long been divided over the death penalty, with nearly half of states banning capital punishment outright and just a handful of others carrying out most of the nation's executions each year.
The longstanding but uneasy relationship with executing the nation's worst criminals has been on clear display in recent weeks, first following a botched lethal injection in Tennessee and later after the military announced plans to livestream a death by firing squad. Both have prompted fresh calls for abolition from death penalty opponents and led supporters to publicly grapple with how to humanely carry out government executions.
When Christa Pike was sentenced to die in 1996 after being convicted of murdering a classmate, Tennessee was among 37 states that had capital punishment, and the number of annual executions in the U.S. was on the rise. Since then, 10 states have abolished capital punishment, and executions haven't approached their late 1990s peak.
Still, it is unlikely the U.S. is headed for complete abolition. Thirty inmates have been executed this year, and another eight executions have been scheduled, most of them in Texas and Florida. The military's planned firing-squad execution for Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan is scheduled for Dec. 3.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's announcement Thursday that the military would livestream Hasan's execution shocked even some capital punishment supporters. Vice President JD Vance on Friday questioned whether it would happen and said he wouldn't watch. Retiring North Carolina Republican U.S. Sen. Thom Tillis called a livestream “beyond disgusting."
American attitudes on the death penalty are complicated
While about two-thirds of U.S. adults see the death penalty as morally justified for people who have committed murder, according to a Pew Research Center poll conducted in July, about 6 in 10 say the death penalty does not deter crime. About 7 in 10 say there is some risk an innocent person would be put to death. Gallup’s trend suggests that support for capital punishment has fallen considerably since the 1990s.
Victims' families are often among the most vocal advocates on either side of the debate. The family of Colleen Slemmer, whom Pike was convicted of killing, has supported Pike's execution.
On the opposite side is Rachel Sutphin, a Presbyterian pastor whose father was killed in the line of duty as a sheriff's deputy. The man convicted of killing him was the last person Virginia executed, in 2017. Sutphin was part of a coalition that successfully argued for abolishing the death penalty in the state in 2021. She said the Pentagon's announcement was so shocking it might push her back into advocacy work.
“This place where (in) the name of revenge, taking an eye for an eye, has become socially acceptable and has almost become a form of entertainment -- that very much concerns me,” she said.
In Tennessee, Republican legislators weren't backing off their support for the death penalty after Pike survived her attempted execution Oct. 1. Instead, they contemplated returning to the electric chair or allowing firing squads. Idaho recently made the firing squad the state's primary execution method, viewing it as more humane because the death is quicker and the chances of botching it are remote.
Idaho state Republican Rep. Bruce Skaug, a retired attorney who introduced that legislation, said he believes the death penalty should be rare but that once the court issues such a punishment, it’s the government’s duty to “carry it out properly.”
But Skaug was surprised by the Pentagon's announcement and still pondering it Friday.
"That’s a difficult one for me to swallow.”
Public executions used to be common in the U.S.
From the Revolution and into the 20th century, American executions were often public and sometimes treated like mass entertainment. But no public executions have taken place since the late 1930s.
Brenner Fissell, vice president of the National Institute of Military Justice, said public executions “are seen by most civilized societies as grotesque and barbaric.” Almost every European nation has abolished capital punishment.
But, Fissell added, he did not know of any legal obstacles that would prohibit the administration from livestreaming Hasan’s execution.
“You don’t have a right to a secret death,” he said.
But Robert Blecker, a professor emeritus at New York Law School, said there are arguments in favor of making executions public. He said it forces the government to take responsibility for executing someone.
“Shouldn't the people have access to what's being done in their name?” he said. “If we can't stomach and can't tolerate it, then abolish it."
Religious institutions highlight conflicting attitudes on death penalty
American culture is replete with portrayals of clergy being around execution, either advising and comforting the condemned or even occasionally giving a moral lecture from the gallows before a hanging. They have been a major part of the ongoing debate over capital punishment.
Blecker, who agrees with some criticism of how capital punishment is administered but believes it is morally appropriate in a few cases involving the worst criminals, said that idea came from the ancient Hebrews and Greeks. They reasoned that failing to adequately punish criminals polluted the population as a whole.
Hegseth's church and denomination were co-founded by archconservative pastor Doug Wilson, who supports capital punishment.
Christian denominations such as the Southern Baptist Convention and the Lutheran Church--Missouri Synod support the death penalty, citing Biblical passages that mandate retributive justice under an authority granted by God to punish grave crimes. Supporters in these faith traditions view the death penalty as necessary to uphold the moral order and as a just response to the taking of innocent life.
But major religious denominations including the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops and several mainline Protestant denominations have taken official stances opposing the death penalty. Those positions are anchored in their theology of redemption and value for the “sanctity of life.”
Many clergy members, chaplains and volunteers from faith groups provide spiritual counseling, prayer and human connection to death row inmates and their families. Faith-based groups routinely organize prayer vigils and letter-writing campaigns while lobbying legislators to commute sentences or abolish capital punishment.
Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, on Friday issued a statement sharply condemning the military's plans to livestream Hasan's execution.
“This decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered,” he said.

Amid growing uncertainties over AI’s utilisation and its prospects, union IT minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said that the government is working on releasing a consultation paper on regulating the nascent tech. Speaking at the release of the World Bank’s latest World Development Report on the subject of ‘The Promise of Artificial Intelligence’, Vaishnaw said the timing is right for India to formalise AI regulation and the upcoming consultation paper will establish the foundational basis for future AI regulation. The regulatory blueprint is also likely to sharpen focus on AI safety and security, navigate the deepfakes risk as well as ensuring adequate skill development necessary to optimise the utilisation of AI. On the deepfake epidemic, Vaishnaw identified AI-morphed content as a “nuisance which can cause huge problems in society” while noting they establish dangerous precedents and narratives that mislead the public. He added that the quality of these is improving continuously. The minister further said that AI and emerging technologies cannot be effectively managed through legislation alone. Hence, the government intends to pursue a techno-legal solution with the active participation of industry stakeholders. “The industry has to take the primary responsibility,” said Vaishnaw, regarding issues such as cybersecurity, safety, user harm, psychological disorders, and deepfake proliferation. Notably, the IT minister had previously emphasised that the IT Act is becoming obsolete and India needs a new legal framework to regulate AI. Reports had also hinted that the Centre was looking at formulating a new framework for AI regulation. As frontier AI models’ capabilities are evolving, the government has increasingly focused on tightening rules to mitigate the harms caused by proliferation of AI-generated content. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) had proposed amending the IT Act to require online platforms to label all deepfakes and AI-generated content as “synthetically generated information.” The news also comes amid a storm over global tech giant Meta’s handling of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on its platforms like Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. A BBC investigation earlier this year alleged that Instagram ads were directing users towards Telegram channels offering CSAM material for sale, resulting in the company facing summons from MeitY and an inquiry by the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR). Following the episode, Meta and Google both ultimately agreed to report content on child abuse to Indian law enforcement authorities.

Public safety, past lapses: Why Delhi Police denied CJP permission for Jantar Mantar protest
Delhi police said the right to protest is a fundamental right but that granting permission also requires authorities to consider the rights of other citizens.
Delhi Police has denied permission to the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) to hold a protest at Jantar Mantar on October 10, citing short notice, alleged violations during earlier demonstrations and concerns over public safety and law and order. The police also defended the restrictions imposed in New Delhi, saying they were necessary to prevent overcrowding and ensure the safety of protesters, residents and commuters.
In a letter dated October 9, addressed to CJP co-convener Saurav Das and joint secretary Balkrishna, the New Delhi district police said the group's communication submitted on October 7 was merely an intimation of the proposed protest and did not constitute a duly submitted application seeking permission.
The police said existing guidelines require applications for programmes at Jantar Mantar to be submitted at least 10 days before the intended date.
Deep Dive
The police said the right to protest is a fundamental right but that granting permission also requires authorities to consider the rights of other citizens and residents.
It cited traffic congestion, safety concerns and the potential disruption of public life as reasons for regulating demonstrations.
Why Delhi Police is citing earlier protests
The police referred to the July protests at Jantar Mantar, saying permission had been granted for a one-day demonstration but that it continued for around a month. In its statement on X, the police said more than 200 personnel were injured during the protests and alleged that the participation of people with criminal antecedents contributed to the violence.
Hindustan Times reported on July 27, citing Delhi Police officials, that police had identified 2,873 people through CCTV footage linked to the July 20 march towards Parliament. Of these, 989 were found to have criminal antecedents, according to the officials.
The cases included murder, robbery, sexual assault and other offences. The police claims about the criminal antecedents of those identified were attributed to officials and should not be read as convictions.
The July 20 march saw clashes at several locations in central Delhi. An FIR accessed by HT alleged that protesters assaulted police personnel, damaged public property and attempted to breach Parliament security. The allegations formed part of the police account of the violence.
In its October 9 letter, Delhi Police said the continuation of an earlier CJP protest beyond the permitted hours had resulted in serious law and order problems and a deterioration in public order.
The police also claimed that women constables had been molested and assaulted by people protesting at Jantar Mantar during the previous week, describing the incidents as deeply troubling.
CJP had estimated 500-600 people for June protest
Documents submitted by CJP to Delhi Police show that the group had estimated a gathering of 500-600 people for its June 20 demonstration at Jantar Mantar.
In an application dated June 17, the group said the protest would be against alleged irregularities and paper leaks in competitive examinations, including NEET-UG and CBSE board examinations, and would demand the resignation of then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
The application specified a protest from 10 am to 5 pm and listed Sonam Wangchuk as a participant. The accompanying undertaking committed the organisers to maintaining order, deploying volunteers, following police directions and keeping the gathering within the permitted limit of 1,000 people.
Delhi Police granted permission for the June 20 demonstration, but the protest continued into June 21.
The eventual turnout of thousands, at the protests which lasted over a month, was also far greater than what CJP had sought permission for.
Police says Jantar Mantar can accommodate 1,000 people
In its statement on X, Delhi Police said Jantar Mantar could accommodate around 1,000 people at a time. It argued that authorities needed advance information about the number of expected participants to arrange traffic diversions, emergency access and safe crowd movement.
The police said Delhi's economic activity and daily life could not be brought to a halt every time a protest took place. It said the restrictions were temporary measures intended to regulate the movement of people, prevent overcrowding and protect protesters, residents, shopkeepers and others in the area.
The police also referred to Supreme Court directions issued on July 23, 2018, concerning the regulation of protests, saying the applicable guidelines had to be followed strictly.
Delhi Police and central security agencies have reviewed their handling of the July protests, identifying security lapses and preparing for further demonstrations. The review included concerns about food deliveries allowing people to remain at Jantar Mantar overnight and broken pavement stones and walls that could pose security risks. The report also noted that a Supreme Court-appointed committee was examining allegations of police excesses during the July protests.
Cops denied BSF permission to protest at Jantar Mantar too
Meanwhile, nearly 400 former Border Security Force (BSF) cooks, water carriers and women tradesmen from various states, under the banner of the Alliance of All Ex-Paramilitary Forces, staged a peaceful protest near the BSF headquarters, seeking reinstatement in service. The alliance's general secretary, Ranbir Singh, shared a copy of a Delhi Police letter denying them permission to hold a protest at Jantar Mantar on October 9 and 10. The letter, issued around a month earlier, cited rules against holding a hunger strike continuously for two days at Jantar Mantar and asked the organisers to cooperate with Delhi Police.
“Police denied permission citing different rules for us to protest at Jantar Mantar for two days. So we held protests near the BSF headquarters today. These people were duped by cyber fraudsters who helped them get NSDC skill development certificates, which were later found to be forged. These are people who served in the BSF during Operation Sindoor but lost their jobs after the department learnt their certificates were not accredited by the NSDC. The fact is they also did not know and submitted what they got,” Singh said.
What is CJP protesting against?
CJP has been demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. The group has continued its campaign through demonstrations and public statements, including a protest in Mumbai on October 2.
The proposed October 10 demonstration at Jantar Mantar was part of the group's effort to press its demands. Delhi Police said the organisers were proceeding without the requisite permission and that the request could not be granted in the larger public interest.
The police said people should be able to raise their concerns peacefully, but organisers must follow the prescribed process so that authorities can ensure the safety of participants and the public.

Two Indian cartoonists, Satish Acharya and Manjul, recently revealed that their Instagram accounts and posts were withheld in India, following orders from the government. While the former’s account was restored on October 6, the latter’s post remains unavailable in India.
On September 23, The Indian Express reported that election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months to decisions concerning electoral-roll management and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), including changes to Form 6, voter deletions and restorations, the centralisation of electoral-roll data, and appeals against decisions in West Bengal.
The investigation, based on internal notes and correspondence reviewed by the newspaper, showed that the two commissioners repeatedly said certain decisions had been taken without their knowledge or approval by chief election commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, with Sandhu at one point describing an SIR-related change as “unauthorised and illegal.” Both Acharya and Manjul had posted cartoons satirising this case.

According to that report, this government takedowns surged specifically after the Cockroach Janta Party-led students’ protest against the NEET exam irregularities in June and July. Alt News had earlier reported that in February, the government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021. The amendment reduced the time available to social media platforms to remove or disable access to unlawful content from 36 hours to three hours after receiving a valid court order or a “reasoned intimation” from the appropriate government or its authorised agency. Nikon says the video that originally won first place in its Small World in Motion contest “did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI.” BBC reports that the original first place video from Dr. Ning Xu claimed to show “tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving in the airway of a child with the respiratory condition PCD.” Nikon said last week that it was reviewing the video following skepticism online about its authenticity.
Nikon microscopic video competition winner disqualified for using generative AI
Nikon says it’s revisiting its competition rules after the original winner’s video was too good to be true.
In a comment on LinkedIn, Dr. Xu admitted to using AI for the video: “An unsupervised neural-network method was subsequently used for AI-assisted post-processing to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images from the super-resolution optical imaging.”
Dr. Xu’s video has now been disqualified and appears to have been removed from Nikon’s website. A video from Nguyen Nam Nhat now holds first place, according to the contest’s updated rankings. Space has plenty of room for more megaconstellations, but only if all operators are willing to share information about where their satellites are and where they’re going, a top executive at SpaceX and its AI subsidiary said this week.
Michael Nicolls, SpaceX’s vice president for Starlink and president of Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company, xAI, used a presentation Tuesday at the International Astronautical Congress in Turkey as a clarion call for improved data-sharing among satellite operators.
SpaceX’s Starlink constellation now has more than 11,000 satellites, about two-thirds of all active spacecraft in low-Earth orbit. Radars and telescopes routinely track thousands more pieces of space junk.
Starlink is, by far, the largest satellite constellation in operation today. But if you buy the buzz, Starlink is just the tip of the iceberg. SpaceX has revealed plans to launch up to a million satellites for a new constellation, called Starmind, to deploy AI computing capacity in low-Earth orbit. Amazon is in the early stages of launching a network of thousands of satellites to compete with Starlink, and two Chinese megaconstellations are now in full-scale deployment.
Law of large numbers
All of this raises the question of how to mitigate the risk of a collision in orbit, an event that could create thousands more pieces of space junk, potentially triggering a self-perpetuating cycle of debris generation. The risk of a collision on any given day is fantastically low. Space is vast and empty, and low-Earth orbit is a long way from filling up. SpaceX and most other Western operators de-orbit their rockets and satellites at the end of their missions to prevent additional debris in orbit.
“That said, the law of large numbers says that if it can happen, it will happen,” Nicolls said.
There’s still a long way to go to improve tracking, awareness, and coordination in orbit. This is sometimes called space traffic management. No global treaties or regulations require satellites to broadcast their locations and maneuvers or mandate coordination among satellite operators. Without rules of the road, it is up to governments and companies to set norms of behavior.
“Once you can track this debris, and if you can track it well, these are like obstacles on a road. If you can measure them, you can predict where they’re going to be, and you can avoid them,” Nicolls said. “What you can’t avoid is other operators who maneuver without telling you where they’re going to go. We have many examples of this on Starlink, unfortunately.”
Nicolls presented several examples of satellites from other operators closely approaching Starlink satellites as they zip around the Earth at 5 miles per second. The examples did not suggest nefarious intent, such as spying or an attempt at striking a Starlink in orbit. Instead, the other satellites conducted maneuvers and changed their trajectories without their owners informing anyone.
“Either they were not publishing their ephemeris to us, or they were not considering the ephemeris of others when they were maneuvering, and these led to conjunctions of tens of meters to hundreds of meters,” Nicolls said. “Way too close to comfort.”
Michael Nicolls, senior vice president of Starlink at SpaceX and president of xAI, speaks at the International Astronautical Congress in Antalya, Turkey, on Tuesday, October 6.
Credit:
International Astronautical Federation
Michael Nicolls, senior vice president of Starlink at SpaceX and president of xAI, speaks at the International Astronautical Congress in Antalya, Turkey, on Tuesday, October 6.
Credit:
International Astronautical Federation
An ephemeris contains information about a satellite’s location and movement. Some operators may not want to share this information, believing secrecy might provide a competitive or strategic advantage. But if spaceflight is to be sustainable, it is vital to err on the side of openness rather than secrecy.
“The minimum standard in low-Earth orbit needs to be that you know where your satellite is, and you know where it’s going. You need to be able to predict where your trajectory is, and that prediction needs to be reliable,” Nicolls said.
SpaceX lauds itself as the benchmark for orbital stewardship. It pretty much has to be, with so many Starlinks in orbit and so much of its business relying on space.
The company has lowered the altitude of the entire active Starlink constellation below 500 kilometers (310 miles), an adjustment that provides three benefits. It moved the network away from other heavily trafficked regions in low-Earth orbit, expedited reentry for any failed Starlink satellites, and improved service for Starlink customers. All of SpaceX’s new-generation Starlink V3 satellites, which began launching on the company’s Starship rocket last month, will fly even lower, at about 350 kilometers (217 miles).
SpaceX also publishes ephemeris data for its Starlink satellites and has asked other operators to share their data, too. Without ephemeris sharing, operators rely on tracking data or their own satellites’ collision avoidance capabilities.
A camera onboard a Starlink satellite captured this view showing a close encounter with another satellite in orbit.
Credit:
SpaceX
A camera onboard a Starlink satellite captured this view showing a close encounter with another satellite in orbit.
Credit:
SpaceX
Starlink satellites, for example, use onboard navigation cameras to detect other objects in orbit. SpaceX calls the system Stargaze, and it now tracks about 90 percent of maneuvering satellites that intersect Starlink orbits, Nicolls said.
That is good, but it would be better if all operators agreed to be more open about what their satellites are doing. It is now a “fairly common occurrence” that Starlink satellites detect an upcoming close encounter and autonomously maneuver out of the way, Nicolls said. If there’s not enough to steer away from a close encounter, Starlink satellites can hunker down at the time of greatest danger. These “ducking maneuvers” involve pointing the satellite to minimize the chance of a collision, Nicolls said.
Starlink satellites perform about 1,000 collision avoidance maneuvers per day to get out of the way of functioning satellites or bits of space debris. In the last few months, Nicolls said Starlink satellites have steered clear of about 650 active satellites from other operators. Only half of those 650 come from operators that participate in ephemeris sharing with SpaceX, he said.
What about China?
“In particular, it’s been very challenging to share data with international operators,” Nicolls said. “There has been good progress here. There have been some good stories here on how we’ve begun to share data. For example, we share data closely with the Chinese space station as well as some other Chinese satellite operators, but there are many that we do not, and we have no information about where those satellites are or where they’re going.”
A chart in Nicolls’ presentation suggested the problem largely lies with Chinese and Russian satellites. But some in the United States, Europe, and Japan also decline to share.
“My fundamental ask here is that we need to make headway here and begin sharing data across all vehicles, from whatever country you are, with us and with others, to promote a safe operating environment,” Nicolls said.
Nearly all Chinese satellite operators decline to publicly share their satellite ephemeris data.
Credit:
SpaceX
Nearly all Chinese satellite operators decline to publicly share their satellite ephemeris data.
Credit:
SpaceX
What do SpaceX’s competitors think? Ars asked the head of Amazon Leo, Rajeev Badyal, about coordinating with Starlink, his chief competitor in the satellite broadband market. Amazon has 396 satellites in orbit today, with hundreds more awaiting launch when their rockets are ready to take them to orbit.
“Space safety is paramount to us as well,” Badyal said. “Every launch we do, we actually coordinate with SpaceX. We coordinate with others who have satellites. We let them know where we’re going to drop them off, how we’re going to orbit raise, etc. So we have regular meetings with companies like SpaceX to exchange data.
“So, for us, sharing ephemeris or sharing the information necessary for space safety is a non-issue,” Badyal said. “We’re big proponents of making sure that all of us operate in this domain in space in a coordinated fashion because [the] consequences of not doing so are significant for everybody, and there’s no reason not to.”
Amazon Leo’s first-generation constellation will consist of 3,232 satellites, and the Federal Communications Commission in February approved Amazon’s request for a 4,504-satellite second-generation network. Amazon has filed for FCC approval for an additional 5,105 satellites for direct-to-device connectivity, but the company is still far from matching the size of the Starlink fleet.
“Obviously, SpaceX is the largest constellation out there,” Badyal said. “We work with them hand in hand. In terms of China and adversaries, that’s something I can’t comment on at the moment. At some point, we will have to coordinate, or it’ll end up being a negative thing for everybody, especially if they get to scale.”
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

The Sentinelese, living on North Sentinel Island in the Bay of Bengal, are one of the most isolated peoples on earth.
Part of an archipelago governed by India, it is prohibited by law to venture within 5km of their island. And when a missionary did manage to land on the beach in 2018, he was killed by bow and arrow.
Yet none of that was to deter influencer Mykhailo Polyakov, who last year filmed himself arriving on North Sentinel Island, and leaving a can of coke on the beach.
Features writer Elle Hunt documents the rise of a new breed of influencer, travelling around the world, and streaming to millions their attempts to contact the uncontacted – despite the warnings of indigenous rights groups that the consequences could be fatal, both for the social media stars and the communities they risk exposing to disease.
Helen Pidd also speaks to Ecuadorian indigenous rights activist María José Andrade Cerda about the rights and wrongs of this new world.

Teen McDonald’s employee killed after 16-year-old coworker attacked him, cops say
Reginald ‘RJ’ Harrell, 17, was working on his scheduled day off when he was fatally stabbed inside the restaurant restroom, his family says

A 16-year-old high school student faces a murder charge after allegedly fatally stabbing a 17-year-old coworker inside a Texas McDonald’s restaurant.
Harris County Sheriff Ed Gonzalez identified the victim as 17-year-old Reginald “RJ” Harrell, a senior at Cypress Creek High School who planned to become a welder after graduation. The teen was working Wednesday at the fast-food location on Louetta Road in Cypress, a suburb northwest of Houston, on what was supposed to be his day off, according to his family.
Police responded to a report of an in-progress stabbing around 11:30 p.m. When officers arrived, they found Harrell in the restroom with multiple stab wounds. Coworkers tried lifesaving measures before first responders arrived, but Harrell was pronounced dead at the scene.
“He did not have to go out like this. He didn’t have to be murdered. He did not deserve this at all,” Harrell's mother, Denisha Dennis, told CBS affiliate KHOU 11. “I want the kid responsible; I want justice for my son, because I don’t have my son no more.
“He’s gone. He was only 17. And I can’t talk, I can’t hug him, he can’t say, ‘Ma, I love you.’”
The 16-year-old suspect remained at the location and was detained immediately by responding deputies. He was later booked into the Harris County Juvenile Detention Center on murder charges. Authorities have not released his identity due to his age.
The victim’s family said they were struggling to understand what triggered the violence inside the restaurant.
“I’m hurt, because I just don’t understand how you can just take someone’s life like that,” Harrell’s sister, Kourtnee Dennis, told KHOU 11. “I don’t know what happened in the bathroom, I don’t know what corresponded, but I feel like he didn’t deserve to be murdered.”
She added: “I would have never thought that the last time he walked out my door to go to work would be the last time that I see him and talk to him.”
It remains unclear what triggered the attack or whether prosecutors will attempt to try the suspect as an adult.
The restaurant remained temporarily closed Thursday as a cleaning crew worked inside, with a sign on the front door turning customers away. In a statement, McDonald’s owner-operator Michael Gutierrez expressed condolences to Harrell’s family.
“We are saddened by this tragedy, and our hearts are with the victim’s loved ones and all those impacted,” the statement read. “Right now, our focus is on the well-being of our restaurant employees, and supporting them as they process these events.”
Everette Penn, an associate professor and director of the Texas Juvenile Crime Prevention Center at Prairie View A&M University, told FOX 26 Houston that transferring a juvenile to the adult court system involved a rigorous judicial review.
“That is going to be selected and chosen by the court,” Penn said. “Now the court will probably look at this, there are circumstances we don’t know that are not available to us but the court has to look at this and determine: what was the state of mind of the youth, what were the circumstances, environment, and background information to determine whether this person could be tried as an adult?
“That’s a very difficult decision, and the court does not take it lightly because that makes for a different path for the individual.”

Sahibzada Farhan celebrated his elevation to the Pakistan T20 captaincy with a 52-ball 89 as Sri Lanka was beaten by four wickets on Friday.
Farhan carried Pakistan to 187-6 in 18.5 overs as he smashed 10 fours and four sixes. Maaz Sadaqat smacked 50 off just 29 balls, and Pakistan took a 1-0 lead in the three-match series.
Opening batter Lahiru Udara’s 91 gave Sri Lanka a fighting total of 182-8 against a new-look Pakistan pace attack that featured debutants Mohammad Imran and Razaullah.
Rawalpindi will also host the remaining two games on Sunday and next Tuesday.
The opening pair of Farhan and Fakhar Zaman (21) didn’t allow the Sri Lankan pacers to settle down in the powerplay as they combined for 54 off 31 balls.
Tall fast bowler Dushmantha Chameera’s two overs in the powerplay went for 32 runs.
Sadaqat struck two sixes and a four in the first four deliveries he faced against Eshan Malinga and settled the chase in the brisk stand of 92 off 53 balls with Farhan.

Sadaqat completed his maiden T20 half-century off just 28 balls before he fell on the next ball, trapped lbw by Maheesh Theekshana (2-36).
Sri Lanka hit back briefly when Chameera grabbed his 100th T20 wicket by having Hasan Nawaz caught behind down the leg side and Theekshana clean-bowled Saim Ayub on 8 by a delivery that kept low.
When Farhan, who counterattacked Theekshana with a six and three fours in one over, finally holed out to a spectacular diving catch by Sahan Arachchige at midwicket, Pakistan was only three runs from victory.

But Udara revived Sri Lanka by putting on 60 runs with Kamindu Mendis (23) against the spinners, and another 57 runs with Dasun Shanaka (18).

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.
