Fired OpenAI employees question the company's commitment to safety
Three former OpenAI employees are raising concerns over the circumstances of their dismissals and the company's commitment to safety, amid intense public scrutiny of the artificial intelligence industry's ability to responsibly develop the technology.
The former employees, Mikita Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, alleged that OpenAI fired them last week over pretexts and punished them for either being outspoken about safety or working with outside researchers. They also expressed worries the company may walk back a recent safety commitment.
OpenAI has repeatedly denied the allegations. It said the employees were fired for mishandling sensitive information and said the company has not abandoned its safety commitment.
The dispute comes at a fraught time for the AI industry and OpenAI in particular. Over the summer, OpenAI's agents hacked into companies, communicated with each other without authorization and attempted to cover their tracks. Unlike chatbots, agents are AI systems that can carry out tasks autonomously for an extended period of time.
The most serious hack, of software company Hugging Face, contributed to the resignation of a researcher at rival Anthropic who issued dire warnings about the trajectory of the technology. The resignation captured the attention of figures outside of the AI field including lawmakers. Many, including some executives of the top AI companies, have called for various ways to avert disaster, including slowing down the development of the most advanced AI.
In the meanwhile, OpenAI has been reviewing its agents' activities in recent months and notifying organizations whose digital infrastructure has been affected.
As a response to the safety concerns, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on Sep. 12 that the company will follow its rival Anthropic in expanding access to third-party evaluators, who assess the safety of AI systems and the practices of developers.
The three employees dismissed by OpenAI last week worked on teams that focus on AI safety and making the company's models follow human intentions and values. Two of them were involved in investigating the Hugging Face hack.
In a letter to OpenAI's safety leadership that the fired employees posted on X this week, they urged the company to stay committed to working with third-party researchers, to preserve human's ability to monitor model behavior and to "continue to support an open and transparent culture of dialogue" between in-house safety researchers and external ones. They also warned their firings were having a chilling effect on their former OpenAI colleagues.
In a statement OpenAI posted on X, the company said it is still committed to bringing in third-party evaluators and that it agreed with the fired employees's recommendations. The company said the three were fired last week because they "violated clear policies on handling sensitive information."
The former employees have disputed OpenAI's explanation of their firings. None of them responded to NPR's interview requests.
"In the exit call, I was told OpenAI no longer trusts me because I was speaking too much to third party safety organizations, implying I leaked company [intellectual property]. I never shared company IP," Balesni wrote on X on Thursday. He said he was involved in investigating the OpenAI agents' hack on Hugging Face.
"If OpenAI has specific concerns, I invite them to write to us directly. I expect they will not, because our firing was pretextual," Balesni continued.
He said he worried that OpenAI will use the firings as an excuse to cut off its relationship with Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), a nonprofit that focuses on evaluating risks of humans losing control of AI. OpenAI allowed researchers from METR and Redwood Research, another AI safety research organization, to examine internal records related to the Hugging Face hack.
A second fired OpenAI employee, Korbak, was the technical point of contact for the METR/Redwood Research investigation. "I was told verbally I was fired because of the way I communicated with METR. No details on what I said or did or when. No other reasons were given and nothing was put in writing," Korbak wrote on X, echoing Balesni's concerns.
The report produced by METR and Redwood Research in the wake of the Hugging Face hack shed light on the scale of the attack as well as the degree to which the agents acted in undesirable ways. The authors of the report called the investigation "brief" and many in the AI safety field have called for expanded access to independent evaluators at AI companies to make sure they investigate similar incidents or other safety concerns thoroughly.
In a statement to NPR, METR declined to comment on the OpenAI employees' firings.
Wang, the third OpenAI employee fired last week, coined the word "pacing," which describes a way of slowing down development of the most advanced AI systems so that safety can catch up, according to the letter she and her two colleagues sent to OpenAI's safety leadership. The term was invoked in an open letter calling for such a slowdown signed by over a thousand staff members from top AI companies in July, after the Hugging Face hack.
Wang wrote on X that she was fired over accessing an executive's email. But she said she had access to the inbox for work reasons in the past and wasn't able to get IT to remove the access once she no longer needed it.
"The reasons that we were provided for our terminations are simply not adding up. We're hearing people are now being told vague rumors internally to discredit us," Wang wrote. "The message to everyone still at OpenAI is clear: raise concerns or work closely with outside safety groups, and you could be next, without being told why."
OpenAI said in a statement to NPR that the three terminated employees violated policies more than once, and the mishandling of information went beyond their work with an outside evaluation group.
OpenAI also shared an internal memo from an unnamed research leader that it said was shared with the company on Wednesday, before the three ex-employees took to social media.
In the memo, the research leader said the company "strongly" agreed with the three ex-employees' recommendations. "We do not terminate employees for raising concerns," the leader wrote.
"OpenAI leadership is saying they strongly agree with our letter. Let's see how that pans out," Wang wrote on X.

Nvidia-backed data centre firm scraps IPO as AI valuation concerns deepen
- Published
Artificial intelligence (AI) data centre company Firmus has scrapped its plans for what would have been one of Australia's biggest-ever stock market listings.
The Nvidia-backed firm said it had made the decision due to "recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions" and that going public would not be in the company or shareholders' best interests.
Firmus had initially announced plans for a stock market debut that valued the company at more than $30bn (£22.65bn).
One investment firm told the BBC that it had decided not take part in the initial public offering (IPO) over concerns about its valuation.
"Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options. We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress," the company said.
Firmus builds and operates liquid-cooled data centres, or what it calls "AI factories", for clients including OpenAI and Meta.
It has operations in Australia, Singapore and other parts of the Asia-Pacific region.
The company's backers include Nvidia and major investment firms Blackstone and Jane Street.
Blackstone declined to comment when contacted by the BBC.
Nvidia and Jane Street have also been contacted for comment.
The decision by Firmus to scrap its stock market listing comes as investors and industry analysts have raised concerns about the hundreds of billions of dollars being poured into AI as the prospects for long-term returns remain unclear.

UniSuper, one of Australia's biggest pension funds, was among the institutional investors that decided not take part in the IPO.
"We think that Firmus indeed has a compelling story. It just doesn't have a compelling valuation," UniSuper's chief investment officer John Pearce said in an update to investors.
He also said UniSuper was concerned that Firmus would have to go further into debt to fund its growth plans.
"It's disappointing. The [Australian Securities Exchange] needs new stories and this could have been one if it was correctly priced," Pearce told the BBC.
Australia has become an attractive destination for data centre investment, thanks to the country's abundant clean energy, natural gas supplies and land availability.
OpenAI boss Sam Altman said earlier this year that Australia could become a world leader in the data centre industry if it wanted to.
There are currently over 160 data centres in the country and plans for more.
That is despite resistance from some Australians who have raised concerns about their environmental impact and the noise they create.
In September, Altman said OpenAI did not aim to list on the stock market this year, citing concerns over the technology's safety that make it "an ill-advised moment" to go public.
The ChatGPT-maker, along with rival Anthropic, have been eyeing blockbuster stock market debuts that would value the firms at more than $1tn each.
AI-related stocks, Nvidia and Oracle, fell in US trading on Thursday after reports that OpenAI's revenues were lower than previously thought.

Did Russia play by the rules in reporting lab worker's death?
A 28-year-old woman died in Russia last week and, since then, speculations about the case have ricocheted around the globe.
The woman was a lab technician at a Russian research institute that studies the plague. As unverified rumors have circulated that she may have contracted the disease from a lab leak, President Trump, the World Health Organization and other leaders are asking for more information.
Russia has insisted this is not a health emergency and stated that its health authorities have not found dangerous pathogens in any of the deceased woman's contacts.
But there are still far more questions than answers.
That uncertainty has global leaders and health experts turning to a law that obligates countries, including Russia, to share exactly this type of information. It's called the International Health Regulations or IHR.
On Wednesday, at a WHO press conference, Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus invoked IHR as the best way to determine current situation in Russia and determine the appropriate response.
"We don't yet have the full picture of this event," he said. "Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks."
Here are the key things to know about the IHR and how it applies in today's world.
Rooted in the 19th century
This law requires countries to share health information that could have international implications. It goes way back to the 1850s with cholera outbreaks in Europe, which led to the creation of guidelines for sharing disease information.
"That's very, very long for international law," says Alexandra Phelan, an associate professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. "Look at the negotiation documents and they're debating: Is cholera caused by a bacteria or miasma [a bad smell]? Like we're really right in the middle of germ theory."
Then, when WHO was founded in 1948, these regulations — then called the International Sanitary Regulations — were adopted. That was one of the organization's first moves. The law has since been amended and updated, most notably after the SARS or Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome outbreak in 2003 and most recently due to COVID-19 pandemic.
A country is supposed to notify WHO if the health event has the potential to cause an international health emergency.
Today, IHR is among the most widely ratified international treaties, with 197 signatories including the U.S. and Russia. (Even though the Trump administration says it has withdrawn from WHO, the U.S. is still bound by the IHR with the exception of some recent amendments.)
One of the core obligations in the law "is that parties or states must notify WHO within 24 hours of detecting a [serious health] event," explains Phelan.
Some events – like a case of smallpox or a new type of influenza — should immediately trigger a notification. For other situations, a checklist helps a country assess whether notification is needed.
Each year, she says, WHO receives thousands of notifications from all over the world and most turn out to be nothing.
The situation in Russia
Some people fear the Russian woman — who died Oct. 2 — had pneumonic plague. That's one of the diseases "explicitly listed" under IHR, says Phelan, as something to assess and notify the WHO.
However, Russia did not notify WHO about this woman's death. Instead, WHO learned about it through media reports and then, on Oct. 3, went to Russia seeking verification and additional information.
"Russia's response, firstly, was delayed," says Phelan. "But also it wasn't comprehensive."
It took Russia several days to respond. On Oct. 6, health officials told WHO there were no cases of plague in the region and that the woman was hospitalized with severe pneumonia of unknown origin before she died. They also explained that health authorities had placed about 200 contacts in quarantine.
WHO asked Russia for more information, including about lab tests conducted, public health measures and the health status of the woman's contacts. However, as with many international laws, there's no mechanism to make countries comply with the law and share information.
Phelan says the next few days and weeks will be key in understanding how much information Russia is going to share. If they aren't fully transparent, she hopes pressure from other countries either convinces Russia to comply with IHR or, at least, helps keep up the norm of other countries respecting IHR and notifying WHO about future health events.
That kind of notification is critical if the world is to be ready to respond and contain future outbreaks, says Lawrence Gostin, who directs the WHO Center on Global Health Law and is a professor at Georgetown University.
"This case shows the good, the bad and the ugly of the IHR," he says.
"Legally, this is the only thing that's holding Russia to account," Gostin explains. And yet, "you have countries that are hiding the ball."
He believes that the risk to the general population from the current situation in Russia is likely very low. But, for him, the fact that countries can disregard the IHR notification requirements is a "blaring siren about how unprepared we are" to quickly control health threats.

An Anthropic model submitted a false homicide tip to Philadelphia police
The tip thankfully landed in the department's spam folder.
Philadelphia police appear to have been caught in one of the most bizarre cases of "rogue" AI behavior yet. Per CBS News, the police department disclosed on Friday that an Anthropic model generated and submitted a false homicide tip to its PhillyUnsolvedMurders website, which the department set up to gather tips from the public related to unsolved homicide cases.
Anthropic notified Philly police of the incident on October 7. According to information the company shared with PPD, it said a model was carrying out a test of a random selection of websites when it emailed the false tip. The submission was flagged as spam and subsequently wasn't investigated. The incident occurred on July 18, but wasn't discovered by Anthropic until September 28, at which point the company halted the testing that led to the false tip.
Anthropic did not immediately respond to Engadget's comment request. Anthropic told Philadelphia police it would publish a report on Friday describing what happened, alongside "other instances of unintended model behavior."
"Philadelphia Police are providing this information to the public ahead of that publication in the interests of full government transparency and accountability," the police department said in a statement shared with Engadget. "The department's regular investigative process for crime tips requires human review and vetting before any tips are disseminated for investigative follow-up. Regardless of who submits information or how it reaches the department, a tip is a lead to assess – not an established fact."
Based on the descriptions police shared, the offending "model" may have been an autonomous agent. "Rogue" AI agents have been all over the news in recent weeks after a group of OpenAI ones hacked the LLM database Hugging Face in July. Since then, many other AI labs, including Anthropic, Meta and China's Moonshot, have disclosed similar incidents involving their own models and agents. However, in each case the reason the models escaped containment was due to a misconfiguration in their respective sandbox environments. Philadelphia police say there's no sign this most recent incident led to "unauthorized access to police systems or a compromise of department data."

In Summary
- Sennheiser has updated its Momentum Wireless series and has launched the Momentum 5 Wireless headphones.
- The Momentum range has been famous mainly for its sound quality, but brings more to the table with the Momentum 5 Wireless, including elements like spatial audio and head tracking, and a sleeker carrying case.
- However, along with these upgrades, comes an upgraded price tag as well, which puts the Momentum 5 Wireless in the same price league as the Sony WH-1000XM6. It is still the master of sound, but can it also challenge others in areas like ANC and calling?
Whenever someone asks us to recommend ANC headphones with great audio quality, Sennheiser’s Momentum Wireless series is among the first to come to our minds. Yes, they are very good in other departments too – they are premium flagship headphones after all – but their real strength has been their sound. If someone prioritizes top-notch ANC and calling or even slightly more bass-y mainstream sound, the momentum (pun intended) shifts towards the likes of the Sony WH-1000 XM series, Bose’s QuietComfort and JBL’s Tour series. The Momentum 5 Wireless could change that. With it, Sennheiser has upped its ANC and calling game considerably, while adding a few new dimensions to its already strong audio performance. The result: perhaps the most mainstream Momentum Wireless ever, and one that can compete in many departments, and not just audio.
Table of Contents
Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless Design and Appearance: Flatter, and a little flash
In terms of design, the Momentum 5 are a refined version of the Momentum. The outer parts of the cups are flatter, and the finish is cleaner. We got the Denim variant, which has a dark blue exterior with mauve-colored cushioning on the earpads and headbands, giving the headphones a very distinct dual-tone look. While most of the headphones are made of plastic, the headband also has a cloth-like, textured finish, which is a classy touch. Rather unusually, there are a lot of shiny elements on the Momentum 5 – there are metallic colored circles with the Sennheiser logo at each of the ends of the headband, as well as microphones in metallic enclosures on the earcups, two of which have Sennheiser branding.
The right ear cup contains all the ports and buttons: a single control button, a 2.5 mm audio jack and a USB Type-C port. There is also a line of LEDs next to the button to show connectivity and battery status. There are no volume control buttons or a 3.5 mm jack (Sennheiser has opted for a 2.5 mm one, although there is a cable that allows you to connect the headphones to a device with a 3.5 mm jack), but the outer part of the right earcup has a touch panel.
The right and left earcups are clearly marked on the inner part of the earcups. The earcups fold 180 degrees but not inwards, which means that they cannot fold up completely, which means that one cannot just bunch them up and put them in a bag. The hinges around which the earcups move are well built, and although the headphones are mainly made of plastic, they have a very solid feel to them.
At around 290 grams, the Momentum 5 Wireless are on the heavier side (the Sony WH-1000 XM6 are about 255 grams), but thanks to all the cushioning, are comfortable to wear. The clamping force is also just right, keeping the headphones in place without making us feel that our head was being squeezed. While they will stay in place during a brisk walk or even a jogging session, we would advise against using them while working out as they do not have any IP rating.
The Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless have been released in an assortment of colors, although they are currently available in black and blue. The black ones are understated and elegant, but the blue ones will turn heads with their dual tone and metal accents. They come in a smart, flat hard case, with a slightly recessed section that makes them easy to carry. It is a tough case and is slim enough not to take up too much space in your backpack or bag. There are two cables in the package: a Type-C to Type-C and a 2.5 mm to 3.5 mm.
Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless Specs and Features: Hello, spatial audio, head tracking, more mics and much more…
The Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless are a big step forward from the Momentum 4 Wireless, although they come with a similar-sounding 42 mm Dynamic Driver. Whereas Sennheiser had in the past avoided features like head tracking and spatial audio, these are very much present in the Momentum 5 Wireless, which come with 3D Spatial Audio, head tracking and support for Dolby Atmos. They also come with 8 microphones for hybrid active noise cancellation, which is double the number on the Momentum 4 (and claim to deliver three times superior ANC), although still less than the 12 on the Sony WH-1000 XM6.
There are considerable improvements on the audio front too – the headphones now come with aptX Lossless as well as adaptive, and users now have access to an 8-band equalizer (the Momentum 4 had a 5-band EQ), which they can completely customize as well. Like the Momentum 4, the Momentum 5 also supports hi-res audio wirelessly as well as through the Type-C port.
Apart from this, the Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless come with Bluetooth 5.4, active noise cancellation (ANC), an anti-wind mode, multiple device connectivity, on-head detection, own voice detection, and, if you have a compatible dongle, also a gaming mode. And in a very notable move, the Momentum 5 Wireless come with a removable and replaceable battery (Sennheiser says even a user can do so using a Philips screwdriver) which can deliver up to 57 hours of audio with ANC on. In spec and feature terms, the Momentum 5 Wireless are a big step up from the Momentum 4 Wireless.
Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless Interface and App: Business as usual
In terms of interface, the Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless are very similar to the Momentum 4 Wireless. All the controls are on the right earcup and are a blend of touch, taps, and swipes. The single button is used to switch the headphones on and off, and long-pressing puts the headphones in pairing mode.
Gestures are a little complicated. Sliding your finger up and down regulates the volume, which is fine and works smoothly. A single tap pauses and resumes audio; sliding your finger horizontally from back to front takes you to the next track, while sliding it from front to back takes you to the previous track. Sliding forward and holding triggers fast forward, while sliding backward and holding results in a rewind. Two taps let you switch between ANC and transparency mode, while two taps with two fingers turn Dolby Atmos on and off. One can accept a call by sliding a finger forward and end a call by sliding it backward. It is not a super intuitive set of instructions and takes a bit of getting used to, especially the gestures that involve finger sliding.
However, pinching and expanding your fingers, which should decrease and increase transparency levels, take a bit of getting used to. One cannot customize these gestures or the button, and while there are tone and voice prompts, there is no way to invoke a virtual assistant from the headphones, which is a bit odd these days.
Detailed controls and settings of the headphones are available on the Sennheiser Smart Control + app, which works smoothly with both iOS and Android. One can tweak the levels of ANC one needs (our tip: leave it at Adaptive, where it works best), turn Immersive Audio (or spatial audio) and head tracking on and off, find your headphones, check features, get updates, and also turn touch controls on and off. The app also gives you access to the 8-band equalizer, which has 8 presets (Speech Clarity, Rock, Pop, Dance, Hip-Hop, Classical, Movie, and Jazz), as well as options to let the software create your own Sound Personalization profiles. You can even set different presets and noise cancellation levels for different places – for instance, I set the headphones to switch to transparency mode when I am home, and to a high ANC mode when I am at my favorite cafe. It actually works very smoothly. The app is simple and easy to use. It does not offer the kind of options one gets on JBL’s companion app, but is classically Sennheiser – focusing on strong basics.
Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless Sound Quality: Upping the bass, adding soundstage, without sacrificing detail
Sennheiser’s Momentum range has always been known for its detailed yet well-balanced sound. And the Momentum 5 Wireless deliver the same level of detail that we are used to in the series, but there is one subtle change – these have a slightly higher accent on bass. The result is a sound that is warm and pleasant. Sennheiser’s handling of the mids (generally the vocals) is masterly as usual – voices sound clear and are never overwhelmed by other frequencies.
There is a slight reduction in the level of treble, though, giving these a slightly softer sound. This might annoy some of the purists, who love tinkling treble, but will please most listeners. There is a bit more “punch” to the Momentum 5 Wireless than any of their predecessors, but it is important to note that this does not come at the cost of clarity. If anything, the slight stress on bass gives the Momentum 5 Wireless a slightly richer sound and a distinct audio flavor, different from the Momentum 4 Wireless, which now seem a little plain in comparison. There is a “Bass Boost” option in the app, but even switching it on does not make the bass overwhelming or rumbly. In many ways, the Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless’ handling of bass is similar to what we used to get from Bose in 2016 – warm without ever getting fuzzy.
Whether it is watching films, playing games, listening to podcasts or a wide variety of music, the Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless deliver detailed, clear and pleasant sound. Of course, one can change the frequency levels using the excellent equalizer options in the companion app, but it is a fair chance that you will love how the Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless sound right out of the box.
Spatial audio or Immersive audio with Dolby Atmos helps in creating a wider soundstage, and enabling head tracking allows you to get the feeling of being actually in a room in which audio is playing, as every time you move your head, the source of the sound changes subtly, just as it would in a real room. Do keep in mind, though, that using immersive audio will reduce the volume levels a bit. Speaking of volume levels, the Momentum 5 Wireless are classic Sennheiser – you will get a sense of loudness at maxed-out volumes but are unlikely to ever feel in danger of being deafened (as can happen with some other brands).
There are a few minor irritants. The Head Detection system is a little too sensitive at times, so even moving the headphones slightly sometimes led to the audio pausing. Even sudden movements of the head sometimes triggered it. Perhaps this could be addressed in a software update. Similarly, it would be great if one could control ANC levels through a pinch or an expand gesture, just as one can change transparency levels. Finally, we do wish Sennheiser would put volume control buttons back on the Momentums – the swipe up and down are not as convenient.
Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless ANC, Calls and Battery Life: Finally, a contender in all categories
Perhaps the most dramatic change in the Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless as compared to the Momentum 4 has been the improvement in both ANC and call quality. While the Momentum 4 Wireless is supposed to be the boss in terms of audio quality, its ANC and call handling abilities were decent, rather than exceptional. The Momentum 5 Wireless changes that. The ANC on the headphones was streets ahead of what we got on the Momentum 4 Wireless or even the more recent HDB-630. The headphones were able to drown out a fair degree of the hum of the Metro and the traffic, and made it easy to work even in relatively loud cafes. No, they do not deliver the sort of Sounds of Silence that the Sony WH-1000XM6 serve up, but they are not too far behind, and can easily match them in most general circumstances. We also feel they are comfortably ahead of the Bose QuietComfort series in this regard. Transparency mode, however, needs a bit of work as external sounds can sometimes be a little muffled, although it is very usable.
Call quality has also improved significantly and is on par with other flagships. You cannot tweak your own voice or that of the speakers as you can on JBL’s headphones, but call clarity is excellent, and most of the people we spoke with did not even realize we were using headphones, which is the litmus test for calling.
Battery life on the Momentum 5 Wireless is similar to that of the Momentum 4. Sennheiser claims 57 hours with ANC, and we got through close to ten days of regular use on a single charge, which involved 5-6 hours of daily usage. Sennheiser also claims that ten minutes of charging can give one up to seven hours of audio, and this is once again close to our experience – we generally got between 5-6 hours. We have been told that the battery will easily last 4-5 years, so the need to change it manually is unlikely to arise soon, but having the option is reassuring. Switching between devices was smooth – once paired with two devices, the Momentum 5 Wireless moved to whichever one produced sound.
Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless Review Verdict: Should you buy?
The Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless are available for Rs 39,990 (USD 399.95). That is significantly more expensive than the Momentum 4 Wireless, which were launched at Rs 34,990 (USD 349.95), but had been available for about Rs 26,990 (USD 199.95) for the past year or so. But with that higher price come very significant improvements, especially in ANC and call quality, as well as a slightly warmer, richer sound. Purists and hardcore loyalists might not like this, but they can always set matters right with the equalizer or go for the Sennheiser HDB 630, which are arguably the best audiophile-level Bluetooth headphones around and cost about Rs 4,000 more.
The Momentum 5 Wireless face stiff competition from the Sony WH-1000XM6, which come with a similar price tag, and are pretty much the bosses in the ANC segment. A detailed comparison of these two is coming up soon, but we can safely say that the Momentum’s improved ANC means that the days of “if you want great audio, get the Momentum, and if you want great ANC, get the Sony” are over. The Momentum 5 Wireless are the most mainstream-sounding Momentum headphones we have used, and deliver great sound without compromises on ANC and call quality. They are easily the best-sounding ANC headphones you can get for under Rs 40,000 (USD 400), and this time the ANC rocks as much as the sound does!

A leading pro-Kremlin Russian military blogger with reported ties to Russia’s intelligence services has been arrested in Montenegro, after warnings of attempts to destabilise the Balkan country, officials have said.
Mikhail Zvinchuk, the founder of the influential Rybar war blog, was detained on Friday alongside his wife and three other Russians by police and security agents in the Adriatic resort town of Risan, on suspicion of spreading Russian influence, local media reported.
Montenegro’s prime minister, Milojko Spajić, confirmed Zvinchuk’s detention in a post on X, saying it followed warnings that the country would face attempts at destabilisation and hybrid warfare.
The Montenegrin news outlet Vijesti reported later on Friday that Zvinchuk and the other detainees were to be expelled from the country on national security grounds.
The Russian Telegram news channel Baza said officers detained Zvinchuk at the luxury Mövenpick hotel in Risan. It said the group was taken to Podgorica, Montenegro’s capital, for questioning and their phones and passports were confiscated.
Founded in 2018 by Zvinchuk, a former press officer at Russia’s defence ministry, Rybar is one of the most popular Russian military blogs covering the war in Ukraine, with more than 1.5 million subscribers on Telegram. It forms part of a sprawling online media ecosystem that promotes Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.
But Rybar’s activities extend well beyond Ukraine, with the channel promoting pro-Kremlin narratives in Africa and the Middle East. More recently, it has been accused of amplifying far-right narratives surrounding the migration crisis in Ceuta, a Spanish enclave in north Africa.
“At the moment, the project team is in contact with Russia’s foreign ministry, which is working to resolve the situation. Since there were no violations of local legislation, we expect all detainees to be released,” the channel said on Telegram.
Britain sanctioned Zvinchuk and Rybar in December 2025 over their role in spreading Kremlin propaganda and undermining support for Ukraine. The British government said Zvinchuk received funding from the Russian state-owned defence conglomerate Rostec, and worked with members of Russia’s intelligence services.
The US has separately accused Zvinchuk of attempting to interfere in the 2024 presidential election, offering a reward of up to $10m for information about those involved.
Days before his arrest, Zvinchuk boasted on social media that he had managed to enter Montenegro despite being subject to western sanctions and an entry ban. He mocked a border guard who, he said, had searched his belongings but failed to check his name against a database.
The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said Moscow was aware of Zvinchuk’s detention and would work to secure his release.
Russia’s former president Dmitry Medvedev suggested Moscow could detain European and American citizens to use in prisoner exchanges to secure Zvinchuk’s release. “We will probably have to replenish our pool of prisoners for exchange with European and American idiots in order to get our own people back,” he wrote on social media.
The arrest is likely to further strain relations between Montenegro and Russia, which have long been tense. In 2016, Montenegrin authorities accused Russian operatives of plotting with Serbian ultranationalists to stage a coup, allegations Moscow denied.
Montenegro, which joined Nato in 2017 and is seeking membership of the EU, imposed sanctions on Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The country recently approved plans to end visa-free travel for Russian citizens from 1 November, closing off a popular holiday destination for Russian tourists as it brings its visa policy into line with the EU.
